## Page 5

Preface
This is the proceedings of the selected papers presented at Chinese Materials
Conference 2017 (CMC2017) held in Yinchuan City, Ningxia, China, July 06 –12,
2017.
The Chinese Materials Conference (CMC) is the most important serial confer-
ence of Chinese Materials Research Society (C-MRS) and is held each year since
the early 1990s. Chinese Materials Conference 2017 had 37 symposia covering four
ﬁelds of energy and environmental materials; advanced functional materials;
high-performance structural materials; and design, preparation, and characterization
of materials. More than 5500 participants attended the conference, and the orga-
nizers received more than 700 technical papers. By recommendation of symposium
organizers and after peer-reviewing, 434 papers are published in the present pro-
ceedings, which are divided into four volumes of
Part 1: Advances in Energy and Environmental Materials
Part 2: High Performance Structural Materials
Part 3: Advances in Materials Processing
Part 4: Advanced Functional Materials
This is the volume for Part 2 including 111 papers selected from 9 symposia of
C01: powder metallurgy; C02: high performance aluminum alloys; C03: high
performance titanium alloys; C04: superalloys; C06: metal matrix composites; C07:
space materials science and technology; C08: rare metals and refractory melts; C10:
nano-structured metals and alloys.
The editors would like to give the thanks to the symposium chairs and all the
paper reviewers of this volume, and the thanks should be also given to Mrs. Yiming
Jia and Mr. Yongzheng Zhang for their hard work of compilation and typesetting
for each paper in this volume.
Beijing, China Yafang Han
March 2018

## Page 17

Effects of Internal Oxidation Methods
on Microstructures and Properties
of Al 2O3 Dispersion-Strengthened
Copper Alloys
Feng Chen, Zhiqiao Yan and Tao Wang
Abstract With Cu–Al alloy powder as raw material and Cu 2O powder as oxidant,
two internal oxidation methods, namely step-by-step internal oxidation-reduction
method (referred to as the step-by-step method) and integrated internal
oxidation-reduction method (referred to as the integrated method), were respec-
tively adopted to achieve the oxidation of Al. Then hot extrusion without canning
was applied to prepare Al
2O3 dispersion-strengthened copper alloys. The effects of
the two internal oxidation methods on microstructures and properties of the alloys
were compared. The results show that both the step-by-step method and the inte-
grated method can achieve the complete oxidation of Al. However, the excessive
oxidant can not be reduced thoroughly in the integrated method. The residual
oxidant increases oxidation of the sintered body during hot extrusion and the
formed copper oxides distribute in the grains as well as at the grain boundaries.
While in the step-by-step alloy, the copper oxides mainly distribute at the grain
boundaries. The step-by-step method improves electrical conductivity and ductility,
but lowers hardness and strength. The integrated alloy has worse ductility and lower
electrical conductivity, but strength and hardness are higher. The step-by-step alloy
has better comprehensive properties, and its electrical conductivity, hardness, ten-
sile strength, yield strength and elongation is 89% IACS, HRB 69 –72, 425 MPa,
394 MPa and 27.2%, respectively.

## Page 18

Introduction
Al2O3 dispersion-strengthened copper (Cu –Al2O3) alloys exhibit not only excellent
electrical and heat conductivities but also outstanding strengths at room and elevated
temperatures. Therefore, these alloys are widely used as resistance welding elec-
trodes, lead frames, and integrated-circuit sealing materials [ 1, 2], where high elec-
trical and heat conductivities and high strength at elevated temperatures are required.
Internal oxidation is the most successful method to prepare Cu –Al2O3 alloys, in
which the vital step is to oxidize Al into dispersion-distributed Al 2O3 particles by
adding excessive oxidant, and then to sufﬁciently reduce the redundant oxidant. With
Cu–Al2O3 powder prepared by internal oxidation as raw materials, many methods
such as hot pressing (HP), hot extrusion (HE), spark plasma sintering (SPS) and
high-velocity compaction (HVC) are applied to prepare the high-performance Cu –
Al2O3 alloys [ 3–7]. Currently, the typical technology for industrialized production
Cu–Al2O3 alloys is as follows. Achieving Cu –Al alloy powder by water or gas
atomization, mixing with excessive oxidant and heat treating in closed container at
800–1000 °C, then breaking the agglomerated powder to pieces and reducing
redundant oxidant, following by canning, degassing, pressing, hot extrusion and cold
drawing to get the ﬁnal alloys [8]. In this method, internal oxidation and reduction are
separately conducted to ensure complete reduction, and canning is employed to
reduce the oxidation of copper during hot working. Therefore, the prepared alloys
have both excellent mechanical and electrical properties. However, the technology
has shortcomings such as complex process and long production cycle, which result in
high production cost. To simplify the procedure and reduce cost, internal oxidation
and reduction carrying out in one step is tried, and thus the extra breaking powder to
pieces after internal oxidation is obsolete. Few researches have been reported so far
about the internal oxidation methods on the microstructures and mechanical prop-
erties of Cu –Al
2O3 alloys.
In this study, the effects of two internal oxidation methods on microstructures
and properties of Cu –Al2O3 alloys, namely the traditional step-by-step internal
oxidation-reduction (referred to as the step-by-step method) and the novel inte-
grated internal oxidation-reduction (referred to as the integrated method), were
thoroughly compared to provide reference for lowing the cost and adjusting
properties of Cu –Al
2O3 alloys.
Experimental Methods
Preparation of Cu –Al2O3 Alloys Cu-0.18 wt% Al alloy powder ( −100 mesh) and
Cu2O powder ( −325 mesh) as oxidant are weighted and mixed according to certain
proportion. Two internal oxidation methods, as shown in Fig. 1, were used to
prepared Cu –Al2O3 alloys (0.34 wt% Al 2O3). The parameter in the same step was
identical.
2 F. Chen et al.

## Page 19

Method I: The step-by-step method
The mixed powder was internal oxidized at 900 °C under nitrogen for 2 h, broke
and reduced at 900 °C under hydrogen for 2 h to obtain the Cu –Al2O3 alloy
powder. Then the as-prepared powder was ﬁrstly pressed by cold isostatic pressing
(CIP), sintered at 900 °C under hydrogen for 2 h, then hot extruded without can-
ning at 930 °C following by cold drawing, and ﬁnally annealed at 850 °C for 1 h to
prepare Cu –Al
2O3 alloy.
Method II: The integrated method
The pressed mixed-powder was successively heat treated under nitrogen and
hydrogen to complete internal oxidation-reduction-sintering in on one step. Then
the identical process as method I was carried out to prepare Cu –Al2O3 alloy.
Characterization The density was determined by the Archimedes method, and
microstructures and fractography were observed by optical microscopy (OM) and
scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Electrical conductivity was tested using an
FD-101-type eddy-current device. The hardness (HRB) was measured using a
Rockwell hardness tester. Tensile tests were done on an Instron 8802 testing
machine with the crosshead moving rate of 0.5 mm min
−1 and the testing samples
were machined into dog-bone shape with a length of 90 mm and a gauge length of
30 mm.
Results and Discussion
Density and Microstructures The green density is usually 80 –85% for Cu –Al2O3
alloy powder formed by CIP. In the following sintering, the dispersed Al 2O3 par-
ticles enhance the initial potential energy of copper diffusion, which cause volume
diffusion dif ﬁcult to start and hence the density after sintering has no obvious
improvement [ 9]. For the mixture powder of Cu –Al alloy and Cu
2O pressed by

CIP, the green density is also about 85%. After the integrated treatment of internal
oxidation-reduction-sintering, the density still has no obvious improvement. In the
following hot extrusion and cold drawing, severe plastic deformation can effec-
tively eliminate residual pores and increase the density obviously. The ﬁnal density
of two Cu –Al2O3 alloys reaches 8.80 g cm −3, close to the theoretical density of
8.85 g cm −3.
SEM and OM images are shown in Figs. 2 and 3, respectively. The samples
seem very dense, and no pores are observed, which is consistent with the tested
density value. But many gray granular inclusions are observed in two alloys. EDX
test shows that these gray particles contain Cu and O, and should be copper oxides.
By contrast, the quantity of the gray particles in the integrated alloy is larger and the
size is signi ﬁcantly bigger than those in the step-by-step alloy (Fig. 2). It is also
found that the gray particles in the integrated alloy mainly scatter in the grains as
well as at the grain boundaries (Fig. 3b). But the gray particles in the step-by-step
alloy mainly distribute at the grain boundaries (Fig. 3a).

## Page 21

Figures 2 and 3 clearly show that preparation methods have an important effect
on morphologies and distribution of oxides. It is considered that the oxides origi-
nate from the following two ways. One is the original added Cu
2O which is not
reduced completely in the subsequent steps, referred as the original oxides. Another
is the oxides caused by reacting between Cu and oxygen during hot extrusion,
referred as the secondary oxides. During the step-by-step method, the Cu –Al
powder was ﬁrstly internal oxidized by Cu
2O. After internal oxidation, the powder
microhardness enhances greatly, and the lattice constant decreases to the value of
pure copper. Hence it is believed that Al should be oxidized fully. At the same time,
the powder are sintered together due to heat generating during internal oxidation.
Additional steps such as breaking and sieving are inevitable before reduction. The
as-sieved powder can still keep loose after reduction due to the pinning effect of the
formed Al
2O3 particle, which guarantees a complete reduction and no excessive
oxidant survives. After further CIP and sintering, the body is preheated to 900 °C
before hot extrusion. Owing to the 80 –85% relative density and without canning,
oxygen in air can easily enter into the interior of compacts through pores. This
oxidation mainly occurs in the pore surface because the exposure time at high
temperature in air is very short. Therefore, in the step-by step alloy, the granular
inclusions are mainly the secondary oxides. They generally exhibit a zonal distri-
bution parallel to the direction of extrusion and drawing (Figs. 2b and 3a).
During the integrated method, the mixture powder of Cu –Al alloy and Cu
2O was
ﬁrst pressed by CIP, followed by internal oxidation and reduction. The as-pressed
body reaches about 85% relative density and shortens the diffusion path of oxygen
atom, which is believed to be more helpful for internal oxidation than the mixture
powder with loose pack. However, the as-pressed body is more dif ﬁcult to be
reduced completely and some excessive Cu
2O particles thus remain as original
oxides. By comparing Figs. 2 and 3, it can be seen that the number of gray particles
in the integrated alloy are larger. It indicates that the original oxides can promote
oxidation degree during hot extrusion and lead to formation of more secondary
Fig. 3 OM images of Cu –Al2O3 alloys by two preparation methods (parallel to extrusion
direction), a the step-by-step alloy; b the integrated alloy
Effects of Internal Oxidation Methods on Microstructures … 5

## Page 22

oxides. In addition, there are a lot of gray particles with small size in the two alloys,
and those in the integrated alloy are relatively larger in numbers and disperse more
widely, as shown by comparing Fig. 2b, d. Apart from dispersing in the grain
boundaries, some oxides lie in the grains due to deep diffusion of oxygen (Fig. 3b),
which indicates that the original oxides not only cause number of the secondary
oxides increase, but also cause the formation position transferring from the
boundaries to the inners of grains. The original oxides and the second oxides also
generally exhibit zonal distribution (Figs. 2d and 3b).
Electrical Conductivity and Hardness Electrical conductivity of the step-by-step
alloy is 89% IACS, higher than that by the integrated alloy with 84% IACS (shown
in Table 1). The difference is related with the oxides distribution.
According to Mathiessen Rules, electrical conductivity is affected by resistivity
caused by impurities [ 10]. Compared with impurities at the grain boundaries, those
in the grains can cause much larger lattice distortion, which will lower electrical
conductivity drastically. For example, the solid solution of copper containing trace
Fe, with 0.023% only, electrical conductivity will reduce to 86% of pure copper. If
Fe is not dissolved and just precipitates from the mechanical mixture, electrical
conductivity reduces slightly and is higher than 99% of pure copper. Copper oxides
in the two alloys play the role of impurities. In the integrated alloy, the oxides
distribute in the grains as well as at the grain boundaries. In the step-by-step alloy,
the oxides mainly distribute at the grain boundaries. Oxides in grains could cause
lattice distortion, which reduce electrical conductivity obviously. As mentioned
above, the number of oxides in the integrated alloy is larger. Therefore, the inte-
grated alloy has lower electrical conductivity than that of the step-by-step alloy.
According to Orowan mechanism, the number and size of oxides will signi ﬁ-
cantly affect the alloy hardness. Compared to the step-by-step alloy, both big and
small size oxides in the integrated alloy have larger numbers, which contributes to
the increased hardness. Thus hardness of the integrated alloy is higher than that of
the step-by-step alloy, with HRB 73 –77 and HRB 69 –72, respectively (shown in
Table 1).

Tensile Properties It is illustrated in Table 1 that tensile strength of the
step-by-step alloy and the integrated alloy is 425 and 446 MPa, respectively. Yield
strength is 394 and 374 MPa, respectively, and the corresponding yield ratio ( r
0.2/
rb) is 92.7 and 83.9%. Elongation is 27.2 and 13.7%, respectively. The difference
in tensile strength is similar with that in hardness, and is also caused by copper
oxides. Oxides acting as a secondary phase can improve the alloy hardness and
strength to some extent. However, they are harmful for ductility. Tensile strength of
the integrated alloy is higher 5% than that of the step-by-step alloy, but elongation
of the former is only half of the latter. Yield ratio of the step-by-step alloy is higher
than 90%, which indicates good resistance to high temperature softening [ 11, 12].
Many dimples emerge in the two tensile fracture morphologies (shown in
Fig. 4), which indicates ductile fracture. In contrast, dimples in the step-by-step
alloy have more uniform size, deeper depth and contain less second phases, which
verify good ductility (Fig. 4a). Dimples in the integrated alloy are shallower and
have many oxide particles in the bottom of dimples (Fig. 4b). These particles
usually act as fracture sources and deteriorate ductility.
Summary
For both the step-by-step and the integrated method to prepare Cu –Al2O3 alloys, Al
in the Cu –Al alloy can completely oxidize. But the latter makes against complete
reduction of the excessive oxidant. Residual oxidant will increase oxidation degree
of the sintered body during hot extrusion, and the formed copper oxides distribute
not only at the grain boundaries but also in the grain interiors. Oxides in the
step-by-step alloy are mainly distributed at the grain boundaries. The step-by-step
method is helpful to improve electrical conductivity and ductility, but lower
strength and hardness slightly. Compared to the integrated alloy, the step-by-step

Effects of Al Content on the Physical
Properties of Al 2O3
Dispersion-Strengthened Copper Alloys
Zhiqiao Yan, Feng Chen and Tao Wang
Abstract Based on three kinds of CuAl alloy powders with Al mass fraction of
0.18, 0.55 and 1.95%, respectively, as raw materials and Cu 2O powder as oxidant,
three dispersion-strengthened copper alloy powders with Al 2O3 content of 0.34,
1.00 and 3.19%, respectively, were prepared by internal oxidation using the optimal
internal oxidation parameter. Hot pressing was subsequently adopted to prepare
Al
2O3 dispersion-strengthened copper (Cu –Al2O3) alloys. The effects of Al 2O3
content on microstructures and properties of alloy powders and sintered alloys were
studied. The results showed that the microhardness of three alloy powders after
internal oxidation was signi ﬁcantly improved and increased with increasing Al
2O3
content. But the difference between powders with 1.00 and 3.19% Al 2O3 content
was small. The relative densities of sintered alloys with lower Al 2O3 content, i.e.
0.34 and 1.00%, were both above 99%. However that with higher Al 2O3 content,
i.e. 3.19%, was only 97.8%. With increasing Al 2O3 content, electrical conductivity
decreased and hardness increased obviously. The electrical conductivity and
hardness (HRB) of three alloys were 86.0, 71.5, 60.0% IACS, and 68.8, 84.3, 91.0,
respectively.

## Page 26

Introduction
Unique combining strength and electrical conductivity with high levels of thermal
stability, Al 2O3 dispersion-strengthened copper (Cu –Al2O3) alloys are materials
developed for wide range of applications. Because of their superior properties, Cu –
Al2O3 alloys have been used as resistance welding electrodes, lead frames, accel-
erators and electrical connectors [ 1–4]. For resistance welding electrodes used in
welding galvanized sheets, Cu –Al2O3 alloys exhibit several superiorities such as a
long life (4 –10 times of Cr –Zr–Cu), no ablation and no adhesion and so on. On
condition that electrical conductivity meets demand, softening temperature, hard-
ness and strength at elevated temperature are further improved with increasing
Al
2O3 content. With the rapid development of mechanical manufacturing industry,
the demands on dispersion-strengthened copper alloys with higher Al 2O3 content
are increasing.
Powder metallurgy combining with deformation processing is widely used to
prepare Cu–Al2O3 alloys nowadays. And Al 2O3 content is obliged to be limited in a
low level, usually less than 1.2%, in order to ensure the yield [ 5]. Researches about
dispersion-strengthened copper alloys with higher Al 2O3 content are rarely
reported.
In this paper, Cu –Al2O3 alloy powders with Al 2O3 content in a wide range
(0.34–3.19%) were prepared by internal oxidation and consolidated by hot pressing.
Considering that the application of Cu –Al2O3 alloys in this study is focused on
electrical materials, electrical conductivity and hardness are mainly investigated
besides microstructures.
Experimental
Raw materials were three kinds of CuAl alloy powders with Al mass fraction of
0.18, 0.55 and 1.95%, respectively. Cu
2O powder was used as oxidant. Each CuAl
alloy powder was uniformly mixed with oxidant according to certain proportion.
The optimal internal oxidation parameter was adopted to prepare three kinds of
Cu–Al
2O3 alloy powders, and then hot pressing at 950 °C under 50 MPa for 1 h
was done to prepare the ﬁnal alloys.
The density was determined by the Archimedes method. Particle size distribu-
tion was measured by a laser particle size analyzer. The phase was examined
through an X-ray diffraction (XRD) and microstructures were observed by optical
microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscope (SEM). Electrical conductivity
was tested using an FD-101-type eddy-current device. Microhardness (HV
0.01) and
hardness (HRB) were measured using a Zwick microhardness tester and a Rockwell
hardness tester, respectively.
10 Z. Yan et al.

## Page 27

Results and Discussion
Powder properties As the large density difference between Cu and Al, water
atomization with great cooling rate is usually used to prepare CuAl alloy powders
with homogeneous element distribution. Figure 1 shows the SEM images of three
CuAl alloy powders. It can be seen that the shapes of particles become more
irregular with increasing Al content.
From the XRD patterns (Fig. 2), it can be observed that only Cu peaks are
present in three CuAl alloy powders. With increasing Al content, peaks shift toward
the small angle correspondingly. For CuAl alloy powders with 0.18, 0.55 and
1.95% Al content, respectively, the corresponding positions of Cu (111) peak (2 h)
are 43.28°, 43.15° and 42.92°, respectively. During the water atomization process,
Al dissolves into Cu and causes lattice distortion. When Al content increases, the
Cu lattice constant becomes large and therefore leads to peak position shifting
toward the small angle. Generally speaking, the more severe lattice distortion will
contribute to improve microhardness. But the microhardness of CuAl alloy is not
increased obviously when Al content is lower than 0.55%. The microhardness
(HV
0.01) values of CuAl alloy powders with 0.18 and 0.55% Al content are 72 and
73, respectively, which are almost the same. When Al content is further increased to
1.95%, the microhardness is dramatically increased to 89. It seems that some other
factors such as grain size, oxygen content and so on in ﬂuence the microhardness of
powders.
When the CuAl/Cu
2O mixture powder was internal oxidized above 900 °C,
some sintering occurred between the powder particles due to local high tempera-
tures caused by the exothermic reaction. After this treatment, the particle size
increases (Table 1) and the number of ﬁne particles obviously lessens (Fig. 3). At
the same time, the positions of Cu (111) peak of three powders all increase to
43.32°, which corresponds to a decrease of the Cu lattice constant to 0.3615 nm,
and consists with the exact value of the lattice constant of pure Cu. The phe-
nomenon indicates that the dissolved Al element is completely oxidized into Al
2O3
and separated from Cu matrix [ 6, 7]. Microhardness (HV 0.01) of three Cu –Al2O3
alloy powders at this state is 132, 165 and 162, respectively, increasing by 83.3,
127.8 and 82.0% when compared with the original CuAl alloy, respectively.

by conventional compaction. In addition, volume diffusion, which is a major
densiﬁcation mechanism, is drastically suppressed by Al 2O3 particles in pressure-
less sintering. Hence pressure-assisted sintering or work deformation is usually
inevitably used when high or full density is required. In this experiment, hot
pressing (HP) was applied to consolidate Cu –Al
2O3 alloy powders.
During HP, powders are in a thermoplastic state under the simultaneous action of
heat and pressure. Plastic deformation and creep, which are unimportant in pres-
sureless sintering, can be major densi ﬁcation mechanisms in HP. At the early stage
of densi ﬁcation, plastic yielding can be the major densi ﬁcation mechanism. The
plastic deformation between particles maybe regarded as identical to that occurring
in a hardness test using an indenter. Then, if the indentation stress r
i satisﬁes the
yielding condition (Eq. 1), densi ﬁcation by plastic deformation occurs.

Here, rY is the yield stress of the material. As the contact area increases with

stops. According to microhardness and Eq. ( 1), rY at room temperature of
Cu–Al2O3 alloy powders with 0.34, 1.00 and 3.19% Al 2O3 content can be calcu-

with 1.00 and 3.19% Al 2O3 content should be more dif ﬁcult to densify than that

that with 3.19% Al 2O3 content. It implies when the external pressure can not
improve densiﬁcation by plastic deformation mechanism at the ﬁnal sintering stage,
creep mechanism plays a major role for densi ﬁcation.

The OM images of three Cu –Al2O3 alloys are shown in Fig. 4. There are few

the alloy with 3.19% Al 2O3 content, which also indicates the alloys with lower

consistent with the result obtained by the Archimedes method. In addition, grain
size seems ﬁner with increasing Al
2O3 content. In HP, grain boundary diffusion will
be restrained due to the pinning effect of the dispersed Al 2O3 particles. The pinning
effect becomes strong with increasing the Al 2O3 content in the alloys. Therefore,
the alloy with higher Al 2O3 content has ﬁner particle size.
Electrical Conductivity As listed in Table 2, electrical conductivity of three
Cu–Al2O3 alloys are 86.0, 71.5 and 60.0% IACS, respectively. That is to say,
electrical conductivity obviously decreases with increasing Al 2O3 content.
Comparing with electrical conductivity of the alloy with 0.34% Al 2O3 content, the
values of the alloys with 1.00 and 3.19% Al 2O3 content were decreased by 16.9 and
30.2%, respectively.
According to Mathiessen Rules, electrical conductivity is affected by resistivity
caused by grain boundaries and impurities [ 8]. With increasing Al 2O3 content, grain
size obviously re ﬁnes and the number of grain boundaries increases, which leads to
increasing of electron scattering and decreasing of electrical conductivity.
Furthermore, the alloy density decreases simultaneously, the effective
cross-sectional of conductivity reduces. This will also cause electrical conductivity
to decrease. In addition, Al
2O3 is an electrical insulator. Increasing Al 2O3 content
will lessen the volume fraction of conductive Cu matrix, and thus electrical con-
ductivity decreases also.
Hardness Hardness of three Cu –Al2O3 alloys are HRB 68.8, 84.3 and 91.0 (shown
in Table 2), respectively, i.e. the value increasing with increasing Al 2O3 content.
Comparing with hardness of the alloy with 0.34% Al 2O3 content, the values of the
alloys with 1.00 and 3.19% Al 2O3 content were increased by 22.5 and 32.3%,

In general, hardness is directly related with alloy density and increases with
increasing density. For dispersion-strengthened alloys, hardness is also related with
particle size and dispersed phase content besides density. With increasing Al 2O3
content, the alloy density decreases but grain size becomes ﬁne. Both ﬁne-grain
strengthening and dispersion strengthening are be bene ﬁcial to increase hardness.
Summary
Three Cu –Al2O3 alloy powders with Al 2O3 content of 0.34, 1.00 and 3.19% were
prepared by internal oxidation of CuAl alloy powders with Al content of 0.18, 0.55
and 1.95%, respectively. After internal oxidation, the microhardness of Cu –Al
2O3
alloy powders is obviously improved and increases with increasing Al 2O3 content.
But the difference between powders with 1.00 and 3.19% Al 2O3 contents is small.
Relative density of alloys prepared by hot pressing reaches 99% for powders with
lower Al
2O3 content ( /C20 1.00%), and that with 3.19% Al 2O3 content is 97.8% only.
Al2O3 content has a inverse in ﬂuence on electrical conductivity and hardness. With
increasing Al 2O3 content, the electrical conductivity decreases and hardness
increases obviously. The electrical conductivity and hardness (HRB) of three alloys
are 86.0, 71.5 and 60.0% IACS, and 68.8, 84.3 and 91.0, respectively.

Abstract Beryllium is used as neutron multiplier in the form of a pebble bed. Basic

Introduction
The Helium Cooled Ceramic Breeder (HCCB) blanket that will be tested in ITER
under the form of Test Blanket Modules (TBMs) located in a common equatorial port
of ITER. In order to improve the tritium breeding ratio of solid-state tritium breeder
TBM, thereby ensuring the tritium self-sustaining of future commercial reactors, a
large number of neutrons must be added to the fusion reactor. Beryllium has been
extensively studied as a neutron multiplier in the high heat and high radiation extreme
working environment for solid-state breeder TBM around the international general
selection [1–6]. At present, Beryllium pebbles are fabricated by PREP method [7–10]
used as neutron multiplier in the form of a pebble bed [ 11, 12]. Basic characteristics
of the beryllium pebbles are required to the design of blanket.
The samples were fabricated by PREP method at Baoji Haibao Special Metal
Materials Co. Ltd. to produce different sizes Be pebbles. The sphericity and the
grain size were measured from the cross-sections of beryllium pebbles using optical
microscopy. The chemical compositions of ingots were examined and
microstructure of beryllium pebbles were analysed by scanning electron microscope
(SEM). Energy Dispersive Spectrometer (EDS) was used to qualitatively analyze
the components of the micro-regions by line scanning and spot scanning. The size
distribution of the pebbles accords with the normal distribution. The sphericity of
the pebble is excellent, and no hollow ball and satellite ball. It is mainly composed
of peritectic and small amount of dendrite Structures.
Experiment Equipment
Baoji Haibao Special Metal Materials Co. Ltd. has plasma rotating electrode
facilities. Figure 1 shows the PREP equipment (FMD-1), southwestern institute of
physics unites Baoji Haibao Special Metal Materials Co. Ltd. to fabricate neutron
multiplier material, the beryllium pebbles. FMD-1 equipment consists of the parts
and systems below.
Fig. 1 PREP equipment
18 Y. Jia et al.

## Page 35

1. Atomization room, a helium plasma is used to melt the end of a rapidly rotating
bar and molten droplets are spun off and solidify in ﬂight in a helium atmosphere.
2. Material rotating and axial movement machine room, which has two supporting
hollow rods.
3. the material advancing room, and the controller.
4. Electric motor room, which has tachometer, gear case and motors, to rotate the
material.
5. Vacuum system, which has mechanical pump, diffusing pump and detecting
instrument, to vacuum the working room and powder cans.
6. Plasma generator, which has stick tungsten cathode to melt the bar.
7. Gas system, which has two parts, argon and helium gas bar, to aerate the
equipment with mixed inert gas.
8. Powder collecting can, consists two tandem cut-off valves.
9. Cooling water system.
10. Operating ﬂoor.
11. Power supply.
The main parameters of equipment are that the diameter of atomization room is
2 m, the pressure of the inert gas is 0.13 MPa, equipment volume is 3.5 m
3, the
power is 120 KW, the max rotating speed is 15,000 r/m, the max current of plasma
is 1500 A, and the voltage 50 V, the grain size of powder is 45 –2000 um.
As the beryllium sphere is toxic, during the process of fabrication and experi-
ment, safety protection measures is taken according to the national standard
GBZ2-2202. As for the treatment of waste gas, every equipment has a dust col-
lecting cover above, which can absorb waste gas by negative pressure into main
exhaust duct. Exhausted gas will be treated in total. When the quantity is massive, a
spray tower should be used. After effective ﬁltration, it will be emitted to general
atmosphere within the limit of beryllium percentage of 0.0005 mg/m
3. As for
experimental fabrication, the waste gas should be treated with bubbling vacuum
cleaners before emission. The waste water treatment is that the waste water should
be pumped into a treatment tank which has quicklime and stir continuously. When
the density goes up, CO
2 is used to combine Ca(OH) 2 and Be or BeO powders into
composed nontoxic oxide, which will be abandoned after ﬁltration. A special water
treatment equipment will be used to deal with the toxic powder and compound
while massive manufacturing.
Experiment Process
The spinning self-consumed beryllium electrode is ﬁtted in FMD-1 equipment, then
shut it down and vacuum. When the vacuum degree comes to 0.005 Pa, 90% of
highly puriﬁed helium gas and 10% of argon gas will be charged. Distribute the gas
evenly by gas circulation pump. Cooling system is activated, plasma is produced,
and the rotating speed and the current of plasma is controlled to expected value by
Synthesis of Beryllium Pebbles Using Plasma Rotating Electrode … 19

## Page 36

electrode rotating motor. The plasma gun is moved before the bar which starts
melting by plasma beam. Molten liquid, which is broken into droplets, is spun off
the electrode and solidify into sphere powders by the in ﬂuence of centrifugal force
and surface tension and ﬁnally drop into powder collecting system. Activate the
electrode advancing machine to make the material advancing speed and melting
speed equal, thus keep the distance between plasma gun and the end of bar constant.
The producing process is showed by Fig. 2.
The choice of producing parameters is ﬁrstly in according to the specialty of
beryllium and asked grain size range, thus deciding the rotating speed of electrode
then the current of plasma. Therefore, this experiment chose the grain size of 0.6 –
1.2 mm, voltage 35 –40 V, current 400 –500 A, bar advancing speed 50 mm/min,
rotating speed 8000 r/min.

electrode were studied and basic performance characterization was conducted in
every batch of beryllium spheres. Table 1 is the pebble chemical composition.

Conclusion
1. The PREP equipment has tight structure and simply controlled process
parameters.
2. Beryllium pebbles produced by PREP method is melted partially in vacuum,
which reduces the pressure for the protection of beryllium outside.

with the optimal processing parameters.

surface is smooth. The content of beryllium is mainly decided by that in the

Preparation and Characterization
of Fine 316L Stainless Steel Powders
Prepared by Gas Atomization
Yingying Chen, Zhiyu Xiao, Haiping Zou, Shangkui Li and Aihong Li
Abstract Atomization technique has the powder production advantages of high
production ef ﬁciency, low cost and good sphericity. In this paper, 316L stainless
steel powders were prepared in nitrogen atmosphere by using self-designed nozzles.
The ﬁne powders yield, particle size distribution, particle shape and microstructure
of powders prepared by different nozzles and different pressure were studied.
Particle analyzer was used to characterize the powders. Results show that the
powders produced by more complex nozzle structures and higher pressure have
higher yield and better effect sphericity. The slender powders are fewer. The
average elongation is below 0.4, and the average O.Bluntness values are above 0.6.
With the decrease of pressure, the average of O.Bluntness value increases and the
sphericity of powders is improved. The average outgrowth values are below 0.2,
and the satellite powders are lesser when the pressure is greater. The ﬂowability of
the 316L stainless steel powders prepared by lower pressure were better, while the
powders prepared by the higher pressure have extremely poor ﬂuidity. The ﬂuidity
was signi ﬁcantly improved after sieving the ﬁne powders less than 25 µm. The
surface and the internal microstructure of 316L stainless steel powders prepared by
different processes are mainly cellular and dendrite structures.

Introduction
In recent years, additive manufacturing (3D printing) has attracted wide attention.
The quality of metallic powders is the key to 3D printing, directly affecting the
performance of the ﬁnished products. However, most kinds of the metallic powders
have to be imported in China. The range and characterization methods of metallic
powder (ASTMF3049) include chemical composition, ﬂowability, particle size and
particle size distribution, morphological character, apparent density, tap density etc.
[1]. Compared with other preparation methods for metallic powders, atomization
technique has the advantages of high powders production ef ﬁciency, low cost and
subsphaeroidal. It is one of the main preparation methods for metallic powders [ 2].
3D printed stainless steel has the characteristics of excellent resistance to corrosion,
high temperature resistance, abrasion resistance, resistance to creep, high strength
and good gloss appearance, which makes it widely used in the aerospace, medical
equipment, automobile industries, and other ﬁelds [3]. In this paper, 316L stainless
steel powders were prepared by atomization technique under different processing
conditions. Particle analyzer and scanning electron microscope were used to
characterize the prepared powders and analysis the effects of different processing
methods on the yield of ﬁne powders, particle size, particle shape and
microstructure in order to provide the technical basis for the application of 316L
stainless steel powders.
Powder Preparation and Experiment Method
Experimental Materials
Self-designed nozzle structures were combined with tightly coupled atomization to
prepare 316L stainless steel powders. The nozzles with ring seam, ring hole, hole
seam combination, hole seam groove combination were tested to study the effects of
nozzle structure on the yield of the ﬁne powders, as shown in Fig. 1. Then the best
nozzle structure was used to prepare 316L stainless steel powders under different
pressure conditions and the in ﬂuence of different pressure conditions on the yield of
ﬁne powders were analyzed. In the process of atomization, the inert gas atmosphere
ensures low oxygen content in 316L stainless steel powders. The factors in ﬂuencing
the atomization process include the heat of the metal ﬂow, atomizing pressure,
nozzle structure and the tube diameter etc. In this paper, the heat was 1610 ± 10 °C
and the tube diameter was 4.5 mm. Atomization with pressures of 1.5, 2.7 and
3.5 MPa was named A, B and C processes, respectively.
Experimental Methods The MASTERSIZER 2000 particle size analyzer was
used to analyze particle size distribution of the prepared powders. The particle
shape of the prepared powders was analyzed by Flowcell FC200S + HR particle
size analyzer (Belgian Occhio Company). The ﬂowability and apparent density of
26 Y. Chen et al.

structure of the powders were observed by NOVA NANO SEM 430. The
microstructure of the polished and corroded sample was observed by scanning
electron microscope.

The In ﬂuence of Different Nozzle Structure and Atomizing Pressure on the

yield of ﬁne powders can reach 36.43%, and the yield of ﬁne powders is greatly
improved. The yield of ﬁne powder can be further improved to 41.51% when the
nozzle with hole seam groove structure is adopted.

Powder O.Bluntness
The geologist introduced the concept of “Wv”to track the movement of the grains
of sand in the water. In 1919, Wentwort and others measured the surface curvature
of the particles and calculated the mean value of the maximum internal tangent
diameter to describe the phenomenon that the square rock was gradually worn into a
circle. The most famous is the reference graph designed by Krumbein in 1941, as
shown in Fig. 4, which is widely used in oil exploration and mining industry.
Nowadays, computers are so powerful that these calculations can be easily
accomplish. The larger the O.Bluntness, the more the particle shape closer to the
circle. Table 5 shows the O.Bluntness patterns and their calculated values of 316L
stainless steel powders prepared by different processes.
Figure 5a shows the relationship between the O.Bluntness and volume fraction
of 316L stainless steel powders prepared by different processes. As can be seen
from the ﬁgure, about 60% of the powders can reach 0.6 and above, and about 50%
of the powders can reach 0.9 or above. The mean O.Bluntness values of the
powders are 0.659, 0.64, 0.62, respectively for Process A, B, C, and the average
values are above 0.6. The powders are nearly spherical.

Figure 6 shows the surface morphology of the powders. The surface microstruc-
tures of larger size particles (30 –50 µm) are dendritic with satellite particles
attaching to the surface; For small particles (10 –25 µm), dendrites gradually
transform into cellular structures. This is due to the slow cooling speed of the large
particles. There is enough cooling time to form dendrites. The small particles are
cooled faster, and the grains have no time to grow into dendrites, forming mainly
cellular structures.

Abstract The differences of microstructure and mechanical properties of die steel
(1.2709) prepared by selection of laser melting (SLM) process and traditional
casting-forging process were studied. Sample A was prepared by SLM process.
Sample B was prepared by mixing process (half volume using conventional casting—
half volume of forging process application SLM). Sample C was prepared by tradi-
tional casting –forging process. Three sets of samples were subjected to the same
process of solution treatment and aging treatment. The microstructures and
mechanical properties of the three groups were studied. The results showed that the
microstructure of sample A was a homogeneous and dense plate-like martensite
structure, and they were different in phase distribution. The microstructure observa-
tion of sample B indicated that the part of the conventional casting-forging process
consisted of martensite and carbide particles, but the SLM process consisted of a
uniformly distributed elongated martensite structure. In the region of different

Microstructure and mechanical properties
Introduction
Additive Manufacturing (AM) is also called 3D printing technology [ 1, 2], it is an
advanced technology based on the principle of discrete-stacking, which can forming
the three-dimensional computer-aided design (CAD/CAM) model directly without
any other technology [ 3]. Selective Laser Melting (SLM) is the most widely used
technology in the additive manufacturing technology, which slicing the
three-dimensional model of the workpiece ﬁrst and then using laser beam [ 4] which
controlled by the scanning system to irradiate the material in the molding area to
make the metal powder selectively melted. After each slice is scanned, the powder
delivery system is completely covered with the new powder. Repeating the two
actions until the completion of scan of all the slices and ﬁnal realization of
cumulative molding of workpiece layer by layer.
At present, SLM technology has made rapid development in the mold design and
manufacturing. Iron-based alloys (mainly steel) are with rich resources, low prices,
easy to use [ 5] and easy to recover and so on. Therefore, it is widely used in
industrial production and life. Conventional cutting material manufacturing meth-
ods can produce a wide variety of iron-based materials at low cost. However, the
traditional method of manufacturing has always been the existence of many pro-
duction processes, long production cycle and other issues. SLM can quickly and
cost-effectively fabricate complex iron-based parts/molds, making up for the
shortcomings of traditional manufacturing methods [ 6]. Therefore, it is very
important to study the forming process, organization and performance of iron-based
alloy SLM. At present, iron-based alloy SLM forming still has some problems.
Firstly, the forming densi ﬁcation is the key common problem in the study of
iron-based alloy SLM forming. Secondly, choosing process parameters improperly
can lead to spheroidization effect and produce micro-cracks, which will reduce the
forming density [ 7].
36 M. Zheng et al.

## Page 52

Secondly, due to iron-based alloy laser rapid melting/solidi ﬁcation of the
forming mechanism, making the formation dif ﬁcult to control. Furthermore, the
alloying elements such as Cr, Mn and Ni in Fe-based alloys have an effect on the
forming structure [ 8, 9], and the mechanism has not been studied deeply. In
addition, SLM technology, if used in the manufacture of complex mold, forming
parts must have excellent mechanical properties [ 10, 11], such as high hardness,
good wear resistance and so on. These mechanical properties are closely related to
the compactness of the forming part and the uniformity of the microstructure.
However, to the best of our knowledge, there are few studies on the phase
transition process and phase transition mechanism of Fe-based alloy laser forming,
and the analysis of the mechanism of phase change is insuf ﬁcient. It’s necessary to
further study the internal relationship between the phase composition and the
microstructural evolution [ 12] of the Fe-based SLM composites and the process
parameters, which can make SLM technology more mature to use in complex
structural parts/mold production.

was manufactured by Germany EOS Corporation. Before the test, the powder was
dried to reduce the effect of moisture absorption on the quality of the molded
sample. The morphology of 1.2709 die steel metal powder was shown in Fig. 1.
Sample preparation process is under the vacuum environment. According to the
technical standards, the thickness of powder is 50 lm. Sweeping the powder on the
surface of the component and remove the substrate. Use DK7735 wire cutting
machine to cut the parts.

of samples were subjected to solid solution strengthening at 840 °C, followed by
aging treatment at 490 °C for 6 h. The microstructures and mechanical properties of

Results and Discussion
Macroscopic Morphology and Physical Parameters As shown in Fig. 2, samples
A, B and C produced by different processes were cut into standard Charpy impact
specimens after the same heat treatment process [ 13]. The surfaces of the three
samples are intact, compact and smooth.
Using a vernier caliper and one ten thousandth of a high-precision balance to
measure the appearance and quality of A, B, and C samples which have been
subjected to wire cutting. The results of obtaining the geometry and density are
shown in Table 2. The results show that the density of the sample prepared by SLM
is high and the relative density of the molded sample is close to 100%.
Mechanical Properties Toughness is an indication of the capacity of a material to
absorb energy before failure and is dependent on strength as well as ductility [ 14].
The mechanical properties of the three specimens were tested: impact toughness
values a
KV, aKU, impact absorption energy KV 2,K U2. The experimental results are
shown in Table 3, and the difference between the impact toughness value and the
impact absorption energy of the sample A, the sample B and the sample C is within
15%. The mechanical properties of sample C are the best, the mechanical properties
of sample B are the worst, and the mechanical properties of the three samples are
not very different.
When compared to conventionally produced 1.2709 die Steel, the impact
toughness of SLM processed specimens is reduced by 10%. However, the impact
toughness of sample B was reduced by 10 –15% which using a mixing process (half
of the volume using conventional casting –forging process and half volume appli-
cation of SLM process).

## Page 56

is formed by laser melting the pre-metal powder. In the laser melting process, the
cooling rate is very fast because the metal bath with the pre-section model of rapid
movement. When the temperature reaches the martensitie transformation temper-
ature, part of the austenite is rapidly transformed into martensite. With the solution
treatment at 840 °C, the alloying elements in the sample were uniformly and
completely dissolved in the matrix. And then 490 °C aging treatment, the treatment
time is 6 h. Most of the alloying elements are precipitated again and dispersed in
the matrix in the form of precipitated strengthening phase, which is hindered by
dislocation movement. So SLM sample strength is improved, but the plasticity is
reduced.
The solidi ﬁed tissues are lath martensite. Many parallel slats form a bundle of
strands, and the striped martensite consists of strands of different bits. Different
orientations of the stripes intersect into a certain angle, the strip width is larger, but
the size is uniform and dense. The microstructures of the samples show a laser
scanning trajectory in the SLM molding technique. During the preparation of the
test piece, the metal powder melts into a liquid phase, and line and a line are
overlapped between the laser scanning trajectories. The track width after lap is close
to the laser spot diameter of 100 lm. Since the laser two-way scanning is used in
the preparation of the sample [ 5], the microstructures are formed in a different
direction.
Samples B were prepared using a mixed process (half of the volume using
conventional casting-forging half the volume of the SLM process). The pattern of
sample B is shown in Fig. 5a. The metal powder was spread on a forged 1.2709 die
steel substrate with a powder thickness of 50 lm. When the high-energy laser
sweeps through the metal powder, the heat source melts the metal powder while
melting the partially forged substrate. As the forging matrix mainly composed of
martensite and carbide and hardness and strength higher than the SLM matrix,
resulting in remelting of the forging matrix and molten metal powder in the role of

Conclusions
(1) Workpieces of SLM process 1.2709 die steel are with high density, the relative
density is close to 100%.
(2) The microstructure of the 1.2709 die steel sample prepared by the SLM process
is a homogeneous and dense plate-like martensite structure, and they are dif-
ferent in phase distribution. The 1.2709 die steel samples were prepared by a
mixed process (half of the volume using conventional casting-forging processes
and half the volume of the SLM process). The traditional casting-forged parts
consisted of martensite and carbide particles, the microstructure of the parts of
SLM process is even-distributed long strip martensite structure. In the region of
different forming process, there is a transition region with a width of 40 lm.
The transition zone is relatively loose and the defects are relatively more.
(3) The impact toughness values aKV and aKU, the impact absorption energy KV 2
and KU2 were increased by the trend of 1.2709 die steel prepared by mixing the
process (half of the volume using the traditional casting-half volume applica-
tion SLM process), SLM process and traditional casting-forging process. The
results show that the mechanical properties of the three sets of samples are
within 15%.

Abstract Rapidly solidi ﬁed 7075 Al alloy ribbons were prepared by
melt-spinning. Sintered 7075 compacts with ﬁne-grain microstructure were
obtained by spark plasma sintering of the chopped melt-spun ribbons at different
sintering temperatures. The corrosion behavior of the sintered 7075 alloy was
examined and compared to that of the 7075-T6 bulk by electrochemical and
immersion experiments carried out in NaCl solution. Microstructures of the con-
solidated samples before and after corrosion tests were examined by optical
microscope and scanning electron microscope. Ratios of corrosion after immersion
tests were measured by an image analyzing software. Results of this study suggest
that the sintered material exhibited slightly poorer corrosion resistance than the bulk

material.

Introduction
Rapid solidi ﬁcation (RS) with cooling rate of 10 4–106 Ks−1 can produce alloys
with unconventional characteristic such as extended solute solubility, less segre-
gation, better homogeneity, much ﬁner grain size and in some cases, even the
formation of nano-crystalline and amorphous phases [ 1]. Melt spinning is among
the most commonly used methods that can signi ﬁcantly modify the alloy

## Page 61

microstructure [ 2]. Recent researches on the rapidly solidi ﬁed Al alloys are mostly
concentrated on Al –Si–X alloys, which are aimed at automotive applications such
as connecting rod, cylinder sleeve, piston and valve retainer etc. [ 3–5].
Heat-treatable aluminum alloys are extensively used in various industries because
of their low density and general acceptable mechanical properties. The outstanding
high strength 7075 aluminum alloy (Al –Zn–Mg–Cu) has been widely used in
aerospace industry [ 6]. The remarkable mechanical properties of the 7075 alloy are
mainly attributed to the nano sized precipitation and sub-micron sized dispersoids
formed from those alloying elements. The presence of these precipitations and
intermetallic phases complicates the electrochemical behaviors of the alloy. Other
than the basic alloying elements, appreciable amounts of minor constituents or
impurity elements such as Si, Ti etc. may intensify the corrosion susceptibility of
the alloy. Corrosion involving Al alloys has long been a perplexing problem in
aviation industry [ 7]. For instance, pitting degrades the fatigue properties of 7075
alloy signiﬁcantly [8, 9]. The presence of corrosion pits shortened the fatigue crack
initiation life by a factor of two to three and decreases the fatigue crack initiation
threshold by about 50% [ 9]. Few studies concerning the rapid solidi ﬁcation of 7075
alloy were performed [ 10–12]. For instance, Rokni et al. investigated the
microstructural evolution of gas atomized 7075 Al powder during high-pressure
cold sprayed deposition. However, no corrosion experiment was performed [ 10].
They obtained high quality coatings with limited porosity. The severely deformed
particle/particle boundaries lead to the formation of an ultra ﬁne-grain structure and
a low density of large angle grain boundaries. While, for small grains precipitates
were distributed primarily at grain boundaries. In a recent study conducted by Qu
and his co-workers, they found discrete, but chain-like grain boundary precipitates
together with some dispersively distributed nano-sized matrix precipitates in a
sprayed formed and T6 heat-treated 7075 alloy (with a grain size about 30 lm)
[11]. The presence of continuous Mg and Zn containing precipitations at grain
boundary has signi ﬁcant effect on the corrosion behaviors of the alloy. But they did
not perform any corrosion study. Up to now, limited work has been done on the
electrochemical characterization of melt-spun 7075 Al alloy.
In this study, 7075 ribbons were obtained by melt-spinning. The ribbons were
then sintered into compacts by spark plasma sintering. Corrosion behavior of the
7075-T6 bulk and sintered materials were studied and compared by using elec-
trochemical and immersion corrosion tests.
Experimental
Melt-spinning 7075 ribbons were produced under vacuum (2.0 /C210−3 Pa) by
using a WK-II melt-spinning machine (Physcience Opto-electronics Co., Ltd.,
Beijing), having a copper wheel with a diameter of 230 mm rotating at 2500 r.p.m.
By employing a crucible gas pressure of 250 mbar, a crucible nozzle of *1.0 mm,
46 S. Ngai et al.

## Page 62

a distance between nozzle and wheel of 2.25 mm and an angle between crucible
and off-centre line of 3°, ribbons of *40 µm thick, 1.8 –2.0 mm wide and 70 –
1000 mm in length were obtained. The temperature of the melt before ejection was
750 °C (about 100 °C above the liquidus).
Spark Plasma Sintering The rapidly solidi ﬁed ribbons were cut into small chips
of about 2 mm /C23m m /C20.1 mm in size. About 6 g of this chips was placed into
a 20 mm diameter graphite mold and sintered at 450, 500 and 520 °C under vac-
uum (1 /C210
−3 Pa) by using a Dr. Sinter Type SPS-825 spark plasma sintering
apparatus (Sumitomo Coal Co. Ltd, Japan). The heating rate and soaking time were
50 °C/min and 15 min, respectively. An uniaxial pressures was maintained constant
at 30 MPa during sintering. Density of the samples was measured by using
Archimedes method.
Electrochemical Tests Only samples sintered at 500 °C were being used in
electrochemical tests and immersion tests. Before each single experiment, samples
were ground by a wet 2000 grit SiC paper. All electrochemical experiments were
carried out in 0.1 M NaCl solution (450 mL) using a standard three-electrode cell
(PAR), involving a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) and a graphite counter
electrode. Electrochemical corrosion potential (E
corr) was collected by a potentiostat
(IVIUM VERTEX). Potentiodynamic polarization scans (PD) were conducted with
a starting potential 300 mV below the open circuit potential (OCP) under a scan
rate of 0.2 mVs
−1. The open circuit potential was measured from an open circuit
setup (OC) after a holding time of 8ks. Values of corrosion current density (I corr)
were determined from Tafel plots of the polarization data. The experiments were
carried out in air under a constant temperature of 25 °C. The reported values are
averages from three individual measurements.
Immersion Tests All samples were ground to a 2000 grit ﬁnish before immersion
tests. After 7 days of immersion in 0.1 and 0.6 M NaCl solution, corrosion products
were removed by cleaning the samples in 7% HNO
3 under ultra-sound.
Microstructure of these samples was examined by an optical microscope (Leica
DMI 5000 M) before and after immersion tests. Scanning electron microscopy
(Zeiss Merlin) was employed to perform microstructural characterization. Ratios of
corrosion characteristics after immersion tests were measured by an image ana-
lyzing software (Image J), using a grey scale threshold based image segmentation
method. Each reported ratio is an average of 11 measurements.
Material Characterization Microstructure of the samples was characterized using
optical and scanning electron microscopy. All samples were prepared by standard
metallographic techniques. The ribbon was mounted in epoxy resin at room tem-
perature prior to grinding and polishing. Sample hardness was measured by using a
load of 100 g, and each reported hardness value is an average of 10 different tests.

Results and Discussion
Figure 1 is SEM micrographs showing dendritic structure on the free-side of the
melt-spun 7075 ribbon. Due to the rapid cooling caused by the fast spinning Cu
wheel, the wheel-side (chill side) of the ribbon is a thin featureless zone and it
connected to the free-side with a transition zone consist of columnar grain structure.
Due to the outgrowth of columnar grains, the free-surface of the ribbon is not
perfectly smooth, as shown in Fig. 1a, tiny bumps and ridges can be seen. The large
round shaped grains (about 2 –3 lm in diameter with very weak dendritic growth on
the rim) found in Fig. 1b are evidence of the outgrowth of columnar grains from the
chill side of the ribbon, while, the rest are mostly dendrites with dendritic arm
spacing less than a micron.
Figure 2a shows typical microstructure of the 7075-T6 bulk material (plain
view). Irregular shaped intermetallic particles can be seen clearly aligned along
lines in the rolling direction. Figure 2b shows microstructure of the 7075 sample
sintered at 500 °C. After sintered at 500 °C for 15 min, a sintered compact with a
relative density of 98.6% was obtained, only limited number of pores can be
observed. In contrast to the bulk sample, very few intermetallic particles can be seen
sparsely distributed in the sintered sample. It indicated that as a result of rapid
solidiﬁcation, most of the solute atoms are remained dissolved in the alloy matrix or
the intermetallic particles are too small to be detected.
Figure 3 shows the effect of sintering temperature on the grain size of the
sintered samples. Grain growth is obvious and the growth rate increased sharply
when the sintering temperature is higher than 500 °C. Thus, 500 °C was chosen to
be the optimal sintering temperature in this study and the resulting grain size is
about 17 lm, which is quite small when compared to that of the bulk alloy (about
82 lm). The measured density and hardness of the sample sintered at 500 °C are
listed in Table 1.

higher. Similar trend can be observed in the corrosion rate (I corr, current at corrosion
potential). The lower corrosion resistant of the sintered 7075 alloy is because of the
existence of porosity, since NaCl solution can penetrated into the surface pores and
corroded the sub-surface grains just below the sintered alloy surface. Although the
porosity is not high at all in the studied sample, the exposed pores did affect
adversely on the corrosion behavior of the sintered sample. However, it is believed
that the signi ﬁcance of the quality of inter-particle bonding is the dominant factor in
this case, since Al alloys are hard to be sintered because of the protective surface
oxide. As pointed out by Spencer and Zhang: “Coating with better inter-particle
bonding will be less subjected to localized attack. ” [13]. From Fig. 2, it is obvious
that the quality of inter-particle bonding in the sintered sample is not comparable to
those of the bulk sample.
Figure 5 shows optical micrographs of the bulk and sintered samples after
immersion in 0.1 and 0.6 M NaCl solution for 7 days. For comparison, the area
ratios of the corrosion characteristic in different samples are listed in Table 2. Pits
and pores both appeared as dark areas in the micrographs, so they cannot be
distinguished by image analyzer. The cathodic protection zones (CPZ) are white
areas around the pits. Many corrosion craters with different sizes can be seen in the
bulk samples after immersion tests, especially for those immersed in 0.6 M NaCl
solution.
By careful inspection, these craters are quite shallow and bumpy at the bottom.
These craters are believed to be originated from the pitting of anodic zones that
located at or in the vicinity of grain boundaries and caused intergranular corrosion
(IGC). The progressing IGC eventually leads to the falling out of the surface
material and leading to craters. Large irregular shaped corrosion craters that found
in the bulk samples are absence, but typical feature of pit corrosion that surrounded
by cathodic protecting zone can be seen in the sintered samples. The localized
pitting attack is usually associated with the embedded particles in the matrix that
exposed to the open surface. Pits may either initiate at the matrix near noble
particles, which are cathodic to the matrix, or at active particles, which are anodic to

Conclusions
Rapidly solidi ﬁed 7075 Al alloy ribbon obtained by melt-spinning were sintered
into compacts with a relative density of 98.6% by spark plasma sintering at the
optimal sintering temperature of 500 °C. Results on Corrosion behavior of the 7075
bulk and sintered materials indicated that porosity adversely affected the corrosion
behavior of the material in NaCl solution. The sintered material exhibited slightly
lower corrosion resistance than the bulk 7075 alloy. Immersion experiment results
showed that even in a harsher environment (0.6 M NaCl solution), there is not
much decrease in corrosion resistance of the sintered 7075 as compared to the bulk
material.

Preparation of Fe/Fe 3O4 Soft Magnetic
Composites by Spark Plasma Sintering
Shuhan Lu, Jihang Ren and Zhankui Zhao
Abstract Fe/Fe3O4 soft magnetic composite was prepared with the method of
physical coating method by spark plasma sintering. In this way, its sintering
interface was improved. It solved the problem that hot pressing curing soft magnetic
composites have low densi ﬁcation. The Fe/Fe
3O4 was observed at different sin-
tering temperatures and the in ﬂuence of the chemical composition and
microstructure properties was analyzed. The material density was higher and
interface was combined with high performance. The resistivity decreases because
the element changed with higher temperature. The morphology and structure are
characterized by SEM, EDS and XRD, respectively and the electric properties are
tested. In the end part we discuss the pros and cons of SPS method on synthesizing
Fe/Fe
3O4 soft magnetic composites and its potential application in industries.
Keywords Soft magnetic composites /C1Spark plasma sintering
Electrical properties
Introduction
Most of the composite materials, which are used in high frequency, are made by hot
pressing sintering with adhesive bonding. The organic or inorganic binder such as
epoxy can reduce magnetic core, and then the electrical and magnetic conductivity
are in ﬂuenced accordingly. Above all the organic and inorganic coatings are not
magnetic materials and do not have good magnetic properties and electrical con-

ductivity [ 1]. The coating layer of magnetic composite material has a great in ﬂu-
ence on the its performance [ 2, 3]. And the holes of the coating layer in the metal
bulk are serious after warm compaction [ 4]. The phenomenon has de ﬁnite inﬂuence
on the mechanical properties. The density of their coating layer is inferior [ 5–7].
On account of its property of low temperature, energy saving and rapid, spark
plasma sintering becomes a rapid rise of sintering method [ 8]. Firstly, the powders
are preloading molding. Then they access to prepressing block pulse current and
make the powders sintered together. Under the high energy pulse current, low
intensity of pressure and experiment of uniaxial, the materials are sintered. SPS
(spark plasma sintering) is a new rapid molding method [ 9]. The mechanism of its
sintering has not been analyzed thoroughly. There are still different ideas and
assumptions on the theory of SPS. The main reason is that the joule heat and applied
load promoted the process of sintering and densi ﬁcation. By the reason of dielectric
difference between adjacent particles, the samples are applied on high energy and
produce electric spark [ 10]. For the quantity of heat produce by 6000 °C, electric
spark and discharge of pulse pressure, the energy density is up to 106 J/cm
2. Then it
can promote the disintegration of the surface of powder particles and the gas strip-
ping. The particle surface can be clean and combined. The electric spark is appeared
in 1 –2 s between particles. After discharge, the form of materials is made further
densiﬁcation by current under the temperature below the melting point [ 11]. And at
the end of the curing stage, the samples realize the ultimate densi ﬁcation by
mechanical pressure. The results show that the Fe
3O4-coated iron powder has soft
magnetic composites. Working for Katie Jo Sunday, Fe 3O4 coated Fe powder was
cured by hot pressing sintering. However there were many holes on the coating layer.
Although the number of holes can be decreased by increasing hot-pressing tem-
perature, its mechanical and magnetic properties can be affected [12]. Relative to heat
pressing sintering, the discharge plasma sintering is relatively short sintering time to
ensure the size of original powder particles which control the particles, the phase
reaction and decomposition, nanometer structure improve the interface strength [ 13].
Experimental Methods
The iron power (purity of 99.9% 200 lm) were mixed by 10 wt% Fe3O4 (purity >99%
100–300 nm). The process of coating the iron powder and Fe 3O4 particles were
carried out for 30 min with 400 r/min in a high energy planetary ball milling equip-
ment. Then the mixed powder was sintered by SPS (Model 1050 the Spark Plasma
Sintering system, Sumtomo Company, Japan) in a cemented-carbide model at pres-
sure of 550 MPa at temperatures of 407, 507, 607 and 707 °C. For the contrast
experiment, the holding time was set as 3 min, and samples were 15 mm in diameter
and 3 mm in thickness.

Figure 1 shows the SEM micrograph for iron powders before (Fig. 1a) and after

The nice Fe 3O4 nano-powder on the coarse Fe particles are shown in Fig. 1b. The
nano-particles have larger ratio surface area and surface energy. And the adsorption
effect can be easily produced between the particles. Compared with different con-
ditions, the samples were in accordance with the material morphology by SPS, such
as Fig. 1c–f. As the temperature increased, the hole is less and the samples are
denser. At the same temperature of circumstances, we found that the number of the
hole of circumstance lessen after sintered and holding time. Although the original
pure iron powder is hollow, the heat preservation treatment can also reduce the
number of empty. In addition, the granule did not grow obviously and keep the
original size. But the granule has been shaped, which was caused by the impact of
axial compression and plasma discharge. The cell wall layer in the sintering sample
was nanometer Fe
3O4 particles.

with heat holding for 3 min. XRD data of all samples is found obviously a-Fe

Conclusions
In the present work, Fe 3O4-coated Fe soft magnetic composites were prepared and
densiﬁed by SPS. Compared to hot pressing, Fe/Fe 3O4 soft magnetic composites
with higher density and resistivity can be obtained at lower sintering temperature
and pressing pressure.

Liming Zou, Xin Liu, Huanwen Xie and Xinhua Mao
Abstract High quality Ti –6Al–4V alloy powders were prepared by plasma
rotating electrode process (PREP). Three different rotating speed were selected.
After sieved, three kinds of powder with different size distribution were consoli-
dated by hot isostatic pressing (HIP). The phase compositions, morphologies and
microstructures of the powders and HIPed samples were characterized. Mechanical
properties of HIPed Ti –6Al–4V alloys also were investigated. The results showed
that the proportion of small particles increased with the increasing rotating speed.
Alloy prepared by powders distributed in 100 –150 lm possesses the best
mechanical properties.

Introduction
Titanium alloy has some advantages such as high speci ﬁc strength, good corrosion
resistance and excellent biocompatibility, so it has been widely used in many ﬁelds
[1–4]. However, the cost of producing titanium alloy by traditional processing
method such as casting is very high, so it is essential to developing low cost
manufacturing techniques, such as powder metallurgy (PM) method [ 5, 6]. In

Now the research hotspot is focusing on preparation of high quality titanium
alloy powder. There exist two main methods to fabricating high quality titanium
alloy powders. They are Plasma rotating electrode process (PREP) and gas
atomization (GA) [ 7–9]. Compared with GA, powder prepared by PREP is more
suitable for HIP. It can be used for producing spacecraft such as missles, rockets. In
the current study, The effect of powder characteristics on properties of HIP sample
has not been reported.
There are relationships between the quality of powders prepared by PREP and
the process parameters such as billet diameter, rotating speed and so on. The
relation between particle size and these parameters can be seen form the following
equation [ 10].

where d presents the average particle size, r presents the surface tension, D presents
the billet diameter, n presents the rotating speed and q presents the billet density.
The purpose of this paper is to investige the relationship between rotating speed
and properties of Ti –6Al–4V alloy powder prepared by PREP. What is more, the
effect of particle size on mechanical properties of Ti –6Al–4V alloy HIPed using
prepared powder also be investigated.
Experimental
Ti–6Al–4V alloy powders were prepared by PREP. The rotating speed was selected
12,000 RPM, 18,000 RPM and 20,000 RPM under an Ar atmosphere (99.99%)
respectively. The PREP equipment consisted of a stainless-steel atomization
chamber. Then prepared powders were divided into three different particle size
distribution.
Powders with different particle size were ﬁlled into stainless steel cans and
degassed. Subsequently, cans were sealed gas tight and HIPed at 980 °C by HIP
equipment (QIH-15, Sweden), for 4 h under a pressure of 140 Mpa. Then the
reaction layer was removed from samples.
Powders and consolidated samples were etched with kroll reagent (HF 2%,
HNO
3 4% and H2O 94%) for 15 s. The element composition of powders such as Ti,
Al, V with different particle size was tested. The oxygen content of powders and
HIPed samples were measured by a Nitrogen/Oxygen Determinator (TC600, LECO
Co.,). The phase composition of powders was investigated by X-ray diffraction

microstructure of HIPed alloys were were analyzed using the scanning electron
microscope (SEM) (JEOL JXA-8100). The tensile mechanical properties of the
HIPed samples were tested using a universal testing system (MTS TestStar 810).

Figure 1 shows the SEM images of prepared Ti –6Al–4V alloy powder. The

hollow powder basically (Fig. 1b).
Figure 2 shows particle size distribution of Ti –6Al–4V alloy powder prepared
by PREP at rotating speed of 15,000 RPM, 18,000 RPM and 20,000 RPM
respectively. The key particle size indicators such as D10, D50 and D90 for
powders prepared with different rotating speeds also are shown in Table 1. With the
increasing of rotating speed, the peak of distribution moves to the left. And the
particle size distribution becomes narrower and narrower. The average particle size
increases with decreasing rotating speed. D50 of particle size decreases from 193 to
114 lm when rotating speed increases from 15,000 RPM to 20,000 RPM. For
powders prepared at rotating speed of 20,000 RPM, the particle size mainly dis-
tributed in 50 –250 lm, but that is 85 –550 lm at rotating speed of 15,000 RPM.
It can be seen from XRD patterns of prepared Ti –6Al–4V alloy powder with
three different particle size. It composed of a′ martensitic phase. Because the
cooling speed is very fast during PREP, so the metastable phase forms. Figure 3b
shows the phase is needle shape.

and O all decrease with increasing particle size. Because boil point of Al element is

Conclusion
Ti–6Al–4V alloy powders prepared by PREP have spherical morphologies. There
exist a small number of satellite ball and no hollow powder. With the increasing of
rotating speed, the proportion of small particles become larger. The alloy powders
compose of a′ martensitic phase. With the increasing of particle size, the content of
elements such as Al, V and O all decrease. The content of oxygen for powders is
less than 0.1%. The microstructure of the HIPed alloys is mainly equaixed grains
and lath like grains. Alloy prepared by powders distributed in 100 –150 lm pos-
sesses the best performance.

Introduction
Aluminum–magnesium alloy is an ideal structural material because of its reason-
able strength, better ductility, strong corrosion resistance and excellent welding
performance. It has been widely used in automotive, aircraft, ship and cryogenic
applications [1, 2]. However, it belongs to a group of non-heat treatable alloys with
medium strength for the coarse precipitation phase from aging process [ 3]. In order
to acquire better mechanical properties, work hardening and micro-alloying come to
be the effective ways.
It is well known that recrystallization is a predominant softening mechanism in
the hot working [ 4]. It has been shown that aluminum alloy 5083 is susceptible to
recovery and recrystallization. Nie et al. [ 5–7] have been committed to the relevant
researches of aluminum alloy containing Er. It has been shown that Zr and Er
additives in aluminum alloy can form thermal stable coherent Al
3(Zr, Er) precipi-
tates which can pin dislocation and subgrain boundaries to inhibit recrystallization
during thermal processing [ 7].
A new type Al –4.5Mg–0.7Mn–0.2Zr–0.2Er alloy was developed based on tra-
ditional Al –Mg–Mn–Zr alloys by adding trace Er. However, few investigations
have been reported on the microstructure, mechanical properties of the hot-rolled
alloy. The purpose of this paper is to study the effect of different hot-rolling tem-
peratures on the mechanical properties of the alloy and its corresponding structural
changes.
Experimental Procedure
The chemical composition of the alloy is shown in the Table 1. This alloy was cast
by a conventional melting and casting route. As-cast Al –6Er, Al–4Zr and Al –10Mn
master alloys, commercial pure aluminum and magnesium were taken as the
starting raw materials. Appropriate amounts of the starting materials were melted in
a crucible by heating furnace to 780 °C and the melt was poured in cast iron mold
at about 720 °C. The compositions of the alloys, analysis by inductively coupled
70 X. Li et al.

## Page 84

plasma atomic emission spectroscopy, are given in Table 1. The as-cast alloy was
subjected to two-step homogenization, which was at 280 °C for 8 h plus 470 °C for
10 h. After homogenization, the samples were hot-rolled with a starting temperature
470 °C and 80% reduction, annealed 1 h at 470 °C and then rolled at 470, 350,
200 °C with the reduction of 50%. For tensile tests, the sheets annealed at various
temperatures were machined according to the ASTM standard specimens with
25 mm gauge length. All of the specimens had an axis along the longitudinal
direction. The tensile test was performed at a constant strain rate of 2 /C210
4/s with
the load direction parallel to the specimen axis. The morphology of the residual
phase was examined on FEI Quanta 650 FEG scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
Thin foils for TEM analysis were prepared by twinjet polishing with an electrolyte
solution consisting of 30% HNO
3 and 70% methanol at −30 °C. TEM observations
were carried out on a JEM2010 transmission electron microscope (TEM) with a
200 kV accelerating voltage.
Results and Discussion
Mechanical Properties The tensile test results are shown in the Table 2. The
ultimate tensile strength (UTS) decreased from 423 to 378 MPa (10.6% decrement),
and the yield strength (YS) decreased from 376 to 310 MPa (17.6% decrement),
whereas the percentage of elongation increased from 10.4 to 15.4% for the
hot-rolled temperature increased from 200 to 350 °C. Similarly, for the hot-rolled
temperature increased from 350 to 470 °C, the ultimate tensile strength
(UTS) decreased from 378 to 330 MPa (12.8% decrement), and the yield strength
(YS) decreased from 310 to 238 MPa (23.3% decrement), whereas the percentage
of elongation increased from 15.4 to 23.0%.
It can be observed that the tensile strength and yield strength increased with the
rolling temperature, while elongation showed an opposite trend. The trends of the
tensile strength, yield strength and elongation are shown in the Fig. 1. From the
ﬁgure, we can infer that in the vicinity of 350 °C, a better match can be got between
strength and elongation.

The instrumented impact results of hot-rolled Al 5E83 samples at different
temperatures are presented in Fig. 2. The impact behavior of the three conditions at

Impact toughness values of hot-rolled Al 5E83 alloy at temperature 200 °C is

(nearly 32% increase) after 350 and 470 °C hot-rolling.
Microstructure Characterizations The SEM fracture graphs of tensile samples of
the hot-rolled Al 5E83 alloy at different temperatures (200, 350, 470 °C) are shown
in Fig. 3. In Fig. 3a, there were many quasi cleavage small facets and a small
number of dimples and tearing edges, which is a transition fracture between
cleavage fracture and dimple fracture, which belonged to quasi cleavage fracture. In
Fig. 3b, the fracture is composed of tearing edge, dimple and a small amount of
quasi cleavage facets. Meanwhile, the intergranular fracture is found to belong to
the ductile brittle mixed fracture. In Fig. 3c, the fracture consists of a large number

of tearing edges and dimples, with a large number of small equiaxed dimples due to
