The SEM fracture graphs of impact samples of the hot-rolled Al 5E83 alloy at
different temperatures (200, 350, 470 °C) are shown in Fig. 4. The fracture
behavior of the samples tested under impact load is different from that of tensile test
due to different load forms [ 8–10]. The basic difference between both types of
fracture surfaces was due to the fact that the tensile specimens results in tensile
fracture; whereas, Charpy impact specimens exhibited shear inducing fracture. The
fracture morphologies are different in different areas of the impact specimen, due to
non-uniform stress distribution in the specimens. With the increase of temperature,
the number of dimples in impact fracture increased gradually, and the dimples
became deeper and deeper, fracture mode of the alloy changed from ductile brittle
mixed fracture to ductile fracture.
During the melting and solidi ﬁcation process of the alloy, the coarse particles
precipitated and then the particles crushed during the rolling process and arranged
along the rolling direction (shown in the Fig. 5). Under impact loading, the dis-
locations piled up in the second phase particles, resulting in stress concentration. So
that the second phase particles ruptured or separated within the matrix, making the

initiation of crack. It has been shown in previous studies that the second phase
particles have a signi ﬁcant effect on the subsequent rolling performance of the
material. The coarse second phase particles have a detrimental effect on the ductility
and toughness of the alloy [ 11–13].
Figure 6 shows the TEM microstructures of the experimental alloy hot-rolled at
different temperatures. In the case of rolling at 200 °C, the grains are typical of
rolling deformation grains, and a large number of dislocations are entangled in the
grains. A small amount of subgrains appeared in some regions, but the subgrain
boundaries are very unclear and the dislocations density is very high (Fig. 6a).
When the temperature increases to 350 °C, there are many subgrains in the
deformed grains, while the subgrain boundaries are easily recognized. The dislo-
cation density of subgrains obviously reduced. The dislocation did not occur,
migration and other large changes, and there are still dislocations in the organi-
zation (Fig. 6b). In this process, the major occurrence of the organization is a
dynamic recovery. With the temperature coming to 470 °C, the dynamic recrys-
tallization occurred inside the grains, and the dislocation is density decreased
obviously, the size of the subgrains increased, and the dislocation density in the
subgrains was very low. We can see the characteristics of subgrain coalescence and
large angle migration (Fig. 6c).

## Page 88

With temperature increasing to 350 °C, tangled dislocation rearrangement, dis-
location tangles become regularized, and the subgrain boundaries occurred. The
process mentioned above is a typical dynamic recovery process. Higher temperature
or lower strain rate can provide a higher driving force or more time for the dislo-
cation movement [ 14]. Thus, it can be seen that there are many dislocation walls
occurring and then turning into subgrain boundary as shown in Fig. 7a. In addition,
there also occurs numerous dispersed Al 6Mn particles and Al 3(Er, Zr) precipitates
in grain interior and boundaries. The Al 6Mn particles and Al 3(Er, Zr) precipitates
can pin the dislocations movement (Fig. 7b) and the subgrain boundaries sliding
(Fig. 7c, d). These particles hindered the growth of subgrains and the migration of
grain boundaries, thereby inhibited the dynamic recrystallization of Al –4.5Mg–
0.7Mn–0.2Zr–0.2Er alloy and ﬁnally improve its thermal stability [ 15].

Conclusions
The microstructure and mechanical properties of 5E83 alloy have been studied, and
the following conclusions can be drawn:
1. The tensile strength and yield strength increase with the hot-rolled temperature,
while the elongation and impact toughness show the opposite trend. When the
hot-rolled temperature is 350 °C a better match between strength and impact
toughness can be realized.
2. The second phase particles lie at the bottom of the dimples, and arrange along
the rolling direction. The coarse second phase particles have a detrimental effect
on the ductility and toughness of the alloy.
3. When the rolling temperature is 350 °C, the major occurrence of the organi-
zation is dynamic recovery. The Al
6Mn particles and Al 3(Er, Zr) precipitates can
pin the dislocations movement and subgrain boundaries slide,hinder the growth
of subgrains and the migration of grain boundaries, thereby inhibit the dynamic
recrystallization of Al –4.5Mg–0.7Mn–0.2Zr–0.2Er alloy and improve its ther-
mal stability.

Microstructure and Properties
of Spray-Formed Si –30Al Alloy Used
for Electronic Packaging
Hongwei Liu, Shuhui Huang, Zhihui Li, Baiqing Xiong,
Yongan Zhang, Xiwu Li, Hongwei Yan and Lizhen Yan
Abstract The microstructure and properties of spray-formed Si –30Al alloy was
studied in this paper, which was used for electronic packaging. Hot isostatic
pressing was used to compact the ingot, and then electroplating and brazing was
carried out. The results showed that, (1) the Si –30Al alloy comprised a-Al phase,
pseudo eutectic phase and primary silicon phase; (2) the ﬂow deformation of a-Al
phase and pseudo eutectic phase ﬁlled pore defect making the alloy compacting by
HIP; (3) the alloy could be electroplated and brazed easily, and no pore defect was
observed in electroplated coating and weld.
Keywords Spray-formed Si –30Al alloy
/C1Electronic packaging
Microstructure /C1Properties
Introduction
Si–Al alloy is ideal material for electronic packaging industry, because of thermal
expansion coef ﬁcient matching with GaAs or Si, high thermal conductivity, low
density, easy to electroplating and brazing. Also, the cost of Si –Al alloy is lower
than the other electronic packaging materials as metal matrix composites and so on
[1–4].
Nowadays, Si –Al alloy is mainly prepared by powder metallurgy and spray
forming. The powder metallurgy technology has some disadvantages, such as, the
ﬂow process is long and complex, the energy consumption and costs are fairly high,
and the oxidation is hard to avoid, which limits its application in producing Si –Al
alloy. By comparison, the spray forming is more suitable for preparing Si –Al alloy,
because of short process, slight oxidation and uniform distribution of elements
[3–6].

## Page 92

The Ospey company produced Si –50Al, Si –40Al and Si –30Al alloys through
spray forming, and the alloys has been used for electronic packaging industry
successfully. Physical property and processing performance of the Si –Al alloys
need further research [ 6–8].
The Si –30Al alloy is prepared spray forming, and then hot isostatic pressing is
used to compact the ingot. The microstructure evolution is researched during
electroplating and brazing. The main properties of Si –30Al alloy, which is used for
electronic packaging, are discussed in this work.
Materials and Methods
Si–30Al alloy is spray-formed by the equipment of SF-500, which is a self-made
machine for spray forming. The schematic diagram of spray forming and the ingots
are shown in Fig. 1. The cylindrical samples of U180 /C2300 mm is machined from
the ingot. The samples are canned by pure aluminum for hot isostatic pressing
(HIP), and the parameters of HIP are 570 °C/200 MPa/4 h. Microstructures are
observed by Carl Zeiss Zxiovet 200MAT optical microscopy (OM), JSM-7001
scanning electron microscope (SEM) and JEOL JEM-2010 transmission electron
microscopy (TEM). Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) is performed by using
a NETZSCH STA 409C/CD in the temperature range 20 –600 °C in an argon
atmosphere with heating rate of 10 K/min.

Results and Discussion
Metallograph of spray-formed Si –30Al alloy is shown in Fig. 2. The grains are ﬁne
and well-distributed, and some pore defect distributed in the matrix t randomly. The
primary silicon phase is about 50 lm, and they have no obvious dendrite orien-
tation which causes anisotropy of the alloy.
The SEM and line scanning of Si/Al interface is shown in Fig. 3. As can be seen
that, the content of Si in primary silicon phase is more than that in matrix and the
opposite phenomenon can be observed at the content change of Al.
The TEM of spray-formed Si –30Al alloy is shown in Fig. 4. The three kinds of
phases are shown in Fig. 4a, which are a-Al phase, pseudo eutectic phase and
primary silicon phase. The chemical content of the phases are determined by EDS
(energy dispersive spectrometer) as shown in Table 1. The matrix is composed of
a-Al phase and pseudo eutectic phase, and lamellar structure of the pseudo eutectic
phase can be observed in Fig. 4b.
DSC curves of spray formed Si –30Al alloy and casted Si –30Al alloy are shown
in Fig. 5. As can be seen that, the endothermic peaks of the two alloys are 566 and
575 °C respectively. So it is proved that again, the spray formed Si –30Al alloy
contains non-equilibrium eutectic phase (pseudo eutectic phase).
The hot isostatic pressing (HIP) are carried out at 570 °C/200 MPa/4 h.
Metallograph of spray-formed Si –30Al alloy after HIP is shown in Fig. 6.
Compared with Fig. 2, pore defect almost disappears, and the form of primary
silicon phase is unchanged. It is shown that, the ﬂow deformation of a-Al phase and
pseudo eutectic phase ﬁlls pore defect making the alloy compacting during HIP.
Three-point bending test is carried out after HIP, and bending Strength of
spray-formed Si-30Al alloy is about 180 MPa. The fracture is shown in Fig. 7 after
the test. Both ductile fracture (position 1) and brittle fracture (position 2) are
observed, so the mechanical property of the alloy comes from mechanical mixture
of a-Al phase, pseudo eutectic phase and primary silicon phase. The chemical

## Page 98

Summary
The Si–30Al alloy has been prepared spray forming, and the microstructure used to
characterize the process of HIP, electroplating and brazing.
1. The Si –30Al alloy comprises a-Al phase, pseudo eutectic phase and primary
silicon phase, and some pore defect can be observed.
2. During hot isostatic pressing, the ﬂow deformation of a-Al phase and pseudo
eutectic phase ﬁlls pore defect making the alloy compacting and the form of
primary silicon phase is unchanged.
3. Three-point bending strength of spray-formed Si –30Al alloy is about 180 MPa.
The alloy can be electroplated and brazed easily, and no pore defect is observed
in electroplated coating and weld.

Effect of Erbium –Zirconium Composite
Modiﬁcations on the Microstructure
and Mechanical Properties of A356
Aluminum Alloy
Liantao Ji, Wei Wang, Hui Huang, Shengping Wen, Kunyuan Gao
and Xiaolan Wu
Abstract The Al–7Si–0.3 Mg (A356) alloys with various contents of the rare earth
element Er, Zr were prepared by the conventional casting technique. The effect of
Er, Zr composite modi ﬁcations on the microstructure and mechanical properties of
A356 alloys was investigated using the optical microscopy (OM), scanning elec-
tronic microscopy (SEM), energy spectrum analysis and mechanical testing. The
results show that addition of 0.3 wt% Er and Zr had an excellent re ﬁning effect on
a-Al grains and a modi ﬁcation effect on Si containing phase in the as-cast state. The
size of a-Al dendrite reduced, the acicular eutectic Si became short rod-shaped or
granular. When Er and Zr content was 0.3 wt%, the tensile strength and hardness of
the alloys reached up to maximum values.

## Page 100

Introduction
The A356 alloy (Al –7Si–0.3 Mg) has well casting properties, corrosion resistance,
weldability and high speci ﬁc strength, which is widely used in automobile industry
and aerospace industry, and which is also made whole ideal of thin-walled com-
plicated casting, casting of aluminum alloy. However, Silicon content is higher in
A356 alloy, in the as-cast condition, the eutectic Si containing phase exhibits a
typical acicular or coarse plate-like morphology, resulting in poor mechanical
properties. These coarse microstructures also include that the a-Al dendrites and
other intermetallic phases in the alloy [ 1]. It is well known that the coarse
microstructures in the cast unmodi ﬁed A356 alloy, cause the decrease of the tensile
properties, especially elongation, as which act as premature crack initiations and
then fracture in tension [ 2]. Therefore, the modi ﬁcation of these coarse phases is
very important to improve the mechanical properties of the as-cast A356 alloy. The
grain re ﬁnement and Si containing phase modi ﬁcation techniques are used.
Among many methods to re ﬁne the coarse microstructure, the addition of rare
earth re ﬁning agent in conventional casting is one of the most important methods
due to its simplicity and effectiveness. In previous studies, the addition of Al –Ti,
Al–B, Ai –Ti–B, Al –Ti–C, and Al –Ti–B–RE master alloys can play the role of
obvious grain re ﬁnement [ 3–6]. The Al –Sr master alloy is widely used to modify
the morphology of the eutectic Si and that has achieved a remarkable effect [ 4–10].
In recent years, the modi ﬁcation of rare earth (RE) elements on the Al –Si–Mg
alloys have received more and more attention. Yu et al. [ 11] found that the addition
of Y to ZL107 alloy, the size of a-Al dendritie reduced, and the acicular eutectic Si
became short rod-shaped or granular. When Y content was 0.1 wt%, the tensile
strength and hardness of the alloy were maximum. Rao et al. [ 12] and Huang et al.
[13] found the re ﬁning effect of Sm-modi ﬁcation and La-modi ﬁcation for the
as-cast ADC12 Al –Si–X alloy, respectively. Sm was an effective modifying agent
for the eutectic Si of ADC12 alloy, when 1.0 –
1.5 wt%Sm was added to the alloy,
the coarse acicular eutectic Si was modi ﬁed into ﬁne particle or short rod structure.
Shi et al. [ 14] observed that 0.2 –0.4 wt%Gd had an wonderful re ﬁning effect on
primary a-Al dendrites and a modi ﬁcation effect on eutectic Si. The mechanical
properties were very poor in as-cast state with the addition of Gd in the alloy.
Rare earth elements has a large number of Segregation coef ﬁcient, in the
solidiﬁcation process in the solid-liquid surface segregation, the formation of a
larger composition undercooling, promote nucleation, re ﬁne the grain size. It has
been found that the erbium(Er) –zirconium(Zr) compound addition has a remarkable
reﬁning effect on the coarse microstructures [ 15–17]. Therefore, the present work is
to investigate the optimum addition amount of Er –Zr to modify the eutectic silicon
of A356 alloy and its effect on the mechanical property.
88 L. Ji et al.

## Page 101

Materials and Examinations
The raw materials for casting were pure Al (99.99 wt%) and pure Mg (99.99 wt%)
and Al –21.2 wt%Si and Al –6.2 wt%Er and Al –3 wt%Zr master alloys. The base
alloy was melted in a graphite crucible at 760 °C by using a 12-KW electric resis-
tance furnace. The modifying agent was added after degassing was completed to
adjust the chemical compositions. The rare earth Er and Zr composite agent was
added to the alloy as 0, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6 and 0.8 wt% (Table 1). The metal mold
was preheated to 350 °C before casting. The surface of the melt was skimmed and
then the melt was poured into the metal mold (180 mm /C2100 mm /C230 mm) at
720 °C. The samples were then treated with a standard T6 schedule.
The microstructure was observed with a metallurgical microscope (OLYMPUS
PMG3) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and the average grain size and the
average aspect ratio of the Si phases were statistically calculated by quantitative
analysis software in 15 ﬁelds. The phase composition was analyzed by an X-ray
diffraction (XRD) and the mechanical properties were examined using a material
test machine (MTS810) with a loading speed of 1.0 mm/min. The hardness
(HV) was tested by a hardness tester (HXD1000TM/LCD); nine samples for each
group were measured to obtain the average value.
Results and Discussion
Effect of Er –Zr Composite Addition on Re ﬁnement of a-Al Grains The
microstructures of A356 alloys with different Er –Zr contents are shown in Fig. 1 in
the as-cast state. The mean diameters of a-Al dendrites in A356 alloys with dif-
ferent Er –Zr contents were measured with quantitative metallography. It can be
found that the size of a-Al dendrite in A356 alloy gradually decreased with
increasing Er –Zr content. The mean diameters of a-Al dendrites in A356 alloys
without Er –Zr contents is about 130 lm. And when the amount of Er –Zr was
0.3 wt%, the mean diameters of a-Al dendrite is about 90 lm With the increase of
Er–Zr, the grain size of a-Al has little change. The shape and distribution of a-Al
dendrite became uniform. In a prior study, the diffusivity of Er in a-Al is

more nucleation places for Zr atoms. Primary Al 3Er phases and Al 3Zr are the reason
of re ﬁnement of a-Al dendritic structure. On the other side, Er, Zr were surface
active elements in A356 alloys, and it was very easy to accumulate in the

After addition of Er –Zr to A356, Al
3Er, Al 3Zr or Al 3 (Er, Zr) compounds formed,
which can act as the heterogeneous sites to promote nucleation of the a-Al dendrites
and the a-Al grains nucleation increased, resulting in grains re ﬁnement. At the same
time, the addition of Er –Zr will increase the composition of super-cooling, the
eutectic reaction could crystallize at higher super-cooling temperatures, so the
nucleation rate increased, remarkably.
Effect of Er–Zr Addition on Morphology of Eutectic Si Phases. Figure 2 shows
the morphologies of the eutectic Si in A356 alloys with different Er, Zr contents. As
shown in Fig. 2a, the eutectic Si in unmodi ﬁed alloy is characterized by coarse
acicular or plate-like morphology. After 0.15 wt% Er –Zr was added to A356 alloy,
the size of eutectic Si become ﬁner, however, there are still some plate-like eutectic
Si phases observed (Fig. 2b). When Er, Zr content was equal to or more than 0.3 wt
%, the eutectic Si was modi ﬁed completely, and the shape of the eutectic Si became
short rod-shaped or granular (Fig. 2c–f). Enrichment of the modi ﬁcation element on
the surface of Silicon phase was strengthened, and the growth of eutectic Si in the
largest was inhibited to a great degree. Whereas, the Er, Zr content reached 0.8 wt%,
the size and morphology of eutectic silicon are not obvious. Figure 3 shows the

Effect of Er –Zr Addition on Mechanical Properties. Figure 5 shows the change

the fracture mode of alloy tends to ductile fracture.

## Page 105

Conclusions
(1) The addition of 0.3 wt% Er –Zr had an excellent effect on the re ﬁnement of a-
Al grains and the morphology of eutectic Si phases in the as-cast state.
(2) When Er and Zr were added to A356 alloy, the acicular or coarse plate-like
morphology eutectic Si became short rod-shaped or granular, large ﬂakes of
eutectic Si were not observed.
(3) The mechanical properties of A356 alloy ﬁrstly increased and then decreased
with Er, Zr content increasing. 0.3 wt% Er –Zr composite modi ﬁcation of the
alloy and T6 treatment yielded the highest strength and elongation of the alloy.

/C1 Aluminum alloy /C1 Microstructure evolution
Hot deformation
Introduction
Aluminum alloy with high strength and low density is applied widely in the ﬁled of
aerospace industry [ 1]. The hot deformation is commonly used to process alu-
minum alloy. During hot deformation, aluminum alloy undergoes different cycles
of heating, holding, deformation and cooling [ 2]. These physical processes sig-
niﬁcantly change the microstructure of the material and then affect the properties of
the ﬁnal products. In order to re ﬁne the microstructure and improve the mechanical
properties, it is very important to control recrystallization volume fraction of the
material [ 3].
Dynamic recrystallization behavior of aluminum alloy has been extensively
studied. Han et al. [ 4] found that the increase of recrystallization fraction leads to
lower strength and fracture toughness. Kannan and Raja [ 5] reported stress corro-
sion resistance of aluminum alloy can be improved by inhibiting recrystallization.
Recrystallization has an adverse effect on the mechanical properties, occurrence of
recrystallization can decrease strength, corrosion resistance and toughness [ 6].
The prediction and control of the microstructure is one of the most important
problem in the modern aluminum industry [ 7]. With the fast development of
computer and mathematical modeling, we can conduct microstructure modeling on
mesoscale by different models such as CA method [ 8], Monte Carlo (MC) method
[9] and Phase Field (PF) method [ 10] etc. CA method has become an important
technique for predicting the evolution of microstructures. CA model can output the
average grain size, the volume fraction of recrystallization and stress-strain curve
etc. In addition, the morphology and distribution of the hot deformation
microstructure can be obtained. CA method has been used to simulate dynamic
recrystallization, static recrystallization and phase transformation successfully [ 11].
The hot deformation behavior of 7085 aluminum alloy was studied though the
Gleeble experiments. A CA model is developed to simulate the dynamic recrys-
tallization during hot compression. The CA model is validated by the experimental
data, good agreement is found between the simulated and the experimental results.
96 J. Zhang et al.

Model Description and Experimental Details
Cellular automata are algorithms that simulate transformation of complex systems
[12]. The transformation rules determine the state variable of a cell as a nonlinear
function of the state variable of the cell itself and the state variable of the neigh-
bouring sites. The automata of dynamic transformation occur though the application
of transformation rules. For the purpose of simulating the DRX behavior of 7085
aluminum alloy, the simulation area is subdivided by an array of cells of 912 /C2 912
sites, they are made up of a regular lattice, the whole lattice corresponds to a real
domain of 912 lm /C2 912 lm.

dislocations are produced by work hardening and disappeared by dynamic
recrystallization. To simulate the deformation behavior and microstructure evolu-
tion of 7085 aluminum alloy, the Kocks-Mecking model has been used [ 13]:

growth of recrystallized grain. The simulation of the nucleation process is based on
a large number of experimental observation during the initial recrystallization
process. The nucleation occurs mainly at grain boundaries. Many ﬁne grain of
equiaxed grains will appear at the grain boundary.

Model of Growth
After the emergence of the new equiaxed grains, the grain boundary moves out-
ward, The new grain gradually grew up and the old grain gradually disappeared, the
dislocation density gradually decreases in the process of nucleation and growth.

energy produced by the deformation, the rate of recrystallized grain growth v can be

specimen and the press indenters, graphite was used as a lubricant in the isothermal
compression test. The scheme of Gleeble tests is shown in Fig. 1, it is divided into

Results and Discussion
The stress-strain curve of 7085 aluminum alloy obtained by hot compressive tests in
shown in Fig. 3. The true stress-strain curve for DRX behavior can be divided into
three stage: working-hardening stage, dynamic softening stage and steady state
stage. The ﬂow stress increases signi ﬁcantly to peak value caused by work hard-
ening, and decreases attributed to the occurrence of dynamic recrystallization
subsequently. The stress presents a steady state stage with the further increasing
strain, the stress does not change violently with the change of strain. Which indi-
cates the synergetic role of working hardening and dynamic softening.
The parameters used in this article are shown in Table 2.
Microstructural simulation of 7085 aluminum alloy was implemented using a
large number Gleeble experimental parameters. To test the reasonableness of the
model, The simulation results and the EBSD experimental results are compared and
analyzed. Figure 4 shows the simulated microstructures and the experimental
results. The different colors displays the different grain, the size and morphology of
the grain between simulated microstructures and the experimental results are very
similar.

Figure 6 show the simulation results of 7085 aluminum alloy. The grain
boundaries become slender, a large amount of deformation occurs in the grain. The
nucleation of recrystallization mostly appearances at high angle grain boundaries, a
lot of ﬁne grain of equiaxed grains can be seen. The reason is that the energy is high
at the grain boundary, recrystallization is easy to occur.
Figure 7 shows the process of the dynamic recrystallization with the deformation
increase: the original grain suffer from plastic deformation and is elongated. During
this period, the rapid increase of dislocation density, especially the disharmony
between two adjacent grains, there will be a lot of dislocation at the grain boundary,
subgrain boundaries is made up of dislocation, a large number of recrystallized
grains will be produced at the old grain boundary. Eventually, these grains grow up
slowly and the deformed coarse grain are replaced by ﬁne equiaxed grains.
Figure 7 shows the microstructures of 7085 aluminum alloy. As the strain
increases, the coarse grain is elongated. It can be observed that a great deal of
recrystallized grains at the grain boundary. Moreover, there are some equiaxed
grains appeared at triangle grain boundary, these grains grow up gradually in the
follow-up process.

## Page 117

Conclusions
The microstructure evolution of the 7085 aluminum alloy was researched by
simulations and experiments. The simulation results can accurately re ﬂect the actual
process of dynamic recrystallization.
1. The ﬁne equiaxed grains start to appear at the grain boundaries when suffer-
ing from plastic deformation, recrystallization happened easily where the dis-
location density is very high. The dislocation density plays prominent part in
DRX of 7085 aluminum alloy.
2. The strain have a major impact on the recrystallization volume percentage and
the average grain size during DRX. When the deformation temperature and the
strain rate are determined, the recrystallization volume percentage increases
while the mean grain radius decreases slowly with the deformation increase. The
higher the temperature, the smaller the average grain size, because the higher the
temperature, the higher the activity of dislocation, which can provide more
energy for recrystallization nucleation and growth.

Aging Time on the Microstructure
and Mechanical Properties of A356
Alloy by Semi-solid Processing
Peng Qi, Bolong Li, Wenjian Lv, Shasha Dong, Tongbo Wang,
Ning Li and Zuoren Nie
Abstract An investigation was carried out to study the effects of aging time on the
microstructure and mechanical properties of A356 alloy by semi-solid processing.
The alloy was subjected to solution treatment for 4 h at 540 °C, arti ﬁcial ageing
was carried out at temperature (170 °C) and different time (0 –24 h). The results
revealed that the needle-shaped eutectic Si phase in as-cast ingot was transformed to
globular shape compared with that by solution treatment. Meanwhile the Chinese
script p-Fe(AlMgSiFe) phase was transformed to smaller and uniformly distributed
b-Fe(AlFeSi) phase, the elongation increased obviously. With the increasing of
aging time, the elongation decreased, and the ultimate tensile strength increased.
When the aging time was 4 h, the alloy achieved the optimal mechanical properties.
The micro-hardness was 121HV, ultimate tensile strength was 329 MPa, and the
elongation was 15%. From the fracture morphology, the fracture for alloy aging for
4 h showed more dimples. With the increasing of aging time, the ultimate tensile
strength and the elongation decreased.

Introduction
A356 casting alloy is widely used in the auto-motive industry because of the good
speciﬁc mechanical properties [ 1]. Meanwhile semisolid metal processing (SSM) is
widely used in Al –Si alloys due to the spherical primary a-Al phase particles
structure and good mechanical properties [ 2, 3].
A356 alloy is a heat treatable casting alloy which can be strengthened by pre-
cipitation of Mg
2Si after T6 treatment [ 4]. Solution treatment at a relatively high
temperature to dissolve Mg-rich particles formed during solidi ﬁcation to achieve a
high and homogeneous concentration of the alloying elements in solid solution [ 5].
The precipitation of Mg 2Si during aging heat treatment is affected strongly by
morphology and size of eutectic silicon in the as-cast condition and aging heat
treatment time. Thus the proper aging process is very important and necessary for
the se alloys to obtain superior mechanical properties.
In this work, the semi-solid slurry of A356 alloy is subjected to solution treat-
ment for 4 h at 540 °C, arti ﬁcial ageing was carried out at temperature (170 °C) and
different timing (0 –24 h). The effects of aging time on the microstructures, tensile
properties and fracture morphology were studied in detail.
Materials and Experimental Procedures
In this study, the chemical composition (wt%) of A356 alloy is shown in Table 1.
The liquidus temperature and solidus temperature of this alloy were determined by
differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) method, as shown in Fig. 1, and they were
618 and 553 °C, respectively.
The raw materials were commercial pure aluminum, pure magnesium and
Al–20Si and Al –50Cu master alloys. The preheated pure aluminum, Al –20Si and
Al–50Cu master alloys were placed inside the crucible. When the temperature of
molten was 700 °C, the pure magnesium was added. After 5 min, the melt was
degassed with 2 wt% C
2Cl6 and the slag was skimmed. After that, the pouring
temperature of the metal was 630 °C, and it was poured into a stainless steel
container preheated to 600 °C. Then the stainless steel container was immediately
transferred to electromagnetic stirrer. The stirrer was started at frequencies of 10 Hz

a holding furnace. It was held about 5 min at temperature of 585 °C. Then the
container was quenched for maintaining the microstructure. Finally, the semi-solid
A356 alloy slurry was obtained. The ingot was taken out from the container when
the melt was changed into solid ingot.
The ingots were cut into square samples (10 mm /C210 mm /C25 mm) from the
bottom edge of the samples for aging treatment. The samples were solution treated
at 540 °C for 4 h, followed by quenching in cold water. The specimens were
immediately arti ﬁcially aged at 170 °C for different periods of time varying from 0
to 24 h. After ageing, the samples were taken out of the furnace at different time
intervals and air cooled to room temperature.
After polishing, the surface of the sample was etched with a solution of 10 vol%
concentrated HF in 90 vol% H 2O for microstructural studies, and the holding time
was about 15 s. The microstructure of the as-cast and the heat treated specimens
were examined using optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron microscopy
(SEM).
The Vickers ’s hardness measurements were carried out using a Viclcer ’s hard-
ness tester operated at a load of 10 kgf. The hardness values reported are an average
of at least nine symmetrical indentations. Tensile specimens were prepared
according to the GB/T228.1-2010 standard, as shown in Fig. 2. Elongation and
tensile strength were tested on the 810MTS (Material Test System) tester with a
stretching rate of 2 mm/min, and each tensile test data were tested in three times.
The fractures of tensile specimens at different aging time were observed under the
scanning electron microscopy (SEM).

Figure 6 shows the statistics of mechanical properties with different aging time.
From the Fig. 6a, hardness of ingot by solution treatment for 4 h at 540 °C without
aging treatment increases from 78HV to 84HV, in compared with the as-cast
samples. Meanwhile, with the increasing of aging time, the hardness increases. The
optimal value of hardness was 121HV when the aging time was 4 h. With the
increasing of aging time continuously, the value of hardness decreased, and then
increased again reaching the second peak (at 17 h). At the ﬁnal stage of aging, the
hardness of the alloy decreases as a result of over-aging. As can be seen, double
aging peaks are present in the age-hardening curve of semi-solid A356 alloy. It has
been reported [ 10] that the age-hardening behavior is related to the precipitation
sequence of alloys, the ﬁrst aging peak is the result from the high-density GP zone
(especially GP II zones), while the second one is from metastable phases.
Figure 6b shows the tensile strength of ingot treated by different aging time. The
ultimate tensile strength of ingot by solution treatment for 4 h at 540 °C without
aging treatment was increased from 212 to 250 MPa, in compared with the samples
without heat treatment. Meanwhile, the value of elongation was increased from 6.7
to 18.8%, it was increased about 180%. After solution treatment, the morphology of
eutectic silicon particles and p-Fe(AlMgSiFe) phase in the A356 alloy fabricated by
semi-solid process changes from long, coarse plate-like to ﬁne spherical or rod-like.
It is seen that ﬁner and more spherical eutectic silicon particles and p-Fe
(AlMgSiFe) phase in heat treated samples improve the elongation signi ﬁcantly.
With the increasing of aging time, the ultimate tensile increases, but the elon-
gation decreases. The optimal value of ultimate tensile strength was 329 MPa when
the aging time was 4 h, and the value of elongation was 15.3%. It is well accepted
that precipitates are mainly responsible for strengthening of the alloys after arti ﬁcial
aging. As the increasing of aging time, the ultimate tensile strength was decreased,
the value of elongation was decreased obviously. A subsequent decrease of the
ultimate tensile strength and elongation, with increasing aging time can be asso-
ciated with the transformation of the coherent b″ phase into the semi-coherent b′
phase [ 6].

The results of mechanical properties were consistent with the analysis of

Figure 7 shows the fracture morphologies of tensile samples at different aging
time. As shown in Fig. 7a, the tensile fracture morphology without heat treatment
included shrinkage hole, tearing rage and cleavage plane mainly. The fracture
modes of tensile specimen were complex, and contained internal defect fracture,
cleavage fracture and quasi cleavage fracture.
However, the fracture morphologies by solution treatment for 4 h at 540 °C
without aging treatment was mainly composed of dimple. The fracture modes
belong to the mixture of ductile fracture. Meanwhile, the fracture of ingot by
solution treatment for 4 h at 540 °C and aging treatment for 24 h at 170 °C, there
existed cleavage plane. According to the comparison, there was corresponding
relationship between the fracture morphologies and the elongation of the ingot.
Conclusions
1. The needle-shaped eutectic Si phase in as-cast A356 alloys fabricated by
semi-solid process was transformed to globular shape after solution treatment.
The elongation increased from 6.7 to 18.8% due to the change of eutectic Si.
2. The optimal value of ultimate tensile strength was 329 MPa, the elongation was
15.3% with the solution treatment for 4 h at 540 °C and aging treatment for 4 h
at 170 °C.

as-cast alloy. Cu, Fe and Mn elements have obvious segregation at grain bound-

intracrystal. The undissolved phases in the grain boundaries are mainly Al

treatment system is 525 °C /C2 24 h. And the optimal double-stage homogenization

Introduction
Al–Li alloys are widely used in aviation and aerospace industries because of their
low density, high elastic modulus, high strength and high damage resistance [ 1–5].
It is considered to be one of the most ideal lightweight high-strength structural
materials for the aerospace industry in twenty- ﬁrst Century. Al –Cu–Li alloy has
been listed as an important development direction of aerospace structural materials
in western countries.
2297 Al–Li alloy, belongs to one of the third generation of Al –Li alloy, which is
invented on basis of the 2197 alloy by reducing the content of lithium and adjusting
other alloy elements, is used in aircraft fuselage and other parts instead of 2124
aluminum alloy, improved the corrosion resistance and comprehensive perfor-
mance. The plane fuselage changed less frequently and reduced the repair time.
However, there is serious interdendritic segregation in the as cast 2297 Al –Li alloy,
causing a large number of dif ﬁculties in the production of hot rolled 2297 plates.
Studies showed that the interdendritic segregation seriously deteriorates the prop-
erties of Al –Cu–Li alloys [ 6–9]. The result of homogenization greatly in ﬂuenced
the thermal processing, microstructures and mechanical properties of Al –Cu–Li
alloy. Despite details studies of homogenizing treatments in various kinds of
aluminum alloy, less attention was focus on the 2297 alloy. The aim of the present
study is to investigate the features of the microstructure evolution during homog-
enization with the help of DSC, OM, SEM and EDS analysis. Homogenization
kinetic analysis derived binding experiments. And get the best homogenization
treatment of 2297 alloy.
Experimental
The chemical composition of 2297 Al –Li alloy consisted of Cu 2.42, Li 1.49,
Mn 0.28, Mg 0.032, Ti 0.026, Zr 0.092, Si 0.015, and Al (mass fraction, %).
Single-stage homogenization treatment system is 505 –545 °C for 24 h, interval
10 °C. Double-stage homogenization treatment system is 460 °C for 20 h and

525 °C for 24 h. Differential thermal analysis was carried out by SDT-Q600 dif-
ferential thermal analyzer. Take Al 2O3 as the reference standard, the temperature
was increased from 25 to 600 °C, and heating rate was 10 °C/min. The sample is
milled by 600# ! 1000# ! 1500# ! 2000# ! 5000#, and then polished by
2.5# and 1.0# diamond polishing paste. After drying, Keller reagent (1 mL, HF,
1.5 mL, HCL, 2.5 mL, HNO
3 and 95 mL) is used to ﬁnish the corrosion.
Then ZEISS, AXIOVERT-200MAT optical microscope were used for metallo-
graphic analysis. The microstructure of the alloy in different states was observed by
JEOL JSM-7001F scanning electron microscope. The composition, quantity and
distribution of second phases of the alloy were analyzed by EDS.
Results and Discussion
As-cast Microstructure Analysis As shown in Fig. 1, as-cast microstructure and
SEM analysis of 2297 alloy. It can be seen that the alloy grain interface is a cellular
interface between plane and dendritic, and there are a large number of
non-equilibrium eutectic phase and Fe and Mn containing phase at grain boundary
(Fig. 1b, c). According to solidi ﬁcation theory [ 10], the shape of the alloy crystal is
determined by its inherent properties and the temperature ﬁeld near the solid/liquid
interface in the crystallization process. Most of the solid-liquid interface of an alloy
(rough type solid –liquid interface structure parameter a /C20 2). Under the positive
temperature gradient, the grain interface is easy to form a plane perpendicular to the
direction of heat dissipation. However, it is easy to form dendritic grain under
negative temperature gradient. As shown in Fig. 1a, its cellular interface is a
transition from planar to dendritic interface. When the alloy contains impurity
elements such as Fe and Mn, the cellular interface will be generated at the positive
temperature gradient, and the groove of the cellular interface provides the condi-
tions for the enrichment of elements such as Cu, Fe and Mn. Under SEM obser-
vation, as shown in Fig. 1d, e, it can be seen that the non-equilibrium eutectic
microstructure at the grain boundary groove shows gray or white like-bone struc-
ture. As shown in Fig. 1d, e, like-bone organization be analyzed by EDS, as shown
in Table 1. The results showed that A and B (gray organization) were contain Fe
and Mn phase, the content of Fe was as high as 10.85 and 12.05%, respectively,
which can’t be dissolved into the alloy foundation. EDS analysis results of C and D
(white organization) showed that the atomic ratio were close to Al
2Cu phase.
The mapping analysis of the as-cast alloy is shown in Fig. 2. It can be seen that
obvious segregation exists at grain boundaries about Cu, Fe and Mn elements.
Among them, the enrichment of Cu elements is the most serious. The degree of
elements enrichment gradually decreased from grain boundary to crystal. But the
distribution of other elements is relatively uniform, which is consistent with EDS
analysis. That is, the groove of cellular interface provides the conditions for
enrichment of Cu, Fe, Mn and other elements. Grain boundary is also a favorable

Single-Stage Homogenization Treatment Figure 3 shows the DSC curve as-cast
and homogenized of the 2297 alloy. From the as-cast DSC curve, it can be seen that
the alloy exhibits an obvious endothermic peak at 529 and 537 °C. 529 °C is the
initial melting temperature of low melting point eutectic phase. Homogenization
temperature should be lower than 529 °C. Ensure the eutectic structure does not

## Page 133

melt. Solute atoms diffuse suf ﬁciently to the alloy matrix. Finally, the segregation
and composition of dendrites are eliminated [ 12]. Homogenization temperature was
extended to 545 °C. Homogenization temperature of the alloy is 505 –545 °C for
24 h, the interval is 10 °C. As shown in Fig. 3, two endothermic peak have dis-
appeared when the alloy were homogenized at 529 and 537 °C. This indicates that
the eutectic phase at low melting point has been dissolved to the alloy matrix.
Figure 4 is the metallographic structure of the 2297 alloy after homogenizing
treatment for 24 h at different temperatures. As shown in Fig. 4a, when the temper-
ature is low, there is still a lot of non-equilibrium eutectic structure at the alloy grain
boundary after homogenized at 505 °C for 24 h. Macro-organization still has the sign
of dendrite or cellular interface, and the grain boundaries are thick and curved. When
the temperature increases to 515 °C, as shown in Fig. 4b, dendrite edge of the alloy is
slightly relieved, but it still exists. Grain boundary is graduallyﬂattened and reﬁned as
the temperature increases to 525 °C, as shown in Fig. 4c. Dendrite morphology was
eliminated. Most of the residual phases at the grain boundaries have been dissolved.
When the temperature continues increases to 535 °C (over 529 °C), the grain
boundaries of the alloy is more straight and re ﬁned. The grain size change is not
obvious, but there is overheating risk. When the temperature increases to 545 °C, as
shown in Fig. 4e, obvious triangular grain boundaries and remelting balls appear in
the alloy. Most of the grain boundaries begin to melt, i.e., there is a severe over
burning organization. Comprehensive consideration, 525 °C for 24 h is a suitable
single-stage homogenization treatment system.
Double-Stage Homogenization Treatment In double-stage homogenization
system, Robson and Prangnell [ 13] predicts by coupling model that the temperature
of the ﬁrst stage should be 0.88 times of the single-stage homogenization tem-
perature. The precipitated Al
3Zr particles more disperse distribution resulted from
J. D. Robson ’s model. At the same time, the width of no Al 3Zr precipitation band is
narrow. Therefore, the ﬁrst-stage homogenization temperature is set to 460 °C.

Conclusions
In the present study, microstructure evolution of 2297 Al –Li alloy during
homogenization process are investigated by OM, SEM, EDS and DSC analysis.
And the corresponding homogenization kinetic analysis is studied. The following
conclusions can be obtained:
1. 2297 alloy has serious dendrite segregation in the as-cast structure. Cu, Fe and
Mn elements have obvious segregation at grain boundaries, and the degree of
enrichment decreases gradually from grain boundary to intracrystal. The
undissolved phase at grain boundary is mainly Al
2Cu phase and Fe and Mn
containing phases.
2. Suitable single-stage homogenization treatment system is 525 °C /C2 24 h. There
is a risk of over burning of the alloy when the temperature is above 535 °C.
Severe over-burn tissue occurs in grain boundaries when the temperature is
above 545 °C.
Fig. 7 Curves of

3. Suitable double-stage homogenization system is 460 °C /C2 20 h + 525 °C /C2 24 h.
After double-stage homogenization treatment, the grain boundary non-
equilibrium eutectic phase is fully dissolved. And the segregation of dendrite is
eliminated. But there is not dissolved Fe and Mn containing phase at grain
boundaries. The double-stage homogenization treatment system is consistent with
the results of kinetic analysis.

The Microstructure Evolution
of Al –Mg–Si–Mn–Er–Zr Alloy
During Homogenization
Xiang Zhang, Hui Huang, Xiaoli Liu, Yifei Liu, Hongbo Wang,
Shengping Wen, Kunyuan Gao and Xiaolan Wu
Abstract The formation of non-equilibrium intermetallic phases during solidi ﬁ-
cation signiﬁcantly deteriorates the mechanical properties of Al –Mg–Si–Mn–Zr–Er
alloy, but homogenization heat treatment can effectively reduce these residual
phases. Therefore, it is necessary to study the evolution of these non-equilibrium
intermetallic phases during different homogenization treatment. In this study, the
methods we used are OM, SEM in combination with EDS, XRD and TEM. The
results showed that non-equilibrium intermetallic phases between grains are mainly
Al
0.5Fe3Si0.5,A l 0.7Fe3Si0.3 and Al 5Mn12Si7. After homogenization, the main
residual phase is Al 5Mn12Si7. Compared with single homogenization, two-stage
homogenization can effectively reduce the homogenization time and is good for the
precipitation of ﬁned Al
3(Er, Zr) particles.

Introduction
Al–Mg–Si–Mn alloy is strengthened by heat treatment, with medium strength, good
corrosion resistance, weldability and good processing performance [ 1–4], it can be
processed into bars, plates, pipes and pro ﬁles, widely used in construction, auto-
motive, aircraft, high-speed trains etc. The heat treatment process of Al –Mg–Si–Mn
alloy is mainly composed of three parts: homogenization treatment, solid solution
treatment and aging treatment. The homogenization heat treatment directly affects
the quality of subsequent machining and subsequent heat treatment effect.
Homogenization heat treatment is an important process before extrusion or
rolling of Al –Mg–Si–Mn alloy. First, the solidi ﬁcation of the alloy is
non-equilibrium solidi ﬁcation. After alloy solidi ﬁcation, the composition is not
uniform, and the segregation of intragranular component is very serious. At the
same time, there are a large number of dendritic phases between the grains, which
called b-AlFeSi [ 5–7]. These dendrite or trip-shaped b-AlFeSi phases are hard and
brittle and may become stress concentration source for the alloy, resulting in the
decrease of the mechanical properties and ductility of the alloy [ 8, 9]. Second,
Mn-containing dispersoid particles are precipitated during the homogenization,
these particles have high density and high thermal stability, which are nucleus of
nucleation of strengthening phase [ 10, 11]. During homogenization treatment, the
dendritic b-AlFeSi phases transform to ﬁne a-Al(FeMn)Si [ 12] phases, which is
more easier for hot rolling or hot extrusion, because its morphology is less likely to
cause stress concentration and more conducive to deformation than b-AlFeSi [ 13].
In addition, the homogenization process can make a large number of Mg
2Si par-
ticles dissolve into the matrix, so that the distribution of atoms in the matrix is more
homogeneous.
In recent years, many scholars [ 14, 15] in the study of micro alloying found that
trace elements in the alloy can not only play the role of ﬁne grains, and may affect
the aging precipitation of the main strengthening phase. Add trace amounts of Zr
and Er to the alloy is of great concern. Some studies [ 16, 17] have shown that after
adding trace Er and Zr, the alloy can form Al
3(Er, Zr) particles, which directly
inﬂuences thermal and mechanical properties of the alloy after heat treatment. In the
paper, we mainly study the effects of different homogenization treatment on the
microstructure morphology of the Al –Mg–Si–Mn–Zr–Er alloy. As a basis for
further research.
Experimental
The chemical composition (wt%) of the Al –Mg–Si–Mn–Zr–Er alloy used in this
research is shown in Table 1. Specimens with dimensions of 12 mm /C212 mm /C2
7 mm were used for homogenization treatments. Six types of homogenization con-
ditions were conducted below: 565 °C/6 h, 565 °C/10 h, 565 °C/16 h, 565 °C/24 h,
130 X. Zhang et al.

565 °C/48 h, 330 °C/10 h + 565 °C/10 h. The cooling method of the sample after
homogenization treatment is air cooling.
After homogenization treatment, the sample was grind and polished, and then the
corrosion was carried out with Keller reagent, and the metallographic observation
was performed with Olympus BX51M metallographic microscope. Statistical of the
area fraction of the intergranular residual phases was measured using the image
analysis software Image-pro Plus 5.0. The morphology and EDS of the residual
phase was examined on SU8020 scanning electron microscopy. The XRD phase
analysis of homogenized samples was carried out by using SHIMADZU XRD-7000.
The experiment using JEOL2100 transmission electron microscope to observe
micrographs of the precipitates in the samples, the working voltage of TEM is
200 kV. First, the sample to be tested mechanically thinned to about 80 lm, then
punched into discs with a diameter of 3 mm. Next, the samples were twin-jet pol-
ishing in the solution of 30% HNO
3 in methanol at −25 to −30°C and 20 V.
Results and Discussion
Microstructure Characteristics of As-Cast Alloy Figure 1 is the microstructure
of the as-cast Al –Mg–Si–Mn–Zr–Er alloy, Fig. 1a for the casting optical
microstructure, it can be seen that the alloy casting internal segregation is very
serious, the internal composition of the grain is not uniform. There are also a large
number of dendrite or trip-shaped b-AlFeSi phases which formed during
non-equilibrium solidi ﬁcation process, we can see that this dendrites and
strip-shaped residual phases along the grain boundary distribution, the interface
between the three grains especially gathered. Around these residual phases, there
are a few disc-shaped particles, which are segregation of related elements.
Figure 1b is a secondary electron scanning image of the cast alloy. It can be seen
that there are gray dendrite phase and white particles in the casting alloy. The EDS
analyses show the chemical composition of them as Table 2. As we can see, the
gray dendritic residual phases mainly composed of Al, Si, Mn, Fe, and the white
particles mainly composed of Al, Mg, Si, Er.
Figure 2 shows Backscattered electron (BSE) microstructure and the corre-
sponding element distribution in the as-cast Al –Mg–Si–Mn–Zr–Er alloy. It can be
seen from the images that the residual phases are mainly distributed between the
grains, the morphology of residual phase in the intergranular phase is dendritic and
elongated. In addition, there are some disc-shaped residual phase in the grains, and
these disc-shaped residual phases mainly consist of Al, Mg, Si and Er.

homogenization.
Conclusions
In the present research, the microstructural evolution of a new type Al –Mg–Si–Mn–
Er–Zr alloy during homogenization was investigated. The results show that:
1. With further prolonging of homogenization time, the non-equilibrium inter-
metallic phases accumulated at grain boundary partially dissolved into the
matrix and signi ﬁcantly reduced.
2. In the Al –Mg–Si–Mn–Er–Zr alloy, the residual phases in the intergranular are
mainly Al
0.5Fe3Si0.5,A l 0.7Fe3Si0.3 and Al 5Mn12Si7. During homogenization,
Mn elements in the matrix will replace some Fe in the intergranular AlFeSi
phase. After homogenization, the main residual phase is Al
5Mn12Si7.
3. The optimum homogenization process is 300 °C/10 h + 565 °C/6 h, which is
beneﬁcial for the precipitation of Al 3(Er, Zr).

Effect of Intermediate Annealing
Temperature and Aging
on the Mechanical Properties
and Conductivity of Al –0.2Mg–0.35Si–
0.3Ce Wire Rod
Yuna Wu, Hengcheng Liao and Jianfeng Zhang
Abstract The present study investigated the effect of intermediate annealing
temperatures on the microstructure, mechanical properties and conductivity of Al –
0.2Mg–0.35Si–0.3Ce wire rod, which experienced hot extrusion (named as E), cold
drawing (named as D), annealing (named as A) and cold drawing, i.e. EDAD. And
four intermediate annealing temperatures (150, 200, 250, 300 °C) were carried out
for investigation. Microstructure observation shows that no recrystallization occurs
in the wire rod when annealed at 150 and 200 °C. However, it occurs when the
annealing temperature reaches 250 °C. Tensile tests indicate that the ultimate ten-
sile strength (UTS) of the as-EDAD samples ﬁrstly increases to a maximum value
of 218 Mpa when the annealing temperature increased to 150 °C, and then
decreases dramatically with the temperature continuously increasing. However, the
elongation and conductivity of the as-EDAD samples just go oppositely. The
conductivity of the sample annealed at 300 °C reaches 57.1%IACS, which is about
3.3%IACS higher than that of the sample without annealing. The effect of aging
(190 °C for 20 h) on the mechanical properties and conductivity of as-EDAD
samples was also investigated. Results show that the variation trend of UTS,
elongation and conductivity of the EDAD-aging samples is similar to that without
aging. The UTS decreases after aging, however, elongation and conductivity both
increase.

Introduction
Al–Mg–Si alloys are widely used in transmission lines due to their light weight,
good corrosion resistant, excellent strength and high conductivity [ 1–3]. Addition
of Ce can remarkably improve the ﬂuidity, castability and electrical conductivity of
Al–Mg–Si alloys [ 4, 5]. Al –Mg–Si–Ce alloy has become a newly developed
conductive alloy that has excellent combination of castability, strength, and con-
ductivity in shape casting [ 6–8]. It has good potential to be a candidate for overhead
wires.
Hot extrusion and cold drawing are usually carried out to prepare the wire rods
[9, 10]. Work hardening is the most important negative factor that impedes the deep
deformation of aluminum alloy, due to the existence of high-intensity dislocations.
Several strategies have been proposed to solve this issue. Liu et al. [ 11] developed a
modiﬁed thermo-mechanical process by adjusting the sequence of solution, aging
and deformation to improve both the electrical conductivity and strength in Al –Mg–
Si–(Cu) alloy. Yoshida et al. [ 12] used “alternate drawing ” to produce aluminum
wires by alternating the drawing direction of every 1 pass, which can give higher
ductility, however, lower tensile strength. Mirzaei et al. [ 13] investigated the effect
of aging on the dislocation density of 2024 Al alloy caused by large strain rolling.
Besides, Proper intermediate annealing also can eliminate stress of aluminum wire
effectively and thus improve the ductility and processability. However, almost no
systematic study has been carried out on the effect of heat treatment on Al –Mg–Si–
Ce wire rod. The present study investigated the effect of intermediate annealing and
aging on the mechanical properties and conductivity of Al –0.2 Mg –0.35Si–0.3Ce
wire rod. Four annealing temperatures were studied.
Experimental Procedure
The experimental alloy with a nominal composition of Al –0.2 wt%Mg –0.35 wt%
Si–0.3 wt%Ce was prepared in a melting/vacuum furnace, using commercial purity
aluminum ingot, Al –12.5 wt%Si and Al –12.18 wt%Ce master alloys, and mag-
nesium ingot (commercial purity, 99.8 wt%Mg). The melt was cast in a cylinder
iron mold with an inner diameter of 60 mm and a plate-like iron mold with a cavity
of 200 mm /C2 100 mm /C2 20 mm. After homogenized at 560 °C for 6 h, the
cylinder billets were immediately water-quenched and then kept in fridge. The
chemical composition of the studied alloy was measured by an ARL-3460 spec-
trum, which contains 0.36 wt%Si, 0.21 wt%Mg, 0.10 wt%Fe, balanced with Al.
The addition level of Ce is 0.3 wt%.
The cylinder billets were extruded at 510 °C with an extrusion ratio of 36. After
extrusion, the formed rods were water-quenched at once, the diameter of which is
10 mm. The drawing was carried out at room temperature and the passes were as
follows: 10 mm-9 mm-8 mm-7 mm-6 mm-5.5 mm-5 mm-4.5 mm-4 mm-3.6 mm-
140 Y. Wu et al.

## Page 152

3.4 mm-3.2 mm-3 mm. When the rod was drawn to 4.5 mm, intermediate
annealing was carried out at 150, 200, 250, 300 °C for an hour respectively. The
rod was drawn to 3 mm ﬁnally after being cooled to the room temperature. The
hot-extruded, cold-drawn, intermediate-annealing samples were named as E, D, A
respectively. So the ﬁnally wire rod is named as EDAD sample.
Tensile test was carried out on a CMT5105 electronic universal testing machine
at a constant crosshead speed of 2.0 mm/min. The conductivity test was examined
by QJ36 type one-twinned brachial electric bridges, and the measured electrical
resistance was converted to conductivity according to International Annealed
Copper Standard by the conversion formula:
%IACS ¼ 0:017241 /C2 l
R /C2 s /C2 100% ð1Þ
where %IACS is the conductivity (International Annealed Copper Standard); l is
the length of samples; R is the electrical resistance of the sample measured by
twinned bridges; s represents the cross section area of samples. As a reference, the
mechanical properties and conductivity of samples without intermediate annealing
were also evaluated. All data are an average of at least three samples.
Optical microscope (OLYMPUS BX-60M) with polarized light was used to
examine the microstructure.
Results and Discussion
Figure 1 shows the optical microstructure of Al –0.2Mg–0.35Si–0.3Ce wire rod
with and without intermediate annealing. A sample annealed at 300 °C (as shown in
Fig. 1b) was compared to another sample without annealing (as shown in Fig. 1a).
It indicates that the coarse second phases are rather stable, and no obvious change

Before aging, when annealed at 150 °C, the UTS of the sample is the highest. It
is because at this processing temperature, there will be a number of b″ strength-
ening phases in the matrix, as reported by Ding et al. [ 14]. Though recovery may
also happened, which will soften the matrix. However, the strengthening effect by
b″ will stronger. So the UTS at this annealing temperature is the highest. When the
annealing temperature increased to 200 °C, the soften effect from recovery will be
enhanced and the strengthening effect from precipitation of b″ phases will be
weakened. So the UTS decreased and the elongation increased. When the annealing
temperature increased to 250 °C, apparent recrystallization occurs, which will
soften the matrix dramatically, as can be seen from Fig. 2d. And at this processing
temperature, the b″ strengthening phase will grow up and turn into b′ or Mg 2Si
phase. So the UTS decreases signi ﬁcantly and the elongation increases more.
After aging at 190 °C for 20 h, the UTS decreases nearly 20% respectively
compared to that before aging, as can be seen in Fig. 3a. It is mainly related to the
soften effect from recovery.

annealing temperature increases to 300 °C. After aging at 190 °C for 20 h, the

During annealing processing, recovery and recrystallization occur, which will
decrease the high dislocation intensity and lattice distortion formed during drawing
and the reinforcing phases will also decreases. Besides, with the grains grow up,
grain boundaries (GBs) decreases. The reduction of these defects (dislocations,
point defects, reinforcing phases, or GBs) will decrease the scattering of conducting
electrons at these defects [ 15]. So with the increasing of annealing temperature, the
electron conductivity increases.
Conclusions
(1) Intermediate annealing has a signi ﬁcant effect on the tensile strength and
conductivity of Al –0.2Mg–0.35Si–0.3Ce wire rod.
(2) When annealing at relatively low temperature ( /C20 200 °C), no recrystallization
occurs in the wire rod, and a higher UTS and lower conductivity were obtained.
The highest UTS of Al –0.2Mg–0.35Si–0.3Ce wire rod reaches about 218 MPa
when annealed at 150 °C.
(3) When the annealing temperature is 250 °C, obvious recrystallization occurs and
the UTS of the wire rod greatly decreases, while the conductivity increases. The
highest conductivity is 57.1%IACS when annealed at 300 °C.

Precipitate
Introduction
As we all know, Al –Zn–Mg–Cu (7xxx) alloys possess a broad usage in the aircraft
and military ﬁelds, due to the high strength/density ratio. Aluminum alloy has a low
density and its high strength is decided by ﬁne precipitates with nanoscale size,
which are formed in ageing treatment and provide the majority for strengthening
effect [1–3]. Due to different service condition and property requirement, a series of
ageing tempers have been developed and solidi ﬁed for the Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloys
during the past decades, such as T6, T7X and RRA treatments. Based on usage
requirement, different ageing treatment regulate alloys with performance diversity.
The T6 peak-aged Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloy has the highest mechanical strength, but
low resistance to stress corrosion cracking [ 4–6]. At two-step over-aged T7X
tempers, the stress corrosion susceptibility is improved but with a 10 –20% penalty
for strength level if we set T6 temper as the basis [ 7]. For the sake of improving the
combination property, the three-step RRA heat treatment is proposed which has a
corrosion resistance as good as that of the T7X tempers, while maintaining a
strength levels near to that at T6 temper [ 8, 9].
During the past decades, researchers have con ﬁrmed that microstructures of ﬁnal
products are controlled by ageing treatments, which matrix precipitate size and
distribution, continuous and discontinuous distribution of grain boundary precipi-
tate as well as the width of precipitate free zone [ 10–12]. Accordingly, products
with various performance characteristics are obtained and applied in different parts
of aircraft and weapons. Hence, it is quite necessary to quantize nanoscale pre-
cipitates and this will be helpful to relate them with service performance. In the past
decades, researchers have focused on the relationship between ageing treatments
and overall performance [ 13–16]. In other words, service requirements are the main
factor for product application and analysis on microstructures is not deep enough.
As a conventional approach on microstructure observation in Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloy,
148 K. Wen et al.

## Page 159

TEM combined with HRTEM can also be used to quantitatively analyze nanoscale
precipitate characteristics with some analysis tools [ 17–19]. Besides, traditional Al –
Zn–Mg–Cu (7xxx) alloys for aerospace application possess a zinc content of about
5.0–8.0 wt% and researches on alloys which possess a zinc content (>9.0 wt%) are
still limited. Compared with the traditional Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloys, the alloy with
high-zinc content has higher strength and improved overall performance and a
better application prospect. So it is of practical signi ﬁcance to investigate such
alloys.
In this work, a quanti ﬁcational study is implemented on the ageing precipitates
with nanoscale size in a high-zinc alloy which suffers diverse ageing tempers (T6,
T74 and T77) by TEM techniques. The precipitate diameter distribution and
average diameter size are proposed.
Experimental Procedure
The researches were launched on samples extracted from an Al –9.54Zn–2.10Mg–
1.69Cu alloy extrusion with in ﬁnitesimal Zr, Fe and Si elements. The samples were
solution treated with an optimized regime of 475 °C/4 h, followed by
water-quenching and one-step T6, two-step T74 and three-step T77 ageing treat-
ments. The detailed ageing tempers and related properties are listed in Table 1.
A HVPC-1000 Vickers hardness survey meter was used to monitor ageing hard-
ening processes and each hardness datum was extracted from the average value of
nine effective values. The electrical conductivity was measured by a current elec-
trical conductivity meter performed under indoor temperature and the value is also
gained by nine effective ones. Tensile specimens were machined to a gauge of
U8 /C2 50 mm (M8) and the tensile direction was parallel to extrusion orientation.
The tensile speed was two millimeters per minute and the result of three effective
duplicate samples were averaged to obtain a tensile value. Disk samples for TEM
observations were extracted from metal sheets with a line cutting thickness of about
three millimeters. Then they were manually rubbed to a thickness of 40 –50 mm.

Results and Discussion
Tensile Properties, Hardness and Electrical Conductivity
The tensile properties combined with hardness as well as electrical conductivity of
the specimens after one-step T6, two-step T74 and three-step T77 ageing treatments
are summarized in Table 1. It can be perceived that the alloy with T6 peak ageing
state has the highest ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 698 MPa, whereas its
electrical conductivity possesses a lowest value (17.5 MS m
−1). At T74 over ageing
states, the UTS decreases severely while its conductivity reaches 22.0 MS m −1.I t
declares that an increment in electrical conductivity from T6 to T74 state is in
accordance to a penalty in strength decrease. The T77 treated alloy has an ultimate
tensile strength comparable to that of the T6 treated alloy, and its electrical con-
ductivity is in between that of T6 and T74.
TEM Observations
Figure 1a–f provides the selected-area diffraction patterns (SADPs) in 100hi Al and
112hi Al orientations for the alloy with T6, T74 and T77 states. The intense
diffraction spots observed from the matrix have been demarcated. As for the alloy
with T6 state, the spots and rays at 1/3 and 2/3 of {220} position in 100 hi Al and
112hi Al orientations, respectively, stem from semi-coherent η′ phase. Some
apparent spots representing coherent GPII zones are found around a half of {311}
positions in 112hi Al orientation. Hence, the man precipitates in the T6 samples are
GPII zone and η′ phase. In the case of the alloy with T74 state, it is obvious that
diffraction spots of η′ phase are quite clear. Besides, some emanative spots around
1/3{220} and 2/3{220} positions reveal that η phase in the T74 alloy is abundant,
which reveals the main precipitates under T74 state are η′ phase and η phase. In the
T77 samples, some GPII zones are found in the SADPs while the spots and rays
come from η′ phase are still apparent, which uncover the main precipitates of the
alloy under T77 state. The dominating precipitates for the present alloy under T6,
T74 and T77 states are summarized in Table 2.

Based on the SADPs and HRTEM analysis, matrix precipitates (MPs) and grain

MPs also decreases. Compared with the T6 and T74 alloy, the matrix precipitates of
the T77 alloy (Fig. 3c) have intermediate characteristics. Intuitively, the size of

than that of the T74 alloy. The precipitate distribution for the T77 alloy has a
similar trend as the size.
The grain boundary precipitates (GBPs) of the T6 alloy exhibit approximately
continuous distribution and the size is quite small. In the T74 alloy, the size of
GBPs enlarges and an obvious discontinuous distribution of GBPs appears. In the
T77 alloy, the size of GBPs is close to that of the T74 alloy and an obvious
discontinuous distribution appears.
Here we can see that the characteristics of MPs for the T77 alloy are close to that
of the T6 alloy while the GBPs are approximate to that of the T74 alloy. In order to
acquire quantitative precipitate characteristics with different ageing states, the
statistical-based analysis is performed on the basis of BF TEM observations.

Statistical Analysis of Matrix Precipitate Projection Along
110hi Al Orientation
The shape of GPII zone, η′ phase and η phase is discoid and they precipitate at
{111}Al plane. In the perspective of 110hi Al orientation, the phases are projected as
ellipse, plate or rod. Hence, in the consideration of errors, it is reasonable to regard
the max diameter of the projections as the size of the matrix precipitates. Owing to
the limited observation condition of TEM technique, namely, abundant precipitates
in low magnitude images with relatively large measurement error while small
number of precipitates in high magnitude images with less measurement error, so
we choose a suitable magnitude to calculate precipitates. Several images are
selected and hundreds of precipitates in them are calculated. The diameter of pre-
cipitates is measured by a tool in IPP software and all the measured data are divided
into groups with a gap of 1 nm. Hence, the percentages of these gaps are calculated.
Besides, in order to ensure the accuracy, the number fractions no more than 1% are
abandoned.
The results of the alloy with T6, T74 and T77 ageing tempers are shown in
Fig. 4. It serves to show that the T6 alloy has a majority in precipitates with a
diameter no more than 2 nm and almost no precipitate has a diameter larger than

Discussion
The dominating strengthening modes of Al –Zn–Mg–Cu (7xxx) alloys are precip-
itation strengthening and dispersion strengthening. Dislocation movement can be
signiﬁcantly hindered by phases and the corresponding strain ﬁeld around them.
The TEM observations indicate that the primary precipitates are GPII zone and η′
phase with characteristics of small size and dispersive distribution for the T6 and
T77 alloys. Meanwhile, the main precipitates in the T74 alloy are η′ phase and η
phase which own semi-coherency and non-coherency with the matrix. Besides, the
size and distribution exhibit big dimension and scattering. Apparently, dislocations
could shear the coherent and semi-coherent precipitates of the T6 and T77 alloys, so
we can describe the strengthening effect by [ 20]:

strength levels than the T74 alloy. Besides, the T77 alloy possesses a broader
precipitate diameter distribution than the T6 alloy while both have more than a half
percentage of precipitates with a size less than 2 nm. That is the reason for a little
lower strength for the T77 alloy compared with the T6 alloy.
Conclusions
In this study, the characteristics for precipitates in a high-zinc Al –9.54Zn–
2.10Mg–1.69Cu alloy treated by T6, T74 and T77 ageing tempers are investigated.
The results of SADPs and HRTEM observations declare that the primary precipi-
tates are GPII zone and η′ phase in the T6 and T77 alloys while η′ and η phase in
the T74 alloy. The Bright ﬁeld TEM observations reveal that the matrix precipitates
for the T6 and T77 alloys have small size and dispersive distribution while that for
the T74 alloy has big size and sparse distribution. Quantitative precipitate char-
acteristics including diameter distribution and average diameter size of matrix
precipitates have been deduced by an image processing implemented on TEM
images projected along 110hi
Al orientation. The results reveal that the T6 and T77
alloys have more than a half percentage of precipitates with a size less than 2 nm
while the T77 and T74 alloys have broad precipitate distribution range till 14 and
16 nm, respectively. The grain boundary precipitates for the T6 alloy have con-
tinuous distribution with small size while that for the T74 and T77 alloys distribute
intermittently with big size.

Abstract Isothermal compression tests of the Al –9.4Zn–1.9Mg–2.0Cu alloy were
carried out at the temperature ranging from 300 to 460 °C and the strain rate from
0.001 to 10 s
−1, and the deformation degree was 70%. Flow stress curves show that
the ﬂow stress decreases with the increasing deformation temperature and the
decreasing strain rate. The measured ﬂow stress was corrected because of the effect
of friction. The corresponding corrected stress values are lower than measured stress
values. The effect of friction is far greater when hot-deformations occurred at lower
temperatures or higher strain rates. A constitutive equation considering the effect of
strain on material constants (i.e. a, n, Q and A) are established based on the
Arrhenius-type equation. Compared with the experimental results, the ﬂow stresses
calculated by the constitutive equation have a high precision with the correlation
coefﬁcient of 0.95. Results show that higher deformation temperatures and lower

Keywords The Al –9.4Zn–1.9Mg–2.0Cu alloy /C1 Hot deformation
Flow behaviors /C1 Constitutive model
Introduction
The ﬂow behavior of metals during hot working deformation process is very
complex because of the comprehensive effect of heat effect and mechanical force
[1]. The ﬂow behavior is a re ﬂection of the microstructure evolution that containing
the hardening and softening appearance [ 2]. To design the aluminum alloy forming
process, hot rolling, forging and extrusion, the understanding of ﬂow behavior is
very important and essential which is described by a constitutive equation model in
a mathematic form [ 3]. A reasonable constitutive model is crucial for the accurate
description of ﬂow behavior, there are three main constitutive equation model
categories: phenomenological constitutive model, physical-based constitutive
model and arti ﬁcial neural network constitutive model [ 4, 5]. In terms of aluminum
alloys, the hyperbolic sine Arrhenius-type model, which is the earliest and most
common constitutive model, was proposed by Zener and Hollomon [ 2], and Sellars
and Tegart [ 6]. Li et al. [ 7] investigated the deformation behavior of AA7050 and
proposed a developed constitutive equation considering the strain compensation.
Dong et al. [ 8] developed a constitutive model of AA6N01, which was applied to
simulate a extrusion process of a complex cross-section pro ﬁle. The constitutive
equation model can be used in computer code to optimize the forming parameters of
metals [ 9]. Therefore, researches that focused on constitutive equations are devel-
oped to get a more accurate constitutive model.
Aluminum alloys have been pay much attentions for their low density, optimal
mechanical properties and recyclable character [ 10]. High alloying aluminum
alloys, Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloys, with high strength-to-density ratio, high fracture
toughness and good stress corrosion cracking resistance, have been widely used for
automotive and aerospace industries [ 11, 12]. To improve the integrated perfor-
mance of Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloys, hot deformation is an essential and effective
process. There are tremendous efforts have been done for hot deformation resear-
ches including ﬂow stress behaviors, constitutive equation models and
microstructure evolution [ 13–15]. However, there still need to further investigate on
the workability and optimize the hot deformation process parameter of Al –Zn–Mg–
Cu alloys.
The object of this study is to investigate the in ﬂuence of strain, strain rate and
deformation temperature on the compressive deformation of the Al –Zn–Mg–Cu
alloy. A comprehensive model describing the relationship of the ﬂow stress, strain
rate and temperature of the alloy at elevated temperatures is proposed. The validity
of descriptive results based on the proposed constitutive equation is investigated.

Experiments
Table 1 shows the composition of a high Zn content Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloy that was
used in this study (wt%). After homogenized at 470 °C for 24 h, the direct chill
casting ingots were made into cylinder specimens with 10 mm in diameter and
15 mm in height. Hot-compression tests were conducted at the Gleeble-1500D
thermo-simulation machine under four kind of temperatures (593, 633, 673 and
713 K) and ﬁve kind of strain rates (0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10 s −1). The procedure of
compression tests was shown in Fig. 1, each specimen was heated to the defor-
mation temperature by 10 K/s rate, and then held temperature to get the heat
balance for 3 min. At the end, the tested specimens were quenching in water
immediately, and their height reduction is 70%.
Results and Discussion
Flow Stress Behavior and Friction Correction As shown in Fig. 2, two groups of
true stress-true strain curve were obtained at different deformation conditions. All of
curves display a similar shape, where the ﬂow stress increases rapidly at ﬁrst and then
follows a constant state, suggesting the ﬂow and microstructure evolution have the
similar law at a wide range of deformation conditions. As the deformation temper-
ature increases and the strain rate decreases, the true ﬂow stress decreases, indicating
deformation temperatures and strain rates determine the alloy ’s workability
effectively.

Constitutive Equations of Flow Stress for the Al –Zn–Mg–Cu Alloy The rela-

by the Arrhenius equation based on the true stress-true strain curves. According to
the hyperbolic law in Arrhenius-type equation [ 2, 17], the Zener-Hollomon
parameter can represents the deformation temperature and the strain rate effect on
the hot compression progress.

According to the results, the value of R is 0.996 and of AARE is 2.45%. Therefore,
the developed constitutive equation model here could describe the ﬂow behavior

accurately.
Conclusions
Isothermal hot compression tests were conducted under different conditions that
deformation temperatures range from 320 to 440 °C and the strain rate range from
0.001 to 10 s
−1. The following conclusions were drawn:
(1) The alloy showed a steady characteristic in terms of ﬂow stress under most of
deformation conditions. The ﬂow stress increased with increasing strain rates
and decreasing deformation temperatures.
(2) Because of the friction effect, the measured ﬂow stress was corrected. The
higher the temperature or the larger the strain rate was, the more serious the
friction effect became.
(3) An improved constitutive equation was proposed, considering the effect of
temperature, strain rate and true strain. The calculated ﬂow stresses are highly
consistent with the measured values, indicating that the developed constitutive
equation possesses a preferable prediction capability.

Abstract Effect of RRA treatment on the mechanical properties and microstructure
of Al –Zn–Mg–Cu–Er–Zr aluminium alloy was researched by hardness measure-
ment, conductivity measurement, exfoliation corrosion measurement, transmission
electron microscopy (TEM). Discussed the relationship between the regression
treatment and composite properties of the alloy. The study found that the hardness
of RRA treated alloys ﬁrst rise and then decline with the increasing of regression
time, but the corrosion performance is increasing all the time. After pre-aging
treatment 120 °C/24 h, regression treatment 180 °C/60 min, re-aging treatment
120 °C/24 h, the combination property of the alloy is optimal, the hardness, con-
ductivity and the exfoliation corrosion grade are respectively: 207.6 HV, 33.53%
IACS, PC. At this moment, it is found from the TEM observations that the matrix
precipitates are small and dispersed, resemble to T6 temper. The grain boundary
precipitation out phases are discontinuous distribution and the relatively wider PFZ,
similar to the T73 temper.
