## Page 179

Introduction
Al–Zn–Mg–Cu aluminium alloys characterized by its good mechanical properties
and lower physical density are applied abroad in the territory of transportation and
aerospace [ 1–3]. However, there is a more prominent problem which is the cor-
rosion resistance not ideal can be reduced with increasing strength [ 4, 5]. The T6
temper is restricted owing to the highest strength but the lower corrosion resistant
[6, 7]. Some literatures [ 8–10] reported that the key problem of T6 temper to
corrosion is solved by use of the over-aged treatment for instance T7X but with a
certain degree reduction of the strength of T6 state. Therefore, the optimum aging
process can combine high strength and good corrosion performance should
explored. The RRA treatment invented by Cina et al. [ 11], which can realize the
goal of the good overall performance included strength and corrosion resistance.
The RRA treatment contained three procedures. Primarily, the pre-aged treatment,
which was alloy in the T6 state or under-grade state. Secondly, the alloy retro-
gressed at upper temperature a period time. And last, the pre-aged treatment was at
a lower temperature for long time with slightly alike to the T6 temper [ 12, 13]. The
important procedure of three-step aging was retrogression, which can allocated the
dissolution of GP zones, η and η′ precipitates in the aluminium matrix grains and
coarsening of GBPs in the grain boundaries. Oliveira et al. [ 14] founded that when
the alloy was retrogressed 200 °C for 40 min, the obtained mechanical properties
and corrosion properties were similar to the T6 and T7X states. Ranganatha et al.
[15] discovered that in the retrogression treatment, the dissolution of precipitates
(GP zones and the particles of η and η) were unstable in the grains, but when
retrogression temperatures extended to above 180 °C, which can obtain more
efﬁcient in dissolving the precipitates and the grain boundary precipitates became
coarsen and discontinuous distribution. Fang et al. [ 16] reported that for the sake of
achieving better combination property, the retrogression process for a short time at
different retrogression temperature range 200 –260 °C, afterward water or
air-cooling quenching and last re-aging process with the initial T6 process, but The
whole treatment is very dif ﬁcult to realize and control in real production. In this
paper, the impact of slow heating RRA treatment process on the microstructure and
properties of the experimental alloy studied and discussed. These results will show
the optimum RRA treatment parameters suitable for industrial production.
Experiment
The experimental material offered by Southwest Aluminium Co. Ltd. China which
was taken from on the 40 mm thick hot extruded aluminium alloy pipe with
chemical component of Al –5.6Zn–2.1Mg–1.2Cu–0.1Mn–0.1Er–0.12Zr (in wt%)
170 X. Wang et al.

alloy. First solution treatment, the alloys temperature rise from 30 to 470 °C with
the velocity of 110 °C/h and kept 2 h at 470 °C, then quenched at room temper-
ature water. And last proceed RRA treatment. The RRA treatment procedures was
listed in Table 1. The hardness was determined on a HXD-1000TM/LCD machine,
and seven points were tested in every sample to get the mean value. The con-
ductivity was tested with a SIGMATEEST2.069. The exfoliation corrosion test was
performed at 25 °C in the light of the exfoliation corrosion (EXCO) test in the light
of GB/T 22639-2008. TEM thin foils mechanical polished to less than 80 lm and
punched into diameter discs of 3 mm. Subsequently, the samples were twin-jet
polishing in the solution of 30% HNO
3 in methanol at −25 to −30 °C and 20 V.

Figure 1 shows the hardness of the experimental alloy, it can be observed that
hardness increased ﬁrstly and then decreased with increasing of retrogression time
after Pre-aging treated. However, the peak value obtained time were different
because of different retrogression time, and the time reduced with increasing of
retrogression temperature. When retrogression temperature at 180 °C, the hardness
after retrogression treated was also rise ﬁrstly and then drop with increasing of
retrogression time, but the curve ﬁrstly decreased to a minimum value, then
increased to a maximum value, eventual decreased as further increasing of retro-
gression time.
The conductivity of experimental alloy RRA processed at different states are
described in Fig. 2. It can be observed that conductivity of the alloy rose with
increasing of retrogression time both retrogression treated and re-aging treated. And
the conductivity of alloy treated by re-aging were always larger than retrogression
treated at the same retrogression temperature. The curves climbing speed rising with
increasing of retrogression temperature.
The exfoliation corrosion rating scale of the experimental alloy RRA treated at
different conditions are shown in Table 2 and Figs. 3, 4 and 5 show the EXCO
properties of studied alloy RRA treated at different conditions. According to GB/T
22639-2008, the EXCO resistance of the alloy increased with increasing of retro-
gression time when treated at the same retrogression temperature. The whole EXCO

decreased, but the RR treated samples ﬁrst dropped and then increased and
dropped at last. The conductivity of different RRA treated and RR treated

Composition Optimization Study
on 7N01 Aluminum Alloy
Wenlin Gao, Gang Sun, Qingmei Ma, Changde Lu, Xiangjie Wang,

Abstract The effect of Mn, Mg, Zn and Zr elements on the microstructure and
mechanical properties of 7N01 aluminum alloy was studied by hardness, electrical
conductivity, tensile test, optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron micro-
scopy (SEM), which was based on the optimal extrusion and heat treatment process.
Results show that a new alloy with optimum properties combination is found and its
composition is Al –4.6Zn–1.55Mg–0.6Mn–0.15Cr–0.1Zr–0.03Ti (wt%), of which
ultimate tensile strength and yield strength are 421.3 and 369.2 MPa respectively,
and the phases are (Fe, Mn)Al
6, η(MgZn2) and a small amount of η′(MgZn).

## Page 188

Introduction
7N01 aluminum alloy belongs to the category of Al –Zn–Mg alloys, which Contains
4–5% zinc (mass fraction) and 1 –2% magnesium (mass fraction). Because of its
excellent welding performance and heat treatment strengthening ability, its
deformed materials are often applied to the manufacture of the welded structural
parts with high strength and high fracture toughness [ 1, 2]. η(MgZn
2) and T
(Al2Mg2Zn3) phases not only have great solubility in matrix, but also their solu-
bility changes drastically with the temperature rise and fall, so the Al –Zn–Mg alloy
has excellent precipitation hardening ability. The development of ultra-high-
strength aluminum alloy abroad mainly follows the direction of high strength, low
toughness-high strength, high toughness-high strength, high toughness and corro-
sion resistance. The design of alloy composition is characterized by that an
increasing alloying extent and the content of Fe, Si and other impurities are getting
lower. Additionally, trace elements are added more reasonable [ 3–5]. In recent
years, a series of in-depth studies on the composition, homogenization and solid
solution treatment process, prestretching process, heat treatment system and pro-
cessing technology of 7xxx aluminum alloy have been carried out, but there is still a
certain gap with the international level [ 6–10]. In this paper, the effects of Mg, Zn,
Mn and Zr elements on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the alloy
were studied by means of reasonable melting and casting process, extrusion process
and heat treatment process, which provides the evidence for the development of
high performance alloy.
Experimental Procedure
Composition Design In this paper, the in ﬂuence of the main alloying elements on
the microstructure and properties of 7N01 aluminum alloy is taken full consider-
ation. Refering to the range of 7N01 Al alloy composition, the content of Mg, Mn,
Zn and Zr elements are set as the main variables to design alloy composition.
Table 1 shows the composition of the 7N01 aluminum alloy.
Experimental Design The pure aluminum was melted in a medium frequency
induction furnace. The Al melt was transferred into theﬁrst crucible resistance furnace
at 780 °C. Cr, Mn, Zn and Zr were added to the Al melt at 780 °C. Mg and Al –5Ti–B
were added to the Al melt when the temperature of the second furnace was stabilized at
780 °C. Then it was poured into the ﬁrst crucible resistance furnace at 780 °C. The
melt was degassed by C
2Cl6 at 740 °C, then cast at 720 °C. The ingots were
homogenized at 530 °C for 10 h. The bars were then extruded into Al plates (The
extrusion process parameters are shown in Table 2). The Arti ﬁcial aging treatment
system was insulation temperature at 95 °C for 5 h, and then 160 °C for 8 h.
180 W. Gao et al.

## Page 189

The conductivity was measured by sigmascope conductivity meter at room
temperature. Vickers hardness was measured with a load of 3 kg and a duration
time of 15 s by 452-SVD automatic turret digital vickers hardness tester. The
tensile test was carried out by shimazduo universal testing machine. The tensile
speed was 5 mm/min and the strain curve was recorded by a 40 mm extensometer.
The samples that coated in anode by reagent (38 mLH
2SO4 + 43 mLH 3PO4 +
19 mLH2O) were used for optical microscopy observations. The SSX-550 scanning
electron microscopy and energy spectrum microanalyser were used for observing
microstructure and analyzing composition.
Results Analysis
Optical Microscopy Observations The software image-Pro plus6.0 was used to
measure the grain size of the ingot. The microstructures of sample coated in anode
are shown in Fig. 1. Compared with the average grain size of the 9 groups of
samples, the grain size of the alloy 1 is about 202.8 lm, which indicates that the
grain reﬁnement level of the component is not good. The grain sizes of the alloys 6,
8 and 9 are approximately 89.2, 94.4 and 75.6 lm, respectively. The other ﬁve
groups’ grain sizes are range from 100 to 120 lm. Relatively speaking, the grain
size of the alloy 9 is the optimal. Considered of the national standard of the
aluminum alloy products, the average grain grade of the alloys reach 3.0 or exceed,
the grain grade of the alloys 6, 8 and 9 arrives 4.0.

The microstructures of the alloys 1 –9 after extrusion without aging are shown in
Fig. 2. We can observe the completely recrystallized structure in alloys 1 and 2.
The partial recrystallization occurs in alloys 3, 4 and 6. The recrystallization not
occurs in alloys 7, 8 and 9, especially the extrusion traces of alloy 9 are clear and
ﬁne.
The recrystallization of alloys 1 and 2 is mainly due to the low content of
alloying elements, especially the lack of Mn is not bene ﬁt to suppress recrystal-
lization during the extrusion process. And grains of the alloys 3, 4, 6 and 7 are
extruded to break up due to the large grain size of the as-cast bars and the extrusion
temperature does not reach the recrystallization temperature. So the slender and
continuous microstructure is formed. Extrusion traces of the alloys 8 and 9 are ﬁne
and uniform because of the small grains of as-cast bars, and no recrystallization
occurs.

Hardness and Conductivity Analysis Figure 3 is the histogram of the hardness
and conductivity of the 9 as-cast alloys. The Vickers hardness values of the as-cast
alloys 2, 3, 6 and 9 are relatively high, which are 123.03, 121.40, 123.03 and
119.57 HV, respectively. However, Vickers hardness values of alloy 4, 7 and 8 are
relatively low, which are 108.30, 107.10 and 103.6 HV, respectively. On one hand,
hardness of as-cast alloys is generally related to the amount of solid solubility and
grain size. The greater the amount of solid solution, the greater the hardness of the
alloys. On the other hand, it is also related to grain size of the ingot. The ﬁner the
grains, the better the hardness and toughness. So the hardness value re ﬂects the
ingot structural properties to a certain extent [ 7–9].

conductivity of alloy 8 is the lowest of 23.83% IACS. The conductivity is closely
related to the lattice distortion. The regularity of the lattice has a great relationship

Tensile Properties Test Figure 5 is the line chart of the tensile test of the 9 alloys
after casting, solid solution, extrusion, aging and tensile properties test. The vari-
ation tendency on tensile strength and yield strength of the 9 alloys is consistent.
The as-aged alloy 9 has the highest tensile strength and yield strength, and their
values are 421.26 and 369.21 Mpa. The as-aged alloy 1 has the lowest tensile
strength and yield strength, and their values are 346.89 and 313.53 Mpa. However,
The as-aged alloy 1 has the highest elongation, and its value is 18.6%. The as-aged

variation tendency of tensile strength and yield strength has a turning point at alloy

Conclusion
The casting grain size of the alloy 9 is the smallest and the most uniform to grade
4.0. After extrusion and aging, both the grain size and the extrusion traces are
uniform, resulting in no recrystallization occurring.
The composition of the optimal alloy is Al –4.6Zn–1.55Mg–0.6Mn–0.15Cr–
0.1Zr–0.03Ti (wt%), which tensile strength and yield strength are 421.26 and
369.21 Mpa, respectively. This excellent alloy exceeds the standard of automotive
7N01 Al alloys.
The main phases of the as-cast alloy are (Fe, Mn)Al
6, η(MgZn2), and a small
amount of η′(MgZn), the excellent performance of the Al alloy owes to the exis-
tence of these phases.

Abstract This study aimed to explore the correlation among forging process,
structure and mechanical performance of advanced 2219 aluminum alloy forged
ring. The microstructure of the alloy forged ring in tangential, radial and axial were
analyzed by Optical microscope (OM), Scanning electron microscopy (SEM),
Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) test. The results
show that the microstructure of 2219 aluminum alloy forged ring is a plate-like
structure and the precipitation phases distributed along the rolling direction. Among
which, ﬁne Al
2Cu particles uniformly distribute in the grain. The hardness and

was tested. The results indicate that the hardness perpendicular to the axial plane is
153.7HV, and the tensile performance of the alloy along the tangential direction is
the highest. By observing the microstructure of the fracture, it is founded that the
dimple in the tangential is deeper and smaller, and the elongation in tangential are

Introduction
With the rapid development of the rolling technology, large-scale forged ring is
widely used in numerous industrial ﬁelds, such as machinery, automobiles, trains,
ships, petrochemicals, aerospace and atomic energy. Especially the high-strength
aluminum alloy forged rings, as the indispensable structural material, are deeply
researched. With the increasing demand for aluminum alloy forgings, higher
strength and plasticity and stronger fracture toughness are necessary [ 1–4]. The
aluminum alloy forged ring in the high-power launch vehicle needs not only large
size, but also high mechanical properties. 2219 aluminum alloy, known as LY19, is
one kind of Al –Cu–Mn alloy, which belongs to the heat treatment and strengthened
deformed aluminum alloy. The mechanical properties of 2219 aluminum alloy can
be improved greatly after solution and aging treatment, and higher corrosion and
cracking resistance were available after T8 heat treatment (T8 heat treatment is that
the alloy after the solid heat treatment, it is cold processed and then arti ﬁcially aged)
[5–7]. So, for the large-sized forged ring of 2219 aluminum alloy, which would be
used in the in the rocket tank forged ring [ 8–13] still needs to be further studied.
A lot of researchers in the world have studied on the performance of 2219 alu-
minum alloy for a long time. Yang [ 14] studied the microstructure and mechanical
properties of 2219 aluminum alloy sheet during the drawing process and discussed
the stress-strain curves and microstructure evolution under different
pre-deformation, the results showed that the alloy have more compact precipitates
and get higher strength when the pre-deformation is about 2%. Zheng [ 15] reported
that the effect of cold deformation on 2219 aluminum alloy aging precipitation and
hardening behavior during aging process and discussed the competitive relationship
between deformation strengthening and second phase strengthening during 2219
aluminum alloy sheet deformation aging processing; Mondol et al. [ 16] studied the
microstructure and tensile properties at different temperature of 2219ScMg alu-
minum alloy, 2219ScMg aluminum alloy was made by adding 0.8%Sc and 0.45%
Mg to 2219 aluminum alloy. However, there is little research on the performance of
large-sized 2219 aluminum alloy forged ring.
Based on above, it is important to study the correlations of forging process,
microstructure and mechanical properties of advanced 2219 aluminum alloy

in tangential, radial and axial of the alloy were observed, and the correlation

aluminum alloy large-sized forged rings.

Results and Discussion
Microstructure of 2219 Aluminum Alloy Large Forged Ring Figure 2 presents
that the phase on the surface of 2219 Aluminum Alloy analyzed by EDS, there are
many strip-like and block-like particles. It is found that the mass fraction of Al and
Cu is 50.3 and 49.7% from the spectrum components, it should be Al
2Cu. It is
pointed out in the literature [ 17] that 2219 rolled annealed plates contain many
strips or spots phase Al 2Cu. Figure 4 shows that the phases are Al 2Cu. These
phases are elliptical, the maximum size of the particles is 11.74 lm, the minimum is
4.88 lm, the average size is 7.59 lm (Fig. 3).
In order to research the microstructure, the specimens were made along tan-
gential, radial and axial direction (Fig. 5). OM test was made perpendicular to the
tangential radial and axial plates (Fig. 6). It is observed that the alloy is Strip
structure, like streamline. The largest deformation direction is tangential, which
consisted with the result of ring rolling. Figure 7 showed that Al
2Cu phase dis-
tributed in the grain and its ’boundary. Most of the grains have recrystallized after
the solid solution treatment, forming a clear equiaxial crystal structure. Figure 6
shows that these phases distributed along rolling direction, segregation phe-
nomenon is found in axial, dispersion-distributed in tangential, which would cause
performance variety among three directions.
Hardness of 2219 Aluminum Alloy Large Forged Ring In order to research the
hardness, the specimens were made along tangential radial and axial (Fig. 8).
Table 2 shows that the hardness in three directions is different, the hardness of the
alloy in the tangential, radial and axial directions is 139.4HV, 153.7HV, 149.8HV
respectively and the average hardness is all above 139HV. The maximum hardness
is 153.7HV, appeared in axial, because the grain is elongated most along the
tangential. But the hardness in the three directions is similar, the difference is not
more than 15HV.

Microstructure of Fracture From Fig. 10, it is found that there are dimples on the
whole fracture surface, indicating that the fracture is ductile. Among the three
directions, the difference is that tangential fracture is smaller and deeper than radial
and axial fracture, which illustrates that the plastic deformation is more obvious in
the tangential direction before fracture, so the plasticity in tangential is better, which
just explains the tangential elongation, yield strength is higher than in axial and
radial. The fracture mode of 2219 aluminum alloy is typical ductile fracture, and the
fracture mechanism is micropore aggregation fracture. Figure 11 shows that the
particles at the bottom of the fracture dimple are Al 2Cu. The broken Al 2Cu phases
at the partial fractures are the crack source when cracked, resulting in stress

concentration and reducing the tensile properties of the alloy. Therefore, the
solution treatment temperature should be controlled, so, if the Al 2Cu can restore to

Conclusions
1. The microstructure of 2219 aluminum alloy is consist of Al matrix and the
second phase Al 2Cu. The tensile fracture feature is a typical ductile and, the
fracture mechanism is microporous accumulation fracture. The second phase
located at the bottom of the dimple is Al 2Cu. The forged ring is elongated along
the tangential direction and the tangible dimple is the smallest and deepest. The
elongation is the highest, and tensile performance is the best along the tangential
direction.
2. The difference of the hardness in forged ring tangential radial and axial is not
great, no more than 15HV. The hardness along different directions is greater
than 139HV, indicating that there is no big difference about the vertical and
horizontal hardness of the product.
3. The tensile properties of the forged ring in the tangential, radial and axial are
similar, but the tangential performance is optimal with the tensile strength of
438.3 MPa, the yield strength of 321 MPa, the elongation of 20.5% and the
elastic modulus is 72.75 Gpa.

Effect of Yield Function on the Stamping
Springback of Aluminum Alloy
Mingdong Huang, Lei Fu, Li Lee and Cheng Liu
Abstract The springback of aluminum alloy sheet after stamping is much larger
than that of the steel sheet of the same strength. This is one of the reasons for the
aluminum alloy sheets not yet being widely used in stamping automobile parts. The
quality of springback prediction for a sheet metal forming process depends on a
precise material model. In this paper, an A-pillar was selected as an example to
investigate the effect of yield function (Hill ’48, Barlat89 and Barlat2000) on the
predicted springback of automotive parts pressed from the 5754 aluminum alloy
sheet. A ﬁnite element model was established using commercial stamping software
PAMSTAMP2G. The parameters of the material models were derived from the
uniaxial and biaxial tensile tests. The stamping experiments of A-pillar were carried
out to obtain the springback values of actual parts. The springback values of the
stamped parts were measured by the 3D scanning technology. The comparison
between the predicted values and experimental ones shows that the predicted
springback using the Barlat2000 yield function is the best.

Introduction
In recent years, automobile light-weight technology has become a key target for car
manufacturers because of increasing concerns about energy consumption, envi-
ronmental emission, and safety. Aluminum alloys as a kind of light material are
increasingly used in the automotive industry, with an average increase of 6% per
year. However, the aluminum alloy yield stress over Young ’s modulus ratio is
smaller than for steel, the springback of aluminum alloy is larger than the same
strength steel. It is well known that the factors affecting the stress distribution will
lead to changes in springback of parts. Therefore, How to improve the precision of
springback calculation is especially important and has always been a hot research.
During the past decades, many researchers have studied what factors affect the
springback and how to improve the accuracy of the springback simulation.
Finite element analysis (FEA) has been considered as an effective way of sim-
ulating predicting springback [ 1, 2]. Volkan Esat et al. [ 3] analyzed bending and
springback of different aluminium materials with different thickness used com-
mercially available FEA software. Using ﬁnite element analysis, the amount of
springback in terms of springback factors, bent angles and displacements can easily
be obtained. Wang et al. [ 4] described the hardening behavior of QP980 by the
NSK Swift model. The procedure of material constants determination with the
tension test data for the NSK Swift model is illustrated thoroughly for further
application. The inertia relief approach is also illustrated and further employed in
springback calculation to examine the accuracy and ef ﬁciency. However, the above
studies do not have a springback prediction for complex aluminum alloy parts.
In order to improve the prediction capability of springback in the ﬁnite element
analysis, many researchers have established a variety of material constitutive
models [5–9]. Yoshida et al. [ 10] presented new experimental data of elastic –plastic
stress–strain responses of two types of steel sheets and indicated some important
points in constitutive modeling for such large-strain cyclic elastic-plasticity by
comparing the results of numerical stress –strain responses calculated by typical
constitutive models of a mixed isotropic –kinematic hardening plastic potential with
the corresponding experimental observations. Chung et al. [ 11] formulated com-
bined isotropic-kinematic hardening law based on the modi ﬁed Chaboche model to
account for the Bauschinger effect and the transient behavior.
The aim of this paper is to compare three plastic yield functions (Hill ’48,
Barlat89 and Barlat2000) to show their relevance on the prediction of springback
behavior for 5754 aluminum alloy. A ﬁnite element model was established by using
commercial stamping software PAMSTAMP2G for simulating the springback
process of an A-pillar. The uniaxial and biaxial tensile tests were conducted to
obtain the basic material parameters needed to simulation. Then the stamping
experiments of A-pillar were conducted. The comparison between the predicted
values and experimental ones shows that the predicted springback using the
Barlat2000 yield function is the best.
200 M. Huang et al.

## Page 209

Tensile Tests and Material Models
In the present work, 5754 aluminum alloy sheets were selected. In order to obtain
the basic material performance parameters which needed to simulation, uniaxial and
biaxial tensile tests were conducted.
Uniaxial Tensile Tests Uniaxial tensile specimens were cut from sheets along RD
(rolling direction), 45° to RD and TD by using a miller. ASTM E8 standard was
followed to conduct the uniaxial tensile tests. The elongation of the material is
about 18%. The results of tensile tests were shown in Table 1.
Biaxial Tensile Tests The biaxial tensile tests carried out in accordance with the
ISO 16842 [ 12]. Figure 1 shows the shape and dimensions of the cruciform test
piece. The experiment equipment of biaxial tensile test is shown in Fig. 2 [13]. The
test materials were subjected to biaxial stretching with the tensile loads, F
x and Fy,
being in ﬁxed proportions. For this research, seven different load ratios, Fx:
Fy = 4:1, 2:1, 4:3, 1:1, 3:4, 1:2, 1:4, were applied. The average strain values of the
two tensile directions were measured by four biaxial strain gauges. The
cross-sectional area was calculated based on the volume invariance principle, and
then the stress of two tensile directions was determined. The stress –strain curve
obtained from a uniaxial tensile test in the rolling direction of the material was
chosen as a reference data for plastic work. Based on the principle of equal work of
plastic work, the yield strength under different load ratios were calculated. The
experimental results were shown in Fig. 3.
Material Models Select a suitable material model for stamping simulation can
improve the accuracy of simulation. The constitutive model of simulation mainly
includes hardening model and yield function. In this paper, the Voce hardening
model was selected for describing the ﬂow behavior of the material. Accurately
describing the yield behavior of the sheet metal is very important for studying the
sheet metal plastic deformation. The sheet metal which is pre-processed or rolled
shows the obvious anisotropy. Researchers have proposed a number of anisotropic
yield functions. The commonly used anisotropic yield functions are divided into
three series: the Hill series, Hosford series and Drucke series. In this research, the
effect of yield function (Hill ’48, Barlat89 and Barlat2000) on the aluminum alloy
stamping springback was studied. According to the results of uniaxial tensile tests
and biaxial tensile tests, the anisotropic coef ﬁcients of yield functions are shown in

Numerical Simulation and Results
Finite Element Model Taking an internal A-pillar of an automobile body as an
example, the in ﬂuence of yield function on springback prediction was studied. The
model of the A-pillar is shown in Fig. 4. The geometry of initial blank is
1345 /C2 640 mm and the blank thickness is 2.0 mm.
In this paper, the stamping springback simulation of the A-pillar was carried out
by using commercial stamping software PAMSTAMP 2G. The tools of A-pillar were
designed to make the left and the right A-pillar in one mould. So the tools structure
was symmetrical structure. In order to enhance the computation ef ﬁciency, only one
side of the model was simulated and analyzed. The ﬁnite element model is shown in
Fig. 5. The model includes punch, die, blank holder and blank. The blank is
elastic-plastic body and the tools are rigid body. The simulation process is divided
into four steps:
(1) The ﬁrst step was the gravity process. The blank fell naturally on the blank
holder by gravity, the friction coef ﬁcient between the blank and the tools was
set to 0.12;
(2) The second step was the holding process of the blank holder. The die moved
downward, and closed with the blank holder. The blank holder force was set to
400 kN;
Fig. 4 Model of the A-pillar
Fig. 5 Finite element model
of A-pillar deep drawing
204 M. Huang et al.

## Page 213

(3) The third step was the stamping process. The die moves at a constant speed to
forming the blank. The explicit computing was used to calculate the above
steps;
(4) The last step was the process of springback. For springback with contact, it is
convenient to use an advanced implicit solver which enables the involvement of
contact. A gravity option must be used in this kind of simulation. In springback
with contact simulation, no blank locking was set because the blank position
was clearly determined by the punch.
Results and Discussion The stamping experiments of A-pillar were conducted.
A 3D laser cutting machine was used to remove the trimming of the part. The
A-pillar part is shown in Fig. 6.
The surface of the A-pillar was scanned by a 3D scanning device. Then the point
cloud data of the component surface was obtained. The simulation data of the
A-pillar after springback are calculated by Hill ’48, Barlat89 and Barlat2000 yield
function respectively. In order to evaluate the effect of yield function on the pre-
cision of the part, the Geomagic Qualify software was used to compare the
experimental results with the simulation data. The comparison results are shown in
Fig. 7. The comparison method was based on the minimum ﬁtting method.
As can be seen from Fig. 7a, there is a large deviation of Hill ’48 simulation
results at both ends of the A-pillar. The deviation of the left end is larger than
1 mm. In Fig. 7b, the springback deviation calculated with the Barlat89 yield
function is smaller than the results of Hill48 yield function. However, the simu-
lation results are still very different from the experiment results. In Fig. 7c, the
deviation values between the calculated and experimental springback are within
±0.5 mm. The calculation results of Barlat2000 yield function are more precise
than the results of the previous two yield function.
In order to quantify the effect of yield function on the springback, the deviation
proﬁle of simulation and experimental results was plotted, as can be seen in Fig. 8.
The deviation was calculated by Hill ’48, Barlat89 and Barlat2000 yield function. It
can be seen from the Fig that the corresponding area fraction with deviation smaller
than 0.5 mm were 69.3, 78.4 and 90.3% respectively. But the proportions of cal-
culation error within −1.00 to −0.50 and 0.50 –1.00 by Hill ’48, Barlat89 and

Conclusions
A FE-model for predicting the springback was established. The uniaxial and biaxial
tensile tests were conducted for obtaining the model parameters for the hardening
model and the yield functions. The Hill ’48, Barlat89 and Barlat2000 yield functions
were applied to the ﬁnite element simulation for the springback of 5754 aluminum
alloy A-pillar. The comparison between the predicted values and experimental ones
shows that:

(1) The simulation results obtained using the Hill ’48 yield function is very much
different from the experimental results. Therefore, the Hill ’48 is not a suitable
yield function for the deformation behavior of aluminum alloy.
(2) The Barlat89 yield function gives a better result than the Hill ’48 yield function.
However, the predicted results also deviate a lot from the experimental results,
and the simulation accuracy is not acceptable.
(3) The simulation results obtained by the Barlat2000 yield function agree with the
experimental results best. Therefore, the Barlat2000 yield function is the
appropriate option in the ﬁnite element simulation of sheet metal forming
process of aluminum alloy with the highest accuracy among the three functions.

Abstract Aluminum drill pipes have low density, high speci ﬁc strength and good
stress corrosion resistance, possessing a huge application potential in the oil dril-
ling. The 1953 alloy belongs to the Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloy, and it is one of the most
promising aluminum alloy materials for petroleum drill pipe. In this paper, the 1953
aluminum alloy were studied by hardness tests, conductivity tests, tensile tests,
optical microscope and scanning electron microscopy. The results show that there
are a large number of AlZnMgCu phases and a small amount of Fe and Si impurity
phases after extrusion. After the solution treatment, the AlZnMgCu phases have

Introduction
Drill pipes are mainly used for jointing at the bottom of the drill tool, transferring
power and torque, and transporting drilling ﬂuid in the drilling process, etc. [ 1].
They are a kind of the main tools in the drilling and oil industry [ 2]. But drill pipes
are often the weak link in the whole drilling equipment. Because their working
conditions are the worst in the drilling operation. Compared with conventional steel
drill pipes, aluminum drill pipes have low density, high strength and good stress
corrosion resistance; further, aluminum is non-magnetic [ 3–6]. In practical appli-
cation, aluminum drill pipes can signi ﬁcantly increase drilling depth, drilling speed
and drilling ef ﬁciency, having obvious advantages [ 7]. Therefore, aluminum alloys
are now becoming ideal light structure materials for drilling. Abroad, aluminum
drill pipes have been used in the oil industry for decades. The actual application of
aluminum drill pipes show that they are reliable products, having a broad appli-
cation prospect [ 8]. Now the main representative materials are D16T, AK4-1T1,
1953T1 in Russia and AA2014, AA7075 in the United States, etc. [ 9–11] Among
them, 1953T1 and AA7075 belongs to Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloy. They have the high
yield strength at room temperature with higher impact toughness than other alu-
minum alloys [ 12, 13].
The Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloys have a strong aging strengthening effect through
quenching and aging. The determining factor of ageing strengthening effect is the
degree of supersaturation. Solution heat treatment can improve the solid solubility
of solute atoms in the substrate, increase the drive force of phase change in the
process of aging and affect the grain size and shape. Furtherly, it in ﬂuences the
properties of the alloy [ 14, 15]. Based on the 1953 aluminum alloy, through the
analysis of the extruded structure, this paper discussed the in ﬂuence of solution and
aging treatment process on its organization and performance.

Experimental
The compositions of the 1953 aluminum alloy studied are listed in Table 1.
After homogenization treatment, the ingot blank of U 450 (Inner diameter
125 mm) /C2800 mm were extruded into the pipe of U 147 /C213 mm. The
as-extruded samples were solution-treated and then water-quenched to room tem-
perature; after quenching, the samples were immediately aged at 120 °C for 24 h.
The solution treatment conditions are shown in Table 2. Based on the optimized
solution treatment, the samples were aged at 110, 120, 130 °C for 24 h and 120 °C
for 4, 12, 36, 48 h.
The vickers hardness testing was performed on a 430 SVD hardness tester and
each hardness value was obtained by averaging ﬁve measurements. The electrical
conductivity was performed on a WD-Z eddy-current conductivity gauge. The
tensile tests were performed at room temperature using a MTS-810 testing machine
at a tensile ratio of 1 –2 mm min
−1 and three measurements were made to obtain the
average value. The microstructure and morphology of samples were examined on
Zeiss Axiovert 200 MAT optical microscope after polishing and eroding with
Keller reagent, and JEOL JSM 7001F ﬁeld emission scanning electron microscope.

Results and Discussion
The In ﬂuence of the Different Second-Stage Solution Temperatures on the
Microstructures and Mechanical Properties of Alloys The metallographic
microstructures of the studied alloys are shown in Fig. 1. It can be obviously
observed that the grains are elongated along the extruding direction and the
microstructures are ﬁbrous (as shown in Fig. 1a). There are a large number of
precipitated phase particles and a small amount of residual phase distributed along
the extrusion direction in the crystal and grain boundaries.

During multi-stage solution, the ﬁrst-stage prompts the alloy elements to dis-
tribute ﬁnely at grain boundary and promotes recovery to generate, which reduce
the driving force of recrystallization. Then the recrystallized grains are hindered to
grow up after the second-stage solution treatment, which avoids the atoms to grow
up and recrystallize due to the high temperature during single-stage solution
treatment.
After solution treatment at different second-stage solution temperatures (as shown
in Fig. 1b–f), recrystallization occurs in both alloys. And their grains are similar. The
recrystallization fraction and average grain size of the alloy are calculated by EBSD,
the results are shown in the Fig. 2a, b. After 440 °C/1 h + 470 °C/1 h solution
treatment, the recrystallization fraction and average grain size is small. When the
temperatures of second-stage solution treatment are greater than 470 °C, the
recrystallization fraction and average grain size increases.
Figure 3 shows the SEM microstructures of studied alloys. Table 3 shows the
EDS results of the typical second phases. It can be seen that the images are similar
to the metallographic microstructures. The grains are elongated along the extruding
direction, and there are a large amount of precipitated phase particles and some
residual phase distributed in the crystal and grain boundaries (as shown in Fig. 3a).
The conclusion can be ascertained from the EDS results. The particles of larger size
in dark color are impurity phases with Fe (as shown in Fig. 3b.A). The bright white
particles which small and distributed widely are AlZnMgCu phases (as shown in
Fig. 3b.B). The black particles are impurity phases with Si (as shown in Fig. 3b.C).
After solution treatment at different second-stage solution temperatures (as shown
in Fig. 3c–g), the phases of AlZnMgCu have disappeared, only impurity phases
with Fe and Si which are dif ﬁcult to dissolve remained (as shown in Fig. 3c.D).
With the temperature of solution treatment increasing, the morphology of impurity
phases with Fe and Si do not change signi ﬁcantly.
Figure 4a, b show the curves of hardness, electrical conductivity and mechanical
properties in T6 aging state (120 °C/24 h) at the different second-stage solution
temperatures. It is clear that the hardness reached maximum after 440 °C/

Mechanical Properties of Alloys The hardness, electrical conductivity and
mechanical properties of alloy at different aging process are shown in Table 4. With
the increase of aging temperature, the conductivity increases, while the strength and
hardness increase ﬁrst and then decrease. With the increase of aging time, the
conductivity and hardness increases rapidly, and then tend to be slowly increasing.
The yield strength and tensile strength ﬁrst increase and then decrease, reaching the
maximum at 440 °C/1 h + 470 °C/1 h solution treatment. But the elongation is
decreasing.
Conclusions
(1) The grain of 1953 aluminum alloy become ﬂat and ﬁbrous along the extrusion
direction after extrusion. There are a large number of AlZnMgCu phase par-
ticles and a small amount of impurity phases with Fe and Si distributed along
the extrusion direction on the grain boundaries.
(2) The suitable solution treatment of 1953 aluminum alloy is 440 °C/1 h +
470 °C/1 h. The residual phases in the alloy are mainly impurity phases with Fe
and Si, and the mechanical properties are relatively better. When the temperatures
of second-stage solution treatment are higher than 470 °C, the recrystallization
fraction and average grain size increases. When the time of second-stage solution
treatment is greater than 60 min, the recrystallization fraction does not change
signiﬁcantly.

Inﬂuence of Cooling Intensity Difference
Between Upper and Lower Surface
to the Residual Stress Distribution
of 7050 Aluminum Alloy Plates
Junqiang Wang, Guanmei Niu, Zhongyu Yang, Hailong Cao
and Cheng Liu
Abstract Residual stress of aluminum alloy thick plates causes distortion in sub-
sequent machining operations for aircraft components. During spray quenching the
different cooling rates applied across the plate thickness to produce residual stresses.
If differential cooling is applied to the upper and lower surfaces, this could lead to an
asymmetric distribution of residual stress on both sides of plate. This in turn causes
potentially uncontrollable part distortion and dimensional inaccuracy during the
machining operation. In this study, a ﬁnite element (FE) model, taking into account
of the different cooling intensity on the upper and lower surfaces, was established to
predict the residual stress. Residual stress was measured using an ultrasonic stress
measuring apparatus. The results showed that the residual stress on the upper surface
was −174 MPa when the applied water ﬂux was 350 m
3/h, and −194 MPa on the
opposite surface where the corresponding water ﬂux was 300 m 3/h. This was found
to be in good agreement with the simulation results. It was found that the residual
compressive stress on the surface with the higher cooling intensity was smaller than
the side with lower intensity which is contrary to conventional wisdom. Therefore,
based on the difference of cooling intensity on the two surfaces, the guidance for
utilizing the roller-quenching-equipment can be derived ﬁnally.
Keywords 7050 aluminum alloy
/C1 Aerospace /C1 Residual stress
Quenching /C1 Pre-stretching process /C1 Finite element model
Introduction
Aluminum alloy 7050 is widely used for aeronautical and aerospace structural parts
due to its high speci ﬁc strength and good processing performance [ 1]. In order to
improve structural strength, safety performance and weight reduction, conventional

## Page 230

part assemblies are being replaced gradually by monolithic component machined
from large aluminum plates having a thickness between 60 and 200 mm [ 2, 3].
Therefore, 7050 aluminum alloy plate represents an essential material in modern
aviation industry. During the manufacturing of 7050 thick plate, a super saturated
solid solution is needed to bene ﬁt its subsequent age strengthening. Thick plate
quenching is commonly performed using roller-quenching-equipment where cool-
ing water is sprayed on the upper and lower surfaces of a thick plate. Limited by
equipment performance and quenching parameters, the upper and lower surfaces of
roller-quenching-equipment often apply an unequal water ﬂux which causes
inconsistent cooling rates on both sides of the plate. This promotes the development
of nonuniform residual stress distributions. However, because of the inherent
rigidity of thick sections, the distortion of 7050 plate is small and it is dif ﬁcult to
observe the nonuniformity effectively by using conventional methods. Therefore, it
is difﬁcult to provide guidance for the adjustment of water ﬂux on both sides of the
plate.
Recent advances in ﬁnite element (FE) technology have enabled heat treatment
simulations to be performed that can accurately predict temperature and stress ﬁelds
and other microstructural properties. Quenching simulations for 7050 aluminum
alloy have been performed using the FE method by various researchers [ 4–6]. Guo
established a FE model of spray quenching for 7050 aluminum alloy and the
simulation model was corrected based on measured temperature curve of quenching
[7]. Li predicted the quenching residual stress of a cross-shaped component by FE
software [ 8]. Xiong established three cooling FE models of a single nozzle on the
plate surface, and evaluated the model which provided good correlation with
experimental data [ 9].
In this study, an FE model of quenching is developed to study the effect of
different cooling intensities on opposite sides of a 7050 plate during spray
quenching. And the effect of different cooling intensities on the residual stress was
analyzed. Residual stress was measured using an ultrasonic stress measuring
apparatus. Based on the simulated and measured results, the difference in cooling
intensity on the upper and lower surface of roller-quenching-equipment can be
assessed based on the residual stress difference, for which the guidance for the
uniformity of the quenching residual stress can be provided.
FE Simulation Model
To study the in ﬂuence of differential cooling intensity applied to the upper and
lower surfaces on the residual stress distribution, a fully coupled 3D thermome-
chanical model was developed. The dimensions of the aluminum plate being
modeled were 80 mm (thickness) /C2 1200 mm (width) /C2 5000 mm (length) as
shown in Fig. 1. The plate was modeled using 213760 C3D8T elements. Due to the
steep thermal gradient that is generated during quenching across the thickness, an
element size of 10 mm (thickness) /C2 15 mm (width) /C2 15 mm (length) was used
222 J. Wang et al.

## Page 231

to ensure conformity and to optimize the computational time. Fully constrained
boundary conditions were applied to the center of the plate to re ﬂect the constraints
in quenching process.
The 7050 aluminum alloy was assumed to have isotropic properties and obey the
von Mises yield criterion. Poisson ’s ratio and density were speci ﬁed as 0.33 and
2800 kg/m 3. Other properties such as elastic modulus, yield strength, thermal
expansion coef ﬁcient and thermal conductivity of 7050 aluminum alloy plate in
quenched state were also assigned using values taken from the literature [ 10].
During the spray quenching process, the upper and lower surfaces and sides are
in contact with cooling water so the thermal losses were modeled using 4-node
elements extracted from model surface. Convective heat loss was determined using
Newton’s law of cooling [ 11] which can be stated as:

Experimental Setup
Spray quenching trials were carried out using industrial roller-quenching -equip-
ment where the water ﬂux on the upper and lower surfaces was 350 and 300 m 3/h
respectively and the roll speed was 150 mm/s. As the heat transfer coef ﬁcient
cannot be measured directly, it was derived from experimental cooling curves taken
at different thickness positions. Three blind holes were drilled in the plate with two
of them drilled at 5 mm depths from the upper and lower surfaces respectively
while the last one was drilled from the lateral side of the plate to the center. Then K
thermocouples were inserted and mounted using a high temperature glue.
At the center of the plate surface, heat transfer can be approximately represented
as one dimensional heat conduction. Based on the temperatures of the plate center
and 5 mm surfaces, the upper and lower temperatures can then be calculated [ 11].

To verify the in ﬂuence of cooling intensity difference between the upper and
lower plate surfaces on the residual stress distribution, the residual stress on the
upper and lower surfaces were measured using an ultrasonic stress measuring

surfaces can be measured. The measurement positions used are shown in Fig. 2.

Results and Discussion
Heat Transfer Coef ﬁcient Cooling curves measured and predicted by the simu-
lation model are shown in Fig. 3. Results show the simulation results agree rea-
sonably with the measured values.
The heat transfer coef ﬁcients of upper and lower surfaces in quenching process
can be calculated by Eqs. 4 and 5. When the temperatures of surface became greater
than 100 °C, the heat transfer coef ﬁcient increased with the decrease of the surface
temperature. After the surface temperature became lower than 100 °C, the heat
transfer coef ﬁcients decreased with cooling process. The peak value of the heat
transfer coef ﬁcient in spray quenching process appears at 100 °C, which is in
accordance with other published research results [ 14, 15]. The cooling intensity of
the upper surface is larger than the one of the lower surface, and the heat transfer
coefﬁcient of the upper surface is also relatively large compared with the lower
surface.

transversal directions, a 1/4 part section was utilized. The predicted residual stress
distribution of the upper and lower surfaces in the rolling direction is shown in

As showed in Fig. 8, temperature change process can be divided into three
stages.
S1 Stage Temperature of upper and lower surfaces decreased at the beginning of
the quenching process. While contraction was hindered by the center material and
then the tensile stress was produced. The yield strength was relatively low due to
the high temperature in this state. Then compression strain was produced at the
plate center and tensile plastic strain was produced at the plate surface. Because the
temperature of the lower surface was higher than the one of the upper surface, and
the yield strength and elastic modulus of lower surface was lower than the values of
the upper surface, this means the plastic deformation of lower surface is easier
leading to the results that the tensile plastic strain of lower surface is larger than
upper surface with the cooling shrinkage. So the shrinkage of the lower surface is
less than the upper surface in this stage.
As showed in Fig. 9, plastic strains appear on both sides of surface and plate
center. At the end of S1 stage, temperature of the upper surface cools to 20 °C,
while temperature of the lower surface reduces to 200 °C, and the temperature of
the plate center is 450 °C. So the stress of upper, lower and center of plate reaches
the yield strength at their temperatures respectively from 0 MPa of pre-quenching.

S2 Stage As showed in Fig. 9, plastic strains of this plate don ’t change in this
stage. Temperature of lower surface reduces from 200 to 20 °C, and the cooling
contraction is hindered by the material of the plate center, while the upper surface
temperature does not change in this stage.
Under the contribution of the lower surface contraction and the equilibrium
condition of force, tensile stress of the upper surface slightly decreases, and com-
pressive stress of center slightly increases. Figure 10 shows that the elastic strain of
the upper and lower surface is equal to that of the end of S2 stage, while the
temperature of the plate center does not descend to room temperature yet. So the
stress of the upper and lower surface is higher than yield strength at 200 °C but
lower than yield strength at 20 °C. The stress of plastic center is higher than the
yield strength of 450 °C (the beginning of S2 stage) but lower than the yield
strength of 350 °C (the end of S2 stage).

S3 Stage Temperature of plate center falls from 350 to 20 °C in this stage. As
showed in Fig. 9, the plastic strain of upper, lower and center is stable, so elastic
strain is dominant in this stage. However, plastic strain of the lower surface is larger
than that of the upper surface, which means the amount of cooling shrinkage on the
lower surface is greater than that of the upper surface, and the length of the lower
surface is greater than that of upper surface.
Temperature of plate center reduces from 350 to 20 °C in this stage, the tem-
perature of upper and lower surface cools to 20 °C at the end of S2 stage. The
shrinkage of the plate center is hindered by the outer surfaces, and then the tensile
stress appeared at the end of the quenching.
The upper and lower surfaces are compressed by the contraction force of the
center. Based on the analysis of S2 stage, the length of the lower surface is great
than that of the upper surface in this stage, which leads to the greater compressive
effect to the lower surface. Therefore, at the end of quenching the compressive
residual stress of lower surface is higher than that of the upper surface.

Based on the analysis of results, it can be inferred that the difference of cooling
intensity between the upper and lower sides of the roller quenching equipment by
measuring the difference of residual stress on both sides of the 7050 aluminum alloy
plate. This information can be used to provide guidance for adjusting the cooling
intensity of roller quenching equipment and to improve the uniformity of residual
stress distribution for 7050 aluminum alloy plate.
Summary and Conclusions
In this paper, an FE model was developed to study the effect of different cooling
intensity on the upper and lower plate surfaces during water-spray quenching. The
model was used to study the residual stress distribution that developed in thick 7050
plate during the quenching process. The accuracy of the residual stress predictions
were veri ﬁed using ultrasonic stress measuring apparatus. Based on the results
obtained, the following conclusions can be made:
(1) The residual stress gradually changes from a compressive stress state on the
surface to a tensile stress state in the center.
(2) For the two sides of 7050 aluminum alloy plate, the residual compressive stress
on the surface with the higher cooling intensity is smaller than that lower,
which is contrary to conventional wisdom.
This work shows that the residual stress measurement can be used to assess and
identify non-symmetrical cooling and can be used to modify the cooling water ﬂux
on both sides of the plate accordingly. This information can be used to provide the
232 J. Wang et al.

## Page 241

guidance regarding the adjustment of the roller quenching equipment, and the
uniformity of quenching and residual stresses between both sides of the plate can be
improved.

Effect of Solution Treatment
on the Microstructure and Fatigue
Properties of 7050 Aluminum Alloy
Xiang Xiao, Wei Li, Jian Zhao and Cheng Liu
Abstract The primary requirement of aircraft design is safety. The fatigue fracture
is dif ﬁcult to detect and prevent, which is a major safety hazard during aircraft
service. In this paper, the in ﬂuence of solution heat treatment on the microstructure
and resistant of fatigue crack growth of 7050 alloy is investigated. For one-stage
solution heat treatment, with the solution temperature increases, the area fraction of
the coarse constituent phase decreases and the recrystallization fraction increase,
and conresponsively the strength and fracture toughness increase and the fatigue
crack growth rates decrease. Under the two-stage solution heat treatment, the alloy
has the best fatigue crack growth resistance compare with the one-stage solution
heat treatments. The effect of solution heat treatment on the properties can be
understood on the basis of the combined in ﬂuence of the constituent phase and the
recrystallized fraction.
Keywords Aluminum alloy 7050
/C1 Solution treatment /C1 Microstructure
Fatigue properties
Introduction
Based on the aircraft design principles, the high strength aluminum alloys with
better fatigue resistance is developed [ 1–3]. 7xxx series aluminum alloys has
excellent performance including high strength, and excellent fracture toughness,
which are applied as structural engineering materials [ 1–5]. Many investigations
focus on the microstructures and properties of 7xxx alloy [ 3–7]. Robson [ 3]
investigate the microstructural evolution in AA7050 during post homogenization
cooling, and its in ﬂuence on behaviour during preheat, hot rolling, and solution

## Page 243

treatment. Lin and Starke [ 4] developed the effect of the Cu content and recrys-
tallization fraction on the property of fatigue crack growth in 7xxx alloys.
Generally, the heat treatments of 7xxx alloys is very important to improve the
combination properties [ 8]. During solution treatment, the coarse phase dissolves
and thus increase the supersaturated solid solubility of the matrix. Han et al. [ 8] ﬁnd
that the enhanced solution treatment can greatly decrease the content of the coarse
particles, and thus improve the fracture toughness of the 7050 alloy. Despite
detailed studies of the in ﬂuence of solution heat treatment on the microstructure and
properties, less attention is paid to the effect of solution treatment on the resistance
of fatigue crack growth in the 7xxx alloy. In this paper, the in ﬂuence of different
solution heat treatment on the microstructure and resistance of fatigue crack growth
of the 7050 alloy are studied.
Materials and Methods
The material is 70 mm thick 7050 alloy plate in hot rolled status. The plate is
solution heat treated under different conditions, as shown in Table 1, and then age
at 121 °C/6 h + 163 °C/12 h.
The samples location for metallographic observation is at the 1/4 of the thick-
ness. The microstructure observation of the samples is examined on JSM-6480
scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry
(EDX). The recrystallization fraction and the area fraction of particles is analyzed
by Image-Pro-Plus software. Nine images of each specimen are observed at a
magniﬁcation 200 times.
The tensile tests are conducted on Instron 5882 testing machine according to the
GB/T 228-2002 standard in the 1/2 thickness location of the plate. The plane-strain
fracture toughness tests are performed in the T-L orientation based on the ASTM
E399 standard. Fatigue crack growth testing are followed by ASTM E647 stan-
dards. The CT specimens for testing is located at the 1/4 thickness in the T-L
orientations as shown in Fig. 1. Fatigue crack growth testing is conducted at
R = 0.1. Pre-cracking is conducted at a DK of 8 MPa pm at the range of 10 –
20 Hz.

The Tensile Properties
Figure 7 shows that, under the one-stage solution heat treatment, the ultimate
tensile strength and yield strength increases with the increasing in temperature. The
strength reaches peak under the C-type heat treatment. With the temperature
increases, the coarse particles redissolves more fully, increasing the solution
supersaturation and precipitate strengthening effect, which has contributed to the
improvement of the strength.
Fracture Toughness
Figure 8 shows the value of K IC of the aged alloy with different solution heat
treatments. The results show that under one-stage solution treatment, the value of
K
IC increases with the increasing of temperature.
Many researchers present that the constituent coarse particles fracture occurs
previously [9–11]. The less the coarse particles on the fracture surface, the better the
facture toughness. The incoherent particles precipitate along grain-boundary make
the slip transfer dif ﬁculty, and bene ﬁts the strain localization. In 7050 alloy, the
crack mainly propagates along the high-angle grain boundaries [ 11, 12].
With the two-stage solution heat treatment in this paper, the content of con-
stituent particles and recrystallization fraction is lower than those of the one-stage
solution heat treatment, as shown in Figs. 4 and 6. It is reasonable that the
two-stage solution treatment resulting in the excellent fracture toughness.

It is worth noting that with the solid solution temperature increases, the area

Figure 9 shows that the da/dN values decreases with the solid solution temperature
increasing. It depicts that the impact of constituent phase on the resistance of fatigue
crack propagation is effective than that of recrystallization. Although the area
fraction of coarse particles under two-stage solution treatment is close to those of
the high temperature C-type one-stage solution treatment, seen in Fig. 4, the
resistance of fatigue crack propagation is better than those of this sample, seen in
Fig. 9. This is mainly due to the reduction of the recrystallization fraction in the
two-stage solution treatment, as shown in Fig. 6. The fatigue cracks easily propa-
gate along the recrystallized grain boundaries. The two-stage solution heat treat-
ment improves the solution supersaturation without increasing the total content of
alloying elements, while reducing the coarse phase content and decrease the
recrystallization fraction, results in the improvement of the resistance of fatigue
crack growth, which can improve the comprehensive performance of the 7xxx
aluminum alloy.

## Page 251

Summary
(1) With the solution temperature increase, the coarse constituent phase dissolves
into the matrix, while the recrystallization fraction correspondingly increases.
The strength, fracture toughness increases and the fatigue crack growth rates
decrease with the higher of solution temperature. The effect of constituent phase
on the property of fatigue crack growth resistent is more signi ﬁcant than that of
recrystallization fraction under one-stage solution heat treatment.
(2) The two-stage solution heat treatment is effective in decreasing the area fraction
of the constituent phases and the recrystallized grains compared with the
one-stage solution treatment, and hence in comprehensively improving the
strength, and resistance of fatigue crack growth of the 7050 alloy.

The subgrain boundaries could retard the propagation of corrosion. Compared with

Introduction
Al–Zn–Mg alloys have been widely used as structural materials due to their high
speciﬁc strength, excellent welding performance and satisfactory formability [ 1].
However, the con ﬂict of strength and corrosion performance has become one of the
bottlenecks to limit the application of these alloys [ 2]. To improve the overall
properties of ultra-high strength aluminium alloys, extensive studies have been
carried out. There are two main ways: the ﬁrst is to develop new heat treatment
processes to regulate precipitates at the grain boundaries [ 3, 4] and the second is to
form new dispersoids by adding trace elements to inhibit recrystallization and grain
growth while improving strength and corrosion resistance [ 5–8]. Generally, the
addition of Zr can effectively improve strength, re ﬁne grains and inhibit recrys-
tallization. The improvements of these properties are owing to the formation of
Al
3Sc dispersoids [ 9]. However, not much work has been carried out on the effect
of Zr on localized corrosion behavior of Al –Zn–Mg alloy.
In this work, an attempt has been made to further understand the mechanism of
better resistance to localized corrosion due to Zr addition based on grain structure
characterization by OM and grain boundaries microstructure characterization and
microchemistry examination by STEM.
Experimental
The hot-rolled thick plates of aluminium alloy with thickness of 3 mm were used
and the nominal compositions of the alloys have been shown in Table 1. The
samples were held at 470 °C for 1 h and then water quenched to room temperature.
After that the samples were aged at 120 °C to the highest strength.
The IGC immersion test was performed according to the IGC test standard of
GB7998-1987. The corrosive solution was made up of 57 gNaCl + 10 mLH

Discussion
The intergranular corrosion resistance is associated with the grain structure, the
precipitates at the grain boundaries and the PFZs [ 13]. Al–Zn–Mg–Zr alloy retains a
lot of ﬁne subgrains with LAGBs. The precipitates at the subgrain boundaries are
similar to those in the matrix and there are almost no PFZs at the subgrain
boundaries, which reduce the electrochemical dynamic of intergranular corrosion,
cut off the anodic corrosion channels to some extent and delay the corrosion
propagation along grain boundaries [ 10].
η phase has lower Ecorr than the aluminium matrix. GBPs (mainly η phase),
PFZs and the interior of the grains form corrosion micro cell. GBPs and PFZs often

## Page 259

preferentially dissolve as anodes, forming anode corrosion channels along the grain
boundaries [14]. The GBPs in Al –Zn-Mg specimens exhibit a higher content of Zn
and Mg than those in the Al –Zn–Mg–Zr specimens, which increase the electro-
chemical activity and decrease the resistance to corrosion [ 15]. The average size of
GBPs and the average width of PFZs in Al –Zn–Mg alloy are bigger than those in
Al–Zn–Mg–Zr alloy, which also promote dissolution of grain boundaries.
Conclusion
(1) Al –Zn–Mg–Zr alloy has smaller IGC and EXCO depth compared to Al –Zn–
Mg alloy. Zr addition can improve the resistance to localized corrosion of Al –
Zn–Mg alloy.
(2) Zr inhibits recrystallization and re ﬁnes grains. The unrecrystallized
microstructure could retard the corrosion propagation.
(3) The GBPs in the the Al –Zn–Mg specimens exhibit a higher content of Zn and
Mg than those in the Al –Zn–Mg–Zr specimens, which increase the electro-
chemical activity and decrease the resistance to corrosion. The average size of
GBPs and the average width of PFZs in Al –Zn–Mg alloy are bigger than those
in Al –Zn–Mg–Zr alloy, which also promote dissolution of grain boundaries.

## Page 261

Preparation and Corrosion Performance
of Silane/Ce Films on 7N01 Aluminum
Alloy
Sha Peng, Lin Sun, Hua-qiang Lin, Yun-lai Deng and Ming-an Chen
Abstract The protective bis-[triethoxysilylpropyl]tetrasul ﬁde (BTESPT) silane
ﬁlms doped with cerium were prepared on surface of 7N01 aluminum alloy by
dip-coating method. Single variable tests were used to obtain optimal silane con-
centration, curing temperature and cerium salt concentration. Fourier Transform
Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and scanning electron microscope (SEM) were used
to characterize structure of the formed ﬁlms. Corrosion performance of the ﬁlms
was evaluated by potentiodynamic polarization, electrochemical impedance spec-
troscopy (EIS) and soaking tests. The results show that the corrosion resistance of
the silane ﬁlm on 7N01 aluminum alloy is improved greatly by doping of Ce into
the silane ﬁlm. The proper silane volume fraction is 5% and the curing temperature
is 100 °C. The optimum cerium nitrate doping into the silane solution is
5 /C210
−3 mol/L.

## Page 262

Introduction
7N01 aluminum alloy is a kind of medium strength alloy, which has been widely
used in aerospace and railway transportation, etc. However, it is subjected to cor-
rosion by aggressive media like chlorine in the environment during service.
The most commonly used pretreatment for aluminum alloys are chromium
conversion coatings, which can provide excellent adhesion performance to organic
coatings coupled with self-healing ability. However, chromium-based compounds
are con ﬁrmed to be carcinogenic [ 1, 2]. Thus, it is needed to look for other
“self-healing” systems for replacement. Rare earth elements conversion ﬁlm on
aluminum alloy substrates behaves better. Besides, polymer coating is widely used
to protect the metal substrates from corrosion. However, the adhesion between alloy
substrate and polymer coating is not as good as expected, which could result in
peeling off of the coating [ 3, 4]. Silanes are hybrid molecules, possessing both
organic and inorganic functionalities. The hydrolysable inorganic functional groups
will establish covalent bonds with metal substrates, whereas the organic functional
groups are compatible with organic painting systems. By cross-linking of silanol
groups in the hydrolyzed silane molecules, the silane ﬁlm with Si –O–Si network
will be formed on the metal substrates [ 5–17], which provides a physical barrier to
penetration of water and electrolyte toward metal substrates. However, there are
some micro cracks and defects in the silane ﬁlm, leading to corrosion by the
electrolyte easily [ 18, 19]. Cerium salts like cerium nitrate not only possess cor-
rosion inhibition property but also self-healing property. Cerium ions will protect
the damaged zones from corrosion by forming cerium oxide or hydroxide [ 20–33].
Therefore the organic-inorganic hybrid ﬁlm by silane coupling agent doped with Ce
has become the most promising environment-friendly substitutes for chromium
conversion coatings [ 33–38].
The aim of the present work is to investigate the effects of three main factors,
silane concentration, the curing temperature of the silane ﬁlm and the cerium nitrate
concentration doping into the silane solution, on corrosion protection to 7N01
aluminum alloy.
Experimental
Pre-treatment of Aluminum Alloy Surface The 7N01 aluminum alloy coupons
were cut into size 15 mm /C215 mm /C22 mm panels. The obtained panels were
boiled in boiling water for 20 min, then sonicated in ethanol for half an hour,
washed with deionized water, dried in air, immersed in 0.3 M NaOH solution for
5 min, cleaned with deionized water and drying at room temperature. Then the
substrates were polished with SiC paper of grits 320 –1500, rinsed by tap water.
Next they were cleaned using ethanol and deionized water, dry in air before used.
256 S. Peng et al.

## Page 263

Preparation of Silane Solution The bis-[triethoxysilylpropyl] tetrasul ﬁde silane
solution was prepared by dissolving X% (v/v) of the silane in ethanol 95-X% (v/v)
and deionized water 5% (v/v). Doped silane solution was prepared by doping
cerium nitrate with different concentrations: 5 /C210
−1,5 /C210−2,5 /C210−3 and
5 /C210−4 mol/L into the previously prepared 5% silane solution. Due to the proper
concentration of cerium nitrate is 5 /C210−3 mol/L, more speci ﬁc cerium nitrate
concentrations, i.e. 1 /C210−3,3 /C210−3,7 /C210−3 and 9 /C210−3mol/L, were set up
to optimize the concentration. The doped silane solution was stirred for 0.5 h and
kept for 96 h before use.
Preparation of Silane Films The substrates were immersed in above prepared
silane solutions for 3 min and then curd at 100 °C (80, 120 °C) for 2 h in blast
oven to promote the cross-linking of silane.
Characterization of Silane Films The surface morphologies of the samples were
observed by ZEISS scanning electron microscope (SEM) operated at 20 kV. Energy
dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis was used for the chemical composi-
tion. A Nicolet spectrometer (Nicolet Nexus 670) was used to record the FTIR
reﬂection spectra on the samples. Sixty-four scans were collected for each mea-
surement over the spectral range of 500 –4000 cm
−1 with the solution of 2 cm −1.
Electrochemical Measurements and Soaking Test The potentiodynamic polar-
ization and Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) tests were carried out in
3.5 wt% NaCl aqueous solution at ambient temperature with a CHI Model 660E
electrochemical work station, in a three-electrode system with the sample as the
working electrode, a saturated calomel electrode as the reference electrode, and a
platinum panel as the counter electrode. The area exposed to the solution for the
samples is 1 cm
2. The polarization tests were conducted at a scanning rate of
0.002 v/s. The EIS measurements were carried out at the OCP. Soaking tests were
carried out in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution at ambient temperature.
Results and Analysis
Potentiodynamic Polarization Tests Figure 1 displays polarization curves of the
bare alloy and substrates pre-treated with different silane concentration in 3.5 wt%
NaCl solution (the curing temperature was 100 °C). Generally, anodic region
represents dissolution process of aluminum alloy substrates with increasing of
potential, cathodic region indicates cathodic hydrogen evolution reaction due to
water reduction. As shown in Fig. 1, the slope of the polarization curves in cathodic
region have little change, while the cathodic branches of the curves tend to a lower
corrosion current density with the addition of silane. It indicates that cathodic
hydrogen evolution reaction is suppressed to some extent by silane surface treat-
ment. The anodic current density of the samples treated with the silane reduced too,
indicating the silane ﬁlm somehow delays the dissolution process of aluminum

## Page 271

Discussion
In order to promote silanol groups in solution, silane hydrolysis conditions should
be controlled strictly. The silane concentration is a factor that affects the content of
silanol groups in the hydrolyzed solution [ 5, 6]. Curing of the silane ﬁlms will affect
the cross-linking of the silanol groups and interfacial interactions between silanol
groups and the substrate. The above results demonstrate that for 7N01 aluminum
alloy substrate the suitable silane volume concentration is 5%, and the curing
temperature is 100 °C.
Although the formed silane ﬁlm provides a physical barrier effect on electrolyte
uptake, it cannot offer a long-term protection to corrosion of the substrate. The
micro-pores in the silane ﬁlm favor the penetration of aggressive species to inter-
face between the silane ﬁlm and the substrate. In addition, the ﬁlm will lose its
protection function to substrates when it is damaged accidently during service.
Cerium salt is widely accepted as a good corrosion inhibitor for different metals
like aluminum alloys, magnesium alloys and galvanized steels [ 20–39]. It has been
reported that cerium hydroxide and cerium oxide deposit in the cathode area, which
hinders the transfer of electrons and thus reduced the corrosion rate. These Ce
4+
ions oxidized from Ce 3+ in the solution can be incorporated in the silane ﬁlm,
leading to the formation of Si –O–Ce network, which will enhance the physical
barrier effect of silane ﬁlm [ 38, 39]. The above results demonstrate that for 7N01
aluminum alloy substrates the optimum concentration for cerium nitrate doping in
the 5% silane solution is 5 /C210
−3 M. Doping cerium nitrate into the silane ﬁlm is a
procedure that combines the corrosion inhibition property of the cerium ions and
the physical barrier effect of silane ﬁlm. It should be noted that the silane –Ce
hybride ﬁlm can behave “self-healing” effect [34, 36, 39].
Conclusions
For 7N01 aluminum alloy substrates, the silane-Ce hybrid ﬁlm formed on its sur-
face can provide a relative longer-term protection to the substrates due to incor-
poration of Ce ions into the silane ﬁlm. Doping cerium nitrate into the silane ﬁlm
has combined the physical barrier property of the silane ﬁlm and the corrosion
inhibition property of the cerium ions. The proper volume fraction of silane is 5%
(v/v) and the curing temperature is 100 °C. The optimum cerium nitrate doping in
the 5% silane solution is 5 /C210
−3 mol/L. Excess higher or lower than
5 /C210−3 mol/L will result in a negative effect on the anti-corrosion property of the
formed ﬁlm.

Analysis on Causes of Flaring Cracks
in Thin-Walled 5A02 Aluminum Alloy
Tubes
Chuan Wang, Defu Li, Jie Hu, Guoqiang Chai, Shengpu Liu
and Zuoming Sun
Abstract In ﬂaring process of some thin-walled 5A02 aluminum alloy tubes ( “the
tubes”) upon cold rolling and annealing, longitudinal cracks occur at the ﬂared
ends. In order to ﬁgure out the reason for these ﬂaring cracks, observations and
experiments are conducted on the cracks at ﬂared ends by means of macroscopic
examination, metallurgical microscope, scanning electron microscope, energy
spectrometer and electronic universal testing machine. The experimental results
show that for the tubes with ﬂaring cracks, both the grain size and the difference
among grain sizes are large. The distribution of second phase particles is nonuni-
form and aggregation of precipitation phase exist. The cracks nucleate and prop-
agate under stress in regions where the inclusions are located. The defects, such as
scratches and pitting, existing on the inner surface of the tubes, cause the nucleation
and propagation of cracks in the defect regions under stress.

Introduction
The 5A02 aluminum alloy is one of Al –Mg series anti-rust aluminum alloy. It
cannot be strengthened by heat treatment, with low Magnesium content, high
plasticity and good formability. But its strength is low, which can be improved by
cold deformation [ 1]. Different sizes of thin-walled 5A02 aluminum alloy tubes
have been widely used in the ﬁeld of aviation, especially for the manufacture of fuel
lines and tubes in speci ﬁc systems for aircrafts [ 2]. One of tube connecting methods
requires ﬂaring process. Occasionally, the tubes partially crack at the ﬂared ends in
ﬂaring process. The cracks usually occur in the middle part of the ﬂared ends.
Figure 1a shows the macroscopic morphology of cracks after ﬂaring process.
Figure 1b is the SEM image of the ﬂared cracks, showing that the cracks start from
the widest part in the middle and extend longitudinally. The cracks have a negative
impact on product quality and normal use, and therefore it is necessary to inves-
tigate causes of the cracks for ﬁnding out further solutions.
Materials and Methods
Materials In this experiment, thin-walled 5A02 aluminum alloy tubes with outer
diameter of U22 mm * 1 mm (outer diameter * wall thickness, same as below) are
used. Production process is as following: Hot Extrusion ! the First Rolling !
Cutting ! Acid and Alkali Washing ! Intermediate Annealing ! Checking and
Repairing Materials ! the Second Rolling ! Checking and Repairing Materials !
the Third Rolling ! Alkali Washing to Remove Oil ! Final Annealing.
Methods Perform heat treatment of the U22 mm * 1 mm thin-walled tube prod-
ucts with different technological parameters using a chamber electric furnace,
investigate effects of annealing temperatures and cooling methods on grain size,

ﬂaring cracks. Different scenarios of annealing process for the ﬁnished product are

Take longitudinal specimens from the tubes. After process of initial grinding, ﬁne
grinding, mechanical polishing, and ultrasonic cleaning, the size and distribution of
the second phases and inclusions are observed by SEM JSM-6510. Using energy
spectrometer, the element proportion of both the second phases and inclusions are
detected. After process of electrolytic polishing and anodic ﬁlm coating, the lon-

Axiovert-200MA-Zeiss.
The tensile test is carried out by means of a WDW-300 electronic universal
tensile testing machine. Sand the inside and outside surfaces of the specimens with
sandpaper to eliminate defects. Upon con ﬁrmation of laminating the tubes without
cracks by ﬂattening test [ 3], the longitudinal tensile strength, yield strength and
elongation of the tubes after heat treatment are measured according to GB/T and
228.1-2010 [ 4], and the yield ratio is calculated. After ultrasonic cleaning, the
tensile fracture surface is observed by SEM (JSM-6510).
The tubes with a size of 22 mm * 1 mm are ﬂared by using a 72° rotating
conical tool on a ﬂaring device. The conical tool is lubricated by kerosene, and
keeps a constant feeding speed.
