Effect of the Second Phase Particles on Flaring Cracks Precipitated second
phase particles in the alloy have a signi ﬁcant effect on recrystallization behavior,
grain size and mechanical properties of the alloy [ 8]. The existence of the second
phase particles increase recrystallization driving force, and large size particles
(more than 1 lm) can act as nucleation sites for recrystallization to promote
recrystallization nucleation. Densely dispersed and ﬁne dispersed phase has strong
pinning effect on large-angle grain boundaries and low-angle grain boundaries, and
thereby inhibits the recrystallization process [ 9]. Mg is the main alloying element in
5A02 aluminum alloy. It is solid soluble in matrix a (Al) aluminum and functioned
as solution strengthening element. Fe and Si are impurity elements and form rec-
ognizable azure Mg
2Si phases and polygonal blocky (Fe, Mn) Al 6 phases in the

strengthening effect [ 11]. Nevertheless, because magnesium is oversaturated in
solid solution a (Al), the precipitated Mg 2Si phase is dif ﬁcult in nucleation, with
less core and large size precipitated particles, which has no advantage to reduce the
recrystallization grain size. For hard and coarse (Fe, Mn) Al
6 phases, ductility
decreases near them and therefore cracks tend to occur during the ﬂaring process.
Hot extrusion and multi-pass rolling make the coarse casted phases change into
small shape. Although dispersed phases are bene ﬁcial to hinder grain boundary
migration and to obtain ﬁne crystalline microstructure, nonuniformly distributed
and coarse second phase may incur coarse grain microstructure, which causes
cracks to appear in the ﬂaring process. Figure 5 is a SEM image of dispersed
second phases. Figure 6 is SEM image of nonuniformly distributed and coarse
second phases.
Effect of Inclusions on the Flaring Cracks It is observed that small inclusions
exist in the tubes by SEM. As shown in Figs. 7 and 9, the inclusions are different in
size and shape. Impurities in the ingot are not thoroughly puri ﬁed during casting,
and then become inclusions. Inclusions break into small pieces under subsequent
extrusion and rolling deformation. In the forming process of ﬂaring, the inclusions
will be separated from the metal matrix and produce microcracks under compres-
sive stress; With caliber of the ﬂared ends becomes larger, the microcracks become

It can be seen from the formula that the bigger the ﬂaring rate is, the bigger the
ﬂaring deformation degree is. When the deformation degree in ﬂaring process
becomes too large (reaches or exceeds a certain limit), cracks will occur at the ﬂared
ends. If causes described in 2.1 –2.5 are not found at cracking parts after macro-
scopic and microscopic observations, it can be inferred that tube cracks may be
caused by the ﬂaring rate reaching the limit.
Effect of Annealing Process on Mechanical Properties of Flared Tubes Yield
ratio (R p0.2/Rm) is an index to re ﬂect the formability of materials [ 13]. Large yield
ratio presents strong anti-deformation capability, which means plastic deformation
is not easy to occur. Small yield ratio presents higher forming limit and better
formability, which means ﬂaring formation is easier to be processed. The breaking
elongation of the tubes also re ﬂects the plasticity of the material. The larger the
breaking elongation is, the greater the plasticity is, which means low possibility to
crack [ 14]. Figure 6 shows curves of the yield ratio and breaking elongation under
different annealing temperatures, after heat preservation for 45 min, air cooling and
water cooling. It can be seen that the yield ratio of the unannealed tubes is large,
and the breaking elongation is small. After annealing process, the yield ratio
decreases signi ﬁcantly, while the breaking elongation increases signi ﬁcantly.
With the increase of annealing temperature, the yield ratio decreases. When the
annealing temperature is 410 °C, the yield ratio reaches the minimum value, while
the breaking elongation reaches the maximum value; as the temperature continues
to rise, the yield ratio becomes larger, while the breaking elongation becomes
smaller. The mechanical properties in air cooling state are better than that in water
cooling state. Therefore, the mechanical properties of the ﬂared tubes are optimal
when the annealing temperature of 410 °C and air cooling, which is bene ﬁcial to
ﬂaring formation (Fig. 14).

## Page 285

Conclusion
(1) The optimum annealing conditions of the tubes are annealing temperature
410 °C, holding for 45 min, air cooling, by which the microstructure with small
and uniformly distributed grains can be obtained. When the annealing tem-
perature is 370 and 390 °C, due to the existence of a certain amount of ﬁbrous
structure, ﬂaring cracks prone to occur. When the annealing temperature is
430 °C, coarsening recrystallized microstructure occur, and ﬂaring cracks
intend to occur as well.
(2) The cracks occurred easily when the nonuniform and coarse second phase
particles are distributed. This is because nonuniformly distributed second phase
particles easily incur coarse recrystallized microstructure, leading to a ductility
decrease near the coarse second phase particles.
(3) The inclusions in the tubes easily separate from the metal matrix and cause the
microcracks under stress, so ﬂaring cracks tend to appear near the inclusions.
(4) ﬂaring cracks tend to appear at the defects on the inner surface of the tubes
during process of multi-pass rolling.
(5) If the ﬂaring rate exceeds the ﬂaring deformation limit, cracks will occur at the
ﬂared ends.

Effect of Quenching Rate
on the Exfoliation Corrosion of 7020
Aluminum Plate
ShengDan Liu, Chen Guo, ZhenShen Yang, HuaQiang Lin, Lin Sun,
YunLai Deng and XinMing Zhang
Abstract The exfoliation corrosion resistance of 7020 aluminum plate treated with
different quenching rates after solution treatment was investigated through standard
exfoliation corrosion (EFC) immersion tests combined with scanning electron
microscopy (SEM). The results showed that the EFC resistance of this alloy plate
decreased with the decrease of quenching rate. The corrosion rank ranged from EA

Introduction
Al–Zn–Mg based alloys are widely used in aerospace and automotive industries
due to their high strength to weight ratio, good ductility and good welding property
[1]. The heat treatment is performed in several steps involving a solution treatment
followed by a rapid quench, and then aged. Slow quenching often leads to drop in
the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance after aging, so it is very
imperative to control the quenching rate [ 2]. As has been recently reported by
Kessler, below quench rate of about 150 K/min such alloys cannot be considered as
quench insensitive since a signi ﬁcant amount of quench-induced precipitation can
be detected such as MgZn
2 (η-phase) and Al 2Mg3Zn3 (T-phase) [ 3].
7020 aluminum are susceptible to different forms of corrosion such as exfolia-
tion corrosion (EXCO), inter-granular corrosion (IGC) and stress corrosion crack-
ing (SCC) [ 4]. In order to understand these corrosion mechanisms, a lot of
researches have been done. This present study tries to understand the correlation
between the quenching rate and the exfoliation corrosion.
Experimental Procedures
The alloy used in this study is 7020 aluminum alloy rolling plate with thickness of
12 mm. It has a composition (in wt%) of 4.65%Zn, 1.13%Mg, 0.15%Cu, 0.18%Cr,
0.14%Zr, 0.36%Mn, 0.41%Fe, 0.043%Ti, 0.14%Si and balance Al. The size of the

## Page 289

Results
Exfoliation Corrosion Evaluations The surface morphology of the aged speci-
mens during immersion is closely related to the quench rate. The specimens sub-
jected to slower quenching inclined to be corroded. Figure 1 shows that with the
increase of immersion time, localized corrosion tended to be more serious for all
specimens. After 48 h, notable layering and penetration into the specimen could be
seen in all specimens, for the specimen quenched in cold water the exfoliation
rating was EA, while greater penetration and loss of metal could be seen in the
specimen quenched in boiled water with the exfoliation rating of EB, what ’s more,
the corrosion status of the specimen quenched in air with the exfoliation rating of
ED was more serious than that of specimen quenched in boiled water. All speci-
mens were covered with black corrosion products.
Microstructures In addition to visual examination results, Optical micrographs of
cross-section can help to better understand the corrosion behavior, see Fig. 2.
Maximum depth of penetration of corrosion was measured and from Table 1 we
know that the maximum depth increased when decreasing the quench rate.
The SEM images in Fig. 3 show the precipitates near the grain boundaries in the
7020 aluminum alloy plate treated with different quenching rates. Obviously the
grain boundary coverage ratio by the precipitates increases with the decrease of
quenching rate. For the samples quenched in cold water, only some large bright
particles can be clearly seen (Fig. 1a). These are phases containing Al, Fe, Mn, Si
which have not been completely dissolved into the Al matrix during solution heat
treatment. When the quenching rate decreased to 165 °C/min (boiled water
quench), a lot of submicron GBPs can be clearly observed. This suggests that some
second phases precipitate on grain boundaries during the quenching process. When
the quenching rate is dramatically decreased into 38 °C/min, both the amount and
size of GBPs increase remarkably, indicating a higher grain boundary coverage
ratio by precipitates compared with the other two conditions (Fig. 1c). Even, the
grain structure is “depicted” by the GPBs in Fig. 1c owing to the precipitates on
grain boundaries. Therefore, these results show us that the quench sensitivity do
exist when the quench rate decreases dramatically.

Discussion
Many previous investigations on 7000 series alloy indicate that the low resistance to
exfoliation corrosion due to slow quenching is closely related to the changes in
microstructure and microchemistry near grain boundaries, however the individual
inﬂuence of each factor is not totally understood [ 5].
Grain boundary is a place where defects, impurities and alloying elements are
enriched. That ’s the reason why it is not as stable as the matrix. The electrode
potential of GBPs, PFZs and the matrix are not the same. It was reported that the
potential of η phase at GBs was −0.86 mV, while that of PFZs and matrix were
−0.57 and −0.68 V respectively [ 6]. Therefore it is reasonable to detect that η phase

Healing of Double Oxide Film Defect
Under Holding Pressure in A357 Alloy
Shanguang Liu, Chuanbiao Luo, Guoai Li, Zheng Lu
and Shenglong Dai
Abstract The bonding possibility of the double oxide ﬁlm defect was investigated
by holding pressure during solidi ﬁcation after holding in liquid A357 alloy for
13 min. The defect was modeled experimentally through contacting the oxide ﬁlm
layers of the A357 alloy. The composition and morphology of the oxide ﬁlm layers
were studied by SEM and EDX. The results show that the bonding area of the oxide
layer increased with the holding pressure during solidi ﬁcation. This is due to the
extrusion ability among the porous spinel gets stronger with the increase of holding
pressure, which means the liquid metal, could ﬂow through the porous spinel much
easier.

## Page 294

Introduction
Aluminum alloy castings have been widely used in the automotive and aerospace
industries. However, one signi ﬁcant drawback of aluminum castings is the double
oxide ﬁlms, which forms when the free surface of the molten metal folds upon
itself with some gas and entrained in the bulk liquid by surface turbulence [ 1].
The double oxide ﬁlms may promote the formation of other defects, such as
hydrogen pores [ 2–4] and Fe-rich phases [ 5] before the solidi ﬁcation and cracks in
the castings.
The oxide ﬁlm layer on the liquid aluminum alloy and the bonding possibility of
the two layers of a double oxide ﬁlm defect has attracted a wide attention. Tenorio
et al. [ 6] suggested the ﬁrst oxide formed on the liquid of commercial purity Al
alloy was an amorphous alumina layer. Then the amorphous oxide ﬁlm transformed
to c-Al2O3 or a-Al2O3. The transformation to a-Al2O3 is accompanied by a 24 pct
decrease in volume of the oxide, which would result in cracks in the double oxide
ﬁlm [ 7]. The cracks result from the transition make the melt contact with the
trapped air. Nyahumwa et al. [ 8, 9] revealed that the air entrapped in double oxide
ﬁlm could be consumed after an incubation time due to the transition. By utilizing
real-time X-ray radiography, Raiszadeh and Grif ﬁths [10] obtained that the volume
of a trapped air bubble decreased with time.
Aryafar [11] investigated the bonding possibility of double oxide ﬁlm defects in
A356 alloy by analyzing the variation of composition and morphology of these
layers, and concluded that the transformation of alumina to spinel was the main
reason of the two layers bonding with each other at several points. The subsequent
transformation from spinel to MgO in holding times of 13 min caused a strong
bonding between the two oxide layers. Amirinejhad et al. [ 12] studied the com-
position and possibility of bonding of oxide layers of Al melt with different content
of Mg. Their results supported the transformation mechanism and found that the
kinetics of these transformation depend on the Mg content of the melt. The higher
the content of the Mg, the transformation of MgAl
2O4 to MgO started earlier, and
the bonding time between Al bars decreased. Bakhtiarani ’s results [ 13] studied the
bonding possibility of oxide ﬁlm layers in Al –4.5Mg (wt%) alloy melt in which the
oxide ﬁlm layers were MgO. The results showed that no bonding points were
observed even after a holding time of 16 h. It means that possible healing mech-
anism of the double oxide ﬁlm layers is the transformation which involves the
rearranging of the atoms in oxide layers occurred during the holding time.
Strong bonding between the two oxide layers always need long time, ensuring
the transformation of MgAl
2O4 to MgO. However, the effect of holding pressure on
the bonding mechanism of the double oxide ﬁlm is not clear. In this study, the
experimental method used by Aryafar and Raiszadeh [ 11] was used to obtain the
double oxide ﬁlm. Then the Al bars were solidi ﬁed under different holding pressure
to examine effect of the holding pressure during solidi ﬁcation on healing possibility
of the double oxide ﬁlm.
290 S. Liu et al.

## Page 295

Experimental Procedure
The commercial alloys of A357 were prepared in a resistance heated furnace. The
composition of the alloys is shown in Table 1. The alloys were subsequently
poured into permanent molds in the shape of bars after degassing by bubbling pure
argon (99.99%) into the melt for 30 min.
The bars were machined to cylinders with the dimensions of Ø19 /C2 100 mm.
The contraction bases of the two sylinders were polished to 9 lm. Then the bars
with contacting the polished bases were inserted into a seamless extruded steel tube
with dimensions of Ø20 /C2 210 mm. The tube was surrounded by silica sand mold
(thickness was 20 mm) with 5% sodium silicate and CO
2 gas as a binder. The role
of sand mold is capable of controlling the liquid metal inside the tube to solidify at a
relatively slow rate during pressurizing process (Fig. 1).
The tube with sand mold was transferred to a resistance heated furnace with the
preset temperature of 1023 K. The melting time of the bars at the temperature was
measured in a separate experiment using a K-type thermocouple inserted in the
middle of the steel tube. The melting time was 420 s.
The ambient atmosphere may ﬂow into the trapped atmosphere between the two
oxide layers through the gap between the oxide layer around the bars and the inside
wall of the steel tube. The gap can be eliminated by removing the oxide layer
around the top of the upper bar with a sharp tool as soon as the melting of the Al
bars was completed.

The photograph of the oxide layers under different holding pressure during solid-

without holding pressure. No bonding points were observed. While the bars

without holding pressure in Fig. 2a. In the case of holding pressure at 600 kPa
during solidi ﬁcation, larger bonding areas were formed (Fig. 2c). It took a certain
force that could not be measured by tensile test machine to separate the bars with
holding pressure of 600 kPa.
Figure 3 shows the SEM micrograph of the oxide layer in Fig. 2a. The oxide
layer was smooth and no bonding points were observed. The EDS analysis revealed
that the ﬂat oxide layer, which contains relatively high content of magnesium, was
mainly composed of spinel and MgO. While the protrusion with lower magnesium
and oxygen content was the liquid metal extruded from the centre of these
protrusions.
Figure 4 displays the SEM micrograph of the oxide layer shown in Fig. 2b with
holding pressure of 300 kPa during solidi ﬁcation. The compositions of the oxide
layer and protrusions were similar with the Al bar without holding pressure. The
amount of the rose-shaped protrusions on the oxide layer increased obviously. The
grain boundary behind the oxide layer could be observed clearly.

The transformation of reaction Eq. ( 1), which occurs at the melt-oxide interface,
is associated with a volume expansion of about 18% [ 6]. The variation of volume
results in a local build up of stress and causes the alumina layer to fail. The fresh
A357 melt could then extrude through the ruptured oxide to form the rose-shaped
protrusions.
Yan [ 14] pointed out that the density of the casting was improved with the
increase of holding pressure due to the enhanced extrusion and in ﬁltration ability
among dendrites in counter-pressure casting. The extrusion ability of the liquid
metal through the failed alumina layer could still be enhanced. On the other hang,
the capillary force in the extrusion process was not the resistance but the driving
force due to the newly melt can wet the alumina once oxide layer was eliminated [ 7,
15]. Accordingly, with the increase of holding pressure, the extrusion ability of
liquid metal through the roughness spinel increased, causing the two oxide layer
bonded to each other by more and larger points than that without holding pressure
during solidi ﬁcation.
Conclusions
All of the alumina had transferred to porous spinel in the holding time of 13 min.
With the increase of holding pressure, the extrusion ability among the porous spinel
becomes strong. Compared with the process without holding pressure, more liquid
metal could ﬂow through the spinel resulting in larger bonding area and stronger
bonding between the two oxide layers. Meanwhile, the grain morphology could be
observed on the oxide layer after solidi ﬁcation due to the double oxide ﬁlm contact
with each other closely under the effect of holding pressure.

Keywords ADC12 alloy
/C1Y modi ﬁcation /C1Microstructure /C1Impact toughness
Introduction
Die cast aluminum alloy with high speci ﬁc strength, good corrosion resistance,
electrical conductivity and heat conductivity has been widely used in automotive,
electronic, communication and aerial industries. Especially with the rapid devel-
opment of automobile industry all over the world, the mechanical properties of
automobile die cast parts fabricated by aluminum alloy are becoming higher and
higher. At present, Al –Si–Cu series die cast alloys including ADC12 exhibit high
casting strength, low coef ﬁcient of thermal expansion, good corrosion resistance,
casting property and cutting performance, and is widely used in the automobile
gearbox, engine housing, air valve and so on. However, its present main problem is
relatively low strength and poor ductility where the elongation is not generally more
than 2% at ambient temperature. The researchers have tried to ameliorate the
microstructure and enhance the performance by adding the rare earth RE [ 1–11].
Compared with La, Sm and Ce, Y being rich in reserves exhibits the unique
regularity of the extracellular electron distribution leading to large solid solubility in
aluminum. Meanwhile, it can purify the aluminum melt effectively. The present
authors have found that the as-cast microstructure can be re ﬁned signiﬁcantly when
0.85%Y (mass fraction) is added into ADC12 alloy. The Si-rich phase changes
from long needle or plate to short rod or globosity. Meanwhile, few acicular new
phase Al
3Y precipitates. The tensile strength and elongation reach 225 MPa and
3.5% at ambient temperature, respectively, which increase by 20 and 133% com-
pared with the corresponding values of ADC12 alloy, respectively [ 12]. Impact
toughness, an important dynamic mechanical property for engineering structural
materials, can affect the performance and structural reliability signi ﬁcantly.
However, the effect of RE on the impact toughness of ADC12 alloy has not been
investigated so far. Therefore, the present paper is focused on studying the evo-
lution on impact toughness when 0.85%Y is added into ADC12 alloy and subse-
quently the two alloys are solution-treated. Then, the inherent relationship between
the impact toughness and the microstructure is established, and the effective way to
obtain aluminum alloy with high impact toughness is put forward.
298 Z. Huang et al.

## Page 302

Experimental
Two alloy ingots were prepared by melting ADC12 alloy ingot and Al –28.22%Y
(mass fraction) master alloy in an electric resistance furnace. When the melt tem-
perature of ADC12 alloy ingot reached 973 K, the master alloy was added into the
melt. Then, the melt was stirred twice within 1 h to ensure the compositional
homogeneity. After adding the re ﬁne and degassing agents, the melt was held at
1033 K for 30 min. When the temperature cooled to 973 K, the melt was poured
into the wedge permanent mold with a preheated temperature of 523 K, and then
as-cast samples were obtained. Then they were solution-treated at 793 K for 8 h in
a heat-treating furnace, and water cooled to obtain the solution-treated samples.
Y content was measured by inductively coupled plasma analyzer (ICP, JY
Ultima2). All specimens were etched with 4% HNO
3 (volume fraction) in ethanol.
Then, microstructural observation was carried out on optical microscope (OM,
Leica DM IRM), scanning electron microscope (SEM, MLA 200 and JEOL
JXA-8100) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, FEI Quanta 200). Phase
analysis was carried out on X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D/MAX-RC) with Cu K a
radiation. Standard unnotched impact specimen with dimension of 10 mm /C210
mm /C255 mm was tested on the pendulum impact testing machine at ambient
temperature. Fracture morphology was observed using SEM.
Results and Discussion
Figures 1 and 2 show the OM and SEM graphs of as-cast ADC12 and
ADC12-0.85Y alloys, respectively. According to the phase diagram of Al –Si–Cu
alloy, the as-cast microstructure of ADC12 alloy composes of gray a-Al matrix,
dark long needle or plate Si-rich phase, light irregular Al 8SiFe2 phase and few
Al2Cu phase (see the arrows in Figs. 1a and 2a). When 0.85%Y is added, the
as-cast microstructure is re ﬁned signi ﬁcantly. Meanwhile, the long needle or plate
Si-rich phase disappears completely, and the Si phase precipitates between den-
drites by short rod or globosity (see Figs. 1ba n d 2b).
Figure 3 shows the EDS spectra of as-cast ADC12 and ADC12-0.85Y alloys,
and the results are listed in Table 1. It can be seen that the as-cast microstructure of
ADC12 alloy composes of a-Al matrix, long needle or plate Si-rich phase (see
spectrum 3 in Fig. 3a), irregular Al –Si–Fe phase (see spectrum 1 in Fig. 3a) and
few small block Al –Cu phase (see spectrum 2 in Fig. 3a). When 0.85%Y is added,
the acicular Al –Y phase appears in addition to the abovementioned phases (see
spectrum 2 in Fig. 3b and spectrum 3 in Fig. 3c).
In order to determine the phase composition, the XRD spectra of as-cast ADC12
and ADC12-0.85Y alloys are compared (see Fig. 4a). It is seen that the XRD
spectrum of as-cast ADC12 alloy consists of most a-Al matrix, Si phase and few
Al
2Cu and Al 8SiFe2 phase peaks. When 0.85%Y is added, the peak of Al 3Y phase

ADC12 alloy (see Fig. 5). The cleavage steps and river patterns in the impact
fracture of the two alloys decrease signi ﬁcantly. Meanwhile, the dimples increase
obviously and become deeper. Especially, the impact fracture of ADC12-0.85Y
alloy changes from the brittle fracture to the ductile fracture, where the large deeper
dimples exist. It is consistent with the change in the impact toughness for the two
alloys (see Fig. 9).
The main factors affecting the impact toughness of material include grain size,
impurity defect and second phase. The ﬁner the grain size is, the larger the area of
grain boundary is, the more the energy consumed into the deformation in a certain
region and the crack propagation is, and the better the impact toughness is. Grain
boundary is the resistance to the crack propagation. The decreasing dislocation
piled up to grain boundary can reduce the stress concentration. The total area of
grain boundary increases, and the impurity concentration on grain boundary
decreases, which can inhibit the intergranular brittle fracture. Grain boundary is the
disordered region for atomic arrangement, and the adjacent grains exhibit different
(a) ADC12 (b) ADC12-0.85Y

graphs with high magni ﬁcation
(a) ADC12 (b) ADC12-0.85Y

Enhancing the Impact Toughness of ADC12 … 303

## Page 307

orientations. Therefore, when plastic deformation pass through grain boundary from
one grain into another grain, it is dif ﬁcult due to the large grain boundary resistance.
In addition, the change sliding direction can consume more energy compared with
the intragranular deformation. Impurity defects on grain boundary can weaken the
grain boundary and increase the tendency of intergranular fracture. Meanwhile,
impurity defects within one grain maybe the place for crack initiation. Compared
with the matrix, the second phase maybe the site for crack initiation, and play a
detrimental effect on the impact toughness of material. The harmful effects can be
weakened effectively by few ﬁne dispersed second particles [ 14].
In the present paper, all impact toughness tests are carried out at ambient tem-
perature, and the difference in the impurity defects is slight for all specimens.
Therefore, grain size and second phase become the main in ﬂuencing factors. The
impact toughness of material mainly composes of the powers for elastic deforma-
tion and plastic deformation, respectively. For aluminum alloy, the power for
plastic deformation, mainly re ﬂected in the initiation and propagation of crack,
exhibits larger than the power for elastic deformation. Therefore, the factor is
mainly reﬂected in the crack initiation and propagation. Generally, under the impact
force, crack should generate at the interface between a-Al matrix and the second
phase. a-Al matrix, a solid solution, exhibits low strength and good plasticity, while
the second phase, an intermetallic phase, does hard and brittle. Under the impact
force, material becomes the plastic deformation. The microcracks ﬁrst initiate on the
phase boundary owing to no synchronization between plastic deformations for two
phases, and propagate until to fracture. Thus, the impact toughness is relative to the
strength of a-Al matrix and morphology, size, distribution and volume fraction of
the second phase [ 14].
For ADC12 alloy, as-cast microstructure exhibits coarse, and meanwhile many
long needle or plate Si-rich phase exists. Crack is easy to initiate the interface
between the long needle or plate Si-rich phase and a-Al matrix, and propagate until
to fracture. Therefore, the alloy exhibits the very poor impact toughness, where the

value anK is only 3.8 J/cm 2. When 0.85%Y is added, the as-cast microstructure is
reﬁned signi ﬁcantly. Meanwhile, the long noddle or plate Si-rich phase disappear
completely, and changes to short rod or globosity between dendrites, which can
weaken the harmful force on the impact toughness. Therefore, the alloy exhibits the
much better impact toughness, where the value a
nK increases to 10.8 J/cm 2. After
solution treatment, partial second phases dissolve into a-Al matrix, resulting in an
increase in the strength of a-Al matrix. At the same time, the long noddle or plate
Si-rich phase in ADC12 alloy disappears completely, and the second phases in the
two alloys exhibit short rod or globosity leading to weaken the harmful effect
obviously. Taking the abovementioned two factors, the impact toughness of the two
alloys becomes further better. Especially, the value a
nK increases to 21.9 J/cm 2 for
ADC12-0.85Y alloy, with the amplitude by 476% compared with the as-cast value
for ADC12 alloy.
Summary
When 0.85%Y is added into ADC12 alloy, as-cast microstructure is re ﬁned sig-
niﬁcantly. The coarse primary a-Al dendrites changes into ﬁne cellular and equixed
grains, and the Si-rich phase does from long needle or plate to short rod or glo-
bosity. Meanwhile, few acicular new phase Al 3Y precipitates. After solution
treatment, the long needle or plate Si-rich phase disappears completely, and partial
second phases dissolve into a-Al matrix. The remaining second phases precipitate
by short rod or globosity, and the segregation degree between dendrites decreases.
Alloying with Y and heat treatment are one of the effective methods to enhance the
impact toughness of ADC12 alloy. When 0.85%Y is added and the alloy is
solution-treated at 793 K for 8 h, the value a
nK can reach 21.9 J/cm 2, with the
amplitude of 476% compared with the corresponding as-cast value of ADC12 alloy.
Meanwhile, the fracture exhibits the typical ductile fracture with dimples.

Effects of Mn Content on Microstructure
and Hardness of 6061 Aluminum Alloy
Xingyu Ding, Yongqi Cheng, Peng Zhang, Yong Dong,
Zhengrong Yao and Peisong Jiang
Abstract Microalloying is an effective way to improve material properties. By
means of scanning electron microscope/energy spectrum, X-ray diffraction, met-
allographic analysis and hardness tests, the effects of microalloying element Mn on
as-cast, homogenization, aging microstructure and hardness were investigated in the
basic of 6061 aluminum alloy. The results showed that the as-cast 6061 alloy
consisted of the primary Al, the irregular strip-shaped Al
8(FeMn)2Si phases,
ﬁshbone-shaped Al 5(FeMn)Si phases and Mg 2Si phases. Through microalloying,
the morphology of phases transformed from irregular strip into ﬁshbone obviously
as Mn content increased. After homogenization process, Mg 2Si phase dissolved
into the alloy matrix but iron-rich phase cannot. With the increase of Mn content,
the phase transformation of ﬁshbone-shaped Al
5(FeMn)Si to particle-shaped
Al8(FeMn)2Si occurred. During solution-aging treatment, higher Mn content
could promote the precipitation of stable phase b(Mg2Si). Mn had a signi ﬁcant
effect on the morphology of the crystalline phases which had a direct in ﬂuence on
the hardness of aluminum alloy. It was found that the addition of 0.24 wt% Mn to
6061 aluminum alloy could make the as-cast and aging alloys achieve the maxi-
mum hardness value 67 and 105 HBW, respectively.

Keywords 6061 aluminum alloy /C1Constituent /C1Hardness /C1Mn
Introduction
6061 aluminum alloy, because of its quite high speci ﬁc strength, good corrosion
resistance and excellent formability, has been widely applied in the ﬁeld of aero-
space, transportation and construction [ 1, 2]. The segregation of 0.3 –0.4 wt%
impurity Fe in the interdendrite usually induces the formation of coarse inclusion
phases, which have an adverse in ﬂuence on mechanical properties of the alloy [ 3,
4]. The previous researches showed that [ 5–7], some transitional elements Mn, Cr,
Zr added in the alloy can improve the property of this 6-series alloys. The effects of
those microalloying elements on microstructure and mechanical properties in
6XXX alloys, especially Mn element, have been reported more and less. However,
few researches on the effects of minor Mn added in the basic of speci ﬁc alloy were
reported. In this paper, the effects of Mn content on as-cast, homogenization and
aging microstructure and hardness of 6061 alloy aluminum were investigated to
obtain an optimal Mn content.
Experimental Procedure
Smelting materials: industrial 6061 aluminum alloy, Al –50%Mg, Al –5Ti–1B and
Al–10%Mn intermediate alloys.
The above-mentioned alloys were added in a certain order and melted in the pit
furnace. The melting temperature was set as 750 °C. The way of re ﬁnement was
blowing Ar with the rotor revolved. After adding Al –5Ti–1B alterant for 10 min,
the melt was poured into the iron die with the size of 35 mm /C245 mm /C2150 mm.
By the way, minor Mg was added to replenish the melting loss of Mg from the
original 6061 aluminum alloy. Based on experimental study, it was known that the
content of melting loss of Mg was about 80 wt%. Hereby, four alloys with different
Mn content were prepared. Chemical composition of the experimental alloys is
shown in Table 1. The sample pieces were cut with the size of 10 mm /C210
mm /C210 mm. The mixed acid 1 mL HF, 1.5 mL HCl, 2.5 mL HNO
3 and 95 mL

treatment for 175 °C /C210 h. Diffraction peaks of the phases which were detected

Metallographic microstructures of the alloy under as-cast, homogenizing and

tester with digital display.
Results and Discussion
Effects of Mn Content on As-Cast Microstructures of the Alloys Optical
micrographs and SEM photographs of the as-cast alloy with diverse Mn content are
shown in Fig. 1. As can be seen from (a
1)–(d1) of Fig. 1, as-cast microstructures are
composed of the primary a(Al) and low-melting eutectic distributed in the matrix,
and they come into being dendritic network with different degree. This is due to
non-equilibrium eutectic structure formed during the solidi ﬁcation process under
overquick cooling rate and distributed along the boundary and dendrites of the
grains, which leads to the formation of the a(Al) solid solution. Comparing four
groups of alloys, it shows that when the initial Mn content is 0.24 wt%, as-cast
microstructures of 0# alloy seem to be the best with ﬁne and uniform equiaxed
grains, of which dendritic crystals are eliminated obviously. As Mn content
increases, the extent of dendritic grains becomes more serious and the grains begin
to coarsen. The re ﬁnement effects of Mn on as-cast microstructure are due to the
heterogeneous nucleation of Mn. The interaction between Mn and Al can lead to

But over a certain amount of Mn, it will signi ﬁcantly increase supersaturation of the
solid solution and reduce composition undercooling of the crystallization front

can be seen from the scanning electron micrograph as shown in Fig. 1 that there are
a large number of crystalline phases in the as-cast alloy, including irregular

2Si
phase, which increase with the Mn content. Combining the X-ray diffraction

2)–(d2), Point 1 is the irregular

phase. The X-ray diffraction peak shows the Al 8Fe2Si and Al 5FeSi phases without
Mn element. However, the presence of Mn element is detected in the EDS spectrum
(Table 2), and the ratio of (Fe + Mn)/Si is the same as that of Fe/Si of Al 8Fe2Si and
Al5FeSi phases, indicating that Mn has a certain function of substitution of Fe [ 9].
When Mn content is 0.24 wt%, the crystalline phases appear irregular strips pri-
marily without ﬁshbone shape obviously, indicating that the segregation degree of
the microstructures is low. With the increase of Mn content, the crystalline phases
of the alloy appear complex and staggered ﬁshbone shape, which are distributed on
the boundary and dendrites of the grains largely. It has no doubts that the segre-
gation degree of the microstructures is serious. Also it is found that the morphology
of the crystalline phases changes from irregular strip to coarse ﬁshbone with the
increase of Mn content.

Effects of Mn Content on Aged Microstructures of the Alloys The metallo-
graphic structures achieved from solution-aging treatment under the condition of
535 °C /C275 min + 175 °C /C210 h are shown in Fig. 5. It can be seen that the
lattice dendrites existing in the as-cast alloy gradually stretches after the aging
treatment, the grain boundary tends to be straight and the grains show equiaxed
crystal state. Compared with the as-cast alloy, the grain is not coarsened, indicating
that under the solution-aging process, the microstructure of the alloy is in the
direction of its favorable development. The analysis results of EDS with scanning
electron show that the type of crystalline phases does not change after annealing
treatment. This is because the solid solubility of the impurity Fe element in the
matrix is very low, and diffusion rate of Mn under the temperature of solidus line is
very slow, which make the AlMnFeSi phase extremely dif ﬁcult to dissolve in the
aluminum matrix [ 11]. With the increase of Mn content, the precipitation of black
spot-shaped phases in the microstructure increases obviously. These phases are
proved to be b(Mg
2Si) phase. This indicates that the precipitation of b(Mg2Si)
equilibrium phase could be promoted when Mn content reaches a high value.
Effects of Mn Content on Hardness of the Alloys The variable hardness curves
of the alloys as-cast and annealing with Mn content are shown in Fig. 6. It can be
seen that when the initial Mn content is 0.24 wt%, as-cast and aging hardness are
the largest, Brinell hardness reaches about 67 and 105 HBW, respectively.

Solution-aging treatment increases its hardness by 56.7%. With the increase of Mn
content, as-cast and aging hardness begin to decrease, and decreased degree of
as-cast hardness is more serious than that of aging hardness. When Mn content is
0.34 wt%, as-cast hardness is about 55.2 HBW and aging hardness is 99.5 HBW.
The upgrade rate of the hardness from solution-aging treatment is about 80.2%.
When Mn content exceeds 0.34 wt%, as-cast hardness tends to increase slightly,
while the aging hardness decreases further. When Mn content is 0.45 wt%, as-cast
hardness is 58.44 HBW, aging hardness is 93.5 HBW, and the improvement of the
hardness is about 60%. When Mn content exceeds 0.45 wt%, as-cast hardness and
aging hardness improve a few. When Mn content is 0.53 wt%, as-cast hardness and
aging hardness are 59.12 and 95 HBW, respectively. The solution-aging treatment
increases its hardness by 60.65%. The results show that the as-cast alloy with
0.34 wt% Mn content can maximize the strengthening effect according
solution-aging process, but for the as-cast alloys with other Mn content, the effects
of which make no difference. From the comprehensive and overall comparison, the
as-cast alloy with 0.24 wt% Mn content can achieve the highest hardness. As the
positive correlation of the strength and hardness, it can be seen that the addition of
the appropriate amount of Mn can make 6061 aluminum alloy to obtain higher
strength performance.
Analysis and Discussion The aging strengthening effect of aluminum alloy is
related to its coherent and semi-coherent precipitated phase in the aging process.
For the Al –Mg–Si alloy, the sequence of precipitated phase is SSSS ! GP
(spherical) ! b″ (needle) ! b′ (rod) ! b (Mg
2Si) [ 12]. It begins to form a
spherical GP area, then grows rapidly, elongates along the matrix [100] direction
and becomes acicular b″ phase, which makes the matrix generate compressive
stress to improve strength of the alloy. Continuing to raise temperature or prolong
time, a semi-coherent b′ transition phase will be formed. Finally, at the interface of
b′ and the matrix, b(Mg
2Si) phase is formed by the depletion of the b′ transition

## Page 318

phase. Because of its complete loss of cohesive relationship with the matrix, so the
appearance of b phase means that the hardness and strength of the alloy decrease
signiﬁcantly. In addition, the order of enhancement is b″ > b′ > b.
Relevant studies showed that in the homogenization or solution process of the
alloy, Mn dissolved in a(Al) phase can form a no coherent Mn-containing dispersed
hard point phase with the matrix, which can not be cut by dislocation [ 13]. It can be
used as a nonuniform nucleation core of the aging strengthening phase b′(Mg2Si) to
promote its precipitation, so as to strengthen the alloy and make it achieve higher
strength and plasticity [ 14]. This indicates that an appropriate amount of Mn content
can improve the aluminum alloy microstructure and enhance its performance. On
the other hand, for Al –Mg–Si alloy, AlFeSi and AlMnSi and other secondary
strengthening phases consume a part of Si required by the main strengthening b″
and b′ phase necessarily [ 15], and excessive Mn will promote the precipitation of b
equilibrium phase, which greatly weaken the enhanced effect of aging treatment.
Therefore, too high Mn content will lead to the decrease of the strength and
hardness of the alloy. Considering the effects of Mn on the strength synthetically,
the strength of 6061 aluminum alloy achieves maximum value when Mn content is
0.24 wt%. But mechanical properties of 6061 aluminum alloy will decrease with
Mn content increased sequentially.
Summary
1. The as-cast alloy had irregular strip-shaped Al 8(FeMn)2Si, ﬁshbone-shaped
Al5(FeMn)Si and a little Mg 2Si crystalline phase. As the Mn content increased,
the morphology of the phases transformed from irregular strip into ﬁshbone
obviously.
2. After homogenizing treatment, Mg 2Si phase dissolved into the alloy matrix.
With the increase of Mn content, the phase transformation of ﬁshbone-shaped
Al5(FeMn)Si to particle-shaped Al 8(FeMn)2Si occurred.
3. During solution-aging treatment, higher Mn content can promote the precipi-
tation of stable b (Mg2Si) phase.
4. When adding 0.24% Mn to 6061 aluminum alloy, the as-cast and aging alloys
achieved the maximum hardness value 67 and 105 HBW, respectively.

Abstract Homogenization heat treatment on an Al –0.92Mg–0.78Si–0.60Zn–
0.20Cu–0.12Zr alloy was investigated by OM (optical microscopy), DSC (differ-
ential scanning calorimetry), energy dispersive X-ray diffractometry (EDX), and
SEM (scanning electron microscopy) in the present work. The results indicated that
with homogenization temperature increasing, the grains enlarged and the secondary
phases dissolved into matrix gradually. The residual phase was Fe-rich particle after
the alloy homogenized at 550 °C for 24 h and Zr-containing particle with larger
size precipitated. While grains of the alloy with almost no change were observed
after double-stage homogenization treatment, and the phases dissolved into matrix
completely and Zr-containing particle with smaller size precipitated. Meanwhile the
size of Zr-containing particle changed little with prolongation of second-stage time.
The ideal homogenization process for the alloy was to homogenized at 430 °C for
10 h, subsequently followed by 550 °C for 24 h.

competitiveness of their products [ 1, 2]. Car body accounts for 30% of the total
weight, and it is obvious for car to reduce the weight of car body. Therefore,
more and more aluminum alloys are used for body panels replacing steel sheets.
Al–Mg–Si alloys are considered among the most promising candidates for
aluminum automotive body panel applications, due to their favorable corrosion
resistance, weldability, low scrap compatibility and low cost [ 3, 4].
As heat treatable aluminum alloys, homogenization is a signi ﬁcant process for
Al–Mg–Si alloys. The alloy investigated in the present was Zr addition.
Composition of the alloy was different from the previous work. Zr element was
usually added to Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloys, and two-stage homogenization heat treat-
ment was used [ 5, 6]. The Zr containing phase precipitated during homogenization
treatment, which effectively inhibited grain growth during homogenization and the
occurrence of recrystallization during hot deformation. Considering the precipita-
tion of Zr-containing particles and the dissolution of coarse phases, the investiga-
tion of Al –0.92Mg–0.78Si–0.60Zn–0.20Cu–0.12Zr alloy was necessary.
Experimental Procedure
Chemical composition of the alloy was Al –0.92Mg–0.78Si–0.60Zn–0.20Cu–
0.12Zr (wt%). The alloy used in the present work was prepared from high-purity
aluminum, magnesium, copper, zinc, Al –10Mn, Mg –30Zr and Al –14Si master
alloys. The raw materials were melted in a graphite crucible in an electrical resis-
tance furnace and then cast in a cast iron mould at 700 °C. The microstructure of
the alloy was studied by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), optical micro-
scopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive X-ray
diffractometry (EDX) analysis. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) under an
argon atmosphere was performed using an equipment of DSC NETZSCH STA
409C/CD, the temperature ranged from 20 to 600 °C with 30 mg Al (99.99%) as a
reference, and the heating rate was 10 °C/min.

Microstructural Evolution of the Alloy After Double-Stage Homogenization
The addition of Zr with 0.1 wt% can form Zr-containing dispersoids during
homogenization, which can effectively pin the grain boundary and hinder the
enlargement of grains [ 9, 10]. After single stage homogenization treatment of 550 °
C for 24 h, the Zr-containing phase has big size and low content, which has an
weak effect. Hence, a double stage homogenization treatment regime is employed
and 430 °C for 10 h is regarded as the ﬁrst step homogenization regime on the
grounds of the double stage homogenization regimes of Zr-containing 7000 series
aluminum alloys. The second step homogenization temperature employs 550 °C
and the second step homogenization time is investigated to ensure a suitable double
stage homogenization regime.
Figure 6 gives the optical microstructure of the alloy with single and double
stage homogenization treatments. After double stage homogenization treatment, the
dendritic structure is completely diminished, the phase dissolve suf ﬁciently and the
grain boundary is ﬁne. With the prolonging of the second step homogenization
time, no obvious enlargement of the grains is observed. Compared with the single
stage homogenization treatment, the grain size of the alloy treated by the double
stage homogenization treatment is smaller.
The SEM morphology of the alloy with single and double stage homogenization
treatments are shown in Fig. 7. It can be seen that the phase dissolve suf ﬁciently
and the remaining phase is Fe-rich phase. An analysis is performed on the

Conclusions
The as-cast alloy was typical dendritic structure. The AlCuMgSi and Mg 2Si phase
dissolve completely while Zr-containing phase has bigger size after homogenization
treatment at 550 °C for 24 h. After two-stage homogenization treatment at 430 °C
for 10 h and 550 °C for 24 h, the residual phase was Fe-rich phase, and the
Zr-containing particle with smaller size precipitated. Meanwhile the size of
Zr-containing particle had little change with prolongation of second-stage time.

Microstructure and Stress Corrosion
Behavior of MIG Welded Joint
Al–Zn–Mg Alloy
Lingying Ye, Wenqing Yang, Chuqi Jiang, Huaqiang Lin,
Shengdan Liu, Jianguo Tang, Yunlai Deng and Xinming Zhang
Abstract The microstructures and stress corrosion behaviors of the welded joint in
a MIG welded Al –Zn–Mg alloy were investigated by slow strain rate test and OM,
EBSD, TEM observation. The results indicated that the stress corrosion cracking
index of welded joint is bigger than the base metal, which means the stress cor-
rosion resistance of base metal is better than MIG welded joint. The stress corrosion
of MIG welded joints mainly occur in the weld zone and heat affected zone, which
indicates that they are the weak areas of welded joints. The fracture mode of the
joint in 3.5% NaCl solution are intergranular brittle fracture and partial trans-
granular dimple fracture, while that of base metal is only transgranular dimple
fracture. The microstructure is coarse equiaxed grain in welded zone, and there is
virtually no strengthening phase in this zone. In the fusion zone, ﬁne columnar
grains and equiaxed grains are distributed at different sides. There is the ﬁbrous
phase in the base metal, and the microstructure of heat affected zone is similar to
this zone. But in the heat affected zone, recrystallization occurs and the grains grow
obviously. And the strengthening phases in the quenching zone are completely
dissolved, but their particles in over aged zone became coarseobviously.

Introduction
Al–Zn–Mg alloys have been widely used in the manufacturing industry of
high-speed trains for their light weight, high speci ﬁc strength, good corrosion
resistance, and nice machinability. Because of their weldability, Al –Zn–Mg alloys
are commonly applied to the manufacture of welded components. Welding methods
of Al –Zn–Mg alloy are numerous, such as Friction stir welding, laser welding,
electron beam welding, argon arc welding, and metal inert-gas welding, but in
high-speed train manufacturing, MIG welding is still the most commonly used
method of welding [ 1]. However, in the process of welding, Al –Zn–Mg alloy is
susceptible to the welding thermal cycle, which reduces its mechanical properties,
corrosion resistance, and greatly changes the grain structure. Especially, the change
of stress corrosion resistance plays an important role in the reliability and safety of
train during service. Accordingly, the research of microstructures and stress cor-
rosion behaviors of the Al –Zn–Mg alloy MIG welded joint have great signi ﬁcance.
So far the microstructure and mechanical properties of the welded joint of Al –Zn–
Mg alloys have been studied by many researchers [ 2–11]. However, the research on
the stress corrosion behavior of the welded joint is very scarce, and not
well-rounded. Therefore, the relationship between stress corrosion resistance and
microstructure of the welded joint was investigated in this paper, it has a positive
signiﬁcance to improve the stress corrosion resistance of the welded joint of the Al –
Zn–Mg alloy.
Materials and Experimental Procedures
Materials The Al –Zn–Mg 7020 alloy extrusion section material was used as base
metal in this work, the welding plate is 10 mm in thickness, which is welded by
x-shape groove butt weld form, and the welding direction is perpendicular to the
extrusion direction of the sheet metal. The ﬁller wire is ER5356 with 1.8 mm
diameter, the chemical composition of base metal and ER5356 ﬁller wire are listed
in Table 1.
Experimental Procedures Slow strain rate test is carried out according to GB/T
15970.7-2000 standard, and standard samples of this test are produced by WEDM
according to HB7235-1995 standard. Along the direction of the plate thickness of
the welded plate, the samples were divided into three groups, outer surface,
enter-layer, and inner surface. The preparation consists of sanding the surfaces of

samples carefully, washing with acetone, then rinsing samples with distilled water
and drying them. Before loading samples, the 150N preload is applied to eliminate
the clearance between the ﬁxture and the gears. The corrosion medium is 50 °C
3.5% NaCl solution, and the inert medium is made of 50 °C silicon oil. The tensile
strain rate is 10-6s-1. After the slow strain rate tensile test, the samples were washed
and dried, and ﬁnally the surface corrosion features were observed by SEM.
The microstructure of the welded joint and base metal was observed by
OLYMPUS GX71 optical microscope. Before observing the microstructure, the
surface of the sample is etched with mixed solution (100 ml: 83 ml
H
2O + 1 ml HF + 16 ml HNO 3 + 3 g CrO 3). EBSD based on FEI-Sirion type 200
ﬁeld emission scanning electron microscopy are performed to observe the macro-
scopical texture and microcosmic grain orientation, and electropolishing is per-
formed before the alloy was observed. In addition, the morphology of precipitates
of different areas were studied by Tecnai G2 F20 ﬁeld emission gun transmission
electron microscopy (FEG TEM).
Results and Discussion
Slow Strain Rate Test Welded joint samples and base metal samples of slow
strain rate test were divided into three groups, outer surface, enter-layer, and inner
surface, each group was respectively tested in 50 °C 3.5% NaCl solution and 50 °C
silicone oil, The stress-strain curve obtained from the test is shown in Fig. 1.A s
shown in Fig. 1, the tensile strength of the welded joint is lower than that of the
base metal, so does the elongation. No matter the welded joint or base metal,
elongation and tensile strength of samples in 50 °C 3.5% NaCl solution are obvi-
ously lower than those of samples in 50 °C silicone oil. That means both the welded
joint and the base metal have certain sensitivity to stress corrosion in 3.5% NaCl
solution.
According to HB7235-1995 standard, I

Microstructure Characterization In order to analyze microstructure transforma-
tion, MIG welded joints are usually divided into four zones, including weld zone
(WZ), fusion zone (FZ), heat affected zone (HAZ) and base metal (BM), as is
shown in Fig. 4. The weld zone, with coarse equiaxed grains, is a typical charac-
teristic of casting microstructure [ 12] (in Fig. 5a). The reason is that, the mechanism
of melting solidiﬁcation is similar to the casting mechanism; the ﬁller wire is melted
rapidly by welding thermal cycle, and then solidi ﬁed rapidly. In general, due to the
microstructure of coarse equiaxed grain in the weld zone, once the crack occurs, the
dislocations at the crack tip will increase rapidly, then forming a large slip step,
which is conducive to the initiation and expansion of the stress corrosion crack.
This is also one of the reasons why the weld zone become a weak area of welded
joints [ 13]. In addition, some defects in the weld zone may become the source of
stress corrosion cracking, thus increasing the stress corrosion sensitivity of the weld
zone. Obviously, the plasticity and strength of coarse equiaxed grain is poor, so the
tensile strength and elongation of welded joints are lower than those of the base
metal in the slow strain rate test of welded joints. From Fig. 5b, there is an obvious
boundary area at the junction of weld zone and heat affected zone, namely the
fusion line. It is obviously that the microstructure of the fusion zone near the weld

Figure 8 shows TEM micrographs of different zones. There is virtually no
strengthening phase in the weld zone (in Fig. 8a), the reason for this is that a part of
the alloying element will be consumed during the process of welding [ 16]. The heat
affected zone can be divided into two parts according to the difference of the
inﬂuence of welding thermal cycle: the quenching zone and over ageing zone, as is
shown in Fig. 8b, c. The quenching zone is located in the heat affected zone near
the welding seam side, from Fig. 8b, it can be seen that the second phase particles
in quenching zone are very few, the reason is that the strengthening phases in the
quenching zone are dissolved under the in ﬂuence of the welding heat cycle and
high temperature, then the cooling rate is faster than the precipitation rate of the
second phase in the solid solution, resulting in the secondary phase being too late to
produce. As is shown in Fig. 8c, the over ageing zone, which is relatively far away
from the welding seam side, there are large amounts of coarse second phases in
there. This is because the over aging zone is far away from the weld zone, the
inﬂuence of welding thermal cycle on material is similar to over aging, the second
phase particles dissolved and re-aggregated into coarse strengthening phases, it is
also one of the important reasons for the decrease of mechanical properties of heat
affected zone. In addition, due to the different distribution of the secondary phases
in the quench zone and over aging zone, the electrochemical corrosion is more

are dispersed evenly in the base metal.
Summary
The stress corrosion cracking index of MIG welded joint of Al –Zn–Mg Alloy is
0.04966, bigger than that of base metal, 0.04629, and the tensile strength and
elongation of MIG welded joint are obviously lower than the base metal. The weak
areas of welded joints are weld zone and heat affected zone.
The microstructure of the fusion zone near the weld zone is ﬁne columnar grain,
as well as ﬁne equiaxedgrain. The grains in weld zone are coarse and equiaxed, and
due to the typical characteristic of casting microstructure, this zone become one of
the stress corrosion weak areas of welded joints. The microstructure of base metal
and the heat affected zone are both extrusion microstructure features, but the grains
of heat affected zone are obviously recrystallized and grown up. Most of the grains in
the heat affected zone are recrystallized, the grain size range of this zone is 0 –40 lm,
while most of the grains in base metal are deformed, the grain size range is 0 –20 lm.
There is almost no strengthening phase in the weld zone, which is one of the
reasons why the weld zone is the weak area of welded joints. In the quenching zone,
due to the in ﬂuence of the welding heat cycle and high temperature, there are few
strengthening phases left because most of them are dissolved. In the over aged zone,
the in ﬂuence of welding thermal cycle on material is similar to over aged, the
second phase particles dissolved and re-aggregated into coarse strengthening pha-
ses, therefore, the mechanical properties of the heat affected zone seriously
decreased. In addition,due to the different distribution of the second phase in the
quench zone and over aging zone, the heat affected zone becomes one of the weak
areas of stress corrosion.

Coarse Grain Layer on Stress Corrosion
Cracking Resistance of Al –Zn–Mg Alloy
Lingying Ye, Xuebin Yao, Huaqiang Lin, Shengdan Liu, Yunlai Deng
and Xinming Zhang
Abstract The correlation between chemical composition, multiphase microstruc-
ture and stress corrosion performance of Al –Zn–Mg alloy with different thickness
coarse grain layers was studied by optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron
microscope (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), tensile test and four
point bending stress corrosion performance test. The results indicated that the
thickness of coarse grain layer of three kinds of Al –Zn–Mg alloy pro ﬁles used in
the test were about 200, 400 and 900 lm, while the stress corrosion cracking
(SCC) resistance and strength of specimens with coarse grain layer decreased with
increase of coarse grain layer thickness. Among different pro ﬁles, the stress cor-
rosion cracking resistance of specimens with coarse grain layer and center layer
without coarse grain layer exhibited the difference with the change of coarse grain
thickness.
Keywords Al–Zn–Mg alloy
/C1Coarse grain layer /C1Stress corrosion cracking
Introduction
Al–Zn–Mg alloy is the most ideal welding structural material and has been widely
used in the body of high speed train because of its high strength, good extrusion
performance and weldability. However, due to the stress corrosion cracking

## Page 339

(SCC) problem, the application of the alloy in the train body is limited [ 1–3].
According to relevant reports, in the process of extrusion, the surface of Al –Zn–Mg
alloy usually has a coarse grain layer, which will have an adverse effect on the
mechanical properties of aluminum alloy. However, it is found that the coarse grain
layer can also be used as an effective corrosion protection layer to retard the
corrosion cracking of the inner metal, thus improving the stress corrosion resistance
of the material [ 4].
In previous research, they found that stress corrosion cracking in Al –Zn–Mg
alloy mainly extends along grain boundaries, therefore, grain boundary plays a
major role in stress corrosion cracking [ 5]. For the ﬁne grain structure, the grain is
small, and there are lots of subgrain and grain boundaries. The corrosion medium
can easily penetrate from many grain boundaries and the cracks can expand con-
tinuously, so the tendency of stress corrosion is accelerated. For the coarse grain
structure, because the grain is coarse and high grain boundaries are less, the crack
propagation channel is correspondingly reduced and the crack stagnation or inter-
crystalline turning easily occurs. As a result, the crack propagation rate is reduced
and thus SCC sensitivity decreased [ 4, 6]. However, does this mean that the more
coarse grains are, the better stress corrosion resistance will be? The study showed
that grain re ﬁnement leads to formation of homogeneous sliding mode and small
size grain boundary precipitates, and the homogeneous slip model is helpful to
improve the material stress corrosion resistance [ 7]. In addition, Wu et al. [ 8] also
studied the effect of grain size on stress corrosion sensitivity of Al –Zn–Mg alloy
and found that the stress corrosion sensitivity of the large grain Al –Zn–Mg alloy is
higher than that of the small grain alloy, and pointed out the stress corrosion
sensitivity is related to GBPs area fraction. Thus, although coarse grain layer can
delay crack propagation, the coarse grain layer has higher stress corrosion sensi-
tivity. However, the different thickness coarse grain layers on SCC of Al –Zn–Mg
alloy are seldom reported. It is necessary to investigate the correlation between
thickness of coarse grain layer and SCC of material.
In this study, three kinds of Al –Zn–Mg alloy materials with different thickness
coarse grain layer, including the surface with coarse grain layer and center ﬁne
grain layer, have been tested by tensile test and four point bending stress corrosion
performance test. And the TEM of coarse grain layer and center ﬁne grain layer of
three kinds of Al –Zn–Mg alloy materials have been observed. The objective was to
comprehensively identify the correlation between alloying elements, microstructure
and SCC performance in Al –Zn–Mg alloy.
Experimental
The test materials are three kinds of Al –Zn–Mg alloy pro ﬁles with thickness of
10 mm and the numbers are 1#, 2# and 3# respectively. The chemical composition
of the three pro ﬁles is shown in Table 1. The main differences between the three
338 L. Ye et al.

## Page 340

proﬁles are on Cr and Zr element, the 2# and 3# pro ﬁles contain almost no Cr and
Zr element, while the 1# pro ﬁle contains Cr and Zr element.
The optical microscopy (OM) and transmission electron microscopy
(TEM) were used to observe the microstructures of the pro ﬁles on a MX3000
optical microscope and FEI TECNAI G220 transmission electron microscope. The
specimens for OM were grinded, then polished and anodized in Chromic acid
solution (83 ml H 2O + 1 ml HF + 16 ml HNO 3 + 3 g CrO 3). Thin foils with
diameters of 3 mm for TEM were prepared by double jet-polishing in electrolyte
solution of HNO3 and methyl alcohol (3:7) at −30 °C. Tensile tests were carried out
on a DDL100 testing machine and the tensile rate is 2 mm/min.
Characterizing four point bending stress corrosion sensitivity by two methods.
Firstly, the loading specimen was together with bending device in corrosion
medium with high acid, high oxygen and high salt. Second, observing the change of
shape and appearance of sample with time. Four point bending stress corrosion
sensitivity of material environment system are evaluated by the fracture time and
fracture morphology. According to the national standard GBT 15970.2-2000, four
point bending specimens with thickness of 3 mm are selected. Two parallel spec-
imens (perpendicular to the extrusion direction) are taken at the outer surface with
the original surface and the center of the plate thickness of the 1# pro ﬁle, the 2#
proﬁle and the 3# pro ﬁle. After calculating the load de ﬂection, through four point
bending beam ﬁxture as shown in Fig. 1 to bend the specimens to a certain
deﬂection. Then, it was immersed in the corrosive medium (3 g/L NaCl + 30 g/L
K2Cr2O7 + 36 g/L CrO 3) at 90 °C atmospheric environment.

Discussion
Due to the difference in chemical composition or extrusion process, the coarse grain
layer with different thickness appeared on the surface of the three pro ﬁles. Among
them, the thickness of the coarse grain layer of 1# pro ﬁle containing Cr and Zr
elements is only about 200 lm because of recrystallization is inhibited, which is
lower than the 2# pro ﬁle of 400 lm and 3# pro ﬁle of 900 lm. In addition, in the
effect of chemical composition and extrusion process, recrystallized fraction of the
center ﬁne grain layer for three pro ﬁles exhibits differences. The recrystallized
Fig. 5 Four point bending fracture SEM of coarse grain layer: a 1# pro ﬁle, b 2# pro ﬁle, c 3#
proﬁle
Fig. 6 Four point bending fracture SEM of center ﬁne grain layer: a 1# proﬁle, b 2# proﬁle, c 3#
proﬁle
342 L. Ye et al.

## Page 344

fraction of 1# pro ﬁle is 37.5%, while the recrystallized fractions of 2# and 3#
proﬁles reach 51.5 and 53.3% respectively, as shown in Fig. 7.
In addition, the results of strength test for three pro ﬁles basically meet the
Hall-Petch theory. That is, with the re ﬁnement of the grain, the higher the strength
of the material, the better the plasticity. The specimens with smaller coarse grain
thickness of 1# pro ﬁles exhibit higher strength and plasticity, while with coarse
grain layer becomes thicker of 2# and 3# pro ﬁles and has more coarse grain, the
strength and plasticity decrease. Similarly, compared with the 3# pro ﬁle with
thicker coarse grain layer, the strength and plasticity of 2# pro ﬁle is better than that
of 3# pro ﬁle. The data statistics ﬁnd that the average size of center ﬁne grain for 1#,
2# and 3# pro ﬁle are 19.8, 17 and 20.5 lm respectively, so the grain size of center
layer for three pro ﬁles has no obvious difference. That is why the strength of the
center ﬁne grain layer for three pro ﬁles has no obvious difference, which is about
400 MPa.
The test results show that the specimens with coarse grain layer of 3 kinds of
material exhibited different stress corrosion cracking resistance. That is, with the
increase of coarse grain layer thickness, the stress corrosion cracking resistance
decreases gradually, which is mainly related to the grain size of the material. The 1#
proﬁle has thinner coarse grain layer and less coarse grain, so it shows better stress
corrosion cracking resistance. While the coarse grain layer thickness of 2# and 3#
proﬁles is up to 400 and 900 lm respectively, with the volume fraction of coarse
grain is larger, so they show poor stress corrosion cracking resistance. In particular,
the surface with coarse grain layer of 3# pro ﬁle exhibited the worst stress corrosion
cracking resistance.
However, due to the effect of chemical composition or extrusion process,
recrystallized fraction of the center ﬁne grain layer for three pro ﬁles exhibits dif-
ferences, as shown in Fig. 7. According to relevant reports, the stress corrosion
cracking resistance of Al –Zn–Mg alloy is related to the recrystallization fraction.
The stress corrosion cracking resistance of Al –Zn–Mg alloy decreases with the
increase of recrystallization fraction [ 9]. But the stress corrosion cracking resistance

test results of center ﬁne grain layer indicate that the center ﬁne grain layer of 2#

in this stress corrosion cracking resistance test. Therefore, the reason of stress

ference is surely coarse grain layer thickness.
So why 2# pro ﬁle has better stress corrosion cracking resistance? At present, the
explanation about stress corrosion cracking of aluminum alloy has two main points:
(1) the anodic dissolution theory, this theory was put forward by Dix [ 10] in 1940,
that the anodic dissolution of GBPs leads to intergranular stress corrosion cracking;
(2) hydrogen induced cracking theory, from the beginning of 1970, people grad-
ually realized that hydrogen should be the main factor affecting stress corrosion
cracking of Al –Zn–Mg alloy [ 11, 12]. Sun et al. [ 13] successfully measured ele-
ment distribution in Al –Zn–Mg alloy grain boundary by three-dimensional atom
probe. They found that there was segregation of “free” Mg elements on the grain
boundaries of the peak aged alloy and MgZn 2 phase was not hydrogen traps. This
latest results show that the partial segregation of Mg and its complex interaction
with hydrogen is probably the main reason for the hydrogen cracking induced of
Al–Zn–Mg alloy. Therefore, based on the theory of anodic dissolution, the higher
the MgZn 2 phase area fraction in grain boundary, the faster the stress corrosion
cracking growth rate is under MgZn 2 phase rapid dissolution on open circuit, the
higher the stress corrosion cracking sensitivity. Figure 8 is the distribution of GBPs
for three pro ﬁles in the bright ﬁeld image. From the ﬁgures, we can ﬁnd that the
GBPs area fraction of three pro ﬁles is gradually reduced, but their stress corrosion
cracking resistance do not increased gradually, the center ﬁne grain layer of 2#

of 3# pro ﬁle

## Page 346

proﬁle has better stress corrosion cracking resistance, which indicates that the
anodic dissolution may not be the only mechanism of stress corrosion cracking.
Sun’s study shows that with the increase of GBPs area fraction, aluminum alloy
stress corrosion cracking resistance increased ﬁrst and then decreased. When the
GBPs area fraction is high, anodic dissolution plays a major role in stress corrosion
cracking, stress corrosion cracking resistance decreases with increase of GBPs area
fraction. And when the GBPs area fraction is low, hydrogen induced cracking plays
a decisive role, stress corrosion cracking resistance increases with the increase of
GBPs area fraction [ 14]. Therefore, the GBPs area fraction of 1# pro ﬁle center layer
is high, the stress corrosion cracking resistance is controlled by anodic dissolution,
and therefore the stress corrosion cracking resistance is poor. GBPs area fraction of
3# pro ﬁle center layer is low and the stress corrosion cracking resistance is con-
trolled by hydrogen induced cracking, thus the stress corrosion cracking resistance
is lower than 2# pro ﬁle.
Figure 9 shows surface crack appearance of four point bending stress corrosion
resistance test. We can ﬁnd that the surface cracks of specimens with coarse grain
layer are more tortuous, while the surface cracks of center layer are straighter. It
indicates that the coarse grain layer as a kind of effective corrosion barrier can delay
propagation of cracks because of coarse grain has less high angle grain boundaries
and crack propagation channel. Therefore, the stress corrosion cracking resistance
of specimens with coarse grain layer is better than the center ﬁne grain layer for 1#
proﬁle. But the test results of 2# and 3# pro ﬁles showed the opposite trend, which
indicates that although the coarse grain layer can be seen as an effective barrier
against corrosion and delay stress corrosion cracking, but the GBPs area fraction of
coarse grain layer is less (Fig. 8), this also increases the sensitivity of hydrogen
induced cracking. Therefore, the coarse grained layer with lower thickness can be
used as an effective corrosion barrier to retard the stress corrosion cracking of the
material. However, the coarse grained layer with larger thickness is harmful to the
stress corrosion cracking of the material.

## Page 347

Conclusions
(1) Due to the in ﬂuence of Cr, Zr and other factors, the coarse grain layer thickness
of three kinds of pro ﬁles studied in this experiment are about 200, 400 and
900 lm respectively. The strength and ductility of surface with coarse grain
layer decreases obviously with the increase of coarse grain layer thickness for
three kinds of pro ﬁles, but the strength of center ﬁne grain layer has no
obviously difference.
(2) The stress corrosion cracking resistance of the specimens with coarse grain
layer decreases with the increase of coarse grain layer thickness, while the
stress corrosion cracking resistance of the specimens with coarse grain layer
and center ﬁne grain layer for different pro ﬁles exhibits difference with the
change of coarse grain layer thickness.
(3) The coarse grain layer can restrain propagation of cracks, but the GBPs area
fraction of coarse grain layer is less and it will increase the sensitivity of
hydrogen induced cracking. So the coarse grain layer with lower thickness can
improve stress corrosion cracking resistance, but the coarse grained layer with
larger thickness is harmful to the stress corrosion cracking of the material.

## Page 349

Effect of RRA Treatment
on the Microstructure and Fatigue
Behavior of 7020 Aluminum Alloy
Yong Wang, Yunlai Deng, Shengdan Liu, Zhaojun Shan,
Jianguo Tang and Xinming Zhang
Abstract The fatigue crack growth (FCG) behavior and fatigue strength of 7020
aluminum alloy in an over aged treatment and two retrogression and re-aging
(RRA) treatments were investigated. The microstructures and fractographies were
observed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron
microscopy (SEM). The result showed that RRA-treated alloys have faster FCG
rate than over aged alloy at lower DK region due to the dense non-shearable
precipitates. And the RRA120 alloy re-aged at 120 °C/24 h has a relatively faster
FCG rate than RRA150 alloy re-aged at 150 °C/12 h. RRA-treated alloys have
higher fatigue strength than over aged alloy. The fatigue strength corresponding to
10
7 cycles of over aged, RRA120 and RRA150 conditions are 114, 129 and
118 MPa, respectively. The effect of RRA treatment on the fatigue property is
mainly caused by its ﬁner and more dispersed precipitates and narrower precipitate
free zone (PFZ).

## Page 350

Introduction
7020 aluminum alloy is widely used in high speed train because of its high speci ﬁc
strength, good formability and weldability [ 1]. One of the major problems during
their use is the low resistance to stress corrosion cracking (SCC) in T6 temper. The
resistance to SCC of the material can be signi ﬁcantly increased by two-stage
over-ageing treatment T7X but it also reduces the strength. A new three-step heat
treatment, commonly called retrogression and re-aging (RRA) treatment, solved the
contradiction by enhance the SCC resistance of the alloy while retaining its original
strength [ 2]. RRA treatment comprises three steps [ 3, 4]: (1) pre-aging heat treat-
ment: the alloy is treated to the state of under aging or peak aging. (2) retrogression
heat treatment: the alloy is treated at a high temperature for a short period of time so
that part of precipitates formed during pre-aging are redissolved. (3) re-ageing heat
treatment: the alloy is treated for a longer period of time at a lower temperature.
Many studies have shown that different aging treatments and the resultant
microstructures have noticeable impact on the fatigue properties of precipitation
hardening aluminum alloys [ 5, 6]. The microstructure characteristics such as grain
size, primary phase morphology and recrystallization degree, which have signi ﬁcant
inﬂuence on the fatigue property, do not change during ageing treatment. Therefore,
the difference of fatigue properties in different ageing conditions is mainly caused
by the difference of precipitates size and morphology in grain interior and grain
boundary, and the precipitate free zone (PFZ) in grain boundary. Many researchers
[7–9] have proposed that under aged alloys have better FCG resistance than peak
aged and over aged alloys due to the reversibility of dislocation motion. But Gurbuz
[10] found non-shearable coarse particles in over aged alloy retard FCG because the
dislocations loop and bypass the precipitates and thus increase the strain hardening
rate. Xia [ 11] proposed that the prolonged retrogression treatment and re-aging
treatment of 7050 aluminum alloy was bene ﬁcial to FCG resistance because dis-
locations can slip freely in the spacing between the large precipitates. Therefore, it
is necessary to do further research on the effect of ageing, especially RRA condi-
tions, on the FCG and fatigue crack initiation, with a view to improving the fatigue
behavior by heat treatment.
In the present work, an over aged condition and two RRA treatments with
different re-ageing temperature and time were chosen to study the effect of aging
treatment on the microstructure of the alloy. And the mechanism of the difference in
fatigue crack initiation and FCG was further discussed.

Experimental
A commercial 7020 aluminum alloy has been used in this work. The chemical
composition of the 7020 aluminum alloy are shown in Table 1. 7020 alloy was
casted, homogenized, hot extruded, press quenched before aging treatment. Table 2
shows the details process of the over aged and two different RRA treatments.
The fatigue crack growth tests were conducted on a material testing system
(MTS Landmark Servohydraulic Test System) according to ASTM Standard E647.
Compact tension (CT) specimens were used and they were prepared by wire cutting
from the extrusions in L-T orientation. The tests were conducted in constant load
control mode at room temperature in laboratory air. The stress ratio (R = r
min/
rmax) is 0.1 and the frequency of loading was 10 Hz.
TEM examinations were performed on the Tecnai G 2 20 ST microscope oper-
ated at 200 kV. The thin foils for TEM test were reduced to less than 100 lmb y
mechanical thinning and punched into discs with a diameter of 3 mm. The discs
were thinned by twin-jet electropolishing subsequently at −30 °C and a potential
difference of 20 V. The solution composition is 30% nitric acid and 70% methanol.
The observation of fatigue fracture surface was ﬁnally inspected by SEM operating
at 20 kV.
Results
Mechanical Properties Table 3 represents the hardness and tensile properties of
the alloy. The tensile strength of RRA treated alloys is comparable to T6 temper.
And the hardness and strength of RRA120 alloy are relatively higher than that of
the RRA150 alloy. For the over aged alloy, the tensile strength decreased by 13.9%
and yield strength decreased by 18.8% compared to RRA120 alloy. The elongation
of the over aged, RRA120 and RRA150 alloys are 15.5, 14.9 and 15.1%,
respectively.

Discussion
The total fatigue life of materials is composed of two parts: the cycle number of
fatigue crack initiation and the cycle number of fatigue crack growth to fracture.
And the FCG stage contains near-threshold region, Paris region and ﬁnal rupture
region. The fatigue crack initiation and FCG at lower DK region are mainly
discussed.
A large number of studies [ 14] have shown that the alloys in under aged con-
dition have good FCG resistance due to the their small precipitates and the
reversibility of dislocations movement in the plastic zone at the tip of fatigue crack.
Since the small precipitates in under aged alloys are coherent and shearable, dis-
locations move back to the opposite direction on the slip plane when the stress is
unloaded. It reduces the local stress concentration and the plastic accumulation,
thus reducing the FCG rate. On the other hand, non-shearable precipitates retard the
reversible slip of dislocation. The change in the size of the precipitates causes
different mechanisms when the dislocation passes through the particles. Kov ács
[15] have studied both the cutting and bypassing mechanisms and got the following
equations:
