where: scutting and sorowan are the critical shear stress of the cutting and bypassing
mechanisms, R is the average particle radius, f is the volume fraction of precipi-
tates. It can be seen from the above equation that the critical shear stress of the
cutting mechanism enhanced with the increase of the volume fraction and the
average particle radius, while the bypass mechanism decreases with the decline of
volume fraction and the increase of average particle radius. There is a critical size,
the dislocations cut off the precipitates when their size is less than it, and bypass the
precipitates when their size is greater than it. The critical size is about 3 nm for Al –
Zn–Mg alloy [ 15–17]. Therefore, the precipitates in RRA conditions are not
sheared although they are relatively small.
At lower DK region, the plastic zone at the front of fatigue crack is very small.
This means the slip distance of dislocations is short while the spacing of precipitates
in the over aged alloy is relatively large. The probability of dislocations interacting
with precipitates is low in over aged alloy which has large precipitates size and
wider spacing, thereby promoting the slip reversibility, ﬁnally reducing the FCG
rate. So the FCG rate of over aged alloy is relatively slower. The RRA alloys show
high FCG rate because the dense precipitates retard the reversible slip of disloca-
tions, and RRA120 alloy has a relatively faster FCG rate than RRA150 alloy at
lower DK region. Xia [ 11] also found that larger precipitates caused by prolonged
re-aging time can reduce the FCG rate in Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloy. At higher DK
region, the plastic zone is large and dislocation slip distance increases greatly. The
precipitates both in over aged alloy and RRA treated alloys retard the reversible slip
of dislocations seriously. But the wider PFZ and the larger grain boundary pre-
cipitates in over aged alloy make it easy to crack and promote a faster FCG.
In contrast to the FCG rate, the RRA120 alloy has the highest fatigue life and
fatigue strength limit. Suresh [ 18] have pointed that the proportion of fatigue crack
initiation can reach 80% of the total fatigue life in the smooth specimen. Therefore,
the results of fatigue life are not inconsistent with the FCG results. The wide PFZs
and coarse grain boundary precipitates are detrimental to fatigue behavior. The soft
PFZs lacking solute atoms are prone to plasticity localization due to their lower
strength. Furthermore, the large incoherent grain boundary precipitates are easily
cracked from the interface with the matrix and promote the formation of voids in
grain boundary, thus results in the initiation of fatigue crack [ 19]. From Fig. 1,i ti s
obvious that the width of PFZ in RRA alloys are narrower than that in over aged
alloy, especially the RRA120 alloy, which has a PFZ width of only 64 nm com-
pared to the over aged alloy with a PFZ width of 104 nm. The size of grain
boundary precipitates in over aged alloy is the largest and it is the least in RRA120
alloy. In addition, the dense precipitates which are non-shearable in nature in the
Effect of RRA Treatment on the Microstructure and Fatigue … 357

## Page 358

RRA alloy lead to more homogeneous deformation and the absence of localized
plasticity, and reduce the possibility of void formation. Therefore, RRA treated
alloys have relatively high fatigue life and fatigue strength limit.
Conclusions
(1) The precipitates in RRA-treated alloys are ﬁne and dense compared to coarse
precipitates in over aged alloys. And the size of precipitates in RRA120 is
smaller than that of the RRA150 alloy. The width of PFZ in over aged alloy,
RRA120 and RRA150 alloy are 104, 64 and 80 nm, respectively.
(2) RRA-treated alloys have faster FCG rate than over aged alloy at lower DK
region due to the dense non-shearable precipitates. And RRA120 alloy has a
relatively faster FCG rate than RRA150 alloy.
(3) RRA-treated alloys have higher fatigue strength than over aged alloy. The
fatigue strength corresponding to 10
7 cycles of over aged, RRA120 and
RRA150 conditions are 114, 129 and 118 MPa, respectively.

Static Recrystallization Grain Size
Model of 5083 Aluminum Alloy
Qingsong Dai, Yunlai Deng, Lingying Ye, Xu Liu and Weihua Zhao
Abstract The in ﬂuence of material initial grain size, deformation temperature,
strain rate and true strain on the static recrystallization grain size of 5083 aluminum
alloy after hot deformation was studied by thermal compression test with
Gleeble-3800 simulated machine. The grain size model of static recrystallization of
5083 aluminum alloy was established according to the experimental results. The
results show that the static recrystallization size of 5083 aluminum alloy decreases
with the increase of true strain or strain rate, and increases with the increase of
deformation temperature or original grain size, and the true strain has the greatest
effect. The predicted value of the static recrystallized grain size model exhibits a
good agreement with the experimental data.
Keywords 5083 aluminum alloy
/C1Static recrystallization /C1Grain size prediction
model
Introduction
The dynamic softening behavior such as dynamic recovery and dynamic recrys-
tallization is easy to occur for aluminum alloy during the process of hot defor-
mation, and the static recovery and static recrystallization will continue to take
place in the space after the hot deformation when the dynamic recrystallization is
not completed [ 1, 2]. In order to predict the grain size of aluminum alloy after the
hot deformation and optimize the process parameters, it is necessary to study the
inﬂuence of thermal deformation process parameters on the static recrystallization
grain size, and establish the relationship between hot deformation parameters and

microstructure evolution. 5083 aluminum alloy, because of its light, corrosion
resistance, easy molding and other characteristics, is widely used in lightweight
vehicle [ 3–5]. At present, the study is mainly focused on the corrosion resistance,
welding performance, forming properties, rheological behavior, dynamic recovery
and dynamic recrystallization, static recovery and static recrystallization behavior
[6–9]. However, the effect of thermal deformation parameters on the static
recrystallization size is seldom to report. In hot rolling or forging processes, it is
usually necessary to control the ﬁnal microstructure of the product by process
parameters. Therefore, it is important to study the in ﬂuence of hot deformation
process parameters on the static recrystallization grain size of 5083 aluminum alloy.
In this paper, the effects of different initial grain size and thermal deformation
parameters on the static recrystallization grain size of 5083 aluminum alloy were
studied by thermal simulation test and metallographic test, and the static recrys-
tallization grain size model was established.
Experimental
The chemical compositions (wt%) of the 5083 aluminum alloy studied are as
follows: 4.65Mg –0.49Mn–0.29Fe–0.11Si–0.1Cr–0.03Zn–,0.03Ti-(bal.) Al.
Cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 10 mm and a height of 15 mm were
machined from the material. The hot compression test was carried out on a
Gleeble-3800 thermal simulator and the hot compression conditions are shown in
Table 1.
The sample was heated to the deformation temperature at a rate of 10 °C/s and
warm for 5 min, then subjected to a thermal simulation compression test. After the
compression, kept the temperature of the sample until the static recrystallization
volume fraction reached 95% or more, immediately put it into the water, freezing

## Page 363

recrystallization nucleation will be, thus the number of grains after recrystallization
is increased, and the size is smaller [ 10–12].
Figure 1b is the static recrystallization grain size of samples 2#, 4#, 5#. It shows
that the static recrystallization size of 5083 aluminum alloy increases with the
increasing deformation temperature. Because the dislocation density of the material
is smaller when the deformation temperature increases, and the recrystallization
nucleation rate is greater than the grain growth rate, so the number of recrystallized
grains decreases and the grain size becomes larger [ 10–12].
Figure 1c is the static recrystallized grain size of samples 2#, 6#, 7#, 8#. The
static recrystallization of average grain sizes corresponds to the strain rate of 0.01,
0.1, 1, 10 s
−1 are 118, 82.9, 54.2, 35.4 lm. There is shorter time for dynamic
recrystallization when the strain rate is higher, then the storage energy and driving
force become greater for the static recrystallization, nucleation rate is higher, and
thus the recrystallized grain amount is larger, the grain size is smaller [ 10–12].
Figure 1d is the static recrystallized grain size of samples 2#, 9#, 10#. The static
recrystallization average grain sizes corresponds to the of true strain 0.36, 0.69, 1.2
are 130, 54.2, 32 lm. The larger the strain, the smaller the recrystallization grain is,
because the strain is greater, the dislocation density after the deformation is greater,
when the storage power is higher, the driving force of the static recrystallization
becomes greater, the nucleation rate recrystallization grains and small size is higher
[10–12].

Measurement of Residual Stress
in As-Quenched 7055 Aluminum Plate
by Various Methods
Hongwei Yan, Xiwu Li, Zhihui Li, Ya ’nan Li, Shuhui Huang,
Lizhen Yan and Yong ’an Zhang
Abstract The accuracy of different residual stress measurement methods has
always been the research focus from the beginning of research on residual stress. In
this study, both conventional and newly-developed methods were applied to
measure the residual stress in as-quenched 7055 aluminum plate. Methods such as
hole drilling, X-ray diffraction based on sin
2W and cos a approaches, crack com-
pliance method and neutron diffraction method were used. In the meanwhile, ﬁnite
element simulation was used to obtain the residual stress distribution as a com-
parison. The results showed that among the methods studied, X-ray diffraction
method has the greatest test error due to its shallow test depth. However, if the
measurement condition was well controlled, the error could be acceptable. The
absolute values of residual stress obtained by X-ray diffraction method were slightly
greater than hole drilling method. If calculated with the reasonably chosen crack
compliance function, the test result was similar to neutron diffraction method.
Under different quenching conditions, all the studied methods showed that the
greater the quenching cooling rate, the greater the absolute value of residual stress.
Keywords Aluminum alloy
/C1 Residual stress /C1 Measurement
Introduction
Even though challenged by composites, 7xxx series aluminum alloys are still the
most important structural material and are widely used in aviation industry. With
the rapid development of aviation manufacturing, the design concept of integral
component is more accepted and proved to be effective in improving service life

## Page 368

and overall performance. Meanwhile, materials manufacturer has been improving
their equipment capability in recent decades. Industrial developed countries have
developed processing and manufacturing technology for aluminum alloy plates and
die forgings with maximum thickness over 200 mm and maximum length/weight
over 300 mm/3900 kg, respectively. However, severe quenching process is inevi-
table because the strengthening of 7xxx series aluminum alloy depends on the
precipitation of supersaturated solid solution which is obtained by quenching
process. Thus, residual stress is introduced by quenching. Residual stress in
products could be detrimental to their fatigue life and stress corrosion cracking
resistance, and additionally it will result in unexpected machining distortion [ 1, 2].
Precise characterization is the foundation of research on residual stress. The
parameters of residual stress control techniques and evaluation of residual stress
management both rely on its accurate measurement. After decades of research, test
standards of conventional techniques for residual stress measurement such as X-ray
diffraction and hole drilling have been developed, and novel techniques such as
X-ray diffraction based on cos a method and ultrasonic method based on critically
refracted longitudinal waves keep emerging [ 3]. Yet different measurement meth-
ods have their own advantages and limitations, and they differ from each other in
terms of measurement depth, scale and resolution. In this study, detailed investi-
gation was carried out on measurement of quenched-in residual stress in 7055
aluminum alloy plate specimens. Methods such as hole drilling, X-ray diffraction
based on sin
2W and cos a approaches, crack compliance method and neutron
diffraction method were applied and the results were compared with each other and
ﬁnite element simulation of residual stress distribution [ 4].
Experimental Procedure
Specimens Details Measurements were performed on 7055 aluminum alloys plates
with the thickness of 27 mm. Specimens with the size of 162 mm in rolling
direction and 81 mm in short transverse direction were wire cut from rolled plate.
Then the specimens were solution treated in an air circulation furnace at 470 °C for
1 h followed by 475 °C/1 h, and the heating time between 470 and 475 °C was
0.5 h. After the solution treatment was ﬁnished, the specimens were quenched into
several different quenchant at various temperatures (Table 1). Finally, the speci-
mens were aged at 120 °C for 24 h to be stabilized in case that the residual stress
distribution changed.
Measurement Methods Considering the comparability of the results, measure-
ment order was set to obtain residual stress information in the same position with as
many methods as possible. The measurements were performed as the following
order.

Hole Drilling Method Hole drilling residual stress test was carried on with RSD-1

Crack Compliance Method Aslot was cut on the specimen to monitor the stress

the crack could be calculated [ 11].
Results and Discussion
Residual Stress Distribution Along the LT Direction Figure 2a, b shows the
distribution of residual stress along longitudinal direction and transverse direction,
respectively. The measurements obtained by hole drilling method and X-ray
diffraction method based on sin
2W approach show similar trend. The residual stress
distribution tends to be uniform between 0 and 30 mm from the center. Then, with
the further increase of the distance to the center, the magnitude of the compressive
stress decreased, and tends to be zero. Compared to residual stress obtained by
simulation, the variation of residual stress shows a similar trend. The measured
residual stress in the uniformly distributed zone along the longitudinal direction and
transverse direction are around −175 and −200 MPa, respectively. The test results
show a slight ﬂuctuation, which might be caused by operation difference.
Residual Stress in Samples with Different Quenching Conditions Furthermore,
the X-ray and hole drilling method were applied to measure the residual stress in
specimens which were quenched into various quenchants at different temperatures
to control the cooling rate. As is shown in Fig. 3, sample 5, which was quenched
into NaCl solution, has the greatest residual stress. With the decrease of the
quenchant’s cooling capacity, the residual stress in sample also decreases. The error
bar in the ﬁgure also shows that X-ray diffraction method has a greater measure-
ment error compared to hole drilling method. Due to the wave length of the selected
X-ray, the measurement depth of X-ray diffraction method is limited to several
microns. The test error of X-ray diffraction method was affected by the measure-
ment depth and local texture. The measurement depth of hole drilling method is
around 2 mm. Thus, the measurement error of hole drilling method is relatively
smaller.
X-ray diffraction method based on cos a approach was applied to verify the
accuracy of the newly developed method. The test was performed on the sample

quenched in 20 °C water. The test results show the measured residual stress is
around −200 MPa. The accuracy of this method is acceptable. Moreover, because
the test time of this approach is drastically shortened, this method could be
promising in ﬁeld measurement (Table 2).
Internal Residual Stress Measurement Figure 4 shows the residual stress in
samples that were tested in the previous section. Crack compliance method was
used to measure the residual stress distribution along the short transverse direction.
X component and Y component were obtained by two cuts along two directions.
For the specimen quenched in 20 °C water, which is the most commonly used
quenchant in practical manufacture, the magnitude of compressive stress is about
180 MPa, and the pull stress in the center is about 170 MPa. The X component is
smaller compared with Y component. When the cooling capacity of the quenchant
decreases, the absolute value of residual stress in sample tend to decrease. And this
is consistent with the measurement of residual stress on the surface.

Summary
Among the methods studied, X-ray diffraction method has the greatest test error due
to its shallow test depth. However, if the measurement condition is well controlled,
the error can be acceptable. And the further reduction of test error of X-ray
diffraction method relies on statistical analysis on repeated test and establishment of
standard test procedure applied to aluminum alloy. The absolute values of residual
stress obtained by X-ray diffraction method are slightly greater than hole drilling
method. If calculated with the reasonably chosen crack compliance function, the
test result is similar to neutron diffraction method. Under different quenching
conditions, all the studied methods show that the greater the quenching cooling rate,
the greater the absolute value of residual stress.

Introduction
Al–Zn–Mg–Cu (7xxx series) alloys possess a usage period for almost a century due
to the extensive applications in aerospace and military industry to make various
fuselage, wing beam, rib, wing wall, and so on [ 1, 2]. Satisfactory combinations of
high strength, yield-strength ratio, preferable fracture toughness, ﬁne corrosion
resistance and practicable fatigue property have increasingly made it crucial in
aforementioned ﬁelds [ 3]. Due to accelerating development of industrial applica-
tion, high level demands of service performances for 7xxx series aluminum alloys
are proposed, which means the alloy design turns to higher content designing of
major alloying elements (mainly the zinc element) [ 4]. In the past twenty years,
several new 7xxx alloys are registered, namely 7136 alloy, 7056 alloy and 7095
alloy, which have almost one percent enhancement on zinc content compared with
typical 7055 alloy registered in the 1990s [ 5–7].
Compared with traditional 7xxx series aluminum alloys (5.0 –8.0 wt% zinc
content) [8–12], high-zinc alloys (no less than 9.0 wt% zinc content) have relatively
faster ageing response degree and bigger number density of precipitates [ 13].
Furthermore, the variation of ageing precipitation kinetics and property perfor-
mance has some differences from the traditional ones [ 14]. Accordingly, the
microstructure variation of the high-zinc ones has its characteristics. Early resear-
ches have proved that traditional alloys endure obvious periods of one-step ageing
treatments [ 15]. That means a certain time to peak-ageing state and then access
over-ageing state with a typical ageing temperature of 120 °C. That is also the
reason of choosing 120 °C/24 h as a commonly used peak-ageing treatment regime
for traditional ones [ 13, 16]. Accordingly, precipitation characteristics have ﬁne and
dispersive matrix precipitates and continuously distributed grain boundary precip-
itates in common [ 17]. However, equivalent researches on high-zinc alloys have
found the variations of microstructure of high-zinc alloys compared with the tra-
ditional ones. TEM technique can observe precipitates in hundred within an image,
which makes it possible to be used to represent geometric features of precipitates
with general image analyses. Thus, statistics obtained from several images can
successively quantize the precipitates [ 18].
In the present study, a high-zinc Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloy treated at several ageing
temperatures is fully studied on the aspects of hardness, electrical conductivity and
378 Y.-Q. Fan et al.

## Page 377

tensile properties. The microstructures with typical under-ageing, peak-ageing and
over-ageing state are observed by TEM observations and the characteristics of
matrix precipitates are quantitatively investigated.
Experimental Procedure
The researches were launched on samples extracted from an Al –9.2Zn–2.0 Mg –
1.9Cu alloy extrusion with in ﬁnitesimal Zr, Fe and Si elements. The samples were
solution treated with an optimized regime of 460 °C/1.5 h, followed by
water-quenching and ageing treatment at 100, 120 and 140 °C. A 430 VSD Vickers
hardness survey meter was used to monitor ageing hardening processes and each
hardness datum was extracted from the average value of nine effective values. The
electrical conductivity was measured by a current electrical conductivity meter
performed under indoor temperature and the value is also gained by nine effective
ones. Tensile specimens were machined to a gauge of U10 /C260 mm (M10) and
the tensile direction was parallel to extrusion orientation. The tensile speed was two
millimeters per minute and the result of three effective duplicate samples were
averaged to obtain a tensile value. Disk samples for TEM observations were
extracted from metal sheets with a line cutting thickness of about three millimeters.
Then they were manually rubbed to a thickness of 40 –60 mm. Every ﬁve disks are
used to create minute holes by contrary jetted methanol solution with a quarter of
nitric acid. The sample preparation temperature is no higher than −20 °C under a
voltage pressure of 10 –30 V. TEM examinations were conducted on a F2010
transmission electron microscope machine. The matrix precipitate size distribution
was measured from the TEM images with the aid of an Image Plus Pro software.
Results and Discussion
Hardness, Electrical Conductivity and Tensile Properties
The hardness values of the alloy aged at (100, 120, 140) °C are shown in Fig. 1a.
First the alloy aged at 100 and 120 °C is under discussion. The hardness exhibits a
rapid increase during the initial few hours, a more placid increase up to 24 h and
then maintain a platform till 128 h with little ﬂuctuations. Here the hardness values
of 120 °C are larger than that of 100 °C during ageing processes and the platform
periods for them are 210 –216 and 212 –221 HV, respectively. As for the alloy aged
at 140 °C, the hardness takes almost 12 h to reach a peak value of 218 HV,
maintains a relatively short period till 28 h and then decreases continuously.
Correspondingly, the electrical conductivity, as shown in Fig. 1b, also presents
quits rules. Here we can see that the electrical conductivity increases with the

enhancing of ageing temperature or the prolonging of ageing time. From the initial
ageing point to the last point, the increase rates of electrical conductivity at 100, 120
and 140 °C enlarge successively. Among them, the enhancement from 120 to 140 °C
is more remarkable than that from 100 to 120 °C.
Based on aforementioned hardness and electrical conductivity results, tensile
properties of the alloy aged at 120 °C are proposed, as shown in Fig. 2. From 6 to
72 h, the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) has small ﬂuctuations and almost main-
tains a terrace with a strength value range of 692 –697 MPa. The yield strength
(YS) shows an obvious increase within the initial 24 h and then maintain a platform
with a strength value range of 655 –659 MPa. The elongation has no conspicuous
increase or decrease trend and is larger than 10%. So it is reasonable to consider that
the alloy aged by 120 °C/24 h has the peak-ageing (PA) state with UTS, YS,
elongation and electrical conductivity values of 697 MPa, 655 MPa, 12.9% and
17.3 MS m
−1, respectively.

TEM Observations
The selected area diffraction patterns (SADPs) for the alloy treated by UA, PA and
OA states, which are projected along <100> and <112> orientations, are shown in
Fig. 3. The matched diffraction spots for <100> and <112> orientations from the Al
matrix have been labelled. As for the alloy with UA state, the corresponding spots
at {1,1/4,0} and {1,7/4,0} in <100> projection come from GPI zone which is
coherent with the matrix. In these two positions, the diffraction spots are quite
obvious. The spots and rays at 1/3 and 2/3 of {220} position along <100> and
<112> orientations, respectively, represent semi-coherent η′ phase. Some legible
coherent GPII spots are found near a half of {311} position in <112> orientation.
Hence, the man precipitates in the UA samples are GPI zone, GPII zone and η′
phase. In the case of the alloy with the PA state, it is obvious that the corresponding
spots from GPII zone and η′ phase are still quite clear, which reveals the main
precipitates under PA state are GPII zone and η′ phase. In the PA samples, no
distinct GPI zone or GPII zone are found in the SADPs while the spots and rays
representing η′ phase are plain, which uncover the dominating precipitates of the
alloy under OA state. This demonstrates that the primary precipitates evolve from

“GPI zone, GPII zone and η′ phase” to “GPII zone and η′ phase” to “η′ phase” with

Based on the SADPs analysis, matrix precipitates (MPs) and grain boundary
precipitates (GBPs) of the UA, PA and OA alloy are observed, as shown in Fig. 4.
The matrix precipitates show small dimension and dispersive distribution. With
ageing degree deepening, the size of matrix precipitates enlarges and a signi ﬁcant
increase in the amount of big size precipitates happens. In the UA alloy, most
matrix precipitate has an upper size limit of about 6 –7 nm and distribute densely. In
the OA alloy, the size of matrix precipitates enlarges obviously with an upper size
limit of about 10 –12 nm. The precipitate distribution is sparser than that of the UA
alloy. As the ageing degree deepens to the OA state, the size of matrix precipitates
increases furtherly and the upper size limit is about 14 –16 nm. Among them, the
amount of big size precipitates for the OA alloy is obviously larger than that of the
PA alloy. The precipitate distribution is more scattered compared with the PA alloy.
The grain boundary precipitates show a similar trend. In the UA alloy, the grain
boundary precipitates exhibit approximately successive distribution and the size is
quite small. In the PA alloy, the size of grain boundary precipitates enlarges and an
obvious discontinuous distribution of them appears. In the OA alloy, the size of
them furtherly enlarges and the degree of discontinuous distribution deepens.

Here we can see that the size of precipitates has an obvious enhancement from
the UA state to the PA state to the OA state. The matrix precipitate distribution
becomes increasingly broader while the average matrix precipitate size becomes
larger and larger. The discontinuous degree of grain boundary becomes more
severe.
Conclusions
In this work, the microstructure characteristics combined with precipitate geomet-
rical features, electrical conductivity, hardness and tensile properties in a high-zinc
Al–9.2Zn–2.0Mg–1.9Cu alloy treated by single stage ageing treatments are
investigated. The conductivity increases continuously at the ageing temperature of
100, 120 and 140 °C while the hardness increases severely in the initial period and
then maintain a platform of 100 and 120 °C. The hardness increases severely in the
initial period and then decrease continuously at the ageing temperature of 140 °C.
The tensile strength keeps a platform while the yield strength increases in the initial
24 h and then maintain a platform. Based on property measurements, the samples
with typical under-ageing state, peak-ageing state and over-ageing state are selected
to observe microstructure. The results of SADPs observations indicate that the main
precipitates in the alloy evolve from “GPI zone, GPII zone and η′ phase” to “GPII
zone and η′ phase” to “η′ phase” when the ageing state transforms from the UA
state to the PA state to the OA state. The Bright ﬁeld TEM observations reveal that
the precipitate characteristics has big variations from the UA state to PA state to OA
state. As the ageing degree deepens, the average matrix precipitate size become
larger, the matrix precipitate size distribution become broader and the grain
boundary precipitate size become larger.

Classiﬁcation and Evolution
of Porous Defects in Spray-Formed
Al–Zn–Mg–Cu Alloy
Shuhui Huang, Hongwei Liu, Zhihui Li, Baiqing Xiong,
Yongan Zhang, Xiwu Li, Hongwei Yan and Lizhen Yan
Abstract The porous defects classi ﬁcation in spray-formed Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloy
was investigated in this paper during spray forming, hot isostatic pressing (HIP) and
homogenization. Metallographic microscopy and scanning electron microscopy
(SEM) were used to study the microstructure and porous defects. The results
showed that, there were four kinds of porous defects in spray-formed alloy, which
were distinguish by the reasons of formation and shape. The ﬁrst kind, the second
kind and the third kind porous defects contain gas, while the forth kind porous
defect did not contain gas. The forth kind porous defects can be eliminated by HIP,
but the other three only can be compressed to be smaller. After homogenization, the
porous defects with gas grew up and was observed easily again, unless some porous
defects connected with ingot surface through the other porous defects which could
exhaust gas during HIP. The second phase in the ingot restored back mostly after
the homogenization treatment of 440 °C/12 h + 474 °C/48 h.
Keywords Spray-formed
/C1Aluminum alloy /C1Porous defects classi ﬁcation
Evolution
Introduction
7000 ultra-high strength aluminum alloy is widely used in aerospace industry,
because of high speci ﬁc strength, corrosion resistance and high toughness [ 1–3].
Spray forming is one of rapid solidi ﬁcation technologies, which can be applied to
produce spray-formed ultra-high strength aluminum alloy with exceeding 15 wt%
alloy elements, and tensile strength can be raised to 800 MPa by spray forming. But
porous defect is inevitable in spray-formed ingot and cannot be eliminated [ 4–8].
The reasons of the porous defects formation in spray-formed ingots are in ﬂuenced

by many factors. The integrity and continuity of ingots are damaged by porous
defects, and then the properties of the ﬁnal products will have bad performance,
which restricts the application of spray forming technology in industry [ 9–15].
The purpose of this work is to research the porous defects classi ﬁcation and
forming mechanism in spray-formed Al –Zn–Mg–Cu alloy, the revolution of porous
defects in hot isostatic pressing (HIP) and homogenization are investigated too.
Materials and Methods
7xxx aluminum alloy (chemical composition: Al –10.8Zn–2.8Mg–1.9Cu–0.12Zr) is
spray-formed by the equipment of SF-500, which is a self-made machine for spray
forming. The schematic diagram of spray forming and the ingots are shown in
Figs. 1 and 2, respectively. During spray forming process, the 750 –800 °C alloy
melt is blown into fog by nitrogen with 0.7 MPa. The cylindrical samples of
U180 /C2300 mm is machined from the ingot. The samples are canned by pure
aluminum for hot isostatic pressing (HIP), and the parameters of HIP are 460 °C/
120 MPa/8 h. Homogenization treatment of 440 °C/12 h + 474 °C/48 h is carried
on after HIP.
Microstructures are observed by Carl Zeiss Zxiovet 200MAT optical microscopy
(OM). Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) is performed by using a
NETZSCH STA 409C/CD in the temperature range 20 –550 °C in an argon
atmosphere with heating rate of 10 K/min.

Results and Discussion
The porous defects in spray-formed ingots cannot be eliminated thoroughly, but
they can be diminished by post-processing. The causes of the formation of porous
defects are different, and the porous defects will be classi ﬁed according to the cause
of the formation. The fraction of liquid phase is lower when the material ﬂow
reaches the deposition surface of spray forming ingot, then a class of the porous
defects appear among the solid phase as called the ﬁrst type porous defects. The
solid particles and semi-solid particles are assembled on the deposition surface of
spray forming ingot, and the interstice among the particles is very dif ﬁcult to be
ﬁlled up by liquid phase. Then the ﬁrst type porous defects form and is shown in
Fig. 3. As can be seen that, the morphology of the ﬁrst type porous defects is very
irregular, and the size is from several microns to several hundred microns. The
interface spreads all over solid particles, and this kind of porous defects contain gas.
The fraction of liquid phase is higher when the material ﬂow reaches the
deposition surface of spray forming ingot, then some gas will be caught by large
droplets, which leads to the second type porous defects. The representative
Fig. 2 Spray-formed ingots
Fig. 3 Microstructure of the ﬁrst type porous defects

## Page 386

microstructure of the second type porous defects is shown in Fig. 4. The second
type porous defects is spherical because of large internal pressure. Compared with
the ﬁrst type porous defects, the size is equivalent to several grains and the interface
is smoother. The grain boundaries and precipitate are coarser than that in matrix,
and the reason is that heat dissipation is more dif ﬁcult in the inside of defects, which
causes the grain boundaries and precipitate on the inner surface have enough time to
grow up. The second type porous defects contain high-pressure gas and is closed.
When turbulence appears in the material ﬂow, it is possible to generate the third
type porous defects which own the characteristics of both the ﬁrst and second type
porous defects. The representative microstructure of the second type porous defects
is shown in Fig. 5. As can be seen that, the morphology of the third type porous
defects is very irregular, and the size is from several microns to several hundred
microns. This kind of porous defects contained gas and the probability of connected
with each other is greatly induced.
The forth type porous defects come from solidi ﬁcation shrinkage of the liquid
phase on the deposition surface of spray forming ingot, which is shown in Fig. 6.
The forth type porous defects distribute along grain boundaries and is about several

After hot isostatic pressing (470 °C/120 MPa/8 h), the microstructure of

The spray-formed ingot is machined to cuboid (10 /C210 /C250 mm) after hot

because of it closed, and the inner surface cannot diffuse connection with each

types porous defects may gas assembles in the part, then the transition which is
similar with the second type porous defects occurs. The second phase on inner
surface of recurrent porous defects is smaller and less than that on the original
porous defects, and the grain boundary is thinner too.
Summary
(1) The porous defect in spray-formed ingots is inevitable, and the porosity is
around 10% in spray-formed aluminum alloy.
(2) According to the cause of formation, the porous defect in spray-formed alu-
minum alloy can be divided into four types. The ﬁrst type porous defects forms
when the fraction of liquid phase is lower than solid phase on the deposition
surface of spray forming ingot, and the ﬁrst type porous defects contain gas.
The second type porous defects forms when the fraction of liquid phase is
higher than solid phase on the deposition surface of spray forming ingot, then
some gas will be caught by large droplets, which leads to the second type
porous defects. When turbulence appears in the material ﬂow, it is possible to
generate the third type porous defects which own the characteristics of both the
ﬁrst and second type porous defects. The forth type porous defects come from
solidiﬁcation shrinkage of the liquid phase on the deposition surface of spray
forming ingot.
(3) When the porous defects do not contain gas or contain gas but it can be exhausted,
the porous defects can be eliminated through hot isostatic pressing. When the
porous defects contain gas and it cannot be exhausted, gas will be compressed and
assemble in the part after hot isostatic pressing, and then it appears again as
spherical shape during homogenization heat treatment at 474 °C.

The In ﬂuence of Homogenizing of 6351
Aluminum Alloy on the Heating Method
of Extrusion
Li Wan and Yunlai Deng
Abstract This paper studies the in ﬂuence of different homogenizing process on the
heating method of extrusion by means of metallographic microscope and eddy
current conductivity meter. The results show that there are a large number of
rich-Fe/Mn particles in 6351 alloy matrix by homogenizing in 560 °C. The rates of
cooling after homogenizing have little effect on the long-time heating and
heat-preservation heating before extrusion. The method of heating at a temperature
higher than 500 °C before extrusion and then cooling in air is bene ﬁcial to the
low-temperature and high-speed extrusion of 6351 alloy. If the total time of heating
and extrusion is within 10 min, the samples which cool rapidly after homogenizing
can be extruded at low-temperature and in a high-speed with the eddy-current
heating.
Keywords 6351 aluminum alloy
/C1The cooling speed of homogenizing
Low-temperature /C1High-speed extrusion
Introduction
The 6000-series aluminum alloy belonging to Al –Mg–Si alloy is the heat-treatable
alloy. It has medium-strength, good welding performance and corrosion resistance.
Hence, it has been widely used in transportation and structural engineering like
bridges, cranes, the roof structure, transport vehicles, ships [ 1–3]. Because the
component of 6000 aluminum alloy contains a certain amount of high melting point
elements like Mn and Cr, it is widely believed in the industry that the presence of

such high melting point elements can lead to the formation of thick Mg 2Si phase
during the process of cooling-homogenizing. And the thick phase will signi ﬁcantly
impact the mechanical property of extruded products [ 4, 5]. So, an advanced
requirement is raised for the alloy, which contains the heterogeneous nucleated
points like Mn and Cr. In order to provide the reference date of industrial pro-
duction, this paper has researched the evolution rule of Mg 2Si phase during the
homogenizing process systematically.
Material and Methods
The 6351 aluminum alloy casting rods were fabricated by the 20T semi-continuous
casting line. The chemical composition of 6351 alloy were shown in Table 1. The
temperature range of casting is 720 –740 °C and that of re ﬁning is 730 –750 °C. The
time for re ﬁning is between 20 and 25 min. The diameter of casting rods is
160 mm. The size of samples cutting from casting rods are 5 * 20 * 20 mm. The
conductivity is tested on the D60K digital conductivity instrument. The metallur-
gical structures are observed by ZEISS Axio Vert.Al metallurgical microscope.
Results and Analysis
Homogenized Heating Figure 1 shows the casting sample and the metallographic
structure which is homogenized for 6 h at different temperature. It can be seen from
Fig. 1a that, due to the rapid cooling during casting process, there aren ’t a large
number of second-phase particles in grain but there are a lot of primary phases in grain
boundary. With the increase of the heating temperature, the primary phases in the
grain boundary are dissolving gradually, but the second-phase particles are still
massive in the grain boundary even at 560 °C (as shown in Fig. 1g). However, with
the increase of the homogenizing temperature, the number and the size of thick
second-phase particles increase gradually. If the holding temperature is above 440 °C,
the quantity of thick second-phase in the grain decreases by degrees. And they are
almost dissolved into matrix structure when the holding temperature is 560 °C. During
the whole homogenizing process, the ﬁne and dispersed second-phase particles are
considerably separated out in matrix structure.
The typical SEM in different homogenizing heating stations is shown in Fig. 2.
From Fig. 2a, there are two kinds of primary phase structures. The one is black and

The Heating Before Extrusion The evolution of Mg
2Si phase during the heating

Heating Method With the demand for the function reliability and dimensional
accuracy of extrusion pro ﬁle increasing, more and more corporates are in favor for
the eddy-current heating in gradient. But how to control the heating process in order
to improve the production ef ﬁciency by extruding in low-temperature is the key
problem. Because a large number of Mg
2Si phases are separated out in matrix
during the slow-cooling after homogenizing, the alloy like 6351 doesn ’t adopt to
the low-temperature extrusion with the eddy-current heating. Thus, this work
mainly considers the situation that the casting rod cools rapidly after homogenizing
(the cooling rate > 250 °C/h). The samples shown in Fig. 6 are heated in 440 and

Conclusions
(1) A large number of rich-Fe/Mn particles exist in the matrix structure of 6351
aluminum after 560 °C homogeneous heat treatment.
(2) The cooling rate after homogenization has little effect on the long heating mode
before extrusion.
(3) The method of heating at higher than 500 °C then cooling in air before
extrusion is bene ﬁcial to the low-temperature and high-speed extrusion of 6351
alloy.
(4) The sample of rapid cooling after homogenization could be processed through
low-temperature high-speed extrusion method by controlling the total time of
heating and extrusion within 10 min.

Effect of Zr Content on Microstructure
and Mechanical Properties
of Al –Mg–Si–Cu Alloy
Y. P. Sun, X. H. Zhou, W. B. Xu, J. M. He and W. X. Wang
Abstract Effect of Zr content on microstructure and mechanical properties of
Al–Mg–Si–Cu alloy were investigated by means of metallograph microscope,
tensile test and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The results show that the
main precipitate is AlCuMgSi phase in Al –Mg–Si–Cu alloy after cold rolling.
Zr element plays a dominant role in re ﬁnement of grains. With the increase of
Zr content, numerous dislocations are found in Al –Mg–Si–Cu alloy, together with a
large amount of complex phase containing Zr element precipitate within the grains.
When the content of Zr is 0.7%, the tensile strength and elongation of Al –Mg–Si–Cu
alloy are 490 MPa and 10%, respectively.
Keywords Al–Mg–Si–Cu
/C1 Zr /C1 Microstructure /C1 Mechanical properties
Introduction
Al–Mg–Si–Cu alloy has been widely used in aviation, rail transportation, auto-
mobile, ship and building materials due to the advantages of light weight, high
strength, easy forming and excellent corrosion resistance, and so on [ 1–3]. In recent

years, it has become one of the most urgent problems to develop lightweight alloys
with better comprehensive properties [ 4–6].
Adding alloying elements in Al –Mg–Si–Cu alloy can improve its recrystal-
lization temperature. For different transition elements, their in ﬂuence on recrys-
tallization temperature is also not alike, such as Zr, Ti, Mo, Mn. As has been
reported, the recrystallization temperature can be controlled by adding trace ele-
ments. Meng et al. [ 7] have reported that the recrystallization temperature of alu-
minum alloy can be improved signi ﬁcantly by adding Sc elements, the elongation
can also be increased at the same time. Svenningsen et al. [ 8] found that
Al
4Cu2Mg8Si7Cu phase appears in Al –Mg–Si alloy by adding Cu elements.
Moreover, the rich-Cu elements in grain boundaries will reduce the corrosion of
Al–Mg–Si–Cu alloy. At the same time, adding proper amount of trace elements can
form a strengthening phase in a-Al matrix, which will improve its mechanical
properties signi ﬁcantly. Meng [ 9] has reported that adding V in Al –Mg–Si–Cu
alloy can obtain Al
3V phase, and equiaxed grain structure was formed and the grain
growth was suppressed by recrystallization nucleation during hot extrusion, thus,
the mechanical properties of wrought Al –Mg–Si–Cu alloy could be improved.
Bahrami [10] studied the in ﬂuence of Zr elements on the homogenization treatment
of alloy, the results show that the addition of Zr has no signi ﬁcant effect on the
eutectic Mg
2Si phase of as-cast aluminum alloy, but it changes the morphology of
Mg2Si phase to a nearly spherical shape after hot extrusion. Further investigations
show that of Zr can improve the tensile strength and elongation for as-extruded
Al–Mg–Si alloy from 160 MPa and 3.2% to 292 MPa and 9.5%, respectively.
In this paper, Zr was added to a Al –Mg–Si–Cu alloy to study the effect of its
content on evolution of microstructure and mechanical properties prepared by large
strain rolling.
Experimental Procedure
The chemical compositions of Al –Mg–Si–Cu alloy are listed in Table 1. The
melting temperature is 760 °C. The alloys were ﬁrst homogenized at 560 °C for
24 h, then hot rolled from 14 to 4 mm by multi passes at 250, 300 and 400 °C, with
a total reduction rate of 71.4%. The plate was soluted at 510 °C for 80 min and
aged at 195 °C for 13 h. Then cold rolled from 4 to 2 mm, the reduction rate is
50%. The microstructures of Al –Mg–Si–Cu alloy was observed by means of

Results and Discussion
Microstructures Figures 1 and 2 show the microstructures of Al –Mg–Si–Cu alloy
with different Zr content fabricated by cold rolling. As shown by the diagrams, the
grain size becomes ﬁner with the increase of Zr content. After cold rolling, the
second phases is mainly distributed within the grains, which is due to the dissolve
of impurity phase into a-Al after homogenization. After aging treatment, the
AlCuMgSi phase and rich Zr phase are uniformly precipitated in the alloy, and Zr
element can form typical dispersed phases. According to the literature [ 10, 11], Zr
can precipitate a ﬁne Al3Zr phase with the size of 0.01 –0.1 lm in aluminum alloy,
and Al 3Zr has a strong pinning effect on the climb and slip of dislocation.
Furthermore, Al3Zr phase also has a effect of stabilize the deformation structures of
Al–Mg–Si–Cu alloy.

Abstract The effect of upsetting and cogging Technique on Microstructure and

Introduction
The beta-titanium alloy has complex microstructures that can obtain the best
strength and toughness by heat treatment and plastic match. In the aerospace and
ship industry, the beta-titanium alloys obtained important application, for example,
can be used for the big cross section structure. Typical beta titanium alloys are:
Ti-38644, b-CEZ, Ti-5553, Ti-15-3 and Ti-1023, these alloys basically some
special the requirements in the aerospace ﬁeld, and gradually replaces the original
titanium alloys with industry recognition [ 1–4].
The Ti-38644 is a meta-stable b titanium alloy, the nominal composition for the
alloy is Ti –3Al–8V–6Cr–4Zr–4Mo. The alloy has high tensile strength and cor-
rosion resistance. The Ti-38644 alloy can be machined into spring, high strength
fasteners and so on because of good cold working performance [ 5, 6]. The b-CEZ is
a highly alloyed, high-strength meta-stable b titanium alloy, the nominal compo-
sition of the alloy is Ti –5Al–4Zr–4Mo–2Sn–2Cr–1Fe. The strength of the alloy can
reach 1200 –1400 MPa by solution and aging treatment. The b-CEZ titanium alloy
can be used for the air compressor disc and large structural parts and so on in the
ﬁeld of aerospace [ 7–9].
In this paper, the effect of multiple upsetting and cogging technique on
microstructure and mechanical properties of b titanium alloys has been studied, so
as to obtain the optimum processing technology, reasonable heat treatment condi-
tions and stable microstructure of b-CEZ and Ti-38644 alloys. The purpose for this
paper is to determine the connection between the hot working process parameters
and microstructure of b-CEZ and Ti-38644 alloys.
Experiment Procedure and Materials
The Ti-38644 and b-CEZ alloy ingots with a diameter of 440 mm were smelted
three times by the vacuum self-consuming arc furnace. After the ingots were forged
in the b-phase zone, they were drawn up along the axis to the square billet.
The b-CEZ billet is subjected to single and multiple upsetting and cogging in the
a + b phase region. The low phase transition temperature of Ti-38644 alloy leads to
processing dif ﬁculties, so the Ti-38644 billet is conducted to single and multiple
upsetting and cogging test in the transformation temperature above 100 °C or in the
b phase region. The Ti-38644 and b-CEZ alloy billets are drawn and rounded in the
a + b phase region, and then forged into the bars with a diameter of 150 mm.
The phase transition temperature of the Ti-38644 alloy is about 760 °C. The
phase transition temperature of the b-CEZ alloy is about 890 °C.
The tensile samples of the Ti-38644 were solution-treated at 760 °C for 15 min
air cooling, then aged at 570 °C for 6 h air cooling. The tensile samples of the
b-CEZ were solution-treated at 780 °C for 1 h, air cooling, then aged at 570 °C for
4 h, air cooling.

Results and Discussion
Macrostructure of Bars Transverse macrostructure of single and multiple
upsetting and cogging of the Ti-38644 and b-CEZ alloy bars are shown in Fig. 1.
From the ﬁgure, it can be seen that the transverse macrostructure of Ti-38644 alloy
bar is not obviously re ﬁned after multiple upsetting and cogging because the pro-
cess temperature for the Ti-38644 was in b phase region. The transverse
macrostructure of b-CEZ alloy bar is obviously re ﬁned, uniform and forging dead
zone macrostructure signi ﬁcantly re ﬁned after multiple upsetting and cogging
because the process temperature for the b-CEZ was in a + b phase region.

and b-CEZ titanium alloy bars at the room temperature after single and multiple
upsetting and cogging. From the table, it can be seen that the tensile strength of
b-CEZ is about 1264.5 MPa for once upsetting and cogging, after multiple
upsetting and cogging, the tensile strength increases to 1363 MPa, the increment is
about 8%. After multiple upsetting and cogging, the elongation of b-CEZ increases
to 6.5%, the increment is about 18%, the reduction of area increases to 23%, the

increment is about 44%. The tensile strength of Ti-38644 is about 1154.5 MPa for
once upsetting and cogging, after multiple upsetting and cogging, the tensile
strength increases to 1221 MPa, the increment is about 6%. After multiple upsetting
and cogging, the elongation of Ti-38644 increases to 7.5%, the increment is about
7%, the reduction of area increases to 27%, the increment is about 26%.
So, the tensile strength and the elongation of b titanium alloy bars have been
improved slightly after multiple upsetting and cogging, but the reduction of area has
been increased signi ﬁcantly. The comprehensive mechanical properties of the b
titanium alloy bars would be improved because of the re ﬁned and uniform grains by
multiple upsetting and cogging. The grains of the square billet have been elongated
along the ﬂow direction of the metal during the drawing process. After the defor-
mation reaches a certain degree, grains have been crushed; and then, during the
upsetting process, the crushed grains would be elongated along the direction per-
pendicular to the stretch because the square billet would be compressed and
deformed under the action of the external force. After repeated upsetting, the grains
become smaller and smaller, ﬁnally re ﬁned and equiaxed.
Microstructure of Bars The microstructures of Ti-38644 alloy bar after single and
multiple upsetting and cogging are shown in Fig. 2a, b. From the ﬁgure, it can be
seen that the microstructure after multiple upsetting and cogging is re ﬁned obvi-
ously. The microstructures after once upsetting and cogging is coarse equiaxed
grains (Fig. 2a), after multiple upsetting and cogging, the coarse equiaxed grains
are signi ﬁcantly re ﬁned and uniformed (Fig. 2b). The microstructures of b-CEZ
alloy bar after once and multiple upsetting and cogging are shown in Fig. 2c, d.
From the ﬁgure, it can be seen that the microstructures after once upsetting and
cogging is coarse equiaxed grains without obvious b grain boundary and lath-shape
a precipitated in coarse equiaxed grains (Fig. 2c); the microstructures after multiple
upsetting and cogging are obviously re ﬁned and homogenized, and the ﬁne
needle-like and lath-shape a would be precipitated in equiaxed grains (Fig. 2d).
Mechanical properties of the material are improved greatly because the upsetting
and cogging process changes the axial forging streamline to a radial distribution and
it effectively increases the uniformity of the internal structure of the alloy.

Conclusions
(1) The ﬂow stress of b-CEZ and Ti-38644 titanium alloys decreases with the
increase of deformation temperature, but the degree of the ﬂow stress reduction
get slow down.
(2) For the b-CEZ and Ti-38644 alloys with multiple upsetting and cogging, the
equiaxed microstructure become ﬁne and uniform, b grain boundaries are very
clear, small acicular and lath-shape a phase also precipitate in the equiaxed
grains, and the microstructure difference is small between transverse direction
and longitudinal one.
(3) The multiple upsetting and cogging can signi ﬁcantly improve the reduction of
area and the mechanical properties of b-CEZ and Ti-38644 titanium alloys with
the re ﬁned and uniform grains.

Evolution in a High Temperature
Ti Alloy with Erbium
Tongbo Wang, Bolong Li, Xu Qiao, Peng Qi and Zuoren Nie
Abstract The effect of thermo-mechanical deformation on the microstructure was
investigated by isothermal compression and microstructure characterization. The
mechanical response of as-casted Ti –6.2Al–3Sn–5Zr–0.5Mo–1.0Nb–0.4Si–0.2Er
titanium alloy was sensitive to the deformation temperatures and strain rates. The
true stress increased with the increase in the strain rate and decreased in tempera-
ture. The discontinuous dynamic recrystallization of b phase was promoted with the
increase in temperatures. Global a phase generated during the deformation at a
temperature of 980 °C. The (Ti, Zr)
3Si and participated phase were dissolved into
the matrix above 950 °C, which acted as the homogenizing annealing process.
However, novel participated phases with an average diameter of 20 nm generated.

Introduction
High temperature titanium alloys have been applied in fabricating the compressor
discs and blades at a temperature of 600 °C, because of their high speci ﬁc strength,
excellent mechanical properties up to high temperature and good corrosion resis-
tance [ 1]. The elevation of service temperature should be promoted to modify the
thrust-weight ratio of Engine in aircraft [ 2].
Ti–Al–Sn–Zr–Mo–Si series titanium alloy was modi ﬁed by rear-earth Er to
generate re ﬁned grain size and alterative silicide, which improved the strength and
toughness at elevated temperatures [ 3]. Therefore, Ti –Al–Sn–Zr–Mo–Nb–Si–Er
titanium alloy has been developed with excellent high temperature strength and
creep resistance. The compound with Er was generated during the casting process.
The effect of compound on the deformation behavior need further study in the
Ti–Al–Sn–Zr–Mo–Nb–Si–Er titanium alloy. Meanwhile, the effect of thermo-
mechanical deformation on the microstructure evolution in a high-temperature
titanium with erbium should be investigated to modify the cogging process [ 4].
The deformation behavior and microstructure evolution of Ti –Al–Sn–Zr–Mo–
Nb–Si–Er titanium alloy were studied in this paper. Additionally, the effect of
thermo-mechanical deformation on the microstructure was clari ﬁed by isothermal
compression and microstructure characterization.
Experimental Procedure
The as-casted Ti –6.2Al–3Sn–5Zr–0.5Mo–1.0Nb–0.4Si–0.2Er titanium alloy was
isothermally compressed on a Gleeble-3500 simulator. The cylindrical specimens
were 10.0 mm in diameter and 15.0 mm in height. The isothermal compressed
temperature was raged from 920 to 1070 °C at 30 °C intervals, and the strain rates
was 0.001 –10 s
−1. The cylindrical specimens were heated to the corresponding
testing temperature with a constant heating rate of 10 °C s −1, and kept for 300 s
before the isothermal compression so as to acquire a uniform deformation tem-
perature in the entire specimen. Moreover, the true strain-stress curves were auto-
matically recorded during the isothermal compression test.
The micro-structures were observed by optical microscope (OM), scanning
electron microscope (SEM), and transmissions electron microscope (TEM). OM
samples were ground, polished, and etched with Keller ’s solution. Then the samples
were observed by Olympus BX51M optical microscope (OM). SEM samples were
only ground and polished, and then were analyzed by SUPRA 55 scanning electron
microscope.
Longitudinal sections of samples were analyzed by a JEM-2010F transmission
electron microscope (TEM). Samples were mechanically polished to thin sheets.
Disks with a diameter of 3 mm were twin-jet electro-polished in a 60% HClO

Mechanical Response Figure 1 shows the ﬂow stress –strain curves in the
isothermal compression of Ti –Al–Sn–Zr–Mo–Nb–Si–Er titanium alloy. For the
whole curves, the true stress increased with the increase in the true strain, and then

became much more stable. It was attributed to the balance between work hardening
and dynamic softening. At the same temperature, the true stress increased with the
increase in the strain rate. The increase in the true stress resulted from the block of
dislocation motion at a higher strain rate.
Meanwhile, the true stress increased with the increase in temperature. It was
attributed to heating effect, dynamic softening, and phase transformation. With the
increase in temperature, the dislocation slipping became easier due to the heating
effect. Dynamic softening, such as dynamic recovery and dynamic recrystallization,
was also the factor for the decrease in stress. Meanwhile, a phase was transformed
into b phase in the a + b region, and then totally transformed into b phase beyond
1010 °C. Because of more stimulating dislocation slipping systems, the deforma-
tion resistance was much lower than that of a phase.

Conclusions
(1) For the as-casted Ti –6.2Al–3Sn–5Zr–0.5Mo–1.0Nb–0.4Si–0.2Er titanium
alloy, the true stress increases with the increase in the strain rate and decreases
in temperature.
(2) The dynamic recrystallization of b phase is promoted with the increase in
temperatures, which is a discontinuous process, including nucleation and
growth of b grain.
(3) The global a phase generates during the deformation at a temperature of 980 °C,
while ﬁner lamellar a phase generates by phase transformation during the
deformation above 1010 °C. The (Ti, Zr)
3Si and participated phase dissolves
into the matrix above 950 °C, but novel participated phases with an average
diameter of 20 nm generate.

Thermal Stabilities of Ti-600 Alloy
Pancake
Liying Zeng, Xiaonan Mao, Quan Hong, Yunlian Qi
and Yongqing Zhao
Abstract Thermal stabilities at ambient temperature were studied on Ti-600 alloy
before and after being exposed at 600 °C for 100 h. Fractography morphologies
were investigated, and fracture mechanism analyzed. The results indicated that the
strength of the alloy sample after thermal exposure decreased 1% or so, the elon-
gation decreased about 49%, indicating that the plasticity decreased abruptly during
the exposure process. For the as-solutioned plus as-aged samples, the cracks
originate from the center of the fracture, dimple typed fracture can be found in the
fractographies. After thermal exposure, only cleavage facets can be observed in the
fractographies, the fractures propagate along the interfaces of lamellar a phases.
The fractography of the tensile specimen prior to and after thermal exposure pre-
sented the feature of intergranular fracture, transgranular plus intergranular rupture,
respectively. These results are caused by the precipitation and the existence of the
brittle oxidizing layers. The cracks formed in the oxidizing layers ﬁrst and then
propagated into the matrix during the tensile tests. Oxygen ﬁltration in the surface
layer was one of the important reasons for the decrease of plasticity. The major
deformation mechanism for Ti-600 alloy without and with thermal exposure is
dislocation slips pass-through a bundles, a/b phase boundary slips during the
tensile deformation process at ambient temperature, respectively.

Introduction
The application temperature for metal materials depends on their heat resistance and
thermal stability. While for Ti and Ti alloys, these are two contradicted factors.
When the heat resistance improves, the thermal stability would decrease at the same
time. That’s one of the main reasons why the using temperature has been restricted
to be not higher than 600 °C for heat-resisting Ti alloys. When further upgrading
the heat resistance for high-temperature Ti alloys, more and more attention has been
paid on their thermal instability. At present, the heat resistance can be easily
obtained for Ti alloys which can be used at 600 °C or even higher temperature for a
long time, but it ’s relatively difﬁcult to solve their thermal stability [ 1, 2]. As one of
major mechanical properties for high-temperature Ti alloys, the thermal stability
can be judged by the loss factor of plasticity before and after thermal exposure,
which would characterize the maintaining capability for plasticity and ductility of
alloys exposed at higher temperature for longer time [ 2, 3].
Thermal stability can be divided into microstructure stability and surface sta-
bility. Two factors in ﬂuence the thermal stability for high-temperature Ti alloys
during thermal exposure process for long time, one is oxygen in ﬁltration at the
surface, the other is the inner microstructure variation.
Recent study aimed at understanding the tensile property at ambient temperature
for Ti-600 alloy prior to and after being exposed at 600 °C for 100 h was inves-
tigated in this paper. Combined with the observation of fractography morphologies,
dislocation structures, tensile fracture mechanism was analyzed, and the factors to
cause the decrease of thermal stability were also discussed.
Experimental Materials and Procedure
A near- a high-temperature titanium alloy named after Ti-600 was used in this
study, the nominal composition for the alloy is Ti –6Al–2.8Sn–4Zr–0.5Mo–0.4Si–
0.1Y. A 504 kg ingot was produced by electrode consumption vacuum arc furnace.
The b transus temperature for the alloy is 1010 °C or so. The alloy was forged at
1100 °C from 440 mm starting diameter to 100 mm bars. Then diameter 100 mm
bars were upset to diameter 140 mm pancakes at 1025 °C, the deformation rate is
about 49%. The tensile and thermal stability samples were cut from the pancakes
and were solution treated at 1020 °C for 1 h, air cooling, then aged at 650 °C for
8 h, air cooling. And some samples were machined to tensile samples and exposed
at 600 °C for 100 h, air cooling. Then tensile tests were conducted for both sam-
ples. Tensile tests were conducted with smooth cylindrical specimens having a
422 L. Zeng et al.

## Page 419

5 mm diameter by 25 mm gauge length using an Instron-1185 electron tensile
machine at a strain rate of 3.3 /C210−3 s−1.
The samples for microstructural examination were cut from the tensile speci-
mens for both conditions, mounted ﬁrst in bakelite and then polished following
standard metallographic practice. Subsequently the samples were etched using
Kroll’s reagent and were examined using Olympus PMG3 optical microscopy.
Fractographies after tensile interrupted tests were performed on JSM 6460
scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Thin foils for TEM observations were pre-
pared from longitudinal sections of fatigued specimens. They were mechanically
thinned on papers with grades 600 and 1200 to a thickness of 60 lm, then elec-
trolytically thinned to electron transparency with a solution composed of 6% per-
chloric acid, 20% butyl glycol, and 70% methanol at −30 °C. Microstructures were
observed on JEM 200CX transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
Results and Discussions
Tensile Properties Before and After Thermal Exposure Table 1 shows the
tensile properties of Ti-600 alloy at ambient temperature before and after being
exposed at 600 °C, for 100 h. From the table, it can be seen that after appropriate
thermal treatment, the alloy possesses moderate strength and relatively higher
plasticity, the ultimate strength (UTS) for the alloy at ambient temperature is about
1093 MPa, the elongation (EL) is up to 10%, and the reduction of area is 18.0%.
While after thermal exposure, the UTS and YS decrease 1% or so. And the plas-
ticity decreases obviously. Elongation is only 5%, its conservation rate is 51.0%,
and the reduction of area is also only 5.8%, its conservation rate is only 32.2%. The
results above indicate that the strength for the alloy decreases a little bit, and its
plasticity decreases sharply.
Fractographies for the Tensile Samples Before and After Thermal Exposure
Fractography for the alloy prior to thermal exposure is shown in Fig. 1a, c, e.
Scanning electron microscopy observations shown in Fig. 1a reveal the overall
morphology at low magni ﬁcation to comprise a rough, obvious necking, shear lip at
the rim with nearly 45° direction to the tensile axial. High magni ﬁcation obser-
vation of this region reveals tearing edge, small amount of cleavage plane, as shown
in Fig. 1c, e. And the boundary between cleavage plane and dimples are not clear.
The fractography has the feature of dimpled ones.

Fractography for the alloy after being exposed at 600 °C, for 100 h is shown in
Fig. 1b, d, f. Many fractured facets and local dimples can be found, bright tearing
edges exist in the facets. The fractography has the feature of compound ones. Its
fracture ﬂuctuation is larger than that in the samples without thermal exposure, as
shown in Fig. 2d. And cracks are initiated at the surface of the specimens. Long
strip-like fractured planes and tearing edges can also be seen, as shown in Fig. 2f.
The strip-like fractured planes correspond to the lamellar a phases in the alloy, and
the fracture proceeds along lamellar a phases [ 1]. This may have relation with
oxygen in ﬁltration at the surface and the inner microstructure change.

Comparing the ﬁgures in Fig. 1, it can be seen that most of the cracks are
initiated at the center and at the surface, respectively for the specimens without and
with thermal exposure. For the specimens without thermal exposure, most of the
morphologies are dimple-type ones, the ﬂuctuation at the fractography surface is
rather large, cleavage fracture along a certain cleavage planes occur only at local
regions, the boundaries between the cleavage plane and the dimples are not
apparent. While for the specimens being exposed at 600 °C for 100 h, fracture
facets and a certain amount of tearing edges can be found, and the fractures
propagate along a lamellar boundary, the morphology is different from that of
specimens without thermal exposure. There are two reasons to cause above phe-
nomenon. One is for the certain notch effect originating from the oxygen in ﬁltration
layer at the specimen surface after thermal exposure, which would accelerate the
origination and propagation of the cracks, and the fracture origin would change
from the center part to the specimen surface. The other is for the inner
microstructure, for the near a type Ti-600 alloy, large quantity of phases may
precipitate from the alloy during high temperature long time thermal exposure
process, stress concentration can be easily generated at the phase boundaries as the
blocks for the slips, and the cracks originate and propagate along phase boundaries
in priority.
For the specimens with thermal exposure, precipitated phase (silicides etc.)
would exist, and oxygen ﬁltration layers ( a brittle layers) can also be found at the
sample surface. Fine cracks can be easily induced in these layers, and premature
fracture would form in the samples. These layers prior to split, cracks will propagate
towards from the surface to inside of the samples, and cracks can be seen at the
surface of the specimens at macro-fractography, as shown in Fig. 1b. As the cracks
further expand to the inner part of the specimen, the cracks will prior to propagate
along weak microstructure regions, and the tensile failure mechanism will also
change, different fractography would be formed comparing with specimens without
thermal exposure. At macroscopic view, the strength for the alloy decreases a little
bit, and its plasticity decreases obviously. As the deformation magnitude is rela-
tively big, much more tearing edges can be seen at fractography for the specimens

with thermal exposure. The results above indicate that oxygen ﬁltration at the
surface is one of major factors in ﬂuencing the thermal stability.
Optical Microstructures of Ti-600 Alloy Prior to and After Thermal
Exposure Figure 2 shows the optical microstructures for Ti-600 alloy before and
after thermal exposure. The alloy was solution treated at 1020 °C ( b transus tem-
perature is 1010 °C or so). When the solution treatment temperature increased to
above the b transus temperature, evenly distributed transformed b microstructure
can be found in the alloy, and the microstructure for the alloy is ﬁne lamellar a plus
b, the grain size is lager than 100 lm, as shown in Fig. 2a. The morphologies of the
alloy after thermal exposure are almost the same as that of the alloy before thermal
exposure. Only the size of primary b grains coarsens a little bit. The grain
boundaries and lathes are relatively smooth for the sample before thermal exposure.
While for the sample after thermal exposure, a certain amount of lathes become to
bend, short and ﬁne lathes can be found. The results above also indicate that the
alloy possesses microstructure stability, and the surface oxidization may have lager
inﬂuence on the tensile properties for the alloy after thermal exposure.
Factors Affecting the Thermal Stability From the data listed in Table 1, it can be
seen that as-SAT Ti-600 alloy possesses favorite strength and ductility at ambient
temperature, and the strength for the alloy with thermal exposure will decrease a
little bit, and its plasticity will decrease sharply. Both of oxygen ﬁltration at the
surface and the change of microstructure will affect the tensile properties for Ti
alloys during the thermal exposure process at 600 °C for 100 h [ 1, 2].
During the thermal exposure process, besides the oxygen ﬁltration at the surface,
10% or so oxygen ( a stabilizing element) would dissolve in the space of Ti lattices,
and enriched oxygen a layers would be formed [ 4]. With higher heating temper-
ature, longer holding time, the thickness for the enriched oxygen a layers would be
thickened, manifesting the steady increase of micro-hardness at the surface. The
distance towards the surface is farer, the increase amplitude of micro-hardness
would tend to be lower and lower [ 5]. Figure 3 shows the curve of micro-hardness
versus depth from the surface. From the ﬁgure, it can be seen that the
micro-hardness is very high at the surface, and is smaller and smaller when the
distance from surface become larger and larger, and tends to be as similar as the
matrix Ti-600 alloy at last.
Enriched oxygen a layers with high micro-hardness, low ductility would be
formed in Ti-600 alloy after thermal exposure, and they are tend to be easily torn at
the surface [ 6, 7]. Figure 4 shows the optical microstructure for Ti-600 alloy tensile
specimens at longitudinal section. No cracks can be found at the failure surface for
the samples without thermal exposure, as shown in Fig. 4a. Many deep and shal-
low, thin and thick, ﬁne cracks can be found at the failure surface for the samples
after thermal exposure, as shown in Fig. 4b. During the tensile test process, with the
increase of deformation, ﬁne cracks caused by oxygen
ﬁltration layer at the surface
would expand continuously to the inner part of the specimens. When the tensile
stress surpasses the tolerance stress, the specimens would failure. Oxygen ﬁltration
layers exist in thermal exposure specimens, a brittle layer would prior to split
426 L. Zeng et al.

## Page 423

during the tensile process, cracks propagate from the surface to inside, and the
tensile failure mechanism is different from that of specimens without thermal
exposure. So, oxygen ﬁltration is one of the major factors affecting the thermal
stability for the alloy.
The ﬁne cracks are the common surface morphology for Ti alloys after being
exposed at high temperature plus tensile tests. The main reason for this phe-
nomenon is the failure and breakage for the oxide ﬁlm. As an active element, Ti can
react easily with oxygen and nitrogen in the air, and a layer of low ductility oxide
ﬁlms should formed at the surface [ 7]. When the alloy was put in high temperature
environment, the oxidization rate should increase rapidly. After being exposed at
600 °C for 100 h, the content of oxygen increases sharply to 0.27% detected by
chemical analysis. And a layer of oxidation ﬁlm would be formed at the same time.

The analysis result of XPS (X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) indicates that the
ﬁlm is composed of TiO, TiO 2,T i 2O3,T i 2N, which coincide with the result in
reference [ 8]. So, at the following tensile deformation process, when a/b phase
boundaries slip for the thermal exposure specimen, the oxidation ﬁlm would apt to
split for its low ductility, and ﬁne cracks would be prone to be formed at the
surface.
In addition, different morphology micro-cracks would also exist at the specimen
surface. They can be divided into two types according to forming mechanism [ 1].
One type is the crack formed by the splitting of oxide ﬁlm caused by a/b phase
boundaries slip, its length-width ratio is small, it moves mostly towards the
direction of 60 –90° with tensile direction for the specimen, and the amount of this
crack is relatively small. The other type has no direct relation both with deformation
mechanism and microstructure for the alloy, its length-width ratio is relatively
large, it moves mostly towards the direction perpendicular to tensile direction for
the specimen, and the amount of this crack is relatively big, most of the
micro-cracks at the specimen surface are this type.
Deformation Mechanism Prior to and After Thermal Exposure It is noted that
the deformation for high-temperature Ti alloys was achieved by three mode of b
grain boundary slip, dislocation slip among a phase, a/b phase boundary slip [ 2, 9].
At different processing and experiment conditions, the three deformation mecha-
nism would have different effect on deformation mode for alloys, and diverse
failure mechanism would be caused.
Figure 5 shows the dislocation morphologies for Ti-600 alloy without and with
thermal exposure. It can be seen that long distance slip lines would be found both in
two kinds of specimens after tensile tests. And slips across a bundle exist in the
alloy.
The critical resolving shear stress (CRSS) to actuate prism slips, basal slips and
pyramidal slips rises consecutively in a-Ti [ 10]. The prism (10-10) slips have the
lowest CRSS value among the slip systems in a phase [ 11]. So, the major slip
deformation mode is the prism (10-10) slips for a-Ti at ambient temperature.
Fig. 5 Bright ﬁeld TEM image of dislocations in Ti-600 alloy without ( a) and with ( b) thermal
exposure, showing the long distance slip across through a and b phases
428 L. Zeng et al.

## Page 425

Figure 6 shows the typical prism slips in a phase for Ti-600 alloy. From the ﬁgure,
it can be seen that the prism (10-10) slips exist in a phase for the alloy after thermal
exposure after tensile tests.
The results above indicate that the main deformation mechanism for Ti-600 alloy
without and with thermal exposure is dislocation slips pass-through a bundles, a/b
phase boundary slips during the tensile deformation process at ambient temperature.
But the proportion of the two deformation mechanism in the total deformation is not
the same, which would cause different failure mode for the alloy after tensile tests at
ambient temperature. The fractography of the tensile specimen prior to and after
thermal exposure presents the feature of intergranular fracture, transgranular plus
intergranular rupture, respectively. This is obviously due to the relatively higher
strength of the boundaries for the tensile specimen after thermal exposure at
ambient temperature, which would put larger obstruction on slips. The plastic
deformation is mostly achieved by intracrystalline deformation, the strength of the
alloy depends on the strength of grain itself, and the fractography presents the
feature of transgranular fracture.
Summaries
Tensile properties variation, fractography features were investigated for Ti-600
alloy pancake prior to and after thermal exposure, and the fracture and deformation
mechanism are also analyzed and discussed. The main conclusions can be drawn as
follows:
1. The strength for the alloy after thermal exposure is slightly lower than that for
the alloy without thermal exposure, and the plasticity decreases to only 5%.
2. The cracks initiate at the center for the specimens without thermal exposure, the
fractography presents the feature of dimple-type fracture. And the cracks initiate
at the specimen surface for the specimens with thermal exposure, cleavage

and expand to the matrix alloy. Oxygen ﬁltration is one of the major factors
decreasing the ductility for Ti-600 alloy.
4. The major deformation mechanism for Ti-600 alloy without and with thermal
exposure is dislocation slips pass-through a bundles, a/b phase boundary slips
during the tensile deformation process at ambient temperature. The fractography
of the tensile specimen prior to and after thermal exposure presents the feature
of intergranular fracture, transgranular plus intergranular rupture, respectively.

Abstract The elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed-bend method is
feasible. Under the action of pushing force, expanding-diameter and bending
moment of horn mould, the elbow generates composite deformation including
bending and compressing deformation along axial direction and off-center
expanding-diameter deformation along circumferential direction. The expanding-
diameter deformation reduces wall thickness, while the compressing deformation of
belly is greater than that of back, and result in thickening wall thickness on belly
and eccentricity. The wall thickness ﬂowed from belly to back along two sides of
horn mould during expanding-diameter to compensate for thinned wall thickness on
back of elbow during off-center expanding-diameter. The wall thickness uniformity
of elbow was related to design of horn mould, pushing temperature and temperature
ﬁeld and pushing rate. The temperature of Ti75 titanium alloy elbow made by
expanded-diameter and pushed-bend method was chosen in two phase region. It can
reduce the deformation resistance and improve the alloy plasticity, and the elbow
