Introduction
Since the elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed-bend method was
invented by Japan in 1970 [ 1, 2], this method had widely used in various kinds of
materials elbow production after nearly 40 years development. In the 1990s, this
method had been applied to long radius elbow production of titanium alloy and high
temperature alloy with hard deformation feature [ 3, 4].
Titanium alloys is considered as hard deformation alloy comparing with steels is
because titanium alloy is characteristic of hexagonal with fewer slip crystal system.
So the plastic deformation is dif ﬁculty in room temperature. In addition, the strength
and plasticity of titanium alloy generate obvious changes with temperature
changing in high temperature deformation. The high temperature sensibility results
in narrow working region. Furthermore, the low heat conductivity requires long
heating time and badly heating uniformity. The crack easily takes place, once in
case the deformation temperature and temperature uniformity of titanium alloy is
controlled badly. However, titanium alloy is an excellence structure material with
low density, high strength and corrosion resistance especially in sea water and sea
atmosphere environments, which is called as sea metal. Titanium alloys has
superior erosion resistance in sea water with high rate, and erosion corrosion rate is
very low when the sea rate reach up to 36.6 m/s. The moving liquid with suspended
substance possibly results in serious damage to cupper alloys and aluminum alloys
when sea water carry wearing grains of sand. However, little effect is subjected to
titanium alloys. Therefore titanium alloys are ﬁrst choice materials in shipbuilding
pipeline designing.
Ti75 alloy is a near a titanium alloy with medium strength alloy for ship-
building, it is suitable to produce plate, bar, forging, pipe, wire, casting and pipe
ﬁttings for using in pressure pipeline of ship. Titanium alloy has higher speci ﬁc
strength and better erosion corrosion resistance comparing with traditional pipeline
material of copper alloy, so the higher designed liquid rate of titanium pipe is
permitted. The pipe can reduce diameter and wall thickness to reduce structure
weight of pipeline, and titanium alloy has same lifetime with ship without changing
material and maintenance in long active time.
In past pipeline designing of titanium alloys, almost elbow was used long radius
elbow with greater than or equal to 1.5 of relative bending radius which is ratio of
radius to wall thickness. With pipeline designing development to miniaturization
432 J. Chen et al.

## Page 429

and light weight direction, short radius elbow is urgent to be used in pipeline
designing to reduce space usage and to increase compact structure [ 5]. The seamless
elbow which is to be expanded-diameter and pushed bend by using seamless pipe
avoids axial welding seam of elbow made by pressed-disc and welded-disc method
and circumferential weld seam of shrimp waist elbow made by welded sheet metal
pipe. The increasing smoothness of inside diameter of elbow can reduce liquid
turbulent ﬂow. Furthermore, elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed bend
method is suitable for batch production.
When the elbow with same outside diameter is made by expanded-diameter and
pushed-bend method, the expanding-diameter deformation of short radius elbow is
1.5 times of long radius elbow, the compression deformation of short radius elbow
is 1.34 times of long radius elbow. For the short radius elbow, the smaller the
bending radius is, the greater the compressing and expanding deformation is
comparing with long radius elbow [ 5].
The deformation feature and structure evolution rule of Ti75 titanium alloy
elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed-bend method are studied to search
changes of microstructure and properties.
Experiment and Measurements
The Ti75 titanium alloy ingot with 620 mm diameter is melted three times in
consumable electrode vacuum furnace by using zero grade titanium sponge, Al –Mo
intermediate alloy, aluminum bean and nuclear grade zirconium sponge. The ingot
is forged into bar after repeated upsetting and drawing out processing, than the bar
is machined into pipe to be used for expanded-diameter and pushed-bend elbow. In
order to decrease the in ﬂuence of pipe stock on wall thickness uniformity and
induction heating temperature of elbow, the pipe production should be to ensure
straightness, roundness and uniformity of wall thickness.
The short radius elbow with DN 600 diameter made by expanded-diameter and
pushed-bending method is carried on expanded-diameter and pushed-bending
machine. The horn mould is connected with front-end of core rod. The pipes are
progressively arranged on core rod and pushed onto horn mould to deform into
elbow by pushing force acted on pushing hoop. The ﬁnished elbows directly enter
into ﬁnished production groove which is excavated down under ﬁnished elbow, and
then cool down subsequently. The pipe and horn mould are heated to deformation
temperature by special induction heating coil surrounding pipe and horn mould.
The pipes heated to deformation temperature can reduce deformation resistance and
improve deformation plasticity. The temperature of expanded-diameter and
pushed-bend is selected two phase region and b phase region. The deformation
temperature is measured by using portable infrared thermometers, AR892.
After annealing in two phase region, the samples are investigated effect of
processing temperature on mechanical properties and microstructure after cutting
down along cross and axial direction of pipe and elbow. The mechanic properties

are carried on Instron 1185 tensile testing machine. The microstructure is observed
on Olypus PMG optical microscope.
Results and Discussion
Strain Analysis of Elbow During Expanded-Diameter and Pushed-Bend
Procedure The straight pipes generate complex deformation consisted of com-
pressing bend deformation along axial direction and circumferential
expanding-diameter along circumferential direction under the common action of
expanding-diameter force of horn mould, pushing force of pushing machine and
force moment. As far as the elbow deformation is concerned, the deformation
degree and stress on belly and back position of elbow is different. The belly of
elbow shorten length due to suffered compressing deformation along axial direc-
tion, however the back length of elbow almost keep consistent with that of pipe, so
it is considered that little compressing deformation occur on back of elbow along
axial direction [6–10]. But bending deformation all exist on belly and back of elbow
due to ﬂexural torque of horn mould.
The wall thickness of elbow has thinned trend under the action of expanding
diameter of horn mould along circumferential direction; however, the thicken wall
thickness of elbow on belly make circumference expanding-diameter deformation
off-centering. During off-center expanding-diameter, the thicken wall thickness of
elbow on belly due to compressing deformation move to elbow back along two
sides of horn mould to make up for reduced wall thickness of elbow on back which
is result from expanding-diameter deformation [ 8]. Therefore, the belly and beck of
elbow can keep same wall thickness.
Strain diagrammatic sketch of elbow made by expanded-diameter and
pushed-bend method is shown in Fig. 1. It can be seen that the strain distribution
gradually reduces from belly to back as a whole. But the belly strain in center of
elbow along axial direction has local increasing phenomenon, because the center of
Fig. 1 Diagrammatic sketch
of elbow strain
434 J. Chen et al.

## Page 431

elbow along axial direction restricted by head and end of elbow is dif ﬁcult to release
strain. The exiting higher strain is easy to generate fold and non-smooth surface.
Inﬂuence of Processing Parameter of Expanded-Diameter and Pushed-Bend
Method The shape of elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed-bend method
is closely relative to designing of horn mould [ 11]. The center line of horn mould
can be descript by using continuous and smooth mathematics curve.
Because the elbow generates compressing and bending deformation along axial
direction and expanding-diameter deformations along circumferential direction on
the position of horn mould. The bending deformation degree along axial direction is
so high that it is needed to reduce deformation degree on per unit length of center
line along horn mould. The beginning bending radius and bending angle should be
increased in designing horn mould processing to extend the length of center line
and decrease bending deformation degree. Excessive thinned wall thickness should
be avoided to assure wall thickness uniformity [ 12].
The deformation temperature and temperature distribution of elbow is very
important. Reasonable pushing temperature can ensure the suitable match between
pushing force and high temperature yield strength of alloy.
Because pipes are arranged in series on core rod, and the push force acted on
push hoop behind of pipe is delivered to heated pipe. The heated pipes at optimum
temperature generate expanded-diameter deformation along circumference direction
and pushed-bend deformation along axial direction on position of horn mould.
Deformation resistance of pipe became larger at lower temperature, then the metal
deformation became dif ﬁculty and the friction force between pipe and horn mould
increase. All these results bring about higher pushing force and higher bearing force
of core rod. Sometimes the core rod comes into being vibration and the needed
pushing force easily overload the equipment capacity. But if the temperature of
elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed-bending method is so high that
oversize grain growth and surface serious oxidation of pipe occur. The overtop
pushing temperature decrease strength at high temperature, the pipe obviously
became too soft to contend against pushing force, and easily bring about fold and
wrinkle, ﬁnally lead to failure of elbow forming.
As a whole, the deformation temperature of short radius elbow is selected in two
phase region. The temperature of short radius elbow is higher than that of long
radius elbow due to greater compressing and expanding-diameter deformation.
Titanium alloy is used higher temperature and lower pushing rate because of higher
strength and lower plasticity comparing with pure titanium.
Because the surface area of large diameter elbow is so oversize that temperature
seriously decreases and deformation resistance force increase due to large cooling
area. As a result, the insulation measure should be adopted to prevent temperature
from falling too fast during heating pipe.
The temperature ﬁeld distribution during pushing elbow is required that the pipe
circumferential temperature is uniformity, and the axial temperature progressive
increase, that is to say, the reshaping section temperature of horn mould is not less
Microstructure and Properties of Large Diameter Elbow of Ti75 … 435

## Page 432

than deformation shaping section temperature. This is in favor of pushing out
ﬁnished-product from horn mould and keep deformation smoothly and easily.
The pushing rate of elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed-bend method
has important effect on wall thickness uniformity. In generally, the belly wall
thickness thickens rapidly because of compressing deformation. The pushing rate is
so fast that the thicken wall thickness has no time to ﬂow from belly to back and
give rise to thickening wall thickness of belly. If the pushing rate is too slow, the
circumferential expanding-diameter deformation rate is higher than axial
pushing-bend compressing rate, so the belly has no thicken wall thickness to make
up recover thinned wall thickness of back, ﬁnally the back wall thickness became
thinning.
Microstructure and Properties of Elbow Made by Expanded-Diameter and
Pushed-Bend Method The tensile properties of pipe are shown in Table. 1. The
pipe has tensile strength of 770 MPa, plasticity of 15% and area reduction of 60%.
The microstructure of pipe is shown in Fig. 2. The pipe microstructures in trans-
verse and axial direction consist of primary a phase and intergranular transfor-
mation b phase, the primary a phase with 10 lm size is characteristic of equiaxed
shape, massive shape and a small amount strip shape. The a lamellar space interval
is about 2 –3 lm in intergranular transformation b phase structure.
The microstructure of Ti75 titanium alloy elbow made in two phase region after
annealing is shown in Fig. 3. The microstructure include equiaxed primary a phase
and intergranular transformation b phase structure, a lamellar with 1 –1.5 lm
thickness in intergranular transformation b phase is thinner than that of pipe,
because the wall thickness of pipe before machining is thicker than that of elbow,
and result in lower cooling rate and thicken a lamellar.
The microstructure of elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed-bend
method in b phase region after annealing is shown in Fig. 4. The microstructure is
typical Widmanstaten structure which has coarse b grain with clear a phase grain
boundary, different orientation a colony of 80 –200 lm size distributing in b grain.
a lamellar basically parallel each other in the same a colony and has nearly same
orientation. The elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed-bend method in b
phase region has higher deformation temperature than phase transition point, so the
pushing force decrease obviously and increase pushing rate, while the
microstructure and properties may be deteriorate.

strength and yield strength before annealing is evidently lower than that of pipe and

Conclusions
1. The elbow made by expanded-diameter and pushed-bend method is feasible.
Under the action of pushing force, expanding-diameter and bending moment of
horn mould, the elbow generates composite deformation included bending and
compressing deformation along axial direction and off-center expanding-
diameter deformation along circumferential direction. The expanding- diame-
ter deformation reduces wall thickness, while the compressing deformation of
belly is greater than that of back, and result in thickening wall thickness on belly
and eccentricity. The wall thickness ﬂows from belly to back along two sides of
horn mould during expanding-diameter to compensate for thinned wall thick-
ness on back of elbow during off-center expanding-diameter.
2. The wall thickness uniformity of elbow is related to many factors, such as
design of horn mould, pushing temperature, temperature ﬁeld and pushing rate,
but the most important factor is design of horn mould.
3. The temperature of Ti75 titanium alloy elbow made by expanded-diameter and
pushed-bend method is chosen in two phase region. The two phase region
processing can reduce deformation resistance and improve alloy plasticity, and
the elbow keeps properties and microstructure consistent with pipe. The
microstructure of elbow with primary a phase and intergranular transformed b
phase is same with that of pipe. The elbow made in b phase region easily
produce grain over burning and overgrowing,and the microstructure of elbow
made in b phase region is typical widmanstanten structure.

Fatigue Behavior and Failure Analysis
of Ti-6Al-4V Forging with High Oxygen
Content
Yunxi Liu, Wei Chen, Zhiqiang Li, Bin Tang and Gang Yao
Abstract The microstructure, texture and HCF (high cycle fatigue) behavior of a
Ti–6Al–4V forging with 0.20 wt% oxygen were investigated. The material was
composed of 80 vol% of equiaxed ap grains and 20 vol% of transformed b (bT).
Average size of the ap phase was about 14 lm. EBSD analysis indicated a weak
basal texture with intensity of 2 times random. The forging billet exhibited a good
combination of ductility and strength performance and the mechanical properties
did not show obvious anisotropy. The fatigue life had a large scatter and the mean
life increased as the stress level decreased. The minimum life and POF = 0.1% life
of the samples increased with the decrease of stress level. The difference of the
feature of facets at the fatigue crack initiation region is considered to be the main
cause of fatigue life scatter. The formation of the faceted area in fatigue crack
initiation area results from the nucleation site of fatigue crack located in grain
clusters with similar orientation.

Introduction
As one of the typical a + b titanium alloys, Ti –6Al–4V has been widely applied in
the aerospace ﬁeld because of its excellent properties, including strength, toughness
and fatigue performance [ 1–3]. Combining with diffusion bonding, Ti –6Al–4V can
be superplastic formed to various hollow structures, such as wide chord fan blades
that have been used in Rolls-Royce ’s Trent engines for several decades.
Oxygen is an a stabilizer for titanium alloy and can also increase the strength by
solid solution strengthening [ 4–8]. Typical Ti –6Al–4V alloy for structural appli-
cation usually contains 0.15 –0.18 wt% of O to obtain a balance of strength and
toughness. However, for the high cycle fatigue (HCF) driven components such as
fan blades, keeping O at the highest level of ASTM Grade-5 is an effective way to
optimize the HCF performance since HCF property of a material is proportional to
its yield strength. In this paper, the microstructure and texture features of a Ti –6Al–
4V forging with 0.20 wt% O were studied. The high cycle fatigue behavior and
fracture mode were also investigated. A statistical model was used to analyze the
fatigue life distribution.
Materials and Methods
The chemical composition of the studied Ti –6Al–4V forging is listed in Table 1.
The oxygen content is 0.20%, which is the upper limit of regular Ti –6Al–4V.
Microstructure samples were prepared by conventional metallographic method.
Chemical etching was carried out using Kroll reagent (HF: HNO 3:H 2O = 1: 3: 7),
then the microstructure was observed by optical microscope (OM). The volume
fraction of each phase and primary a-grain size were measured using ImageJ
software and linear interception method, respectively. Electron backscatter
diffraction (EBSD) samples were prepared by a similar method. Afterwards, texture
analysis was carried out on a JSM-7001F ﬁeld emission SEM with an EBSD probe
of TSL system. The scanning regions were no less than 500 /C2500 lm, and the
step length was 1 lm. Then the experimental data were processed and analyzed by
the TSL OIM Analysis 6 software.
The room temperature tensile specimens were prepared according to GB/T
228.1-2010, as shown in Fig. 1a, and the strain rate was set to be 0.001/s. Smooth
cylindrical fatigue specimens were prepared according to GB/T 3075-2008, as
shown in Fig. 1b. The stress ratio and the test frequency were 0.1 and 100 Hz

Results and Analysis
The microstructures of the material are shown in Fig. 2. The material consists of
about 80 vol% of globular primary- a(ap) particles and 20 vol% transformed- b (bT).
The microstructure is relatively uniform, and the ap grains are in contact with each
other. In Fig. 2a, b, the original grain boundary a can still be observed but it was
broken into separate ap grains with low angle boundaries during the forging pro-
cess. The average grain size of ap is about 14 lm. The bT is composed of secondary
a and b lamellae, among which the b lamella is relatively thin(0.6 –1 lm). The
microstructure of the surface section (L-T plane), transverse section (T-S plane) and
longitudinal section (L-S plane) is quite similar, which indicates the isotropy of the
forging.
The GODF (grain orientation distribution ﬁgure), PFs (pole ﬁgures), IPFs (in-
verse pole ﬁgures) and GBMDF (grain boundary misorientation distribution ﬁgure)
of the Ti –6Al–4V forging are shown in Fig. 3. It is found that the orientation
distribution of the forging is relatively random (Fig. 3a), but some grain clusters
exhibit a preferred orientation (red grains in Fig. 3a). The pole ﬁgures (Fig. 3b)
show that the c axis of a few grains was oriented along the normal direction of the
forging, but the overall (0001) intensity is only 2 times random. It can also be seen
from the [001] inverse pole ﬁgure (Fig. 3c) that the billet has a weak basal texture.
Comparing with the Ti –6Al–4V rolled plates, there is no obvious crystallographic
texture in this Ti –6Al–4V forging. Figure 3d shows that there are still some green
and red grain boundaries within the primary agrains, indicating the existence of low
angle boundaries, which represents subgrains inside. Most of the blue lines in
Fig. 3d are high angle boundaries between a and b lamellae.
The tensile tests in Table 2 show that the Ti –6Al–4V forging exhibits good
ductility and strength properties. The tensile properties along the transverse and
longitudinal directions are similar, indicating that there is no anisotropy, which is
consistent with the EBSD results in Fig. 3. The tensile fracture surface shows a
typical cup-cone feature (Fig. 4a). The crack started from the center of the sample

With regard to the ductile material, the fatigue life is generally considered to
have a normal distribution function [ 9]. Therefore, the cumulative probability of
fatigue failure can be expressed in the form of normal probability, resulting in the
cumulative probability distribution space (POF-N
f) of fatigue failure [ 10–13]. In
engineering safety analysis and design, the fatigue life of POF = 0.1% is usually
used to evaluate the minimum safety life [ 9] of the material. The cumulative fatigue
failure probability distribution of 475, 500 and 525 MPa for forging samples is
shown as POF-N
f in Fig. 6a. Linearization ﬁtting of the normal probability at each
stress level is shown by the dotted line in the ﬁgure, and the results of the
parameters of each line are shown in Table 3. As is shown, the ﬁtting r value of
each stress level is greater than 0.9, indicating that the fatigue failure probability at
these stress levels has a good linear correlation relationship, which implies that the
specimens have single distribution mode of fatigue life. In addition, from 525 to
475 MPa, the ﬁtting line ’s slope gradually increases with the decrease of stress
level, indicating that the dispersion of fatigue life tends to decrease. However,
extending to the whole stress level range tested, combining with the analysis of
Fig. 5, the regularity of fatigue life dispersion of the forging is not explicit with the
stress level.
The mean life, minimum life and POF = 0.1% life of forging samples at various
stress levels are shown in Fig. 6b. The POF = 0.1% life were acquired by means of
the extrapolation of ﬁtting lines. The ﬁgure shows that the minimum fatigue life
tends to increase with the decrease of stress level and the POF = 0.1% life has some
correlation with the minimum fatigue life. The minimum fatigue life at the same
stress level will signi ﬁcantly affect the POF = 0.1% life. Moreover, the mean life
also shows the same trend, although the 500 MPa line is an exception. In reality,
the minimum fatigue life is the weak link property of titanium alloys and it is more
random than the mean life.
All samples exhibited typical fatigue fracture features. The fracture surface can
be divided into three zones: crack initiation region, the propagation region and ﬁnal
fracture region [ 14]. The representative SEM images of the Ti –6Al–4V fatigue
fracture surface are shown in Fig. 7. The sample exhibited 2,038,774 cycles at the

500 MPa stress level. The fatigue crack initiated close to the surface (Fig. 7a), and
the crack initiation region is usually accompanied by the occurrence of facets
(Fig. 7b). Obvious river patterns can be observed from the macro images in the
propagation region. Fatigue striations can also be observed, and their direction is in

of dimples are observed in the ﬁnal fracture region due to overload.
Figure 8 shows the SEM images of two samples tested at 500 MPa. The fatigue
life is 2,038,774 and 5,293,788 cycles, respectively. In the former sample, there are
several smooth initiation facets (IF) adjacent to each other, and they connected with
surrounding propagation facets (PFs) to form a larger faceted area (Fig. 8b). This is
consistent with the phenomenon of fatigue facets observed in typical Ti alloys
[15–22]. This may be due to the fact that the fatigue crack nucleation area located in
the region of several grains with similar orientation (Fig. 3). On the contrary, there
is only one initiation facet in the crack initiation region of the latter specimen, and
then the crack extended through the PFs (Fig. 8d) without forming a faceted region
similar to the former one. The difference of the feature of facets at the fatigue crack
initiation region is considered to be the main cause of fatigue life scatter.

Summary and Conclusions
(1) The Ti –6Al–4V forging is composed of about 80 vol% of equiaxed ap grains
and 20 vol% of bT. The average ap grain size is about 14 lm and the b lamella
thickness in bT is about 0.6 –1 lm. The forging exhibits a weak basal texture
and the intensity is 2 times random.
(2) The forging billet exhibits good ductility and strength properties, and the
mechanical properties do not show obvious anisotropy. The fatigue life has a
large scatter and the mean life increases with the decrease of stress level. The
minimum fatigue life tends to increase as the stress level decreases and the
POF = 0.1% life has some correlation with the minimum fatigue life. The
minimum fatigue life is the weak link property of titanium alloys and it is more
random than the mean life.
(3) The difference of the feature of facets at the fatigue crack initiation region is
considered to be the main cause of fatigue life scatter. The formation of the
faceted area in fatigue crack initiation area results from the nucleation site of
fatigue crack located in grain clusters with similar orientation.

Abstract In order to further improve the usage temperature of high temperature
titanium alloy, two kinds of near a titanium alloy ingots with Er and Re were

conditions, namely, b phase region and near b phase region were investigated by

Introduction
Some excellent properties of titanium alloys make it widely used. It is utilized as
materials for fan and compressor blades of aero-engines [ 1–3]. In recent years,
people have paid more attention to the research of titanium alloys and its use
temperature has also been raised to 600 °C. Instead of steel or other super alloys,
titanium alloys can reduce the quality of the engine and increase the engine thrust
weight ratio [ 4–7]. With the rapid development of the aircraft industry, new
advanced aero engines offer new requirements for the study of high temperature
titanium alloys. To meet this demand, many high temperature titanium alloys were
developed [ 8].
Because rare earth elements have very negative chemical potential, it has higher
afﬁnity with oxygen, nitrogen and other gases than titanium. Furthermore, it is an
active surfactant, that can decrease the surface tension of the alloy and increase the
activation energy of the nucleation [ 9]. Therefore, the addition of rare earth element
has become a trend in the development of high temperature titanium. For instance,
Ti-60 contains 0.2% mass fraction of Nd and has good thermal stability and high
temperature oxidation resistance. Ti600 contains 0.1% mass fraction of Y, its
tensile strength and high temperature durability are good. In particular, the creep
performance of Ti600 exceeds the IMI834 [ 6, 10]. Because of the chemical bonding
between Re and Si, the thermal stability of the alloy can be improved, so we add Re
to our alloy.
In this paper, the two alloys containing equal amounts of Er and Re were
prepared. The elements contained in the two alloys are Ti –Zr–Al–Sn–W–Si–Nb–
Mo–Re(Er). Besides, their effects on our alloy were investigated.
Experimental Procedures
We smelted the alloy three times in the furnace and casted at the third time. The cast
ingot is cylindrical. Phase change will appear at 1003 °C. Isothermal forging in
multiple directions was used for preparing the alloy. The forged temperatures were
1050 and 980 °C, respectively. The ingot was heated in the ZY-LS1600 resistance
furnace and the heating time was 40 min. When the heating process ended, we
began to forge the alloy. The deformation amount of upsetting is 40%, and the
deformation amount in the long direction is 30%. After the ﬁrst step of forging, we
tempered the ingot 10 min, and then started the second forging. Air cooling is used
in this forging process. The DDL50 test machine was used to obtain tensile data.
SU8020SEM and QUANTA650SEM were used to shoot microstructures.
452 Y. Jin et al.

## Page 448

Results and Discussion
Figure 1 is the cast microstructure of the two kinds of alloys, both of them are
widmanstatten structure. We can see from the picture that the alloys containing Er
and Re have almost the same grain size, which is about 400 –500 lm. The lamellar
of the alloy containing Re is more slender.
Microstructure After Forging
Figure 2 shows the different structures obtained by adding Er and Re at different
forging temperatures. Titanium alloy is very sensitive to the temperature, and the
structure of the forging is different at different temperatures [ 11]. It is easy to obtain
lamellar structure after appropriate forging in b phase region. If the heating tem-
perature is lower than the b transition temperature and the deformation is suf ﬁcient,
equiaxed structure will be obtained. This alloys forged at 1050 °C either with Er or
Re are basket-weave microstructure and the b grain boundary is obvious. There is
not much difference between the two alloys after forging at 1050 °C, except the
lamellar that containing Re is more slender. The microstructure forged at 980 °C is
duplex microstructure, which is composed of primary equiaxed a and transformed
b phase [ 12]. The grains of equiaxed a are relatively larger in the alloy that
containing Re.

Mechanical Properties After Forging
Figure 3 is the tensile curves and Table 1 is the tensile data of the two kinds of
alloys. Comparing with that of the alloy forged in b phase region, the tensile
strength at room temperature increased by 40 –50 MPa and the yield strength
increased by 70 –80 MPa and the elongation increases by about 2% of the alloy
forged in near b phase region. Under two kinds of forging conditions, the perfor-
mance of the alloy containing Re is higher than that of Er alloy. The yield strength
increased by about 20 MPa and elongation increased by about 2%. In comparison
with the high temperature tensile properties after forging, the high temperature
performance of forging at 980 °C is better than that of forging at 1050 °C. The
tensile strength of the alloy that containing Er forged at 1050 °C is the highest, but
its elongation rate is the lowest. The tensile strength and yield strength of the alloy
that containing Re forged at 1050 °C is relatively lower. The elongation rate of the
alloy that containing Er forged at 980 °C is the highest. In conclusion, the com-
prehensive performance of containing Re forged at 980 °C is the best.

## Page 450

The analysis of the structure can further explain the properties of the alloy. Our
alloy contains primary equiaxed a phase forged at 980 °C. The existence of voids
and cracks is an important reason for the fracture of the sample. When the crack
meets the equiaxed a phase, it can’t go straight forward and can only bypass it. This
way of passing makes it lose more energy. The larger the primary a particle, the
greater the crack growth encounter. Therefore, the tensile specimen can produce
greater deformation before fracture and obtain higher tensile plasticity and strength.
Hence, the alloy has obtained better properties after forging at 980 °C. When
forging at 1050 °C, the alloy forms basket weave microstructure with lamellar a
phase and b phase. The same habit plane in this microstructure makes the slip easy
to carry out. Coarse slip zones and voids will also appear at this time. That is, the
crack initiation is easier. So the plasticity is going to fall [ 13–15]. Therefore, the
duplex microstructure forged at 980 °C has the best performance. The lamellar of
the alloy containing Re is more slender after forging at 1050 °C. The equiaxed a of

Conclusions
By studying the effect of Er and Re on the alloys, we mainly get the following
conclusions:
(1) The microstructure is basket-weave microstructure after forging at 1050 °C and
duplex microstructure can be obtained after forging at 980 °C.
(2) The properties of the two alloys containing Er and Re are better as forged at
980 °C than that at 1050 °C.
(3) The comprehensive performance of the alloy containing Re forged at 980 °C is
the best.

Analysis of Friction and Wear Behavior
of Vacuum Nitriding on Ti80 Titanium
Alloy
Lei Li, Xiaonan Mao and Quan Hong
Abstract Titanium alloy has light weight, low young modulus, small coef ﬁcient of
thermal expansion and good corrosion resistance properties. Especially for high
corrosive hydrogen sul ﬁde and carbon dioxide, titanium alloy shows excellent
resistance. With the replacement of Ni based alloy with titanium alloy, titanium oil
pipes have become one of the development directions of high temperature and high
pressure wells. Recently, the titanium alloy tubing has been used in Yuanba gas-
ﬁeld, indicating that titanium alloy tubing has entered a practical stage in China.
However, because of the low hardness, high friction factor, poor wear resistance,
serious adhesive wear, the erosion of crude oil and the friction of the sucker rod
have a great in ﬂuence on the wear properties of the titanium alloy tubing. These
deﬁciencies will become one of the main constraint factors for the development of
titanium alloy oil tubes. In order to solving this problem, in the present paper we
improved the tribological performance by means of ion nitriding on Ti80 alloy. The
microstructure, surface morphology, hardness tester and wear resistance of the
material were analyzes by means of XRD, SEM, Vickers hardness tester and wear
and abrasion tester. The results showed that the tribological performance of Ti80
alloy oil tubes is improved by ion nitriding process.

## Page 454

Introduction
The demand for oil and nature gas will double in the next ten years, because of the
rapid development of world economy. Yuanba gas ﬁeld is an important position in
key exploration areas of Sinopec Group in China. The gas reservoirs in Changxing
area are deep buried, high temperature, high pressure, high corrosive hydrogen
sulﬁde and carbon dioxide. The corrosion environment is very complex. Therefore
Yuanba gasﬁeld is one of the highest risk projects for onshore gas ﬁeld operation in
the world, and the service conditions of oil pipes are very abominable.
Titanium is recognized for its highest strength-to-weight ratio among all metals.
Elevated temperature property is also an outstanding merit comparing with other
metals. Chemically, the excellent resistance to corrosion is the most noted property
of titanium. Comparing with the nickel based alloy, titanium alloy has light weight,
low young modulus, small coef ﬁcient of thermal expansion and better corrosion
resistance properties. Especially for high corrosive hydrogen sul ﬁde and carbon
dioxide, titanium alloy shows excellent resistance [ 1–3]. With the replacement of Ni
based alloy with titanium alloy, titanium oil pipes have become one of the devel-
opment directions of high temperature and high pressure wells [ 4]. However,
because of the low hardness, high friction factor, poor wear resistance, serious
adhesive wear, the erosion of crude oil and the friction of the sucker rod have a
great in ﬂuence on the wear properties of the titanium alloy tubing [ 5–8]. These
deﬁciencies will become one of the main constraint factors for the development of
titanium alloy oil tubing.
The nominal component of Ti80 alloy is Ti –6Al–3Nb–2Zr–1Mo. Ti80 alloy is
one of the 850 MPa-level corrosion resistant near alpha titanium alloys of China.
Ti80 alloy has high strength, good corrosion resistance and good weldability, and
its comprehensive property is better than that of TC4 alloy [ 9–11]. Ti80 alloy has
excellent impact toughness, fracture toughness and corrosion resistance. Ti80 alloy
is widely used in ship and underwater weapons, bolts, shafts and corrosion resistant
shells in the form of plates, bars, forgings and so on. Recently, the Ti80 tubing has
been used in Yuanba gas ﬁeld, indicating that titanium alloy tubing has entered a
practical stage in China. In order to improving the tribological performance of Ti80
for its application, we perform surface treatment by means of ion nitriding on Ti80
alloy. The microstructure, surface morphology, hardness tester and wear resistance
of the material were analyzes by means of XRD, Vickers hardness tester and wear
and abrasion tester. The results showed that the tribological performance of Ti80
alloy oil tubes improved by ion nitriding process.

Sample Preparation and Measurements
In order to getting uniform composition, Ti80 alloy used in the present work was
three-times melting ingot, with the process of vacuum arc furnace melting — vac-
uum skull furnace melting — vacuum arc furnace melting. Though a series of hot
forging, Ti80 alloy ingot eventually deformed into square bar (80 * 80 * 500 mm).
Its chemical composition is presented in Table 1.
The b transformation temperature (T b) was measured to be approximately
1010 °C. The Ti80 alloy bar had been subjected to a large number of hot forging in
a + b region. Finally, a homogenous bimodal microstructure was obtained which
consisted of equiaxed a phase within a ﬁne transformed b matrix, as shown in
Fig. 1. The microstructure is uniform and nearly equiaxed, with grain size of about
15–30 lm.
The tensile specimens were electro-discharged machined from the square bar
with a gauge length of 25 mm and a diameter of 5 mm. The results of room
temperature mechanical properties are shown in Table 2.
The Ti80 ion nitriding sample had been pretreated with the process of surface
polishing— ultrasonically cleaned in alcohol — drying. Ion nitriding of Ti80 samples
was performed using a pulsed ion nitriding facility (type LDMC-15A). The cross

Results and Discussion
Figure 2a shows the surface of nitrided sample. The color of nitrided layer is light
brown. Figure 2b shows the microstructure of nitrided sample. The white particles
are titanium nitrides. The thickness of nitrided layer is about 150 lm, but only the
top 40 lm is dense zone.
Figure 3 show the X-ray diffraction pattern of the nitrided sample. The result
indicates that the nitrided layer is composed of TiN, Ti 2N, TiN 0.3. From the
intensity of the diffraction peaks, it is obvious that the content of Ti 2N and TiN 0.3
are higher than TiN. The diffraction peaks of Ti are very weak. That means the most
atoms near the surface are nitrided.
It is worth noting that the diffraction peaks of Ti
3Al are observed. During the ion
nitriding of titanium alloy, the stability of TiN is higher than that of AlN. Therefore,
the formation of titanium nitride is easier than aluminum nitride. The diffusion
behavior of ion nitriding of titanium alloy has been studied by Magnan [ 12]. At the
beginning of ion nitriding process, TiN is formed at the surface of Ti alloy. With the
decrease of Ti atoms, the concentration of aluminum atoms increases at the inter-
face of nitride layer and the matrix. In order to dissolve the accumulated Al atoms,
Ti
3Al intermetallic compound formed.

Conclusion
The tribological performance of Ti80 alloy and nitrided Ti80 alloy has been
investigated in this paper. A 150 lm nitrided layer is obtained by ion nitriding on
Ti80 alloy sample. The nitrided layer is composed of TiN, Ti 2N, TiN 0.3. The
hardness of nitrided samples is 887HV and decreases steeply along the depth. The
nitrided layer shows excellent wear resistance under the load of 50 N. The mass
loss is much smaller than original samples. But under large load of 200 N, the
brittle nitrided layer is damaged immediately at the beginning of the test. The dry
sliding friction and wear mechanism of Ti80 sample and nitrided sample is abrasive
wear and adhesive wear.

Effect of NaOH Concentration
on the Microhardness and Corrosion
Resistance of Titanium
by Acid-Hydrothermal Method
Ying Xu, Bian Wang, Yanqing Cai and Zizi Zhang
Abstract To enhance the microhardness and corrosion resistance of modi ﬁed pure
titanium, TiO 2 nanostructure has been prepared on titanium substrate by
acid-hydrothermal method. The morphology of the titanium surface underwent
change from nanosheets to nanorods with the increase of NaOH concentration,
which was performed by the scanning electron microscope (SEM). A mixture of the
anatase TiO
2 and rutile TiO 2 were formed on the synthesized titanium surface
measured by X-ray diffraction (XRD). Microhardness was measured by micro-
hardness tester and the hardness rose sharply and then declined gradually as the
increase of NaOH concentration, showing a considerably high hardness value of
361HV with NaOH concentration of 5 M (PAN-5). In addition, the corrosion
resistance was examined in SBF by electrochemical methods. The polarization
curve demonstrated that the corrosion resistance was optimal when the NaOH
concentration was 5 M. Therefore, the hardness and corrosion resistance of tita-
nium, with the appropriate morphology of nanorods, were optimized as the NaOH
concentration was 5 M.

Introduction
Commercially pure titanium and its alloys were attractive materials in industrial and
biomedical applications owing to their good corrosion resistance, mechanical
properties, chemical stability and biocompatibility in the human body [ 1, 2]. The
characteristic of these materials was due to a passivation layer of amorphous tita-
nium dioxide, which was naturally oxidized during exposure to air on the surface
[3, 4]. Although the oxides act as barrier layers between the hosting tissues and the
titanium implant, it was too thin and got disrupted easily under the action of body
ﬂuids to provide full corrosion protection [ 5]. Besides, the hardness of pure titanium
also needs to be enhanced [ 6, 7]. So the corrosion resistance and hardness on
titanium surface must be improved by its modi ﬁcation.
The modi ﬁcation techniques included mechanical methods (e.g., sandblasting,
grinding, polishing, etc.), chemical methods (e.g., acid corrosion, sol-gel method,
chemical vapor deposition, etc.), electrochemical methods (anodic oxidation, etc.)
and physical methods (physical vapor deposition, ion implantation, thermal spray,
etc.) [3, 5, 8, 9]. Recently, great interest had been placed on the surface modi ﬁcation
of biomaterials by hydrothermal methods, which offered a simple and cost-effective
technique to produce thin, ﬁrmly attached oxidative layers [ 10, 11].
The attractiveness of nano titania was largely ascribed to its unique properties,
including high corrosion resistance, non-toxicity and stable property. So the main
aim of the present study was to produce nano TiO
2 on titanium surface by
acid-hydrothermal methods and examine their effect of NaOH concentration on the
microhardness and corrosion resistance of titanium. The surface roughness of
titanium could be improved by acid treatment, which was favorable to mechanical
bonding with bone tissue [ 12].
Materials and Methods
Sample Pretreatment and Acid Treatment Commercial pure titanium samples of
dimensions 10 mm /C2 10 mm /C2 1 mm, with the purity of more than 99.7%, were
spark cut from plates. The titanium plate was ultrasonically rinsed with acetone,
ethanol, and distilled water (each for 10 min). Then the titanium was immersed in
5 wt% oxalic acid concentration at 100 °C for 2 h, rinsed with distilled water, and
dried at room temperature.
The pre-treated specimens were etched in an acid mixture composed of 50 mL
of 0.29 M HNO
3 and 0.53 M HF at a temperature of 25 °C for 10 min. Then the
samples were rinsed, ultrasonic cleaning twice in distilled water and were subjected
to surface treatments.
Sample Preparation of Hydrothermal Synthesis Acid treated samples were
placed in a Te ﬂon container (50 mL) containing 35 mL NaOH to 75% full volume
with four concentration of 1, 3, 5 and 10 M, respectively. The Te ﬂon container was
468 Y. Xu et al.

## Page 463

placed in a stainless steel autoclave for hydrothermal treatment at a temperature of
130 °C for 12 h. Then the samples were immersed in 0.3 M HCl concentration for

For the surface treatments, acid, hydrothermal and NaOH concentration were
sequentially performed, and each surface treatment group was shown in Table 1.
Surface Characterization The crystalline phases of the synthesized were identi-
ﬁed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Japan, D/MAX2500PC), The X-ray source was
CuKa radiation and the 2 h range was 20 –80 °C with a scanning step size of 0.02°.
The morphology of the surface was observed by scanning electron microscopy
(SEM, Japan, S-480).
Microhardness Test The microhardness was measure by Vickers microhardness
tester (HVST-1000ZA). The indentation load used 10 g with 4-sided pyramid with
square base and an apex angle between opposite sides of 136 ± 15°. Higher loads
could cause problems as a direct result of load dependence of hardness and pro-
moting the occurrence of localized microscopic cracking [ 13]. To minimize
uncertainties from measurement and ensure complete deformation, an indentation
load of 10 g for a dwell time of 15 s was chosen. At least ﬁve points were randomly
made on modi ﬁed surfaces of each sample.
Electrochemical Test The corrosion resistance was determined by electrochemical
workstation (CHI760C) during exposure in SBF with pH = 7.4. The components
and concentrations of the SBF concentration were given in Table 2. The reference
electrode was a Ag/AgCl electrode and auxiliary electrode was Pt electrode. Before
beginning, all electrochemical measurements were performed after the open circuit
potential (OCP) stabilized. The rest potential was considered to be attained when
the potential changed less than 2 mV over 30 min. The initial scan potential and the
ﬁnal scan potential were ±50 mV superimposed on the open circuit potential value
with a speed of 1 mV/s. Relevant parameters of free-corrosion potential (E
corr),
free-corrosion current (I corr) and corrosion rate related to the corrosion resistance
were obtained by Tafel analyses of the corresponding dynamic polarization curves.
Non-modiﬁed samples were used as reference.

Apart from the peaks of the titanium substrate, the anatase phases and rutile

peak intensity of rutile did not change greatly, for the reason that the changes of the

TiO
2 increased with the intensities of progressively NaOH concentration.
The acid treatment could etch most oxidation ﬁlm on the titanium surface with
mixed acid of HF and HNO 3. It played a very important and dominant role on
different morphology in the growth process of TiO 2 nanostructures after immersed
in NaOH concentration. Generally, the vegetation process of TiO 2 nanostructures
by hydrothermal method proceeds through several stages. During the addition of
NaOH, Ti(OH) 3
+ formed by hydrothermal treatment caused owing to the effect of
OH− (Eq. 1). Simultaneously, the hydrated Ti dioxide (TiO 2/C1 nH2O) was generated

fragments or a layered structure (Eqs. 3 and 4). Titanate was formed after the
sodium titanate reacted with H + after immersed in HCl (Eq. 5). Since the heat
treatment did cause a signi ﬁcant impact, TiO 2 generated by the pyrogenic
decomposition of sodium titanate forms as a layered structure (Eq. 6). The unstable

It was discovered that the shape of the nanostructure which gradually changed
from the titanium surface of TiO 2 structure was affected by NaOH concentration in
Fig. 1. The main reason was the increase of NaOH concentration could make the
productivity of titanate, which was generated by reaction with titanium and NaOH
concentration increase. At the same time, titanate could also provide more energy to
accelerate the titanate into TiO
2. If the driving force is insuf ﬁcient, the titanate
concentration was too low to curled up rods. Titanate decomposition speed takes
place quickly with increasing of NaOH concentration, which occured too rapidly to
achieve the uniform growth after curled of TiO
2 and make the nanorods aggregated
to reduce the energy (Fig. 1d).
By above knowable, the morphology of the titanium surface underwent changed
from nanosheets to nanorods with the increase of NaOH concentration. Besides, the
different NaOH concentration did not change the chemical composition of titanium
surface, just change the peak intensity of anatase. Thus, a coating mostly composed
of anatase TiO
2 and rutile phases TiO 2 was formed on the surfaces after
hydrothermal treatment.
Microhardness Hardness evaluation was an important part of mechanical behavior
evaluation of metallic biomaterials. Table 3 showed the hardness results of the P,
PAN-1, PAN-3, PAN-5 and PAN-10 groups. The zero point represented the pure
titanium (P). It was noteworthy that different NaOH concentration displayed higher
hardness than P group. The hardness gradually heightened as the NaOH concen-
tration increase in a range of 1 –5 M, showing a considerably high hardness value of
361HV increase to 5 M (PAN-5). Out of this range, the hardness slowly dropped to
slightly lower values with increasing NaOH concentration. The hardness was
approximately 341HV, however, was higher than that of pure Ti with aqueous of
PAN-10 sample.
The reason for this could be two-fold: ﬁrst, The TiO
2 nano-structures prepared
by hydrothermal methods were typically harder than metallic ones on account of

Conclusion
In this study, acid-hydrothermal treated TiO 2 nanostructures were obtained by acid
solution (HF and HNO 3) and NaOH solution in order. The main conclusions of
microhardness and corrosion resistance were summarized as follows:
(1) Acid treatments with HF and HNO 3 were effective in increasing the surface
roughness of titanium surface with ridge structure of angular stepped.
(2) The surfaces morphology of the sample was changed by acid-hydrothermal
methods from nanomaterials to nanobars with the increase of NaOH concen-
tration. The hydrothermal treated samples consisted of a mixture of the anatase
and rutile phases of TiO 2.
(3) The microhardness of the titanium specimen was signi ﬁcantly higher after the
heat treatment. The hardness prominently increased and then slowly dropped to

## Page 470

Effects of Forging Temperature
on Microstructure and Mechanical
Properties of 650 °C High Temperature
Titanium Alloy
Dandan Li, Lihua Chai, Ziyong Chen, Tounan Jin, Guodong Shi,
Yanfang Jin and Zongyue Feng
Abstract The microstructure and mechanical properties of the alloy Ti –Al–Sn–Zr–
Mo–Nb–Ta–Si–C–Er forged at different temperature were discussed. The micro-
scopic observation showed that both forged alloys consisted of basket weave
structure, the alloy forged at 1000 °C had some lamellar a phase turning to
equiaxed a phase, and its a lamellae was ﬁner than that forged at 1050 °C, which
coincided with the theoretical expectation. The mechanical properties at room
temperature and 650 °C were measured, and the results showed that the forged
alloy at 1000 °C possessed better mechanical properties. Compared with the alloy
at 1050 °C, the alloy forged at 1000 °C has a high strength and slightly better
elongation. The result showed that with the decrease of forging temperature, the
strength and ductility increase, the size of a lamella reduces, and the number of
equiaxed a phase increases. The excellent comprehensive mechanical properties of
the alloy are obtained by forging at 1000 °C.
Keywords High-temperature titanium alloy
/C1Forging temperature
Microstructure /C1Mechanical properties
Introduction
Titanium and its alloys are widely used for aerospace applications due to their low
density, high speci ﬁc strength, high temperature resistance and corrosion resistance
[1–4]. Titanium alloys can be classi ﬁed into ﬁve categories: a, near- a, a + b,

## Page 471

metastable b and b titanium alloy. In contrast with a and b titanium alloys, the
nearly a titanium alloy has higher creep strength and elevated temperature
instantaneous strength. Nowadays, near- a titanium alloys have attracted extensive
research interests due to their excellent mechanical properties, especially high
thermal stability and good weld-ability, it is used for discs and blades in the
compressor of aero engine, with service temperature up to 600 °C [ 5–8]. With the
instantaneous temperature of some new aerocrafts is up to 650 –700 °C in ﬂight,
which requires a higher temperature titanium alloy used for the components of
aircraft engines [ 9].
In recent years, as the developing of aviation industry of our country and the
increasing number of ﬂight accidents, there is a growing emphasis on the structure
of crashworthiness performance, the research on the high performance of high
temperature titanium alloys becomes an urgent problem that should to be solved.
Forging can be effectively used for the increase of mechanical properties in titanium
alloys [10, 11]. The titanium alloy is sensitive to the heating temperature, the slight
change in the heating temperature leads to a sharp drop in deformation resistance,
using isothermal forging or near isothermal forging can reduce or eliminate the
effect of mold chill and material strain hardening, signi ﬁcantly reduce the defor-
mation resistance and improve the forming performance of the blank [ 12–15].
It has been reported that the forging temperature of titanium alloy is the main
factor determining the microstructure and mechanical properties of forgings. In this
paper, the microstructure and the mechanical performance of titanium processed by
multiple forging at different temperature are studied.
Experimental Procedures
The alloy Ti –Al–Sn–Zr–Mo–Nb–Ta–Si–C–Er was fabricated by melting in Ar
atmosphere using water-cooled copper crucible vacuum induction melting furnace.
The cast ingot obtained is shown in Fig. 1.
Cylindrical blanks were cut from the cast ingot by wire electrical discharge
machining, and the size is U60 mm /C2150 mm. The blanks were subsequently
coated with an anti-oxidation coating, Ti-1200, to prevent severe oxidation, and
then they were wrapped in insulated cotton to prevent excessive cooling of spindles
during forging. The treated spindles adopted a multi direction free forging at def-
erent temperatures and speed 0.02 s
−1, tempered two times during forging, and the
total reduction of treated spindles was about 80%. After forging, the treated spin-
dles were air cooled. Forging temperature were about 20 –30 °C above or below the
(a + b)/b transition temperature.
Samples with a size of 6 /C28 /C210 mm
3 were cut from the ingots and forged
spindles respectively, which were chemically corroded after grinding and polishing
with metallographic abrasive papers (from #400 to #2000) and Polishing cloth. The
corrode solution is 2 pct hydro ﬂuoric, 4 pct nitric acid and the rest water. The
478 D. Li et al.

## Page 472

microstructural observation was performed using SU8020 SEM by Secondary
electrons scanning electron microscopy after metallographic corrosion.
The tensile tests were performed on the CMT 5205 GL tensile machine. Room
temperature tensile tests were performed at strain rates of 5 /C210−4 s−1, and high
temperature tensile tests were performed at the temperature of 650 °C and strain
rates of 1 /C210−3 s−1. After the tensile tests, the fractographs characterization was
performed by scanning electron microscopy using backscattered electrons.
Results and Discussion
Tensile Properties As-forged Ti–Al–Sn–Zr–Mo–Nb–Ta–Si–C–Er alloy with 80%
deformation was the starting state in the tensile property tests. Tensile curves of the
forged alloys at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 2, and the tensile results
are summarized in Table 1. Compared with the alloy forged at 1050 °C, the room
temperature and high temperature ultimate tensile strength of the alloy forged at
1000 °C increases by about 35 MPa, and the yield strength at room temperature
and high temperature increases by about 60 and 45 MPa respectively. In addition,
the elongation of the alloy forged at 1000 °C also increased. Obviously, as shown
in Fig. 2, with the decreases of forging temperature that from 30 °C above the
(a + b)/b transition temperature to 20 °C below, strength and ductility notably
increases.
Fracture Analysis SEM observations of the fracture surface of tested at room
temperature and 650 °C of the samples forged at different temperatures are shown in
Fig. 3. Figure 3a, b are the fracture morphologies of samples forged at 1050 °C, the
fracture surface of samples that tested at room temperature exhibits brittle fracture
mode by plentiful tearing ridges. At 650 °C, it is the mixture mode of cleavage
fracture and ductile fracture, which include a small amount small and shallow

The change of mechanical properties is closely related to the microstructure.
Figure 5 illustrates the microstructures of samples after forging at 1050 and 1000 °C.
It could be observed that the b grains were distorted after forging at 1050 °C, the
grain size is decreased, the lamellae a in the b grains are distorted and bent under
stress. During the forging process, b grain boundary solution dissolved, when the
temperature falls below the ( a + b)/b transition temperature, the lamellae a and a
small amount of b phase precipitated on the original b grain boundary, with the
temperature decrease, the lamellae a phase precipitated from the inside of the grains.
After 1000 °C forging, the crushed original b grains could be seen, grain boundary is
no longer obvious, the a lamellae in the grains was distorted, shredded, and the
dynamic globularization of a lamellae could be observed. Compared with the forged
alloy at 1050 °C, the a lamellae in the sample of forged at 1000 °C is smaller, and the
ﬁne a lamellae could increase the strength of the titanium alloy, and the equiaxed a

phase in 1000 °C forged alloy could improve the plasticity. The reason which

1050 °C, is that the ﬁne a lamellae and the equiaxed a phase increased the strength
and ductility of the alloy respectively.
Conclusions
The effect of forging temperature on microstructure and mechanical properties of
650 °C high temperature titanium alloy have been investigated. The following
conclusions are drawn:
1. With the decrease of forging temperature from the 30 °C above the ( a + b)/b
transition temperature to 20 °C below, the strength and ductility notably
increase, the size of a lamella reduces, and the number of equiaxed a phase
increases. An excellent comprehensive mechanical properties can be obtained
by forging at 1000 °C.
2. The fracture surface of the alloy by forging at 1050 °C exhibits brittle fracture
mode and it shows ductile fracture mode at 1000 °C forged.

Forging Technology and Microstructure
and Mechanical Properties of a Novel

Zongyue Feng, Lihua Chai, Ziyong Chen, Tounan Jin, Guodong Shi,
Yanfang Jin and Dandan Li
Abstract In this paper, the Ti –Al–Sn–Zr–Mo–Si series high temperature titanium
alloy is designed by using the electron concentration theory and the ﬁrst principles
calculation. The ingot of a novel high temperature alloy was prepared by induction
skull melting (ISM) in a water cooler copper crucible, then three different kinds of
forging technology (two steps of axial forging, two steps of lateral forging and two
steps of multi-directional forging) are employed for the Sub b forging at 1050 °C
and the near b forging at 980 °C. It shows a basket-weave microstructure after sub
b forging at 1050 °C. While after the near b forging at 980 °C, the alloy shows a
duplex microstructure with a little amount of primary a-phase and mechanical
properties is better than the alloy forging at 1050 °C. The grains undergoing a two
steps of multi-directional forging is ﬁner and more uniform, and the properties is
more excellent for the alloy.

Introduction
In recent years, with the rapid development of science and technology, aerospace
industry has become more and more urgent for new structure materials with high
strength, low density and high temperature resistance [ 1]. Titanium alloy has been
widely used in frontier ﬁelds such as war industry, ocean, petroleum and chemical
industry recently due to it have many advantages, such as low density, high speci ﬁc
strength, high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, good weldability and
low coef ﬁcient of linear expansion. At present, advanced aero engines require
higher mechanical properties, thermal stability and oxidation resistance of materials
at high temperature. The traditional materials can ’t meet the engine performance,
and the application of high temperature titanium alloy can improve the engine thrust
weight ratio, high temperature resistance and oxidation resistance. Therefore, in
recent years, all countries in the world have put development of new high tem-
perature titanium alloy in a vital position [ 2–4].
At present, the domestic and foreign high temperature titanium alloys, such as
IMI834, Ti-1100 and Ti60 etc., can be used at only 600 °C. With the development
of the aerospace industry, the temperature has been unable to meet the new
requirements of spacecraft using existing high temperature titanium alloy, therefore
we need to develop to meet the new high temperature titanium alloy Ti-(6 –7)Al-(2–
3) Sn-(8 –10)Zr–Mo–Nb–W–Si–Er using above 650 °C [ 5–7].
In this paper, the microstructure and the mechanical performance of titanium
processed by three different kinds of forged technology at different temperature are
studied. The specimens manufactured by two steps of multi-directional forging at
980 °C [ 8–10] exhibit high strength and concomitant good ductility, the method is
capable used for production of titanium alloys with superior mechanical properties
of industrial [ 11, 12].
Experimental Procedures
Using electronic concentration theory, the ﬁrst principles calculation and the latest
research results at home and abroad, Ti-(6 –7)Al-(2–3)Sn (8–10)Zr–Mo–Nb–W–Si–
Er series high temperature titanium alloy with properties close to 650 °C is
designed. The ingot of titanium alloy was prepared by induction skull melting
(ISM) in a water cooler copper crucible, and its solidi ﬁcation structure was con-
trolled to obtain homogeneous and non segregated high quality ingot.

rates of 1 /C210−3 s−1.

Conclusions
In the study, the effect of forged technology on microstructure and mechanical
properties of a novel titanium alloy of high temperature resistant to 650 °C tem-
perature was investigated. The conclusions are drawn as following:
1. The microstructure of Ti-(6 –7)Al-(2–3)Sn-(8–10)Zr–Mo–Nb–W–Si–Er alloy
has a remarkable in ﬂuence on the mechanical properties of the high temperature
titanium alloy, and the strength of the alloy is obviously improved with a ﬁne a
lamellae and the equiaxed a phase.
2. With the forged temperature decreases from the 40 –50 °C above the ( a + b)/b
transition temperature to the 20 –30 °C below, the strength of the alloy has a
remarkable increases. An excellent mechanical properties could be obtained by
near b forging at 980 °C
3. Under the same forged temperature condition, the mechanical properties of
Ti-(6–7)Al-(2–3)Sn-(8–10)Zr–Mo–Nb–W–Si–Er alloy is the best among all the
alloys in this paper after two steps of multi-directional forging.

Failure Mode of Ductile Hole Formation
in Thick Ti –6Al–4V Targets Having
Equiaxed and Lamellar Microstructures
Chao Zheng, Xiurong Zhu, Haiying Xin, Zhiwen Shao, Huan Wang,
Huaxin Peng, Xingwang Cheng and Fuchi Wang
Abstract The 40 mm Ti –6Al–4V thick targets having equiaxed and lamellar
microstructures were normally impacted by 12.7 mm and 14.5 mm arm-piercing
projectiles. The Ti –6Al–4V targets having equiaxed microstructure showed better
ballistic impact property compared with the Ti –6Al–4V targets having lamellar
microstructure. The analysis of macro-damage and micro-damage features revealed
that the failure mode of ductile hole formation in 40 mm thick Ti –6Al–4V targets
should be divided into three stages: cratering, steady penetration and perforation.
The role that adiabatic shear bands played varied in the different stages of pene-
tration. In the stage of steady penetration, the plastic deformation was concentrated
in adiabatic shear bands to coordinate with the squeezing into of the projectile.
While in the stage of perforation, adiabatic shear bands were still failure paths for
the formation of spalling fragments from the rear surface.

Introduction
Since 1990, Burkins et al. [ 1] evaluated the effect of thermo-mechanical processing
on the ballistic limit velocity for ELI grade Ti –6Al–4V. They reported that the
failure mode for plates processed both in the b region and in the ( a + b) region is a
combination of bulging, petaling and spalling. Bartus [ 2] found that the ballistic
limit velocity of BASCA treated Ti-5553 plates was lower than that of STA treated
ones. It is a pity that the analysis on micro-damage features was not included in
these papers.
The adiabatic shear instability of titanium alloys has long attracted the concerns
of the materials scientists, and the roles that adiabatic shear bands, shorten as ASBs,
play in Ti –6Al–4V targets have already been investigated by Woodward [ 3], Grebe
et al. [ 4], and others. Adiabatic shear bands were always thought to be failure
channels for further catastrophic capacity loses. Leppin and Woodward [ 5] inves-
tigated the failure mode of thin plates of titanium alloys impacted by ﬂat and
conical projectiles. Me-Bar and Rosenberg [ 6] found that the Ti –6Al–4V plates
processed by different heat treatments showed two kinds of failure modes including
ductile hole formation and plugging. Martinez et al. [ 7] concluded that the for-
mation of adiabatic shear bands and cracking induced by adiabatic shear bands
increased with increasing impact velocity, forming a cylindrical ﬂow regime which
ﬁnally led to plugging. Recently, Sukumar and Singh [ 8] pointed out the crucial
role played by adiabatic shear bands and ASB induced cracks in b-CEZ titanium
targets. Zheng et al. [ 9] reported the improved ballistic impact property found in the
Ti–6Al–4V targets having bimodal microstructure with thick a plates in the
transformed b. But so far, investigations on the roles that adiabatic shear bands play
in failure mode of ductile hole formation in thick Ti –6Al–4V targets are still quite
limited.
In order to ﬁnd the role that adiabatic shear bands play in failure mode of ductile
hole formation in thick Ti –6Al–4V targets, 40 mm thick Ti –6Al–4V targets having
equiaxed and lamellar microstructures were normally impacted by 12.7 and
14.5 mm AP in this work. Metallurgical observations were done to analyze the
macro-damage and micro-damage features of the impacted thick Ti –6Al–4V
targets.
Methods and Materials
Quasi-static tensile tests were conducted at a strain rate of 10 −3 s−1 using an Instron
testing machine according to GB/T 228-2002. The dynamic compression properties
were tested at a strain rate of 10
3 s−1 using the Split Hopkinson Compression Bar
introduced in [ 10]. The ballistic impact experiments were conducted in the terminal
ballistic laboratory, as shown in Fig. 1. The targets machined in dimensions of
150 /C2150 /C240 mm were ﬁxed in the target rack at a point of 10 m from the gun,
494 C. Zheng et al.

## Page 486

and the velocities of the projectiles were measured by circle targets. The projectiles
used were 12.7 and 14.5 mm AP, and the cores of the projectiles are illustrated in
Fig. 2. The cores were made from Steel T12A with a hardness of 65 HRC, and the
mass of the cores of the 12.7 and 14.5 mm AP is about 30 and 40 g, respectively.
The initial velocity of the 12.7 mm AP was about 840 m/s, and the velocity of the
14.5 mm AP was about 960 m/s.
The materials are forged 50 mm thick Ti –6Al–4V plates, which were subjected
to different thermo-mechanical processing to obtain the equiaxed and lamellar
microstructures. The plate forged in the b region had a typical b-processing
structure of plate-like a and inter-granular b (designated as the lamellar
microstructure), while the plate forged in the a + b region had a typical structure of
equiaxed a and inter-granular b (designated as the equiaxed microstructure) [ 11].
Both of the plates were then annealed at 800 °C for 2 h, followed by air cooling.
After ballistic impact, all the targets were recovered. The recovered targets were
sectioned parallel to the penetration direction: half was used to measure the
parameters of macro-damage features; the other half was grinded, polished and
etched with a Kroll solution (H 2O 88 mL, HF 2 mL, and HNO 3 10 mL) for met-
allurgical examination to investigate the micro-damage features.

Results and Discussion
Microstructure and Mechanical Properties The optical micrographs of the Ti –
6Al–4V plates having equiaxed and lamellar microstructures are shown in Fig. 3.I n
the equiaxed microstructure, about 33 vol% of b is present at the triple points of a
grains, and the grain size of the equiaxed a is about 20 lm. In the lamellar
microstructure, the volume fraction of b, the colony size and the thickness of a
platelets were measured to be about 36 um, 200 –500 and 3 –5 lm, respectively.
Tensile data of the equiaxed and lamellar microstructures are listed in Table 1. The
hardness, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation of the equiaxed
microstructure are higher than those of the lamellar microstructure. With the
presence of the equiaxed a phase, the equiaxed microstructure showed better
combination of strength and elongation properties than the lamellar microstructure.
It is interesting to ﬁnd that the equiaxed microstructure shown an improvement of
about 3% in strength, and about 32% in elongation compared to the lamellar
microstructure. The difference in the plastic properties of the Ti –6Al–4V plates
having equiaxed and lamellar microstructures can also be found in the fractographs
of the tensile specimens, as shown in Fig. 4.
The true stress-strain curves obtained from the dynamic compression tests are
shown in Fig. 5. It is well known that a good combination of strength and ductility
properties can provides better ballistic performance due to a larger product of stress
and plastic strain under the quasi-static or dynamic stress-strain curves, which is a
measurement of the energy absorbed by a specimen until adiabatic shear failure

combination of ductile hole formation and spalling fragmentation [ 12]. It is obvious
that the spalling fragments from the rear surface were more serious in the lamellar

Grace et al. [ 13] has provided an analytical approach to the problem of rod
penetration of plate targets, at impact velocities extending to the hydrodynamic
regime, wherein the process takes place in two separate phases: an initial pene-
tration into the plate target followed by perforation of the target until the rod exits
the target rear surface. Since the failure mechanism of thin Ti –6Al–4V targets has
been discussed by Leppin and Woodward [ 5] and Me-Bar and Rosenberg [ 6], we
suggest that the failure mechanism involved in thick Ti –6Al–4V targets should be
divided into three phases: Cratering, characterized by an avalanche of spalling
fragments from the face surface; Steady penetration, characterized by the formation/
propagation/interaction of adiabatic shear bands and the nucleation/coalescence of
microvoids/microcracks; Perforation, characterized by an avalanche of spalling
fragments from the rear surface and the detaching of plugging fragments; A
schematic illustration of the failure mechanism of thick Ti –6Al–4V targets is shown
in Fig. 7. Figure 8 shows the recovered cores of the 14.5 mm AP, the plugging and

Micro-damage Features of the Ti –6Al–4V Targets Impacted by the 12.7 and
14.5 mm AP The moment when the projectile hit the Ti –6Al–4V target, a shock
wave generated which may have motivated the initiation and propagation of dis-
locations and the formation of twinning. Then strains developed at a high strain rate
and dynamic deformation became the crucial factor affecting the ballistic perfor-
mance. Homogeneous plastic deformation and adiabatic shear localization are
always the dynamic deformation mechanisms involved in Ti –6Al–4V targets.
Figure 9 shows optical micrographs of the 40 mm thick Ti –6Al–4V targets
having lamellar and equiaxed microstructures normally impacted by 12.7 mm
AP. The areas observed were cut from the red rectangles in Fig. 6a, b. It is clearly
seen that lots of adiabatic shear bands (ASBs) formed at an angle of 45° to the
impact direction. More microcracks/microvoids were observed in the adiabatic
shear bands in the lamellar microstructure than in the equiaxed microstructure.
ASBs induced microcracks/microvoids would further form macrocracks which
ﬁnally led to loses of capacity. The roles that adiabatic shear bands played can be
better understood by observing Zone I-III in the perforated 40 mm Ti –6Al–4V
targets impacted by the 14.5 mm AP, as shown in Figs. 10, 11 and 12.
Figures 10, 11 and 12 are optical micrographs of the areas cut from the red
rectangles marked Zone I-III in Fig. 6. Figure 10 shows Zone I of the perforated
Ti–6Al–4V targets. Few ASBs can be seen for an avalanche of spalling fragments
from the face surface.
Figure 11 shows Zone II of the perforated Ti –6Al–4V targets having lamellar
and equiaxed microstructures normally impacted by the 14.5 mm AP. Adiabatic
shear bands without any microcracks/microvoids were observed in both cases. The
pattern of propagation of the adiabatic shear bands were tree-type in the equiaxed
microstructure and chain-type in the lamellar microstructure. The effects of
microstructure on the propagation and interaction features of adiabatic shear bands
in Ti–6Al–4V alloys have been discussed by Gu and Nesterenko [ 16] and Liu et al.
[11, 17]. In lamellar targets, the microstructure is inhomogeneous even within the
same prior beta grain. It is expected that such lamellar microstructure with plate-like
a and intergranular b would cause a zigzag slip path resulting in bifurcation and

Figure 12 illustrates Zone III of the perforated Ti –6Al–4V targets having
lamellar and equiaxed microstructures normally impacted by the 14.5 mm AP. The
role that adiabatic shear bands played has changed. In the stage of perforation,
adiabatic shear bands in thick Ti –6Al–4V targets are still failure channels causing
further capacity loses. It is clearly seen that both the equiaxed and the lamellar
targets showed formation of spalling fragments. In the lamellar target, the ﬁrst layer
of spalling fragments were thrown away, while the second and third layers of
spalling fragments were still attached to the target. In the equiaxed target, no
spalling fragment was thrown away. The spalling fragments observed were caused
by fracture through coalescence of microvoids/microcracks along the adiabatic
shear bands, as can be seen within the dotted circles in Fig. 12. So we consider that
spalling fragments from the rear surface of the Ti –6Al–4V targets are caused by two
main factors: propagation of ASBs, and ASB induced cracks. It should be pointed
out that the spalling fragments were caused by perforation during ballistic impact,
which is different from spalling that occurs due to the tensile stress generated by the
interaction of two rarefaction waves caused by ﬂy impact experiments [ 18, 19].
Table 3 lists the dimensions of the adiabatic shear bands observed in the thick
Ti–6Al–4V targets. In the equiaxed and the lamellar Ti –6Al–4V targets, the
dimensions were not uniform. The maximum ASB thickness measured in the
lamellar targets was about 50 lm, which is much thicker than that what was also
measured in the equiaxed targets. This agrees with previous studies [ 20, 21]o n
steels and aluminum alloys showing that the width of the ASB decreases when the

## Page 494

strength of material increases. However, the depth that the ASBs propagated into
the matrix was smaller in the lamellar targets than in the equiaxed targets. The
length of the ASBs increased with the increasing projectile caliber and velocity in
both the equiaxed and the lamellar targets, and in the equiaxed targets the ASBs
were much longer than in the lamellar targets.
Conclusions
Thick Ti –6Al–4V targets forged in the ( a + b) region show better ballistic per-
formance than thick Ti –6Al–4V targets forged in the b region. Ductility has an
important impact on the ballistic impact properties of thick Ti –6Al–4V targets.
The analysis of the macro-damage and micro-damage features reveals that the
failure mode of ductile hole formation in 40 mm thick Ti –6Al–4V targets should be
divided into 3 stages: cratering, steady penetration and perforation. The behavior of
adiabatic shear bands plays a crucial role in ballistic performance of thick Ti –6Al–
4V targets. In the stage of steady penetration, the plastic deformation is concen-
trated in adiabatic shear bands to coordinate with the squeezing into of the pro-
jectile. While in the stage of perforation, adiabatic shear bands are still failure paths
for the formation of spalling fragments from the rear surface.

Tribological Behavior of Graphene
Reinforced 600 °C High Temperature
Titanium Alloy Matrix Composite
Mingyu Wu, Guangbao Mi, Peijie Li, Jianming Cai
and Chunxiao Cao
Abstract Graphene reinforced high temperature titanium matrix composite syn-
thesized by spark plasma sintering (SPS) was prepared from mixed powders of
graphene oxide (GO) and 600 °C high temperature titanium alloy (TA29). SEM,
EDS, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, UMT and SRV tribotester were employed to
investigate the microstructure and tribological properties. Microstructural studies
indicated that the added graphene oxide was substantially decomposed into gra-
phene during the sintering process and did not cause a signi ﬁcant increase in
oxygen content of the TA29 matrix. Graphene was observed to remain after the
sintering process and be evenly dispersed in the TA29 matrix. The friction coef-
ﬁcient and wear rate under room temperature and light load were reduced by 15 and
60% respectively, because the graphene dispersed in the matrix was proved to
improve the conditions of the frictional interface by self-lubricating effect. The wear
rate under high temperature and heavy load was reduced by about 25% for the
increasing in the yield strength of graphene reinforced TA29 matrix composite.
