Introduction
Titanium alloys have many excellent performances, including high strength, cor-
rosion resistance and wide range of service temperature. Therefore, titanium alloys
are widely used in aviation, chemical and medical ﬁelds. However, the wear
resistance of titanium alloy is relatively poor [ 1–3]. The concept of using new
nanometer materials to strengthen titanium has promoted the development of tita-
nium matrix composite with excellent properties. With the deepening of
graphene-related research, graphene reinforced titanium matrix composite has
become one of the research frontiers.
Graphene is a kind of carbonaceous material with excellent performance. The
carbon atoms form a single-layer planar network structure by sp
2 hybridization [4].
Graphene has many excellent properties such as high speci ﬁc surface area
(2630 m 2/g), high thermal conductivity (5000 W m −1 K−1 at room temperature),
high fracture strength (125 GPa), and high Young ’s modulus (1.1 TPa) [ 5].
Therefore, the addition of graphene can improve the performance of the matrix
material in many aspects. Several studies have shown that the addition of a certain
proportion of graphene to aluminum alloys [ 6–8], copper alloys [ 9–11], magnesium
alloys [ 12] and nickel-based superalloys [ 13] can improve many properties,
including the strength, elastic modulus and wear performance. However, due to the
large difference in the density between titanium and graphene, the high chemical
activity of titanium and the narrow process window of preparing composites, the
preparation of graphene reinforced titanium alloy composite is more dif ﬁcult. Thus
the corresponding research started later and is relatively less.
600 °C high temperature titanium alloy is the key material of current and future
high performance aeroengine, which has obvious advantages in speci ﬁc strength,
including low cycle fatigue performance and fatigue crack propagation resistance. It
can be used for key components such as compressor blisk and case, and can
signiﬁcantly reduce the weight of the engine structure instead of using traditional
steel or other superalloys [ 14]. Therefore, in this study, graphene was added to the
600 °C high temperature titanium alloy (TA29) matrix to prepare graphene rein-
forced high temperature titanium alloy composite. With focus on tribological
behaviors, the addition of graphene and densi ﬁcation process parameters were
analyzed to investigate the in ﬂuence on tribological properties and its mechanism.
Experimental
The TA29 titanium alloy bar was prepared by using vacuum arc remelting
(VAR) and forging, with the nominal composition of Ti-5.8Al-4.0Sn-4.0Zr-0.7Nb-
1.5Ta-0.4Si-0.06C. Powders with the diameter of 100 –150 lm (powder 1) and
150–220 lm (powder 2) were prepared by argon atomization and selected by
ultrasonic vibration. The natural graphite was used as raw material to prepare
506 M. Wu et al.

## Page 498

graphene nanosheets by Hummers method, and the thickness was controlled within
several atomic layers. The microstructures of TA29 powders and graphene oxide
nanosheets were shown in Fig. 1. The powder 1 and the powder 2 were mixed with
0.3 wt% graphene oxide in the anhydrous ethanol respectively by the combination
of ultrasonic dispersion and mechanical stirring to obtain the mixed graphene/TA29
titanium alloy powder. The mixed powder was rapidly sintered at 1000, 1050, 1100
and 1150 °C at a heating rate of 50 –100 °C/min using a spark plasma sintering
(SPS) process after dried in the oven for several hours and vacuum treatment.
Finally densi ﬁed cylindrical samples were obtained after heat preservation for
5–8 min at the highest temperature and pressure.
Tribological experiments were performed on the UMT-3/SRV-4 tribotester,
including the determination of friction coef ﬁcient and wear rate at room temperature
and light load/high temperature and heavy load conditions. Si 3N4 ball was used as
the counterface and point contact was employed. Under the condition of light load,
the load was set as 3 N, the stroke was set as 3 mm, the reciprocating frequency
was set as 2 Hz, and the loading time was set as 30 min. Since the friction and wear
mechanism of the titanium alloy at high temperature and heavy load is different
from that at room temperature, the friction coef ﬁcient and the wear rate at high
temperature are measured by SRV-4 tribotester. Following parameters were set,
including the temperature of 350 °C, the load of 200 N, the frequency of 20 Hz,

Results
Microstructural Characteristics Figure 2a, b are the metallographic structures of
the TA29 alloy without the addition of graphene oxide prepared by the spark plasma
sintering process. The phase transition point of TA29 alloy is about 1050 °C.
With the increase of temperature from 1000 to 1150 °C, TA29 alloy should have
gradually changed from the equiaxed a-phase to the acicular b phase. However,
because of the rapid heating rate of SPS sintering process, the time when temperature
of the composite was above the phase transition point lasted only 5 –6 min, the grains
did not have sufﬁcient time to complete the transformation from a phase to b phase,
so the microstructure eventually appears as lamellar a phase.
In the TA29 alloy added with 0.3 wt% graphene oxide, the microstructure is mainly
composed of TA29 alloy, because of the relatively low proportion of graphene
oxide. Compared with TA29 alloy sintered at the same temperature without adding
graphene, the matrix structure is not signi ﬁcantly different. But the difference is
that, as shown in Fig. 2a, a relatively uniform layered structure can be observed in
the matrix of the TA29 alloy to which graphene oxide is added. Analyzed by EDS,
the mass fraction of the major constituent elements of the matrix and lamellar
structure in Fig. 2 is shown in Table 1. The proportion of oxygen in TA29 matrix
added with graphene oxide is consistent with that of the sintered samples without
addition of graphene oxide, indicating that the addition of graphene did not cause a
signiﬁcant increase in oxygen content in the matrix.

region.

In the temperature range in this study, ΔG varies between −142.55 and
−147.31 kJ/mol, which means this reaction is spontaneous thermodynamically.
From this view, during the SPS process, graphene and titanium should sponta-
neously react and form TiC. XRD was employed to measure the amount of formed
TiC (Fig. 5). However, the results show that this reaction hardly occurred in the
actual sintering process. The strength of the 36° and 42° standard diffraction peaks
of TiC in the samples added with graphene oxide did not increase signi ﬁcantly
compared to the samples without addition of graphene oxide. It can be concluded
that during the sintering process, TA29 hardly reacted with graphene, and the
graphene can remain in the TA29 matrix after SPS.

Discussion
Tribological Properties Under Room Temperature and Light Load The tri-
bological properties of the graphene reinforced TA29 alloy are affected by many
factors, including the addition of graphene oxide, the sintering temperature and the
initial powder particle size.
In this paper, due to the absence of lubricants, the friction condition should be
classiﬁed as dry friction. It has been concluded that the main wear mechanisms of
titanium alloy under low-speed and low-load friction conditions are abrasive wear
and adhesive wear [ 16]. Due to the higher hardness of the counterface in the test
process (Vickers hardness of TA29 alloy is 400 –500 HV, while Vickers hardness of
Si
3N4 is about 2200 HV), the adhesive wear is not easy to occur. Figure 9a shows a
clear image of plough, which is the typical structure of abrasive friction, and EDS
has proved that wear debris in Fig. 9b contains Si
3N4 (Table 2). Therefore, it can be

concluded that at room temperature and under the load of 3 N, the main wear

Figure 9b, c show the microstructure of the scratches of sample without addition
of graphene oxide. Obvious plough on the matrix can be observed along the sliding
direction. The plough is caused by the fact that the abrasive particles were pressed
into the interface under the load and the cutting of the sample surface occurred with
the relative movement of the friction pair. In this process, the matrix material
accumulated along the plough on both sides, but was soon ﬂattened in the subse-
quent friction process, which resulted in a certain degree of plastic deformation of
the material surface. With the continuous accumulation of plastic deformation, the
surface of the material began to partially peel off and form lamellar exfoliation. This
caused many uneven lamellar structures on the interface, deteriorating the friction
environment and resulting in higher friction coef ﬁcient and wear rate.

According to Fig. 9d, compared with samples without graphene oxide, the
surface of samples with graphene oxide is much smoother, and no obvious exfo-
liation is found on it. As the graphene oxide has been transformed into graphene
structure during the sintering process, the improvement of tribological properties
should be ascribed to the existence of graphene in the matrix. In contrast to Fig. 3a,
it can be seen that the original lamellar structure in the matrix has transformed into
circular plates. As shown in Table 3, the carbon content around the plate is much
higher, indicating the circular plate is mainly composed of graphene. As shown in
Fig. 10, with the occurrence of wear on the interface, the graphene is gradually
dispersed around the site of the original graphene and ﬁnally a local lubricant layer
of graphene is formed on the surface, thereby improving the friction environment
on the interface. The role of graphene as a lubricant layer to reduce the friction
coefﬁcient and improve the wear resistance has already been con ﬁrmed [ 17].
Therefore, in this study, the reason for the decrease in the coef ﬁcient of friction
should be attributed to this “wear-cover-lubrication” mechanism of graphene.
Tribological Properties Under High Temperature and Heavy Load Compared
with the room temperature and light load conditions, no improvement in friction
coefﬁcient of the sample added with graphene oxide is found under the temperature
of 350 °C, load of 200 N and reciprocating frequency of 20 Hz. This is mainly
because the wear mechanism has changed in the case of high temperature and heavy
load. Under these circumstances, abrasive wear is no longer the main wear
mechanism, oxidation wear and delamination wear have become the main mech-
anisms. Crack and delamination occur on the interface, deteriorating of the friction
environment, resulting in a sharp increase in friction coef ﬁcient. The effect of this
change in the friction mechanism exceeds the lubricant effect of graphene in this

Compression tests conducted by Gleeble proves that the yield strength of graphene

resistance of TA29 alloy by increasing its yield strength.
Sintering temperature is another factor that affects the tribological properties of
graphene reinforced TA29 alloy. With the increase of sintering temperature, the
friction coefﬁcient and wear rate of sintered samples show a decreasing trend, and
there is a signi ﬁcant change at 1000 –1050 °C. The reason for this effect can be
divided into two aspects, the density of the sintered sample and the hardness of the
material.
For properties of powder metallurgy samples, the density is a factor that can not
be ignored. There has been a literature on the relationship between density and
strength in materials [ 19].

In order to determine the effect of the sintering temperature on the tribological
properties of the graphene reinforced TA29 alloy, the degree of densi ﬁcation of the
samples at different sintering temperatures was measured. As shown in Fig. 11,
there are obvious pores in the sintered samples at 800 °C. The samples sintered at
1000 °C are not completely dense, white the samples sintered above 1050 °C have
high density which almost does not increase as sintering temperature continues to
rise. Therefore, according to Eq. 4, with the increase of sintering temperature the
porosity of the material decreases, thus the friction coef ﬁcient and wear rate also
decrease. And when the sintering temperature changes from 1000 to 1050 °C, there
is a transition from incomplete densi ﬁcation to complete densi ﬁcation, so that the
friction coefﬁcient and wear rate are greatly decreased.
Figure 12 is the result of the microhardness test of sintered samples with dif-
ferent parameters. As the sintering temperature increases, the hardness of the
sample gradually increases. Because the hardness ratio of abrasive particles to
material matrix is about 4.9, which is much bigger than 1.2, the wear condition
should be classi ﬁed into hard abrasive wear. Therefore, the increase in hardness of
matrix can improve the abrasion resistance rapidly [ 22]. According to the Archard
equation, the in ﬂuencing factors of abrasive wear can be analyzed.

In this study, the effect of initial particle size on tribological properties of TA29
was also discussed. According to Fig. 7a, above 1050 °C, the powder particle size
has little in ﬂuence on the friction coef ﬁcient, but below 1050 °C, the in ﬂuence is
more obvious. According to the law of densi ﬁcation in the process of spark plasma
sintering, the smaller particle size of the initial powder is, the faster the densi ﬁcation
of the material will be. Sintered below 1050 °C, the powder 1 and powder 2 differ
in density, so according to Eq. 4, sample with smaller initial particle size has lower
porosity and better friction and wear properties. At 1050 °C, the densi ﬁcation
process has been basically completed, and the density difference between powder 1
and powder 2 is not obvious. Therefore, the effect of particle size on friction and
wear properties is not obvious in this temperature range.
Conclusions
In this paper, the graphene reinforced TA29 alloy matrix composite was success-
fully prepared by spark plasma sintering. The friction and wear properties,
inﬂuencing factors and mechanisms were investigated by adjusting the addition of
graphene, sintering temperature and initial powder diameter. The following main
conclusions are reached.
(1) The graphene oxide added to the TA29 alloy is decomposed to graphene, and
the graphene can be retained after spark plasma sintering at 1150 °C. The
decomposition does not cause obvious increase in oxidation degree of TA29
alloy matrix.
(2) Graphene can be relatively evenly dispersed in the TA29 alloy matrix, and the
tribological properties of the composite are signi ﬁcantly improved. Under room
temperature and light load, friction coef ﬁcient decreases by about 15% and
wear rate decreases by 60%, while under high temperature and heavy load, the
wear rate is reduced by about 25%. In the wear process, graphene can play the
role of self-lubricating material under the light load at room temperature, and
rely on the mechanism of “wear-cover-lubrication” to form local graphene
lubricating layer, thus improving the interface state of friction and wear. Under
518 M. Wu et al.

## Page 510

high temperature and heavy load, graphene can reduce the delamination wear,
and improve the wear resistance by increasing the yield strength of TA29 alloy.
(3) The mechanism of the initial powder particle size on the tribological properties
is re ﬂected in the effect on the densi ﬁcation process. At 1000 °C or below,
sintering with a smaller particle size results in faster densi ﬁcation rates to
improve the tribological properties. At 1050 °C or above, there is no signi ﬁcant
difference on ﬁnal tribological properties between powder 1 and powder 2.
(4) The effect of sintering temperature on the friction and wear properties is
reﬂected in the degree of densi ﬁcation and hardness of sintered samples. At
1050 °C or above, the sintering temperature has no obvious effect on the degree
of densi ﬁcation. With the increase of sintering temperature, the hardness of
sintered sample increases, and the tribological properties of graphene reinforced
TA29 alloy matrix composite.

In Situ Notched Tensile Fracture
of TC21 Alloy with Different
Microstructures
Hui Shao, Di Shan, Kaixuan Wang, Yongfeng Ding, Yunjin Lai,
Guojun Zhang and Yongqing Zhao
Abstract In order to investigate the notched toughness of TC21 alloy, different
types of microstructures (lamellar, basketweave and equiaxed microstructure)
prepared by different forging and heat treatment processes were studied. The
microstructure was observed through the in situ SEM tensile technology. The
cracks were found initiated along b grain boundary, lath a/b interface and equiaxed
a/b interface. The crack easily propagate along the slip damage in the plastic area of
the crack tip. The notched toughness of the TC21 alloy with the lamellar
microstructure was found to be the highest among the three ones.

Introduction
TC21 alloy, as a raw material of the aerospace structural parts, could be subjected to
thermal or thermo-mechanical process to achieve various combinations of strength
and toughness [ 1]. The property controlling depends on the microstructure of TC21
alloy [2]. The coarse acicular or plate-like a structure has the high fracture toughness
due to the secondary micro-cracking and the crack-branching [ 3]. The equiaxed a
structure could improve the ductility and the strength of TC21 alloy [ 4, 5].
At present, the slotting, the stairs and the thread are usually processed in TC21
workpiece due to the application requirement. These notches could result in the
stress concentration, which promotes the formation of crack [ 6, 7] and causes the
failure of the workpiece early. Thus it is necessary to evaluate the notch toughness of
TC21 alloy. Until now, the notched toughness mechanism of TC21 titanium alloy
with different microstructures has a few studies.
In this paper, the in situ SEM observation is employed to identify the in ﬂuence
of the microstructure on the damage accumulation at the notch. The relationship
between the slip morphology and the crack initiation is analyzed for TC21 alloy
with different microstructures. The energy consumption of fracture process was also
discussed to evaluate the notch toughness of TC21 alloy.
Experiment Procedure and Material
The b transformation temperature of TC21 alloy is about 945 °C. The lamellar
microstructure (LM) was gained by heating at 1000 °C for 1 h following furnace
cooling. The basketweave microstructure (BM) was gained by the b ﬁeld forging
and following heating at 920 °C for 1 h and air cooling. The equiaxed
microstructure (EM) was gained by the a plus b ﬁeld forging and then heated at
930 °C for 0.5 h and furnace cooling. All in situ tensile specimens with a notch
radius of approximately 0.2 mm were prepared by the machining and the electro-
chemical polishing process (Fig. 1).
The specimens were put into tensile test apparatus SM-TS40 in SEM JXA-840
with the maximum load of 5000 N and elongation of 20 mm. Notch tensile tests
were conducted in the air at a constant displacement rate of 0.06 mm/min. The slip
morphology and crack initiation were revealed by the in situ observation. The
scanning electron microscopy examination was used to observe the surface topo-
graphic features. The electron backscatter diffraction test was performed with a
scanning step size of 0.5 lm, and related patterns were recorded on an oxford
instruments nordyls camera.

Results
Microstructure Characteristic Figure 2 shows the morphology images of dif-
ferent microstructures. For LM microstructure (Fig. 2a), the several variants of a
colonies with the average size of 83 lm in one grain are obtained. The average
thickness of a lath is about 2.5 lm. The grain boundary a phases are observed to be
of two types (zig-zag appearance and smooth appearance). After the forged process,
the lath a and grain boundary a phases are broken up into the short bar alpha phase.
The BM microstructure is developed with lath a thickness of about 5 lm (Fig. 2b).
It is noteworthy that the ﬁne secondary a phase precipitates from the preserved b
phase during the cooling process. Compared with the BM microstructure, the
thicker a phase with the average size of 10 lm distributes in the b matrix in the EM
microstructure (Fig. 2c).
Orientation Characteristic After forging deformation, the burgers relationship
((0001)

microstructure. The pole maps of the BM and EM microstructures with the
70 lm /C270 lm area are shown in Fig. 3, respectively. Although the scanned area

According to our previous experimental results and other works, the slip trans-

Figure 5 shows the crack initiation processes of different microstructures. For the

interface (Fig. 6e), and then propagates by the crack bridging (Fig. 6f). For the EM
microstructure, the slip lines are localized in a and b phases, respectively (Fig. 6g).
With the increase of displacement, the deformed a phase amount is increased
seriously (Fig. 6h). The crack is ﬁnally developed at the equiaxed a/b interface
(Fig. 6i).

Discussion
Slip Behavior of Different Microstructures Figure 6 shows a wide quantity of
slip lines initiated along *35° angle with principle stress in the LM microstructure.
The large-size colony is deformation unite in the LM microstructure. The slip line
could easily transfer from a lath into neighboring one due to the burgers rela-
tionship (Fig. 6a). In the BM microstructure, some bar-like a phases are divided
and broken by the slip arranges along the thickness direction (Fig. 6b). For the EM
microstructure, most of slip lines are pinned on the phase interface due to the
serious destruction of burger relationship, which could easily cause the slip
incompatibility and crack initiation in TC21 alloy (Fig. 6c).
Crack Propagation For the LM microstructure, the crack propagates along the a/b
interface or b grain boundary (Fig. 7a). While the b boundary hinders the slip line
inheriting into adjacent one apparently, resulting in the slip damage in the plastic
zone of the crack tip. These observations are accordance with the previous results
[8–10]. While the main crack of the BM microstructure propagates by connecting
the small micro-crack along the a phase interface in the plastic zone (Fig. 7b). The
Fig. 7 Crack propagation path in the front of notch during the in situ tensile test: a LM
microstructure, b BM microstructure and c EM microstructure
In Situ Notched Tensile Fracture of TC21 Alloy with Different … 527

## Page 519

crack propagation could be hindered by the a phase perpendicular to the crack path.
In the EM microstructure, the crack propagates along the a phase interface or slip
band within the a phase (Fig. 7c), which has no obvious hindering in the crack
propagation due to the slip damage of the crack tip [ 11, 12].
Fractographic Analysis The LM microstructure has better plasticity than others
for the notched TC21 alloy. This is decided by the large plastic zone at the tip of the
crack (Fig. 8). The plastic area is hardly observed along the fracture path in the BM
and EM micostructures. The cleavage fracture is observed due to the crack prop-
agation along (0001) a or (10-10) a face in the LM microstructure (Fig. 9a).
Figure 9b, c show the elongated and equiaxed dimples in the BM and the EM
microstructure, respectively. It is indicated that the fracture stresses of the BM and
EM microstructures are high due to the deformation mechanism.

## Page 520

Summary
In the present study, the in ﬂuence of microstructure on the notched fracture of
TC21 alloy is investigated by the in situ SEM observation. The crack initiated at the
phase interface plays an important role in the fracture process. The notched
toughness and plasticity of the lamellar microstructure are the best due to the large
plastic area at the crack tip.

Shengchuan Chen, Xiuyong Li and Daoyu Xu
Abstract The Gr9 /20 /C20.3 mm alloy tube with high-quality small size
extra-thin walls was manufactured in this paper. The surface quality of the tube was
improved by controlling the surface quality of the extruded tube and the interme-
diate tube and adjusting the clearance between the mandrel and the tube. The
methods of controlling the rolling deformation and Q value and annealing tem-
perature were adopted to solve the matching problem on comprehensive perfor-
mance of Gr9 titanium alloy tube. The measure of controlling the tube size
deviation and the rolling feed were taken to obtain high-precision ﬁnished tube. The
result shows that the Gr9 titanium alloy ﬁnished tube manufactured by this process
has high strength and high plasticity.
Keywords Gr9
/C1Feed /C1Clearance
Introduction
Gr9(Ti–3Al–2.5V) is a kind of nearly a-type a + b titanium alloy, not only has
good mechanical properties at room temperature and high temperature and corro-
sion performance, but also has excellent cold and hot processing technology
plasticity, formability and weldability [ 1], becoming the ﬁrst choice in the aero-
space and other high-end materials. It is still in the development stage in China for
high quality and small-sized and ultra-thin-walled Gr9 titanium alloy tube. The
main problems that need to be solved urgently are: the control of high precision size
of ﬁnished tubes; How to obtain excellent comprehensive performance of ﬁnished

tubes; How to improve the inspection quali ﬁed rate of ﬁnished products to achieve

the rolling feed in pass. The matching of Gr9 titanium alloy tube is solved by
controlling the rolling deformation and Q value and annealing temperature. By
controlling the surface quality of the extruded tube and the tube for intermediate
pass, and rolling process parameters, the surface quality of ﬁnished tubes was
solved in order to improve the inspection quali ﬁed rate [ 2].
Experimental Methods and Processes
The experimental raw materials are 0-grade sponge titanium, AlV55 intermediate
alloy and aluminum bean, and after two vacuum self-consuming arc furnace
smelting, the preparation of the Gr9 titanium ingots with phi 600 mm is prepared.
The ingot was drilled into billet and then bored and the package was made into
hollow billet, which is prepared by the 1600T hot extruder into /55 /C29 mm tube
blank, and is rolled into /20 /C20.3 mm ﬁnished tube after multi-pass. In order to
ensure the excellent surface quality and the performance of the tube, the pass
processing rate is controlled at 40 –70%, the Q value is controlled at 1.5 –2.5, and
the appropriate annealing temperature is selected. Through the surface treatment of
the tube billet and the middle tube billet, It has eliminated the surface crack and
shrinkage of the tube, and improved the pass rate of the detection tube.
Using Instron 5982 electronic universal testing machine to test room temperature
tensile properties of the annealed tube, CSR value and ﬂaring, ﬂattening as well.
The inner wall of the tube was observed by OLYMPUS GX51 metallographic
microscope. The HV-30 micro vickers hardness tester was carried out on the tube
surface hardness, the outside micrometer on cold-rolled tube outside diameter size.
Among them, the tensile test was conducted according to GB/T 228-2002 《metal
material at room temperature tensile test method 》.
Results and Discussion
The Dimensions and Surface Quality Control of Gr9 Titanium Alloy Tube
Blank In order to ensure the high accuracy of the ﬁnished tube (OD tolerance
±0.03 mm, the wall thickness tolerance ±0.01 mm), the size accuracy is strictly
controlled from the beginning of the tube blank. According to the design of rolling
process, the /55 /C29 mm tube is ﬁrst rolled on a two-roll high rolling mill, and
then rolled into ﬁnished tube in the multi-roll mills. According to the correction
ability for two-roll mill is bigger, the ability for multi-roll is smaller and the
dimensional tolerances that the ﬁnished tube needs to achieve, starting from the
532 S. Chen et al.

## Page 524

tube billet design and controlling the size requirements for each pass [ 2]; The
rolling process uses high precision molds to control the tube size to ensure the size
precision of the ﬁnished tube.
In order to ensure the surface quality of the ﬁnished tube, the inner and outer
surface should be treated. This is because the inside and outside surface of extruded
tube are relatively rough and have small cracks, and the surface oxide is thicker (as
shown in Fig. 1), which has a great impact on both the subsequent processes and
the quality of the ﬁnal product. When rolling with a small defect and an oxide layer,
the defects in the tube will be deteriorated, at the same time the oxide layer will be
pressed into the tube surface, which affects the surface quality (as shown in Fig. 2).
If the defects in the inner and outer surface are not removed and entered into the
rolling stage, it will be passed down, which will seriously affect the detection
passing rate of the ﬁnal product.

## Page 525

It can be seen from Table 1 that the hardness of metal matrix is quite different
from that of surface oxidation layer. During the process of rolling, the tube is
subjected to greater tensile stress, which causes cracks in the tube surface.
Effect of Rolling feed on the Surface Quality and Dimensional Accuracy of Gr9
Titanium Alloy Tube It can be seen from Table 2 that cracks start to appear on the
outer surface of the tube when the rolling feed is more than 6 mm. This is because,
with the increase in the amount of feed, resulting in deformation section of the tube
cross-sectional size increases, due to the roll groove and the mandrel size is
determined, resulting in the increase of the deformation, work hardening and
processing stress more and more big. Cracking occurs when processing stress
exceeds the limit stress value of the tube. At the same time, with the increase of the
feed, the radial tensile strain gradually increases, in which the radial tensile strain
increases gradually in the reduced diameter section and the wall thickness section,
while that slowly decreases in the ﬁxed diameter segment [ 3]. This is because in the
reduced diameter section, the tube is only in contact with the roll, and there is a
clearance between the mandrel and the tube, and the opening degree of the aperture
is also larger, so the radial tensile strain generated in the opening area is smaller.
When entering the wall thickness, the tube is in contact with the roll, and the inner
surface is also in contact with the mandrel, thus being squeezed by both internal and
external surface, the opening degree of the aperture is also gradually reduced. The
mental ﬂows along the rolling direction, and some will ﬂow to the open area in
addition, so the radial tensile strain increases gradually [ 3]. After reaching the ﬁxed
diameter section, the pore opening degree reaches the minimum, while this time the
tube has been formed and the size change is very small, so the radial tensile strain
will gradually decrease.
When the feed is too large, the radial tensile strain and the circumferential
compressive strain are still very large in the later stage of rolling, mainly because
the actual size of the tube is large than the size required when the feed is too large.

## Page 526

Under the limitations of the roll and the mandrel, the tube will produce a greater
deformation [ 4], thin time the metal will over ﬂow along the roll clearance, causing
the inner wall shrinkage and surface cracking in the roll clearance area.
It can be seen from Fig. 3 that, the dimensional accuracy of the tube after rolling
becomes worse, and the actual size of that is gradually increased with the increase
of the rolling feed. This is because the deformation of the tube in deformation zone
creases due to the feed increases, resulting in the increase of the metal ﬂow velocity,
and it increases the difference between the mental ﬂow velocity of the tube cir-
cumference points, resulting in tube deformation unevenness, which effects the
dimensional accuracy of the tube [ 5]. On the other hand, the hole curve composed
by the groove and the mandrel is ﬁxed in the cold rolling process, that is the
diameter is ﬁxed in different deformation stages [ 6], It means that the tube rebound
increases when the feed increases, leading to a gradual increase in actual size.
Moreover, the residual stress on the surface of the tube during the rolling process
will increase as the feed increases, which is not unfavorable to the performance of
the cold rolled tube, resulting in the bending. Based on the above results, it can be
seen that excessive feed can seriously affect the size accuracy of the tube after
rolling, and can result in a large actual size than the theoretical size.
From Table 2 and Fig. 3 it can also be seen that in order to ensure the surface
quality and dimension precision, and improve the ef ﬁciency of production,
choosing the feed of 4 mm can better meet the technological requirements in the
process of Gr9 tubes cold-rolling.
Effect of Clearance on Surface Quality (Inner Wall Quality) of Gr9 Titanium
Alloy Tube It can be seen from Fig. 4 that the clearance between the tube and the
mandrel has a great in ﬂuence on the inner wall quality of the tube. The larger the
clearance volume, the more severe the shrinkage of the inner wall and the worse the
Fig. 3 Inﬂuence of rolling feed on outer size accuracy of the cold-rolled Gr9 alloy tube

quality of that. This is because the tube has been reduced by diameters, successive
wall and sizing stage among the cold rolling process. In the reducing phase, the
metal ﬂows to the clearance of the mandrel and the wall by roll radial force, the
internal shrinkage appears due to the instability, the greater the amount of clearance
(that is, the greater the empty reduction), the greater the degree of instability. The
shrinkage will form the inner wall crack when the instability to a certain degree, and
the crack will be deepened along with the increase of empty reduction.
Based the results of Fig. 4, it can be seen that in order to ensure the tube inner
surface quality, the clearance should be chosen to be 0.4 mm in the process of Gr9
cold-rolled tubes. When the amount of clearance is too small (that is, the clearance
is less than 0.4 mm), the screw is too tight in the process of rolling, and it easily
causes intubation in particular thin-walled tubes. While the clearance is too large

Performance of Gr9 Titanium Alloy Finished Tube The temperature of the
ﬁnished product is annealed by different annealing temperature, and the test of
temperature tensile performance is carried out, as shown in Fig. 5. As the annealing
temperature rises, the strength decreases and the plasticity increases. In the tem-
perature range 550 –650 °C, the strength and plasticity of the tube change sharply,
because the tube is in the stress state at low temperature, and it begins to transform
from the stress state to completely amorphous at 550 °C, ends after 650 °C, which
in fully recrystallization, the strength and the plasticity has been stabilized. It can be
seen from Fig. 5 that the ﬁnished tube shows high strength and high plasticity, with
a maximum elongation of 60%.
Flaring test was carried out on the ﬁnished product, with 74° deformation cone
in the axial pressure, making tube diameter 1.2 times of the original diameter after
the permanent ﬂaring, the tube does not appear crack and other visible defects,
which reaches to limit expansion rate of 45% (as shown in Fig. 6). In the ﬂat test,
when the plate is 4.24 mm, the surface of the tube does not appear cracks, tears or
broken, and the ﬁnished product can reach the limit crush of 3.20 mm (as shown in
Fig. 6).
The mechanical properties and process properties of the ﬁnished tube of the
20 /C20.3 mm Gr9 titanium alloy can be shown that it shows excellent compre-
hensive performance. For the CSR test, the CSR value is in the range of 1.3 –2.5 (as
shown in Table 3).

Conclusions
(1) By controlling the size deviation and surface quality of the tube blank, the
surface quality and dimensional accuracy of the subsequent tube are ensured.
(2) In order to ensure the size precision and the surface quality of the ﬁnished
product, the choice of 4 mm feed and the 0.4 mm clearance is advisable.
(3) The ﬁnished products show high strength and high plasticity, and excellent
comprehensive performance, which meet the customer ’s requirement.

Effects of Different Cooling Methods
on Microstructure and Mechanical
Properties of TC4 Alloy
Meigui Ou, Song Zhang, Hongchao Song and Yilong Liang
Abstract In order to investigate the in ﬂuence of the microstructure obtained by
different heat treatments on the mechanical properties, TC4 alloy were heated at
1050 °C for 5 min and cooled to room temperature through different cooling
methods (furnace cooling, open-door furnace cooling, air cooling and water cool-
ing). Subsequently, the microstructure was observed and the corresponding
mechanical properties were measured. The experimental results showed that with
the increase of cooling rate, the microstructure ( a + b) became smaller and ﬁner,
and the rough tensile fractures gradually became ﬂat; the elastic limit and tensile
strength increased and the plasticity decreased. In the uniform plastic deformation
stage, the plastic deformation power reached the maximum (43.50 MJ m
−3) for air
cooling. In the necking stage, the plastic deformation power was the maximum for
furnace cooling and the static toughness reached 110.82 MJ m −3. TC4 alloy
obtained good comprehensive properties in the case of furnace cooling.

Introduction
Titanium and its alloy products, called “third metals”, have attracted more and more
attention because of their high strength and good corrosion resistance. The resource
of titanium is abundant in the crust: the reserve of 34 billion tons rank at the ninth
place of all elements in the world, and China has the largest reserve of titanium.
With the continuous improvement of titanium alloy products ’ quality in the past
years, titanium alloy have been widely used in the ﬁelds of aerospace and marine
industries, chemical, energy, pharmaceutical, transportation, etc. As the industri-
alization and urbanization rapidly develops in recent years, the demand for titanium
alloy products is bound to substantially augment. Therefore, it is an inevitable trend
to optimize the processing and forming of titanium alloys and to investigate new
type of titanium alloys with excellent properties.
Reasonable heat treatment enables the titanium alloys to obtain desirable
microstructure and properties. On the contrary, the undesirable microstructure will
seriously affect the properties of the titanium alloys and even lead to an accident [ 1–
3]. Therefore, it is necessary to reasonably select the parameters of heat treatment
and to effectively control the microstructure. The microstructure at different levels
can be obtained by thermomechanical treatment and heat treated at different cooling
rates [ 4] to improve the mechanical properties.
The microstructure and hardness of TC4 titanium alloy at different temperature
and cooling rate were investigated by Zhanghua et al. [ 5]. They discovered that
when heated at 970 °C and then cooled, the a ! b transition is incompletable and
a phase is primary in the cooling microstructure. When the temperature is 1020 °C
or above, the a phase is stubby and tightly arranged due to low cooling rate by
furnace cooling and air cooling. The effect of different heat treatment processes on
microstructure and mechanical properties of TC4-DT titanium alloy bars was
studied by Wenguang et al. [ 6]: good comprehensive properties can be obtained
after the solid solution and aging at two-phase zone (950 °C/1 h/WQ + 550 °C/
6 h/AC). Wang Huigai also investigated the effect of heat treatment on
microstructure and properties of TC4 titanium alloy [ 7], and the results showed that
the microstructure is composed of small equiaxed b that dispersed a intercrystalline
and a phase; the primary a phase reduced and acicular martensite formed after the
solution treatment.
This paper aims at the correlation between the microstructure and the properties
of TC4 titanium alloy (plastic deformation power, static toughness, etc.), and the
microstructure at different levels (grains, clumps and lamellas) can be obtained by
different cooling methods.

Experimental Procedures
The experimental material is forging bars of TC4 alloy and the chemical compo-
sition of the material is shown in Table 1.
The samples were heated to 1050 °C for 5 min and then cooled to room tem-
perature by different methods (furnace cooling, open-door furnace cooling, air
cooling and water cooling). The correspond cooling rate is 0.05 –1, 0.5 –2, 10 –20,
and 50–100 °C/s, respectively. The observation of microstructure was performed at
room temperature with an OLYMPUS GX3 optical metallographic microscope and
the specimens were corroded by the mixture of HF, HNO
3 and H 2O (HF:HNO 3:
H2O = 1:3:7). The tensile fracture morphologies were observed using SRURE40
scanning electron microscope. The mechanical properties were measured at room
temperature with an electro-hydraulic servo material testing machine (INSTRON
8501).
Results and Discussion
Effects of Different Cooling Rates on Microstructure of TC4 Alloy The
microstructure images of TC4 alloy cooled by different methods are shown in
Fig. 1. With the increase of cooling rates, the size of a colony is 165.14, 110.80,
106.26, and 44.25 lm, respectively. The precipitations of a phase form in a process
of nucleation and growth. The nucleation site, the quantity of crystal nucleus and
the growth rate are related to the composition and cooling conditions of the alloy
[8]. When the cooling rate is slow, a phase ﬁrstly nucleates along grain boundaries
because of small undercooling, and then grows towards crystal interior, forming a
colony with coarse slices. The network-like a phase also can form along grain
boundaries because of the low cooling rate. Whereas, in the case of fast cooling
rate, a phase can nucleate in crystal interior owing to the large undercooling and
then grows in similar orientation and parallelly arranges to form a colony. The size
of a colony will decrease as the cooling rate increases [ 9].
The lamellar structures of a phase obtained by different cooling rates are shown in
Fig. 2. The lamellar thickness of a phase decreases with the increase of cooling rate
and the thickness is 8.47, 1.97, 1.57 and 0.85 lm, respectively.
The fracture morphologies of tensile samples at different cooling rates are shown
in Fig. 3. The tensile fractures change from rough to ﬂat with the increase of
cooling rate. It is seen in Fig. 3d that the fracture is bright and crystalline with few
ﬁber areas, which indicates that there is no obvious plastic deformation before the

Conclusions
1. With the increase of cooling rate, b transition phase of TC4 alloy transforms
from thick a + b, ﬁne ﬂaky a + b, acicular a + b and to a0 phase; the a phase
becomes smaller and ﬁner, and the rough tensile fractures gradually become ﬂat;
the elastic limit and tensile strength increase, and the plasticity decreases.
2. In the case of furnace cooling, the cluster size of microstructure is relatively
large, which makes fewer a/b interfaces and less number of microcrack
nucleations. Moreover, the cracks propagate in the translamellar mode and the
plastic yield region in front of the cracks is large and consumes more energy,
leading to the relatively high static toughness. Therefore, TC4 alloy obtains
good comprehensive properties in the case of furnace cooling.

Fuhui Gao, Min Li and Pan Ding
Abstract This paper studied the effect of wall thickness and specimen diameter on
the mechanical property of TA6V castings. Grain size on the cross section of test
pieces after testing was analyzed by optical metallography and fractography was
observed by scanning electron microscopy. The results show that grain size grown
up with the increasing thickness, meanwhile tensile strength and yield strength
improved with the increasing thickness and specimen diameter. The diameter
selection of tensile specimen should depend on the castings grain size. The crack
initiates at the center of specimen and the fracture mechanism is brittle transcrys-
talline rupture.

Background
TA6V is one kind of titanium alloy which is most consumable and widely used in
aeronautics, astronautics, chemical and health care industry because of its low
density, high speci ﬁc strength, good anti-corrosion property, good high temperature
property and excellent biocompatibility. With the widespread of hot isostatic
pressing technology and improvement of welding methodology, the property of
TA6V castings greatly improved, and now it is widely used in high stressed parts
and structural parts for low pressure compressor of aero-engine.

Grain size is an index which has important in ﬂuence on the mechanical property.
When the other pouring parameters are frozen, the grain size intensely depends on
the wall thickness of castings, because during the solidi ﬁcation process, the liquid
metal solidifying slowly on the thick area, which provides suitable condition for the
grain size growth.
Figure 5 represent the tensile strength, yield strength and percentage elongation
change with different diameter of specimens. Each data in the ﬁgures means the
mean value of two tests with same diameter. The result indicates the value of tensile
strength and yield strength raises with the increasing of specimen diameter, and the
enhancement tendency of tensile strength is faster than yield strength. At the same
time, the percentage elongation decreases from about 4.7 –4% with the specimen
diameter changing from 6 to 15 mm. This tendency is just opposite to the con-
clusion of some other study, which declares that the strength decreases with the
specimen diameter increasing because the probability of inhomogeneous structure
and internal defects is higher with bigger diameter specimen [ 8]. The casting parts
and test bars were treated by hot isostatic pressing which can heal most casting
shrinkage hole, and then inspected by X-ray to exclude indication on the sampling
zone, so specimens used in this paper can eliminate in ﬂuence of the internal defects.

morphology on the fracture surface and the fracture initiated from the center of the
specimen with obvious radiation area. The micrography of Fig. 6b shows typical
cleavage plane on the crack initiation area. The fracture mechanism is

Table 3 shows the maximum grain size for the test bars. The grain of casting
TA6V alloy is coarse and inhomogeneous, usually only several grains on the
observed section. The maximum grain size for specimens is about 8 –10 mm, but
for the /6 mm tensile test specimens, because of its limits of cross section area,
sometimes the big grain was cut off and shown as an incomplete grain on the
section with a dimension of 5 –6 mm, actually which can not represent the real grain
size. The maximum grain size of test bars is about 1 –2 mm larger than that of the
production castings with same wall-thickness. The reason is that the factors which
impact the grain size are complicated, from the aspect of casting structure, the test
bars are cylinders with same thickness, but the production parts have complex
structure with different thickness. During pouring and solidi ﬁcation process, ﬂuid
metal ﬂew from the bottom to top, for the sample structure of test bars, the grains
grew up without obstacle. But for the production parts with complex thickness,
before arriving to the thick-wall area, the liquid passed through a thin-wall zone and
cooling to a lower temperature, so the growth of grain was limited.

According to customer speci ﬁcation, the tensile test specimen with a diameter of
ASTM 1/4 ′ was recommended, but it is smaller than the grain size of TA6V

Summary
(1) The tensile strength and yield strength of investment TA6V castings decreases
while the grains grow with the increasing wall thickness.
(2) If excluding the in ﬂuence of the internal defects and under the condition of
same wall thickness, the tensile and yield strength of investment TA6V castings
increases but the elongation decreases with the increasing specimen diameter.
(3) The fracture initiates from the center of specimens and propagates understress.

Kunjie Luo, Chengtao Li, Fei Xue, Yan Liu, Lu Zhang
and Guodong Zhang
Abstract The high temperature oxidation and high temperature sulfuration
behavior of Inconel 740H alloy were studied by ﬁeld emission scanning electron
microscope (FESEM) and other equipments. The results show that the surface ﬁlm
formed by high temperature sulfuration of 740H alloy was looser and easier to fall
off compared to surface ﬁlm formed by high temperature oxidation. The oxide ﬁlm
obtained by high temperature oxidation contained two layers. The outer one was
mainly composed of Cr
2O3 and Ti 2O3 phase, while the inner one was mainly
composed of Al 2O3 phase. The surface ﬁlm obtained by high temperature sulfu-
ration contained three layers. The outer one was mainly composed of Cr 2O3 and
Ti2O3 phase, the inner one was mainly composed of S and Cr compounds, and the
middle one was mainly composed of inner oxide Al 2O3. The depth of internal
sulfuration zone increases as sulfuration temperature rises.

sulfuration

700 °C ultra-supercritical coal- ﬁred generating units [ 1–3]. These units have
expected steam temperatures of 700 °C. The outer wall temperatures of the tubes
reach 740 –770 °C when washed and corroded by corrosive high-temperature ﬂue

Sample Preparation The test material was 740H alloy ﬁnished tube produced by

2SO4 solution, and the surface of the sample was deposited with a

Discussions
The formation of oxide ﬁlm on the surface of the alloy is controlled by both kinetic
and thermodynamic factors. Elements Cr, Al, and Ti in the alloy are formation
elements in the oxide ﬁlm, and the contents of each are 24.8, 1.5, and 1.1%,
respectively. The contents of Al and Ti are lower than the critical concentration
required to form a single oxide ﬁlm on the alloy surface [ 14]. The activity of
elements Al and Ti is high, but compared with element Cr, the content and element
concentration difference after surface oxidation are relatively small. At the begin-
ning of high temperature oxidation, the capacity of the element Cr to make short
path diffusion along the grain boundary is superior to those of other elements in the
alloy [ 15]. Therefore, the alloy surface mainly forms an oxide ﬁlm dominated by
Cr
2O3. In this test, in addition to Cr 2O3, another main oxide ﬁlm is Ti 2O3, and the
content of Al 2O3 is relatively small. The composition may be dependent on the
diffusion rates of Ti and Al in the 740H alloy matrix. The Cr and Ti elements in the
alloy surface oxidize to form oxides, expanding the volume expands. The formed
oxide ﬁlm is inconsistent with the expansion coef ﬁcient of matrix, thus making the
alloy matrix bear tensile stress and the oxide ﬁlm bear compressive stress. At
extended oxidation time, the stress between the oxide ﬁlm and matrix increases,
leading to micro cracks on the alloy surface and its internal part and providing lanes
for element O in the air to diffuse into the internal matrix [ 16]. Element O diffuses
into the internal alloy through the micro cracks in the oxide ﬁlm or through the
oxide grain boundary. Meanwhile, owing to oxidation consumption of the surface
Al element, the Al element of the internal alloy also diffuses to the outer layer,
promoting internal oxidation between Al and O. The form of oxide is linear or
spiked possibly due to the increased diffusion rate of elements Al and O along the
grain boundary [ 17]. When the surface is coated with Na
2SO4, the following
chemical equilibrium occurs on the surface during hot corrosion/sulfuration [ 16].
Na2SO4 /C29Na2O þ SO3 ð1Þ
SO3 /C29ð1=2ÞS þð 3=2ÞO2 ð2Þ
In the formula above, Na 2O is the alkaline component and SO 3 is the acidic
component. The O 2 obtained in formula ( 2) induces the alloy to oxidize again.
Oxidation and Hot Corrosion Behavior of Inconel 740H Alloy … 563

## Page 553

Owing to the continuous oxidation of the alloy, the O 2 in the molten salt system is
consumed, and thus the oxygen partial pressure of the surface salt deposit –alloy
interface region decreases. The equilibrium of Formulas ( 1) and ( 2) consequently
shifts to the right, thereby increasing the sulfur partial pressure. During this
chemical reaction, the positive activity gradient of S forms between the corrosion
layer and matrix. This formation enables the diffusion of atom S into the internal
740H alloy matrix through the micro cracks or through the oxide grain boundary of
the surface oxide ﬁlm. The atom S then reacts with metal elements in the alloy and
produces metal sul ﬁde. In general, the lattice defect concentration of the sul ﬁde is
higher compared to that of oxide. Therefore, in comparison with that of the oxide,
the rate of metal ion diffusion through sul ﬁde increases, and the corrosion rate of
alloy is accelerated. Meanwhile, atom S is immersed into the alloy matrix to form a
metal sul ﬁde through an autocatalytic process. Even if the sul ﬁde is absent for
further supply, the metal can still be invaded, and the sulfuration process can be
maintained. The diffusion rate of S increases as the temperature rises, and the inner
distribution is dispersed. The sul ﬁde depth increases at 820 °C for 120 h, and
internal sulfuration occurs in the alloy at 26 lm from the surface. Decreased dif-
fusion rate of S is observed at 750 °C, and the distance for diffusing from the
surface to the inner part is limited. Therefore, after 120 h, the internal sulfuration is
concentrated and mainly distributed within 7 lm from the alloy surface.
Conclusions
(1) The oxide ﬁlm obtained by high temperature oxidation of 740H alloy contains
two layers. The outer layer is mainly composed of Cr 2O3 and Ti2O3. The inner
layer is mainly Al 2O3 phase.
(2) When the sulfur-containing salt is deposited on the surface of the 740H alloy,
the obtained surface ﬁlm contains three layers. The outer layer is composed of
Cr2O3 and Ti 2O3 phases. The middle layer is mainly composed of Al 2O3. The
inner layer is mainly composed of S and Cr compounds. The depth of internal
sulfuration zone increases as the temperature rises.
(3) The surface ﬁlm on the 740H alloy generated during hot corrosion is looser and
easier to fall off compared with that generated through high temperature
oxidation.

of Cr28Ni48W5 Alloy Heat Radiant

Jiazhi Tian, Guoli Zhai and Qingchao Tian
Abstract An electric radiant tube in continuous annealing furnace was manufac-
tured by using Cr28Ni48W5 heat resistant alloy with the built-in electric resistance
bars of 0Cr27Al7Mo2 supported by the insulation of high-temperature ceramic
disk. The radiant tube was found to be perforated during the annual routine
inspection. In this study, a failure analysis of the radiant tube was performed by
carefully visual inspection of the failed tube, scanning electron microscopy
observation of perforation samples, and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy
analysis of the tube metals and oxide scales. The used materials were prepared by
centrifugal casting. The analysis showed that there exhibited the microstructure
characteristic of melting and solidi ﬁcation near the perforation hole, and the serious
oxidation had occurred. It is inferred that under the condition of prolonged
high-temperature heating, the creep deformation caused the electric resistance bar
bend to contact the tube inner surface, and then electrical discharge took place and
further melted the tube inner matrix through continuous heating by the release of
electrical arc.

Introduction
Radiant tubes are the most important components of continuous-annealing furnace,
as they are exposed to extreme temperature condition during service. Therefore,
high-alloyed heat-resistant steels are required since they show high creep rupture
strength and good oxidation resistance [ 1]. Many radiant tubes are heated with
electric resistance wires or bars in the inner diameter. Therefore the radiant tubes act
as the role of transferring the heat from the inner diameter to the outer surface, and
generally the minimum lifetime of the tubes is designed for 100,000 h of service at
operating temperatures of higher than 1173 K. Nevertheless, premature failures of
radiant tubes are frequently observed as results of several damage mechanisms,
such as creep, oxidation, thermal shock, and accidental overheating [ 2].
In the present study, a failure analysis was performed on a radiant tube, which
was replaced in the annual routine non-destructive inspection because a perforation
hole had been found in its surface. The service temperatures of the
continuous-annealing furnace ranges from 1123 to 1323 K, and the radiant tube
was made by centrifugal casting with the material of Cr28Ni48W5, while the
built-in electric resistance bars were made of 0Cr27Al7Mo2 supported by the
insulation of high temperature ceramic disks.
Experimental
Visual Examination Pictures of the as-received tube for the investigation are
shown in Fig. 1. The speci ﬁcation of the radiant tube was /101.6 /C26 mm. Visual
inspection revealed that the perforation hole located near the middle of the radiant
tube, as indicated by the arrow in Fig. 1a, and the enlarged hole is shown in Fig. 1b,
exhibiting an irregularly rectangle shape. Many small bulges can be seen homo-
geneously distributed on the tube outer surface, functioning to improve the radiant
efﬁciency.
The specimens for further examination were prepared using an emery cutter, and
the inner surface of the specimens are matched and shown in Fig. 1c, from which
can be seen that there exist other shallow pits near the perforation hole along the
same side (Fig. 1d), while on the opposite side melt-like pile-ups disperse along the
tube inner surface, accompanied by the adhering small round bars, as shown by the
arrow in Fig. 1e, and which were veri ﬁed as the electric resistance bars. Some
sphere particles look like to be the deposit of the solidi ﬁed molten liquid, scatter
over the inner diameter, indicating the occurrence of a sputtering process. There is
no obvious evidence of wall thinning at the visual inspection, except that in the
perforation area.
Analysis Methods All specimens in this study were subject to metallographic
analyses using optical microscope (OM) and scanning electron microscope
(SEM) operated in backscattered mode. Chemical composition of the radiant tube

troscopy equipped in SEM. Microstructural examination was focused on the
transverse section of both the radiant tube and the round bar striped off the tube
inner surface.
Results and Discussions
Chemical Composition The chemical composition of the radiant tube, determined
using glow discharge optical emission spectrometry, is shown in Table 1.
This chemical analysis veri ﬁes that this composition is in accordance with the
nominal chemical composition of 2.4879 (KHR48N, Cr28Ni48W5) steel grade [ 3],
except that the Cr and Ni contents are less than the nominal ones, which might be
attributed to the oxidation loss due to prolonged exposure to high temperature. The
Fe–Cr–Ni based austenitic steels are well-known for its good performance of
mechanical property and oxidation resistance, and have been extensively used in a
variety of heat treat applications such as radiant tubes operated at high temperatures
[4]. It is worth noting that apart from Cr and Ni as the main alloying elements in this
heat resistant alloy steel studied, other elements are also added, like W to improve
the creep strength whereas Si to increase the casting ﬂuidity, and further to form the
protective oxide ﬁlm.

Microstructural Analysis High temperature operation for a prolonged duration
leads to serious damage to the radiant tube due to oxidation. As shown in Fig. 2a,
internal oxidation happens in matrix, and oxidation cavities develop and some have
already coalesced with each other, forming intergranular cracks at grain boundaries.
This phenomenon was reported to occur when the service temperature reaches
1363–1503 K in the case of NiCr steel [ 5]. Hence, it can be argued that local metal
temperatures during service must go up to such high temperatures.
The microstructure of the centrifugally cast material consists of austenite den-
drites delineated by a eutectic M
7C3 or M 23C6 carbides, as shown in Fig. 2b. The
dendrite morphology of the stick-out bulges on the outer surface has been com-
pletely disappeared (Fig. 2c), and a network of internal oxidation cracks has formed
because of long time exposure (Fig. 2d). The chemical composition analysis of the
oxidation product is shown in Fig. 2e, f. Figure 2e indicates that the scale on the
outer surface is composed of composite oxides containing Fe, Cr, Ni and Si (point
A in Fig. 2d), while that on the inner (point B in Fig. 2d) is a composite oxide
containing Fe, Cr, Ni and W (Fig. 2f).
It is known that when exposure to oxidation environment, metal or alloy may
form a protective oxide layer. This Cr28Ni48W5 material is known to have
excellent high temperature oxidation resistance through forming thin and compact
Cr
2O3 ﬁlm. This Cr 2O3 ﬁlm layer is commonly believed to form very quickly and
adhere tightly to the metal which protects it from further oxidation. However,
evidence shows that Cr 2O3 in most places on the outer surface exists in the com-
posite oxides rather than in the presence of the Cr 2O3 ﬁlm, fortunately, some
remains, indicated by the arrow in Fig. 2g and EDS analysis in Fig. 2h, are found
near the area adjacent to the bulges, where the oxide shows different layers.
Nevertheless, the protection of the Cr
2O3 layer is by no means perfect for the scale
is discontinuous and lies on the outside layer. It is reported that if the service
temperature exceeds 1273 K, the stabilized Cr
2O3 ﬁlm becomes unstable and
transforms into volatile CrO3, losing its protective effect [ 6]. Therefore, it can be
concluded that failure occurred when the temperature of radiant tube was higher
than 1363 K, as evidenced by the internal oxidation appearance and the lose of
Cr
2O3 ﬁlm.
Figure 3a shows the morphology of microstructure near the perforation hole
along the tube inner diameter, from which can be seen obviously that there exists a
fusion zone near the matrix connecting the foreign material, which contains Cr, Ni,
Al and Fe, and thus can be identi ﬁed as the mixture of the radiant tube and electric
resistance bar melts. The particles in the fusion zone as shown in Fig. 3b are the
solidiﬁcation precipitates containing Cr, Ni, Al and Fe (Fig. 3c). These particles are
also found existing along the slope of inner hole, as indicated by the broken line
area shown in Fig. 3a, and the enlarged morphologies of regions D and E are shown
in Fig. 3d, e, respectively. There exists an oxide layer covering the inner slope
(Fig. 3e), which means that the perforation hole had formed long before the annual
routine inspection.

tube inner surface, the round bar has also experienced a high temperature oxidation

Perforation Mechanism The melted metal of electric resistance bar fell on the
radiant tube, and subsequently might react metallurgically with the inner surface
material. However, this could not be the cause of perforation, and there are two
reasons responsible for it. Firstly, once somewhere of the electric resistance bar
melted, the fuse should shut off the electric circuit to stop the bar melting, therefore,
there would be no enough quantity of liquid metal falling on the tube to melt the
tube matrix to perforation. Secondly, the oxide layer on the inner surface of the
radiant tube would effectively protect the matrix from the erosion of high tem-
perature melted material.
Based on literature, electrical discharge damage has been a recognized failure
mode, and is also known as electrical arc damage [ 7]. All the evidences including
metallurgical analysis together with visual observation point to that the electrical
discharge damage had occurred on the inner diameter of the radiant tube when the
electric resistance bar was on operation.
Generally, creep can be considered as a signi ﬁcant failure mode under elevated
temperatures, while evidence in the case studied shows the service temperature
exceeding 1363 K. Under such conditions, the temperature of electric resistance bar
should be higher than 1563 K. On the one hand, the electric resistance bar be prone
to fuse because of both the casting defect and the extreme high temperature, other
more, the electric voltage and current would be much higher owing to supply
enough heat; On the other hand, creep deformation would eventually happen under
prolonged exposure to high temperature. When the electric resistance bar elongated
to bend to contact the inner diameter surface under such heating condition, elec-
trical discharge took place and damaged the tube inner surface through continuous
heating by the release of electrical arc, and a process like arc welding occurred, and
eventually leading to the perforation of tube matrix. In fact, this process is recorded
by the trace of solidi ﬁcation precipitation along the perforation slope shown in
Fig. 3. It is inferred that the electrical discharge damage occurred on the top side of
the tube, and the pile-ups formed when the melted metal fell to the opposite down
side.

## Page 562

Conclusions
(1) The failed radiant tube was made of Cr28Ni48W5 alloy with austenitic dendrite
microstructure. The stick-out bulges on the outer surface have been almost
oxidized and covered by layers of oxide, causing the function of improving the
radiant efﬁciency decrease or even lose. Such design is suggested to be aban-
doned in high temperature service because of its high manufacturing cost and
easy loss of function;
(2) Defects such as large area of shrinkage cavity in the electric resistance bar
elevate the electric resistance, leading to the melting of local metal and even-
tually the premature failure of electric resistance bar. Therefore, the bar in cast
state should be replaced by that in the rolled state;
(3) It is veri ﬁed that electrical discharge damage is the direct reason of perforation
in the present case. Much attention should be paid to this kind of failure mode,
and preventive measures concerning the work conditions, such as the service
temperature, the physical properties of the electric resistance bar, and the dis-
tance between the support ceramic disk, should be considered to avoid elec-
trical arc damage. It is proposed that creep deformation should be monitored
during the operation process especially under prolonged high-temperature
exposure.

/C1 CaO crucible /C1 Desulfurization /C1 Vacuum induction melting
Introduction
Superalloys refer to the highly alloyed metal materials, which have great resistance
and strong surface stability to high temperatures (over 873 K) and complex stress
[1, 2]. K4169 superalloy is a kind of precipitation-hardening version of casting alloy
[1, 3] which is basically same as Inconel 718 alloy developed by International Nickel
Company. This superalloy has excellent mechanical and erosion-resisting properties,
and has been widely used in the constructional foundry goods, such as compressor
disk and blades [ 4–7]. Cast superalloys are mainly produced by vacuum induction
melting with oxide crucible. CaO material is one of the most thermodynamical stable
oxides and barely reacts with the alloy melt. Compared with the Gibbs free energy of
formation, CaO has a very low negative value [ 8] that it is a good choice to produce
melting crucibles for nickel-base superalloys. For higher properties required of
aeronautics and astronautics, impurities criterions in K4169 superalloy are stricter
than before. However, it will pick up a variety of impurities during vacuum
induction melting from the raw materials, oxide crucible and residual atmosphere in
furnace, and the impurities have harmful effects on the mechanical properties of the
alloy [ 9, 10]. Sulfur is a detrimental element in the nickel-base superalloys, even a
trace amount of sulfur in the alloy could bring a signi ﬁcant adverse effect on the
properties. Some literature [11–14] have proved that it will not only reduce the creep
resistance of nickel-base superalloys, but also signi ﬁcantly decrease the stress rup-
ture lifetime in high temperature, as the sulfur content increasing in the alloy. In
order to improve the properties of the superalloys, it is necessary to control the sulfur
content strictly and clarify the desulfurization mechanism.
Experimental
High purity Ni –Cr–Fe–Nb quaternary system alloy, as the master alloy, weighting
45 kg was prepared for the experimental raw material. The mass percentage of Ni,
Cr, Nb is 53.45, 19.56, 5.05% and the rest is Fe which is basically same as that of in
K4169 superalloy. Then, the master alloy was divided into parts for carrying out the
following desulfurization experiments. 50 ppm of sulfur by FeS reagent was added
into the melt when the master alloy remelted completely before desulfurization
experiment. The desulfurization experiments were carried out in the 2500 Hz
576 K. Xie et al.

## Page 565

frequency vacuum induction casting furnace (Model: VIM/L-5) with CaO crucible,
and the dimension of the crucible is 140 mm (out diameter) /C2 116 mm (inner
diameter) /C2 200 mm (inner height).
After the furnace chamber was evacuated down to 0.1 Pa, the master alloy in the
CaO crucible was heated to the desired temperatures. Temperature was measured
by a thermocouple (WRe3-WRe25) combined with an infrared pyrometer. Power of
the furnace was manually adjusted on the basis of temperature measurement to
maintain the desired melt temperature and it is assumed that the temperature was
controlled within ±10 °C. At each experimental temperature, the melt was kept for
well-deﬁned periods of time, which were interrupted for sampling a small amount
of melt into quartz tubes. This moment was taken as starting time for the melt
temperature reached the experimental temperature. Sampling was performed at
eight accumulated hold time: 0, 5, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120 min. It is worth men-
tioning that chamber pressure and melt temperature did not change essentially
during the sampling procedure.
The sulfur contents of all samples were measured by the high frequency infrared
carbon-sulfur analyzer (LECO CS844). After melting, the CaO crucible section
contact with melt of each different desulfurization experiments was taken to analyze
the phase compositions by using X-ray diffraction (XRD) (SmartLab). The scan-
ning electron microscope (SEM) (JSM-6301F) equipped with an energy dispersive
X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and electron probe micro-analyzer (EPMA) (JEOL
JXA-8530F) was used to characterize the microstructures, chemical compositions
and quantitative elements distribution at interface of the CaO crucible.
Results and Discussion
Desulfurization of CaO Crucible In the case of no addition of Al and Ti, the
desulfurizing results of Ni –Cr–Fe–Nb quaternary system alloy using CaO crucible
are shown in the Fig. 1a. It can be seen that the sulfur contents in the alloy melt had
a very small drop with the melting time at 1823 K. The results demonstrate that the
desulfurization do not carry out by using CaO crucible alone during the process of
vacuum induction melting. After adding Al and Ti, the desulfurizing results of
Ni–Cr–Fe–Nb quaternary system alloy at 1823 K using CaO crucible are shown in
the Fig. 1b. The sulfur content decreased rapidly after adding 0.6% Al at 1823 K,
and the sulfur content was approaching 27 ppm after 5 min and 6 ppm after
15 min, ﬁnally it reached the equilibrium and maintained at 5 ppm after about
20 min. Adding Ti had a similar effect on desulfurization, the sulfur content in the
alloy melt also decreased sharply to its minimum of 26 ppm after 5 min of adding
1.3% Ti. However, it rose slight again with the extension of re ﬁning time, and it
reached 38 ppm after 120 min. The desulfurization rate of the alloy melt with the
addition of Al and Ti together was very fast, and the change regulation of desul-
furization was almost same as that of adding Al alone. The sulfur content decreased
to 12 ppm after 5 min of re ﬁning and was dropped to 5 ppm ﬁnally.

Fig. 2b. It became fusible slag at the experimental temperature for its low melting
point of 1673 K [ 15]. By adding Ti alone, a small amount of calcium titanate
(CaTiO3) was found on the inner wall of the crucible with the exception of the CaO
and Ca(OH) 2, as shown in Fig. 2c. The melting point of calcium titanate (CaTiO 3)
is 2248 K [ 16] and it kept solid at the temperature of melting. Same as expected,
calcium-aluminate (3CaO /C1 Al2O3) and calcium titanate (CaTiO 3) were detected in
the CaO crucible sample with Al and Ti addition together into melt.
In the reference of desulfurization experiment of liquid iron [ 17], CaS can be
detected. However, the diffraction peak of CaS was not found in Fig. 2 at the three
melt conditions. It may due to the quantity of sulfur content in the alloy material
was very little and the small amount of CaS formed, which is not enough to be
displayed on the XRD diffraction diagram.
The local microscopic regions of the crucible inner wall were examined by scan
electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). As
shown in Fig. 3, the crucible is not a dense material, but porous microstructure.
Owing to this structure, molten alloy could be penetrated into opening pores which
expanded the interface of melt and CaO crucible. Table 1 presented the chemical
compositions of Zone A and B marked in Fig. 3. It was revealed that S element was
enriched on the crucible inner wall.
The elemental distribution of the crucible interface was scanned by electron
probe micro-analyzer (EPMA). At the bigger magni ﬁcation, the CaO crucible

the sulfur content in the 3CaO /C1 Al2O3 slag with different sulfur content and the

From the data in Table 4, it can be seen that the effect of desulfurization is very
obvious by adding Al, and it will seriously affect the effect of desulfurization with
the increase of sulfur content in the 3CaO /C1 Al
2O3 slag. According to the experi-
mental data, the sulfur content can be reduced to 6 ppm by adding 0.6% Al in melt,
and it does not further reduce the sulfur content with the extension of re ﬁning time.
During the desulfurization reaction, the sulfur into the slag is a liquid-liquid reac-
tion. However, it is the solid-liquid reaction when the sulfur entered into the cru-
cible wall from the slag, and its reaction rate is much lower. The sulfur content in
the slag increased rapidly with the desulfurization reaction proceeded, and the
desulfurization rate would decrease greatly and reach a metastable state gradually.
The results of thermodynamics calculation and that of experiment are anastomotic
in a certain extent. The degree of desulfurization mainly depends on the CaS
removed from the slag and the alloy liquid. To further reduce the sulfur content in
the alloy liquid, measures should be taken to enhance the removal of sulfur content
in the slag.
Conclusions
(1) The desulfurization reaction between superalloy and CaO crucible do not carry
out if the melt without Al or Ti addition.
(2) Using CaO crucible, the effect of desulphurization is very obvious by adding Al
in melt and the sulfur content can be reduced to 6 ppm after 15 min. Ti has a
little worse effect on desulfurization for the sulfur concertation rose slight after
it decreases quickly to the minimum of 26 ppm.
(3) At interface of melt and CaO crucible, the desulfurization reaction is 3CaO + 2
[Al]

The thickness of CaS layer is less than 20 lm.

## Page 575

Microstructure and Solidi ﬁcation
Characteristics and Segregation
Behavior of Superalloy K4169
Xiaoliang Li, Bo Chen, Weiwei Xing, Long Zhang, Yingche Ma
and Kui Liu
Abstract The solidi ﬁcation process and segregation feature of K4169 alloy is
studied by DSC, Thermo-Calc simulation and isothermal solidi ﬁcation analyses.
The segregation and precipitation behavior of superalloy K4169 during isothermal
solidiﬁcation at 1360 and 1120 °C have been observed by the means of optical
microscopy (OM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), scanning electron
microscope (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The results stated
that the solidi ﬁcation began with the formation of primary c dendrites, and
accompanied by the formation of MC carbides. During the solidi ﬁcation, Nb, Mo
and Ti were enriched in the residual liquid phase, which eventually lid to the
formation of MC carbides and Laves phases. The liquidus of K4169 was 1354 °C,
and the solidus was 1240 °C. Its solidi ﬁcation sequence can be identi ﬁed as
follows: L ! c at 1354 °C; L ! c + MC at 1290 °C; L ! c + Laves at 1120 °C.
