## Page 576

Introduction
K4169 alloy is an alloy obtained by imitating Inconel 718, which was the
iron-nickel-base cast superalloy strengthened by precipitates c″ and c′. The alloy
have excellent overall performance at −253 to 650 °C [ 1, 2]. The alloy has been
widely used in aerospace industry, nuclear power plants, and petrochemical engi-
neering as well [ 3]. With the continuous development of superalloys, the degree of
alloying of the alloy is getting higher and higher, resulting in a large amount of
segregation of the elements in the superalloy. K4169 alloy contains high Nb and
Mo content (5 wt%Nb and 3 wt%Mo), resulting in greater segregation and even
macrodefects. Segregation problems have now become one of the major barriers to
improve their performance and efforts have been made worldwide to alleviate
coagulation segregation [ 4]. Most researches were mainly divided into two aspects:
First, the processing, in order to reduce the segregation of superalloys, such as rapid
solidiﬁcation, high temperature homogenization, limiting ingot size, powder met-
allurgy, invented many advanced technologies; the second was to adjust the
chemical composition of the main alloying elements in the superalloy and control
the impurity elements in the superalloy [ 5]. Y. Murata et al. [ 6] determined the
solidiﬁcation process of In718 alloy by DTA. Knorovsky et al. [ 7] used the DTA
method to obtain the phase transition temperature during the solidi ﬁcation of the
In718 alloy and presented the pseudo binary image.
However, it is still not clear for the solidi ﬁcation process and the segregation of
elements during solidi ﬁcation of K4169 alloy. Further studies on the solidi ﬁcation
process and segregation characteristics of K4169 alloy are still necessary for better
controlling casting defects. In this study, isothermal solidi ﬁcation experiment, DSC
analysis and Thermo-Cala simulation are employed to investigate solidi ﬁcation
behavior, including liquidus, solidus, the formation temperature of main phase and
solidiﬁcation sequence. Electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) is employed to
analyze the segregation characteristics.
Experiments
DSC Measurement K4169 alloy used in this work were melted in vacuum
induction furnace, the speci ﬁc chemical composition shown in Table 1. The
instrument used in this Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) test was a Netzsch
testing apparatus (model STA449F3) to get temperature of phase transformation.
The specimens used in the DSC testing were cut from the alloy and the mass were
160.35 mg. The experiment was carried out under a dynamic high purity Ar
atmosphere to minimize the effect of oxidation. The experimental procedures,
parameters selection, and data calibration were all referred to general principles of
DSC testing.
588 X. Li et al.

## Page 577

Isolidiﬁcation Solidi ﬁcation Quenching Process Specimens for the isothermal
solidiﬁcation experiments were taken from the master alloy with the size of
U16 mm /C2 12 mm and then placed into alumina crucibles. The samples were
surrounded by alumina powder to minimize the contact area between samples and
air environment, which was favorable for protecting melts from oxidation and
nitrogen absorption during melting and solidi ﬁcation. The sample was heated in a
KBF1700 box resistance furnace to 1450 °C for 15 min to allow the sample to melt
homogenously and then cooled to the set temperature (1360 –1120 °C, taking a
temperature of 10 °C) at a rate of 10 °C/min, after 10 min brine quenching.
Quenched samples were polished by mechanical polishing and observed under
metallography and scanning after chemical etching in a solution of 1HNO3 +
3HCL + 4lycerin at 5 V for 10 s. Sisc IAS image analysis system software was
used to determine the solid volume fraction by optical metallography in a
200/C2 magniﬁed etched sample. Ten ﬁelds of view were taken at least in different
areas of the sample and the average values were taken for better statistical results.
The quenched samples at different temperatures were observed by SEM
(JSM-6301F) and their energy disperse spectroscopy (EDS). The percentages of
major elements in the solid and liquid phases of the isothermal coagulation samples
were determined by the JEOL JXA8530F electron probe. Three samples were
randomly taken from each location on each sample, and the average was taken. The
distribution of alloying elements were analyzed by scanning the precipitated phase
through the electron probe. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) samples were
prepared by jet-beam electropolishing using an electrolyte of 10% perchloric
alcohol solution maintained between −22 and −18 °C, and the voltage was 22 V.
The microstructure and composition analysis of the precipitates were performed
using an FEI Tecnai G2 20 TEM.
Thermo-Calc Calculation The TTNI8 database of Thermo-Calc software was
used to calculate solidi ﬁcation sequence of K4169 superalloy. The chemical con-
stituents of Table 1 used in the calculation. The simulation was performed under
equilibrium condition and the program was calculated every 10 °C from 400 to
1600 °C. At each calculation, the program would de ﬁne the equilibrium phase
according to the lowest Gibb ’s energy. At the same time, the Scheil model was used
to calculate the solidi ﬁcation sequence. The Scheil model was added with the
segregation correction coef ﬁcient in the calculation process, which was carried out
in the non-equilibrium state [ 8]. The Scheil model proceeded to step down every
1 °C until the complete solidi ﬁcation.

Results
DSC Analysis The DSC heating and cooling curves were shown in Fig. 1. The
main phase melting temperature can be derived from the temperature rise curve:
(1) the fusion of the d, (2) the dissolution of the Laves phase, (3) the melting of
carbide MC, and (4) the melting of the c. From the cooling curve can be drawn
from the main phase precipitation temperature: (1) the c matrix began to form,
(2) the carbide precipitated and (3) the formation of Laves from the residual liquid.
This was due to overheating in the warming process and overcooling in the cooling
process, causing a difference in the major phase precipitation temperature. By
analyzing the heat (temperature) curve, the solid-liquidus temperature of the alloy
and the precipitation temperature of the main phase were obtained [ 9], and the
phase transition temperature was the average value of the heating curve and the
cooling curve [ 10].
Microstructure Observation During Solidi ﬁcation In order to understand the
microstructure of the alloy during the solidi ﬁcation process, the microstructures at
different temperatures were observed. Figure 2 displayed the evolution of
microstructures from the isothermal solidi ﬁcation experiments, which revealed the
corresponding volume fraction of liquid phase from isothermal solidi ﬁcation
experiment on K4169 alloy. As shown in Fig. 2, the coarse grains were already
solidiﬁed solid phases, and the uncoagulated liquid phases formed ﬁne dendrites
structures during quenching. So there was no doubt that the alloy was in the all
liquid phase at 1360 °C. After quenching at 1350 °C, the coarse primary solidi ﬁed
grains appeared and the volume fraction of liquid phase decreased to 78.3%,
indicating that the alloy began to solidify at 1350 °C and the liquidus was between
1360 and 1350 °C (Fig. 2b). At 1290 °C, the liquid volume fraction was 16.96%,
and the residual liquid was still continuous in the interdendrite channel (Fig. 2c).
From 1280 °C, most of the alloy had solidi ﬁed and the isolated liquid pools were
observed (Fig. 2d), in which the residual liquid presents an obvious island structure.
Fig. 1 DSC resulted for K4169 alloy during heating and cooling

## Page 579

In Fig. 2e, when the alloy was quenched at 1240 °C, the remaining liquid phase
was 2.81%, less than 3% [ 11]. This meant that the solidus of the alloy was 1240 °C.
The residual liquid phase completely disappeared at 1180 °C.
The precipitation of MC carbide from the liquid of K4169 alloys at 1290 and
1280 °C are shown in Fig. 3. There were lots of tiny rod-like and nodular phases
precipitating at the interdendrite. The species of the MC carbide precipitated phase
was identiﬁed by energy spectrum analysis. In addition, according to EPMA map in
the sample quenched at 1280 °C, C, Nb and Ti were signi ﬁcantly enriched in these
phases, as illustrated in Fig. 4. Meanwhile, Ni, Cr, Fe and Mo were depleted in
these phase. It is well known that Nb and Ti were strong former of carbides.

Moreover, as illustrated in Fig. 5, the bulk carbide have a FCC crystal structure

Figure 6a showed clearly the white phases precipitated from the liquid when the

had a sieve-like structure, which were c/Laves eutectics precipitating around the

Discussion
Solidiﬁcation Characteristics As shown in Table 3, the liquidus, solidus and
precipitation temperature of the main phase of the K4169 alloy were obtained by
Thermo-Calc simulation, isothermal solidi ﬁcation and DSC. The liquidus temper-
ature obtained through simulation was close to the liquidus temperature obtained
from the isothermal solidi ﬁcation experiment, while the DSC analysis result was
slightly lower. Since the specimen used in the DSC experiment was very small
(160.35 mg), and the cooling process was relatively rapid (with a rate of 10 °C/min),
which increased the supercooling degree of the melt. So the liquidus of K4169 alloy
was 1354 °C. The solidus obtained from the Thermo-Calc equilibrium model was
lower than the result obtained from isothermal solidi ﬁcation experiment, and the
result obtained from isothermal solidiﬁcation experiment was lower than the result of
DSC. In this stage, the residual liquid could be long term reserved due to elements
segregation into the residual liquid. Therefore, solidus from the isothermal solidi-
ﬁcation experiment was low because of severe segregation in the ﬁnal solidiﬁcation
stage. In the Thermo-Calc equilibrium model, the calculation was conducted under
equilibrium condition, which underestimated the segregation degree, so there were
no positive segregation elements gathering into the residual liquid in the last stage of
solidiﬁcation. The Scheil model took the segregation of the element into account
during the calculation, but did not take into account the back diffusion of the alloying
element into the solid phase. In the DSC experiment, the solidus was obtained from
the heating curve, so it was not affected by elements segregation. In the industrial
casting process, the elements segregation was inevitable, so it was more reasonable
to select 1240 °C as the solidus of K4169 alloy.

## Page 585

The precipitation temperatures of MC carbide obtained from the DSC experi-
ment showed many similarities to those measured by the isothermal solidi ﬁcation
experiment. In the DSC experiment, the supercooling degree was great in the
solidiﬁcation process, so precipitation temperatures of MC carbide were higher than
those from the isothermal solidi ﬁcation experiment. However, the precipitation
temperatures of MC carbide obtained from the Thermo-Calc simulation showed
many differences from those measured by isothermal solidi ﬁcation experiment. In
the Thermo-Calc equilibrium model, the calculation was conducted under ideal
conditions, so the phase transition temperatures were lower. So the precipitation
temperature of MC carbide was 1280 °C. Carbide precipitated at 1280 °C, at which
point the alloy was not solidi ﬁed, so the carbide was precipitated directly from the
liquid phase.
In the equilibrium simulation experiment, no Laves phase was precipitated, but it
was observed in isothermal solidi ﬁcation and DSC experiments. This indicated that
Laves phase was not the equilibrium phase in the alloy but rather the product of Nb
and Mo and trace element enrichment in the residual liquid phase.
Segregation Characteristics From the previous EPMA results of Table 2 and
Fig. 8, with isothermal quenching temperature decreased, Nb and Mo tended to
segregation into the liquid, which meant that these elements were enriched in
residual liquid phase. In the quenching process, k of Nb and Ti on the samples
quenched at 1280 °C suddenly reduced. This was Consistent with the experimental
results that the tiny nod-like MC carbides precipitated from the liquid phase at
1280 °C. With solidi ﬁcation proceeding, Nb and Mo constantly gathered into the
residual liquid, which resulted in the precipitation of the Laves phase and led to a
very slow solidi ﬁcation rate in the end of solidi ﬁcation.

## Page 586

Summary
(1) The solidi ﬁcation process of K4169 alloy was de ﬁned as follows: l ! c
(1354 °C), l ! c + MC (1280 °C), l ! c + Laves (1120 °C).
(2) The liquidus of K4169 alloy was 1354 °C, and the solidus was 1180 °C. In the
last stage of solidi ﬁcation, because of alloying elements gathering into the
residual liquid, the solidus would be low.
(3) With the solidi ﬁcation proceeding, Ti and Nb accumulated into the liquid,
which promoted the nucleation and growth of MC carbides at the initial stage of
solidiﬁcation. Cr and Fe tended to segregate to the solid. Enrichment of Nb and
Mo in the residual liquid at the last led to the precipitation of Laves.

## Page 587

High Temperature Creep Behavior
and Fracture Characteristics of a 2%Ru
Nickel Based Single Crystal Superalloy
Shuang Liang, Sugui Tian, Zhixin Liu and Delong Shu
Abstract The creep behavior and fracture characteristics of a new type of 2%Ru
nickel base single crystal superalloy was studied through measurement of creep
properties and microstructure observation. The results show that the alloy has good
creep properties at 1070 –1100 °C and 127 –147 MPa. The apparent activation
energy of creep is: Q = 416.8 kJ/mol and the stress index n is: n = 4.67 at the
steady creep stage. The deformation mechanism of alloy in the steady state of creep
is that the dislocation slip in the matrix and climb over the c′ phase in the matrix,
and the dislocation can be cut into the c′ phase in the late stage of creep. Under high
temperature and low stress, the c′ phase of the alloy can form raft structure, and the
crack initiation at the interface between the raft c′ phase and the matrix phase. With
the crack propagation, aggregation and connectivity, the creep resistance of the
alloy decreases sharply, which eventually leads to creep rupture of the alloy.
Keywords Ru
/C1Superalloy /C1Creep /C1Fracture /C1Dislocation
Introduction
Nickel-based single crystal superalloy are widely used in turbine blades and guide
vanes in practical engineering, and its growth direction is [001] orientation, which is
mainly affected by centrifugal force during service, and the direction of force is
basically the same as that of [001] direction [ 1]. Creep is a trend of slow permanent
deformation of materials under the inﬂuence of stress, and the stress when it occurs is
often much smaller than the yield strength of the alloy and lasts for a long time [ 2].

## Page 588

At the same time, the creep becomes more severe with the increase of temperature.
The centrifugal force of Nickel-based alloy blade during service is much lower than
the yield strength of the alloy, and the service process of the blade is accompanied by
higher temperature, which accords with the creep characteristics [ 3]. Creep defor-
mation and fracture are the main forms of material failure. Therefore, it is the
ultimate purpose of studying nickel-based superalloy to improve their temperature
bearing capacity and creep life [ 4, 5].
People added 3%Re and 6%Re to the second generation and the third generation
nickel-based superalloy respectively [ 6, 7], and then added different contents of Ru
on the basis. Then fourth generation and the ﬁfth generation superalloy were
developed. Although Re has higher solution enhancement effect, it has small
reserves in the earth and high price [ 8]. How to improve the creep properties of the
alloy by adding Ru element without adding Re is one of the research directions of
many researchers. The creep behavior and fracture characteristics of non Re/Ru
alloy and Re/Ru alloy have been reported, but there are few reports about Ru
without Re alloy. Therefore, a 2%Ru alloy is designed and prepared in this paper,
and the creep behavior and fracture characteristics of the alloy are studied by means
of creep test and microstructure observation. The purpose of study is to provide the
theoretical basis for the development and application of single crystal alloys.
Experimental Method
A superalloy with 2%Ru nickel based single crystal is designed. The composition of
the alloy is 6Al + 7.5Ta 4.15Cr + 3.9Co + 6Mo + 6 W + 2%Ru (mass fraction),
and the rest is Ni. The mother alloy is melted and stirred by vacuum induction furnace
and poured into the vacuum directional solidi ﬁcation furnace, and the type of the
solidiﬁed furnace is ZGD-2 type vacuum high gradient single crystal furnace. The
heat difference curve of the cast alloy was measured at the drawing rate of 0.08 mm/s
and the pouring temperature of 1500 °C, and the initial melting temperature of the
alloy was determined to be 1324 °C. The heat treatment process is: 1280 °C /C22h ,
A.C + 1315 °C /C24 h, A.C + 1070 °C /C24 h, A.C 870 °C /C224 h, A.C.
The single crystal test bar was fabricated along the [001] direction into the
standard I-type creep specimen. The creep properties of the alloy under high
temperature and low stress were tested and the creep curves were drawn. The
activation energy and stress index of the alloy in the creep steady stage were
calculated according to the creep curve. The microstructure of the alloy under
different conditions was observed under SEM and TEM, and the deformation
mechanism and fracture characteristics of the alloy under high temperature and low
stress conditions were studied.

Experimental Results and Analysis
Creep Behavior of Alloy The two sets of creep curves of the alloy under different
conditions, as shown in Fig. 1. Figure 1a is the creep curve of the alloy under
137 MPa stress conditions at different creep temperatures. When the creep tem-
perature is 1070 °C, the alloy has higher creep life. After 383 h, the alloy fracture,
the creep stable stage is longer, the strain rate is lower, and the strain rate is only
0.0087%/h. When the creep temperature is increased to 1080 °C, the creep life of
the alloy decreases signi ﬁcantly, the creep life is only 220 h. The creep temperature
increased only by 10 °C, and the creep life decreased by 43%, which indicates that
the alloy has strong temperature sensitivity at 1070 °C or higher temperature. When
the temperature is raised to 1100 °C, the creep life of the alloy is reduced to 125 h.
The creep curves of the alloy under 1100 °C and different stress conditions are
shown in Fig. 1b. It can be seen that the creep life of is 218, 125, 51 h respectively
when the stress is applied to 120, 137, 147 MPa respectively. With the increase of
creep stress, the creep life of alloy is greatly reduced. When the stress is increased
from 137 to 147 MPa (increased only 10 MPa), the creep life of the alloy is reduced
by 59%. The strain rate of alloy decreases rapidly with the increase of applied
stress, and the strain rate of the alloy is 0.0203, 0.0397 and 0.0563%/h respectively.
The above experimental results show that the alloy has strong stress sensitivity
under above condition, especially when the applied stress is increased to 147 MPa,
the stress sensitivity of the alloy is the largest.
The strain rate is obtained under the condition of steady state creep according to
the curve dates of Fig. 1, and the relationship between strain rate and temperature and
stress is drawn, as shown in Fig. 2, where the Fig. 2a is the relationship between
strain rate and temperature, Fig. 2b is the relationship between strain rate and stress.
The apparent creep activation energy of the alloy at the steady state creep stage is:
Q = 416.8 kJ/mol and the stress index is: n = 4.67 under the condition of the tem-
perature and stress. Through stress exponent n, it is preliminarily concluded that the
deformation mechanism of alloy at the condition of high temperature and low stress is
that the dislocation slip and climb across the of the c′ phase in the matrix.

## Page 592

Crack Propagation of Alloy The microstructure of the crack propagation in the
near fracture area of the alloy is shown in Fig. 5. It is observed that the initiation of
cracks begin at the c/c′ two phase interface as shown in Fig. 5a, and cracks con-
tinue to grow with creep. There is a tip on both sides of the crack, where the stress is
concentrated. And the crack extends from the tip along the stress axis, as shown in
Fig. 5b. With the creep and cracks continue to expand, cracks formed eventually a
“jujube stone ” type, and its length is about 20 lm, the width is about 3 lma s
shown in Fig. 5c.
It is considered that the c′ phase of the alloy can be transformed into a raft
structure under the condition of high temperature and low stress, which is originally
embedded in the c matrix in common lattice method. In the late stage of creep,
different slip systems can start alternatively and shear each other. The rafted c′
phase appears seriously distorted, and its continuity is also seriously damaged
especially in the near fracture area. The cracks in the alloy sprout in the two phase
interface and expand along the stress axis. With the creep, a large number of cracks
expand and connect, which eventually leads to rapid decrease of the creep resis-
tance of the alloy until the creep fracture. There are the creep fracture characteristics
of the alloy under the condition of high temperature and low stress.
Deformation Mechanism of Alloy The microstructure of the alloy at 30 and 90 h
creep under the condition of 1100 °C/137 MPa, as shown in Fig. 6. Figure 6a is the

## Page 594

of creep, the raft c′ phase of the alloy twist seriously in the stage of creep accel-
eration to creep rupture, which its continuity is reduced. There are many disloca-

shows that the deformation mechanism of alloy is that dislocation slip in the matrix
and climb over c′ phase at high temperature and low stress conditions in steady
creep stage. A large number of dislocation piled up in the interface form stress
concentration with the creep into late creep, which caused the dislocation can cut
into the c′ phase to lead to the decrease of intensity of c′ phase and occurrence of
twisting.
Conclusion
1. Alloy has better creep performance under high temperature and lower stress.
The creep life of the alloy is 383 h at 1070 °C/137 MPa, and the creep life is
125 h when the creep temperature rises to 1100 °C.
2. At high temperature and low stress, the apparent creep activation energy is
Q = 416.8 kJ/mol, and the stress exponent is n = 4.67.
3. Under the condition of high temperature and low stress, the c′ phase of the alloy
can be transformed into raft structure in the alloy. As the observation point is
close to the fracture area, the raft c′ phase distorted seriously.
4. Under the condition of high temperature and low stress, the crack of alloy
initiation in the two phase interface and expand along the stress axis, and then a
large number of cracks expand and connect with the creep going on, which
eventually leads to rapid decrease of the creep resistance of the alloy until the
creep fracture.
5. Under the condition of high temperature and low stress, the deformation
mechanism of the alloy is that the dislocation slip in the matrix and climb over c′
phase at stead stage. At the rapid stage of creep, a large amount of dislocation
accumulates to the two phase interface to form the stress concentration, which
lead to the dislocation cut into c′ phase.

## Page 596

Research and Manufacture
of Short-Flow Hot Extrusion Forming
and Seamless Pipe for GH3625
Superalloy
Yubi Gao, Yutian Ding, Bin Meng, Zhengyi Dou, Xin Gao and Zhi Jia
Abstract In order to obtain GH3625 superalloy seamless pipe, the GH3625
superalloy seamless pipe with U28 /C25.5 mm was developed through short- ﬂow
hot extrusion forming and cold rolling molding process. And a comprehensive
evaluation for the microstructure and mechanical properties of GH3625 superalloy
seamless pipe was conducted. The results showed that the hollow tube has been
successfully extruded the GH3625 superalloy tube with U43 /C29.5 mm under the
condition of ﬁxed extrusion speed of 50 mm/s, preheating temperature of 1150 °C
and extrusion ration of 7.4. The alloy tube was composed of a small amount of
deformation twin and a large number of equiaxed crystal mixed crystal structure,
the average grain size was about 8.6, and the tensile strength at room temperature
and elongation at break were 771 MPa and 52.33%, respectively, showing good
cold working performance and mechanical properties. The performance of GH3625
superalloy seamless pipe after cold rolling and annealing is in accordance with
ASTM-B163-04 international standard.

## Page 597

Introduction
GH3625 superalloy is a representative of a wrought nickel-based superalloy, which
is nickel-chromium alloy solid solution strengthened by its content of molybdenum
and niobium, it the United States alloy uni ﬁed number N06625 [ 1, 2]. Due to
GH3625 superalloy still has high temperature strength and good corrosion resis-
tance and oxidation resistance when it is in the environment service of 600 –900 °C,
this alloy is widely used in the pipeline system of industrial gas turbine, nuclear
power equipment, chemical plant and seawater special equipment, and it is a key
material for aviation, aerospace, nuclear power, petroleum and chemical industry
[3–5].
GH3625 superalloy tube cannot be prepared by hot piercing process because of
this alloy high degree of alloying, high resistance to hot deformation, low process
plasticity and narrow range of hot working temperature and so on. Therefore,
GH3625 superalloy tube is prepared by hot extrusion technology [ 6]. At present,
the domestic and foreign use of traditional pipe production process GH3625 alloy
seamless pipe, the process is GH3625 alloy ingot by forging and blooming machine
after processing into hollow tube, the use of hot extrusion technology to prepare the
pipe, cold rolling/cold drawing and heat treatment process to produce ﬁnished pipe
[7–9]. However, due to the characteristics of GH3625 superalloy, it is easy to form
microcracks or breaks during the process of forging and blooming, which causes
serious cracking of the pipe the hot extrusion process, and thus the production
efﬁciency of the alloy pipe [ 10, 11].
In this work be aimed at the existent problems of forging and blooming process,
to be innovate traditional pipe production process, and a new type of short- ﬂow
GH3625 superalloy seamless pipe preparation method is provided, that is extruded
from hollow ingot mother tube, and cold rolling/cold drawing and heat treatment
process to produce ﬁnished pipe, which avoids the dif ﬁcult to control the forging
and blooming process, reduces the cracks produced in the process of forging and
blooming, and provides high quality hot extrusion billet, improve production ef ﬁ-
ciency and save cost. Therefore, in the paper the hot extrusion forming and cold
rolling molding process of GH3625 alloy are studied, and the comprehensive
evaluation of seamless pipe is carried out.
Experimental

Materials and Technology Co., Ltd. with vaccum-inducing plus electroslag-
remelting (VIM + ESR) U120 mm GH3625 superalloy ingot. The microstructure

Table 1. It can be seen from Fig. 1, GH3625 superalloy ingot dendritic growth has
a clear orientation, and in the area between the dendrites can clearly see the black

## Page 599

Experimental Method In this paper, GH3625 superalloy pipe with U43 /C29.5
mm was successfully machined by short- ﬂow hot extrusion technology. Then,
GH3625 superalloy seamless pipe with U28 /C25.5 mm was developed by cold
rolling technology. The process ﬂow was Smelting (VIM + ESR) ! homoge-
nization treatment ! hot extrusion preparation of the tube ! solution treat-
ment ! cold rolling/cold drawing + heat treatment ! ﬁnished pipe.
Hot Extrusion Forming Technology In order to successfully prepare GH3625
superalloy tube by hot extrusion forming technology on horizontal extruder, it is
necessary to keep the temperature of the blank in the optimum hot working tem-
perature during the extrusion process [ 12], that is to say there are suitable hot
extrusion process parameters, namely the blank temperature, mold preheating
temperature, lubricant, extrusion speed, extrusion ratio and other process parame-
ters. In order to obtain the suitable hot extrusion process parameters, the hot
deformation behavior of the cast GH3625 superalloy was studied based on the hot
working map. The optimum hot working temperature was 1150 –1180 °C, the strain
rate was less than 0.1 s
−1. Meanwhile, numerical simulation of the GH3625
superalloy during hot extrusion process, obtaining a suitable hot extrusion process
parameters shown in Table 2.
When the blank is heated by hot furnace charge, the furnace is heated and heated
to 800 °C. The heating speed is 8.75 °C/min and heated to 1150 °C for holding
time 30 min, so that the blank is heated evenly. The purpose of the hot furnace
charge is to prevent the blank from oxidizing at low temperatures. In order to solve
the blank and extruded cylinder, blank and extrusion mold insulation and lubri-
cation between the problems, it must use a reasonable lubricant. This test uses high
temperature alloy hot extrusion process dedicated glass lubricant, the lubricant for
1120–1180 °C high temperature alloy hot extrusion process. The blank lubrication
method is to apply the glass powder to the outer surface and the inner hole of the
blank to prevent the surface temperature of the blank, and isolate the outer surface
of the blank with the extruding cylinder and the inner hole of the blank and squeeze
the needle The At the same time, the glass pad placed between the hot extrusion die
and blank, isolation blank and mold, play a role in lubrication and protection of the
mold.
Cold Rolling Molding Technology For the energy equipment on the GH3625
superalloy seamless pipe speci ﬁcations, the need for speci ﬁcations U43 /C29.5 mm
hot extrusion tube for secondary development, that is, cold rolling molding. In order

to ensure the smooth progress of cold rolling, the GH3625 superalloy hot extrusion
tube is subjected to solution treatment (1150 °C/1 h/AC) to eliminate the residual

place completely. Get a good plastic processing for subsequent cold processing.
The hot-extruded tube was mechanically polished to remove surface impurities and
scale. The cold rolled pipe with U28 /C25.5 mm was successfully rolled on the
twin-roll cold rolling mill. The cold rolling deformation was about 62%. The
annealing heat treatment (1100 °C/15 min/AC) of the cold rolled GH3625 alloy
pipe eliminates the effect of work hardening and obtains good microstructure and
properties to ensure the reliability of the ﬁnished pipe during service.

metallographic specimens were mechanically ground and polished and chemically

3 + 5 mL H 2SO4 + 90 mL HCl for 1 –3 min. The alloy

method”. The alloy was measured with WDW-100D electronic universal testing
machine, and tensile test according to GB/T 228.1-2010 “Metal material room
temperature tensile test method ”.

## Page 601

Figure 4b, c for the GH3625 superalloy hot extrusion tube microstructure. It can be
seen from the ﬁgure that there are a small amount of deformation twins and a large
number of fully recrystallized mixed crystal structure in the hot extruded tube, with
an average grain size of 16.38 lm (8.6°). GH3625 superalloy tube deformation
twins occurs in the hot extrusion process, the plastic deformation method mainly
has slip and twin, due to the large extrusion ratio has produced in the process of hot
extrusion of the larger shear stress, the twins are complementary when the slip is not
easy, usually appear in the slip caused by the stress concentration area, the twins
required shear stress is much larger than the slip. The twins are produced by
mechanical deformation, are lenticular or sheet, deformation twin or mechanical
twin. The complete recrystallization is in the hot extrusion process in addition to the
high-density of dislocation pile-up the triple line boundary and the boundary of
bowing grain boundary, but also in the twin and twin boundaries to provide a
favorable recrystallization nucleation position [ 13].
Microstructures of Cold Rolling Tube GH3625 superalloy hot extrusion tube
after solution treatment, the tube surface by mechanical grinding as shown in
Fig. 5a. Figure 5b, c for the GH3625 superalloy hot extrusion tube after the
solution treatment on the microstructure. It can be seen from the ﬁgure that there are
annealing twins and uniformly equiaxed grains mixed crystal structure, with an
average grain size of 23.48 lm (7.6°). The alloy in the carbide and other precipi-
tates can be completely dissolved into the matrix, the alloy microstructure occur
completely recrystallized, in this solid solution treatment process, the alloy tensile
strength of 740 MPa, elongation of 50%, the alloy has good mechanical properties
and cold plastic molding ability.
The GH3625 superalloy hot extruded tube after solution treatment carry on cold
rolling molding, the cold rolled tube as shown in Fig. 6a. After the cold rolling
deformation of the alloy pipe grain showed a thin strip, and the emergence of a
large number of deformation bands and deformation twin, with an average grain
size of 15.45 lm (8.7°), grain boundary obvious rotation, there grain boundary and
loading pressure axis vertical arrangement of the phenomenon, twin boundaries
clearly visible, There is a linear slip line inside the grain boundary, and the parallel
lines are terminated at the twin boundaries. The twin boundaries and grain
Fig. 4 GH3625 alloy hot extrusion tube and microstructure. a Hot extrusion tube; b cross-section
614 Y. Gao et al.

## Page 602

boundaries have a strong hindrance to the dislocation [ 14], as shown in Fig. 6b.
This is because the GH3625 superalloy belongs to the low stacking fault energy
material, in the cold rolling deformation process, the low stacking fault energy can
not only prevent the dislocation of the slip, so that slip deformation becomes
difﬁcult, while reducing the twin boundaries of the interface energy, the stress of the
alloy before the dislocation is started has reached the stress required for the twin
deformation [ 15]. Therefore, in the cold rolling deformation process is easy to
produce deformation twin.
GH3625 superalloy hot extrusion pipe after cold rolling deformation produced a
signiﬁcant work hardening phenomenon, so that the strength and hardness of the
alloy increased signi ﬁcantly, while the plasticity, toughness decreased signi ﬁcantly
[16, 17]. On the one hand after cold rolling deformation of the work hardening, the
strength of GH3625 superalloy hot extrusion tube is improved. On the other hand,
the deformation resistance of the alloy increased, the plasticity of the alloy reduced,
to make the subsequent processing add dif ﬁculty [ 18]. In order to obtain good
performance, to prevent the alloy pipe in the course of the production of cracks or
even cracking, GH3625 alloy cold rolling pipe must be appropriate heat treatment.
The microstructure of the GH3625 alloy cold-rolled pipe after annealing is shown
in Fig. 6c. It can be seen from the ﬁgure that there are annealing twins and uni-
formly equiaxed grains mixed crystal structure, with an average grain size of
20.18 lm (8.0°).

## Page 603

Mechanical Properties of GH3625 Superalloy During Pipe Making Figure 7
shows the variation of the strength and elongation of GH3625 alloy in different
states. As can be seen from Fig. 7, from the as-cast (VIM + ESR) to the homog-
enization state, the strength of the alloy increases and the plasticity increases. In this
process, the element segregation is eliminated and the hot-worked plasticity of the
alloy is improved. From the homogenization state to the hot- extrusion state, the
strength of the alloy increases, the plasticity decreases, in the process of dynamic
recrystallization, the alloy microstructure appears deformation twins, blocking
dislocation movement, so that the strength of the alloy increases, the plasticity
decreases. From hot extrusion to solid solution state, the strength of the alloy is
reduced and the plasticity does not change obviously. During this process, the grain
is grown in the alloy after the complete recrystallization, and the precipitates such
as carbides in the alloy can be completely dissolved into the matrix. The strength of
the alloy is reduced and the plasticity does not change obviously. From the solid
solution state to the cold rolling state, the strength of the alloy is greatly improved
and the plasticity is remarkably reduced. In this process, the alloy structure occur
the deformation twins and the large of the deformation band and slip bands, the
dislocation density increases, resulting in work hardening, so that the strength of the
alloy greatly improved, plastic signi ﬁcantly reduced. From cold rolling state to
annealing state, the strength of the alloy signi ﬁcantly reduced and signi ﬁcantly
increased plasticity, in this process, the alloy is completely static recrystallization
occurs, to eliminate defects such as dislocations, so that the strength of the alloy
decreases, increasing plasticity, its performance to international standard
ASTM-B163-04.

## Page 604

Conclusions
(1) Through GH3625 superalloy tube short- ﬂow hot extrusion forming process, the
GH3625 superalloy tube with U43 /C29.5 mm was successfully extruded in the
hot extrusion process under the preheating temperature of 1150 °C, extrusion
speed of 50 mm/s and extrusion ratio of 7.4.
(2) GH3625 superalloy hot extruded tube has been developed to the seamless pipe
with U28 /C25 mm by cold rolling process, the average grain size of ﬁnished
pipe is 20.18 lm, tensile strength is 755 MPa, elongation is 52.88%, and the
performance index reached ASTM-B163-04 international standard.
(3) Through the comprehensive analysis of the microstructure evolution and
mechanical properties in the process of GH3625 superalloy short- ﬂow pipe
production process, it is indicated that to eliminate the process of forging and
blooming to produce GH3625 superalloy seamless pipe method is feasible.

Introduction
As a kind of alloy with high strength and excellent oxidation resistance and cor-
rosion resistance under high temperature conditions, GH3625 alloy has attracted
worldwide attention since its inception, especially in chemical industry, nuclear
power, aerospace and so on [ 1, 2]. As GH3625 alloy hot extrusion pipe size is
larger, the wall is thin, and GH3625 alloy itself, high strength materials, low plastic
processing, thermal processing temperature range narrow [ 3], so in the hot extru-
sion process is dif ﬁcult, Accurate control of GH3625 alloy thermal deformation
behavior is more dif ﬁcult. For now, China ’s preparation of GH3625 alloy pipe
extrusion technology is not perfect control. In addition, the hot extrusion program in
the factory is usually based on the actual experience of the technical staff and try to
experiment several times to develop the trial and error method, but because
GH3625 alloy itself is higher cost, labor loss, and the need to start the machine
resources, Resulting in its high production costs, low ef ﬁciency, long cycle time, it
is difﬁcult to solve the actual hot extrusion dif ﬁculties [ 4]. Based on the numerical
simulation technology of ﬁnite element software, the hot extrusion behavior of
GH3625 alloy pipe can be explored from all aspects and angles in a comprehensive,
thorough and detailed way without being bound by the actual experimental con-
ditions [5–9]. Therefore, the use of ﬁnite element software for numerical simulation
analysis has become dif ﬁcult to deform nickel-based superalloy pipe hot extrusion
process research and development of effective path.
By studying the peak temperature and peak squeezing force of the most
important billet in the hot extrusion process, the orthogonal test was carried out by
ABAQUS. The blank temperature and the peak squeezing force were used as the
evaluation indexes to discuss the blank Hot temperature, die angle, extrusion speed,
extrusion ratio and friction coef ﬁcient on the temperature rise and peak squeezing
force of blank. In order to optimize the hot extrusion experiment scheme of
GH3625 alloy pipe, the hot extrusion parameters combination is used to provide the
basis for the actual hot extrusion experiment.

blank U260 /C2 70 /C2 350 mm, extrusion ratio 6.7. The simulation of extruded
blank GH3625 alloy, the mold material for the GH4169 alloy, perforated pin for the
H13 steel, the basic performance parameters in Table 1.
The Establishment of Constitutive Equation GH3625 alloy vacuum induc-
tion + electroslagre melting smelting ingot, the two-stage homogenization treat-
ment. A high temperature hot compression experiment was carried out at a
temperature of 800 –1200 °C and a strain rate of 0.01 –10 s
−1 using a Gleeble-3800

Establishment and Simulation of Finite Element Model in this paper, ﬁnite
element software ABAQUS is used to simulate the hot extrusion of GH3625 alloy
pipe. Deformation process of the existence of heat exchange and friction heat and
other processes, so the use of thermal coupling analysis method. The entire
extrusion process is geometrically symmetrical, the model is treated as an
axisymmetric model, and the perforations and squeeze pads, extrusion cylinders
and molds are treated as a rigid body with heat transfer properties, regardless of
their Plastic deformation. Grid unit type selection CAX4RT, mold die angle
deformation is large, where the grid density is larger than other places, the blank
grid is completely uniform. The extrusion process of metal is a large deformation
process, using adaptive grid technology to improve the convergence, and the use of
mass scaling technology to improve the ef ﬁciency of computing. The simpli ﬁed
ﬁnite element model is shown in Fig. 1.

Conclusion
(1) The rank of impacting factors of the temperature rise for GH3625 alloy pipe hot
extrusion parameters is: extrusion ratio > preheating temperature of the
blank > coef ﬁcient of friction > die angle /C25 extrusion speed.
(2) The rank of the effect of hot extrusion parameters of GH3625 alloy pipe on the
peak extrusion force is: friction coef ﬁcient > extrusion ratio > preheating
temperature of the blank > extrusion speed > die angle.
(3) The hot extrusion process parameters of GH3625 alloy pipe have been obtained
by orthogonal test. The speci ﬁc parameters are as follows: preheating tempera-
ture 1180 °C, die angle 30°, extrusion speed 70 mm/s, extrusion ratio 5, friction
coefﬁcient 0.02. Under the above parameters the peak pressing force is
15.68 MN, the peak temperature is 1197.85 °C, the temperature rise is 17.85 °C.

Hot Deformation Behavior
of NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB Superalloy
Min Yu, Kaihong Cai, Zhenrui Li and Donghui Xie
Abstract NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB alloy is a kind of precipitation hardening
nickel-base superalloy, also is a kind of high temperature and high elasticity alloy.
The chemical elements of the alloy composition is very complex, it includes more
than 4.5% aging strengthening elements of Al and Ti, and nearly 37% solid solution
strengthening elements of Cr, W, Co etc. Because of composition segregation in the
alloy ingot, the dif ﬁculty of hot working is faced. In this paper, the composition
segregation and homogenization annealing process of cast NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB
alloy were studied. The dendrite segregation and its elimination method were
investigated by homogenization annealing experiment. High temperature plastic
deformation behavior of NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB alloy was also studied in this
paper. By thermal simulation compression test, the thermal deformation behavior
and microstructure change under different deformation conditions were analyzed,
which provides a good reference for practical production.
Keywords NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB superalloy
/C1Homogenization annealing
Thermal simulation
Introduction
NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB alloy is a kind of precipitation hardening nickel-base
superalloy, also is a kind of high temperature and high elasticity alloy. It was suc-
cessful developed by Soviet scientists in 1969. As Ni –Cr–W–Co precipitation
hardening alloy, its strength, elasticity and plasticity is better than that of 3J1
(Ni36CrTiAl) and 3J3 (Ni36CrTiAlMo8) at the range −196–600 °C [ 1]. Because of
high stability in the tropical marine atmosphere or some corrosive medium, it is
suitable for manufacturing instrument elastic elements which operates below 500 °C.

The chemical elements of the alloy composition is very complex, it includes
more than 4.5% aging strengthening elements Al and Ti, and nearly 37% solid
solution strengthening elements Cr, W, Co etc. Because of composition segregation
in the alloy ingot, the dif ﬁculty of hot working is increased. At the same time,
because of the high precipitation temperature of the strengthening phase, the
temperature range of the hot working is reduced, and the dif ﬁculty of hot working is
further increased [ 2–4]. The authors carried out research on the segregation of
NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB alloy and homogenization annealing process, combined
with the microstructure and properties of the alloy, and then made the best alloy
homogenization annealing process to improve the properties of hot working. The
authors also studied alloy high temperature plastic deformation behavior by thermal
compression simulation test, and analyzed the thermal deformation behavior and
microstructure changes under different deformation conditions. Then these analysis
results provided a good reference for practical production
Experimental
The experimental material NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB alloy is smelted in a vacuum
induction furnace and re-smelted in a vacuum consumable furnace. The diameter of
the alloy ingot is 200 mm, and its main chemical composition is shown in Table 1.
The samples of homogenizing annealing experiment were made by wire cutting
in the center of the ingot. The diameter of the sample is 10 mm, and the height is
15 mm. The samples were heated to 950, 1050 °C, or 1150 °C, respectively, and
then remained for 4, 8 h, or 15 h. The original microstructure of the sample was
observed by Neophot-21 optical microscope, and the morphology of the sample
after annealing was observed by JSM-6510 scanning electron microscope (SEM),
and the component segregation was analyzed by EDS spectrometer.
The samples of simulation compression experiment were made from of forging
billet. The diameter of the sample is 8 mm, and the height is 12 mm. The tests were
conducted in the Gleeble 3800 thermal simulation machine. In the experiment, the
samples were heated to the deformation temperature at the rate 15 °C/s, remained
for around 180 s, and then compressed in an axial direction. The detailed heating
speciﬁcation is shown in Fig. 1. The deformation temperature was 1000, 1050,
1100, 1150, 1200, and 1250 °C. The degree of deformation was 20%, 50%. The
deformation rate is 0.1 s
−1. In order to obtain ideal microstructure, a hot com-
pression sample should be rapidly quenched by water. And the metallographic
observation surface is perpendicular to the compression axis.

It can be seen that, segregation constant of W is greatest. This is because the high
melting point of W is highest. In the process of solidi ﬁcation of molten steel, high
melting point elements are enriched in dendrite axis, and low melting point ele-
ments enriched in the inter-dendrite.
Taking into account the in ﬂuence of precipitation phase and grain size,
homogenization annealing temperatures are selected 950, 1050, and 1150 °C,
respectively. The microstructures of the samples after treatment are shown in Fig. 4.
In Fig. 4, it can be found that the heat treatment temperature is the same, with the
holding time, the grain size do not change, as shown in Fig. 4e, h. At the same time,
with the increase of temperature, the dendrites gradually disappear, as shown in
Fig. 4g–i.
After different homogenization annealing process, alloy element concentration
distributions are shown in Table 3. Because of the high melting point of W, it is
easy to cause uneven distribution in the process of alloy smelting and solidi ﬁcation.
After the homogenization annealing, the segregation of W has been improved, but it
has not been completely eliminated. Therefore, in order to solve the segregation of
W, besides proper homogenizing annealing, the smelting process of alloy should be
adjusted properly. For the low melting elements Al and Ti, with the increase of heat
treatment temperature and extension of holding time, segregation is obviously

## Page 623

are enhanced, and thus the thermal stability and heat resistance of the alloy is
improved. In this kind of nickel base alloy, the content of c′ phase usually varies
with the sum of Al and Ti content increased, but seldom in ﬂuenced by the ratio of
Ti/Al. Co and Cr preferentially enter the gamma matrix and strengthen the gamma
solid solution. And W not only enters c′ phase, but also the gamma matrix, each
accounted for about 50%, have played a role in strengthening. For the nickel base
alloy, segregation of various elements is related to their solubility in Ni. The
element, such as Co, Mn, Cu, Fe, Cr etc., whose atomic radius is close to Ni, can
form substitutional solid solution. The segregation degree of these elements is low.
Conversely, the elements that can form interstitial solid solutions with Ni, such as
W, C, S, P and so on, have a greater degree of segregation [ 9]. Because of the high
content and the serious segregation of W in NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB alloy, the
plasticity of alloy decreases sharply.
In the crystallization process, due to diffusion, the atoms are in non-equilibrium
state. This state is metastable in thermodynamics, so the atoms are automatically
transformed into a state of balance trend. Therefore, in order to improve the atomic
diffusion ability, the ingot is heated to a suitable temperature, so as to quickly
complete the atomic transformation from non-equilibrium to equilibrium state. For
suitable homogeneous annealing temperature, it is generally required to lower
beginning melting temperature of alloy, and higher than the phase precipitation
temperature of harmful precipitation. On the one hand, the temperature is not too
low, it is necessary to eliminate the harmful, but also to avoid forging new harmful.
Heat time is also not too long, to reduce the production cost. On the other hand, the
temperature is not too high. Because the grain size will be too large and alloy will
de melted at high temperature. That will affect the later thermal processing.
The experiment shows that, annealed at 950 °C, dendrite segregation still exists.
Annealed at 1050 °C, dendrite segregation is obviously improved, but not com-
pletely eliminated. Annealed under the condition of 1150 °C/4 h and 1150 °C/8 h,
although the dendrite segregation is improved, but is not been completely elimi-
nated. Annealed under the condition of 1150 °C/15 h, the homogenization effect is
ideal. So the homogenization annealing temperature of NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB
alloy should be considered at 1150 °C, and the holding time is not less than 15 h.

The true stress-strain curves of samples 20% compressed are shown in Fig. 7.
The true stress-strain curves of samples 50% compressed are shown in Fig. 8. It can
be seen from the ﬁgures that the rheological stress of the alloy during high tem-
perature plastic deformation shows obvious stages. Under different experimental
conditions, the common features of the alloy rheological curve is that, true stress
increases rapidly with true strain at the beginning, then begins to increases slowly
after true strain reaches a certain amount. That is because, in the stage of initial
deformation, the alloy mainly focuses on strain reinforcement, and as the strain
increases, the rheological stress increases rapidly. When the alloy was deformed to
a certain extent, the rheological stress continued to increase because of that the alloy
did not have dynamic re-crystallization at low temperature. As the temperature
increases, the rheological stress grows slowly due to the dynamic response and
dynamic re-crystallization of the alloy [ 10, 11]. At this stage, the softening rate of
the alloy is less than that of the machining hardening rate due to the low dynamic
recovery and dynamic re-crystallization.
With the same deformation rate and deformation, the theological stress increases
rapidly with the decrease of temperature. This is because, with the increase of
deformation temperature, thermal activation gradually strengthen, atomic momen-
tum gradually grow, binding force between atoms is weakened gradually, the

In nickel-based superalloy, due to low fault energy and wide fault ribbon, the
dislocation sliding and climbing get dif ﬁcult, then dynamic recovery gets dif ﬁcult.
So the dynamic re-crystallization is the main softening mechanism during defor-
mation. The true stress-strain curves of NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB alloy and the
microstructure of the compression test prove this point. When the deformation is
50%, the microstructure of the alloy at different temperatures is shown in Fig. 10.I t
can be seen that dynamic re-crystallization occurs in the microstructure at between

1200 °C, the quantity of re-crystallization grains have gradually increased, the ﬁne
re-crystallization grains gradually replace the original coarse grains. That is mixed
grains. At 1250 °C, the dynamic re-crystallization continues to occur, and only a
small amount of original grains exist in alloy. From Fig. 10, it also can be seen that
the re-crystallized grain size of the alloy increases gradually as the deformation
temperature increases.

## Page 628

Conclusion
1. In NiCr19Co6W10Ti3AlB alloy, Ti and Al are mainly concentrate in dendrite,
and W mainly concentrates at the dendrite arm.
2. Homogenizing annealing can effectively improve the forging performance, and
the ideal homogenizing annealing temperature is 1150 °C.
3. At the beginning of the thermal deformation stage, with the increase of strain,
the rheological stress increases rapidly. When the variable reaches a certain
value, the true rheological stress increases slowly, and the rheological stress
decreases with the increase of the deformation temperature.
4. Deformed microstructure is greatly affected by deformation temperature.

Hot Forging Behavior of Inconel625
Superalloy Based on Processing Map
Deshun Sun, Xingzhi Jiang, Jianzhong Shi, Jianhua Huang
and Yongzhong Jiang
Abstract The hot forging behavior of Inconel625 superalloys was studied in hot
compression tests by the thermal mechanical simulator with Gleeble-3800. The
testing conditions were that the maximum strain was 0.8, the deformation tem-
peratures were 950, 1000, 1050, 1100, 1150, 1200 °C, and the strain rates were 0.1,
1, 5, 10, 50, 80/s. The constitutive equation was developed based on true stress
(r)-strain ( e) curves, and the activation energy of Inconel625 superalloy under hot
compression was about 679.6 kJ/mol. The processing map was developed based on
experiment data and the dynamic material model (DMM), which predicted that the
optimum hot working regime of Inconel625 was the compression condition of
1200 °C with 0.1 s
−1, and predicted the instability zones were found out under the
compression condition of 1100 °C with 0.1 s −1, 1200 °C with 1 s −1, 950 °C with
10 s −1 and 1150 °C with 80 s −1. The microstructure under the compression con-
dition were in good agreement with the predictions of the processing map, under the
optimum compression condition of 1200 °C with 0.1 s
−1, the dynamically recrys-
tallized grains were ﬁner and the better mechanical properties, this condition should
be selected to forging. In contrast, the grain sizes were uneven and the mechanical
properties were poorer under the instability compression condition of 1100 °C with
0.1 s
−1, 1200 °C with 1 s −1, 950 °C with 10 s −1 and 1150 °C with 80 s −1.
Therefore, these instability zones should be avoided during hot forging.

## Page 630

Introduction
Nickel-based superalloys are unique high temperature materials used gas turbine
engines, which display excellent resistance to mechanical and chemical degradation
[1]. Inconel625 as newly corrosion resistance superalloy, not only has excellent
corrosion resistance and oxidation resistance, but has excellent tensile and fatigue
properties from subzero to 980 °C. Therefore, Inconel625 promises to be superalloy
for spare parts in the aeroengine. As known, the ingots of Nickel-based superalloys
are unsuitable for mechanical applications: they must undergo thermal-mechanical
working in order to break down the as-cast structure and to reduce the grain size to
acceptable levels. This conversion is achieved in a series of stages, or heats. The
ingot is placed in a furnace and allowed to reach an appropriate temperature for
forging. The deformation of forging applied to the ingot causes substantial
recrystallisation to a ﬁner grain structure. After reheating, the ingot grain size will
be reduced from a few tens of millimeters to a few tens of microns. Therefore, it is
very important to research in the forging characteristic of Inconel625 superalloy.
Over the past years, extensive studies have been carried out to clarify the hot
deformation behaviours of steel, few studies have been carried out to clarify the
forging characteristic of superalloys.
In this paper, isothermal compression tests of Inconel625 superalloy have been
conducted at different temperatures and strain rates in order to characterize the ﬂow
behavior during forging. And in order to assess the stability of the superalloy under
hot working processing, processing map was drawn out with the stress ( r)-strain (e)
curves obtained from the hot compression tests.
Experimental Procedures
The chemical composition of the superalloy-Inconel625 examined in this investi-
gation is given in Table 1. For homogenization, the ingots were annealed in the
temperature range of 950 –1200 °C for plenty of time, and then hot forging, fol-
lowed by water quenching. In order to evaluate the hot working behavior of the
forged specimen, hot compression was carried out using a Gleeble simulator
(Gleeble 3800DSI). The true strain was ﬁxed at 0.8.
The schedules of the hot compression were shown in Fig. 1. As shown in Fig. 1,
the forged cylindrical specimens with 15 mm length and 10 mm diameter were
solution-treated at 1200 °C for 5 min to homogenization, after which the hot
compression was carried out, strain rates were (0.1, 1, 5, 10, 50, 80/s), then

quenching. Using the stress ( r)-strain (e) curves obtained from the hot compression
tests, constitutive equation of hot working and a processing map of Inconel625
based on a dynamic materials model (DMM) were established, and the optimum
and unstable hot working conditions were predicted by the processing map. The
specimens after the hot compression tests were etched using aqua regia
(hydrochloric:nitric=3:1), the microstructures were observed by optical microscopy.
Results and Discussion
High Temperature Flow Behavior Figure 2 depicts the true stress ( r)-strain ( e)
curves for forging specimens deformed at different strain rates of 1100 and 1200 °
C. In general, the ﬂow behavior was characterized by an increase of the true stress
with true strain up to a peak or multi-peaks that is followed by ﬂow softening until
the end of isothermal deformation [ 2]. Work hardening and dynamic recrystal-
lization [3] (DRX) are depicted by the true stress ( r)-strain (e) curves, however, it is
difﬁcult to de ﬁne which component predominates the hot deformation. In addition,
the ﬂow stress level at a certain plastic strain increases with an increase of strain
rates or decrease of temperature [ 4].
Figure 2 shows that curves are divided into three sections, ﬁrst section (slope is
positive) is that work hardening caused by dislocation multiplication; the second
section (slope is close to zero) is that the same levels of work hardening and
softening caused by DRX; the third section (slope is negative) is that softening
predominates the hot deformation.

Conclusions
The deformation behavior of Inconel 625 superalloy in a wide range of tempera-
tures (950, 1000, 1050, 1100, 1150, 1200 °C) and strain rates (0.1, 1, 5, 10, 50, 80/
s) has been investigated and discussed. The following conclusions can be drawn:
(1) The constitutive equation for hot deformation behavior of Inconel 625 super-
alloy has been carried out, and Q = 679.6 kJ/mol, n = 7.6470,
A = 1.35E + 18 s −1, a = 0.00233 MPa −1;
(2) An optimum deformation condition (1200 °C with 0.1 s −1) for heat forging is
determined to be depended on processing map. Under this condition, the grain
is ﬁner and uniformed;

Inﬂuence of Composition Adjustment
on the Microstructure and Properties
of a First Generation Ni-Base Single
Crystal Superalloy DD416
Shuai Zheng, Jian Zhang, Qinghui Wu, Zhenyu Yang and Yushi Luo
Abstract The effects of composition adjustment on the microstructures and
properties of a ﬁrst generation Ni-base single crystal superalloy DD416 were
investigated. Four experimental alloys with adjusted compositions were direction-
ally solidi ﬁed and their microstructures were observed with scanning electronic
microscope (SEM) and optical microscope (OM). The tensile and creep rupture
properties were tested. The results showed that the volumes fraction of eutectic of
the as cast alloys and heat treated alloys were obviously in ﬂuenced by the slightly
adjustment of composition, especially the change of Al and Ti contents. The tensile
properties of the four experimental alloys were similar, but the creep rupture
properties were affected by the adjustment of composition signi ﬁcantly.

Introduction
The single crystal superalloys have been developed from the 1980s [ 1–11], and the
sixth generation single crystal superalloy are under investigation, while the second
generation single crystal superalloys are now the most widely used in the civil and
military planes [ 12–14]. Single crystal superalloys are used as the aeroengine tur-
bine blades and vanes materials, and have the advantages like high temperature
mechanical properties, good heat resistance, good chemical resistance and so on.
The single crystal superalloy compositions are severely controlled to gain the aimed
heat treat window, eutectic volume, c′ volume, c′ size, etc., and with proper heat
treatment the satisfying properties would be gained. But there were not many
literatures about the composition adjustment affects on the microstructures and
properties.
DD416 is a ﬁrst generation Ni-base single crystal superalloy and its notable
feature is its high Al content and Ti content, while its Al content is about 4.7 –5.0%,
and Ti content about 4.5 –4.9%. In the meanwhile there are other alloy elements
such as Mo, Ta, Co, Cr as the solution strengthening elements. The composition
adjustment of alloy elements would infect the heat treat window and its mechanical
properties. In this study, four experimental alloys were investigated to gain the
effects.
Experimental Procedure
The nominal chemistry composition of DD416 and the four experimental alloys are
listed in Table 1. The DD416 was developed as a low density single crystal
superalloy so the Al and Ti contents were determined at a high level, and added
with proper solution strengthening elements of Mo, Ta, Cr, Co. Alloy 1 were
prepared as all the major elements were in the upper limit, and the major elements
were made all in the lower limit in the alloy 2. The Al and Ti elements were made in
the upper limit in the alloy 3, while other major elements were with the nominal
composition. The Al and Ti elements were made in the lower limit in the alloy 4

## Page 641

and other major elements were with the nominal composition. In the following, the
four experimental alloys are named as the All-up alloy, All-down alloy, Al + Ti-up
alloy and Al + Ti-down alloy.
A high thermal gradient industry vacuum furnace was used for the directional
solidiﬁcation. The single crystal bars were solidi ﬁed with the solidi ﬁcation rate of
50 lm/s. The bars were 15 mm in diameter and 170 mm in length. The specimens
for microstructure observation were taken from the top of the bars, and were
wire-cut into ﬂakes parallel to the growth direction and polished. The specimens
were etched with solution (33% acetic acid, 33% nitric acid, 33% water and 1%
hydroﬂuoric acid) which dissolves the c′ phase. The as cast condition microstruc-
tures were observed with optical microscope, and the heat treated condition
microstructures by optical microscope and scanning electronic microscope.
The test bars were heat treated in non-vacuum furnace, and the solution heat
treatment was 1238 °C, 3 h + 1271 °C, 3 h + 1277 °C, 3 h, AC. The aging heat
treatment were 1080 °C, 4 h, AC + 870 °C, 20 h, AC. The bars were then
machined to standard specimen and tested for 760 °C tensile property, 760 °C/
780 MPa, 850 °C/520 MPa, 980 °C/230 MPa, 1050 °C/150 MPa creep rupture
property.
Results and Discussions
The as cast DD416 samples exhibited a two-phase c/c′ microstructure with a
dendritic segregation pattern. And the c/c′ eutectic distributes in the interdendritic
areas. The as cast microstructures of the four experimental alloys were presented in
Fig. 1. Obviously the eutectic volume were in ﬂuenced much by the composition
adjustment as the volumes fraction of eutectic were respectively 8.6, 5.2, 10.8 and
4.8% (Table 2) corresponding to the All-up alloy, All-down alloy, Al + Ti-up
alloy, Al + Ti-down alloy.
Compared with the Al + Ti-down alloy, the volume fraction of eutectic in the
Al + Ti-up alloy increased by about 6.0% with the additional 0.38% aluminum and
0.45% titanium. That is easy to understand because the Al and Ti were the c′
forming elements and segregates to the interdendritic areas. And there was only
0.4% difference of eutectic volume between Al + Ti-down alloy and the all-down
alloy with the difference of 0.38% Co, 0.11% Ta, and 0.1% Mo. It seems that the
volume fraction of eutectic were not affected much by the Co, Ta, Mo in DD416
alloy. Compared with the All-up alloy, the eutectic volume of the Al + Ti-up alloy
increased by about 2.2% when there was additional 0.07% Ti in the Al + Ti-up
alloy, which indicated the Ti content played an important role of the eutectic
volume in DD416.
After the solution treatment the volume fraction of c/c′ eutectic decreased much
of all the four experimental alloys. The heat treated condition microstructures of the
four experimental alloys were presented in Fig. 2. It can be seen that the
microstructures were much different within four experimental alloys, as the volume

corresponding to the All-up alloy, All-down alloy, Al + Ti-up alloy, Al + Ti-down

All-up alloy, while no incipient melting were found in the other three experimental
alloys.
The volume fraction of residual eutectic of all the experimental alloys decreased
dramaticly compared with the as cast condition. The eutectic of the All-down alloy
and Al + Ti-down alloy were almost dissolved into the matrix. But the 5.9%
residual eutectic amount of the Al + Ti-up alloy indicated that that much eutectic
was not easily to be dissolved completely (Table 3).

## Page 645

not that regularly in the All-down alloy and the Al + Ti-down alloy. As the sum of
the Al and Ti contents comes below a point in DD416 alloy, good cuboidal c′
particles can not be gained.
According to the microstructures of the four experimental alloys, the c′
strengthening and solution strengthening both played important role in the creep
rupture properties. The difference of creep rupture life between the All-up alloy and
the Al + Ti-up alloy and that between All-down alloy and the Al + Ti-down alloy
showed the effect of the solution strengthening elements of Mo, Ta, Cr, Co. The
difference of creep rupture life between the Al + Ti-up alloy and Al + Ti-down
alloy exhibited the effect of the c′ strengthening on account of the additional
aluminum and titanium elements.
Conclusions
1. As the single crystal superalloy DD416 composition changes, the volume
fractures of eutectic under the as cast condition and heat treated condition are all
inﬂuenced. The as cast eutectic volumes of Al + Ti-up alloy, All-up alloy,
All-down alloy and Al + Ti down alloy are in the descend order, and so is the
consequence in the heat treated condition.

cantly by the composition change, and the c′ strengthening and solution
strengthening both play important role on the creep rupture properties. The
creep rupture lives of All-up alloy, Al + Ti up alloy, Al + Ti-down alloy and
All-down alloy are in the descend order for the four creep rupture test

Effect of Hot Isostatic Pressing
on the Tensile Property of a Second
Generation Single Crystal Superalloy
Jian Zhang, Huiming Guo, Yunsong Zhao and Yushi Luo
Abstract The hot-isostatic pressing (HIP) process at the condition of 1300 °C/
100 MPa, 4 h was applied on the second generation single crystal superalloy DD6.
Microstructural evolutions of DD6 alloy after HIP and heat treatment were
observed by using optical microscope (OM), scanning electron microscope
(SEM) and electron probe micro-analyzer (EPMA). The tensile properties of DD6
alloy after HIP treatment were tested at 760 and 980 °C. The results showed that the
volume fraction of porosity in DD6 alloy deceased from 0.31 to 0.04% after the
HIP treatment of 1300 °C/100 MPa, 4 h, meanwhile, the dendritic segregation was
homogenized gradually. Compared to the standard heat treatment, the HIP treat-
ment did not change the tensile strength and elongation of DD6 alloy at 760 °C
obviously. While the elongation of DD6 alloy increased from 24.25 to 35.90% at
980 °C.

## Page 648

Introduction
The development of directional solidi ﬁcation and the production of single crystal
turbine blades and vanes have resulted in dramatic improvements in the perfor-
mance of gas turbines [ 1–4]. In single crystal superalloy, the solution temperature
can be raised because grain boundary strengthening elements such as C, B, Hf are
barely used, so that almost all primary c′ precipitates are dissolved in base c phase
and the alloy are more homogeneous. However, micro-porosity located in inter-
dendritic region are still inevitable [ 5], these cast pores are formed during alloy
solidiﬁcation mostly, and related to the solidi ﬁcation conditions and dendrite
structure [ 6, 7]. It is well known that the cast porosities are detrimental to alloy
performance and give rise to a limit to their use potential.
Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) techniques play an important role in the research
and envelopment of superalloy in recent years. In HIP technology, high temperature
and high gas pressure can be simultaneously applied to work pieces. A study has
shown that the microporosity content reduced from 1.0 to 0.035% after HIP for
single crystal alloy PWA1480. However, the yield strength and tensile strength
were not increased obviously, the author believed the reason is that HIP has little
effect on the content of residual eutectic, which is a main in ﬂuencing factor to
tensile strength. Kim and coworkers have concentrated on the effect of HIP on
GTD-111 alloy. They found that the yield strength increased from 521 to
769.1 MPa, and the tensile strength increased from 647 to 1117 MPa. They
believed that the precipitation of c′ during HIP strengthened the alloy further [ 8].
Another research of He shows that the yield strength and tensile strength of K4169
alloy were both increased after HIP treatment, the yield strength by 12.2% and the
tensile strength by 18.9%, this is because the untreated alloy have much more cast
porosities. These porosities reduced the sectional area and cause a stress concen-
tration [ 9]. Up to now, the effect of HIP on single crystal superalloy is still not
researched adequately.
In this paper, the hot-isostatic pressing (HIP) process was applied on the second
generation single crystal superalloy DD6, and the effect of HIP on tensile property
was researched.
Experiments
A second generation single crystal nickel-based superalloy DD6 is selected for the
present work (for alloy composition see Table 1). The single crystal bars (16 mm in
diameter and 180 mm long) were produced in [001] orientation by Bridgman high
rate solidi ﬁcation technique under a high thermal gradient in vacuum furnace. The
orientation of each bar was determined by the X-ray diffraction technology. Only
samples with orientation within 10° deviating from [001] were used. The HIP
procedure is 1300 °C/100 MPa for 4 h, after HIP treatment. The alloys received a
662 J. Zhang et al.

## Page 649

solution and homogenization heat treatment at 1315 °C for 4 h followed by a
precipitation heat treatment at 1120 °C for 4 h and 870 °C for 32 h.
Tensile testing was carried out at 760 and 980 °C. The microstructure of the
samples was observed by light optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) metallographic techniques.
Experimental Results
Microstructure Figure 1a, b shows the typical un-etched microstructure with
different conditions. The cast porosity was observed by optical microscopy, the
pores are mostly located in the interdendritic regions of the microstructure, a total
pore area fraction of around 0.31% in untreated samples. After HIP treated, the
amount of cast porosity is decreased obviously, a total pore area fraction is about
0.04%, and almost all pores with large size were eliminated. Figure 1c, d shows the
Microstructure of DD6 alloy before and after HIP treatment, the amount of residual
eutectic is 1.05% after standard heat treatment, after HIP treatment, it declined to
0.47%. The typical microstructure of alloy after full heat treatment is presented in

Fig. 2. The c′ precipitates appeared as cuboids with the average size of around

The compositions of the dendritic and interdendritic regions were determined by
electron microprobe to investigate the difference in the extent of microsegregation
resulted from HIP treatment. The partition rations k ′ = (dendritic composition/

Tensile Behavior Tensile property tests were carried on at 760 and 980 °C with
single crystal specimens treated under standard heat treatment and HIP treatment.
The effect of HIP on strength, elongation, contraction of area is shown in Table 2.
In 760 °C testing, it can be seen that the yield strength and tensile strength showed
a small increase after HIP treated, but the elongation and contraction of area
changed little. In 980 °C testing, HIP did not lead to a obvious change on the yield
strength and tensile, however, the elongation increased from 24.25 to 35.90% after
HIP treated.

## Page 651

The Fractographs Figure 4a, b shows the fracture surface morphologies at 760 and
980 °C. At 760 °C, the fracture mode is typical shear fracture. Further analysis
revealed that the fracture plane was {111} crystal plane. At high temperature (980 °C),
fracture mode completely changes and homogeneous deformation occurs (Fig. 4c, d).
The fracture surface is characterized by mostly ductile rupture with dimples. HIP
procedure did not cause different at both temperatures.
Examination of the longitudinal sections of the failed specimens revealed the
presence of internal microcracks (see Fig. 5). These microcracks were observed
throughout the gage length of the specimens but with a higher density close to the
fracture surface. The comparison shows that the amount of microcracks is markedly
reduced in the specimens HIP-treated. Further examination of the microcracks
revealed that they initiated from the pre-existing cast porosities (Fig. 6a) and
residual eutectic phase (Fig. 6b). During the later period of tensile testing, the
microcracks start to elongate and link up to each other, increasing the stress in the
remaining undamaged cross section and leading to rupture.

Discussion
Effect of HIP on Microstructure High temperature and high gas pressure
simultaneously applied to single crystal bars in the HIP procedure, under this
condition, alloy elements diffusion is promoted and microporosities are closed
gradually by creep deformation. Some researches demonstrated that the capability
of closing and healing microporosity, and they considered that microporosity
closing is ﬁnished by two steps: (1) Stress-induced collapse of voids. (2) Diffusion
bonding once surfaces of voids come into contact [ 10, 11]. HIP procedure led to a
obviously decrease on the amount of cast porosity. On the other hand, the standard
heat treatment was carried on after HIP procedure, so c′ precipitates were not
affected by HIP. During HIP procedure, alloy elements diffusion was accelerated
under high temperature treatment, a more uniform microstructure with improved
homogeneity was obtained after HIP.
Effect of HIP on Tensile Behavior The fracture mode is typical shear fracture at
760 °C in the tensile test. Under this condition, the major deformation mechanism
is c′ particles shearing by dislocations frequently [ 12]. At 980 °C, the fracture
surface is characterized by mostly ductile rupture with dimples. Dislocations can
hardly cut into c′ particles and the main deformation mechanism is dislocation
slipping and climbing in c phase [ 13].

## Page 653

In both two deformation mechanisms at 760 and 980 °C, the volume fraction
and size of c′ particles are critical in ﬂuencing factor to the tensile property. As
discussed above, c′ particles were not affected obviously by HIP. Thus, HIP did not
appear to have any effect on the tensile property.
At 980 °C, the fracture surface is characterized by mostly ductile rupture with
dimples. Examination of the longitudinal sections of the failed specimens revealed
the presence of internal microcracks (see Fig. 6). These microcracks were observed
throughout the gage length of the specimens but with a higher density close to the
fracture surface. Further examination of the microcracks revealed that they initiated
from the pre-existing cast porosities but no new porosities were formed. During the
later period of tensile testing, the microcracks start to elongate and link up to each
other, eventually lead to rupture. After HIP treated, the amount of cast porosity
decreased obviously, a total pore area fraction is about 0.04%. Linking of micro-
cracks was prolonged and the elongation increased dramatically.
Conclusion
(1) After a 1300 °C/100 MPa, 4 h HIP procedure, a total pore area fraction
decreases from 0.31 to 0.04%;
(2) After HIP treatment, a more uniform microstructure with improved homo-
geneity can be obtained;
(3) At 760 °C, HIP does not show the obvious effect on the strength and elonga-
tion. At 980 °C, HIP also does not lead to an obvious change on strength, but
the elongation increases from 24.25 to 35.90%.
