Effect of Strain on Recrystallization
of a Ni-Based Single Crystal Superalloy
Qian Liu, Lixi Tian, Wenlong Xiao and Chaoli Ma
Abstract The effect of strain induced by compression testing on recrystallization
(RX) of a single crystal superalloy DD6 was investigated. The evolution of surface
structure during annealing at the temperatures of 1000, 1100, 1220 °C was char-
acterized by Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and Energy Dispersive
Spectroscopy (EDS). The element distribution and microstructure of the oxidation
layer after annealing at 1100 °C showed that the main chemical elements were
mainly Al, Ta, Cr, Ni, O. This indicated that the formation process of oxides
included the inward diffusion of O and the outward diffusion of oxide-rich elements
(Al, Cr, etc.). The thickness of RX layer was measured. At 1000 °C, no recrys-
tallization but PFZ (precipitate free zone) was observed under oxidation layer.
However, when annealing at higher temperature, the thickness of RX layer
increased obviously with the increasing deformation strain. Cellular recrystalliza-
tion could be detected in the samples annealed at 1100 °C, whereas isometric
recrystallization and annealing twin formed in the specimen annealed at 1220 °C.

## Page 656

Introduction
Ni-based single crystals (SC) superalloys possess extremely high temperature
strength, fatigue and creep properties. Therefore, they are widely used as turbine
blades and vanes [ 1]. But there are many potential sources that may result in
deformation during the process of manufacturing and processing of a blades or
vanes as well as during service: contraction stresses during cooling of the solid in
the shell mold, removing the ceramic mold and core material mechanically,
stamping identi ﬁcation marks, impact damage, removing of coating residues
mechanically, etc. [ 1]. In addition, high density of crystal defects such as vacancies
or dislocations remained in the cold deformed alloys, which could stimulate
recrystallization when they were heat treated or in service. Due to acting as a weak
sites (crack initiation and propagation sites) during high temperature service, grain
boundaries induced by RX may lead to a signi ﬁcant reduction of high temperature
properties. In previous work, researchers investigated the critical deformation strain
of recrystallization of SC superalloy SRR99, and concluded that the critical strain
decreased with increasing annealing temperature while the thickness of recrystal-
lized layer increased with the heat treatment temperature and pre-compression
strain [ 2].
In this work, the effect of compressive strain on recrystallization of SC super-
alloy DD6 has been studied. Microstructure evolution during different temperature
annealing heat treatment has been investigated by inducing various compression
deformations.
Experimental Procedure
The second generation single-crystal superalloy DD6 in heat-treated condition was
used for the experiment, with its composition listed in Table 1 [1, 3]. Specimens
(5 mm /C25m m /C28 mm) were machined from the SC bar by wire-electrode
cutting, and mechanically polished to get fresh surfaces. Then samples were
compressed at 0.2 mm/min by SANS-CMT5105 along the longtitude direction
([001] direction) at room temperature to induce various plastic strain. After
unloading, SEM observation was conducted on side face of the specimens to
characterize the slip bands. Then, the specimens were subjected to annealed at
1000, 1100 and 1220 °C (The typical service temperature of SC superalloy is
between 1000 and 1100 °C, and the secondary phase c′ solution temperature is
1220 °C.) for 4 h in static air.

In order to reveal the microstructure evolution, heat-treated samples were further
characterize by Apollo 300 scanning electron microscope (SEM), which was
equiped with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and operated at 15 kV.
The SEM samples were ﬁrst mechanically polished and then chemically etched in a
solution of 5 g CuSO 4 +2 0m LH 2O + 20 mL HCl.
Results and Discussion
Slip Bands The surface morphology of the sample before and after compression
was observed by SEM, as shown in Fig. 1. Figure 1a described the sample prior to
deformation, no slip bands were observed. After pre-compression, slip bands could
be clearly detected and the amount of it increased with the increasing pre-strain
(Fig. 1b–e).
Closer inspection revealed that the slip bands intersected with each other and
formed a speci ﬁc angle at about 75°, as illustrated in Fig. 2. When dislocation slips
out of the crystal, slip band forms on the surface. In face centered cubic
(FCC) metals, dislocations can be easily activated along the 〈110 〉 direction on
{111} planes. Since samples in present study were cut from the single crystal, the
surface of the specimens may present a speci ﬁc orientation with {111} slip plane,
which may result in the speci ﬁc angle between slip bands.
Oxidation Reaction and c′ Precipitate Free Zone (PFZ) Microstructure and
element distribution of the sample pre-compressed to 8% and annealed at 1100 °C
for 4 h were demonstrated in Fig. 3. It could be clearly observed that the oxide
layer were rich in Al, Ta, Cr, Ni, O, etc. According to previous investigations [ 4–8]

d 8%; e 10%

## Page 658

and the EDS analysis in present study, the oxide layer could be divided into three
parts. A thin and continuous Al 2O3 ﬁlm formed closely to the PFZ. Next to the
Al2O3 ﬁlm was an intermediate layer mainly composed of Cr 2O3 and spinel phase.
The Outer part was (Ni, Co) O layer. Thus the formation process of oxides included
the inward diffusion of O and the outward diffusion of oxide-rich elements (Al, Cr,
etc.). The impoverishment of c′-rich element (Al, Ta) under the oxide scale resulted
in the transformation of c′ to c, i.e., c′ precipitate free zone (PFZ) formed [ 9]. In the
PFZ layer, nucleation and grain growth of recrystallization could be easier carried
out.
Microstructure of Samples Annealed at 1000 °C Typical SEM images of sam-
ples suffered to different pre-strain and annealed at 1000 °C for 4 h were shown in
Fig. 4. For all the investigated samples, the c′ PFZ and oxidation layer (Ox) could
be distinctly observed. The thickness of oxidation layer and PFZ was measured. It
revealed that the total thickness of oxidation layer and PFZ was almost identical,
about 5.5 lm when the pre-strain increased from 2 to 10%. However, for the
sample suffered a smaller pre-strain, the oxidation layer (Fig. 4a) was thinner than
those in the samples subjected to larger deformation (Fig. 4c, d).
The diffusion coefﬁcient was affected by many factors such as temperature, type
of diffusion, bonding, and crystal structure, concentration of diffusing species and
composition of matrix [ 10]. Among these, temperature has the most profound
inﬂuence on the coef ﬁcients and diffusion rates. Atoms could also diffuse along

## Page 659

dislocations, grain boundary and external surface. Because of the high density of
dislocation and vacancies, the diffusion process would be accelerated in largely
deformed samples, resulting in thicker oxidation layer in them.
Microstructure of Samples Annealed at 1100 °C Figure 5 presented the SEM
images of the deformed DD6 after annealing at 1100 °C for 4 h. The thickness of
oxide layer became signi ﬁcantly greater than those annealed at 1000 °C (Fig. 4).
For samples deformed at small strain (2, 4%), the morphology of PFZ has not been
changed obviously. However, as plastic strain increased, the surface microstructure
distinctly changed. As shown in Fig. 5c, d, cellular recrystallized structure can be
clearly observed (Fig. 5c, d).
With the temperature increasing (below the c′ solvus temperature [ 11]), the
diffusion coefﬁcient increased obviously. For those samples suffered a larger plastic
strain, higher distortion energy was remained in the crystal, which was enough to
drive recrystallization. Recrystallization grains nucleated on the surface in the c′
PFZ, and then grew toward the matrix. Hence there was no c′ precipitates in the
outer side of the recrystallized grains. With grain boundaries moving toward the
matrix, the solute atoms would be suf ﬁcient to precipitate c′, resulting in the for-
mation of c′. In addition, during this stage, the grain boundaries migrated quickly
without inhibition in the moving direction. The diffusion of c′-formation elements,
Fig. 4 SEM images of samples with different pre-strain and annealing at 1000 °C for 4 h: a 2%;
b 4%; c 8%; d 10%

## Page 660

such as Al, along the boundaries could not provide suf ﬁcient elements for con-
tinuous growth of c′. In the ﬁnal stage, the migration of the boundaries slow down,
and the diffusion of c′-forming elements along the boundaries can provide elements
for the growth of columnar c′ precipitates, resulting in the longer columnar c′
precipitates near the boundaries. Similarly, when grain boundaries moving,
c′-formation elements can migrate along another “short-circuit” diffusion paths-
dislocation, so the depth of recrystallized layer increases with the increasing of
dislocation density.
Microstructure of Samples Annealed at 1220 °C After annealing at elevated
temperature 1220 °C for 4 h, equiaxed recrystallized grains [ 12] could be easily
found on the whole surface in cold-deformed samples (Fig. 6). And with plastic
deformation increasing, the depth of recrystallized layer increased distinctly, from
30 lm at 2% plastic strain, to 46.7 lm at 4% plastic strain, and increased to more
than 95 lm at 8% plastic strain. Besides, a large amount of annealing twins [ 13, 14]
could also be observed in the equiaxed recrystallized grains. For those materials
exhibited low stacking energy, annealing twins formed easily when material suf-
fered to plastic deformation and annealing treatment [ 15].

Conclusions
(1) Oxide layers can be observed in DD6 alloy after cold deformation and
annealing treatment. The oxide layers are mainly composed of Al, Ta, Ni, Cr.
And oxide layer causes the depletion of Al near the surface, resulting in c′
precipitate free zone (PFZ).
(2) After annealing at 1000 °C for 4 h, there is no recrystallization even in the
specimen with plastic strain of 10%.
(3) For those sample suffered a larger pre-compression strain, annealing treatment
at 1100 °C for 4 h results in cellular recrystallization.
(4) After annealing at temperature 1220 °C for 4 h, equiaxed recrystallized grains
and annealing twins can be found in a large range area on the surface in
cold-deformed samples.

Abstract As the superalloy K4648 is a high Cr content alloy, the different heat
treatment process affects the precipitation of a-Cr and Cr carbides. In this paper, the
heat treatment experiment of K4648 superalloy was carried out. The results showed
that the morphology and quantity of a-Cr phase in the alloy were very sensitive to

Introduction
K4648 is a high chromium nickel-base cast superalloy, and also an aging precip-
itation strengthening type alloy. The alloy is characterized by high chromium,
mainly used for 900 °C below the strong antioxidant aviation materials parts [ 1–4].
The main strengthening elements of the alloy are Cr, W, Mo, Nb, Al, and Ti. W,
Mo mainly enters the c solid solution to strengthen the matrix, Al, Ti, Nb form
precipitation phase to strengthen the matrix. The alloy is mainly composed of c
solid solution, a-Cr, c′,M

chemical composition for the alloy is that the chromium content is up to 32 –35%. In
general, a certain amount of Cr elements are added in the high temperature alloys to
protect the alloy surface from oxidation and hot corrosion. The higher the Cr
content, the better the corrosion resistance of the alloy, especial to sulfur corrosion,
but the increase of Cr content will inevitably lead to the increase of a-Cr phase
precipitation in the alloy [ 5–7].
The aging treatment process has a great in ﬂuence on the microstructure and
properties of K4648 superalloy. Different heat treatment processes can affect the
precipitation of a-Cr and chromium carbides. In this paper, a series of heat treat-
ment processes of K4648 superalloy were carried out, and the in ﬂuence of aging
treatment on the microstructure and properties of K4648 superalloy was found.
Materials and Experimental Procedure
The chemical composition of the prepared cast steel is shown in Table 1.
In order to eliminate and reduce the gas and the fatigue crack source caused by
inclusions, the prevention of the cast steel in the long-term service during the cycle
fatigue damage and reduce its service life, the steel cast should be obtained by
vacuum furnace. As smelting vacuum <0.6 Pa, the raw material was carried into the
furnace and after melting, the alloy re ﬁning period set in. In order to fully degas, the
inclusions were fully ﬂoated, the harmful elements were fully volatilized, and the
reﬁning temperature and re ﬁning time were strictly controlled during the re ﬁning
period. In this process, power and alloying time should be rational controlled to
prevent the alloy temperature from too high. The molten steel was cast into
mechanical performance test stick to measure the strength and impact toughness.
The alloys were subjected to solid solution treatment at 1180 ± 10 °C/4 h and
aging treatment at different temperatures. The test bars were tested for strength and
impact toughness.
Results and Discussion
The mechanical properties of the alloy after different aging treatment are shown in
Table 2. It can be seen that with the increase of aging temperature, the ultimate
strength decreased, the elongation and the reduction of area increased gradually,
and the impact toughness increased. Among them, from 910 to 930 °C, the ultimate

point of view, at the aging temperature of 930 °C, K4648 alloy had a good com-
prehensive performance.
According to the thermodynamic equilibrium phase diagram of K4648 alloy
(shown in Fig. 1), it can be seen that the c′ phase disappeared completely when the

small amount of c′ phase. When the temperature rised to 930 °C, the c′ phase
disappeared and the content of a-Cr phase decreased. When the temperature con-

did not change signi ﬁcantly.
Figure 2 shows the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of K4648 alloy with
different aging temperatures. In the ﬁgure, the black feather-like phase was the a-Cr
precipitated phase. It can be seen from the ﬁgure that the precipitation phases of
a-Cr changed with the aging temperature. With the increase of aging temperature,
the precipitation of a-Cr in the sample gradually reduced. According to the sta-
tistical properties of the samples treated at different aging temperatures, it may be
concluded that the content of a-Cr precipitates decreases with the aging temperature
increasing, which will decrease the tensile strength of the materials. When the
temperature rised from 910 to 930 °C, the strength change was not obvious, the
elongation and the reduction of area were slightly improved, and the impact per-
formance was improved obviously. The elongation and the reduction of area
increased signi ﬁcantly when the treatment was reduced at 950 °C due to the
decrease of a-Cr content. But the impact toughness change was not obvious. It is
indicated that the reduction of a-Cr content will not always improve the impact
toughness, to a certain extent, there will be in ﬂection point.

Conclusions
The aging temperature has a greater impact on the impact toughness of K4648 high
temperature alloy. In the reasonable temperature range, with the increase of the
aging temperature, the ultimate strength of the alloy decreases, and the impact
toughness ﬁrst increases to the maximum, and then the change is not obvious.
Based on the several tests, the best alloy performance and the most suitable aging
temperature has been obtained for the alloy. Through the thermodynamic equilib-
rium calculation, metallographic observation, electron microscopy analysis and
energy spectrum analysis, the regularity of the change of the structure with the
aging temperature has been established, which provides a reliable theoretical basis
for the best matching of the performance. better comprehensive mechanical prop-
erties can be achieved by the aging treatment of 930 °C/16 h.

## Page 670

Precipitation Behaviors of M 23C6
Carbides and cʹ Phase in Cast IN617B
Alloy During Long-Term Aging
Shuang Gao, Jieshan Hou, Fei Yang, Changshuai Wang
and Lanzhang Zhou
Abstract The precipitation behaviors of M 23C6 carbides and cʹ phase in cast
IN617B alloy during long-term aging was systematically investigated by compar-
ison with previous studying results about wrought IN617B alloy. The results
showed that the morphology of M
23C6 carbides and the nucleation location of cʹ
particles in cast IN617B alloy were distinctly different from those of wrought
IN617B alloy due to the difference of processing method. The microstructure
observation revealed that the morphology of M
23C6 carbides at grain boundaries
(GBs) transformed from ﬁlm-like shape into cellular shape owing to the reduction
in the interfacial energy of GBs. Within the grains the bar-like M 23C6 carbides and
spherical cʹ phase directly precipitated from the c matrix. Moreover, the growth of
M23C6 facilitated the formation of cʹ phase by enriching cʹ-formation elements, and
conversely, dense cʹ phase inhibited the coarsening and decomposition of M 23C6 by
constraining the diffusion of M 23C6-formation elements. In addition, the mecha-
nism of inhibiting effect of cʹ phase on the coarsening of bar-shaped M 23C6 was
discussed.

## Page 671

Introduction
IN617B alloy is a solid-solution strengthened nickel-base superalloy with high
creep rupture strength, superior high temperature corrosion resistance and good
weldability, which is considered as the most promising superalloy candidate in
700 °C Advanced Ultra Supercritical coal- ﬁred power plant [ 1, 2]. Since IN617B
alloy is a newly developed B-alloyed variant of the commercial IN617 alloy, only a
few studies on the microstructural transformation during long-term thermal expo-
sure have been done to date. Moreover, most reports focus on wrought IN617B
alloy while few studies about cast IN617B alloy are reported at present. Recently,
there are some reported cases in Europe and Japan, that IN617B alloy is used to
produce castings or valve components applied in coal- ﬁred power plants [ 2].
However, the microstructure evolution of cast IN617B alloy is not investigated in
detail.
IN617B alloy contains a high content of Cr element and small amounts of Al and
Ti, M23C6 and cʹ are inevitable to precipitate during thermal exposure [ 3–5].
During thermal exposure, it is observed that cʹ precipitates heterogeneously
nucleate at M
23C6/c interfaces and then inhibit the growth of M 23C6 [4]. And Tytko
et al. [ 4] considered that M 23C6 particles grow in the elastically soft (100)-plane of
the matrix resulting in plate-shaped morphology. But some research [ 6, 7] observed
that M 23C6 carbides appeared blocky and distributed homogenously in grains
without growth habit plane during 704 °C thermal exposure. Therefore, it seems
that the crystallographic growth direction and morphology of M
23C6 was not
conclusive in IN617B alloy. Nevertheless, there is a generally received opinion that
the crystallographic growth direction of M
23C6 is parallel to the 〈001〉 directions
and the morphology of M 23C6 appears as octahedral-shape in nickel-base super-
alloys [ 3, 8]. Although the chemical composition of cast IN617B alloy is the same
to that of wrought IN617B alloy, different processing methods will lead to the
difference of mechanical properties and microstructures of both alloys. Due to the
lack of detailed microstructural data of cast IN617B alloy, it makes the investiga-
tion about microstructural evolution necessary and novel. This research character-
izes carbides the precipitation behaviors of M
23C6 carbides and cʹ in cast IN617B
alloy during long-term aging of 700 °C, which is different from that in wrought IN
617B alloy.
Experimental
The compositions of cast IN617B superalloy used in this work were (wt%) 0.004B,
0.04C, 0.34Ti, 1.2Al, 8.54Mo, 12.1Co, 22.21Cr and 55.67Ni. The as-received
material was an ingot provided by the investment casting method. Figure 1 reveals
that the as-cast alloy has an obvious dendritic segregation pattern with some coarse
carbides both on GBs and within grains such as Ti (C, N), M
6C and M 23C6. These
686 S. Gao et al.

## Page 672

carbide types are identical with those in wrought IN617 alloy [ 5, 6, 9, 10]. The alloy
was subjected to solution heat treatment at 1200 °C for 2 h followed water cooling
(WC). Subsequently, aging treatment is performed at 700 °C for 500 and 5000 h.
Observation of the microstructural evolution of each specimen was conducted by
scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectrometer
(EDS), transmission electron microscope (TEM). Before SEM observations, the
surfaces of all samples were polished and then electrolytically etched at room
temperature for 30–60 s at 15 V. Electrolytic etching which stripped away c matrix,
was employed for three-dimension observation of precipitates with an electrolyte
containing 300 ml HCl + 100 ml HNO 3 + 500 ml C 3H8O3. Specimens for TEM
observation were mechanically grounded to 50 lm and then thinned by twin-jet
electro polishing with a solution of 10 ml HClO 4 +9 0m lC 2H5OH at 22 V and
−20 °C.
Results and Discussion
Figure 2 shows the microstructure after solution heat treatment at 1200 °C for 2 h
with WC. It is clear that composition segregation is almost eliminated and carbides
dissolve into the matrix except some blocky and black particles. According to the
corresponding EDS result (Fig. 2b), it is con ﬁrmed that the particle is a Ti-rich Ti
(C, N) carbonitride, which is in agreement with the observation in wrought IN617B
alloy [4, 7]. Due to the relatively stable structure of Ti (C, N), it is hard to dissolved
Ti (C, N) into the matrix although the temperature of solution heart treatment is
higher than the solution point of other carbides. After solution heat treatment, the
residual GB carbides appear as a ﬁlm-like shape. However, some researchers found
that GB carbides in annealed wrought IN617B alloy remained particle-shape or
globular-shape [ 7, 11]. The difference is ascribed to that the solution temperature
Fig. 1 As-cast microstructure of the alloy: a SEM image of the dendritic microstructure;
b backscattered electron (BSE) showing inter- and intra-granular carbides
Precipitation Behaviors of M 23C6 Carbides and cʹ Phase … 687

## Page 673

preformed on cast IN617B alloy is higher than that applied on wrought IN617B
alloy. Due to serious composition segregation and coarse carbides existing in
as-received cast IN617B alloy, higher solution temperature is used to improve the
homogeneity of microstructure effectively. In work reported by Mankins et al. [ 12],
it determined that M 23C6 precipitated between 649 and 1093 °C. At high solution
temperature, the diffusibility of solute atoms increases remarkably. Therefore, GB
carbides dissolve into the matrix more completely than those in annealed wrought
IN617B alloy.
Owing to that the matrix is kept in a supersaturated and unstable state after
solution heat treatment, some precipitates subsequently nucleate during aging.
Figure 3a clearly reveals the three-dimension morphology of carbides after aging for
500 h. Carbides on GBs show ﬁne and cellular particles which are con ﬁrmed as
Cr-rich M 23C6 carbides according to the corresponding EDS result (Fig. 3d). The
formation of ﬁne and cellular particles should be a result of the decomposition of
primary ﬁlm-like GB carbides in solution microstructure. As is well known, cellular
carbides have a smaller surface energy than ﬁlm-like carbides under the situation of
the same volume of materials. Hence, ﬁlm-shape M 23C6 phase in the solution
microstructure is the unstable structure with a relatively high surface energy at high
temperature. When a small perturbation impacts on the phase surface the unbalance
of concentration ﬁeld at the perturbed point results in the dissolution of local phase.
As a result, with the increase of aging time, ﬁlm-shape M 23C6 carbides gradually
decompose into cellular carbides. Therefore, the reduction in the interfacial energy is
responsible for the formation of cellular carbides. Previous studies con ﬁrmed that
such ﬁne and cellular particles on GBs were bene ﬁcial to the creep resistance of
alloys by retarding the movement of GB during elevated temperature creep [4, 9, 10].
Besides, Fig. 3a also reveals that carbides within grains present the bar-shape
morphology. Figure 3b reveals the TEM topography of the microstructure after the
aging for 500 h. It is found that bar-like carbides and circular cʹ particles uniformly
distribute in grains (Fig. 3b). According to the corresponding selected-area
diffraction patterns (SADP) in the ½/C22112/C138 zone axis (Fig. 3c), bar-like carbides are
determined as M 23C6 carbide with a face-centered cubic structure (FCC) crystal

2 h with WC and b EDS of Ti (C, N) carbonitride

structure and a lattice parameter of a = 1.03 nm. Furthermore, it is clear that the
cube-on-cube orientation relationship between M 23C6 and the matrix c is as fol-
lows: ½/C22112/C138 M23 C6 //½/C22112/C138 c and ð110ÞM23C6ð110Þc. In addition, it is found that both cʹ
particles and M 23C6 carbides independently and directly precipitate from c the
matrix after aging for 500 h. This is not agreement with previous research that cʹ
particles nucleated on the surface of M 23C6 carbides with the plate-shape mor-
phology after aging of 100 h [ 4]. This should be attributed to the effects of different
processing methods on the microstructure. Tytko et al. [ 4] observed that a mass of
dislocations forming during forging process pile up on the surface of M 23C6 in
wrought IN617B alloy. The high dislocation density on the surface of M 23C6
carbides will give rise to the high lattice distortion energy which provides the
driving force for the nucleation of cʹ particles. Hence, a correlated growth of M 23C6
and cʹ is observed in wrought IN617B alloy. Furthermore, forging process will also
induce the formation of lattice defects such as twin boundaries, vacancies and
stacking faults. The effect of lattice defects on the morphology of M
23C6 carbides is
important in an austenite matrix [ 13, 14]. However, in cast IN617B alloy, both
dislocations and twins are not observed under TEM (Fig. 3b). In contrast, these

## Page 675

lattice defects are easily observed in wrought IN617B alloy subjected to solution
heat treatment. As a result, M 23C6 carbides in wrought IN617B alloy have the
plate-shape morphology which is different from t bar-like morphology in cast
IN617B alloy. Therefore, the authors deem that processing method exerts a sig-
niﬁcant inﬂuence on the morphology of M
23C6 carbides and the nucleation location
of cʹ phase.
From Fig. 3b, it is clear that the appearance of cʹ particles inﬂuences the growth
of bar-shaped M 23C6. When cʹ particles locate on the growth direction of
bar-shaped M 23C6, the growth of M 23C6 is impeded, as marked by the arrow 1 in
Fig. 3b. Moreover, when cʹ particles locate on the surface of bar-shaped M 23C6, the
curving surface of M 23C6 is caused, as marked by the arrow 2 in Fig. 3b. The above
results indicate cʹ particles have an inhibiting effect on the growth of M 23C6. This is
ascribed to the difference of the chemical composition of cʹ particles and M 23C6
carbides. The cʹ phase with L1 2 ordered structure is an intermetallic compound,
Ni3(Al, Ti) [ 15]. The M 23C6-formation elements, Cr and Mo are depleted in the cʹ
phase, which is con ﬁrmed by Tytko et al. with atom probe tomography [ 4, 16].
Therefore, dense cʹ particles will inhibit the continuous growth of M 23C6 by cutting
off the diffusion of Cr and C into carbides. As a consequence, the growth of M 23C6
carbides will be inhibited effectively during aging. Such stable carbides and ﬁne cʹ
are able to block the movement of dislocations during elevated temperature creep,
contributing to hindering the accumulation of dislocations at GBs and delaying the
initiation of microcracks [ 4]. These bene ﬁcial conditions imply that cast IN617B
alloy has a relatively stable microstructure during long-term aging.
After the aging for 5000 h, the average size of cʹ particles strikingly increases
from 35 to 55 nm while bar-like M 23C6 carbides size has no obvious change, as
shown in Fig. 4a. But M 23C6 carbides on GBs coarsen signi ﬁcantly and transform
into blocky carbides. It can be found that cʹ particles strongly aggregate on the
surface of M 23C6 (Fig. 4b). Moreover, the size and density of cʹ particles in the
vicinity of carbides are larger than those far away from carbides. This indicates that
the growth of M 23C6 carbides facilitates the formation of cʹ particles on the surface
of M 23C6. According to EDS result in Fig. 3d, M 23C6 carbides contain a limited
content of Al and Ti. Consequently, with aging prolonging, the growth of M 23C6
rejects large amount of Al and Ti, which are cʹ formation elements, on the surface
of M 23C6. As a result, the driving force of cʹ phase nucleation on the surface of
M23C6 will be strongly enhanced, which is con ﬁrmed by Yan et al. [ 17], and the cʹ
particles have a higher growth rate than those far away from carbides. Furthermore,
the decomposition of carbides is not observed under TEM and SEM. This is also
attributed to that the cʹ network to constrain the diffusion of formation elements and
then delay the decomposition of carbides during long-term aging. In summary, the
effect of cʹ phase distributing on M
23C6 precipitates is positive, which is conducive
to improve the long-term microstructure stability by forming ﬁne and stable
carbides.
690 S. Gao et al.

## Page 676

Conclusions
Based on the comparison between the present results in cast IN617B alloy and
previous studies about wrought IN617B alloy, it is found that processing method
exerted a signi ﬁcant in ﬂuence on the morphology of M 23C6 carbides and the
nucleation of cʹ particles. In cast IN617B alloy, M 23C6 carbides and cʹ particles
independently precipitate from the matrix. The M 23C6 in grains show the bar-like
morphology which is different from that in wrought IN617B alloy. In addition, the
growth of M 23C6 facilitates the formation of cʹ, and conversely, dense cʹ inhibites
the coarsening and decomposition of M 23C6 by constraining the diffusion of carbide
formation elements.

Introduction
Directional solidi ﬁcation (DS) to form columnar grain structures has been
employed for decades to improve the mechanical properties of Ni-base superalloys
[1–3]. DZ4125L alloy is the ﬁrst generation directionally solidi ﬁed nickel based
superalloy and has been developed by the low segregation technology [ 4]. The
alloy contains quite a bit of c′ forming elements, thus obtains a high volume
fraction of hard c′ precipitates embedded coherently in a soft c matrix. Therefore,
DZ4125L alloy exhibits good mechanical properties and physical properties and
has been used into industrial production [ 5]. However, it is found that the blade
often shows poor castability when the alloy is used to produce hollow blades. The
phenomenon is known as hot cracking [ 6]. Lots of effort has been spent on
understanding the formation of hot tearing. It was found that the modi ﬁcation in
composition of Hf, Ti and Ta can change the hot cracking tendency due to the
inﬂuence on solidi ﬁcation behavior [ 7–9]. Meanwhile, minor elements, such as Zr,
B and C, which generally tend to segregate at grain boundaries (GBs), were also
been reported to have effects on hot tearing tendency [ 10–12].
Our previous work found that the castability of DZ4125L alloy could be
improved by changing thermal gradient of the DS furnace and controlling Ti, S and
P in alloy [ 5]. But it cannot completely eliminate hot cracking. Meanwhile, the
relationship between relatively serious burning loss of Al in alloy and the low yield
of blades began been noticed. Several master alloys which contain lower Al content
exhibit more serious hot tearing tendency. So it is meaningful to investigate the
effect of Al on solidi ﬁcation behavior and castability of DZ4125L, which can be
helpful to developing free hot cracking blades. Besides, Al can also in ﬂuence the
microstructure and mechanical properties of the alloy. Thus, in this paper, a
research of the in ﬂuence of Al on microstructure, mechanical properties, solidi ﬁ-
cation behavior, segregation and castability of DZ4125L alloy was reported. We
hope to provide useful guidance on producing hollow blades.
694 Z. Tan et al.

Experimental
Two alloys with different aluminum proportion were designed according to the
composition range of DZ4125L. All the master alloys were ﬁrst prepared by a
vacuum induction furnace. Then the DS specimens were produced at a constant
withdrawal rate of 6 mm/min in a directional solidi ﬁed furnace. The actual
chemical compositions of two experimental alloys were analyzed subsequently, as
shown in Table 1. All the DS specimens received the same standard heat treatment
as:1220 °C /C22 h/AC + 1080 °C /C24 h/AC + 900 °C /C216 h/AC.
The microstructure of as-cast and heat-treatment alloys were examined by
optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The primary
dendrite arm spacing k
1, secondary dendrite arm spacing k2, and volume fractions
of eutectic and carbides of as-cast alloys were analyzed by the Image-Pro Plus
software. The standard cylindrical specimens for tensile and stress rupture tests
were machined after heat treatment. The tensile and stress rupture tests were con-
ducted at room temperature and 980 °C, 235 MPa respectively. Differential scan-
ning calorimetry (DSC) was employed to determine the critical temperature of
phase formation during solidi ﬁcation, using heating rates of 5 K/min. The tem-
peratures of phase formation were then used to select the quenching temperatures.
The isothermal solidi ﬁcation samples with the dimension of 8 mm /C28m m /C28
mm were cut from the ingots and embedded into graphite blocks with drilling holes.
After desiccation, the graphite blocks were heated up to 1400 °C and held for
10 min, followed by cooling at 15 °C/min to the desired solidi ﬁcation temperatures.
The samples were held at these temperatures for 10 min followed by water
quenching. The microstructures of the solidi ﬁed samples were analyzed by met-
allography, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electronic probe micro
analysis (EPMA). The volume percentage of the frozen liquid phase in the samples
was measured by quantitative image analysis. The segregation coef ﬁcient is de ﬁned
as k′ =C
d/Ci, where k′ is segregation coefﬁcient, Cd is chemical composition of the
element in dendrite core, and Ci is chemical composition of the element in inter-
dendritic regions.

In order to test castability, all of the DS processing parameters were set to meet
industrial standard. The alloy was heated to 1520 °C and held for 5 min before it
was poured into the preheated mold (mold temperature: 1500 °C). A withdrawal
speed of 6 mm/min was used. Fluoroscopic examination was carried out on the
samples to reveal macro and micro cracks. Each alloy was used for 6 blades ’
casting.
Results and Discussion
Microstructure Observation The as-cast microstructures of two alloys are pre-
sented in Fig. 1. The microstructures have same composition of phases: c, c′, c/c′
eutectic and carbides. By analysis of EDS, carbides are identi ﬁed as MC type. With
the decrease of Al content, the composition of phases barely changed. Figure 2
shows the quantitative analysis of dendrite arm spacing ( k1, k2), volume fractions of
eutectic and carbides of Alloy A and Alloy B. It can be seen that the primary
dendrite arm spacing ( k1), secondary dendrite arm spacing ( k2) and the volume
fraction of carbides slightly decreased as the decrease of Al content, while the
volume fraction of the c/c′ eutectic in the interdendritic region decreased signi ﬁ-
cantly in Alloy B. Since Al is generally considered as a eutectic forming element, it
can be explained the noticeable decrease of c/c′ eutectic in the low Al content alloy.
Figure 3 shows the typical microstructures of the two experimental alloys after
heat treatment. It can be seen that the c/c′ eutectic dissolve completely after heat
treatment. Alloy A contains nearly 62% cubic shape c′ phase embedded in c matrix
while the volume fraction of c′ in Alloy B is about 59%. The average c′ phase sizes
of two alloys are 0.51 and 0.45 µm, respectively. The volume fraction and size of c′
phase particles becomes small with decreasing Al content.

## Page 683

Mechanical Properties The tensile properties of Alloy A and Alloy B at room
temperature are shown in Table 2. It can be seen that the yield strength, tensile
strength, elongation and contraction of area all slightly decreased in low Al content
alloy. The difference of tensile properties of Alloy A and Alloy B can mostly be
attributed to the change of microstructure. The Ni-based DS superalloy is mainly
strengthened by hard c′ precipitates. The tensile property of superalloy is strongly
affected by the volume fraction and size of c′ phase. The volume fraction decrease
and the size of c′ phase particles becomes smaller with decreasing Al content.
Therefore, the tensile property of Alloy A is better than that of Alloy B at room
temperature.
The stress rupture properties of two alloys aged at 980 °C and 235 MPa are
shown in Table 3. It can be seen that the stress rupture life decreased signi ﬁcantly
with decreasing Al content. Both of the experimental alloys contain more than half
fraction c′ precipitates as the second phase particle. Hard c′ precipitates can inhibit
the dislocation motion at high temperature and result in the strengthening effect.
Thus, when the volume fraction of c′ phase was reduced in low Al content alloy, the
stress rupture life decreased accordingly.
Solidiﬁcation Characteristics of Alloys The effect of Al on thermo-physical
properties and high-temperature transformations was investigated by DSC instru-
ment. The DSC heating curves of two alloys are displayed in Fig. 4. The initial c′

peak of the ﬁnal temperature difference is named as the liquidus temperature of
alloy (T liquidus). The endothermic peak next to the T liquidus is identi ﬁed as the
carbides transformation temperature (T carbide). The solidus temperature of alloy
(Tsolidus) is described by extrapolation of the onset temperature of the liquidus. The

## Page 685

the ﬁnal period of solidi ﬁcation in both alloys. The change of remaining liquid
volume fraction will led to the formation of shrinkage strain. If the strain cannot be
accommodated by elastic and plastic deformation of the alloy, hot tearing will
occur.
Speciﬁcally, the change of liquid volume fraction within DT
CTR, df/dT, is
believed to have direct correspondence with hot cracking tendency. The higher df/
dT date represents a higher hot cracking tendency since this parameter determines
the strain and the strain rate during solidi ﬁcation. The reason is that during the
critical temperature range ( DT
CTR), the solid fraction is high enough to prevent
feeding and to allow the development of stresses. The df/dT dates were calculated
as 0.61%/°C in Alloy A and 0.57%/°C in Alloy B according to Fig. 5. This indi-
cates that the Alloy B suffer from a little lower strain and strain rate than Alloy A at
the end of solidi ﬁcation.
Another important factor which can in ﬂuence hot cracking tendency is the
dendrite arm cohesion strength during the ﬁnal solidi ﬁcation process [ 14]. It has
been proved that the signi ﬁcantly reduce of dendritic arm spacing would provide a
stronger cohesion strength, which is bene ﬁcial to improve the castability of the
alloy. While in our study, the in ﬂuence in indendrite arm cohesion strength caused
by the change of dendritic arm spacing can be nearly ignored, since it has been
shown that the dendritic arm spacing did not changing dramatically with the
decrease of Al content (Fig. 2).
On the other hand, the distribution form of the residual liquid during the ﬁnal
stages of solidi ﬁcation is another key factor which can also effect the dendrite arm
cohesion strength. It is generally considered when solid fraction incresed above
90%, the solidi ﬁcation process reached the last stage [ 15]. Thus, isothermal
solidiﬁcation microstructures at 1330 and 1310 °C were chosen as the typical forms
of the ﬁnal stages of solidi ﬁcation about two experimental alloys, according to
Fig. 5. Detailed SEM analysis of the remaining liquids is shown in Fig. 6. The
remaining liquids are all signed by colors. It is apparently that the remaining liquid
is much more continuous in Alloy B than in Alloy A at the ﬁnal solidi ﬁcation
process (Fig. 6c), and the liquid still presents a thin continuous network form at a
very low temperature (Fig. 6d). At the end of solidi ﬁcation, the dendrite arms begin
to contact. If the residual liquid exists between the approaching dendrite arms, the
bridging of the arms will be prevented. The continuous residual liquid ﬁlm even can
completely separate the dendrite arms. The more continuous residual liquid means
smaller dendrite arm bridging area and lower cohesion strength. Since the thin
residual liquid is hardly to feed, the smaller cohesion strength in low Al content
alloy can led to higher hot tearing tendency.
Figure 7 shows the value of segregation coef ﬁcient k′ after completely solidi ﬁed
of two alloys. It can be seen that elements such as Al, Ti, Cr, Mo and Ta all tend to
segregate towards the interdendritic regions as indicated by their k ′ less than 1,
while Co and W all tend to segregate towards the dendrite core region and Ni tends

## Page 687

to uniformly distributed in alloys. That result is a little different from some other
researches [ 16, 17]. The segregation degree of Cr, Mo and W decrease with
decreasing Al content, while other elements as Co, Al and Ta are more likely to
segregate towards the interdendritic regions in Alloy B. The segregation behavior of
Ni and Ti is barely in ﬂuenced by the change of Al content. Elements such as Al and
Ta are generally considered as the forming elements of low melting point phase
solidiﬁed within the interdendritic regions. The higher segregation degree of these
elements in Alloy B would lead to certain amount of low melting point liquid exist
in front of dendrite arms, which can cause the formation of the continuous liquid
ﬁlm during the ﬁnal solidiﬁcation processing. This is just consistent with the above
microstructure observation. It is reasonable that the enhanced segregation of
low-melting phase forming elements due to the decrease of Al content led to the
formation of the detrimental thin liquid ﬁlm in Alloy B at the end of solidi ﬁcation,
and then the smaller cohesion strength and higher hot tearing tendency.
Castability Tests All the blades made of shown no crack under the ﬂuoroscopic
examination. However, all six blades cast by Alloy B alloy were observed several
cracks. The typical macro- and microstructure of crack in Alloy B blade are shown
in Fig. 8. It can be obtained that the cracks are hot cracks, which means that the
castability is getting worse with the decrease of Al content. We already found that
the decrease of Al can lead to little lower solidifying stress and smaller cohesion
strength. It seems that the cohesion strength has major in ﬂuence on hot tearing
tendency than solidifying stress in experimental alloys. The reduced cohesion
strength caused by the lower Al content leads to the bad castability in Alloy B.

## Page 688

Conclusions
1. The change of Al content can affect the microstructure in the alloy. The dendrite
arm spacing and volume fraction of carbides slightly decrease while the volume
fraction of the c/c′ eutectic decreases distinctly as the decrease of Al content.
2. With the decrease of Al, the tensile properties at room-temperature slightly
reduce while the stress rupture life decreases signi ﬁcantly at 980 °C/235 MPa.
3. The solidi ﬁcation and segregation behavior of the alloy change when Al content
decreases to 4.58 wt%. During the solidi ﬁcation, the change of liquid volume
fraction within DTCTR slightly reduces, and the residual liquids are more
inclined to remain thin continuous network form. The segregation degree of Cr,
Mo and W decreases with decreasing Al content, while Co, Al and Ta are more
likely to segregate towards the interdendritic regions in low Al alloy.
4. The castability of the alloy is getting worse when Al content decreases to 4.58
wt%. The reduced cohesion strength caused by the decrease of Al content is the
principal reason. Therefore, in order to ensure the quality and higher quali ﬁed
rate of turbine blades, it is better to raise the aluminum proportion when
preparing raw materials.

Abstract Ni-based superalloy HGH163 wire was studied in this paper. The
microstructure and properties of HGH163 wire subjected to different solution
treatments were investigated by the mechanical properties testing, metallographic
microscope and scanning electron microscope analysis. The results show that the
solid solution temperature signi ﬁcantly affects the microstructure and mechanical
properties of HGH163 alloy. With the increase of heat treatment temperature, the
tensile strength decreased, the plastic deformation of grains increased signi ﬁcantly,
changing from the deformed grain to equiaxed ones.
Keywords HGH163
/C1Microstructure /C1Mechanical property /C1Solution treatment
Introduction
Nickel base superalloy has high temperature strength, good oxidation resistance and
thermal corrosion resistance. It has a wide range of applications in aerospace,
nuclear power, petrochemical and other ﬁelds [1–3]. GH163 alloy is a Precipitation
Hardening Nickel Base Superalloy based on nickel-chromium-cobalt, together with
aluminum and titanium elements aging strengthening. GH163 alloy has a higher
yield strength and creep strength, smaller strain aging crack tendency, and good
thermal fatigue performance, formability and weldability. The alloy is mainly used
as the component [ 4] in the combustion chamber and afterburner of the aero-engine.
The ﬂame tube in the combustion chamber is welded by GH163 alloy sheet and is
usually formed by TIG welding.

alloy welding wire was studied in order to obtain the best material structure and

Experimental Materials and Methods
Experimental Materials The experimental material is made of vacuum induction
furnace and electroslag remelting double process ingot. After forging and hot
rolling, the steel wire is drawn to 3.5 mm. The chemical composition of the alloy is
shown in Table 1.
First, the thermodynamic equilibrium phase diagram, the precipitation phase and
the redistribution of elements in the solidi ﬁcation process are obtained by using the
thermodynamic calculation software JMatPro. The cold drawing wire diameter of
3.5 mm were treated by the solid solution temperature of 1000, 1050, 1100, 1150
and 1200 °C. The microstructures of the samples were observed by Neophot-21
optical microscope and the carbide morphology was observed by JSM-6510
scanning electron microscope. The tensile properties of the material at room tem-
perature were tested on the MTS810.22M hydraulic servo universal testing machine
and the hardness of the alloy was tested.
Experimental Results
Thermodynamic Equilibrium Phase Diagram of HGH163 Alloy The thermo-
dynamic simulated equilibrium phase diagram of HGH163 alloy calculated by
JMatPro software is shown in Fig. 1. The initial melting temperature and ﬁnal
melting temperature of HGH163 alloy are 1300 and 1370 °C, respectively. The
main precipitate phases are mainly matrix c and a large number of c′ phases, and
they also contain carbide phases (MC, M23C6), ETA and MU phases. HGH163
alloy contains solid solution strengthening of Cr, Mo and Co, and strengthening of
second phase of carbide and c′ phase. The carbides are precipitated below 925 °C,
and the c′ phase is precipitated below 760 °C. The thermodynamic calculation
results show that the alloy can precipitate a large number of c′ phases in the cooling
process, and the c′ phase can effectively strengthen the matrix and increase the
deformation resistance of the alloy during the deformation process.

Conclusion
(a) HGH163 alloy is strengthened by solid solution of Cr, Mo and Co, and the
second phase of carbide and c′ phase. The c′ phase is precipitated below 760 °
C and it effectively strengthen the matrix and increase the deformation resis-
tance of the alloy during the deformation process.
(b) With the increase of solution heat treatment temperature, the grain of HGH163
alloy gradually changed from elongated grain to equiaxed crystal, and the grain
size of alloy increased rapidly at 1150 °C degrees and above.
(c) The alloy should be treated at the temperature of 1100 –1150 °C, in order to
obtain the microstructure and mechanical properties.

Experimental Procedure
The Ni-11.5Cr-3.0Mo-2.0Al-1.0Nb-0.4Ti-0.05C alloy with different chemical
composition of Al, Mo, Nb and Ti in the experimental alloy is denoted by 1# and 2#
alloy. The alloy was vacuum induction melted and cast into a rough stretch sample,
which were machined to U5 mm standard tensile specimens. The tensile test was
carried out on universal tensile testing machine. Elongation was measured with
strain gauge of 25 mm measurement base. Meanwhile, the possible precipitation
phases of the alloy were determined by thermodynamic equilibrium calculation
software and the corresponding Ni base alloy database. The metallographic sample
for light (LM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was cut from the blank
sample after pouring, which were lightly etched by immersing in a solution con-
sisting of 10 mL H
2SO4 and 2.0 g KMnO 4 in 90 mL distilled water.
Results and Discussion
Thermodynamic Calculation BHAMBRI and other studies [ 4] have pointed out
that the solidi ﬁcation sequence of the Inconel 713C alloy in the equilibrium state is
L+M C ! L + MC + c ! MC + c ! MC + c + c′. Figure 1 shows the ther-

the diagram, the alloy is mainly composed of c, c′,M

## Page 700

Conclusions
The new superalloy consists of Cr, Mo, Al and Ti elements. The microstructures of
the 1# superalloy and the 2# superalloy are similar in the cast structures, which are
mainly composed of the c matrix and a small amount of carbide phase precipitated
in both the grain boundary and grain interior. ﬁne c′ phase between the dendrites is
found in precipitates in 2# alloy, and no c′ phase is found in the 1# alloy.
1# alloy has high strength plasticity at room temperature, with a good tensile
strength of 658 MPa, a yield strength of 312 MPa and an elongation to fracture of
54.0%. And the strength and plasticity of the alloy decrease with the increase of the
test temperature. The tensile strength of 2# alloy at room temperature, 650 and
760 °C are improved, and plastic signi ﬁcantly reduced, compared with 1# alloy.
The content of c′ phase and the second phase precipitation of the alloy increases, so
that the tensile strength of the 2# alloy at room temperature and high temperature is
enhanced, whereas the plasticity was signi ﬁcantly reduced.

Weld Properties of Haynes214 Alloy
Ran Wei, Qingquan Zhang, Huiyun Wu, Chao Wang and Yu Cao
Abstract Haynes214 alloy should be welded together with other alloys when it is
used as brush seal materials. In the present investigation the welding performance
of Haynes214 alloy welded with GH4169 alloy and GH625 alloy was carried out.
The microstructure and mechanical properties of the welding joint under different
conditions were studied. The results showed that no liquation crack or other defect
existed at the welding joint of Haynes214-GH4169 and Haynes214-GH625. After
aging, the room temperature tensile strength of Haynes214-GH4169 and
Haynes214-GH625 welding joints was approximately 94% of Haynes214 alloy.
The high temperature (500 °C) tensile strength of Haynes214-GH4169 welding
joint was about 85% of Haynes214 alloy, while Haynes214-GH625 welding joint
was about 75% after aging.
Keywords Haynes214 alloy
/C1Welding /C1Mechanical properties

Introduction
As Ni –Cr–Al based super alloy, Haynes 214 alloy is widely used in aviation,
aerospace and other ﬁelds due to its excellent high temperature oxidation resistance,
abrasion resistance and good mechanical properties [ 1, 2]. It should be welded
together with other alloys when used as brush seal material. However, few
researches were done on the welding property of Haynes 214 alloy.

## Page 703

Vacuum electron beam welding is a fusion welding process in which a beam of
high-velocity electrons are applied to impact the workpieces, then the kinetic energy
of the electrons is transformed into heat to melt the workpieces under vacuum
condition. It is widely used in automobile, aviation, aerospace, nuclear industry and
other industries owing to its advantages of high welding speed, small thermal
inﬂuence area and small deformation [ 3, 4]. Using vacuum electron beam welding
method, Haynes214 alloy strip was welded with GH625 alloy strip and GH4169
alloy strip respectively. The structure and mechanical properties were studied.
Materials and Experimental Procedure
The materials used in this study were Haynes214 alloy, GH4169 alloy and GH625
alloy strip with the thickness of 0.8 mm. Haynes214 alloy is c′ strengthened alloy,
GH625 is solid —solution strengthened alloy [ 5], and GH4169 alloy is c″ andc′
strengthened alloy [ 6, 7]. The compositions of the experimental alloys are shown in
Table 1. Haynes214 alloy strip was welded with GH625 alloy strip and GH4169 alloy
strip respectively by vacuum electron beam welding method. The welding joints were
respectively represented by Haynes214-GH4169 and Haynes214-GH625.
The line cutting method was used for sampling, and the sampling direction was
perpendicular to the welding direction. The room temperature tensile properties
were investigated with WDW3100 universal testing machine. The Vickers hardness
were tested by micro-hardness instrument (HVS-10). The morphology of samples
were examined with scanning electron microscopy (JSM-6510) after polished and
corroded.
Results and Discussion
Room Temperature Mechanical Properties The initial state of the three alloy
strips is denoted by S (solid solution). Haynes214 alloy is welded with GH4169 and
GH625 alloy, after that the alloy state is called W (welding). In order to simulate the
actual using environment, the samples from the welding joint and the matrix of the
alloys were taken, and then were heat treated at 700 °C by 2.5 h and air cooling,
which is called A (aging).

## Page 704

Figure 1 shows the tensile property of the three alloys after solid solution and aging
at room temperature.
The results in Fig. 1a shows that the yield strength of Haynes214 alloy increased
slightly after aging. The tensile strength and yield strength of GH4169 alloy
increased signi ﬁcantly, while the strength of the GH625 alloy was nearly the same
before and after the aging. Accordingly, Fig. 1b shows that the elongation of
Haynes214 alloy and GH4169 alloy obviously decreased after aging, while the
elongation of GH625 alloy did not change obviously before and after aging. The
reason for this result is that the strengthening phase precipitated from Haynes214
alloy and GH4169 alloy after 700 °C heat for 2 h aging. GH625 alloy is solid
solution strengthening alloy, when heat for 2 h at 700 °C there was no phase
change, so its mechanical properties basically remained unchanged.
Figure 2 shows the contrast of the tensile properties of the welding joint and
Haynes214 alloy matrix. Figure 2a indicates that the tensile strength of
Haynes214-GH4169 welding joint was about 73% of Haynes214, while the
Haynes214-GH625 welding joint was approximately 87%. After 2 h heat preser-
vation at 700 °C, the tensile strength of Haynes214-GH4169 welding joint sig-
niﬁcantly increased, and Haynes214-GH625 joint strength did not change
obviously. After aging, the tensile strength of Haynes214-GH4169 welding joint
was comparable to that of Haynes214-GH625, which was approximately 94% of
Haynes214 alloy matrix. The yield strength of Haynes214-GH4169 is correspond to
the yield strength of Haynes214 alloy, which is higher than Haynes214-GH625
welding joint. Figure 2b indicates that the elongation of the welding seam of
Haynes214-GH4169 and Haynes214-GH625 reduced.
High-Temperature Mechanical Properties To further study the mechanical
properties at service temperature, 500 °C high temperature tensile test was carried
out for the samples. Figure 3 is a comparison of the high temperature tensile
properties of three alloys matrix at solid state and aging state. Consistent with the
tensile property at room temperature, the tensile strength and yield strength of
Haynes214 alloy increased slightly after the aging while the elongation decreased.

superalloy which has been used for a long time in a variety of military and civilian

In recent years, a number of domestic research structures have explored the
alloy, and its mechanical properties, oxidation resistance, hot and cold fatigue
performance were test, but lack of research of high temperature tensile properties.
In this paper, K423A alloy was prepared by means of vacuum smelting, tested at
750–950 °C with MTS. The microstructures of the tested samples were observed by
SEM, witch helped to analyze the effect of alloy microstructure and phase structure
on its high temperature tensile properties.
Materials and Experimental Procedure
The tensile test bar was obtained by vacuum remelting with the induction furnace
witch was also used as an alloying device, machined to be standard test bar. In order
to obtain consistent microstructure, the test bars were equally spaced around the
casting channel in the process of sample casting.
The chemical composition of the test bars is shown in Table 1.
Results and Discussion
The breaking strength, yield strength and elongation were tested at 750 –950 °C
(shown in Fig. 1). Before the start of each temperature experiment, the samples
were incubated at that temperature for 30 min, thereby ensuring stress relief and
tissue homogenization. With the increase of test temperature, the tensile strength
and yield strength of K423A alloy decreased at the same time. When the
test temperature increased from 750 to 950 °C, the tensile strength of the alloy
decreased from 1050 to 483 Mpa, and the yield strength decreased from 825 to
418 Mpa. The elongation of the alloy increased ﬁrst and then decreased when the

preparation, the organization showed a larger dendrites, segregation is more obvi-
ous. As too much the carbide formation elements, there are many types of carbide
precipitation, in the SEM showed a white block or cursive. Microstructure of

The high temperature tensile properties of the material are mainly affected by the

uniformity of the material organization. It can be seen from Fig. 2 that when the
temperature rises from 750 to 950 °C, the degree of segregation of the alloy is
improved obviously, and the uniformity of the structure is improved. At the same
time, some carbides begin to be dissolved or the morphology is improved.

and the precipitation is about 60% of the alloy quality [6]. MC type carbide belongs to
primary carbides, precipitated from the liquid phase, the same temperature above

results in a smaller elongation at 950 °C, but with the cooling process, the phase
disappears at about 850 °C. TCP phases usually have low precipitation temperatures.
X-ray analysis shows that the main phase of the alloy is face-centered cubic, less
carbide and intermetallic compounds can not be given priority detection (shown in
Fig. 3b).
The main precipitated phases of the K423A alloy were analyzed by scanning

Metallurgical Controlling of La
in a Superalloy
Yong-ji Niu, Hai-wen Liu, Zhi-wei Zhang, Ning An, Yang Gao
and Jian-jun Tian
Abstract In this paper, the burning law of La in VIM + ESR
double-smelting-processing was studied in an alloy containing La. The results
showed that the added La was almost burn out when added in after the re ﬁning in a
vacuum induction melting process. However, when La was added at the end of
smelting and before tapping, La can be effectively preserved. The burning rules of
electroslag remelting slag system of CaF
2:Al2O3, CaF 2:Al2O3:CaO and CaF 2:
Al2O3:CaO:La2O3 was examined, and the results showed that the recovery rate of
the ﬁrst two slag series La was between 13 and 19%, and the burning loss of the two
slag series La was not very different. The recovery rate of La in the slag system with
La
2O3 was 10 –13%, the loss of La was signi ﬁcantly over the previous two large
slag systems. But in terms of the La uniform in different parts of alloy ingot the slag
containing La 2O3 was the best.

Introduction
GH188 alloy is a kind of solid solution strengthened wrought cobalt-base super-
alloy, its developed as an upgrade to alloy GH605, it combines excellent
high-temperature strength with very good oxidation resistance, its thermal stability
is better than that for GH605 alloy, and it is easier to fabricate [ 1–5].
One of the major features of GH188 alloy is containing rare earth lanthanum
(La) 0.02 –0.12%, the high content of La ensure the alloy with excellent oxidation
resistance, and improve the processing properties of the alloy. After veri ﬁcation of
production at home and abroad, the better smelting production process of the alloy
is vacuum induction and electroslag remelting duplex smelting process [ 6, 7]. But
this process, especially the electroslag remelting process without protecting atmo-
sphere the element La is easy to burn, and therefore the stability control of La is a
big problem. The main reaction of oxidation loss of La is shown in formula ( 1). The
oxygen potential of La
2O3 in oxygen potential diagram is very low [ 8], even lower
than the Mg and Ce oxide oxygen potential, and therefore La is easier to burn than
Mg and Ce. The control of La is extremely dif ﬁcult. This paper aims at tackling this
problem.

Experimental Method and Main Production Process
The standard composition of test alloy is shown in Table 1. The high-purity raw
materials were used during the smelting test. The experiment of smelting was
carried out in the 25 –500 kg vacuum induction furnace and 300 kg electroslag
furnace (in air). The chemical composition analysis of the H188 alloy ingots was
carried out and the timing of La addition was investigated. The recovery of La
burning under different slag systems was mainly investigated by ESR.

Electroslag Remelting
Due to Electroslag remelting is in atmospheric environment, The oxidation loss of
La shall be great, It is precondition to master the burning out rule of La in elec-
troslag remelting process to obtain quali ﬁed steel ingot. In the case of other
hardware conditions being relatively ﬁxed, the most ﬂexible part of ESR process is
slag system, Therefore, the selection and adjustment of slag system was the focus of
the investigation.
Main Points of Electroslag Remelting Process
1. Crystallizer: Electroslag remelting was performed using 90 and 200 kg crys-
tallizer. The electrode size and slag quantity shall be adjusted according to the
size of the mold. The electrode rods were respectively U80 and U115 mm in
diameter, and the alloy was made by vacuum smelting.

during remelting was tested. Deoxidation test was to add deoxidizer Al powder

3. The sampling position is in the upper, middle and lower part of the ingot body.
Analysis of ESR Test Results
We have carried out multiple batch electroslag remelting tests, and the results are
shown in Table 2. From the test results, as far as the slag system was concerned,
electroslag remelting occurs in three slag systems, and the La in the alloy had a
large burning loss, one of the reasons is the smelting process in the atmosphere. In
the process of melting, the La of the alloy was consumed with oxygen; Another
reason is that after melting in vacuum, the part of La exists in the form of oxides
and sulfur oxides. In the process of ESR, because of the existence of “slag wash-
ing”, those oxides were ﬁltered out [ 6, 7]. In the three test slag systems, the burning
amount of La was the largest in La
2O3 slag system, the recovery rate of La content
(10–13%) was lower than that of the other two slags (13 –19%). But for the uni-
formity of La in electroslag ingot, adding La 2O3 slag system was better than the
other two slag systems. The other two slag systems show little difference in the
recovery of La. The recovery rate of La was slightly higher deoxidation by using
aluminium powder than not deoxidation. The results showed that aluminum powder
deoxidization can remove oxygen in slag, thus, the burning loss of La in the alloy
was protected to a certain extent.
The La
2O3 slag system resulted in the maximum combustion loss of La in
different tests, This was contrary to our expectation, The original intention of
adding La
2O3 was to increase the activity of La 3+ in the slag, Inhibit the oxidation
of La (formula 1) to the right, Thereby reducing the burning amount of La in the
alloy, But the actual test results were contrary to expectations, this may be related to
the change of other physical and chemical properties of molten slag (such as
melting temperature, viscosity, etc.) after adding La 2O3. The addition of La 2O3 in
the slag system enhanced the adsorption of lanthanum oxide and sulfur oxides on
the slag, thus, the ﬁltration effect of “slag washing ” was improved. Figure 2 is the
metallographic examination of inclusions in CaF
2:Al2O3:CaO electroslag remelting
alloy, Fig. 3 is the metallographic examination of inclusions in CaF 2:Al2O3:CaO:

has resulted in less alloy inclusions, smaller particle size and more uniform

Conclusion
1. The timing of adding La is the key to the vacuum induction smelting process. After
the reﬁning period, the added La was almost burned out. With the addition of La
from 0.15 to 1.6% before tapping, the recovery of La increased from 33 to 81%.
The adding amount of La was linear with the analysis result and recovery rate.
2. Electroslag remelting in three slag systems of CaF 2:Al2O3, CaF 2:Al2O3:CaO
and CaF 2:Al2O3:CaO:La2O3, the recovery rate of La in the ﬁrst two slag series

High Temperature Oxidation
of Superalloys in Steam Environment
Zhiyuan Liang, Miao Yu, Yong Gui, Preet Singh and Qinxin Zhao
Abstract High temperature oxidation of superalloys in steam environment was
studied. The experimental results showed that the oxidation resistance of the
superalloys in steam environment was superior to heat resistant steel HR3C. Only
the oxide scale formed on Super 304H steel was spalled at 800 °C. The oxide scales
formed on superalloys Haynes 282 were composed of an external oxide layer of
TiO
2 and Cr 2O3 and an internal oxide layer of Al 2O3, TiO 2 and Cr 2O3. A uniform
MnCr2O4 and Cr 2O3 formed at the surface of superalloys Haynes 120 and Haynes
625. It was concluded that Cr and Ni improved the oxidation resistance in steam
environment. The penetration depth of internal oxides was decided by the contents
of Al and Ti. Finally, the oxidation resistance index of superalloys was compre-
hensively evaluated by the weight gain, oxide scale thickness and Cr depletion
depth.
Keywords Steam oxidation
/C1Microstructure /C1Superalloys
Introduction
Most effective method to increase the boiler ef ﬁciency and decrease emissions is to
increase the steam temperature of modern coal- ﬁred power plants [ 1]. The increase
in the steam temperature of the advanced ultra-supercritical (AUSC) power plants

will require higher grade heat-resistant materials to support the long-term safety and
service reliability of power plants. The oxidation resistance of alloys is one of the
most important factors for the application in AUSC power plants. B. A. Pint
reported the effect of Al + Ti content on the oxidation resistance of high temper-
ature alloys [ 2]. Results showed that increasing the Al + Ti content in alloys
resulted in a higher weight gain at higher temperatures. V. P. Deodeshmukh con-
ducted long-term oxidation experiment in environments containing water vapor [ 3].
Oxidation attack parameter was put forward to evaluate the oxidation performance
of alloys. However, the oxidation behavior of superalloys is not fully understood in
published research.
The aim of this research is to study the steam oxidation of superalloys and to
gain the oxidation mechanism.
Test System and Materials
The oxidation system consists of a gas- ﬂow controller, a steam generator and a
horizontal tube furnace with alumina tube, as shown in Fig. 1. An internal ther-
mocouple was used to measure and control the temperature of test samples. In the
steam generator, water was continuously introduced at the rate of 6 mL/h, into a
separately heated stainless steel vessel to generate a continuous ﬂow of steam with a
rate of 134.4 mL/h for the oxidation experiments. Specimens were placed per-
pendicular to the alumina boat surface so that they were in a constant temperature
zone and did not affect steam ﬂow to other samples.
The nominal compositions of superalloys are listed in Table 1. Samples were
continuously ground by 240#, 400# and 1000# SiC papers and ultrasonically
cleaned in ethanol for 5 min. Samples were weighed before and after the experi-
ment to obtain the mass change using an electronic balance with an accuracy of
10
−4 g. The oxide scale formed on the sample surface was characterized by XRD

Results and Discussion
Figure 2 displays the weight gain of austenitic heat-resistant steel HR3C and
superalloys in steam environment at 800 °C after 336 h. Weight gain of HR3C and
superalloys are listed in following order: Haynes 120 < Haynes 625 < Haynes
617 < Haynes 282 < HR3C. The oxidation kinetics of superalloys in steam envi-
ronment followed parabolic oxidation law. The oxide scale formed on Super304H
is found to be spalled off at 800 °C. Weight gains of HR3C and superalloys
increase when the steam temperature increases from 750 –850 °C due to the rapid
diffusion at higher temperatures, which provides more ions for the nucleation and
growth of the oxide.
Figure 3 shows the cross section of heat-resistant steels and alloys after exposure
to steam environment of 336 h. Haynes 120 and Haynes 625 show excellent oxi-
dation resistance to high temperature steam. The oxide scales developed on Haynes
120 and Haynes 625 are thin and uniform, as shown in Fig. 3a, b. However, the

environment is much severer than other alloys and steel from the viewpoint of the
thickness of oxide scale. Cracks are observed at the inner oxide layer, which are
parallel to the steam/oxide interface. The thickness of oxide scale is in consistent
with the result of mass change. Compared with the oxide on austenitic heat-resistant
steels, the oxide scale on high temperature alloys is continues and stable, providing
protection against steam at high temperature. This phenomenon indicates that the
oxidation performance of steels and alloys is not only greatly affected by the Cr
content but also the Fe content.
Figures 4, 5, 6 and 7 showed the element distribution of cross section of
superalloys in steam environment for 336 h. The external oxide scale is composed
of Ti, Cr and O. Below the Cr-rich external, Cr-depletion zone is formed due to the
outward diffusion of Cr ions as shown in Cr mapping of Fig. 4. The internal oxide
scale consists of Al, Ti and O. The oxidation frontier is mainly composed of Al
oxide. Also, some Ti precipitates are observed underneath the oxide, as shown in
Fig. 4. The formation of Ti oxides may originate from the dissolution of Ti pre-
cipitates. Ti oxides detected at the external and internal oxidation layers are caused
by the high diffusion rate at high temperatures.
Based on the EDS mapping results in Figs. 4 and 7, the Cr depletion depth of
superalloys was obtained, as shown in Fig. 8. The Cr depletion depth in the
cross-sectional of Haynes 282 was biggest in all superalloys, indicating that the
diffusion rate of Cr ion in Haynes 282 was much faster than that of other super-
alloys. Considering the different composition of superalloys, it was induced that
higher Al and Ti provided more paths for the outward diffusion of Cr ion.
Figure 9 displays the X-ray diffraction results of superalloys at 800 °C. The
oxide scales formed on Haynes 120, Haynes 617 and Haynes 625 were Cr

## Page 731

uniform chromia layer. Therefore, the critical Cr content to establish a protective
chromia in steam also were affected by the temperature and environment. From the
viewpoint of the thickness of oxide scale and Cr-depletion zone, the corrosion
performance of HR120 was better that of Haynes 617 and Haynes 282. Alloys
containing higher Cr content could provide more sites per area for the nucleation of
the oxide, promoting the formation of a uniform chromia layer. Once the protective
chromia scale formed on the surface, the oxidation rate would greatly decrease.
For superalloys, elements Al and Ti were chosen as strengthening elements for
the purpose of formation of gamma prime phase. At higher temperatures, Al and Ti
usually formed as internal oxides Al
2O3 and TiO 2 underneath the chromia layer,
which was also reported described in many papers [ 2, 4, 7–9]. Some TiO 2 also
appeared at the outer oxide layer, as shown in Figs. 4 and 9. The formation of TiO 2
was due to the concentration gradient of Ti between the metal and oxide, which
developed Ti doped chromia oxides, accelerating the chromia growth on Haynes
282. For the internal oxidation, Al and Ti easily oxidize along the grain boundary
because of the high activity of metallic atoms and high oxygen partial pressure, as
shown in Figs. 3 and 4. In the grain under the chromia layer, oxides composed of
Al
2O3 and Cr 2O3, which was related to the oxygen partial pressure at those posi-
tion, as characterized in Fig. 4. The main reason was that the required partial
pressure of oxygen to form oxide for Al, Ti and Cr were in the following sequence:
Cr > Ti > Al.
It is interesting that Ti oxide other than Al oxide was only observed around the
pores at the grain boundary in the internal oxidation zone, as shown in Fig. 4. This
phenomenon was also found at the sample exposed in steam for 4 h at 1000 °C in a
previous study [ 10]. This phenomenon indicated that the partial pressure of oxygen
around the pores were relatively higher than that at the grain boundaries. The pores
at the grain boundary were caused by the faster outward diffusion of metallic ions
along the grain boundary, which will leave the cavity at original position, which is
similar to the Kirkendall effect. Coarsening and aggregation of cavities led to the
formation of pores, especially at the high-angle grain boundaries. The pores at the
metal/oxide interface and the grain boundary is a potential disadvantage for the
application in AUSC power plants, which will be the position of crack initiation. If
this alloy is used, the oxide scale may be prone to spall-off due to the compressive
stresses developed during the boiler shut-down or due to thermal cycling.
Summary
Oxidation resistance of superalloys in steam environment is superior to heat
resistant steel HR3C. The oxide scales formed on superalloys Haynes 282 are
composed of an external oxide layer of TiO
2 and Cr2O3 and an internal oxide layer
of Al 2O3, TiO 2 and Cr 2O3. A uniform MnCr 2O4 and Cr 2O3 form at the surface of
superalloy Haynes 120 and Hayne 625. It is concluded that Cr and Ni improve the
oxidation resistance in steam environment. The contents of Al and Ti in superalloys

decide the penetration depth of internal oxides. Oxidation resistance index of
superalloys is comprehensively evaluated by the weight gain, oxide scale and Cr
depletion depth.

Effect of LMC Processing Parameters
on Casting Defects in Large-Scale Single
Crystal IGT Blades
Wenjin Wu, Jingyang Chen, Qing Li, Lin Liu, Lamei Cao, Xin Tang
and Chengbo Xiao
Abstract The effects of liquid metal cooling (LMC) processing parameters
including mold shell temperature, withdrawal rate and metal pouring temperature
on casting defects of large-scale single crystal blades were investigated by
orthogonal experiments. The results of range analysis showed that with the with-
drawal rate increasing from 5 to 8 mm/min, primary dendrite arm spacing (PDAS)
and secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) were re ﬁned obviously. But the
number of casting defects especially stray grains (SG) in transition region and
helical section increased, because the solid-liquid interface became more concave.
With the pouring temperature increasing from 1550 to 1570 °C, the number of
casting defects increased. Dendrite structure was re ﬁned slightly and the
solid-liquid interface became less concave with the mold shell temperature
increased from 1540 to 1560 °C. Finally, the suggestions were proposed to opti-
mize the LMC processing parameters and control casting defects formed during
directional solidi ﬁcation.
