## Page 734

complicates the control of casting defects [ 1]. An effective way to control casting
defects is improving thermal gradient of directional solidiﬁcation. Previous researches
have proved that liquid metal cooling (LMC) process, of which the coolant is
low-melting-point liquid metal, has some advantages in preparation of large-scale
directional and single crystal blades because of its high thermal gradient [ 2].
Recently, LMC processing parameters have been investigated by numerical
simulation and in castings with simpli ﬁed geometrical shape [ 3–9]. Elliott analyzed
the in ﬂuence of the solidi ﬁcation parameters on the thermal gradient in LMC
process, and indicated that the heat transfer coef ﬁcient between the liquid alloy and
the mold shell was the most sensitive parameter of LMC process [ 4]. Lu et al.
studied the effects of mold shell temperature, metal pouring temperature, shell
thickness, withdrawal rate, specimen size and alloy composition on the solidi ﬁca-
tion process, and put forward that thermal gradient angle can be utilized as one of
the ef ﬁcient analysis standards for the optimization of process conditions [ 8]. Li
et al. combined numerical simulation with directional solidi ﬁcation experiments of
simpliﬁed model blades and investigated the in ﬂuence factors of platform stray
grains formation, and pointed out that higher withdrawal rate could promote the
formation of platform stray grains [ 9]. Previous works of numerical simulation and
simpliﬁed model blades contribute to understanding the formation mechanism and
inﬂuencing factors of casting defects during directional solidi ﬁcation. While as for
the directional solidi ﬁcation of large-scale single crystal IGT blades, further
research into the effects of processing parameters on casting defects is needed with
a view of practical application.
In the current study, the in ﬂuences of LMC processing parameters including
mold shell temperature, withdrawal rate and metal pouring temperature were
investigated by orthogonal experiments with a real large-scale single crystal IGT
blades, which may provide experimental evidence for optimizing the processing
parameters of the directional solidi ﬁcation during LMC process.
Experimental Procedures
A new hot corrosion resistance Ni-based single crystal superalloy with high chro-
mium content, which was speciﬁcally developed for marine and industrial gas turbine
applications, was selected for this research. The maximum dimensions of the IGT
blades selected for this study were approximately 210 mm /C2 70 mm /C2 40 mm.
Three LMC processing parameters including mold shell temperature, withdrawal rate
and pouring temperature were investigated by orthogonal experiments. The values of
different processing parameters for four groups of blades are listed in Table 1. The
blades were directionally solidi ﬁed using three-blade mold by LMC process with
assistance of liquid tin coolant.

## Page 735

As-cast blades were etched in HCl:H 2O2 (2:1) to reveal casting defects such as
stray grains (SG) and low angle boundaries (LAB). Following this, specimens were
sectioned 100 mm away from the end of helical section to observe the dendrite
structure by optical microscope. The microstructure of SG and LAB were also
observed by optical microscope. Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) was
used to measure the value the misorientation angle of LAB and SG. Moreover, the
area ratio of primary grains at the platforms of IGT blade were counted in order to
qualitatively assess the effects of processing parameters on the shape of solid-liquid
interface in the vicinity of platform during directional solidi ﬁcation. Minitab 16
software was used to analyze the changing trends of dendrite structure, number of
casting defects and area ratio of primary grain at blade platforms with the change of
LMC processing parameters.
Results and Discussion
Microstructures of Dendrite Figure 1 shows the dendrite structure of blades
solidiﬁed at four processing conditions. It can be seen that there are obvious dif-
ferences in dendrite structures of four groups of blades. The values of primary
dendrite arm spacing (PDAS) and secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) are
listed in Table 2. Figure 2 presents the main effect plots of three processing
parameters on PDAS and SDAS, respectively, from which the variation trend of
dendrite structures with the change of processing parameters can be concluded. It
can be seen that the in ﬂuence of withdrawal rate was much greater than that of mold
shell temperature and pouring temperature. With the withdrawal rate increasing
from 5 to 8 mm/min, the dendrite structures including PDAS and SDAS were
reﬁned obviously, which is consistent with the most widely accepted models
originally proposed by Hunt, Kurz and Fisher [ 10, 11] (Eqs. 1 and 2). PDAS shows
a slightly decrease with the increasing of mold shell temperature and pouring
temperature, it may because the thermal gradient ( G) increased with the increasing
of mold shell temperature and pouring temperature.

Formation of LAB and SG The types of casting defects observed in this study
were mainly stray grains (SG) and low angle boundaries (LAB). It should be noted
that because of the set of grain continuator, no SG was observed at the platform of
blades. Figure 3 shows the morphology of LAB formed at blade platform. The
result of EBSD shows that the misorientation angle of LAB is about 3°. The
differences of thermomechanical stresses between dendrites from grain continuator
and the airfoil lead to small plastic deformation during solidi ﬁcation process,
therefore LAB have inevitably arisen at blade platform [ 12]. Figure 4 shows the
morphology of SG formed at transition section. The result of EBSD shows that the
misorientation angle of SG is more than 22°.
The number of casting defects including LAB and SG of IGT blades solidi ﬁed at
four processing conditions are shown in Fig. 5, which shows that four groups of
blades have signi ﬁcant differences in the level of casting defects. Figure 6 presents
the main effect plots of three processing parameters on the number of casting
defects, from which it can be seen that the number of casting defects increased
sharply with withdrawal rate increasing from 5 to 8 mm/min. With pouring tem-
perature increasing from 1550 to 1570 °C, the number of casting defects also
increased slightly, while change in pouring temperature has no signi ﬁcant effects.
Guo et al. reported that the critical withdrawal rate of LMC processing shall not
exceed 9 mm/min, otherwise, SG may form in the helical section or platform [ 13].
Given that the liquid metal coolant was Ga –In–Sn liquid alloy in their study, of

conducted by Lu showed that the temperature of alloy melt tended to be steady ten
minutes after pouring [ 8]. While the resting time in this study was only three
minutes. The temperature of alloy melt was unstable when withdrawing began,
which may increase the risk of formation of casting defects. The resting time after
pouring may have noticeable effect on the formation of casting defects, further
study should be conducted in subsequent research.

Shape of Solid-Liquid Interface As seen in Fig. 7, the primary grains show
signiﬁcant differences at different processing conditions, which indicated that the
shape of solid-liquid interface was under the in ﬂuence of processing conditions. It is
not difﬁcult to understand that higher area ratio of primary grain represents a less
concave solid-liquid interface. According to the main effect plots (Fig. 8), the shape
of solid-liquid interface became more concave at higher withdrawal rate, while
higher mold shell temperature reversed this effect. Previous work has shown that
the shape of solid-liquid interface become more concave at higher withdrawal rate
[14], beyond that the time of secondary dendrites branching to the platform ends
reduced at higher withdrawal rate [ 9]. The shape of solid-liquid interface became
less concave at higher mold shell temperature, which may be due to the fact that the
branching of secondary dendrites from grain continuators were suppressed at higher
mold shell temperature, so there was suf ﬁcient time for primary grains branching to
platform ends. The result of numerical simulation conducted by Lu indicated that
the change of pouring temperature only affected the solidi ﬁcation of the initial part
of casting, whereas had little in ﬂuence on the subsequent solidi ﬁcation process [ 8].

## Page 740

The platform solidi ﬁed at the later stages of the whole solidi ﬁcation process, which
means that pouring temperature has negligible effect on the shape of solid-liquid
interface near blade platform.
Optimization of Processing Parameters Based on the above analysis, some
suggestions can be proposed from the perspective of reducing casting defects.
Firstly, in order to control casting defects to a low level and obtain a less concave
solid-liquid interface, lower withdrawal rate and metal pouring temperature as well
as higher mold shell temperature should be set in the directional solidi ﬁcation of
large-scale single crystal IGT blades. What is more, the resting time of liquid alloy
after pouring should be prolonged to ensure that a stable temperature of liquid alloy
can be reached.
Conclusions
(1) Primary dendrite arm spacing(PDAS) and secondary dendrite arm spacing
(SDAS) of the airfoil are obviously re ﬁned with the increasing of withdrawal
rate, the increasing of mold shell temperature and pouring temperature to cause
a high thermal gradient, and hence to re ﬁne PDAS.
(2) The number of casting defects tend to increase at higher withdrawal rate and
pouring temperature, whereas change in mold shell temperature has little effect.
(3) The shape of solid-liquid interface becomes more concave at higher withdrawal
rate, while higher mold shell temperature causes inverse effect.
(4) In order to control casting defects of large-scale IGT blades, appropriate lower
withdrawal rate and pouring temperature as well as higher mold shell tem-
perature should be set during LMC directional solidi ﬁcation.

Formation Mechanism of Oxide Scales
Grown on X10CrAlSi18 and 310S
Heat-Resistant Stainless Steels Under
High Temperature in Air
Yuqing Zhou, Dening Zou, Wei Zhang, Yingbo Zhang and Lei Du
Abstract To promote the application of resource-saving heat-resistant stainless
steels, the study on high temperature oxidation behavior and oxide-scales formation
mechanism of X10CrAlSi18 ferritic heat-resistant stainless steels (FHSSs) and
310S austenitic heat-resistant stainless steels (AHSSs) was carried out in air up to
140 h, and the microstructure of oxide scales, oxidation kinetics and thermody-
namics theories, and the classical hypothesis of the third-element effect analyzed.
The results showed that the cost-effective X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs presented good
oxidation resistance at 800 and 900 °C due to the compact multicomponent oxide
scales composed of Al
2O3,C r 2O3, MnCr 2O4 and MnFe 2O4 and good adhesion to
the matrix. However, the oxidation resistance of the alloy at 1000 °C was deteri-
orated, which is mainly due to the non-protective Fe
2O3. The oxide scales of 310S
AHSSs containing Cr 2O3, MnCr 2O4 and inner SiO 2 exhibited good oxidation
resistance, while the internal oxidation of silicon weakened the adhesion to the
substrate.

Introduction
AHSSs have been widely used in power plants [ 1] due to good oxidation and creep
resistance and comprehensive mechanical properties. However, the tight supply and
expensive price of nickel resource make AHSSs uneconomical [ 2], so cost-effective
FHSSs have gradually replaced AHSSs in some applications of high temperature
ﬁelds due to high thermal conductivity, low linear expansion coef ﬁcient and good
mechanical strength and formability [ 3–5]. Nowadays, 310S AHSSs as the main
boiler-pipeline alloys have been widely used in power plants [ 6], and previous
studies [ 7–9] show that FHSSs which contain Al and Si synergizing with Cr may
exhibit extremely good oxidation resistance, so we attempt to substitute 310S
AHSSs by nickel-free X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs with lower Cr content and some Al and
Si elements.
High temperature oxidation resistance of heat-resistant steels is one of the
principal properties applied in power generation, and the key to obtain good
resistance is to establish an external, continuous layer of slow-growing and ther-
modynamically stable oxide scales. Much work has been done on oxidation
resistance of AHSSs, but the oxide-scales formation mechanism of 310S AHSSs is
not explicit enough and the oxidation behavior of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs is not
reported before, so we comparatively investigated the high temperature oxidation
behavior and oxide-scales formation mechanism of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs and 310S
AHSSs to promote the substitution of 310S AHSSs by nickel-free X10CrAlSi18
FHSSs.
Materials and Methods
Chemical compositions of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs and 310S AHSSs are shown in
Table 1. The specimens were cut from hot-rolling plates with dimensions of
30 mm /C215 mm /C24 mm. The surfaces of specimens were grounded with SiC
water-abrasive papers up to No. 2000 to remove the surface oxide skin, and then
cleaned by ethanol and dried in the oven. The total weight of “specimen + crucible ”
both before and after oxidation tests was weighted by microbalance with a reso-
lution of 10
−4 g to obtain the mass gain.
The isothermal oxidation test was carried out in air by box-type
electric-resistance heating furnace, due to the difference of working temperature
between FHSSs and AHSSs, the oxidation temperature of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs is

800, 900 and 1000 °C, while that of 310S AHSSs is 800, 900, 1000 and 1100 °C.
And the oxidation time both is 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120 and 140 h. After the
oxidation test, the variations of mass gain were evaluated to determine the oxidation
kinetics. The cross-section morphologies and chemical compositions of oxide
scales were investigated by scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with
electron dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The phase constitutions of oxide scales
were detected by X-ray diffractometer (XRD). Then the high temperature oxidation
behavior and oxide-scales formation mechanism were researched based on the
oxidation kinetics and thermodynamics theories and the classical hypothesis of the
third-element effect.
Results and Discussion
Kinetics and Thermodynamics Theories and the Hypothesis Wagner theory
[10, 11] con ﬁrms that kinetic curves of oxidation resistance materials obey the
parabolic regime, which is at the initial oxidation stage, the chemical adsorption and
reaction decide the oxide scale formation, and the diffusion of solutes through the
substrate to scale-metal interface mainly by grain-boundary diffusion is important in
determining the compositions of oxide scales under this situation [ 12]. Then at the
oxide scale growth stage, oxidation is controlled by the migration of solutes across
oxide scales by grain boundaries and vacancies. It can be deduced that the slightly
increased mass gain in this stage is attributed to the lower diffusion coef ﬁcients [13]
in compact oxide scales.
The Richardson-Ellingham diagram of thermodynamics theory [ 14] revealing
the relationship between standard Gibbs-free energy and oxidation temperature
indicates the probability and order of chemical oxidation reactions. This exhibits the
afﬁnity between oxygen and other elements and the possible order of oxidation
products. However, the ﬁnal oxidation behavior also combines with the content of
alloy elements and oxidation kinetics.
The classical hypothesis of the third-element effect [ 15–18] is that an element
with an oxygen af ﬁnity between the basis metal and protective oxide-forming
element can promote the establishment of the protective scale by acting as a sec-
ondary getter for oxygen, thereby decreasing the inward ﬂux of oxygen into the
substrate when the primary getter is removed from the surface regions as its oxide.
Meanwhile, the third-element effect also prevents the formation of non-protective
scale by suppressing the outward ﬂux of base metal, such as iron.
Oxidation Mechanism of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs Figure 1a shows the isothermal
oxidation kinetic curves of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs at different temperatures. This
indicates that the mass gain per unit at 1000 °C is apparently higher than that at 800
and 900 °C, and the weight gain curves present a parabolic law of Wagner theory
[10, 11]. XRD analysis of oxide scales of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs at different tem-
peratures for 140 h is shown in Fig. 1b. It should be noted that the oxidation

products of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs are vary with different oxidation temperatures.
The products are Cr 2O3,A l2O3, MnFe2O4 and MnCr2O4 at 800 and 900°C and turn
into Fe 2O3,C r 2O3, MnFe 2O4 and MnCr 2O4 at 1000 °C.
The cross-section EDS analysis of the oxide scales at 800 and 1000 °C for 140 h
is shown in Fig. 2. It can be observed from Fig. 2a that Al, Mn, Si and Cr elements
almost simultaneously diffuse to external, and the content of Al 2O3 in inter part is
relatively high, the content of Cr 2O3 in middle part is slightly high, and Al 2O3,
spinel MnFe 2O4 and MnCr 2O4 almost assemble in the outer part. This is a
homogenous, compact, continuous and well-adherent multicomponent oxide scale.
It should be noted from Fig. 2b that the oxide scale exhibits delamination and the
situation is complicated at 1000 °C, and chromium continuously distributes in the
outer layer and there is a discontinuous distribution of iron in its interior. In
addition, silicon and lots of aluminum exist in the inner layer. As for manganese
and oxygen, they exist in the whole layer of the oxide scale, and manganese mainly
gathers in the outermost and the innermost layers. This indicates that oxide scale of
1000 °C is divided into three layers, the inner layer distributes Al
2O3 and SiO, the
middle layer exists Cr 2O3 and Fe 2O3, and the outer layer is composed of spinel
MnFe2O4 and MnCr 2O4.
Based on the Richardson-Ellingham diagram, the possible order of oxidation
products of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs is: Al 2O3 > SiO 2 > MnO > Cr 2O3 >F e 3O4 >
Fe2O3 [14]. Combined with the theories and the analysis of microstructure of oxide
scales, the formation mechanism of oxide scales of X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs can be
summarized as:
When the oxidation temperature is 800 and 900 °C, at the initial oxide formation
stage, aluminum and silicon have high af ﬁnity for oxygen among other elements, so
they primarily precipitate from the alloy matrix, however, silicon is much less
effective than aluminum in rapidly developing a oxide layer [ 15], so massive Al
2O3
is detected while SiO 2 was not detected at 800 °C. It should be noted form the
hypothesis of the third-element effect that chromium as for the third-element in

X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs facilitates the establishment of Al 2O3 and prohibits aluminum
precipitating out as internal oxides embedded into the substrate, meanwhile,
chromium with high content also generates massive Cr
2O3. Related research [ 19]
shows that with Al 2O3 oxide scales have low growth rates and good thermody-
namically stability compared with those of Cr 2O3 scales. Then at the scale-growth
stage, the vacancies and grain boundaries of oxide scale offer short-circuit diffusion
path for outward diffusion of Fe 3+ and Mn2+ and inward diffusion of O 2− [20]. The
spinel oxides are more stable than binary oxides, so Fe 3+ and Mn 2+ migrating to
external react with oxygen to form MnO and Fe 2O3, then binary Fe 2O3 and Cr 2O3
react with MnO to form spinel MnFe 2O4 and MnCr 2O4 immediately.
When the oxidation temperature is 1000 °C, the third-element effect is reduced
due to the higher temperature, so oxygen solubility and diffusivity in the substrate
largely increase and solutes (such as Al and Cr elements) rapidly deplete at the
initial oxide formation stage. Therefore, that gives a chance for iron to react with

Oxidation Mechanism of 310S AHSSs The isothermal oxidation kinetic curves of
310S AHSSs at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 3a, which illustrates that
the mass gain per unit at 1100 °C is remarkably higher than that at 800, 900 and
1000 °C, and the mass gain curves almost present parabolic regime of Wagner
theory [ 13, 14]. Figure 3b presents the phase constitutions of oxide scales at dif-
ferent temperatures for 140 h. It is found that the oxide scales of 310S AHSSs is
composed of Cr
2O3, spinal [ 21] MnCr2O4 and substrate FeCr(Ni) at 800 °C, while
the substrate FeCr(Ni) is not detected at 900, 1000 and 1100 °C. This reveals that
the oxidation products of 310S AHSSs are same with different oxidation temper-
ature, only the oxide scale is thicken with the higher oxidation temperature.
The cross-section EDS analysis of the oxide scale at 900 and 1100 °C for 120 h
is shown in Fig. 4. It is concluded from Fig. 4a that a continuous and dense external
Cr
2O3 and MnCr 2O4 oxide scale formed, and silicon assembles in the scale-metal
interface and embeds into the substrate, so there exists internal oxidation of silicon
and the scale is not well adherent to the substrate. Figure 4b shows that the higher
the oxidation temperature is, the thicker and rougher the external oxide scale
becomes and the severer the internal oxidation of silicon becomes.
Based on the Richardson-Ellingham diagram, the possible order of oxidation
products of 310S AHSSs is: SiO
2 > MnO > Cr 2O3 > FeO > Fe 3O4 > NiO > Fe 2O3
[14]. Combined with the theories and the analysis of microstructure of oxide scales,
the formation mechanism of oxide scales grown on 310S AHSSs can be summa-
rized as:
At the initial oxide formation stage, SiO
2 primarily forms in the internal oxide
scale due to its highest af ﬁnity with oxygen, and it should be noted form the
third-element effect hypothesis that chromium as for the third-element in 310S
AHSSs will promote the formation of SiO 2, however, the silicon content is low and

## Page 748

silicon is not effective enough in rapidly developing a healing layer of its oxide
[15], so the effect of the third-element is reduced, and SiO 2 forms slowly and
exhibits pronounced protrusions into the substrate. Meanwhile, massive Cr 2O3
formed in the interface due to its high content. Then at the scale-growth stage, the
vacancies and grain boundaries of Cr 2O3 scale offer the short-circuit diffusion path
for outward diffusion of Mn 2+ and inward diffusion of O 2− [20]. It is known that the
standard Gibbs-free energy of the formation for the spinel oxides is more negative
than the binary oxides. Therefore, when Mn 2+ migrates to the outward of scale, it
reacts with oxygen to form MnO, then Cr 2O3 reacts with MnO to form spinel
MnCr2O4 immediately and a diffusion barrier against high temperature oxidation
constitutes.
Conclusion
Nickel-free X10CrAlSi18 FHSSs with lower Cr content and additional Al and Si
elements exhibit good oxidation resistance at 800 and 900 °C due to dense, con-
tinuous and homogenous multicomponent oxide scales containing Al 2O3,C r 2O3,
MnFe2O4 and MnCr 2O4 and well adherent to the matrix, while the oxidation
resistance is deteriorates at 1000 °C mainly because of the formation of
non-protective Fe 2O3 scales. Oxide scales of 310S AHSSs are composed of con-
tinuous and dense Cr 2O3 and MnCr 2O4, but silicon exhibits severe internal oxi-
dation embedded into the substrate. Therefore, the adherence between oxide scales
and substrate and oxidation resistance were relatively deteriorated. X10CrAlSi18
FHSSs can substitute 310S AHSSs applying in the power plants when the oxidation
temperature is not higher than 900 °C.

Heat Treatment of a New Designed
Ni-Based Single Crystal Superalloy
Yichuan Liu, Zheng Tan, Wenshu Tang, Zhi Zheng, Enze Liu,
Jian Tong and Likui Ning
Abstract The heat treatment for a new designed Ni-based single crystal superalloy
was investigated. The solution heat treatment was con ﬁrmed as 1260 °C/2 h +
1280 °C/4 h, AC through differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) curves and
incipient melting experiments. The aging heat treatment was determined as 1120 °
C/4 h, AC + 870 °C/32 h, AC according to the high temperature stress rupture
tests for samples aging at different temperatures. Results showed that the eutectic
was completely dissolved after solution heat treatment. The c′ phase was uniformed
in suitable size after aging heat treatment. The stress rupture test at 1070 °C/
140 MPa showed the rupture life of alloy after heat treatment was 163.25 h. The
segregation degree of alloying elements after heat treatment was decreased
obviously.

## Page 751

Keywords Superalloy /C1Ni-based /C1Single crystal /C1Heat treatment
Introduction
Single crystal (SC) superalloys were widely used for the hot-end components of
aircraft engines, such as guide vane and turbine blade. With the development of
aircraft industry, the higher service temperature and mechanical properties were
required [ 1, 2].
The main strengthening methods of SC superalloys were precipitation
strengthening and solution strengthening. The main strengthening phase of pre-
cipitation strengthening was c′, which has a coherent interface with the c matrix. In
order to get outstanding high temperature mechanical properties, the higher volume
fraction of c′ was needed [3]. As a result, lots of refractory elements such as W, Mo,
Ta and Re were added into the SC superalloys, the total mass fraction of those
refractory elements was increased from 14.6 to 20.7% [ 4]. But the increased content
of those refractory elements would cause higher precipitation trends of harmful
TCP phase [ 5, 6]. In that case, Ru was added to improve the situation. The addition
of Ru could reduce the precipitation tendency of TCP phase [ 7, 8]. However, the
diffusion coefﬁcients of those elements (W, Ta, Re, Ru) were extremely low [ 9], it
was difﬁcult to reduce the degree of segregation through conventional solution heat
treatment [ 10, 11]. Lots of work has been done in order to reach a higher solution
heat treatment temperature [ 12]. Fuchs et al. designed a step wise solution heat
treatment in order to increase the solution heat treatment temperature [ 2, 4].
This new designed Ni-based single crystal superalloy contains about 10% Cr
(wt), which can improved heat corrosion resistance ability and serve in coastal or
maritime.
The purpose of this study was to develop a suitable heat treatment for a new
designed Ni-based SC superalloy, which has a high content of Cr. The solution heat
treatment conditions were chosen by DSC curves and metallographic method [ 13],
the aging condition (mainly the pre-aging heat treatment temperature) was con-
ﬁrmed by metallographic and stress rupture experiment.
Experimental
Experiment Alloy The chemical composition of experiment alloy was shown in
Table 1. The SC bars of diameter 16 mm were produced in a directional solidi ﬁed
furnace. Then the bars were cut as 4 mm thick semi-circular specimens for further
experiment.
768 Y. Liu et al.

## Page 752

Microstructure In order to observe the microstructure of as-cast alloy, the pol-
ished specimens were chemical etched in solutions which contain 20 ml
H
2O + 20 ml HCl + 5 g Cuso 4 for 5 –10 s or electrolytic etched by solutions
contain 40 ml HNO 3 +5 0m l H 2SO4 +1 2m l H 3PO4 at 5 V/30 s. The
microstructure of as-cast alloy was observed by optical microscope (OM) and
scanning electron microscope (SEM).
Solution Heat Treatment Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was employed
to con ﬁrm the solidus and liquidus of the alloy. In order to determine the solution
heat treatment condition, incipient melting experiments were used to con ﬁrm the
incipient melting temperature. The specimens were put into tubular furnace and
heated to 1250, 1260, 1270 and 1280 °C, held for 15 min and then quenched into
water. Those specimens were observed by SEM to con ﬁrm the incipient melting
temperature and the pre-heat treatment temperature. The specimens were insulation
in the box furnace at 1260 °C for 1, 2 and 3 h. Then repeat the incipient melting
experiments at 1280, 1290, 1300 and 1310 °C. Using SEM to con ﬁrm the incipient
melting temperature of the pre-heat treated alloy and chosen the solution heat
treatment temperature.
Aging Heat Treatment Different pre-aging temperatures range from 1080 to
1140 °C were chosen to ﬁnd the suitable aging heat treatment condition. Samples
were aging at different temperatures range from 1080 to 1140 °C step by 20 °C for
4 h. Metallographic method and stress rupture experiments were used to con ﬁrmed
the aging heat treatment condition.
Result and Discussion
As-Cast Microstructure The as-cast microstructures of alloy are presented in
Fig. 1. The alloy exhibit a typical dendritic segregation pattern with certain amount
of ( c + c′) eutectic occurring in interdendritic regions. Through metallographic
method it was indicated that the primary dendrite arm spacing of the as-cast alloy is
332 lm, while the secondary dendrite arm spacing is 41.9 lm and the volume
fraction of eutectic is about 2.07%.
The typical ( c + c′) eutectic and c′ morphologies of as-cast alloy are shown in
Fig. 2. Through statistical the volume fraction of c′ in as-cast alloy is 54.8% and the
size of c′ in dendrite region is 280 nm.

Conclusion
(1) The solidus and liquidus of the alloy are 1335 and 1375 °C and the incipient
melting temperature of as-cast alloy is between 1270 and 1280 °C.
(2) According to the incipient melting experiment, the pretreatment temperature
and the solution temperature is con ﬁrmed at 1260 and 1280 °C and after
solution heat treatment the eutectic organizations is vanished completely.
(3) The rupture life of this alloy at its peak when the pre-aging temperature is
1120 °C, and the heat treatment of this alloy is con ﬁrmed as: 1260 °C/
2 h + 1280 °C/4 h, AC + 1120 °C/4 h, AC + 870 °C/32 h, AC. The segre-
gation degrees of alloying elements after heat treatment decrease.

Abstract Argon gas atomized Ti –43Al–9V–0.3Y alloy powders with oxygen
contents of 1150 and 550 ppm respectively were hot isostatic pressed (HIPed) at
1200 °C and 150 MPa for 3 h to obtain full density compacts. The effect of
powders oxygen content on previous particle boundaries (PPBs) was investigated.
Results show that PPBs only were observed in the HIPed compact produced from
the powders with 1150 ppm oxygen content, and higher oxygen content promoted
the formation of PPBs in TiAl alloy. SEM and TEM analysis proved that the
microstructure at PPBs was a
2/c lamellar. Oxygen was the a2 phase stabilizer, and
it restricted the a ! c transformation but drived the a ! a2 + c eutectoid process
in which the lamellar formed.

## Page 762

Introduction
Intermetallic TiAl alloys are among the most promising candidates as high tem-
perature structural materials of aerospace and automobile engine, due to their rel-
atively low density, high strength, excellent creep properties and oxidation
resistance [ 1–3]. However, their widely application is restricted by low ductility at
room temperature and poor hot deformability. At present, introducing b phase into
TiAl alloys is one of the main methods to overcome the above-mentioned problems,
because b phase is body-centered structure and has more slip systems at elevated
temperature [4]. Small amount of element Y can re ﬁne the grain size and purify the
alloy [ 5]. Powder metallurgy (PM) is an attractive technique to achieve ﬁne and
homogenized microstructure. PPBs is a typical defect in PM alloys [ 6, 7], however
there is limited investigation on PPBs in PM TiAl alloys. Recently, the authors
found that PPBs existed in the HIPed TiAl alloy produced by powders with relative
high oxygen content. Therefore, the characteristics of PPBs in HIPed TiAl alloy and
the effect of oxygen content were investigated in the paper.
Experimental
Ti–43Al–9V–0.3Y alloy powders with two different oxygen contents designed as
P1and P2 were prepared by argon gas atomization. Then the pre-alloy powders
were consolidated by HIPing at 1200 °C/150 MPa/3 h. The HIPed alloys corre-
sponding to P1, P2 were designed as H1, H2.
Table 1 shows the detailed chemical composition of the TiAl alloy powders, in
which the Ti, Al, V and Y composition were tested by inductive coupled plasma
emission spectrometer (ICP), and the oxygen content analysis was performed by
TC 600 oxygen/nitrogen analyzer. The surface oxidation characteristics of the
powders were investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and auger
electron spectrum (AES). In addition, the microstructures of matrix and PPBs were
examined by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with backscattered electron
mode (BSE), while the phases of the HIPed TiAl alloy were identi ﬁed by X-ray
diffraction (XRD), energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDX) and selected area
electron diffraction patterns (SAED). Furthermore, the elemental distribution in
PPBs was detected by electron probe microanalysis (EPMA).

Results and Discussion
The chemical composition of P1 and P2 powders in Table 1 indicates that the major
elements are almost the same but the oxygen content is 1150 and 550 ppm
respectively. Figure 1 presents the particle morphology of P1 and P2 powders.
Most of the powders are spherical except for a few heteromorphic particles.
The surface oxidization characteristics are analyzed by XPS and AES. Figure 2a
displays the Ti2p spectrum whose binding energy are 454.1, 460.2 eV of Ti and
464.1, 458.2 eV of TiO
2. Figure 2b provides the Al2p spectrum with the peaks at
72.9 eV of Al and 73.6 eV of Al 2O3 [8]. The O1s spectrum is in Fig. 2c which
suggests that there are two oxides, TiO 2 (529.9 eV) and Al 2O3 (521.8 eV), and
oxygen (531.1 eV) in the surface of the powders [ 9]. Quantitative analysis
(Table 2) found that nearly 60% of element Ti in P1 transformed into TiO 2 while
element Al is 70%. The Ti transformation in P2 was nearly the same as P1, but 20%
more Al in P2 oxidized compared with P1. Since the sputter rate is 13 nm per
minute and the elements in P1 and P2 became stable after sputtering for 4.5 and
2 min respectively, the depth of oxides are 58.5 nm in P1 and 26 nm in P2. There is
nearly 70% oxygen combining with element Ti and Al in P1 and P2, and it can not
be pumped out at degassing process. After HIPing, the oxygen content in H1 is also
higher than that in H2, which is 930 and 450 ppm respectively (Fig. 3).
The microstructure of H1 and H2 is black phase with average size of *10 lm
surrounded by gray phase, as is shown in Fig. 4a, c. PPBs only formed in H1,
which is lamellar structure shown in Fig. 4b with colony size of *20 lm. EDX
analysis in Table 3 reveals that the molar ratio of titanium and aluminum in black
phase is approximately 1:1 and the gray phase contains a higher content of element

Conclusions
(1) Ti –43Al–9V–0.3Y alloy powders with different oxygen content of 1150 ppm
(P1) and 550 ppm (P2) have been fabricated by argon gas atomization. XPS
spectrum reveals that most of Ti and Al oxide in the surface of the powders and
the depth of oxidation layer in P1 is two times higher than that in P2.
(2) The microstructure of H1 and H2 is ﬁne-grained near gamma, with c and B2
phases. PPBs formed only in the H1 alloy, which indicates that higher oxygen
content promotes the formation of PPBs. The microstructure of PPBs region is
lamellar structure.
(3) XRD analysis shows that a
2 phase has been discovered in H1, while it is hardly
found in H2.
(4) Titanium is rich in PPBs, while aluminum and V contents are relatively low.
TEM/SAED pattern proves that the phases of lamellae in PPBs region are a2, c
and B2.
(5) Since oxygen is the a2 phase stabilizer, it can transfer the path from a ! c to
a ! a2 + c eutectoid process in which the a2/c lamellar at PPBs formed.

## Page 770

Effect of Solution Treatment
on Microstructure and Properties
of GH3625 Alloy Tubes in Different
States
Yutian Ding, Bin Meng, Yubi Gao, Yuanjun Ma and Jianjun Chen
Abstract The in ﬂuence of solution treatment temperature on microstructure evo-
lution and mechanical properties of the GH3625 alloy tubes in different states (hot
extrusion, cold rolled and annealed) were investigated by organization characteri-
zation(OM, SEM) and performance tests (hardness test and tensile test at room
temperature). The results showed that the mixed grain structure of the hot extruded
GH3625 alloy degraded and transformed into uniform equiaxed grain structure, as
the solution treatment temperature was 1000 °C. When the solution temperature
was higher than 1050 °C, the microstructure of the cold rolling GH3625 alloy was
uniform equiaxed grain, and the solution amount of the carbides increases with the
increase of the solution temperature. The microstructure of annealed GH3625 alloy
in the whole solution temperature range (950 –1150 °C) was fully recrystallized
equiaxed grain, and there were a large number of lath-shaped annealed twins in the
grains. The microstructure and mechanical properties of the GH3625 alloy during
the solution treatment were not only affected by the solution temperature, but also
inﬂuenced by the original states. After solid solution treatment at 1150 °C for
60 min and then water-cooling, the tensile fracture modes of GH3625 alloy tubes
under different conditions was ductile fracture. The temperature of 1150 °C can be
used as the reference temperature for optimizing the microstructure and properties
of GH3625 alloy through solution treatment in different states.

Introduction
GH3625 alloy is a solid solution strengthened of nickel-based deformation super-
alloy with Mo and Nb as the main strengthening elements, because of the good
durability, fatigue properties and corrosion resistance at below 650 °C, and the
good strength and toughness at low temperature to 1050 °C temperature range
[1–4]. This material has found widespread applications in industrial gas turbines,
nuclear power equipment, chemical plants and seawater special equipment pipeline
system [ 2, 5, 6]. It is a key component material in aviation, aerospace, nuclear
power, petroleum and chemical industries [ 7, 8]. Seamless tube is one of the
common products of GH3625 alloy. It usually uses hot extrusion forming tech-
nology to prepare tube blank, and then passes through many times cold rolling/cold
drawing processing and heat treatment process [ 9, 10]. In general, solid solution
treatment is required to improve the microstructure, improve the process property,
and even achieve good overall performance after different processes [ 11, 12].
Up to now, many researchers have done a lot of research on the effect of solution
treatment on the microstructure and properties of GH3625 alloy. Liu et al. [ 13]
studied the grain growth behavior of hot rolled GH3625 alloy at 900 –1250 °C, it
was found that the grain growth slowed down due to the pinning of carbides at
grain boundaries, resulting in temperatures lower than 1050 °C. And the mathe-
matic model of grain growth was also established during solid solution treatment at
1100–1250 °C. Fang et al. [ 14] studied the effect of solution temperature on the
microstructure and properties of hot-extruded GH625 alloy. It was found that the
alloy was mainly grain growth after heat treatment at 970 –1180 °C, while the
carbides gradually dissolved with the increase of temperature. When the heat
treatment temperature reached 1150 °C, the carbide can be completely dissolved. It
was also found that the grain size and the second phase were the main factors
affecting the mechanical properties of GH625 alloy at room temperature.
Sundararaman et al. [ 5] studied the precipitation behavior of carbides in the tem-
perature range of 1000 –1200 °C for cold-rolled state 625 alloy, and found that
when the temperature was 1000 to 1050 °C, the bulk M
6C carbide particles
appeared. Similar carbides were not observed when the temperature was above
1100 °C. It was also found that the presence of grain boundary carbides had a great
effect on the fracture mode of the alloy. Thus, the existing research mostly con-
centrated in a state under the in ﬂuence of solid solution treatment on Microstructure
and mechanical properties of GH3625 alloy, but the change of solid solution
treatment on microstructure and mechanical properties, not only in ﬂuenced by
solution treatment process, but also depends on the solution structure status before
treatment.
790 Y. Ding et al.

## Page 772

Therefore, it is necessary to compare and analyze the microstructure and
mechanical properties of GH3625 alloy after solution treatment in different states.
In this paper, the microstructures and mechanical properties of GH3625 alloy tubes
in different conditions were studied by adjusting the solution temperature, in order
to achieve the purpose of optimizing the organization and performance, especially
can provide experimental data and theoretical basis for a variety of other high
temperature alloy after solution treatment and organization performance changes.
Experimental Procedure
The test material was prepared by vacuum induction (VIM) + electro-slag
remelting (ESR) smelting casting. The homogenization treatment was ﬁrst carried
out and then processed into a pierced billet ( U43 /C29.5 mm) by hot extrusion, and
multi pass cold rolling/cold drawing + heat treatment process of the ﬁnal prepa-
ration of size speci ﬁcations for GH3625 alloy tube with a diameter of 28 mm
5.5 mm. The chemical composition of the alloy is shown in Table 1.
In order to ensure that the solution treatment specimen have the original state of
the same organization, the several samples with size of 5 mm /C210 mm /C25.5 mm
were machined from the hot extrusion, cold rolled and annealed of GH3625 alloy
tube along the radial direction, respectively. The samples were subjected to surface
treatment, polished to remove burrs, oil pollution and other dirt. Then, the alloy
samples of three states are put into the tube furnace for solution treatment at the
same time, the temperature is 950, 1000, 1050, 1100, 1150 °C, holding time of
60 min, Cooling method using water cooling. The samples were polished and
mechanically polished in the original sample and different solution treatment
conditions. The polished samples were ﬁrst ultrasonic in alcohol solution for 5 min
and then chemically etched for 3 –5 min using a mixture of hydrochloric acid and
nitric acid (3:1). Microstructure observation was performed using Axiovert 40
MAT metallographic microscope (OM) and Quanta FEG 450 thermal ﬁeld emis-
sion scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Average grain sizes of the alloy was
measured by linear intercept method according to GB/T 6394-2002 《Metal
average grain size method 》. Dimple diameter was measured by Image-Pro-Plus
metallographic software. The tensile tests were carried out in CMT5305 type tensile
testing machine, the average value of three samples in each group was measured.
HVS-1000 type Vivtorinox hardness tester was used to measure the hardness of the
alloy under different conditions, and the hardness values of the ﬁve different points
were measured.

Results and Discussion
Original Structure Observation Figure 1 shows the original microstructure of
GH3625 alloy in different states. Figure 1a is the original microstructure of the hot
extruded GH3625 alloy. It can be seen that the microstructure is composed of a
large amount of complete recrystallization grains and a small amount of incomplete
recrystallization grains. The occurrence of mixed grain structure is due to the
deformation of the hot extrusion process and the extrusion temperature is not
uniform, resulting in incomplete dynamic recrystallization of a small quantity of
grains [ 15, 16]. There are a large number of twin organizations. On the one hand,
their appearance because the GH3625 alloy belongs to low stacking fault energy
materials, thermal deformation of dislocation cross-slip and climb dif ﬁcult to carry
out, the twin are used as a supplement when the slip is not easy [ 10, 17]. On the
other hand, since the extrusion ratio (6.06) is larger during the hot extrusion pro-
cess, a greater shear stress is produced [ 18], and the lower layer fault energy also
reduces the interfacial energy of the twin boundaries [ 19], while low SFE also
reduces the interfacial energy of the twin boundary, the stress on the metal has
reached the stress required for twinning before the dislocation starts, resulting in a
large number of twinning structures. Figure 1b is the original microstructure of the
cold rolled GH3625 alloy, showing the grains are elongated in the direction of
deformation, the grains are thin strips, and a large number of (glide bands) defor-
mation bands and twin bands are present, with the rolling direction of about 35°.
From this we can see, GH3625 alloy after cold rolling deformation, not only the
grain shape changes, and the structural defects within the grains will increase, such
as lattice distortion, resulting in vacancy, greatly increased dislocation density,
resulting in sub-structure (cell structure) and deformation twins and other deformed
organization are produced to increase the resistance of the dislocation movement,
thus increasing the strength and hardness of the alloy, and dramatically decreasing
the plasticity and toughness [ 20–22]. Figure 1c is the original microstructure of the
annealed GH3625 alloy, organization is uniform ﬁne equiaxed grain, and it appears
a large number of annealed twins. The appearance of the annealing twin is that the
GH3625 alloy tube to form a fault in the annealing process, and then continue to
grow, eventually changes the nucleation annealing twins. With the prolongation of

c As-annealed

holding time, high angle grain boundary migration, resulting in the formation of
annealing twins [ 23–25].
Effect of Solution Treatment Temperature on Microstructure of GH3625
Alloy Figure 2 shows the microstructure of the hot-extruded GH3625 alloy after
solution treatment at different temperatures. As can be seen from the graph, when
the temperature is 950 –1000 °C, the mixed grain structure in the hot extruded state
is gradually degraded and transformed into uniform equiaxed crystal structure.
When the temperature is higher than 1000 °C solution treatment, the microstructure
of GH3625 alloy is fully recrystallized equiaxed grain. It is also found that there is a
strip-like twin structure in the organization, this is because in the process of solution
treatment, the grain with the grain boundary movement and growth, the atomic
layer at the grain boundary at the corner (111) stacking sequence on the surface of
the pile will appear accidentally, there will be twin boundaries and along the grain
boundary angle in the formation of twins [ 23, 25]. With the increase of the solution
temperature, the strip-like twins are gradually growing up. In the thickness direc-
tion, the number of twin strips is gradually reduced by the merging mechanism, and
the strips are gradually widened [ 24]. In the length direction, the twins grow up
with the grain boundary migration. After the twins grow up, some of the twin
interfaces gradually disappear due to the movement of dislocations, and the number
of twins began to gradually decrease.
Figure 3 is the microstructure of cold rolled GH3625 alloy after solution treat-
ment at different temperatures. After solution treatment at 950 °C (Fig. 3a), the cold
deformation structure is gradually degenerated, nucleated and formed a new ﬁne
grain structure, but the original grain boundaries of some cold deformed structure
can also be seen. When the temperature increases to 1000 °C (Fig. 3b), the cold
deformation of the organization basically disappeared and the ﬁne recrystallized

completed. When the temperature continues to rise, the grain homogeneously
grows. At the same time, it is also observed that the number of carbides gradually
decreases with the increase of the solution temperature. When the solution tem-
perature is 1150 °C (Fig. 3f), the atomic diffusion is suf ﬁcient and the carbides are
almost completely dissolved back to the austenite matrix. This shows that the
solution temperature has a great in ﬂuence on the carbides of GH3625 alloy. As the
temperature increases, the number of carbide re-dissolution is increasing [ 26].
Figure 4 is the microstructure of annealed GH3625 alloy after solution treatment
at different temperatures. As shown in Fig. 4a–e, the microstructure of GH3625
alloy is basically equiaxed grains with suf ﬁcient recrystallization, and there are a lot
of wide strip-like annealed twins. In addition to, the high-density dislocation of the
triple line boundary, the bow of the grain boundary and the full recrystallization are
due to the low-level SFE of the GH3625 alloy which twin internal and twin
boundaries can also provide recrystallization nucleation location [ 21]. At the same
time, with the increase of the solution temperature, the atomic activity is enhanced,
the recrystallization activation energy is reduced, and the recrystallization is carried
out more thoroughly [ 27]. The appearance of the wide strip-like annealing twin is
due to the original slender twin strips to be gradually widen by the merger
mechanism, large twins of the interface gradually swallowed the strain area grew up
by stepped out of the mechanism [ 24].
Figure 5 shows the effect of solution treatment temperature on the grain size of
GH3625 alloy with different original conditions. In general, with the temperature
increases, the grains grow as a whole and tend to be uniform. From the perspective
of dynamics, the driving force of grain growth is mainly the decline of the total

Effect of Solution Treatment Temperature on the Mechanical Properties of the
Alloy Figure 6 shows the effect of solution treatment temperature on the hardness
of GH3625 alloy in different original states. It can be seen from the ﬁgure, whatever
the hot extrusion, cold state or annealed of GH3625 alloy, and the hardness shows a
decreasing trend with the increase of solution treatment temperature. The new
non-distorted equiaxed grains nucleate at the crystal defects and grow by con-
suming dislocations around the matrix. With the further increase of the solution
temperature, more non-distorted equiaxed grains nucleate and grow at the crystal
defects, decreasing the dislocation density of the matrix, reducing the chance of
dislocations being pinned by the two-phase particles. It also reduces the interaction
between dislocations and weakens the work hardening effect, which shows the
decrease of hardness [ 10, 13]. At the same time, according to the theory of ﬁne
grain strengthening, with the increase of the solution temperature, the average grain
size of the grains gradually increases, resulting in the hardness of the alloy
decreases. Therefore, the microstructure of the alloy is affected by the solution

plastic deformation, the grain becomes very small, while the uneven deformation of
the organization was caused by inhomogeneous structure, so the dimple showed a

dimples is small, the size is larger, the distribution is uneven and the dimple is

that the dimple is evenly distributed. Figure 7f for the annealed fracture morphol-
ogy after solution treatment, many homogeneous, small and shallow of dimples are
observed. Generally, GH3625 alloy will emerge dimples at different degrees after
fracture at room temperature. The presence of dimples is strongly related to grain
boundaries. During the uniaxial tensile test at room temperature, the grain boundary
plays a role of coordinated deformation. However, due to the limited ability to
strengthen the grain boundary, once the ability to lose, the pores are formed by the
micro aggregation fracture mechanism, where there is stress concentration at the
grain boundaries and the triple line boundary, this process determines the number
and distribution of dimples [ 29]. With the continuation of the tensile test, dimple
and dimple connected together, and ultimately fracture, this process determines the
morphology of the fracture surface. Therefore, dimples were observed in the tensile
fracture of GH3625 alloy under different conditions at room temperature.
Figure 8 shows the variation of the dimple diameter (Fig. 8a) and the grain size
(Fig. 8b) of the GH3625 alloy in different states. After careful observation, it is
found that the change of the dimple diameter of the hot-extruded GH3625 alloy at
before and after the solution treatment (1150 °C/60 min/QC) is opposite to that of
the grain size, that is, the grain size becomes larger and the dimple diameter becomes
smaller. After solution treatment (1150 °C/60 min/QC), the plasticity of the hot
extruded GH3625 alloy was improved, which was bene ﬁcial to the subsequent
processing. Compared with the grain size before the solution treatment, the grain size
of the annealed GH3625 alloy after the solution treatment (1150 °C/60 min/QC) is 3
times, and the change of the dimple is not obvious. This shows that annealed
GH3625 alloy not only has good ductility and strength but also has the suitable grain
size. It can also improve the thermal stability and durability of the alloy [ 10]. The
change of the dimple diameter of the cold-rolled GH3625 alloy at before and after
the solution treatment (1150 °C/60 min/QC) is same as that of the grain size, that is,
the grain size becomes larger and the dimple diameter increases. This is because the
solution treatment eliminates the unstable structure of the alloy, the grains grow into

Comparison of Grain Size and Mechanical Properties of GH3625 Alloy with
Different States after 1150 °C Solid Solution The purpose of GH3625 alloy
solution treatment is mainly 3 points. First, the alloy in the distribution of various
non-uniform carbides (MC, M
6C, M 23C6, etc.) possibly dissolved in the matrix to
get single-phase alloy. Second, GH3625 alloy structure can be suf ﬁciently recrys-
tallized to obtain a certain grain size of the equiaxed grain and to meet the com-
prehensive performance requirements. Third, the role of residual stress was
eliminated in order to continue processing forming. Table 2 is the change of grain
size and mechanical properties of GH3625 alloy at different temperatures after
1150 °C solution treatment. It is found that the grain size is suitable and the strength
plasticity matching is good at this temperature. In addition, analysis and discussion
of the in ﬂuence of solution temperature on microstructure, mechanical properties
and fracture modes of GH3625 alloy under different conditions was undertaken.
After a comprehensive consideration, it is considered that 1150 °C can be used as a
reference temperature for optimizing the microstructure and properties of GH3625
alloy by means of solid solution treatment.

Conclusions
1. When the solution treatment temperature is 1000 °C, the mixed grain structure
of the hot extruded GH3625 alloy is degraded and transformed into uniform
equiaxed grain structure. When the solution temperature is higher than 1050 °C,
the microstructure of the cold rolling GH3625 alloy is uniform equiaxed grain,
and the solution amount of the carbides increases with the increase of the
solution temperature. The microstructure of annealed GH3625 alloy in the
whole solution temperature range (950 –1150 °C) is fully recrystallized equiaxed
grain, and there are a large number of lath-shaped annealed twin in the grains.
2. Both the original state and the solution temperature have some in ﬂuence on the
microstructure and mechanical properties of GH3625 alloy.
3. After solid solution treatment at 1150 °C for 60 min and then water-cooling, the
tensile fracture of GH3625 alloy in hot extrusion, cold rolling and annealed state
is ductile fracture.
4. The temperature of 1150 °C can be used as the reference temperature for
optimizing the microstructure and properties of GH3625 alloy by solution
treatment in different states.

## Page 783

Effects of Ce and Dy on the Cyclic
Oxidation Behavior of a Ni-Based Single
Crystal Superalloy
Jieying Bai, Jianhao Wu, Shuhua Xu, Yanling Pei, Lu Qin, Shusuo Li
and Shengkai Gong
Abstract To understand the role of rare earth elements in in ﬂuencing
high-temperature oxidation behavior of the Ni-based single crystal superalloy, a
high Mo-containing nickel-based single crystal superalloy and the derivative alloy
modiﬁed by Ce and Dy were designed. The results of oxidation tests conducted at
1100 °C indicated that doping 0.022 wt% Ce or 0.042 wt% Dy signi ﬁcantly
improved the oxidation resistance of the alloy by reducing the oxide scale growth
rate and enhancing the scale adhesion. The positive effects are probably because the
doped trace of Dy or Ce can combine with O
2− more quickly and reduce the oxygen
contents on the oxide surface which decreases the oxidation rate. At the same time,
it decreases the thickness of oxide scale which results in the reduction of the elastic
strain energy and the weaker tendency to spallation of the oxide scale. But too high
concentration of Dy or Ce was deleterious because its high oxidation rate results in
much more defects which induce cracks easily.
Keywords Ni-based single crystal superalloy
/C1 Rare earth elements
Cyclic oxidation /C1 Oxidation resistance
Introduction
Structural alloys are frequently subjected the environmental attack as well as
mechanical stresses during their service at elevated temperature [ 1]. In order to meet
the high temperature strength, a high Mo content Ni-based single crystal superalloy

## Page 784

has been developed [ 2]. However, the high temperature oxidation resistance of the
alloy at 1100 °C should be further improved in order to meet the severe conditions.
Especially, under thermal cycling in an oxidizing atmosphere, alumina former
alloys oxidize faster than under isothermal conditions [ 3]. Therefore, it is becoming
increasingly important to develop new superalloys with the combination of casta-
bility, strength, oxidation and corrosion resistances and microstructural stability [ 4].
Since 1980s, the research has been focused on the role of rare earth elements
(REE) in in b-NiAl or b-NiAl based alloys. Fortunately, the result indicate that minor
addition of REE imparts a very strong beneﬁt on the spallation resistance [5–9]. From
the 1990s, extensive work has been conducted to explore the mechanism of REE, and
some possible mechanisms were proposed [ 10, 11]. Guo et al. [ 12] investigated the
effects of rare earth elements Sc, Y, Ce, Nd, Dy, Ho and Gd on the microstructure,
mechanical properties and oxidation resistance of NiAl-based eutectic alloys. The
results indicate that the appropriate addition of rare earth element in the NiAl-based
alloys can re ﬁne the microstructure and grains, improve the tensile ductilities and
strengths signi ﬁcantly at room and elevated temperatures, and reasonably improve
the oxidation resistance at high temperature. Some researches [ 13, 14] indicated that
Dy doping NiAl alloy not only reduced the scale growth rate, but also effectively
enhanced the oxide scale adhesion mainly due to the formation of oxide pegs at the
scale/alloy interface. It is believed that the effect of the REE addition on the oxidation
and hot-corrosion resistances for b-NiAl is attributed to inhibiting outward diffusion
of refractory elements (e.g., Mo, Ta and Re) from the substrate [ 15], suppressing the
growth of interfacial voids resulting from the af ﬁnity of Pt to S [ 16, 17].
Though the mechanisms of rare earth elements in ﬂuencing oxidation resistance
of polycrystalline and coating are widely researched, there is still no comprehensive
understanding of the effects of the rare earth elements on oxidation behavior of
Ni-based single crystal superalloy. The present work examined the oxidation
behavior of a Ni-based single crystal superalloy and its derivative alloys modi ﬁed
by Ce and Dy at 1100 °C, and explored the possible mechanisms of rare earth
elements.
Material and Experiment
The high Mo containing Ni-based single crystal superalloy and its four derivative
alloys modiﬁed by Ce and Dy were melted in a vacuum induction furnace. Because
pure rare metal materials are reactive and easily oxidized at room temperature, the
NiDy (which consists of 40 wt% Dy) and NiCe (which consists of 65 wt% Ce)
intermediate alloys were used to prevent the failure of the alloys. Single crystal
superalloys with <001> orientation were prepared in a directional solidi ﬁcation
furnace by using the bottom-seeding technique. The heating temperature was
1660 °C, and single crystals were produced at the withdrawal rate of 100 lm/s. The
real compositions of these alloy rods are listed in Table 1. Inductive coupled-
plasma (ICP) analysis was used to determine the concentrations of the dopants. Due
804 J. Bai et al.

## Page 785

to the melting loss, the concentrations of REE were lower than the nominal
compositions.
The as-cast specimens were cut into pieces of U8 /C2 3m m 3 from alloy rods with
an electric discharge machine. And the samples were ground using SiC abrasive
paper (1000 grid), ultrasonically cleaned in acetone and ethanol before oxidation
testing. The samples were set in the Al
2O3 crucible preheated to constant weight
and the crucible was covered to prevent the caving of the oxides during the
experiment. The cyclic oxidation tests were carried out at 1100 °C in furnace with a
1 h heating cycle, consisting of (1) ramping from room temperature to 1100 °C and
isothermal exposure at 1100 °C for 50 min, (2) cooling to room temperature in
10 min. With two identical samples for the repetition of the experiment and the
oxidation testing was periodically interrupted to weight the mass changes of the
samples by an electronic balance (Sartorious CAP 225D, Germany) with the pre-
cision of 0.01 mg. The mass gain of samples and spallation of the oxide scales were
both observed to evaluate the oxidation resistance of the alloys.
The surface morphology and cross-section microstructure of the specimens after
cyclic oxidation were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Model
JSM-6010LA, Japan) equipped with energy dispersive spectroscope (EDS) and
scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Model FEI Quanta 200F, USA) with back
scattering electron (BSE) detector. The elements distribution of the oxide scales was
observed by electron probe (EPMA, Model JXA-8230, Japan, the spot diameter is
1 lm) with wavelength dispersive (WDS). And the phase compositions of the oxide
scales were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Model D/Max 2500PC Rigaku,
Japan).

Morphology and Microstructure of Oxide Scale The samples of the M alloy and

which leads to the O
2− diffusing to the interface of the oxide/alloy quickly, because
the cracks can provide short-circuit diffusion channels to the cation and anion. It is
well known that diffusion plays an important role in the oxidation and quicker
diffusion leads to the higher oxidation rate. While the spallation does not occur on
0.022 Ce-containing and 0.042 Dy-containing alloys, the oxide scales of these two
alloys are smoother and ﬂatter, which proves that adding a trace of rare earth
elements can improve the plasticity of the oxide scales. On the contrary, 0.052
Ce-containing and 0.085 Dy-containing alloys suffer severe spallation, the substrate
is even exposed on some parts of the oxide surface, the surface oxides mainly
consist of NiO, Ni(Al, Cr)
2O4 and complex oxides of Mo and Ta. According to the
oxidation curve it is easily illustrated that once the severe scale spallation occurred

Summary of Mechanisms of Rare Earth Elements Effect The bene ﬁcial effects
of rare earth elements on the oxidation behaviors of various superalloys have been
already extensively studied by several researchers. Various mechanisms have been
proposed to explain the effects on oxidation behavior [ 20, 21]. It is noted, however,
there is not a speci ﬁc mechanism always responsible for reactive metals effects on
all alloys. In the present case, the mechanisms of positive effects of rare earth
elements on oxidation behavior of superalloys can be interpreted primarily by the
following theory.
It is well known that the crack is often initiated at the interface between the oxide
scale and the alloy matrix. So the stress of Al
2O3 scale can be calculated by the
ﬁnite element method to evaluate the tendency of the crack to initiate in the different
parts of the oxidation systems. Figure 8a shows the average thickness of Al 2O3
scale of ﬁve alloys after 100 h oxidation which is not the thickness before the ﬁrst
fracture. It can be seen that the thinnest Al 2O3 scale of about 2 lm can be observed
in the A alloy. While the thickest Al 2O3 scale of about 7 lm can be observed in the
D alloy. The simple ﬁnite element model was built to calculate the stress

increase to a certain extent, the voids generated by elements diffusion will increase,
and the interfacial fracture toughness will reduce. As a result, the oxide scale is
easily spalled. Larger atoms, in fact, can move much faster than smaller atoms [ 22].
So rare-earth elements whose atom radii are larger can improve the resistance of
cyclic oxidation more signi ﬁcantly.
Conclusions
Cyclic oxidation behaviors of the M alloy and alloys modi ﬁed by rare earth ele-
ments were investigated at 1100 °C. Some conclusions can be drawn as follows:
1. The doping of 0.042 wt% Dy or 0.022 wt% Ce remarkably improves the cyclic
oxidation resistance of M alloy at 1100 °C. But 0.085 wt% Dy or 0.052 wt% Ce
doped alloy performs poorer oxidation resistance. So single crystal superalloys
should be doped appropriate rare earth elements to improve the oxidation
resistance.
2. In the alloy doping by trace Ce, Ce
3+ can combine with O 2− quickly and reduce
the oxygen contents of the oxide surface which can decrease the oxidation rate.
It also decreases the thickness of oxide scale which reduces the elastic strain
energy of the oxide scale. The Dy doped alloy has similar effect compared with
the Ce doped alloy.
3. In the alloy doping by excess Ce or Dy, the voids generated by elements
diffusion will increase, and the interfacial fracture toughness will reduce which
results in the easy spallation of the oxide scale.

## Page 795

Tensile Fracture Characteristics Along
Different Directions of Laminated
Ti-TiBw/Ti Composites with Two-Scale
Hierarchical Structures Fabricated
by Reaction Hot Pressing
Baoxi Liu, Lujun Huang, Xiping Cui, Lin Geng and Fuxing Yin
Abstract The tensile behaviors and fracture characteristics of laminated Ti-TiBw/
Ti composites with two-scale hierarchical structures along different directions were
investigated in detail. The laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites exhibited the highest
tensile strength and fracture elongation along the longitudinal direction.
Multi-necking and interfacial “intercrystalline-like” network fracture dominated the
fracture behaviors along the transversal direction, which are attributed to the high
strain (e
Ti), low strain hardening exponent ( nTi) of Ti layer, and obvious strain mis ﬁt
at the interface, respectively. The longitudinal fracture characteristics of laminated
Ti-TiBw/Ti composites reveals diffuse necking delaying, localized shear band
transferring, tunnel cracks blunting, micro-cracks insensitivity, crack bifurcation
and interfacial delamination absenting phenomena, which are bene ﬁcial to the
toughening the laminated composites.
Keywords Metal-matrix composites (MMCs)
/C1 Layered structures
Damage mechanics /C1 Fractography
Introduction
Titanium matrix composites (TMCs) have been widely used as structural materials
in the aerospace and automobile sectors due to their high speci ﬁc strength, high
special stiffness, high wear resistance and high temperature durability, such as TiB

## Page 796

whisker reinforced Ti6Al4V composites is employed to gas valves of Toyota
automobile in 1998. However, TMCs usually exhibit low ductility and toughness in
comparison with monolithic titanium and its alloys due to the presence of rein-
forcements [ 1, 2]. Natural nacre has superior strength and toughness, which is
attributed to the multiscale hierarchical structures, containing laminated, brick,
projection, bridging, and network structures [ 3]. Lu reported that the metal matrix
composites with multiscale hierarchical structures may possess superior mechanical
properties [ 4]. However, nacre-like materials are rarely focused on the laminated
[5], gradient [ 6] and network [ 2] composites with one-scale structure due to limits
of experimental condition. Herein, metal matrix composites are paid considerable
attention from ancient times, dating as far back as 2750BC, for applications in
shields, blades and swords [ 7], and laminated composites are potential candidates
for use as modern load-bearing structural components because of its good
strength-ductility and strength-toughness balance [ 8–10]. Therefore, metal matrix
composites with laminated reinforcement structure provide a possible solution to
this problem because they exhibit property gradients that are not attainable by
conventional materials [ 11–15].
Laminated composites display different properties along different directions, so it
is important to understand different mechanical behaviors and fracture character-
istics along different directions under various complex stress states, which is useful
for practical applications. However, most investigations mainly focus on the tensile
properties of laminated composites along longitudinal direction rather than
transversal direction due to the weak interfaces or intermetallic layers [ 5, 14].
Laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites with two-scale hierarchical structures fabricated
by reaction hot pressing have shown to possess strong interfacial bonding [ 11, 12].
Therefore, understanding the relationships between tensile direction and perfor-
mance of laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites may prove signi ﬁcant to guide sub-
sequent theoretical estimation of the same, and other laminated composites systems.
Experimental Procedures
Laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites were fabricated using spherical Ti powders,
prismatic TiB2 powders and commercial pure Ti sheets, as reported in our previous
work [ 9]. Microstructural examination was performed using optical microscopy
(OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi S-4700). Tensile tests with a
tensile off-axis angle of 90° (transversal), 45° and 0° (longitudinal)were carried out
using an Instron-5569 universal testing machine at a constant crosshead speed of
2 mm/min. According to the ASTMA370-03a, the dimensions testing tensile samples
with dog bone shape were 52 mm long and 10 mm wide. The effective gage length,
width and thickness were 18, 5.6 and 2 mm, respectively, the more detailed experi-
mental condition and process has been reported in the previous work [ 16]. Herein,
there are 14 and 45 layers along the effective longitudinal direction and transversal
direction, respectively. A total of ﬁve samples were tested along each direction.

Results and Discussions
Microstructure Characteristics Figure 1 shows SEM micrographs of the lami-
nated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites with two-scale hierarchical structures, which is
comprised of laminated and network structures. In the macro scale, the bright
TiBw/Ti composite layer and the dark Ti layer are taken as laminated structures,
whose thickness is around 400 lm. Herein, the TiBw volume fraction in the TiBw/
Ti layer is about 5 vol%, and the Ti layer reveals many coarse a grains as shown in
Fig. 1b, which is reported in the previous work in detail [ 11, 12], In the micro scale,
the distribution of TiBw is taken as network structure as shown in Fig. 1c. TiB
needle-like whiskers has a high aspect ratio, which plays an important role in
strengthening the titanium matrix composites [ 17, 18].

Ti-TiBw/Ti composites along different directions. Table 1 summarizes their tensile
properties in order to assess the effects of the loading direction. The tensile behavior
of the laminated composites along different directions exhibited a linear elastic
stage and a nonlinear plastic deformation stage with reasonable strain hardening
rate. Their elastic modulus (E), yield strength ( r0.2) and ultimate tensile strength
(rb) reveal slight variations. The E, r0.2 and rb of the laminated composites along

Moreover, the ductility ( d) of the laminated composites along different tensile
directions exhibit obvious variations: the laminated composites tested along the
transversal direction exhibit lower d of 11.5%, whereas the laminated composites
along the longitudinal direction obtain a superior d of 20.5%. Along the longitu-
dinal direction, the laminated composites experience a longer uniform plastic stage.
Along the transversal direction, the laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites exhibited a
high ultimate tensile strength of 589 MPa, far beyond that (546 MPa) of monolithic
pure Ti in the previous work [ 12], which is obtained at the same hot pressing
condition, located in the reported values range from 400 to 700 MPa, and the range
of fracture elongation is about 15 –40% [ 21]. This could be attributed to the fol-
lowing factors: (1) the addition of TiBw reinforcement; (2) under a three dimen-
sional stress a constrained Ti layer can be strengthened [ 22, 23].
In order to understand the fracture mode in the laminated Ti-(TiBw/Ti) com-
posites, the fracture pro ﬁle of laminated composites along the transversal tensile
direction was investigated, as illustrated in Fig. 3. The fracture mode in the lami-
nated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites is explained as follows: (a) shear fracture occurred as
a result of nucleation and bifurcation of shear bands in the pure Ti layer; (b) ductile
failure occurs resulted from nucleation, growth and coalescence of micro-voids in
the TiBw/Ti composite layer [ 24]. It is obvious that the main crack propagates
along the interface between the Ti layer and the TiBw/Ti composite layer as shown
in Fig. 3a. It is worth a special mention that obvious multi-necking phenomena are
can be observed in the Ti layers as shown in Fig. 3b. The thickness of the Ti layer
ahead of the main crack reaches to 580 lm from 400 lm, an increase by 45%.
Also, the thickness of the second stacked Ti layer is increased to 473 lm, far
beyond that (425 lm) of the TiBw/Ti composite layer. Therefore, it is understood
that the Ti layer can withstand higher strain for Ti layer than TiBw/Ti composite
layer. Figure 3c shows the macro secondary crack in the TiBw/Ti composite layer,
which is attributed to the nucleation, growth and coalescence of micro-voids

initiation in the Ti layer is typically characterized by shear band. Many micro-voids

in Fig. 3d. Therefore, fracture and failure characteristics of the Ti layer and TiBw/
Ti composite layer mutually affect and compete with increasing stress along with
the transversal tensile test: Ti layers exhibit multi-necking phenomena and many
localized shear bands accompanied with micro voids, the presence of macro sec-
ondary cracks that are initiated by nucleation, growth and coalescence of micro
cracks in the TiBw/Ti composite layer.

According to Fig. 3, the failure mainly occurred at the interface, which may be
mainly attributed to the obvious strain mis ﬁt between Ti layer and TiBw/Ti layer.
Yuan and Wu [ 25] proposed that interface with high strain mis ﬁt serves as the
source of dislocation nucleation, causing necking instability at the interface
according to molecular dynamics simulation. Kassner et al. [ 22, 26] reported that
the growth of unstable voids is initiated by high stress triaxiality at the interface,
which is attributed to mismatch of deformation between the Ti layer and the TiBw/
Ti composite layer. Therefore, it is not surprising that fracture is observed at the
interface.
Moreover, multi-necking is mainly located in the Ti layer as shown in Fig. 3b.
According to the Considere criterion [ 27], diffuse necking can introduce a complex
triaxial stress state in the necked region, leading to localized stress concentration
and inhomogeneous plastic deformation at the diffuse necking point. The initiation
condition of diffuse necking is expressed as follows:
e
necking ¼ n ð7Þ
Thus the strain at the diffuse necking area ( enecking) mainly depends on the strain
hardening coef ﬁcient “n”. With the addition of TiBw, TiBw/Ti composite layer
reveals higher n than that of Ti layer due to dispersion strengthening mechanism:
nc /C21 nTi ð8Þ
Meanwhile, the stain in the Ti layer is higher than that of TiBw/Ti layer
according to Eq. ( 5). Therefore, multi-necking phenomenon is easily formed in the
Ti layer due to high eTi and low nTi during the transversal tensile process.
Figure 4 shows the pro ﬁle fracture characteristics of laminated composites along
longitudinal tensile direction. Many microstructural fracture characteristics can be
observed in the pure Ti layer and TiBw/Ti composite layer: the pure Ti layer reveals
many localized shear bands (Fig. 4a, b), the TiBw/Ti composite layer reveals tunnel
cracks, secondary cracks and voids as shown in Fig. 4c. Combined with the
analysis of microscopic, void nucleation, growth and linkage are the fundamental
causes of ductile fracture. Tunnel cracks and voids can be easily initiated by the
fracture of TiBw. Figure 4d reveals that the macro secondary cracks are effectively
blunted by the adjacent Ti layer.
When the transversal and longitudinal tensile characteristics are compared, the
obvious differences are attributed to plastic instability [ 28]: diffuse necking,
localized shear bands, tunnel cracks and secondary crack. The tensile pro ﬁle
micrographs of the laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composite along longitudinal tensile
direction reveal slighter diffuse necking in the pure Ti layer than that of transversal
Tensile Fracture Characteristics Along Different Directions … 821

## Page 802

tensile samples. The tensile strain of the Ti layer is similar to that of TiBw/Ti layer
during the longitudinal tensile process, and the inhomogeneous plastic deformation
of the Ti layer can be inhibited by strong interfacial bonding. Meanwhile, the high n
can be obtained in the laminated composites along longitudinal tensile direction.
Thereby delaying premature diffuse necking in the Ti layer is shown in Fig. 4a.
Localized shear bands normally follows the diffuse necking, inclining at an angle
along tensile direction. Localized shear bands are associated with dislocation
motion of crystals at the micro level, which can result in stress concentration due to
the reduction of loading cross section and high-localized plastic deformation energy
[28]. Inhomogeneous shear bands are presented in the Ti layer during the
transversal tensile process. However, more shear bands are presented in the Ti layer
which are uniformly separated into many parts by interfaces as shown in Fig. 4a, b.
That is to say, the interfacial constraint can be found throughout the deformation
process rather than during the necking process only. Moreover, Fig. 4c shows that
more tunnel cracks and secondary cracks are observed along the longitudinal
direction than that of laminated composites along transversal tensile direction,
revealing crack insensitivity. In addition Fig. 4c shows the multi-fracture TiB
whiskers along the tensile direction. According to shear lag theory, TiB whisker
with high aspect ratio play a superior role in strengthening and toughening matrix.
TiB whiskers with high aspect ratio can effectively bear load, contributing to the
multi-fractured phenomenon. According to the shear lag theory, those TiB whiskers
whose aspect ratios are beyond the critical value, playing an effectively role in
carrying stress. With the increase of tensile strain, the normal stress of TiB whisker
is gradually increasing and the multi-crack can easily appear in the interior of TiB
whisker with high aspect ratio due to high stress intensity. During the longitudinal
