Figure 5 shows the fracture characteristics of laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites
with two-scale hierarchical structures along transversal and longitudinal tensile
directions. Transversal tensile fracture morphology reveals that the main crack
propagates along the network boundary as shown in Fig. 5a, which is similar to an
intercrystalline fracture. Due to the network structure and the “intercrystalline-like
fracture”, the fracture surface exhibits a rather rough characteristic indicating tor-
turous crack propagation, which can more effectively toughen the composites than
plain crack propagation. The cross section of Fig. 5a shows that the dimples and
tearing ridge line are bene ﬁcial to the toughening effect of the Ti matrix and the
strengthening effect of TiB whiskers. Figure 5b reveals the torturous fracture
characteristics along the longitudinal tensile direction. There are many ﬁned dim-
ples formed in the Ti layer, which can effectively toughen the laminated compos-
ites. Besides the “intercrystalline-like” network fracture, dimples and ridge lines,

some crack bifurcation phenomena are existed in the TiBw/Ti composite layer,

there are no interfacial delamination phenomena due to superior interfacial strength
and toughness. There is Hutchinson ’s criterion relating to interfacial delamination

where ETiB=Ti is the Young’s modulus of the TiBw/Ti composite layer, and Jint is the

determining suf ﬁcient interfacial toughness to prevent interfacial delamination
failure. Nambu et al. reported that the laminated composites can possess superior
ductility absence of interfacial delamination [ 14]. Therefore, laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti
composites fabricated by reaction hot pressing has superior interfacial toughness
beyond JCritical, which can inhibit the formation of interfacial delamination and
exhibit high tensile longitudinal fracture elongation.
Conclusions
1. The laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites with two-scale hierarchical structures
along longitudinal tensile direction can exhibit the highest elastic modulus,
strength and fracture elongation, The transversal/longitudinal elastic modulus
and yield strength of the laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites can be predicted by
lamination theory.
2. Along the transversal direction, “intercrystalline-like” network fracture occurs at
the interface due to the obvious strain mis ﬁt between Ti layer and TiBw/Ti
layer, multi-necking phenomena is occurred in the Ti layer, which is attributed
to high eTi and low nTi.

3. The high fracture elongation of the laminated Ti-TiBw/Ti composites along the
longitudinal tensile direction is attributed to the delay of premature diffuse
necking, load transferring effect of localized shear band, blunting effect of tunnel
cracks and micro-cracks insensitivity, and absence of interfacial delamination.

Enhanced Mechanical Properties
of Al7075 Alloy with Graphene
Nanoplates Prepared by Ball Milling
and Hot Extrusion
Teng Wang, Yitan Zhang, Guodong Li, Chaoli Ma and Wenlong Xiao
Abstract In this study, Graphene Nanoplates/Al7075 (GNPs/Al7075) composites
were prepared by powder metallurgy and hot extrusion. And the microstructure and
mechanical behavior of GNPs/Al7075 composites prepared by ball-milling and hot
extrusion were investigated. Compared with the unreinforced Al7075 matrix, these
composites possess signi ﬁcantly improved stiffness and tensile strength.
Keywords Ball milling
/C1Graphene nanoplates /C1Aluminum composites
Powder metallurgy
Introduction
As structural material, aluminum alloys are widely used in aerospace, automotive
and other ﬁelds nearly 100 years, thanks to its outstanding performance, such as
low density, high speci ﬁc strength, good corrosion resistance and so on. However,
the rapid development of polymer matrix composites in the past decade, gradually
replace the aluminum alloy in somewhere. Although aluminum alloy used pro-
portion on the decline, in the ﬁeld of aerospace and automotive, the utilizing of ultra

## Page 808

strength aluminum alloy percentage increase year by year. So it ’s necessary to
research the ultra strength aluminum alloy. Commonly, it ’s called ultra strength
aluminum alloy which tensile strength is more than 500 MPa. The traditional ways
of strengthening aluminum alloy include solid solution strengthening, precipitation
strengthening, strain hardening and ﬁne-grain strengthening, which are dif ﬁcult to
obtain higher tensile strength. There are two kinds of common method to obtain
ultra strength aluminum alloy, ﬁrstly using other high-performance reinforcement,
such as carbon ﬁber, ceramic particles etc., secondly designing the structure of
reinforcement.
The introduction, assemblage and mutual effect of low-dimensional nanomate-
rials (from 0D to 2D) with bulk 3D metal matrices have provoked striking interest
in condensed matter physics and material science, to research and transform their
amazing properties from nanoscale to the macroscopic world. The addition of
reinforcements brings in some outstanding mechanical and functional properties
into the metal matrix and the features of interface between reinforcements and
matrix materially affect the performance of materials. It is commonly known that
aluminum matrix composites (AMCs) possess distinguished speci ﬁc strength,
modulus, wear resistance and fatigue resistance contrast to traditional unreinforced
material [ 1–3]. Because of its outstanding properties, AMCs are widely used in
aviation, vehicle, and military applications [ 4]. The attendance of Carbon nanotube
(CNTs) and Graphene in the ductile matrix can result in improvements in strength,
stiffness and other satisfactory properties. Although CNTs and GNPs have shown
great potential for enhancing the strength, stiffness and conductivity of metal
matrices, through complicated fabricating processes, the resultant enhancement
efﬁciency is always much lower than expected. This may be put down to the
agglomeration and damage of structure during processing as well as their poor
interfacial bonding and compatibility with metal matrices, delivering a disap-
pointing load-bearing capacity in metal environments [ 5–7].
Graphene (RGO), an amazing material in today ’s scienti ﬁc world, has been
widely known to the human society as the basic structural unit of graphite. It is the
landmark work by Geim and co-workers in synthesizing graphene from graphite
through mechanical exfoliation in 2004 [ 8], which make it possible to start questing
myriad possibilities for using graphene in several areas of applied technology. Such
technological applications range from the ﬁelds of transparent electrodes,
semi-conductors, gas barriers, sensors, super capacitor, biomedical devices and bulk
scale composites for structural applications [ 9–14]. It is demonstrated that the
strengthening and stiffening ef ﬁciencies of RGO in the RGO/Al nanolaminated
composites is considerably higher than those of conventional particle and ﬁber
reinforcements and are also superior to those of CNT in CNT-reinforced Al matrix
composites reported so far [ 15, 16].
In this work, Al7075 matrix composites are reinforced with GNP that containing
more than ten layers of RGO, prepared by balling, hot pressing and hot extrusion.
During the ball milling process, milling balls of small diameter (3 mm) are chosen
to decrease the breakage of reinforcement, in other words keeping the integrity of
RGO, while a high rotation speed and short milling time are adopted to ensure the

## Page 809

Al7075 particle turn into sheet. The optimized preparation parameters that include
temperature and time, are obtained through long-time exploring. The microstruc-
tures and mechanical properties of GNP/Al7075 composites are investigated.
Experiments Procedure
The raw materials of Graphene Nanoplates (GNPs) and Al7075 powders with 300
mesh in diameter were used to produce GNPs/Al7075 composites in the present
investigation. GNPs with the size of 5 –20 nm were provided by Deyang Carbonene
Tech Co. Ltd., China. The morphology of the Al7075 powders is shown in Fig. 1,
and the chemical composition of Al7075 powder is showed in Table 1.
Ball Milling Al7075 powders with different additions of GNPs (0, 0.5, 1.0 wt%)
were loaded in a stainless steel jar with stainless steel balls of 3 mm in diameter
ball-milled by planetary ball mill. The ball-to-powder weight ratio was 20:1 and the
ball milling was conducted at a speed of 350 rpm for several hours under argon
atmosphere. 1.0 wt% stearic acid was added as process control agent to prevent
excessive agglomeration of powder build-up on the milling balls. Ball milling was
introduced to disperse GNPs and strengthen the interface bonding between GNPs
and matrix (Table 2).

## Page 810

Hot Pressing and Extrusion The milled GNP/Al7075 composite powders were
loaded in a stainless steel sleeve with an inner diameter of 23 mm, kept at 673 K
(heating rate: 15 K/min) for 2 h to remove the stearic acid, and then sintered at
773 K for 2 h under 300 MPa uniaxial compressive force. The sintered specimens
were extruded at 743 K at the extrusion rate of 1 mm/min and an extrusion ration of
10:1. There was no special heat treatment for the composites. For the as-extruded
composites, the aging treatment was carried out.
Characterization The microstructures were observed in CamScan Apollo300 ﬁeld
emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The structure integrity of GNP and
MWCNT were examined by Raman spectroscopy (Renishaw in Via) with an Ar
+
laser wavelength of 633 nm. The phase composition was characterized by Rigaku
D/Max 2500 v/pc X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu K
a radiation. The mechanical
performances were tested on Instron 8801 tensile testing machine with the strain
rate of 2 /C210
−4 s−1 at room temperature. The tensile specimens of 3 mm in
diameter and 18 mm in gauge length were machined from the extruded rods. The
tensile direction was parallel to the extrusion.
Results and Discussion
Microstructure SEM was used to observe the raw Al7075 powder and GNPs with
5–20 nm in thickness, and the morphology of the powders is shown in Fig. 1. The
original Al7075 powder had a near-spherical shape with a diameter of 10 lm. From
Fig. 1a it can be observed that the surface of the Al7075 powder is not smooth.
Figure 1b presents the image of GNPs that stacking together more than ten layers.
The uniform dispersion of GNPs is the prerequisite to acquire the high mechanical
performances for the composites. Figure 2 shows that Al7075 powders exhibited
ﬂaky morphology and the thickness of 1 –5 lm after ball milling. From Fig. 2a–c, it
is found that the average sizes are 46, 17 and 8 lm for three powders of pure
Al7075 powder (a), 0.5 wt% GNPs/Al7075 (b) and 1.0 wt% GNPs/Al7075 com-
posite powder (c), respectively. Obviously, the sheet sizes of the powders decreased
by introducing GNPs suffering uniform milling time. Figure 2b, c show the Al7075
sheets were wrapped by GNPs.
In general, the distribution of GNPs by high-energy ball-milling process, play a
key role on their homogeneous dispersion in the Al7075 matrix. This is because the
subsequent hot pressing, sintering and hot extrusion do not in ﬂuence and improve
the dispersion.

Mechanical Properties The specimens were not been heat treated. The mechanical
properties of the designed sample 1 #,2 # and 3#, were evaluated with the tensile and
microhardness tests, and the results are presented in Fig 3a, b, respectively. It can
be seen that GNPs shows outstanding enhancement effects on mechanical perfor-
mances of GNPs/Al7075 composites. With the introduction of 0.5, 1.0 wt% of
GNPs, the yield strength increased from 172 to 253 and 275 MPa, respectively.
And hardness values increased from 81 to 118 and 137. The increase of ultimate
tensile strength of the composites caused by the GNPs ’modiﬁcation was more
remarkable, increasing from 254 to 347 and 385 MPa. It worth noted that the
tensile and hardness values of the composites in this study were incessantly
improved as the GNPs content was added up to 1.0 wt% GNPs, which experi-
mentally con ﬁrms that the GNPs addition plays a crucial role in the as-obtained
composite. As everyone knows that the strength and ductility of metallic materials
usually exhibit trade-off tendency, i.e. the increase of ductility sacri ﬁces strength
and vice versa. It was found that the elongation decreased from 13.4 to 10.3 and
6.1% with the adding of different amounts of GNPs. The trade-off tendency in pure
metals is due to that both strength and ductility are mainly determined by single
factor, the level of dif ﬁculty in dislocation movement [ 17]. Because of reinforce-
ment introduction, however, factors controlling strength and ductility become more
complicated in composites [ 18].

## Page 813

Conclusions
GNPs-reinforced Al7075 matrix composites with different GNPs addition
(0–1.0 wt%) have been prepared via powder metallurgy route, including
ball-milling, hot pressing, sintering and hot extrusion. The yield strength and
hardness of GNPs/7075Al composites monotonically increase by the increasing
GNPs addition. The 1.0 wt% GNPs/Al7075 composites exhibit largest yield
strength and hardness value, which is 1.6 and 1.7 times higher than that of original
7075Al, respectively. Compared to original 7075Al, the incorporation of GNPs
decreases the composite plasticity. The results indicate that GNPs can be a well
reinforcement candidate in metal matrix composites.

Microstructure and Thermal Properties
of SiC/Al Composites for Electronic
Packaging
Tong Lu, Yan Wang, Qiang Yao, Qiong Wang and Yu Hong Zhu
Abstract The SiC particles reinforced aluminum matrix composites for electronic
packaging was prepared by using pressureless in ﬁltration. The microstructures and
thermal properties were investigated. The results shown that the composites were
free of porosity, the SiC particles were distributed uniformly and which interfaces
were well controlled. The bending strength was less affected by different loading
speeds, the experimental results shown that the average bending strength was more
than 360 MPa. By studying the fracture surface of bending specimens, the SiC
particles were brittle cleavage fracture and the matrix was ductile tough fracture.
The thermal performance test results indicated that the coef ﬁcient of linear
expansion increased ﬁrst and then decreasing with the temperature rising, and the
maximum value is 8.25 /C210
−6 K−1 near 300 °C. The thermal conductivity
decreased gradually, when the temperature is 25 °C, the maximum thermal con-
ductivity was 225.7 W m −1 K−1, and the density was 2.95 g/cm 3, meet the
requirements of electronic packaging materials.
Keywords Electronic packaging /C1Aluminum matrix composites
Linear expansion coef ﬁcient /C1Thermal conductivity
Introduction
In recent years, with the development of electronics industry, and the development
goal of microelectronic devices is to miniaturization, high performance and assembly
of high-density. More and more demands on the performance, system thermal
management, quality and functionality are needed for the packaging materials [ 1, 2].
Effective heat dissipation and thermal matching are the most critical requirements for
electronic packaging materials, those requirements promote the development and

## Page 816

processing of composite materials, provide effective solutions for high-performance
packaging [ 3, 4]. The traditional electronic packaging materials include silicon
substrate, metal substrate, ceramic substrate and so on, because of silicon and ceramic
substrate are processing difﬁculties, high cost, low thermal conductivity. The thermal
expansion coef ﬁcient of metal substrate is not match with microelectronics chip,
resulting appear warping in the use. As a result, these traditional materials are
increasingly dif ﬁcult to meet the requirements of the packaging substrate. SiC
reinforced aluminum matrix composites (SiC/Al) are inexpensive, and have high
thermal conductivity, adjustable expansion coef ﬁcient, high speci ﬁc stiffness, low
density and other characteristics, so that the package structure have high power
density, long chip life, high reliability, light weight and other characteristics, show a
good application prospects in the ﬁeld of electronic packaging [ 5].
At present, there are many researches on the preparation process of SiC/Al
composites including injection molding, pressureless in ﬁltration, vacuum pressure
inﬁltration [ 6], extrusion casting [ 7] and powder metallurgy [ 8]. Qu et al. [ 9]
prepared SiC/Al composites with the volume fraction of 58 –70% by powder
injection molding, and thermal conductivity were 170 –220 W m
−1 K−1, linear
expansion coef ﬁcient were 7.0 /C210−6 K−1; Teng et al. [ 10] prepared SiC/Al
composites with the volume fraction of 50% by powder metallurgy, the effect of
SiC particle size and annealing on the microstructure and properties were studied.
The SiC/Al composites were prepared by vacuum-pressure in ﬁltration and the
interfacial structure and stability was studied [ 11]. Pressure in ﬁltration, including
pressure in ﬁltration and extrusion in ﬁltration, the preparation process is dif ﬁcult,
high production costs and it is dif ﬁcult to prepare a small thin-walled electronic
packaging components. Pressureless in ﬁltration is in natural or vacuum conditions,
the molten alloy with high temperature depends on the capillary force to penetrate
the preform, and get the composite material, the key of this method is the SiC
particle surface treatment and penetration uniformity [ 12]. The preparation of
pressureless inﬁltration is a widely used preparation method because of its low cost,
high efﬁciency, high dimensional accuracy and excellent performance. In this study,
SiC/Al composites with volume fraction of 65% were prepared by pressureless
inﬁltration, the microstructure of SiC composites, the distribution uniformity of SiC
particles and the bending properties were studied, and the microstructure and
fracture morphology were analyzed, the effects of temperature on the linear
expansion coefﬁcient and thermal conductivity of the composites were also studied.
Experimental
The SiC/Al composites which were prepared by pressureless in ﬁltration, the matrix
is ZL101 aluminum alloy and the chemical compositions is presented in Table 1,
and the volume fraction of SiC reinforced particles were 65%. SiC particles are
made into preforms ﬁrstly,and then the matrix aluminum alloy is placed in the
upper portion of the preforms, the entire apparatus is pushed into a tubular
836 T. Lu et al.

## Page 817

atmosphere furnace, and the temperature was raised to 800 –1000 °C in nitrogen
atmosphere, heat preservation for 2 –3 h and cooling with the furnace, take out the
sample and the composite material ingots are obtained after remove the upper part
of aluminum alloy. The SANS universal testing machine was used for the
three-point bending test. The samples size was 3.5 mm /C23.5 mm /C255 mm, the
surface roughness were 3.2 lm, the span was 50 mm, the loading speed was
0.2, 0.5 and 1 mm/min, each loading speed has 5 samples. The microstructure and
fracture morphology were observed by ZEISS SIGMA scanning electron micro-
scopy, and the composition of the microstructure and fracture were analyzed by
BRUKER XFlash 6160. The thermal expansion coef ﬁcient were measured by the
German NETCHSCH DIL 402CL thermal expansion apparatus in the range of
25–500 °C. The sample sizes were 3.5 mm /C23.5 mm /C230 mm, the heating rate
of 5 °C/min. Nitrogen was introduced during the test in order to prevent the oxi-
dation of the sample and the nitrogen ﬂow rate was 60 mL/min. The thermal
conductivity were tested at 25 –500 °C by NETCHSCH LFA 467, the sample sizes
were 7 mm /C27m m /C24 mm, nitrogen was introduced to prevent the oxidation of
the sample also, and the nitrogen ﬂow rate was 50 mL/min.
Results and Analysis
Figure 1a is the SEM image of SiC/Al composites, as can be seen from the ﬁgure,
the material is uniform, dense, no obvious microvoids, the combination of SiC
particles and aluminum alloy matrix is good, Figs. 1ba n d 2 are the distribution
maps of all elements in the composite. It can be seen from the ﬁgure that the SiC
particles are evenly distributed in the matrix and the surface of the particles have an
oxide layer, this is due to pre-oxidation before the SiC preform is impregnated, the
surface of SiC particles will produce a certain thickness of the SiO
2 layer after
pre-oxidized, the SiO 2 participate in the interface reaction and generate Si, the
generated Si can improve the wetting of interface and it is conducive to the com-
bination of aluminum and SiC particles [ 13]. At the same time, the reaction heat by
the reaction between the aluminum alloy and the SiC can cause the temperature to
rise, reduce the in ﬁltration angle, and thereby enhancing the two-phase wetting. It
can be seen from Figs. 1b and 2 that the SiC particles are evenly distributed and the
interface is better, larger size of SiC particles are evenly distributed in the aluminum
alloy matrix, and the small size of SiC particles are ﬁlled in the voids which are
formed by the large size of SiC particles, thereby increase the volume fraction of
SiC in aluminum matrix composites.

with smaller particle size are higher. In this experiment, the matrix of aluminum

The thermal conductivity of the sample is calculated according to the measured
thermal diffusivity a, the density q and the constant speci ﬁc heat capacity C
p by
k = a ∙ q ∙ Cp, where k are the thermal conductivity (W m −1 K−1), a are the
thermal diffusivity (mm 2 s−1) and C p are the speci ﬁc heat capacity (J g −1 K−1),
respectively. Table 3 shows the test results of thermal conductivity. It can be seen
from the table that the thermal expansion coef ﬁcient and thermal conductivity
decrease with the temperature rises, and the speci ﬁc heat capacity decreases with
temperature rises. The average thermal diffusivity is 102.8 mm 2 s−1 and the average
thermal conductivity is 225.4 W m −1 K−1 at 25 °C. The thermal process of SiC/Al
is mainly through the phonon of SiC particles and electron of aluminum alloy
matrix. With the temperature rise, the vibration energy of the phonon increase and
the frequency become faster, the probability of collision increases and average free
path reduce, so the thermal conductivity is decrease. For aluminum ally substrates,
the reason for conduction are the collision between electrons and metal ions, and
then the electron kinetic energy is converted into metal internal energy. According
to the molecular motion theory, the temperature higher, the probability of collision
between the metal ions and electrons greater. So the kinetic energy are dif ﬁcult to
spread farther. Therefore, the reason for thermal conductivity decrease with the
temperature rise can be inferred by the thermal mechanism of SiC and aluminum
alloy.
Figure 4 shows the relation between thermal expansion coef ﬁcient and tem-
perature, it can be seen from the Fig. 4 the thermal expansion coef ﬁcient of material
is between 6.9 /C210
−6 K−1 and 8.2 /C210−6 K−1, which have a good thermal
matching with the ceramic substrate. In addition, Fig. 4 shown that the thermal
expansion coefﬁcient of the aluminum matrix composite material increases ﬁrst and
then decreases with the temperature rises, reaching the maximum value of
8.25 /C210−6 K−1 near 300 °C, this is similar to the results of the literature [ 13].
There are two reasons for the coef ﬁcient of thermal expansion increases with
increasing temperature, On the one hand, due to the increase of the thermal
expansion coefﬁcient of the aluminum alloy with the temperature rises, the thermal
expansion coefﬁcient of the composite material increases with the temperature rises,
too. On the other hand, with the temperature rises, the interfacial transmission
capacity of the composites decreases, and the ability of the reinforcement to reduce
the thermal expansion of the aluminum matrix is reduced, and the thermal
expansion coefﬁcient of the composites increases with the temperature rises. As the

more silicon in the matrix leads to sharp increase in the solid solubility of aluminum

Conclusions
1. The SiC/Al composites for electronic packaging are free of porosity by pres-
sureless in ﬁltration, SiC particles are evenly distributed, the interface is better,
larger size of SiC particles are evenly distributed in the aluminum alloy matrix,
and the small size of SiC particles are ﬁlled in the voids which are formed by the
large size of SiC particles, thereby the volume fraction of SiC in aluminum
matrix composites increase.
2. The bending strength are less affected by different loading speeds, the experi-
mental results show that the average bending strength are more than 360 MPa.
By studying the fracture surface of bending specimens, the SiC particles are
brittle cleavage fracture and the matrix are ductile tough fracture.
3. The thermal performance test results show that the coef ﬁcient of linear expan-
sion increase ﬁrst and then decrease with the increase of temperature, reaching
the maximum of 8.25 /C210−6 K−1 near 300 °C, the thermal conductivity
decreases gradually, when the temperature is 25 °C, the maximum thermal
conductivity is 225.7 W m −1 K−1, and the density is 2.95 g/cm 3, to meet the
requirements of electronic packaging materials.

## Page 824

Analysis of Uniformly Distributed Limit
Load for Circular Plate by TSS
Criterion
Siwei Gao, Shunhu Zhang, Guijing Wu and Jian Cao
Abstract In order to analyze the uniformly distributed limit load for circular plate,
a trial function of de ﬂection with cosine form is investigated by the variational
method. With the speci ﬁc plastic work of the Twin Sheer Stress (called TSS for
short) criterion, the internal deformation power is deduced. ATn analytical solution
of limit load based on the TSS criterion is obtained as a function of circular plate
radius a, thickness h and yield stress r
s. Compared with the available solutions
based on Tresca and Mises criteria, it is shown that the present result is the highest,
but the relative error between the present one and the Mises result is only 0.77%.
The de ﬂection increases with the decrease of plate thickness or the increase of the
ratio of r/a, and the limit load decreases with the increase of plate radius.
Keywords Variational method
/C1 Trial function /C1 Twin sheer stress criterion
Simply supported circular plate /C1 Limit load
Introduction
Circular plate is always used in actual engineering ﬁled, and the research of its
plastic bearing capacity is concerned by many researchers [ 1]. The limit load of a
structure refers to the load leading to the instability of the overall structure [ 2]. On
the research of the limit load of simply supported circular plate, the Tresca yield
criterion does not take the intermediate principal stress into account, consequently
the calculation result is conservative and the material would be wasted in pro-
duction. On the other hand, the Mises yield criterion can consider the effect of all
principal stress, but it is dif ﬁcult to be used for obtaining analytical solution because
of its non-linearity [ 3–6]. To solve the above-mentioned problems, a trial function
of deﬂection of simply supported circular plate is set, and the TSS criterion and its
speciﬁc plastic work are introduced to the calculation of the limit load. Moreover,

TSS Criterion and Its Speci ﬁc Plastic Work
The TSS criterion was established by YU Mao-hong in 1983, in which all the stress
components of the stress state and their in ﬂuence on material yield and destruction
have been considered. The TSS criterion could be used in different kinds of cal-
culating limit load of construction equipment such as thin plate, line pipe and so on.
Its mathematical expression is [ 7]:
ð1Þ
The locus of the TSS criterion is shown in Fig. 1.
It can be seen that at the points B0 and A0, the states of the Tresca, Mises and TSS
criteria are the same. The Tresca criterion is the inscribed hexagon of the circle and
the TSS criterion is the circumscribed hexagon of the circle.
Speciﬁc plastic work is also called plastic work per unit volume, which is the
integrand of the power functional of metal forming. The speci ﬁc plastic work based
on the TSS criterion can be shown as [ 8]:

As is shown in Fig. 4, the TSS criterion could predict the upper bound of the

limit load decreases as the radius a increases.
Conclusion
1. A feasible Ritz trial function of simply supported circular plate under uniformly
distributed load is proposed, and the analytical solution of the limit load is
obtained by using the TSS speci ﬁc plastic work. It is shown that the solution is a
function of a, h and r
s.
2. Compared with the traditional results, the analytical solution based on the TSS
criterion is biggest among the existing solutions of the Tresca and Mises criteria,
and the error between the present TSS result and the Mises one is only 0.77%.
3. The de ﬂection obtained by the variational method reaches the maximum at the
center of the circular plate and equals 0 at the edge. Also, it is shown that the
deﬂection decreases as r/a and thickness increase.

Interfacial Diffusion Behavior
of Thermal Bimetal 5J20110 with High
Sensitivity
Donghui Xie, Jing Zhang, Zhi Qin, Min Yu and Weifeng Peng
Abstract The thermal bimetal 5J20110 with high sensitivity was prepared by cold
rolling bonding process, the effect of diffusion annealing temperature and time on
the properties and interfacial diffusion behavior of 5J20110 was studied. Combining
with the principle of diffusion, the diffusion law of interfacial alloy elements was
calculated and analyzed, and the relation that the interfacial diffusion layer thick-
ness varying with diffusion annealing temperature and time was deduced. The
results showed that the diffusion trend of alloy elements enhanced gradually and the
thickness of diffusion layer increased gradually with the increase of diffusion
annealing temperature and time, and the bonding strength and resistivity of the
thermal bimetal varied little. It is found that the interfacial diffusion layer is solid
solution, and the diffusion layer thickness is proportional to the square root of
diffusion time t
1/2 and e−1/T of diffusion temperature T. The formula for the growth
of the interfacial diffusion layer thickness derived in this paper can provide the basis
for optimizing the diffusion annealing process.
Keywords Thermal bimetal
/C1Diffusion annealing /C1Interfacial diffusion layer
Introduction
5J20110, which is composed of Mn72Ni10Cu18 high expansion alloy and FeNi36
low expansion alloy, belongs to the thermal bimetal with high sensitivity and
resistivity, the nominal resistivity is 113 lX cm, and the nominal speci ﬁcd eﬂection
is 20.8 /C2 10
−6/°C. It is mainly used in the ﬁeld of circuit breaker and relay pro-
tection switch, instrument, thermal protector and thermostat. Our company employs
cold rolling bonding process to produce 5J20110 thermal bimetal. In order to
improve the bonding strength of the thermal bimetal and make it soft, the diffusion

## Page 834

annealing is necessary after the composite process. The interfacial alloy elements
are mutually diffused to form a diffusion layer so as to achieve metallurgical
bonding. The interfacial diffusion layer has a decisive in ﬂuence on the properties of
the thermal bimetal. The uniform and moderate interfacial diffusion layer is ben-
eﬁcial to improve the temperature sensitivity, reaction speed, consistency, stability
and service life of thermal bimetal components [ 1]. Therefore, selecting the rea-
sonable diffusion annealing process to control the interface layer is the key to
improve the quality of the thermal bimetal [ 2, 3]. At present, there is little research
on the diffusion law of thermal bimetal interface, and the diffusion annealing
process is limited to empirical experimental research. In comparison, a large
number of studies have been carried out on the interfacial diffusion behavior of
layered composites of nonferrous metals both at home and abroad [ 4–8], such as:
Cu/Al, Ni/Al, Pd/Ni, Kovar/Cu/Kovar and other composite materials. The research
covers the structure, morphology, mechanical properties, thermodynamics and
dynamics of interfacial diffusion. Based on the research results of interfacial dif-
fusion of metal layered composites at home and abroad, this paper takes 5J20110
thermal bimetal as the research object, to study the diffusion behavior of the
interface, and provide the basis for making reasonable diffusion annealing process.
Experimental
The 5J20110 strip specimens with a thickness of 1.6 mm were taken and cut into
100 mm /C2 200 mm blocks after the cold rolling bonding process. The diffusion
annealing experiments at different temperature and time were carried out in a box type
resistance furnace. The recrystallization temperature of Mn72Ni10Cu18 and FeNi36
alloy is 650–700 °C and 700 –750 °C respectively, so in order to make the composite
thermal bimetal strip soften fully, the testing temperature of diffusion annealing
should be not less than the recrystallization temperature of any component alloy. In
this paper, the process parameters of the diffusion annealing are listed in Table 1.
The interfacial bonding strength of the strip after cold rolling bonding and
subsequent diffusion annealing was evaluated by repeated bending test and inter-
facial peeling test. The 10 mm /C2 200 mm strip samples used to do bonding
strength test were taken along the rolling direction of the composite strip at different
diffusion annealing process. In the repeated bending test, the sample is subjected to

## Page 835

repeated bending between 0° and 90° with the bending curvature radius less than
10 mm, and the repeated bending times is recorded when the joint interface is
separated or partially cracked, which is used to characterize the bonding properties.
The peeling test is carried out on the electronical tensile testing machine. Figure 1
shows the schematic diagram of the sample size of peeling test. The applied load is
perpendicular to the joint surface until the composite strip is completely separated,
and the maximum load divided by the width of the sample in the process of
separation is used as the testing result, that is peeling strength. The peeling surface
should be retained after the test in order to observe its morphology and analyze its
composition.
The surface Vickers hardness of component alloys was measured with HVS-10
type Vivtorinox hardness tester, and the microhardness of the diffusion layer in the
micro region near the interface were measured with and FM Semi-automatic
microhardness tester. Before measuring hardness, grinding and polishing should be
carried out on the samples with metallographic abrasive paper.
The resistivity after different diffusion annealing process was measured by
YD2512 type digital ohmmeter according to “ASTM B63-2007 Standard Test
Method for Resistivity of Metallically Conducting Resistance and Contact
Materials”.
Metallographic specimens were intercepted and made on the strip samples after
diffusion annealing. Scanning electron microscope (JSM-6510) was used to observe
the microstructure of the interface zone of the thermal bimetal, and with the aid of
energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), the line scanning analysis was carried out to
study the regional distribution of interface chemical composition and the diffusion
behaviour of interfacial elements. The thickness of the interfacial diffusion layer is
estimated according to the concentration gradient of the diffusion of the interface
element, as shown in Fig. 2 is a schematic diagram of the measurement of the
interfacial diffusion layer thickness. Six samples were taken from each process, and
the thickness of the diffusion layer was measured 2 times for each sample. Then the
average thickness of the diffusion layer was taken as the thickness of the diffusion
layer under the process.

Interface Morphology and Composition The interface microstructure of 5J20110
thermal bimetal after cold-rolled bonding and 900 °C, 3 min diffusion annealing is
shown in Fig. 3. The cold rolled composite strip is mainly mechanic joggle between
the Mn72Ni10Cu18 and FeNi36 component alloys before diffusion annealing, and
the interface is straight and clear. After diffusion annealing, alloying elements of
Mn72Ni10Cu18 and FeNi36 in the interface diffuse mutually and forms metal-
lurgical bonding, which results in the formation of a diffusion layer with a certain
thickness.
Figure 4 illustrates the backscattered scanning electron microscope photograph
of 5J20110 specimens from several diffusion annealing processes. Figure 5 is the
line scanning results of interfacial composition. The diffusion layer with a certain
thickness is formed in the interface of component alloys, but the boundary of
diffusion layer and the component alloy is blurry. With the increase of annealing
temperature and time, the thickness of the diffusion layer has an increasing trend,
and the interface between the diffusion layer and component alloys becomes
increasingly blurred.

Figure 6 is the morphologies of the peeling surface of the 5J20110 thermal
bimetal after peeling off. It is observed that after the interface tearing, the cross
section is dimple, and the interface is clean and no non-metallic inclusions such as
oxides and inclusions appears. It shows that the whole interface has achieved good
metallurgical bonding.
Figures 7 and 8 are the results of EDS analysis of the peeling surface of FeNi36
alloy and Mn72Ni10Cu18 alloy respectively. From the test results, there is an
obvious interdiffusion in the bonding interface. In the peeling surface of FeNi36
alloy, the main element is Mn, and also there is a small amount of Cu, Ni and Fe. In
the peeling surface of Mn72Ni10Cu18 alloy the main element is also Mn. Thus it is
concluded that the peeling tearing is closer to Mn72Ni10Cu18 layer, moreover, the
interfacial diffusion layer is mainly solid solution with Mn as matrix.

Calculation and Analysis of Interfacial Diffusion Process When the interdiffu-
sion of interfacial alloy elements occurs, diffusion velocity of the alloy elements are
different, so a new interface forms after the completion of diffusion, that is the
Matano interface, on the both sides of which the amount of diffusive material
remains unchanged [ 9]. The schematic diagram of interface diffusion is shown in
Fig. 13. As a matter of fact, by the limitation of test methods in this experiment,
Matano interface is dif ﬁcult to observe and measure. According to the principle of
Matano interface, the diffusion process between component alloys is considered as
the diffusion that the amount of diffusive material maintains constant in a
semi-inﬁnite object.
According to Fick ’s second law, assume that the diffusion coef ﬁcient is inde-
pendent of the concentration, the solution of the diffusion equation is as follows:

According to Eq. ( 7), the thickness of the diffusion layer can be estimated by
knowing the diffusion annealing process. It shows that when the temperature is
constant, the thickness of the diffusion layer is in parabolic relationship with time,
and when the time is constant, the thickness of the diffusion layer is in exponential
relationship with the temperature. Therefore, the annealing time can be shortened
by increasing the annealing temperature.
Conclusions
1. The interfacial diffusion layer of 5J20110 thermal bimetal is solid solution, and
the diffusion degree of interface increases signi ﬁcantly with the increase of
diffusion annealing temperature and time.
2. With the increase of diffusion annealing temperature and time, the interface
bonding strength and resistivity varies little.
3. The formula between the thickness of interfacial diffusion layer and annealing
temperature and time of 5J20110 thermal bimetal is deduced, that is,

Abstract The aim of this article is to study the effect of intermediate annealing on
the interface and plasticity of Cu –Ni–Si/Al–Mg–Si clad composite wires. Cu –Ni–
Si/Al–Mg–Si clad composite wires were produced by cold drawing process and
annealed at the temperature from 150 to 350 °C for 0.5 h. The presence of various
intermetallic compounds in different temperature was detected by scanning electron
microscope and EDS analyzer. The mechanical properties were measured by stretch
test. The elongation increased with the temperature increment. The morphology of
fracture showed that intermetallic compounds were tough and brittle. During the
subsequent drawing, the intermetallic compounds were harmful to the overall
structure of composite wires. The elongation cannot identify the plasticity of
copper-clad aluminum (CCA) composite wires accurately.
Keywords Interface
/C1Clad composite wire /C1Plasticity /C1Intermediate annealing
Intermetallic compounds
Introduction
The copper-clad aluminum composite wires have been widely used in cable
industry [1–3]. CCA composite wires combine the excellent conductivity of copper
and low density advantage of aluminum. However, the relatively poor mechanical
properties of pure Cu and pure Al limit their application. The alloying of pure metal
component can improve the performance of CCA, such as Cu/Al –Mg–Sc [ 4]. To
improve the pressure welding property, Cu –Ni–Si is used to replace pure Cu,
because of its good elasticity. And Al –Mg–Si alloy is used to replace pure Al
because of its high strength [ 5].

## Page 848

Drawing is a common method during the manufacturing process of CCA thin
wires. It has the ability to produce good compositional controlled and uniform
composite microwires [ 6]. The plasticity of pure Cu and pure Al is so good that
CCA wires can be drawn directly to the ﬁnal size without any heat treatment.
However, with the multi-pass drawing, the plasticity of Cu –Ni–Si alloy and
Al–Mg–Si alloy reach their limits. Therefore, the intermediate annealing is a sig-
niﬁcant process to the manufacture of Cu –Ni–Si/Al–Mg–Si clad composite wire.
During the heat treatment, the Intermetallic Compounds (IMCs) are inevitable
formed at the contact area of Cu/Al due to the occurrence of diffusion [ 7].
According to the results of former researchers, the kinds of IMCs produced in
various conditions are different. For example, Kim and Sun [ 8] con ﬁrmed that the
existence of IMCs was respectively Al
4Cu9, AlCu and Al 2Cu during the cold
roll-cladding of tri-layered Cu/Al/Cu composite. Abbasi et al. [ 9] discovered a
saturated solid solution region among the IMCs. The existence of IMCs has a
signiﬁcant effect on the properties and the subsequent drawing of CCA wires.
Experimental Procedure
Cu–Ni–Si/Al–Mg–Si clad composite wires were fabricated using Al-0.88Mg-
0.88Si (wt%) bar with a diameter of 20 mm and Cu-2.8Ni-0.68Si-0.19Mg (wt%)
tube with an outer diameter of 21.7 mm. The Cu –Ni–Si alloy was solution treated
at 950 °C for 1 h. The Al –Mg–Si bar was crammed into Cu –Ni–Si tube, then
Cu–Ni–Si/Al–Mg–Si clad bar was drawn to 0.5 mm in diameter. The volume ratio
of Cu –Ni–Si maintains at approximately 15%.
Different annealing temperatures from 150 to 350 °C were performed and
annealing time was 0.5 h. The interface morphology and mechanical property
changes of Cu –Ni–Si/Al–Mg–Si wires were studied. Afterwards the wires were
drawn to a 0.25 mm in diameter respectively.
Microstructure observations were carried out by Leica DM400 optical micro-
scope (OM) and JSM-7001F scanning electron microscope (SEM) with energy
dispersive spectrometer (EDS). Mechanical property were tested using a wire
stretch tester according to GB/T 29197-2012 standard.
Results and Discussion
The interface morphology of Cu –Ni–Si/Al–Mg–Si wires with different annealing
temperature from 200 to 350 °C for 0.5 h are shown in Fig. 1. Below 200 °C,
No IMC exist on the interface. With the temperature increasing, the IMC layer is
observed as shown in Fig. 1b, c. EDS detection indicates that the IMC is Al
2Cu. When
temperature reaches 350 °C, different phases can be distinguished, e.g. Al4Cu9,A l C u
and Al 2Cu respectively, according to EDS analysis, as shown in Table 1. These
results are in accordance with the study of Antoine Gueydan et al. [ 10].
870 Z. Yang et al.

## Page 849

Temperature is the main factor to the formation of various IMCs due to the
improvement of diffusion rates. As we know, ﬁve IMCs exist according to Cu –Al
phase diagram at room temperature, but researchers discover only two or three
phases in most diffusion studies. The formation mechanism of various IMCs is not
clear.
From the Fig. 2, the as-drawn wires exhibit a high tensile strength of 485 MPa
and a very low elongation about 2.3%, which indicates that the wires have gone
through a large deformation. If the wire can be drew continue, it will be snapped.
The intermediate annealing is necessary for the wire to regain plastic processing
capacity. when annealing temperature is higher than 200 °C, the tensile strength
falls down shapely to about 260 MPa, which is close to the strength value range of

Al–Mg–Si alloy. The Cu –Ni–Si alloy has a relatively small effect on the strength of
clad composite wire, due to the volume ratio of Cu –Ni–Si alloy reaches only
15%. Moreover, at low temperature, no aging precipitation of Cu –Ni–Si alloy
occurs and the strength value of that shows no obviously change [ 11]. The tensile
strength of Al –Mg–Si alloy decreases due to the occurrence of recovery and
recrystallization behavior.
While annealing temperature below 200 °C, the elongation of Cu –Ni–Si/Al–Mg–
Si clad composite wires has no signi ﬁcant change. Above 250 °C, the elongation
begins to rise. when the annealing temperature is 350 °C, the elongation reaches at
5%. Because of the recovery of Cu –Ni–Si alloy, the vacancy defect reduces that
promote the elongation of the whole wires. In addition, to some extent, IMCs are of
beneﬁt to the bonding of Cu–Ni–Si alloy and Al–Mg–Si alloy owing to the diffusion.
The bonding is helpful to the synchronous deformation of two alloy matrixes.
The morphology of tensile fractured wires after intermediate annealing at 350 °C
has been observed by SEM, as shown in Fig. 3. The break phenomenon of IMCs
exists on the interface, leading to the separation of Cu –Ni–Si and Al –Mg–Si during
the stretch progress. With the extension of Al –Mg–Si alloy, the sheet-shaped IMCs
adheres to Al –Mg–Si alloy crack. The other part of IMCs with an orderly fracture
adheres to Cu –Ni–Si alloy. All of the above results suggest that IMCs are tough,
brittle, and no ductility. Hug and Billido [12] tested the hardness of the various IMCs,
which showed the IMCs are much harder than Cu and Al matrix. Chen [ 13] con-
ﬁrmed the brittle nature of IMCs in the study of cold roll bonded Al/Cu bimetal sheet.
Figure 4 shows the interfacial morphology of Cu –Ni–Si/Al–Mg–Si clad com-
posite wires drawn to 0.25 mm after different intermediate annealing temperature.
After the annealing at 200 °C, it exhibits a ﬁne interface. However, while annealing
temperature above 250 °C, the IMCs have a negative effect on the interface,
as shown in Fig. 4b, brittle IMC breaks and the generated particle is involved in
Cu–Ni–Si alloy during plastic ﬂow, which may destroy the overall structure of
CCA composite wires.

## Page 852

In Fig. 4c, d, the broken IMCs appear as masses after drawing process. On
account of different plasticity, metallurgic bonding of IMCs and the matrix alloys is
no longer in force. The size of these blocks is more than 1 lm. However, the
thickness of outer Cu –Ni–Si alloy is only about 10 lm. Because of stress con-
centration, the hard blocks have an adverse effect to the wires de ﬁnitely during the
following drawing. Cracks produce near the blocks, resulting in the fracture of thin
Cu–Ni–Si layer.
Summary
In this work, the evolution microstructure of Cu –Ni–Si/Al–Mg–Si clad composite
wires for different annealing and drawing conditions has been investigated. With
the annealing temperature increasing, various IMCs are observed on the interface.
When the wire annealed at 350 °C for 0.5 h, three IMCs layers, Al
4Cu9, AlCu and
Al2Cu respectively, are determined, and that elongation of wires reaches a maxi-
mum value at this condition. However, IMCs break during the subsequence
drawing process, which leads to the fracture of thin Cu –Ni–Si layer, due to their
brittle nature. Elongation cannot identify the plasticity of Cu –Ni–Si/Al–Mg–Si
composite wires accurately.

Thermodynamics and Morphological
Fractal Characteristics of WC
Particulates Reinforced Steel Matrix
Composites by Composite Electroslag
Melting and Casting
Ning Zhang, Chunhong Zhang, Mingfan Zhu and Yinghuai Qiang
Abstract The composite electroslag melting and casting technology was adopted
to produce 45 wt% WC particulate reinforced steel matrix composites. The results
indicated that the WC formation showed a dominant position and displays in a
triangle or rectangle in the WC reinforced steel matrix composites. As a reference
plane, WC grains in the ð0001Þ surface grew up into a stack structure in the way of
hierarchical formation along the 0001 hi direction, ﬁnally formed a three-
dimensional shape with the ð0001Þ surface in a triangle. The fractal dimensions
of WC present different changed with the transformation of the heat treatment
process. When quenched and tempered at high temperature, the fractal dimension
value of two types of WC appeared, and WC phases showed two groups of different
fractal structure with different particle size and quantity. The larger fractal
dimension difference DD corresponded to Fe
3W3C compound carbides, with the
smaller DD to WC particles which keeps the properties and morphology under the
state of forging and annealing. The higher the quenching or tempering temperature,
the larger the fractal dimension difference DD and the greater change of the mor-
phology of WC were obtained.

Introduction
Steel is the most widely used metal material in industry, but in many special
occasions, higher hardness and wear resistance were required for some tool and
pattern materials and wear-resistant parts, consequently, the traditional iron and
steel materials cannot meet these stringent requirements. In recent years, the
application and study on ceramic particulates reinforced metal matrix composites
have received wide attention to further pro ﬁt the excellent overall performance
[1, 2]. A variety of processing methods were adopted to improve the hardness and
wear resistance by incorporating the ceramic particles into steel matrix. The
advantages of steel with excellent plasticity and toughness, and the bene ﬁts of
ceramic with high hardness and wear resistance were both obtained. Appropriate
heat treatment can also be carried out due to the features of low price, high pro-
ductivity, and large size production [ 3].
In this experiment, the composite electroslag melting and casting process was
adopted to prepare the particulates reinforced metal matrix composite; 5CrNiMo
steel was used as matrix and WC particles was used as reinforcement phase [ 4, 5].
In the process of the composite electroslag melting and casting, the effect of WC
hard particles dissolution and precipitation behavior in melt at high temperature
should be analyzed, and the particle morphology, size, and crystal characteristics, as
well as the diffusion phenomenon of W and C elements in the composite interface
of the steel matrix should be discussed, which is an important factor affecting the
performance of composite materials [ 6]. While these are based on the theory of
thermodynamics, through thermodynamic analysis, the phase composition, growth
mechanism, and reaction characteristics of the reaction products in the process of
melting and solidi ﬁcation need to be understood to better control the composite
electroslag melting and casting process.
The as-annealed and as-forged foundry goods cannot be used as ﬁnal products,
which should be received proper heat treatment to obtain better performance [ 7]. In
heat treatment, WC will dissolve and separate out in the steel matrix, causing WC
morphology change, and forming different composition and organizational struc-
ture, so that the overall performance of the composite is enhanced [ 8]. The fractal
has the basic features of self-similarity and scale in-variance, as well as the fractal is
widely existed in the organization and structure of all kinds of composite materials.
The fractal dimensional measurements can be used to characterize some important
properties of this kind of composite [ 9]. Chu et al. [ 10] used the measurement and
calculation method of Sierpinski fractal dimension to carry out fractal study on the
metallurgical structure of diamondite after electroslag remelting, and quantitatively
described the changes of hard phase morphology before and after electroslag
remelting. Sun et al. [ 11] adopted the plasma spraying technology to prepare
878 N. Zhang et al.

## Page 856

composite coating of ceramic particles/Ni alloy, and studied the distribution of
ceramic particles in the metal matrix by using Sandbox method, then gained the
fractal dimension of ceramic particle reinforced composite coatings under different
volume fractions.
In this experiment, the fractal study is carried out on the BSED (backscattered
electron detector) mapping of WC particulates reinforced steel matrix composites
before and after heat treatment by using the measurement and calculation method of
Sierpinski fractal dimension, and the morphology change of the WC particles for
composites was also quantitatively investigated before and after heat treatment.
This is of great signi ﬁcance for the study on change mechanism of the WC phase
performance and the effect of the WC morphology change on the properties of
composites.
Materials and Method
In this experiment, WC particle reinforced steel matrix composites were produced
using the composite electroslag melting and casting technology. The WC particles
were bought in ZhuZhou cemented carbide factory, which were divided into two
speciﬁcations that the coarse particles were 150 mesh (95 –110 lm) and the ﬁne
particles were 300 mesh (45 –55 lm), and the WC particles added was 45 wt%.
The composite electroslag melting and casting process is a new method to
prepare particulates reinforced steel matrix composites. Firstly, recovered waste raw
materials were fabricated into 5CrNiMo steel consumable electrode in
medium-frequency induction furnace by using common casting method, then the
reinforced particulates carrier which is mainly WC was produced by high-energy
whipping ball milling method. Reinforced particulates and consumable electrode
were melted in vertical electroslag furnace with one-armed beam in the form of
dropping, and the dispersed reinforced particulates in the base fusant using elec-
tromagnetic stirring technology. In the end, the fusant was rapidly cooled and
crystallized in water-cooling crystallizer. After that, the semi ﬁnished product was
annealed isothermally and forged, and it would optimize organizational structure
and improve the effect of particulates reinforced steel matrix.
The large differences of physical and mechanical properties between WC par-
ticulates and steel matrix were existed. Before service normally; an appropriate heat
treatment should be adopted to improve the intensity and hardness, and decreasing
internal defects and residual stress. So the process of heating then oil quenching and
tempering at low temperature were adopted. The specimen surface was coated with a
layer of anti-oxidation at high temperature and anti- decarburization coating, then
quenched and tempered according to the heat treatment scheme was shown in Fig. 1.
The oxide-layer on the surface of heat-treated sample was removed by emery
paper, then ground on Buehler AutoMet 250 auto grinding and polishing machine
with different types of emery papers, and polished by mechanical method using
3 lm diamond polishing liquid, ﬁnally polished on Buehler VibroMet 2 vibratory

sive X-ray spectroscopy), respectively.

During the process of the electroslag melting and casting, WC and W 2C were
alternately generated in the molten steel at high temperature. However, when the
solidiﬁcation temperature falls in the water cooling mold, W 2C partly transforms
into WC. The characteristics of the crystal surface are anisotropic. When crystal-
lization occurs in WC, the differences in crystal surface energy will lead to the face
0001ðÞ as the datum plane for the growth of WC grains, and the WC grains will
grow in the form of hierarchical along the direction 0001 hi , which shows the
stacking structure of multilayer, eventually forming a three-dimensional shape with
a unique shape as shown in Fig. 3.

Extraction of The Image Fractal and Calculation of The Fractal Dimension
The samples were scanned by SEM in BSED mode. The characteristics of the images
could be obtained according to the magni ﬁcation which was set. Because black and
white contrast of the back-scattered electron images re ﬂects the average atomic
number corresponding to the position of the sample, the bright-white part of the
images means the W elements are more. On the contrary, the dark-black part of the
image means the W elements are less. So it can be distinguished separately between
enhanced particles and steel matrix, and does not need to carry out the black and
white binarization processing. The BSED images can be extracted from the ImageJ
software to measure the percentage N(r) of the steel matrix, i.e. the measurement of
the residual area under different magni ﬁcations. Each sample was selected ﬁve dif-
ferent parts to take pictures. Then the average value of N(r) was calculated. The
average value of N(r) and the value r of the corresponding ampli ﬁcation are sub-
stituted in Eq. ( 11) to obtain the fractal dimension D of the Sierpinski carpet.
Some parts of the BSED images of the samples with the coarse WC particulars
are shown in Fig. 5. Each row represents a group images of the same sample in the
same area under the different magni ﬁcation.
Each BESD diagram was imported by the ImageJ software, and the percentage
of the remaining area in the composite materials was obtained by the process of the
calculation. Then the data was substituted in Eq. ( 11), and draw the double loga-
rithmic curve by ﬁtting function of the OriginPro software. A part of the ﬁtting
results of the coarse particle WC composite are shown in Fig. 6. The common
logarithm of the percentage of the remaining area is called as the normalized
residual area, and the common logarithm of the image magni ﬁcation is named as
the standard linear scale. The slope value can be calculated automatically by the
software, and the value of k can be expressed as the following equation:

Abstract TiB2/7055 composites with volume fractions of 0, 5.17 and 18.23% were
prepared by two step method. Firstly, the Al/TiB 2 master alloy was prepared by
Melt Self-propagating High-temperature Synthesis method. Then, TiB 2/7055
composite was prepared by adjusting the alloy elements with using this master alloy
as the matrix. Meanwhile, the effect of TiB 2 particle content on hardness and wear
resistance of the composites were studied. The microstructure of the composite was
observed by SEM and TEM. The result showed that the average size of TiB
2
reinforced particles were less than 1 lm and the particles were dispersively dis-
tributed in the grain. With the increasing of the TiB 2 particles content, the hardness
and wear resistance of composites increased. When the volume fraction of TiB 2 was
18.23%, the hardness of composite after T6 aging could reach to 264HB, which is

Introduction
Metal matrix composite has become an important research ﬁeld because of its high
modulus of elasticity, high strength, good wear resistance and dimensional stability
[1–3]. Since the early days of 80s, ceramic particles reinforced aluminum matrix
composites have been used in the manufacture of diesel engine pistons, which has
led to the rapid development of metal matrix composites. The preparation of in situ
particle reinforced aluminum matrix composite can not only improve the compat-
ibility with the matrix, but also be expected to reduce the cost of materials.
TiB
2 particles have higher melting point, hardness and excellent wear resistance
than other reinforcements such as TiC, SiC, Al 2O3 and TiB 2 particles do not react
with most of the metal elements between the matrix and the reinforcement interface.
Therefore, it is a kind of ideal reinforcement for the aluminum matrix composites
[6–12].
It has been reported that the wear resistance can improved by adding a certain
volume of TiB
2 particles, such as TiB 2/Al–Cu [ 2], TiB 2/A356 [ 4], TiB 2/7075 [ 5].
However, for the TiB 2/7055 composite, the contribution of TiB 2 particles on the
hardness and wear resistance still not been reported. The 7055 alloy has such
characteristics as high speci ﬁc strength, excellent processability and excellent
welding performance. Meanwhile after the T77 heat treatment, the alloy has a good
combination of high strength, good corrosion resistance and fracture toughness. It is
currently the best comprehensive performance of ultra-high strength aluminum
alloy. And it can be widely used in the ﬁelds of aerospace and civil industry.
Therefore, although a small part of toughness is sacri ﬁced, the strength and wear
resistance of the matrix alloy are greatly improved by introducing TiB
2 particles to
reinforce the matrix alloy. This will improve the service performance of 7055
aluminum alloy, and has good economic bene ﬁts.
In this work, the hardness and wear properties of TiB
2/7055 composite with
different volume of TiB 2 particles were investigated, and the wear mechanism was
discussed.
Experimental
TiB2/7055 composites were prepared by two step method. Firstly, Al/TiB 2 master
alloy was fabricated by Melt SHS method [ 7, 8]. The content of TiB 2 particles with
different compositions were determined by adjusting the content of aluminum alloy.
892 H. Wang et al.

## Page 870

In this process, high volume fraction of TiB 2 particle reinforced Al alloy was
prepared at ﬁrst, and then the content of aluminum alloy were added in proportion.
So the intermediate alloy were diluted and obtained the composites with various
TiB2 particle content. Furthermore, composite materials were fabricated by
adjusting the alloy elements with using this master alloy as the carrier. The nominal
composition of material is Al-8Zn-2.1 Mg-2.3Cu-0.12Zr (wt%). Table 1 showed
the three samples with different volume fractions of TiB
2 particles, ranging from 0
to 18.23%. Finally, the ingot was extruded into plates with the size of 200 mm
60 mm /C26 mm at about 400 °C with a extrusion ratio of 17:1 [ 7]. The com-
posites were had a T6 treatment which solid solution at 460 °C for 70 min and then
quenched with water and aged at 120 °C for 24 h.
The specimens were cut from the ingots and the paltes to carry through
microstructural characterization. The surface morphology and distribution of TiB 2
particles were observed by Scanning electron microscopy (QUANT200) and the
transmission electron microscopy (JEM2100F). HBRV-187.5DT Motorized Brinell
Rockwell was used to measure the Brinell hardness of the composites.
Abrasive wear tests were carried out on a ML-100 pin disk abrasive wear tester.
The wear test specimens of composites with 4 /C24 /C212 mm
3 were machined by
super CNC wire cutting machine. The specimens are thoroughly cleaned in the
alcohol by ultrasonic cleaning before and after each abrasions. The quality of
specimen was measured by electronic balance of 0.01 g precison, in order to obtain
the mass loss. The speed of the test machine is 240 r/min, the load is 40 N, and the
granularity of sand paper is 100 mesh during the wear test.
Results and Discussion
Table 2 showed the composition of the experimental material, which were tested by
ICP-AES. The component of the composite with different TiB 2 content was stable.
It showed that the method of Melt SHS prepared by experiments was reliable,
reproducible and operational.

Figure 1 showed the microstructure of matrix alloy and composites with dif-
ferent TiB 2 content. From this Fig. 1a, the microstructure of the matrix alloy is
composed of typical discontinuous reticulate coarse dendrites. Compared with the
composite (Fig. 1b, c), the grain structure of composites are re ﬁned because of the
addition of the TiB
2 reinforcement. At the same time, with the increasing of TiB 2
content, the grain size re ﬁnement of composites is more obvious. And the average
grain size of composite with 18.23 vol% TiB 2 particles is 48.3 lm. This is mostly
owing to the common re ﬁnement of the TiB 2 particles and TiAl 3 phases in the
materials [9]. According to Fig. 1d, e, TiB 2 particles with an average size were less
than 1 lm, and part particles were concentrated on the grain boundary. This particle
can not effectively enhance the properties of composites. To improve the condition,
extrusion deformation and heat treatment must be carried out.
Figure 2 shows the microstructures of 18.23 vol% TiB
2/7055 composite at the
state of as-extruded, solid-solution and as-aged. The extruded alloy was deformed
in the direction of extrusion, and the defects in the material were reduced obviously.
Meanwhile, the TiB
2 particles played an important role in strengthening the matrix
due to the difference of thermal expansion coef ﬁcient. Mass of dislocations were
gathered around the TiB 2 particles, which lead to the hardness greatly increased.

## Page 873

Moreover, with the increase of TiB 2 content, the wear rate decreased. This is also
consistent with the increasing trend of the hardness value of the material. When the
volume fraction of TiB
2 is 18.23%, the hardness of the composite after T6 aging
can reach 264HB, which is 14.29% higher than the 7055 alloy (T6 aging), and the
wear resistance is 32.36% higher than the 7055 alloy. It mainly because the
hardness of the composite is higher than the 7055 alloy by high hardness particles
load transfer and sharing. On the other hand, the TiB
2 particles in the composites
were dispersively distributed in the grain. It makes the composites have a higher
carrying capacity, and then reduced the mass loss in the process of wear test, which
result to improve wear resistance.
Figure 4 is the SEM image of matrix alloy and 18.23TiB
2 (vol%)/7055 com-
posite after abrasive wear. From the Fig. 4a, b, the surface of the matrix alloy after
wearing occurred serious plastic deformation, showing the surface of deep furrows
and poor wear resistance. However, the composite wearing surface furrows not only
decreased, also appeared the irregular wear area and irregular furrows. These
irregular areas are mainly TiB
2 particles which has uniformly distributed in the
material, which were peeled off during the abrasive wear. Due to these dispersed
TiB
2 are strongly bonded to the matrix, the ability to resist abrasion is greatly
improved.

Summary
The TiB 2/7055 composites with different volume fractions of TiB 2 particles have
been successfully prepared by two step method.
1. TiB 2 particles in the composites dispersively distribute in the grain, and exhibite
the good bonding in interface.
2. With the increase of the TiB 2 particles, the hardness and wear resistance of
composites increase. When the volume fraction of TiB 2 is 18.23%, the hardness
of the composite after T6 aging can reach 264HB, which is 14.29% higher than
that of 7055 alloy (T6 aging), and the wear resistance is 32.36% higher than
7055 alloy.

Effect of Graphite Content
on the Tribological Properties
of Cu –Graphite–SiO2 Composites
Yifei Ye, Xu Ran, Bozhe Dong and Yanyi Yang
Abstract Cu–graphite–SiO2 composites with different graphite content were fab-
ricated by vacuum hot-pressing sintering. Pin-on-disk friction and wear tester was
used to carry out the friction test and study the tribological behaviors of
Cu–graphite composites. The results show that the fabricated composites had good
compactness and the relative density reached 96.2%. With increasing graphite
content, the density, hardness and electric conductivity of composites all declined.
The friction coef ﬁcient and wear rate both declined at ﬁrst and then increased and
obtained the lowest value (0.198 and 1.062 mg/m, respectively) at 15% graphite.
The composite with 15% graphite showed the best tribological properties. The wear
mechanism of composites with lower graphite content is mainly abrasive wear. The
wear mechanism of the composite with 15% graphite is plastic deformation. When
graphite content increased to 20%, fatigue wear and delamination turned into the
wear mechanism of the composite.
Keywords Cu-graphite
/C1 Graphite content /C1 Friction and wear
Wear mechanism
Introduction
Cu–graphite composites, due to their excellent electrical and thermal conductivity,
favourable self-lubricating property and remarkable corrosion resistance, have been
widely used in brushes, electrical contact materials, bearing materials, etc. [ 1–6].
Graphite can effectively reduce friction and wear, however, numerous amount of
graphite lowers the mechanical properties of the composites [ 7–9]. In order to
increase material strength and wear resistant property, several strengthen phases
(i.e., SiC, SiO
2, and carbon ﬁber) were introduced into Cu-graphite composites

## Page 877

[10–15]. Ramesh et al. [ 11] suggested that higher amount of hard reinforcement in
copper–SiC–graphite hybrid composites leads to enhancement in microhardness
and strength of the hybrid composites, however, ductility decreases. Rajkumar and
Aravindan [ 12] studied tribological performance of microwave sintered copper –
TiC–graphite hybrid composites and found that the formation of mixed smooth
layer improves the wear resistance and reduces the friction coef ﬁcient. In present
years, a large number of investigations emphasize on novel C/Cu materials (such as
carbon ﬁber/Cu, CNTs/Cu and graphene/Cu composites) to expand the application
of copper matrix composites [ 16–20]. But conventional Cu –graphite composites
still have great research value in certain applications [ 21–25].
Because of the relatively simple composition and structure of Cu –graphite
composites, it is essential to select raw materials and optimize preparation tech-
nique, thus obtaining the composite with desirable performance. The shape, size
and content of the material have signi ﬁcance impacts on the performance of the
ﬁnal composites. In this study, considering the better mobility and formability,
atomized copper powder and spherical graphite were adopted as raw materials. Cu –
graphite–SiO
2 composites were prepared by hot-press sintering. Friction and wear
tests were conducted under certain condition to study the tribological behaviors of
the composites. This investigation can provide some valuable experimental infor-
mation to the development of the material used as high-speed train ground brush.
Experimental
Material Preparation The specimens examined were prepared by powder met-
allurgy technology (PM). The sizes of the copper powder, graphite and SiO 2 are
about 4 –7, 24 and 10 lm, respectively. Figure 1 shows the powder morphologies
of atomized copper (a), spherical graphite (b), and SiO 2 (c). Five composites were
prepared according to Table 1. Cu powders were mixed with graphite and SiO 2 to
prepare composite powder mixture of different graphite content. The mixed pow-
ders were cold pre-compacted into a bulk at a pressure of 500 MPa for 1 min and
then were put into a graphite mould (innerdiameter of 30 mm) in a hot-press
sintering furnace. The heating rate was 15 °C/min and sintering temperature was
850 °C. A compaction pressure of 50 MPa was held for more than 1 h.
Physical and Tribological Performance Test The microstructure of the speci-
mens was investigated by using scanning electron microscopy (JSM-5600LV). The
bulk densities of the composites were measured using Archimedes ’method. The
relative density is the ratio of actual density to theoretical density. The hardness of
sintered composites was measured on a Brinell hardness tester (HBS-3000, hard
alloy indenter of 10 mm in diameter, holding 30 s with a pressure of 250 kgf). The
electric conductivity was evaluated by using a digital metal conductivity tester
(Sigma 2008).

Results and Discussion
Microstructure of Composites The Microstructure of sintered Cu –graphite–SiO2
composites is shown in Fig. 2. As can be seen from Fig. 2, the black part is
graphite, the gray part is silica particles and the rest is copper matrix. The graphite
particles are homogeneously distributed throughout the copper matrix. Some of the
silica particles are completely covered in the copper matrix, and some are covered
in the interface of copper matrix and graphite. Spherical graphite was deformed into
ﬂat shape in the process of hot-press sintering and had a directional distribution in
the copper matrix. The micrograph of specimen C1 is shown in Fig. 2a. The size of
graphite particles varies greatly. Figure 2b, c show the microstructure of specimens
C2, and C3, respectively. The size and distribution of graphite particles are more
uniform. When graphite content reaches 20% (see Fig. 2d), the graphite particles
are locally reunite and have a network distribution as a whole. The typical bonding

## Page 880

micrographs of graphite, SiO 2 and matrix are given in Fig. 3. No crack or pore can
be observed from Fig. 3a, b, which reveals good interfacial bonding among three
phases.
Physical Properties of Composites Figure 4 illustrates the variation of physical
properties with graphite content. It is clear that the density of composites decreases
with the increase of graphite content (see Fig. 4a). However, the relative density
shows little change with increasing graphite content, which proves the good
interfacial bonding of each phase in composites on the other hand. Specimen C4
(20% graphite) has a lower relative density than other composites, which may be
related to the pores in reunited graphite particles. Figure 4b shows that the hardness
and electric conductivity of composites distinctly decreases with an increase in
graphite content. The decrease in hardness is because graphite is much softer than
copper matrix, otherwise the increase of graphite content leads to more silica
particles appeared in the interface of copper matrix and graphite, but these silica
particles play a weak matrix strengthening role. The electric conductivity of copper
is much better than graphite, so the copper matrix becomes the main conductive
carrier in composites. The increase of graphite content leads to a decline in the
connectedness of the copper matrix, which ultimately gives rise to the decrease in
electric conductivity.
Friction and Wear Properties The friction curves of composites with different
graphite content are shown in Fig. 5. It reveals the real-time variation of friction
coefﬁcient with time. It can be found that the friction curve of the composite with
5% graphite ﬂuctuates greatly during the whole sliding process and the other there
curves are quite stable after 600 s. This indicates that a small amount of graphite
cannot provide good lubrication and stable friction coef ﬁcient. Moreover, the
friction coef ﬁcient of the composite with 20% graphite is obviously greater than
others. The reason is that the effect of large amounts of graphite on the
microstructure and mechanical properties increases the friction coef ﬁcient. In
comparison with 10% graphite composite, the friction coef ﬁcient of 15% graphite
composite has smaller ﬂuctuations to re ﬂect the optimum friction effect. Figure 6

## Page 882

Wear Mechanism SEM micrographs of worn surfaces of specimens C1, C2, C3,
and C4 are shown in Fig. 7. It can be seen from Fig. 7a that there are lots of wear
debris on the worn surface, besides, deep ploughs along the sliding direction are
observed. In the friction process, the surface of composites was adhered to the
counterpart on the contact point, of which the material partly fell off and became
wear debris under the shear action. At this point, the lubrication of small quantities
of graphite was not so obvious that the wear debris was attached to the friction
surface and produced a plough cutting action. It indicates that the wear mechanism
of specimen C1 is dominantly abrasive wear. Figure 7b presents light and small
ploughs and a few of wear debris. Graphite reduced the friction shear resistance,
which made adhesion points easy to be cut off and not easy to produce massive
exfoliation. The abrasive debris formed at this time were small and with low
hardness, which can be broken during the friction process and eventually trans-
ferred out of the friction surface. It suggests the wear mechanism of the specimen
C2 is adhesive wear. The worn surface of specimen C3 (see Fig. 7c) is relatively
smooth and neat. Copper matrix with plastic deformation covers the SiO
2 and
graphite, and graphite is also deformed under external forces, covering the worn
surface and forming the lubrication ﬁlm. The main wear mechanism is plastic
deformation in this case. Figure 7d shows severe plastic deformation and delami-
nation on the worn surface. A large amount of graphite severely reduced the
hardness and strength of the composite. Copper matrix deformed repeatedly,
resulting in fatigue cracks occurring and gradually expanding in the relatively weak
part of surface that were peeled off in the form of slice layers into wear debris
subsequently. So the wear mechanism of specimen C4 is fatigue wear and
delamination.

## Page 884

Conclusions
Cu-graphite-SiO2 composites have been fabricated and their tribological properties
investigated, and the following conclusions can be obtained:
The fabricated composites have high relative density (reach to 96.2%) but 20%
graphite can reduce the relative density of composites. With increasing graphite
content, the density, hardness and electric conductivity of composites all decline.
The friction coef ﬁcient and wear rate both decline at ﬁrst and then increase and
obtain the lowest value (0.198 and 1.062 mg/m, respectively) at 15% graphite.
When graphite content is lower, the wear mechanism of composites is mainly
abrasive wear, accompanying adhesive wear. Ploughs and wear debriscan be
observed on the worn surface. The worn surface of the composite with 15 wt%
graphite is smooth and neat. Plastic deformation is the wear mechanism in this case.
Keeping on increasing graphite content, fatigue wear and delamination turn into the
wear mechanism of the composite. The composite with 15% graphite has the
optimal tribological properties.
