Design and Numerical Simulation
of a Novel Mixer in Preparing
SiCp/A357 Composites
Yuelong Bai, Zhenlin Zhang, Zhifeng Zhang, Chunsheng Chen
and Jun Xu
Abstract Aim at uniform SiCp-particle distribution in aluminum matrix compos-
ite, a novel mixer for preparing SiCp/A357 composites was designed, and a ﬂow
model based on standard j-e model was developed to simulate the ﬂow behavior of
the SiCp/A357 composites stirred by the novel mixer, at last the structural
parameters of the mixer were optimized and veri ﬁed by numerical simulation and
stir casting experiment. The results showed that the appropriate mixer parameters
were as following: the diameter was 150 mm, the layer spacing was 40 mm and the
gap distance to the crucible was 40 mm. The SiCp particles distributed uniformly in
the aluminum matrix and the stir casting experiment results were in accord with the
numerical simulation, the mixer was effective to produce the high-quality SiCp/
A357 composites.
Keywords Aluminum matrix composites
/C1 Mixer /C1 Numerical simulation
SiCp/A357
Introduction
Due to their low density, low coef ﬁcient of thermal expansion, high speci ﬁc
strength and good wear resistance, SiCp/Al composites have received more com-
mercial attention and been broadly applied to many ﬁelds including car production,
airplane industry and civil engineering [ 1–4].
There are many processing methods for pdoducing SiCp/Al composites, these
methods include powder metallurgy, squeeze casting, liquid metal in ﬁlteration,
spray decomposition and stirring casting [ 5–9]. Among these processing methods
the stir casting is a a low-cost process and it is regarded as the most potential
process for producing large-sized and complicated components. But the distribution
of SiCp is a big problem in stir casting process due to the weak wettability between

SiCp and Al matrix and the high viscosity of the composites slurry. Therefore, an
effective mixer is of key importance for obtaining uniform distribution of SiCp in
the stir casting.
In order to optimize the structure of stirrer, Yao Guini [10] simulated the ﬂow ﬁeld
in stirred tank with multiple impellers used for waste glass particles reinforced
aluminum-based alloy. Hou Shuandi et al. [11] investigated the straight blade turbine
impeller in detail using CFD methods. Pakzad [ 12], Chapple [ 13], Yapici et al. [ 14]
simulated several kinds of radial ﬂow and longitudinal ﬂow in non-Newtonian ﬂuid.
But previous work was mostly focused on Newtonian ﬂuid, and little work have been
done about ﬂow ﬁeld in high viscosity non-Newtonian ﬂuid.
In the present work a novel mixer was designed, and the j-e model coupled with
the apparent viscosity model was used to simulate the ﬂow behavior of the
non-Newtonian SiCp/Al composites. and stir casting experiment was carried out to
verify the simulation results.
Modeling and Simulation Process

ture, opacity and high viscosity, so it is dif ﬁcult to observe ﬂuid ﬂow by physical
method. Computational ﬂuid dynamics (CFD) is a valid method to analysis the ﬂuid
ﬂow [ 15, 16]. In this work, the standard j-e model was used to simulate the ﬂow
behavior.

Simulation Process The j-e model was coupled with the Fluent software, the 3D
modeling of mixer was established by Solidworks software and was imported to the
Fluent software. The mould was meshed by the ﬁnite volume method. The mesh
number was 548309.
The novel mixer was shown as Fig. 1, it includes two layer, the upper layer
included four oblique blades and the under layer included four rectangle grids, The
four blades were set on upper layer to prevent the metal ﬂow from splashing and
keep an stable surface, the four rectangle grids were set on under layer to mix the
SiCp/Al composites melt intensively and to make the SiCp distribute uniformly in
Al matrix. The mix was set in the center of the crucible with 300 mm diameter and
500 mm height, the height h of the SiCp/Al composites melt is 300 mm and the
total weight is about 40 kg.
The ﬂow ﬁeld was simulated by sliding mesh method. The agitation of com-
posites melt was analyzed by k- e model, the SiCp/Al melt was regarded as
incompressible ﬂuid. The ﬂuid ﬂow was assumed as turbulence of approximate
stationary (Re > 1 /C2 10 − 5). The boundary conditions of the mixer were setting
as moving wall. The mixer and the ﬂuid around it were set as moving region. The
mixer was set as rotating synchronously with moving area. The other area was set
as still region, and an exchange interface was set up to realize data communication
between moving region and still region.
The mixer diameter (D), layer spacing (L) and the gap distance (H) to the
crucible were importamt parameters in the mixer, these parameters were investi-
gated in this simulation.

Experimental Method
The experiment was carried out by stir casting in order to verify the mixer, the stir
casting equipment was shown as Fig. 2. The argon pressure of the furnace was
controlled by the pneumatic system. The mixer was driven by a motor and can rise
and fall in the furnace. The aluminum alloy was melted by medium frequency
induction melting furnace, the temperature of the melt was controlled by a ther-
mocouple. The SiCp was added into the melt by the SiCp-feeder. The whole
process was controlled by the control cabinet.
The A357 was used as the matrix aluminum alloy of the composites, its nominal
chemical composites was shown in Table 1, DTA result showed that its liquids
temperature and solids temperature was 614 and 505 °C, respectively. The matrix
alloy was reinforced by SiC particles with its median diameter is 13 lm. In this
experiment the 20% (wt%) SiCp/A357 aluminum matrix composites were prepared.
The preparation process of the includes the following steps: The SiC particles
were preheated to 500 °C for four hours, 28 kg of A357 aluminum alloy was
melted to 720 °C in the intermediate frequency furnace and was carried out
degasssing and slagging-off; the SiCp particles were transferred into the SiC-feeder
and the pneumatic system was ﬁlled with argon. When the melt temperature is
630 °C, the mixer began to rotate with 300 rpm speed and the 7 kg of SiCp
particles was slowly added to the whirlpool of the ﬂuid,when the SiC power was
emptied, the mixer continued to stir for 30 min at 800 rpm stirring rate and 610 °C
melt temperature, after that the SiCp/A357 composites was poured to a cylindrical
mould and shaped the cast billet with 200 mm diameter and 480 mm height.
Metallographic samples were sectioned from the cast billet and prepared by
standard procedure, 0.5% HF solution was used to etched the samples.
Microstructure examination was performed by a Zeiss optical microscope with a
quantitative image analysis system. The position from where the samples were cut
was shown in Fig. 3.

high when H was 40 mm. With the H increasing to 80 mm the ﬂow velocity
decreased and there was a dead zone that could not be stirred strongly near to the
bottom of the crucible. More over, when the H = 40 mm the ﬂow velocity is higher

Experimental Results
The stir casting experiment using the optimized mixer was carried out to verify the
numerical simulation, in the experiment the stir temperature was 610 °C, the stir

It was well known that the SiCp distribution has an important effect on the
mechanical property, the SiCp clusters were great obstacle for the A357 matrix to
wet and resulted in much pores, but also it may result in a great difference including
wear resistance, coefﬁcient of thermal expansion and so on, as shown in Fig. 13.S o
the SiCp particles must distribute uniformly in the matrix. From Fig. 12 it could be
seen that the SiCp distributed uniformly in A357 aluminum matrix and no obvious
SiCp clusters were found, which demonstrate the mixer was effective to produce the
high-quality SiCp/A357 composites.

## Page 896

Conclusions
A ﬂow model of the novel mixer for SiCp/A357 composites stir casting based on
standard j-e model have been developed, it can successfully present the dynamic
evolution of the ﬂow ﬁeld in the stir tank.
A novel mixer has been designed and the optimized mixer parameters are as
follows: the gap distance to the crucible is 40 mm, the layer spacing is 40 mm and
the mixer diameter is 150 mm. The ﬂow velocity increaes greatly and the melt is
stirred strongly by the mixer, but the surface ﬂuctuation of the liquid is gradual.
The experiment results are in accord with results of the numerical simulation.
The SiCp particles distribute uniformly in the aluminum matrix. The mixer is
effective to produce high quality SiCp/A357 composites.

## Page 898

Effect of EPS Porogen
on Microstructure and Properties
of ZTAp/High Chromium Cast Iron
Composites
Mojin Zhou, Yehua Jiang, Xiaozu Zhang and Nan Wang
Abstract The expandable polystyrene was added to the gap in the ceramic preform
which was made of ZrO 2 toughened Al2O3 (ZTA) ceramic particles. Increasing the
porosity of the preform is bene ﬁcial to the high chromium cast iron in ﬁltration and
can obtain the composites of ZTA particles reinforced high chromium cast iron
matrix. In this paper, studied the residues amount of the different porogen in the
preform such as 10 * 20 mesh, 20 * 40 mesh, 40 * 80 mesh, 80 * 120 mesh
and mixing particle sizes were heated to the temperature of 250, 350, 450, 550 °C.
The corresponding composites were obtained under the different conditions and the
interfacial effect, the wear resistance of the composites were observed. At the same
time, the fracture mode of the composites was analyzed. The results showed that the
porosity of preform with mixing particle sizes was the lowest at 550 °C and had the
best interfacial, the highest wear resistance. The fracture mode of the composites
was the particles fracture, metal matrix brittle fracture and the particles shedding
from the matrix.
Keywords Porogenin
/C1 Metal matrix composites /C1 Preform
Three-body abrasive wear
Introduction
The wear resistant castings are mainly used in mining, electricity, cement, agri-
culture and other industries, the annual economic losses of about 40 billion yuan
[1, 2]. At present, most wear resistant materials are mainly traditional high man-
ganese steel and high chromium cast iron, because of its poor wear resistance, poor

## Page 899

toughness that can not meet the needs of industrial development [ 3]. A new wear
resistant material on the structure was invented — metal-based ceramic reinforced
composite materials. It not only has high hardness of the reinforcements, but also
the toughness of the matrix. The composites become a new research ﬁeld in wear
resistant industry development [ 4, 5]. The preparation of ceramic particles rein-
forced metal matrix composites is mainly obtained by adding ceramic reinforced
phase or generating ceramic reinforced phase by in situ reaction. The main draw-
back of the composites is the ceramic reinforcement not uniform distribution in the
metal matrix, and the interface reaction product can not control [ 6, 7]. The ceramic
particles were prepared into ceramic preforms with structure. According to the
properties of the reinforcement and the metal matrix, the desired reaction products
in the interface between the reinforcement and the metal matrix were obtained by
the pretreatment of the ceramic reinforcement [ 8].
Therefore, the structure of the prepared ceramic preform and its porosity have a
direct decisive effect on obtain a metal-based ceramic reinforced composites. The
more common is the layer composites. Because of its porosity is low that affect the
molten metal cast in ﬁltration ceramic preform that restricts its application and
development [9]. The presently effective preform structure usually was made into a
honeycomb structure. Usually, increasing the porosity of the preform by add the
organic porogen into the preform. The porogen means that it was added to the
preform and can be decomposed into volatile substances such as gas or moisture
under high temperature conditions. Therefore, leaving a pore structure in the pre-
form to improve the porosity of the preform and that improve the matrix in ﬁltrate
the preform [ 10]. Commonly used porogen are polyoxymethylene (POM), poly-
acrylamide (PAM), dextrin, starch, ammonium bicarbonate, sawdust, expandable
polystyrene (EPS), polypropylene (PP), polyurethane (PU) and so on [ 11].
Ammonium bicarbonate is instability, easy decomposition in the air and decom-
position speed is accelerate under heat that the ceramic preform is almost no
strength and can ’t use it. The porogen of starch and sawdust can not meet the
requirements because of they are dif ﬁcult to remove. POM was volatilized in the air
will produce formaldehyde and other toxic gases and it not suitable as a pore agent
from the environmental point of view. The hardness of PP beads is too high and the
market price is relatively high that it not be considered as pore forming agent. EPS
beads can regard as a pore forming agents due to its good mechanical properties and
inﬂated under heat [ 12]. However, removal the pore-forming agent and its residue
in the preform will affect the overall properties of the resulting composite.
In this paper, the ceramic preform structure was selected as the honeycomb, the
reinforcements are ZTA ceramic particles, and the porogen is EPS. The effect of the
process curve about removal the porogen in the preform under the same conditions
was studied that effect on the ceramic particles reinforced metal matrix composites,
and it has well guided in the practical production applications.
924 M. Zhou et al.

Experimental Procedures
Sample Preparation The ceramic particles is ZrO 2 toughened Al 2O3 (ZTA;
40 wt%ZrO 2), the particles size is about 1 * 3 mm (Fig. 1a). The metal matrix is
high chromium cast iron (HCCI). The chemical composition of high chromium cast
iron are show in Table 1.
The preform prepare process: weigh two copies of the ceramic powder with 2, 4 wt%
about the ceramic particles. They were added to the porogen and the ZTA ceramic
particles, respectively. The volume fraction of the porogen and the particles was 1:1.
A silane coupling agent with 4 vol% of the porogen and the PVA with 2 wt% of the
particles was added to the porogen and was stirred with the ceramic powder and that
make the surface of the porogen was adhered a layer ceramic powder. Adding 2 wt%
of the binder water glass to the ZTA ceramic particles, and then suf ﬁciently stirring
with the ceramic powder that the ceramic powders distribute uniformly on the surface
of the ZTA particles. Finally, the porogen with the ceramic powder mixed together
with the particles, and then stir evenly, ﬁlled into the mold. The size of the porogen
(Fig. 1b) was selected according to the requirements of the ceramic preform. In this
paper, the particle size was selected from 10 to 20 mesh, 20 to 40 mesh, 40 to 80
mesh, 80 to 120, mixed mesh (10 to 20 mesh:20 to 40 mesh:40 to 80 mesh:80 to 120
mesh = 1:2:1:1) ﬁve different range of porogen.

porogen as follows:

Preparation for the Composites The ZTA particles reinforced high chromium
cast iron matrix composites was prepared by conventional gravity casting process.
The speci ﬁc prepared process is as follows: The oxidized preform was placed in a
predetermined position of the cavity of the sand mold. Using medium frequency
induction furnace for smelting and the pouring temperature is about
1450 * 1550 °C, cool to room temperature and shake-out. The schematic diagram
of the pouring system is shown in Fig. 3a and the composites are shown in Fig. 3b.
Three-Body Abrasive Wear Test The different samples of the composites were
tested by the MMH-5 ring block three-body abrasive wear tester and the size of the
abrasive particles is about 40 * 70 mesh [ 8]. The sample was put into the alcohol
beaker for ultrasonic cleaning about 30 min and each test process about 1 h. Weigh
the wear sample by the one thousandth of a precision electronic balance after clear
and dry and note the data. Each wear process should replace with the new abrasive
particles. The rotating speed of the main axle is 50 rmp/min, and the testing force of
single axle is 50 N and each sample is tested about 5 h. The wear sample size are
shown in Fig. 4. The wear resistance of the composites was measured by volume
loss and calculated as reference [ 13].

Results and Discussions
Residues Amount of Porogen in Preform Figure 5a shows the differential
scanning calorimetry (DSC) curve and thermogravimetry (TG) of the pore forming
agent, and the heating rate is 10 K/min in air (NETZSCH5). It can be seen that the
TG curve has increased in the range of the temperature of below 340, which may be
related to the presence of oxygen in the air. An exothermic peak at 121.2 °C may be
a glass transition temperature. There appear a peak after the temperature of 121.2 °C
that means from the glass change to the rubber state. EPS in the decomposition
process is only one stage, starting from 325.8 °C and end at 431.4 °C. The pyrolysis
products will be further oxidized and the residues in the preform will be further
reduced after 431.4 °C. The residues amount of EPS for the original quality about
7.5% at 600 °C [ 14].
Figure 5b shows the residues amount of the porogen in the preform after slow oxi-
dation of the preform containing different pore sizes at different temperature. It can be
seen that at the same temperature and different pore size of the pore forming agent, the
residues in the pore size of the mixed granules is the lowest. At the same particle size,
different temperature, the porosity of the preform is the lowest at 550 °C. It can be
concluded that the effect of slow oxidation is the best at 550 °C and mixed particle
size, and the residues amount of porogen in the preform is the lowest.
Figure 6 shows the macroscopic morphology and stereo micrographs of the
preform with slowly oxidized which the size of the porogen in the preform is
mixture size and the highest oxidation temperature is 550 °C. It can be seen from
the Fig. 6a known that the pores (Fig. 6b) was formed by the ceramic powder after
oxidation and volatilization in the preform are dispersed between the ceramic
particles, which are improve the porosity of the preform. The holes are intercon-
nected to each other that provide casting channel. The molten metal reduces the
casting pressure during the casting process, which facilitates the combination
between the metal and the ceramic particles.

Analyze the Results of Three-Body Abrasive Wear Test Figure 8 shows the
result of the three-body abrasion test of the matrix and the composite region of
Scheme D. From the results, we can known that the wear resistance of metal matrix
is much smaller than that of the composites. The wear resistant of the composites is
about 8 times than that of the high chromium cast iron, which shows the pore
formation of the porogen does not affect the wear resistant of the composites. It can
be concluded that the EPS as a porogen is bene ﬁcial to the the preform.
Fracture Surface Morphology Analysis of ZTAp/HCCI Honeycomb
Composites Figure 9 shows the fracture surface morphology of the composites
about the four schemes. It can be seen that the fracture mode of the particles in the
composites is mainly achieved by the way of particle fracture or the particles
shedding from the matrix. The way of the matrix fracture between the particles is
mainly brittle fracture. The connection between the matrix and particles was
improved due to the presence of the ITL. When the composites fracture, the HCCI
and the ceramic particles with larger brittleness will appear microcracks ﬁrstly and
then the crack propagates to the interface transition layer.

## Page 907

Conclusions
(1) The ceramic preforms of ﬁve different pore-forming agents with 10 to 20 mesh,
20 to 40 mesh, 40 to 80 mesh, 80 to 120 mesh and mixed particle size were
respectively oxidized to the temperature of 250, 350, 450, 550 °C to removed
the porogen in the preform. With the increase of temperature, the residues
amount of the porogen in the preform decreases, and the interface combined
effect of the composites is improved. The residues amount of the porogen is the
lowest at 550 °C and the mixed particle size is the best, the interface of the
composites with the best results.
(2) The fracture mode of the composites mainly is ceramic particle fracture, particle
shedding and the matrix brittle fracture.
(3) The wear resistance of the composites which obtained by the metal in ﬁltrated
the oxidation porogen of EPS in the preform is about 8 times than that of the
high chromium cast iron.

## Page 908

Preparation and Characterization
of Electroless Copper Coating
on Hollow Glass Microspheres
Dan Liu and Qiang Zhang
Abstract The electroless copper coating was prepared on the hollow glass
microspheres. To reduce the cost, the silver nitrate activator was used instead of
conventional PdCl
2. The coated microspheres were characterized by scanning
electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) and
X-ray diffractometry (XRD). The continuous and uniform Cu coating was obtained
on the microspheres under the optimized electroless process and the thickness of Cu
coating was identi ﬁed to be about 100 nm. The silver nitrate activator has been
demonstrated to be effective replacement for the PdCl
2 activator.
Keywords Hollow glass microspheres /C1 Electroless coating /C1 Copper
Microstructure
Introduction
Nowadays, the increasing electromagnetic wave pollution has become a serious
problem [1, 2], because it will disturb sensitive electrical equipments or even cause
the possible health hazards for humans. Therefore, it is necessary to develop
electromagnetic shielding materials for ef ﬁcient protection [ 1, 3, 4]. Conventional
electromagnetic shielding materials, such as permeability alloy and silicon steel,
have high density. The Cu, Ag or Ni coated hollow glass microspheres, combining
the properties of low density (hollow structure) and high conductivity (metal
coating), are appropriate ﬁllers which can be added into the metal or polymer matrix
to produce light-weight electromagnetic shielding composites.

## Page 909

Electroless plating allows us to obtain continuous and uniform coatings on the
surface of metallic, dielectric and semiconducting materials [ 5]. It also has the
advantages of fast deposition and formation of good coatings at low temperatures.
Consequently, the electroless plating has been widely used for metal coating on
hollow glass microsphere [ 6, 7]. Before the electroless plating of Cu, two pre-
treating processes (sensitization and activation) are necessary for hollow glass
microspheres with nonmetallic surface [ 8, 9]. Compared to the expensive and toxic
PdCl
2 activator, cost-effective AgNO 3 provides an alternative.
In this work, the electroless copper coating was prepared on the hollow glass
microspheres using AgNO 3 activator. The processing parameters were discussed,
and then the microstructure and phase composition were characterized by scanning
electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) and
X-ray diffractometry (XRD).
Experimental
Materials The main elements of the hollow glass microspheres are as follows:
53.99 wt% O, 34.25 wt% Si, 8.26 wt% Ca, and 3.51 wt% Na. Table 1 lists the
typical properties of these hollow glass microspheres.
Figure 1 shows the morphology of hollow glass microspheres. These micro-
spheres have smooth surface and their hollow nature can be revealed by the frac-
tured microsphere. The porosity of these hollow glass microspheres is 84%.
Electroless Plating Procedures Because of the microspheric shapes and low
density (hollow structure), the electroless plating treatment should be controlled
very carefully [ 9]. The typical sequential steps involved in the electroless copper
coating process are as follows:
(1) Pre-cleaning: The hollow glass microspheres were cleaned in the
NaOH + Na
2CO3 solution for 30 min at 25 °C, then were washed with
deionized water and dried at 60 °C for 30 min.
(2) Sensitization: The hollow glass microspheres were stirred in a solution con-
taining 20 ml/L of concentrated HCl (37%) and 10 g/L of SnCl 2, for 20 min at
25 °C. Then the sensitized particles were ﬁltered from the solution and washed
with deionized water, without being dried, straightway removed to the previ-
ously prepared activating solution.

(3) Activation: As mentioned in the sensitization step, the microspheres were then
stirred in a activating solution containing 9 ml/L of ammonia and 10 g/L of
AgNO3 (called silver-ammonia solution), for 15 min at 25 °C, ﬁltered off,
washed three times with deionized water and dried in drying chamber at 60 °C
for 30 min.
(4) Electroless plating: After sensitization and activation pretreatment, the micro-
spheres were transferred to plating bath and stirred at 30 °C for 25 min. The
compositions of plating bath are shown in Table 2. After electroless copper
plating, the hollow glass microspheres were ﬁltered off, washed three times
with deionized water and dried in drying chamber at 60 °C for 50 min.
Characterization The surface morphology of the original and Cu-coated hollow
glass microspheres were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM,
Helios Nanolab600i). The compositions were measured by energy dispersive X-ray
spectroscopy (EDX). The crystalline phases before and after electroless copper
plating were determined by X-ray diffraction (XRD, D/MAX2200).

Results and Discussion
Effect of Microspheres Loading Concentration To ensure the quality of the
pre-treatment process and use appropriate electroless copper plating process, the
morphology of Cu-coated hollow glass microspheres with different loading con-
centrations in the plating bath was observed using SEM and shown in Fig. 1.
It can be seen that, with the decreasing of microspheres loading concentration in the
plating bath from 3 to 1 g/L, the surface of Cu-coated hollow glass microspheres
were covered with increasing copper deposited clusters. Especially for the micro-
spheres with 1 g/L loading concentration, the microspheres were completely
coated, with a thicker coating (Fig. 1c). When the loading concentration is rela-
tively larger, such as 3 or 2 g/L, the plating bath was consumed quickly; therefore, a
continuous and complete coating could not be obtained. Short plating time would
also cause such problems (Fig. 2).
Microstructure Figure 3 shows the SEM morphology of Cu-coated hollow glass
microspheres with 1 g/L loading concentration. From Fig. 3a, b, it can be found
that the surface of all the hollow glass microspheres was uniformly and completely
covered with a layer of Cu. According to the magni ﬁed micrograph in Fig. 3c, it is
conﬁrmed that the continuous Cu ﬁlm is consisted of copper nanoparticles.
The EDX analysis of Cu-coated hollow glass microspheres (Fig. 3d) demonstrates
that the ﬁlm is pure copper, with some O, Si and Ca coming from the base

In the initial stage of electroless reaction, it was catalyzed by Ag atoms on the

Anti-irradiation Performance
of Al –Si–Zn–O Compound Coating
on Kapton/Al Second Surface Mirror
Gang Liu, Huifen Wang, Yujing Li, Bo Zhou and Yangyang Pan
Abstract An Al–Si–Zn–O compound ﬁlm was prepared on the surface of Kapton/
Al second surface mirror by hydrothermal growth and sol-gel methods. The
microstructure, composition, optical and thermal performances of the coatings
before and after irradiation were investigated compared to the unprotected surfaces.
It was shown that the compound coating had a structure of AZO particles coated by
continuously distributed amorphous SiO
2 and displayed denser and smoother. With
this compound coating the resistivity of Kapton/Al second surface mirror to space
proton and electron radiation was greatly improved, while the optical and thermal
performances of the protective coating degraded much less than that of the
unprotected coating.

## Page 916

Introduction
Thermal coating is an important part of thermal control system for satellites and is
vital to the safety of satellites as the optical and thermal control performance of
which will degrade gradually under the effects of space radiation environment when
the satellite is operating on orbit [ 1–6]. Moreover, the prolongation of satellite life
span calls for thermal coating with higher resistivity to space radiation too.
At present, the research on thermal coating protection from space radiation is
mainly on the preparation of optical ﬁlm [ 7, 8]. It has been reported that SiO 2 and
Al2O3 ﬁlm were studied for this purpose [ 9, 10]. The analytical results demonstrate
that although the SiO 2 ﬁlm is continuous and compact but it is brittle and easy to
result in crack, while Al 2O3 ﬁlm is structured with a state of particle aggregation
which is easy to induce holes or spalling [ 11].
In this paper, the hydrothermal growth method and sol-gel method are intro-
duced for the preparation of the Al –Si–Zn–O protective ﬁlm on the surface of
Kapton/Al second surface mirror, forming a structure of AZO particles coated with
amorphous SiO
2, which avoids the brittleness caused by pure SiO 2 ﬁlm or the
non-continuity caused by pure Al 2O3 ﬁlm effectively [ 12–14]. Thus, the resistivity
of the ﬁlm to space radiation is greatly improved.
Experimental
Materials and Equipment The experimental ﬁlm materials are Zn(NO 3)2/C1 6H2O
(AR) and Al(NO 3)3/C1 9H2O. The ﬂexible second surface mirror (Kapton/Al) is served
as the matrix. The irradiation experiment is carried out in a synthesized space
irradiation environment effect simulator (Fig. 1), with the electron radiation dose of
1.6 /C2 10
17/cm2 and the proton radiation dose of 1.6 /C2 1016/cm2.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Atomic force microscopy (AFM) and
Energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) are used to evaluate the morphology and
composition of the ﬁlm.
Samples Preparation and Characterization Firstly, a seed layer is laid on the
surface of Kapton by the pretreatment of hydrothermal method. And then the
precursor is coated on the treated substrate of Kapton with the sol method. Then the
SiO
2–AZO (Al –Zn–O) ﬁlm will be formed after a gel process.
The orthogonal experiment is carried out for the optimization of formulation.
The SEM observation result is shown in Fig. 2 when Zn: Al: Si is 4:1:5. The
surface morphology shows that the AZO particles well dispersed in the SiO 2
continuous phase and the ﬁlm with the thickness of 400 nm is compact, ﬂexible and
well combined with the base, without shedding and scaling. The EDS analysis

optical performance is tested by spectrophotometer, as shown in Fig. 3, which
remains unchanged after the deposition of protective ﬁlm.

Conclusion
The SO2–AZO(Al–Zn–O) compound protective ﬁlm is prepared on Kapton surface
by hydrothermal growth method and sol-gel method with (Zn(NO 3)2/C1 6H2O) and

Depth Distribution of High Energy
Proton in Polyimide Film
Bin Rong Wang, Yan Hua You and Hai Yun Hu
Abstract In order to study the process of high energy proton passing through a
thin ﬁlm, a non-equilibrium statistical model of proton irradiation was established
on the basis of stochastic theory. Considering the statistical model and the elec-
tronic stopping power, the Langevin equation and the corresponding Fokker –
Planck equation were given, then the average passing depth and the changes of
probability density distribution of passing depth with energy or time were calcu-
lated. By analysis, the average passing depth of the high energy proton in the ﬁlm
was calculated. The probability density distribution of the passing depth represents
the probability that protons pass to a certain depth.
Keywords High energy proton
/C1 Polyimide ﬁlm /C1 Passing depth
Statistical distribution
Introduction
The development of space technology plays an important role in the space industry.
There are many irradiated particles in space that have great damage to spacecraft. It
is particularly the destruction of the spacecraft surface by proton irradiation. The
surface of the spacecraft has a thermal control coating material, usually Kapton
ﬁlm. Proton irradiation has great impact on this ﬁlm and the destruction of Kapton
ﬁlm will lead to decline of the spacecraft life [ 1]. As the analog space environment
is more complex, so far, most people use the Monte Carlo method to study the
passing depth of particles in the material [ 2–4] and analyze material performance

changes. In order to further study the mechanism of the incident particles in the
material and analyze the probability variation of the passing depth of incident
particles, in this paper, the Kapton ﬁlm under the proton irradiation is taken as the
object of study. Based on the non-equilibrium statistical theory, when protons
irradiate the ﬁlm, the process of passing in the ﬁlm follows a certain statistical law.
By using this model, we analyze the probability density distribution of the passing
depth with the different incident energy and the relationship between the passing
time and the depth. It may provide a new idea for the further study of the irradiation
process.
Stochastic Growth Equations for Irradiation Damage
Irradiation protons passing in the Kapton ﬁlm is a stochastic collision walking
process, so it can be described by stochastic process equations. Due to the changes
of density of atoms in the passing path of the irradiated proton, it will lead to
stochastic ﬂuctuations in the rate of passing. The passing rate of incident protons is
determined by two parts. The ﬁrst part comes from the average structural back-
ground of the ﬁlm, and the second part is derived from the changes of the target
atomic density in the ﬁlm. Let t is the passing time, x is the passing depth, _x is the
passing depth per second, called the passing rate. Thus the passing rate of protons
satisﬁes the generalized Langevin equation [ 5, 6].
_x ¼ kxðÞ þ b xðÞ ftðÞ : ð1Þ
where kxðÞ is called the transport growth rate of passing depth of protons. It
corresponds to the ﬁrst part. kxðÞ ¼ Ab xðÞ , A is a constant that is unrelated to x, ftðÞ
is the stochastic part of the growth rate called the ﬂuctuation growth rate, b xðÞ is the
ﬂuctuating ampli ﬁcation function, b xðÞ ftðÞ is the rate of ﬂuctuation. It corresponds
to the second part.
Protons passing process in the ﬁlm is similar to the Brownian motion, so the
passing process of the protons in the ﬁlm can be regarded as a Markov process. And
ftðÞ satisﬁes the equation

Analysis and Results at High-Energy Incidence
When high energy protons enter the ﬁlm, the protons interact with the electrons
outside the nuclear of target atom, and mainly generate inelastic collision which is
called ionization damage. Protons make the electrons obtain energy and escape
from the binding of the target atoms to form ionization damage. When the energy of
the incident proton is reduced to a certain critical value the ionization damage
process ends. Next, the incident proton mainly occurs nuclear collision. And this
interaction process is equivalent to low-energy incident proton passing into the
material. In our work, we only consider the interaction of high-energy protons
passing in the ﬁlm. When high energy proton is incident, the Bethe-Bloch formula
can be used for the expression of its stopping power /C0

Conclusions
The evolution of passing of protons in the material has been studied based on the
model of non-equilibrium statistical theory, and the relationship between micro-
scopic parameters and macroscopic properties of proton passing in the material
established. Considering the ﬂuctuations of passing rate in the passing process of
proton, the variation of the passing depth of the proton with the different incident
energy are compared and the proton with different incident energies passing depth
is calculated. According to the size of the incident energy, the average passing
depth of protons can be calculated. This may provide a new method for us to
calculate the passing depth of the different incident particles in the material.

Baohong Zhang, Di Dong, Chengyang Wang and Danhua Zhang
Abstract Three refractory metal composites were prepared by powder metallurgy,
that is. W –7Cu, Mo –10Cu and W –26Re. Properties of the materials were studied,
such as tensile strength, fracture toughness, elastic modulus and ablation resistance.
The results show that W –26Re has the best mechanical properties and ablation
resistance. The tensile strength is 350 MPa at 1600 °C. And the linear ablative ratio
is 3.37%, and the linear ablative rate is 0.006 mm/s at 2500 K of ablation of 600 s.
It has wide potential application in the high-temperature working environment.

Introduction
Refractory metal refers to the metal with a melting point above 1800 °C which
include tungsten (3410 °C), molybdenum (2620 °C), tantalum (2980 °C), niobium
(2468 °C), rhenium (3180 °C) and vanadium (1890 °C). The common character-
istics of them are high melting point and high temperature strength. They are widely
used in high-temperature working environment as ablation resistant materials for
their excellent properties. But a single metal has its limitations. For example, pure
tungsten is very brittle and dif ﬁcult to process. Copper and rhenium have good

toughness and plasticity. In recent years, with the development of science and

Refractory metal and its composite materials show their superiority, especially in
the aerospace, electronic information, energy, metallurgy, nuclear industry and so
on. A lot of research work has been done in refractory materials in the United
States, Japan, France, Britain, Germany and other developed countries [ 1–16]. In
this paper, the mechanical and ablation resistance properties of W –Cu, Mo–Cu and
W–Re materials are studied.
Test Method
Preparation Process Three refractory metals and composites were prepared by
powder metallurgy, including tungsten-copper composite, molybdenum-copper
composite and tungsten-rhenium alloy. The ingredients are W –7Cu, Mo–10Cu and
W–26Re. The preparation process contains powder processing, cold isostatic
pressing, high temperature sintering, in ﬁltration or deformation processing,
mechanical processing.
Test Method Microstructure was analyzed by metallographic and SEM. The
universal electronic testing machine was used to analyze the tensile strength. The
fracture toughness was tested by fracture toughness testing machine. The elastic
modulus was tested by the method of suspended - wire coupling resonance, and the
sample size is U6 /C2160 mm. The high temperature ablation resistance test was
carried out by arc wind tunnel test with the ablation test temperature of 2500 K.
Test Results and Analysis
Mechanical Properties Mechanical properties include tensile strength, fracture
toughness and elastic modulus in this paper.
Tensile Strength Tensile strength of different materials is shown in Fig. 1 at room
temperature, in Fig. 2 at 1600 °C. Each value in the ﬁgure is the average of three
measured data.
It can be seen from the comparison of data that the tensile strength of W –26Re
material is the highest at room temperature, reaching 805 MPa, followed by W –
7Cu, 728 MPa, and the lowest is Mo –10Cu, reaching 522 MPa. At 1600 °C, W –
26Re material has the highest tensile strength of 350 MPa, followed by W –7Cu,
86 MPa, and Mo –10Cu material has the lowest tensile strength, which is only
57 MPa. The comparison shows that the tensile strength of W –26Re is signi ﬁcantly
higher than that of W –7Cu and Mo –10Cu, whether at room temperature or high
temperature.

Analysis and Discussion W–Cu and Mo –Cu are spontaneous sweat materials. The
substrate material is hard so as to resist the erosion of gas, and the toughness of
sweat metal is better and can be used to toughen the substrate material. Therefore,
the strength and toughness of spontaneous sweat materials are signi ﬁcantly
improved. The addition of copper not only improves the mechanical properties of
the material but also increases the thermal shock resistance. When working at high
temperatures, the melting and evaporation of copper can absorb heat, thereby
cooling the material and improving the ablation resistance.

Mechanism of Tungsten Alloy
Guohui Liu, Ling Wang, Yingnan Qin, Guirong Liu and Ning Xiong
Abstract In this study, 93W –5Ni–2Fe tungsten heavy alloy prepared by powder
metallurgy method were tested at 1000, 1100, 1200, 1300 and 1400 °C respectively
for investigating high temperature mechanical properties. Fracture analysis was
carried out by scanning electron microscope and then developing principles of
fracture mechanism obtained. The results showed that as the elevating temperature
in the range of 1000 –1400 °C, mechanical properties of 93W –5Ni–2Fe alloy, such
as tensile strength, elongation, reduction of area and Young ’s module were dra-
matically getting worse. Material becoming brittle, transgranular fracture hardly
found, binder phase tear and interfacial fracture between tungsten grain and binder
phases are domestic fracture mode.

## Page 938

Introduction
Tungsten heavy alloy (WHA) with the unique properties such as high strength, high
hardness, good ductility, good machining performance, low thermal expansion
coefﬁcient, high thermal conductivity, good oxidation and corrosion resistance, is
considered as a reliable material for a wide range of application ﬁelds, for example,
aerospace, electronic information and military ﬁeld [1, 2]. Especially on the ﬁeld of
aerospace so far, tungsten heavy alloy has been more and more frequently applied
to extreme environments, for instance high temperature at 1200 °C and the limi-
tation estimated approximately 1300 °C. In recent years, a loads of researches has
been launched into tungsten alloy mechanical property and fracture mechanism in
room temperature static state at the effort donated by home and abroad scientists.
However, available studies of mechanical behavior at high temperature are rarely
beyond 1100 °C [ 3, 4]. Therefore, in this study, taking 93W –5Ni–2Fe as an
example, the mechanical behaviors and fracture characteristics at temperature span
1000–1400 °C were studied by using the high-temperature tensile test method,
developing principles of tensile strength and fracture mechanism with temperature
in the condition of ultrahigh temperature was explored.
Experimental
93WNiFe alloy adopted in this research was using commercial powders of ﬁne W
powder (3 µm), electrolytic Ni powder and carbonyl Fe powder as raw materials,
prepared by three-dimensional mixer in the light of composition ratio of 93W –5Ni–
2Fe, molded into bar specimen by cold isostatic pressing, and then sintered at
hydrogen atmosphere, ﬁnally vacuum heat treatment. The sample was machined
according to Fig. 1. The specimen was machined following GB/T 228.2-2015 and
with argon atmosphere protection tested by INSTRON 3369 Tensile and
Compression tester. Stretching rate was 2 mm/min. The test temperature were
1000, 1100, 1200, 1300 and 1400 °C respectively. The fracture of specimen
fracture was analyzed by using the model of GSM –6380LV scanning electron
microscope, and the evolution of fracture mode with temperature was observed.
Fig. 1 Sketch of sample for high temperature tensile test

## Page 939

Results and Discussion
Effect of Temperature on Material Mechanical Properties
Table 1 is mechanical property data of 93WNiFe alloy at different temperatures. At
room temperature (RT 30 °C), tensile strength is 936 MPa, yield strength is
670 MPa, elongation is 25%, while in high temperature span of 1000 –1400 °C,
having a signi ﬁcant difference. Figure 2 is 93WNiFe alloy tensile strength with
temperature curve and Fig. 3 is yield strength with temperature curve. As the
ﬁgures shown, both tensile and yield strengths decrease with the increasing tem-
perature when temperature falling the range 1000 –1400 °C, the tensile strength
decreasing from 281 to 102 MPa, yield strength reduced from 200 to 93. 2 MPa.
Moreover, as the temperature increases, tensile and yield strength are getting closer,
yield and fracture tend to be synchronized. Figure 4 is elongation with the tem-
perature curve. The same tendency as tensile and yield strength, the elongation of
the material dramatically decreased with increasing temperature, from 8.5 to 4%,
fracture mode transform into brittle fracture.
Fracture Analysis
Figure 5 is the typical fracture morphology of 93WNiFe alloy at room temperature.
It can be seen that the fracture of tungsten alloy is mainly composed of four kinds of
faults at room temperature, namely tungsten grain transgranular fracture, bonder
phase torn fracture, tungsten-bonder interfacial de-bonding and tungsten-tungsten
interfacial separating. At the room temperature, tungsten grain transgranular frac-
ture and binder phase tearing fracture are mainly fracture mode. Cleavage strength
of tungsten particle is very high, which resulting in material behaving great tensile
strength, and bonding phase tearing also further verifying the high elongation.
Figure 6 is the fracture morphology of 93WNiFe alloy at different temperatures
between 1000 and 1400 °C. It can be seen clearly that the 93WNiFe alloy under the

where, f is the percentage of the fracture. Statistically estimated the proportion of
these fractures, substituted into the equation, value of tensile strength by calculating
is close to that of experiments [ 7]. It indicates that the tensile strength of the
tungsten alloy is closely linked to the fracture morphology. On the other hand,
fracture mode is highly affected by temperature. It can be seen from fracture
appearance that tungsten grain transgranular cleavage fracture and binder phase
ductile fracture are dominant fracture mode at room temperature. When it comes to
1000 °C or above, almost all of the material fractures are tungsten-binder phase
de-binding and tungsten-tungsten interfacial fracture. With increasing temperature,
the bonding strength of tungsten-binder is extremely deteriorated, the tungsten
particles can be easily separated from the bonding phase, and strength of the binder
phase is also signi ﬁcantly reduced. Tensile strength and the elongation of material
macroscopically behaves sharply reduced.
Conclusion
(1) In 1000 –1400 °C temperature range, the tensile strength, yield strength and
elongation of 93WNiFe alloy are gradually decreasing with the increasing
temperature, and the yield strength and tensile strength are getting closer along
with temperature.
(2) The tensile strength of tungsten alloy depends on the fracture mode. In the
condition of high temperature environment, tungsten-binder phase de-bonding
and tungsten-tungsten interfacial separation are mainly fracture mode.
Transgranular fracture at room temperature disappearing at high temperature.
(3) From 1000 to 1400 °C, with the increase of temperature, W –W interfacial
strength and bonding phase strength decreased sharply. Material exhibits
obvious brittle fracture.

Effects of Ce Addition on Mechanical
Properties and Microstructures of Mo
Alloy Wires
Pengfa Feng, Xiaoming Dang, Na Wang, Qinli Yang
and Weicheng Cao
Abstract The effects of Ce addition on mechanical properties and microstructures
of Mo –Ce alloy wires were investigated. The results show that the yield strength
(Rp), tensile strength (R m) and elongation to failure (A%) of Mo –Ce alloy wires
were sensitive to the Ce content. When the Ce content was less than 0.03 wt%, R p,
Rm and A% did not change signi ﬁcantly as comparing with the unalloyed
molybdenum wires; when the Ce content was ranging from 0.06 to 0.09 wt%, R p
and Rm gradually increased, and the decreasing of A% was accompanied; when the
Ce content was ranging from 0.09 to 0.12 wt%, the maximum A% and moderate R p
and Rm were obtained; when the Ce content was ranging from 0.15 to 0.3 wt%, R p,
Rm and A% decreased simultaneously. The optical microstructures of as-sintered
Mo–Ce alloys show that the grain sizes of Mo –Ce alloys were 20 –30 lm, which
were almost equivalent to one quarter of those of unalloyed molybdenum. In
addition, the TEM and XRD analyses show that Ce element homogeneously dis-
persed in the intra- and inter-granular molybdenum substrate in the form of CeO
2
particles during the whole preparation processing. Due to that the lattices of CeO 2
particles were partly coherent with the molybdenum matrix, they not only had the
signiﬁcant grain re ﬁnement and dispersion strengthening effects, but also served to
inhibit the brittle-to-ductile transition behaviors of Mo alloys during the subsequent

Keywords CeO2 /C1 Dispersion strengthening /C1 Fine grain /C1 Lattice mis ﬁt
Molybdenum
Introduction
Molybdenum, a metal with excellent physical, chemical and high-temperature
properties, is an interesting material for applications in lighting-technology, high
performance electronics, high temperature furnace construction and coating tech-
nology. However, its applicability as a structural material is limited because of a
brittle-to-ductile transition around room temperature and the small speci ﬁc strength
at high temperatures in unalloyed molybdenum. Therefore, the strengthening and
toughening technology is one of focuses of molybdenum alloys research.
Since the 1980s, many researches concerning with the strengthening and
toughening technologies of the molybdenum have been carried out [ 1–3]. In the
previous researches, the rare earth elements and their oxides were widely added into
molybdenum to obtain Mo –RE
xOy alloys due to those high melting points, stable
microstructures and high creep resistance [ 4, 5]. According to the literature
investigation, it is found that the most of the researches were focused on the
strengthening and toughening effects and applications of La
2O3 and various lan-
thanum molybdate compounds (La 6MoO12,L a 2Mo4O15,L a 2Mo3O12,L a 2MoO6,
La2MoO5,L a 6Mo4O15, etc.) [ 6–9], and little research was aimed toward the syn-
thesis and characterization of new compounds incorporating cerium oxides and
molybdenum. Therefore, in the present work, the effects and mechanism of Ce
element and its compounds on the mechanical properties and microstructures of
molybdenum alloy wires were experimentally investigated.
Experimental
Chemically pure MoO 2 powders with the purity of 99.97 wt% were used as the raw
material in this work, which were composed of loose particles with the regular
crystal morphologies. The particle size distribution of MoO
2 powders exhibited a
Gaussian curve and the ﬁsher particle size was 2.25 lm. The Ce element was added
into MoO 2 powders in the form of cerium nitrate solution (Ce(NO 3)3/C1 6H2O) with
the commercially available purity of 99.5%, and its XRD pattern was illustrated in
Fig. 1.
974 P. Feng et al.

## Page 946

The stoichiometric compositions of Mo –Ce alloys prepared in the work were
present in Table 1.
Mo–Ce alloy wires were fabricated by the following processing. Firstly,
Ce(NO3)3 solution was smoothly sprayed into MoO 2 powders by the conventional
solid-liquid spraying processing. MoO 2–Ce(NO3)3 mixture powders were then
dried and reduced into metallic Mo –Ce powders by dry hydrogen in a
six-heating-zones tube furnace at 850 to 950 °C. During subsequent processing,
Mo–Ce powders were compacted by the cold isostatic pressing machine at
200 MPa for 10 min and sintered by the appropriate heating programs in the
medium-frequency induction hydrogen furnace at 1900 °C for 28.5 h. Finally, the
as-sintered 17-mm diameter Mo –Ce alloy rods were hot-drawn into 1.8 and
0.18-mm diameter wires.
The mechanical properties of Mo –Ce wires were determined at room tempera-
ture and 1500 °C by WDL-2 tension test machine and Gleeble 3500 thermal-
mechanical simulation system. Their microstructures were observed by the MEF4M
light microscope, S-3400N scanning electron microscope (SEM) and JEM-200CX
transmission electron microscope (TEM), respectively. The grain sizes of the matrix
phases and second phase particles were measured by the quantitative metallography
method via Malvern Morphologi G2 system.

Results and Discussion
Effects of Ce Element on Mechanical Properties of Molybdenum Wires The
tensile properties at the room temperature of the 1.8-mm diameter Mo –Ce alloy
wires as a function of the Ce content are present in Fig. 2. Compared with the
unalloyed molybdenum wires, whose tensile strength and elongation are 700 –
900 MPa and 10 –15% [ 10], it can be found that, except of Mo –0.3Ce alloy, the
other 1.8-mm diameter Mo –Ce alloy wires exhibit much higher yield strengths
(Rp), tensile strengths (R m) and elongation to failure (A%). After the further
analysis, it can be found that when Ce addition is more than 0.06 wt%, R p and Rm
of Mo–Ce alloy wires of 1.8-mm diameter are almost equivalent to those of Mo –Si–
La alloy wires [ 11] and Mo –Y alloy wires [ 12]. Meanwhile, the room-temperature
elongations of all the six Mo –Ce alloy wires of 1.8-mm diameter reach 22.75% or
above, which are far larger than those of Mo –La alloy wires (5 –6%) [ 13], Mo –Si–
La alloy wires (3 –5%) [ 11] and Mo –Y alloy wires (about 10%) [ 12]. Such the
excellent ductility of Mo –Ce alloy is extremely outstanding in the
oxide-dispersion-strengthened (ODS) molybdenum alloys. The results suggest that
Ce element can play an remarkable strengthening effect on molybdenum alloys
without the elongation loss. Because the Mo –Ce alloys have such excellent com-
prehensive mechanical properties, it can be concluded that the Mo –Ce alloy wires
have more superior hot workability than that of the three other ODS molybdenum
alloy wires during the thermomechanical proecessing.
As shown in Fig. 2,R
p,R m and A% of 1.8-mm diameter Mo –Ce alloy wires
exhibit a very strong regular consistency with the changing of Ce contents, which is

and A% of Mo –0.03Ce alloy wire are a little higher than those of unalloyed
molybdenum wire [ 10]. When Ce content gradually increased (0.06 wt%), R p,R m
and A% are simultaneously increased. When Ce content further increased (0.06 –
0.12 wt%), R p and R m exhibit two U-shaped curve, meanwhile the A% exhibit an
inverse curve. It worthy to note that the Mo –0.09Ce alloy wire exhibits the largest

It is well known that the liner-cutting service life of the 0.18-mm diameter
molybdenum wires and ﬁnish qualities of the cutting workpieces are greatly
depended on the room-temperature tensile strength and elevated-temperature
yield-tensile-strength-ratio (i.e. Rp/Rm). Therefore, the room-temperature tensile
strength of 0.18-mm diameter Mo –Ce alloy wires are further measured, as pre-
sented in Fig. 3. It is revealed that when Ce content increased, the
room-temperature Rm of 0.18-mm diameter Mo –Ce wires is ﬁrstly increased and
then decreased, i.e. a typical \ -shaped curve. Especially noted, the Rm of Mo –
0.09–0.12Ce wire exhibits the maximum level of 2500 MPa, suggesting that Mo –
0.09–0.12Ce wire can withstand the maximum tensile load during the liner-cutting
service.
In addition, the elevated-temperature tensile properties at 1500 °C of 1.8-mm
diameter Mo–Ce alloy wires versus Ce content are summarized in Table 2. It can be
found that the curve of the elevated temperature tensile strength versus Ce content
are consistent with the changing at room temperature. Similar to the room tem-
perature tensile properties, Mo –0.09Ce alloy wire reaches the maximum
elevated-temperature yield-tensile-strength-ratio (0.87) and smallest elongation
(3.57%). It indicated that the length of Mo –0.09Ce alloy wires would be kept
excellently stable during the liner-cutting cutting service.
Strengthening and Toughening Mechanism of Ce Element The XRD pattern of
Mo–0.3Ce alloy is given in Fig. 4. It can be inferred that Ce element is dispersed in
molybdenum substrate in the form of CeO
2 particles during the whole preparation
processing. So the strengthening and toughening effects of Ce element on molyb-
denum alloys are mainly dependent on the signi ﬁcant grain re ﬁning roles of CeO 2
particles and the excellent lattice relationship between CeO 2 particles and the
molybdenum substrate.

## Page 949

The Grain Re ﬁnement Roles of CeO 2 Particles The metallographic photographs
of the as-sintered Mo –Ce alloys are shown in Fig. 5. It can be observed that the
grain sizes of Mo –Ce alloys are much smaller than those of Mo –La alloy [ 13] and
Mo–Si–La alloy [ 11], and close to those of Mo –Y alloy [ 12]. Wang et al. [ 14] and
Zhong et al. [ 15] revealed that the grains of molybdenum substrates can be re ﬁned
to less than one quarter of unalloyed molybdenum by Ce addition. The reason for
the ﬁne grain structure is that CeO
2 particles, which are uniformly dispersed in the
intra- and inter-granular molybdenum matrix (the white particulates in Fig. 6a),
would effectively inhibit the growth of molybdenum grains during the whole sin-
tering processing. According to Hall –Petch equation, the homogeneously ﬁne
crystalline structure would guarantee both remarkable strengths and ductility of
Mo–Ce alloys.
The SEM morphologies of the tensile fracture surface of the 1.8-mm diameter
Mo–Ce alloy wires are shown in Fig. 7. It can be observed that the depths of every
dimple are roughly equal, which suggests that the deformation degrees of all the
grains are relatively homogeneous. It can be conclude that the homogeneous
deformation behavior is mainly attributed to the re ﬁned microstructures, which are

Based on the two above equations, the lattice mis ﬁt along /C22111hi of Mo is much
less than 12%, inferring that the lattices of Mo and CeO 2 are completely coherent;
and the lattice mis ﬁt along 110hi of Mo is between 12 and 18%, inferring that the
lattices of Mo and CeO 2 are partly coherent. The lattice mis ﬁt between Mo and
second phase particles is extremely favorable in ODS molybdenum alloys and
beneﬁcial to realize the harmonious deformation of molybdenum substrates and
CeO
2 particles. It is the main reason that Mo –Ce alloys are more ductile than the
other ODS molybdenum alloys at room temperature. The viewpoint is also con-
sistent with the analysis by Nasser et al. [ 18].
Summary
(1) The comprehensive mechanical properties of Mo –Ce alloys are far superior to
the Mo –La alloys and Mo –Si–La alloys. Mo –Ce alloy wires with Ce content of
0.09–0.12 wt% not only exhibit excellent hot workability, but also meet the
requirement of exceedingly good liner-cutting service performance.
(2) Ce elements are homogeneously distributed in the intra- and inter-granular
molybdenum substrates in the form of CeO 2 particles. The strengthening and
toughening effects of Ce element on molybdenum alloys are mainly dependent on
the remarkable grain re ﬁning role of CeO
2 particles and the excellent lattice rela-
tionship between CeO 2 particles and molybdenum substrates.

Constitutive Model
for Molybdenum-Niobium Alloy During
Hot Deformation
Wen Zhang, Xuanqiao Gao, Jun Cheng, Laiping Li, Zhongwu Hu,
Bin Zhao and Pingxiang Zhang
Abstract Isothermal compression of the molybdenum-niobium alloy was con-
ducted on a Gleeble-3800 thermal simulator at the deformation temperature range
of 1100 –1300 °C with strain rates ranging from 0.001 to 10 s
−1 and height
reduction of 50%. The results show that the deformation temperature and strain rate
affected the ﬂow stress during the thermal deformation of molybdenum-niobium
alloy signi ﬁcantly. The true stress –strain curves exhibit a peak ﬂow stress, ﬂow
softening and steady ﬂow behavior. The activation energy ( Q) and stress exponent
(n) of molybdenum-niobium alloy, are calculated. The constitutive equation is
established based on a hyperbolic-sine equations of Arrhenius type.

## Page 955

Introduction
Due to the high melting point, hardness, strength and other unique physical/
chemical/mechanical properties, refractory metals (tungsten, molybdenum, tanta-
lum and niobium, etc.) and their alloys are widely used in military industry,
aerospace, electronic information industry, energy, metallurgy, chemical industry,
nuclear industry and other ﬁelds with a signi ﬁcant importance to the national
economy. With the development of rocket missile technology, aerospace technol-
ogy, aviation jet technology, atomic power technology and other advanced tech-
nology, materials are required to bear a high temperature (above 1500 °C) [ 1–3].
Molybdenum and its alloys have a high melting point (2620 °C), excellent high
temperature mechanical properties, and the density is relatively low, so they are
excellent candidates in advanced ﬁeld [ 4].
For Mo –Nb alloy, the hot deformation condition has signi ﬁcant effect on the
microstructure and properties. In this paper, the thermal compression tests were
carried out for Mo –Nb alloy on Gleeble 3800 thermal simulator, and the effect of
strain rate and deformation temperature on the ﬂow stress was analyzed. The
experimental data of different strain are ﬁtted with the Arrhenius hyperbolic sine
function Model to establish the constitutive equation which can describe the whole
process of hot deformation of Mo –Nb alloy.
Experiment
The high purity Mo –Nb alloy rod was provided by Northwest Institute for
Nonferrous Metal Research. The chemical composition and microstructure of Mo –
Nb alloy were shown in Table 1 and Fig. 1 respectively. The cylindrical com-
pression specimens with size of U8m m /C2 12 mm were cut out from the Mo –Nb
alloy along the longitudinal-axis by wire cutting, and the surfaces were polished.
A series of thermal compression tests were conducted on Gleeble 3800 thermal
simulator to collect thermal deformation data in the deformation temperature range
from 1100 to 1300 °C and strain rate range from 0.001 to 10 s
−1. The specimens
were deformed up to 50%, and the true strain was about 70%. After compression,
the specimens were cut open along the compressive direction for metallographic
observation.

Results and Discussion
Stress–Strain Curves Table 2 and Fig. 2 show the peak ﬂow stresses and true
stress–strain curves of Mo –Nb alloy applied at different temperatures and strain
rates, respectively. According to Fig. 2, the stress increased linearly with strain in
the initial stage of deformation, and the main deformation mechanism is the elastic
deformation and dynamic recovery. Due to work hardening, the ﬂow stress
increased rapidly to peak values with further loading, and then decreased to the
stable values due to the softening effect, showing the characteristics of steady ﬂow.
Figure 3 shows the relationship between the ﬂow stress and loading condition. The
ﬂow stress increased with an increasing strain rate, and decreased with increasing of
the deformation temperature, which indicates that the ﬂow stress during the thermal
deformation of Mo –Nb alloy was affected signi ﬁcantly by the deformation tem-
perature and strain rate. Furthermore, at high temperature and low strain rate
(T /C21 1250 °C, _e = 0.001 s −1), the deformation softening is more signi ﬁcant for
Mo–Nb alloy. It is worth noting that the curves of Mo –Nb alloy show a signi ﬁcant
serrated oscillation for the hot deformation condition of 1100 °C/1 s −1, 1250 °C/
1s −1, 1150 °C/1 s −1 and 1300 °C/10 s −1, because the combined effect of local
temperature elevation, microstructure evolution and deformation instability over-
whelmed work hardening.

The constitutive relation of Mo –Nb alloy established in this study can be used to
calculate the deformation resistance during the hot working process and acted as the
constitutive equation of the ﬁnite element simulation.
Summary
(1) The hot compression tests on Mo –Nb alloy indicate that strain rate and
deformation temperature have a signi ﬁcant effect on the ﬂow stress for Mo –Nb
alloy. The true stress –strain curves have characteristics of steady ﬂow at low
strain rates, while at high temperatures and high strain rates the curves have
characteristics of strain softening.
(2) The relationship between the material constants Q, A, n, a and the true strain is
established by using Arrhenius relation in the hyperbolic sine form, and the
material constants are calculated as A ¼ 2:04 /C2 10
5 s/C0 1; a ¼ 0:0043 mm 2/N;
n ¼ 1:4688; Q ¼ 322:3 kJ/mol.
(3) Including the constitutive equation for the high temperature deformation of
Mo–Nb alloy is established as a function of deformation temperature, strain rate
and strain in the hyperbolic sine form.

## Page 963

Diffusion Bonding Properties of Large
Dimension WTi Alloy Target Bonded
to the Back Plate
Zhaochong Ding, Haiyang Yu, Xiaoyong Wan, Ming Chen,
Yongming Wang and Jifeng Lei
Abstract In this paper, large dimension WTi alloy target for 12 in. wafers was
respectively diffusion bonded to Al alloy, Cu alloy or Mo back plate. Then the
properties test of the overall deformation after bonding, interface microstructure,
bonding rate, tensile strength were conducted. The results showed that after the
large dimension WTi alloy target bonded to the Al alloy or Cu alloy back plate, the
overall deformation was large, the target was easily crack or debonding, so the
reliability was poor. After the WTi alloy target bonded to the Mo back plate, the
overall deformation was small, the bonding rate could reach more than 99%, and
the tensile strength could be more than 50 MPa which was better than the tradi-
tional solder bonding strength (<5 MPa) and could meet the high power sputtering.
Keywords Sputtering target
/C1 WTi alloy /C1 Diffusion bonding /C1 Back plate
Introduction
Tungsten-Titanium (WTi) alloy has excellent performances of low electron
mobility, stable thermo-mechanical performance, and good resistance to oxidation
and corrosion material. The role of Ti in WTi alloy is to increase adhesion of W to

## Page 964

oxide surface and also to improve oxidation resistance [ 1]. The Ti content is usually
5–20 wt%, and W –10 wt% Ti is one of the most widely used W –Ti alloy [ 2]. Since
it was commercialized by Materials Research Corporation (MRC) in 1970, the WTi
alloy has been used extensively in semiconductor fabrication as a diffusion barrier
layer and a capping layer in interconnect metallization. Pure WTi behaves as a
passive barrier between aluminium or tungsten layer and silicon substrate. And the
barrier performance is further enhanced when the layer is stuffed by nitrogen
reactive sputtering or by exposing the deposited ﬁlm to air [ 3]. In addition to being
an effective diffusion barrier, the WTi ﬁlm is also utilized for interconnect metal-
lization in semiconductors, advanced packaging, photovoltaic, light emitting diodes
(LED), micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS). And yet, the step coverage of
WTi ﬁlm is also relatively good, because that the atomic mass of W is high and so
W atom suffers less gas-phase scattering with Ar [ 4, 5].
The WTi ﬁlm is typically formed by physical vapor deposition through mag-
netron sputtering of a WTi alloy target. Due to the high melting point, WTi alloy
target was usually manufactured by powder metallurgy process, such as
pressure-less sintering, hot pressing sintering (HP), or hot isostatic pressing sin-
tering (HIP). The target blank was then machined into a monolithic target or bonded
to the back plate. For the bonded target, on one hand, the bonding rate between the
target and the back plate needs be very high, for example more than 95%, in order
to ensure good thermal and conductivity during sputtering [ 6]. On the other hand,
the bonding tensile strength between the target and the back plate needs be enough
high in order to avoid debonding or falling off. The WTi alloy target and back plate
can usually be bonded by solder or diffusion bonding method. Choice of bonding
method typically depends on the physical, thermal and mechanical properties of
target and back plate material and also application of sputtering targets [ 7]. The
traditional solder bonding involves the use of molten ﬁller metal, such as In, Sn and
alloy, to wet and joint the target and back plate. The solder bonding process is
simple, but the bonding tensile strength is less than 5 MPa which is the solder ’s
breakdown strength [ 8]. For a solder bonding WTi alloy target for 12 in. wafer,
even though the bonding rate can be more than 95%, but because that the solder
material melting point is low, so the target reliability is poor and easily debonding
or falling off during sputtering, especially for high-power sputtering. Figure 1
shows the debonding WTi alloy target with the sputtering power less than 5 kW. So
in this paper, large dimension WTi alloy target for 12 in. wafers was respectively
diffusion bonded to Al alloy, Cu alloy or Mo back plate. Then the properties test of
the overall deformation after bonding, interface microstructure, bonding rate, tensile
strength and etc., were conducted and discussed in order to explore an ideal dif-
fusion bonding solution for high power sputtering.

## Page 965

Experimental Procedures
One diffusion bonding process was that the WTi alloy target was directly diffusion
bonded to Al or Cu alloy back plate by HIP. The Al alloy included 6061Al alloy,
5052Al alloy, and etc. And the Cu alloy included CuZn alloy, CuZnSn alloy, CuCr
alloy, and etc. The vacuum HIP can diagrammatic sketch was shown in Fig. 2. And
the other diffusion bonding process was that ﬁrstly the mixed WTi alloy power and
the Mo back plate were placed in the HP mould, secondly the WTi alloy target
sintering and diffusion bonding to the Mo back plate are completed simultaneously
in the HP furnace. The HP mould diagrammatic sketch was shown in Fig. 3. After
being bonded to the back plate, the overall deformation of the target compound was
tested by feeler gauge, the bonding interface microstructure was observed by
SEM-EDX, the bonding rate was tested by C-axis ultrasonic testing (C-Scan), and
the bonding tensile strength was tested by universal material machine.

Results and Discussion
For the ﬁrst diffusion bonding process, the main HIP diffusion bonding parameters
of Al alloy back plate were the bonding temperature of 450 °C, pressure of
120 MPa, and the pressure holding time of 2 h. And the main HIP diffusion
bonding parameters of Cu alloy back plate were the bonding temperature of 600 °C,
pressure of 120 MPa, and the pressure holding time of 2 h. When the diameter of
the WTi alloy target was small, such as u100 mm, the overall deformation of the
target compound was less than 1 mm, and the bonding rate was more than 99%
with the bonding tensile strength was 20 –50 MPa. But when the diameter of the
WTi alloy target was large, such as u450 mm, the overall deformation of the target
compound was large to 3 –4 mm, and the WTi target cracked and fell off from the
bonding interface which was shown in Fig. 4. When reducing the bonding tem-
perature, even though the target did not crack, but it was dif ﬁcult to bond the WTi
alloy target to the Al alloy or Cu alloy back plate.
So the second diffusion bonding process was conducted, the main HP sintering
and diffusion bonding parameters of Mo back plate was the bonding temperature of
1300 °C, pressure of 30 MPa, and the pressure holding time of 2 h. When the
diameter of the WTi alloy target was as small as u100 mm, the overall deformation
of the target compound was about 0.2 mm, and the bonding rate was more than
99% with the bonding tensile strength was more than 50 MPa. Even the diameter of
the WTi alloy target increased to 450 mm, the overall deformation of the target
compound was just about 0.5 mm, and the target did not crack or fall of from the
bonding interface. Through the SEM-EDX test as shown in Fig. 5, there were no

diffused into the Mo back plate. Through the C-Scan test, the bonding rate was

test data proved that even the 12 in. WTi alloy target could be well diffusion
bonded to the Mo back plate by the second bonding process. The ﬁnish product of

was sputtered with the sputtering power as high as 10 kW, and there was no crack
or debonding.

For the bonding between different materials, such as the WTi alloy and back
plate, the deformation after bonding can hardly avoid which is root caused by the
difference of Coef ﬁcient of Thermal Expansion (CTE). As shown in Table 1, take
the u450 mm WTi alloy target bonded to Cu alloy back plate for example, the CTE
of WTi alloy is about 5.8 /C2 10
−6 K−1, and the CTE of Cu alloy is about
16.5 /C2 10−6 K−1 [9]. When the temperature falls from 600 °C (Bonding temper-
ature) to 25 °C (Room temperature), the theory thermal-shrinkage deformation ( D)
between the WTi alloy and Al alloy is shown in Eq. ( 1).

D ¼ 16:5 /C0 5:8ðÞ /C2 10/C0 6 K/C0 1 /C2 450 mm /C2 600 /C0 25ðÞ K /C25 2:8m m ð1Þ
And the actual deformation value is 3.2 mm which is consistent with the theory
value. From the Eq. ( 1), besides of the CTE differences, the deformation value is
also affected by the bonding temperature fall and bonding area. When the u100 mm
WTi alloy target bonded to Cu alloy back plate, the actual deformation was just
0.7 mm. But when the diameter of WTi alloy target increased to u450 mm, the
actual deformation reached as high as 3.2 mm which was larger than the WTi
alloy’s elastic deformation, so the WTi alloy target cracked from the bonding
interface. To some extent, decreasing the bonding temperature can reduce the
deformation, but low bonding temperature can cause less diffusion and less bonding
strength. So for the ﬁrst diffusion bonding process, the bonding reliability was very
poor, especially for a large diameter WTi alloy target.
For the second diffusion bonding process, on one hand the CTE differences
between the WTi alloy and Mo is small which can dramatically reduce the bonding
deformation. On the other hand, during the sintering and diffusion bonding, the
WTi powder has large surface area and high activation energy which is in favor for
fast diffusion and achieves high bonding strength. So for the second diffusion
bonding process, the bonding reliability was very high, and the WTi alloy target
could meet the high power sputtering.

## Page 971

Conclusions
For the ﬁrst diffusion bonding process, the WTi alloy target has been bonded to Al
or Cu alloy back plate. The overall deformation is large and the target is easily
cracked or de-bonded. So the bonding reliability is poor which is caused by the
large CTE difference between the WTi alloy target and Al alloy or Cu alloy back
plate.
For the second diffusion bonding process, the WTi alloy target has been bonded
to the Mo back plate. On one hand, the overall deformation is dramatically small for
the small CTE differences. On the other hand, during the sintering and diffusion
bonding, the WTi powder has large surface area and high activation energy which is
in favor for fast diffusion and achieves high bonding strength. So the bonding rate
of the 12 in. WTi alloy target can reach more than 99%, and the tensile strength
could be more than 50 MPa which is better than the traditional solder bonding
strength and can meet the high power sputtering.

W–Cu Tube Processing and Structure
Property by Powder Extrusion Molding
Shengli Han, Liqun Cui and Daren Li
Abstract In this paper, W –30%Cu tube with 0.8 mm inner diameter, 8 mm
external diameter and more than 200 mm on length was shaped using powder
extrusion molding and in ﬁltration sintering process. The results showed that the
parameters such as powder loading, hot degreasing temperature and sintering
temperature and time affected the formability and structure property of W –Cu tube.
High properties of W –30%Cu tube with a relative density of 99.6% and an electric
conductivity of 49%IACS were obtained when sintering at 1300 °C for 2 h and the
powder loading was up to 60%. The effects of sintering temperature and time on the
macro-structure and micro-structure were studied.

electrical conductivity of Cu and the high arc erosion of W [ 1, 2]. W–Cu tube with

However, it is known that the W –Cu tube is very dif ﬁcult to shape by powder
compaction, due to the large ratio of length to diameter. Usually the W –Cu tube is
obtained through processing with high cost and low ef ﬁciency [ 4]. Thus, new
processing methods must be introduced to fabricate W –Cu tube [ 5].
Powder extrusion molding is an advanced near net shape technology for powder
metallurgy, which has been rapidly developed in recent years, and has now become
one of the most effective ways to produce tube, rod, strip and other special shaped
products of cemented carbide, high density tungsten alloy, and other metals and
their alloys.
In this work, W –30%Cu tube with 0.8 mm inner diameter, 8 mm external
diameter and more than 200 mm on length was shaped using powder extrusion
molding and in ﬁltration sintering process. The parameters such as powder loading,
hot degreasing temperature and sintering temperature and time will affect the
formability and structure property of W –Cu tube. High properties of W –30%Cu
tube with a relative density of 99.6% and an electric conductivity of 49%IACS were
obtained when sintering at 1300 °C for 2 h and the powder loading was up to 60%.
The effects of sintering temperature and time on the macro-structure and
micro-structure were studied.
Experimental
In this work, W (99.9%, 1 –3 lm) and Cu (99.9%, −400 mesh) powders, from
Gripm Advanced Materials Co., Ltd and Zhuzhou Cemented Carbide Co., Ltd,
China, respectively, were used as raw materials. The characteristics of raw powders
are listed in Table 1. The SEM of raw powders are in Fig. 1. The binder used in this
work was composed of paraf ﬁn wax (PW), liquid paraf ﬁn wax (LPW), high density
polyethylene (HDPE), polyethylene vinyl acetates (EVA) and stearic acid (SA).
The characteristics of the binder are listed in Table 2.
The powder extrusion molding has four steps: feedstock, extrusion molding,
debinding, and sintering. The feedstock for extrusion was prepared by mixing a
proper ratio of powder and binder. The proper ratio of the binder and W –Cu alloy
powder was 70/30 by weight, respectively. Premixing was done with a dry-mixing
apparatus at room temperature and 30 r/min for 5 h. Fine mixing was done in the
single screw extruder (D20, Shanghai, China) at 170 °C and 50 r/min for 2 h.

were formed by extrusion molding. The tubes were cut into 250 mm sections to

Therefore, the binder formula has some limitations. With the binder, powder ﬁlling

The processing parameters of thermal debinding are shown in Fig. 5. Most of the
parafﬁn wax in the form of in ﬁltration, evaporation, and cracking was removed at
250 °C. However, the paraf ﬁn wax in the binder of green extruded tubes will not
decompose, only some soften before 70 °C. After 70 °C, due to rapid cooling the
stress produced during extrusion. Heat preservation in 110 °C for 1 h is to eliminate
these stress. Two heat insulation platforms are set at 110 –145 °C, and the temper-
ature rise is very slow. Paraf ﬁn wax can be further removed by means of osmotic
evaporation at 145–190 °C. At 190 °C, 30% of paraf ﬁn was removed. After 250 °C,
more than 80% paraf ﬁn wax can be removed. Thereafter the heating rate can be
increased by 480 °C, the binder is completely removed. Figure 6 is scanning electron
micrographs of W–Cu tube after thermal debinding, the binder has disappeared from
the sample.
SEM of W–Cu alloy in different sintering temperature are shown in Fig. 7. It can
be seen that the powder particles remain in the original state at 850 °C, sintering neck
between particles is formed at 1200 °C, and the alloy is very dense at 1300 °C. At
1200 °C, the wetting angle of between liquid Cu and W is 20°, and the wetting angle
of between liquid Cu and W is 0° at 1300 °C. At this time, the densi ﬁcation of the
alloy was accelerated. Further increase of sintering temperature, the hole in the alloy
appeared at 1350 °C, the reason may be that the surface tension of liquid phase Cu
increased with temperature, and the ﬂow property was enhanced, which resulted in a
small amount of Cu ﬂuid loss, which resulted in the decrease of the density of the
alloy.
